entries.section: 1. The piety and wealth of Job

paragraphs.text: 1 There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job; and that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil. 2 And there were born unto him seven sons and three daughters. 3 His substance also was seven thousand sheep, and three thousand camels, and five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred she asses, and a very great household; so that this man was the greatest of all the men of the east.
"There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job;
and that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil" [1].

Many of the Fathers see that the book opens with a great praise of him in the words, "There was a man." As Origen says, many are called human beings, yet they behave like beasts of prey, or stupid animals, or reptiles, or birds, and not as men, according to how God, the Lover of mankind, created them.

* This name "man" we do not define as those who are outside define it, but as the Holy Bible defines it. A human being is not everyone who has the hands and feet of a man, nor merely one who is rational, but one who practices godliness and virtue with courage.

St. John Chrysostom * Many call themselves "men" (human beings), but they are not truly so. Some live with the conduct of beasts, while others live with the conduct of reptiles, spewing out their wrath like wild beasts. Therefore David himself says, "Nevertheless man being in honour abideth not: he is like the beasts" (Ps 49:12)...

But surely the word "man" is used of one who bears the image of God (Gen 1:27), who guards his dignity in a fitting manner, and sets the choice between good and evil, and gives his glory to his creation, which rejoices in him and finds its delight in him (Ps 104:31).

So "there was a man in the land of Uz." The region was a desolate wilderness, yet in it was planted... Job was a treasure lacking nothing. He was full of the grapes of the planted vintage. He was perfect (true), like the creation of the true God, for he used his virtues for the sake of the truth without hypocrisy, fulfilling the commandments of God... He worshipped God as God wishes.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem The sons of Edom dwelt in "Uz" in the days of Jeremiah the prophet (Lam 4:21). It is believed that it lay between Damascus and Edom, in the Syrian desert. Some believe that it is Hauran. It lies between Palestine and Arabia, north-east of the river Euphrates, on the caravan route between Egypt and Babylon. Tradition holds that Haran is Job's homeland, east of the Sea of Galilee. It was an exceedingly fertile region, and it contained about 300 small cities.

Perhaps Uz was not far from Ur of the Chaldees, from which Abraham was called. If God called Abraham to raise up from his seed a chosen people, He still had a remnant that bore witness to Him among the Gentiles. And God's plan for humanity is fulfilled when we share with St. John in enjoying this sight: "A great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne" (Rev 7:9).

God brought Abraham out of that corrupt land, where God calls His chosen ones to withdraw from evil. And He permitted Job to remain, that he might be a witness to His divine light in the midst of the thick darkness, like the stars in the darkness of the night.

* To make known the worth of his virtue, we are told where the holy man dwelt, for who does not know that Uz is a Gentile land? The Gentile world was under the authority of the evil one, and accordingly its eyes were closed to the knowledge of its Creator. So let us be told where he dwelt, for in this there is praise of him. He was a good man dwelling among wicked people. It is no great praise to be good in the company of the good; but to be good while dwelling in the midst of the wicked is a testimony that cannot be measured...

For it is said, "And delivered just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked: for that righteous man dwelling among them, in seeing and hearing, vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds" (2 Pet 2:7-8)...
And so Paul says to his disciples, "In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world" (Phil 2:15).

And it was said to the angel of the church of Pergamos, "I know thy works, and where thou dwellest, even where Satan's seat is: and thou holdest fast my name, and hast not denied my faith" (Rev 2:13).
So the Church was praised by the voice of the Bridegroom, who says in the Song of Songs, "As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters" (Song 2:2)...

Rightly it is said of him that he "eschewed evil," for it is written, "Depart from evil, and do good" (Ps 37:27). For truly, good works are not acceptable to God if in His eyes they are stained by being mixed with evil works, as it was said by Solomon, [He who sins in one matter destroys much good] (cf. Eccl 9:18). James bears witness to this, saying, "For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all" (Jas 2:10). Paul says, "A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump" (1 Cor 5:6).
It was fitting, then, to point out how he eschewed evil works, in order to show how the blessed Job was without blemish and steadfast in his good works.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

The word of God bears witness to Job's perfection: "And that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil." 1. Perfect: this is a relative perfection, and it does not mean that he was without sin, but that he seeks perfection and strives to attain it as far as he is able.

* The Apostle speaks of himself as being perfect and not perfect. He counts himself not perfect, looking at how much righteousness he still lacks, yet he is perfect in that he is not ashamed to confess his imperfection and that he presses on to attain perfection.

St. Augustine * There are two forms of perfection, an ordinary form and a heavenly one. One is acquired here, the other hereafter. One is according to human capacities, the other belongs to the perfection of the world to come; but God is just through all, wise above all, perfect in all.

St. Ambrose 1. Upright: in his dealings with God and men, that is, he bears a spirit of simplicity without twisting or inward deviation. What he practices reveals what is in his heart, without malice. He is upright in his conduct, scrutinizing his thoughts, words and actions, faithful in his time and appointments and in the talents given to him. 2. Godly: he worships God with a godly spirit, not in dry formalities without spirit. He strives to fulfil the will of God; in other words, his conduct is in harmony with his worship of God; he fears God lest he offend against His majesty and love. 3. Eschewing evil: the fear of the Lord is a wall surrounding him, so that he does not allow evil to creep into his thought, or his heart, or his conduct.
* It is said that he was upright, "without blemish," and it does not say "without sin"... Why was he without blemish? Because he was upright.
He was "true" because men are liars (Ps 62:9).

He was "true," not in words only but in deeds also. By this he is "a man of truth." For "Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole of man" (Eccl 12:13). Job was zealous for pure conduct; therefore the text says that he was "godly and true," and it brought out the cause of all his virtues, that he feared God... The knowledge of God is made manifest in a person's life, and becomes a guardian of life...

It does not say, "He did not commit evil," but "he eschewed evil"... In another passage: "Lest I be full, and deny, and say, Who is the LORD?" (Prov 30:9). You see that unless a man is careful, satiety is the foundation of deception. But this was not Job's condition.

entries.section: 1. The piety and wealth of Job

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom "And there were born unto him seven sons and three daughters" [2].

With the multitude of his offspring, righteous Job was not preoccupied with his possessions, in order to give a great inheritance to each son or daughter of his; rather, what occupied him was giving them a vast inheritance of prayers, praises, spiritual sacrifices and burnt offerings as a support for them.

Origen sees in the sons and daughters a symbol of the work of the Holy Spirit in the life of the believer, in whom He begets or bears, through his soul as through his body, holy spiritual fruits for the Lord. For the godly man, like Job, has the Spirit of God working in him, so the soul is in harmony with the body, and he is wholly under the guidance of the Holy Spirit. Pope Gregory (the Great) offers us, in detail and at length, symbolic interpretations of the seven sons and the three daughters, of which we quote very little.

* What does the number 7 present to us other than the summit of perfection...? The seven sons represent the order of the preachers, and the three daughters may point to the three classes of believers in the life of the Church... pastors, virgins and the married.

Seven sons are born to us when we conceive by good intention, and the seven virtues of the Holy Spirit are born in us. The prophet gave attention to this spiritual offspring in particular when the Holy Spirit makes the mind fruitful, in these words: [And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the Lord, and shall fill him with the spirit of the fear of the Lord] (cf. Isa 11:2-3). So when wisdom, understanding, counsel, strength, knowledge, godliness and the fear of the Lord are begotten in each of us at the coming of the Holy Spirit, an offspring has been born in the mind, which preserves the lineage of our heavenly honor in life, where it is allied all the more with eternal love.

Surely the seven sons in us have three sisters, since each of them (the sons) works with maturity (manliness) with virtuous inclinations, and so is united with faith, hope and love. For the number 7 will not reach the perfection of the number 10 unless they do everything in faith, hope and love.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

After speaking of his inward wealth, that of the soul, in that he had seven sons, that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, together with three daughters, that is, faith, hope and love, he spoke of his bodily wealth. For the children point to the wealth of the Spirit, and the animals point to the wealth of the body that is sanctified in the Lord. So he suffers neither spiritual want nor bodily want, since the Creator of soul and body satisfies his whole being.
"His substance also was seven thousand sheep, and three thousand camels, and five hundred yoke (pair) of oxen, and five hundred she asses, and a very great household;

entries.section: 1. The piety and wealth of Job

paragraphs.text: so that this man was the greatest of all the men of the east" [3].

With his enormous wealth he was marked by righteousness. The sheep are mentioned first because they were necessary for families: "The lambs are for thy clothing... goats' milk enough for thy food, for the food of thy household, and for the maintenance for thy maidens" (Prov 27:26-27). His servants were very many; all served him and his house.

Among the customs that still remain among shepherds and Bedouin societies is that a person's riches and wealth are estimated not by his land or his houses, but by the livestock he owns. Abraham was very rich in his flocks (Gen 13:2). Lot also had his flocks (Gen 13:5). So Job's wealth is estimated by the number of animals he owns. He mentioned the female donkeys (she asses) because their value was much greater than that of the males on account of the milk that was used for drinking.

Some see that Job's sheep and camels point to the union of the age of the Law with the age of grace. The seven thousand sheep point to the pasture of the Law, which becomes perfect through spiritual touches (the number thousand) in place of the letter; to this pasture are joined the three thousand camels, as the peoples of the Gentiles come to join the pasture of the spiritual Law, and all become one flock with one shepherd.

* Job was rich, but he did not spend his life in luxury without compassion (for others). His house was open to everyone in need, by his will that was full of love. He treated no one with injustice, but helped those who suffered injustice; he provided the necessary needs for widows and orphans. For these are the works of righteousness of the righteous rich man.
Origen

4 And his sons went and feasted in their houses, every one his day; and sent and called for their three sisters to eat and to drink with them. 5 And it was so, when the days of their feasting were gone about, that Job sent and sanctified them, and rose up early in the morning, and offered burnt offerings according to the number of them all: for Job said, It may be that my sons have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts. Thus did Job continually.
"And his sons went and feasted in their houses, every one his day; and sent and called for their three sisters, to eat and to drink with them" [4].

A wonderful picture of a very rich man whom wealth and riches did not preoccupy, nor did they preoccupy his sons; rather all gather in a spirit of love and unity with good management, and they hold a feast in the house of each son in turn, with fellowship with the sisters! His sons held periodic feasts in a spirit of love and unity. Each son held the feast in his turn, gathering his brothers and sisters. The psalmist says, "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" (Ps 133:1).

The following is observed in these feasts: 1. They were held in houses, not in public places, perhaps so that the family would keep its holy character even at feasts and in the midst of joys. 2. The invitation of the sisters is an indication that the feasts were family feasts, and most probably limited to Job's family. 3. Job did not go to the feasts, not out of rigidity, for he seeks the joy and delight of his children as long as it is in the Lord; but his presence as an old man might have in it a kind of not giving the young people the freedom to be merry yet, even if it was in the Lord.

* Great wealth is usually a cause of disputes among brothers. What an inestimable praise of the upbringing of such a father! The wealth of the father and the peace of the brothers together were proclaimed, for while the wealth was divided among them, love was not divided, but filled the hearts of all!
Pope Gregory (the Great)

"And it was so, when the days of their feasting were gone about, that Job sent and sanctified them, and rose up early in the morning, and offered burnt offerings according to the number of them all: for Job said, It may be that my sons have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts.
Thus did Job continually" [5].

Although Job did not take part in the feasts bodily, he took part spiritually in a spirit of tender fatherhood and love. He was zealous for the salvation of their souls, fearing lest they be defiled even in thought, and so be counted as blasphemers against the Holy One.

He feared lest one of them think in the depths of his heart, saying, "My power and the might of mine hand hath gotten me this wealth" (Deut 8:17). Or, as the wise man says, "Lest I be full, and deny, and say, Who is the LORD?" (Prov 30:9).

Job was the priest of the family. He believed that he was unable to sanctify his children, and that this is the work of God; therefore he offered burnt offerings according to their number. He did this not only at the beginning of the feast, nor only at its end, but throughout all the days of the feast, and all the days of the year. "Thus did Job continually." Perhaps he offered a burnt sacrifice for the whole family every day, but in the days of the feasts he offered a burnt offering for each one, because sins, especially those of thought, find in feasts a suitable atmosphere to creep inside.

* If sins committed in ignorance are judged to be so grievous and need a sacrifice to atone for them, a truth to which Job bore witness by offering a sacrifice for his children, what then is to be said of those who commit sin knowingly, or those who in their silence yield to the sinful conduct of others?

St. Basil the Great * He offered his sacrifices for their hidden sins and their unconfessed faults. If Job took such care concerning hidden sins committed without knowledge, how much more, do you think, concerning manifest faults. Notice how he translates the words of the Apostle into action: "And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord" (Eph 6:4), that is, a person takes care of his children. It is a practice of parental protection. Notice to what level of perfection he wished to lead them...

For manifest faults he could correct them, but what could he do about secret sins? Yet it was said to Moses, "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever" (Deut 29:29). At any rate, Job did not ignore even the secret faults in their relation to God, but obliged himself to correct the situation personally by a remedial means. For this means allowed him to strike at the faults and uproot them, and also to teach his children...

You see that he corrected not only their shortcomings in deeds, but also what concerns thoughts, practically fulfilling the words of Christ: "For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts... These are the things which defile a man" (Mt 15:19-20)... You see here a purification that is not Mosaic, nor by the Law, but in an apostolic manner, in that he seeks the purification of their thoughts daily, not only by advising them and giving them counsel, but also by protecting them and praying to God for them. This is not the work of a father only, but also of a priest, though we know that there was not yet a priest...
Some see that there were priests in those days also, such as Melchizedek, whom the people did not choose.
St. John Chrysostom * The very words of Scripture indicate that ignorance is a sin. This is the reason why Job offers burnt offerings for his sons, lest they had sinned unwittingly in thought.

St. Jerome * This statement attributed to Job shows very great godliness. For many people are accustomed to rise early for earthly occupations, and all they think about during the night is the means of amassing wealth or glory or honors, so they hasten to rise to carry out their thoughts in practice. The prophet expresses, in a song of lamentation, what must be said about these: "Woe to them that devise iniquity, and work evil upon their beds! when the morning is light, they practise it" (Mic 2:1). But Job was not occupied with this; rather, at dawn he offered service to God, who makes the light shine... For the true sacrifice is the keeping of the Law and the practice of virtues (Sir 35:1-3). The words of Paul's Epistle to the Hebrews serve us in this as an example: "By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually... But to do good and to communicate forget not: for with such sacrifices God is well pleased" (Heb 13:15-16).

"For Job said, It may be that my sons have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts" [5]. Job's uprightness is clear! He completes his righteousness toward goodness. He is a wise father and an experienced master, a tower (of the stars) marked by prudence, a good guide like one who holds an outer bridle to restrain the inner passions... David was not content to sing those words: "Who can understand his errors? Cleanse me from secret faults" (Ps 19:12), but he also put the commandment of the Gospel into practice. We say that Job walked according to the Law and grace, and according to the commandment of the Gospel: "...Which in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, keep it" (Lk 8:15). He did not take this lightly. John the Theologian wrote on this: "And shall assure our hearts before him. For if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things. Beloved, if our heart condemn us not, then have we confidence toward God" (1 Jn 3:19-21), and the Lord Himself says, "For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies: These are the things which defile a man: but to eat with unwashen hands defileth not a man" (Mt 15:19-20). Let us then be purified from these deeds. Let us seek fruit from our souls every day, for Job was "true and blameless," looking also to what is written: "Thus did Job continually" [5].
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Thus Job purified his children, for one who offers sacrifices for secret sins, how much more does he care about manifest sins?
* Job used a remedy even for the thoughts of his sons.

St. John Chrysostom * "And rose up early in the morning, and offered burnt offerings according to the number of them all" [5]. The saint knew that a feast is rarely held without transgression. He knew that the merriment of feasts must be purified by sacrifices. And the stains that the sons had committed in their persons during their feasts the father washed away by offering a sacrifice... for feasts are often accompanied by passions, and when the body is relaxed by pleasures the heart submits to vain joy. For it is written, "The people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play" (Ex 32:6).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Job was at ease about the conduct of his sons and daughters in their love for one another and their oneness of spirit and harmony together, and he was reassured about their behavior and words, but he did not know what was going on in their thoughts and hearts. He did not take the position of a judge, passing judgment on what was inside them, nor did he stand in negligence, considering himself not responsible for what was in their hearts; rather, in a love full of wisdom he had recourse to God by offering spiritual sacrifices and burnt offerings for each one of them. For He alone knows the hidden secrets, and is able to sanctify the depths.

* "Thus did Job continually" [5]. Job did not cease offering a perpetual sacrifice, just as our Savior offers a burnt offering for us without interruption. He shows His incarnation before the Father for our sake without ceasing. For His very incarnation is an offering for our cleansing; and while He shows Himself as a man He is an intercessor who washes away the impurities of man, offering through the mystery of His humanity a perpetual sacrifice...

Vain is the goodness we practice if it stops before the end of life, for it is vain for one who runs swiftly to stop before reaching the goal. Concerning this the rebuke was given: "Woe unto you that have lost patience!" (Sir 2:14). And so the Truth says to His chosen ones: "Ye are they which have continued with me in my temptations" (Lk 22:28)... So Moses ordered that the tail of the sacrifice be offered on the altar, meaning that every good work we begin we complete with perseverance to the end.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* In general, the commandments of all the saints urge us to this by example, just as Solomon used in Proverbs, saying, "Hear, ye children, the instruction of the Lord, and attend to know understanding. For I give you good doctrine, forsake ye not my law. For I was my father's son, tender and only beloved in the sight of my mother" (Prov 4:1-3). For the righteous father brings up his children well, as he strives to teach others by his upright and virtuous conduct. So that if opposition arises, he is not ashamed to hear this saying: "Thou... which teachest another, teachest thou not thyself?" (Rom 21:2), but rather he is like a faithful servant who is able to save himself and gain others. And as the grace entrusted to him is multiplied he can hear that saying: "Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord" (Mt 21:25).
St. Athanasius the Apostolic

6 Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan came also among them. 7 And the LORD said unto Satan, Whence comest thou? Then Satan answered the LORD, and said, From going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it. 8 And the LORD said unto Satan, Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil? 9 Then Satan answered the LORD, and said, Doth Job fear God for nought? 10 Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side? thou hast blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land. 11 But put forth thine hand now, and touch all that he hath, and he will curse thee to thy face. 12 And the LORD said unto Satan, Behold, all that he hath is in thy power; only upon himself put not forth thine hand. So Satan went forth from the presence of the LORD.
"Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan came also among them" [6].
It is stated in the Jerusalem Targum, Targum Yerushalmi, that the two councils held in heaven, one was on Rosh ha-Shanah, and the second on Yom Kippur.

The angels, the sons of God, would gather together before God to offer Him the fitting praise for His love for the heavenly and the earthly beings, and to present also the prayers of the believers, and to await any mission they might fulfil, for they are servants for those who shall be heirs of salvation (Heb 1:14).

Satan, the proud deceiver, slipped in among them to complain against humanity, especially the believers, for in his envy he cannot bear to see an earthly man grow in the Spirit and take flight as on the wings of a dove to heaven.

All things are open before God; He has no need of angels to carry to Him the prayers of His believers, nor of Satan to disclose the corruption of some believer. But God, in His love for the heavenly beings, grants them the work of love, whether by presenting prayers or by fulfilling His mission. And in His justice He leaves Satan the freedom to complain against whomever he wishes. He hallows the freedom of will in rational creatures, whether at the level of the heavenly orders, or the spiritual powers of evil, or human beings.

We should not wonder at this, for in the vision of Zechariah the prophet, when he saw the Word of God Himself as a high priest bearing our sins like a filthy garment, Satan stood to resist him (Zech 3:1-2).
St. John Chrysostom asks us not to be astonished that the rebel stands among the angels, for what the book presents is in human form so that we may understand the situation with our human mind.

* The angels came, according to the text, and Satan came with them, as he was going about the earth and walking up and down under heaven. What do we understand from this? That the earth is full of demons and angels, and all are under the authority of the power of God, and that the angels stand before God, where they receive orders from Him. And Satan cannot do anything he pleases unless he obtains permission from above... The saying, "Satan came also among them" [6], means only that he too cannot do anything without God's permission.
* What does this expression mean? He is with them in the world, for just as deceitful men and good men are mingled together, so are angels and demons.

St. John Chrysostom Perhaps the utmost a man desires is to enjoy heavenly glory by standing in the midst of the heavenly orders and delighting in the sight of God; so how does Satan stand thus to see God and enter into a dialogue with Him? Without doubt the standing here does not carry the literal meaning; rather, God permitted him the dialogue for the sake of divine justice and to confirm the freedom of rational creation, even in the case of Satan and his wicked hosts. Satan stood as though among the angels, being permitted to speak with God, but he did not enjoy the sight of God's glory, nor did the splendor of the divine glory shine upon him, nor did he experience the sweetness of God's voice as a source of delight, joy and true peace!

So on the great day of the Lord, the true believers will see in the eyes of Christ Jesus a gentle dove, and in His embrace inexpressible glories, but the wicked will see His eyes as a flame of fire, and will not bear to look at Him.

And just as it was said here of Satan that he stood presenting himself before God without enjoying the splendor of His glory, it was said in another place of the angels that they are "ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation" (Heb 1:14), but their being sent forth to serve does not deprive them of enjoying the divine presence and of the divine splendor shining upon them.
* Perhaps some will ask: How can Satan, who fell from his rank because of his pride, stand before the Lord among the angels?
Can he behold the Lord while he is unclean?

The devil and his hosts fell and it is no longer their right to see God, but according to his nature as a spirit he can present himself before God without beholding Him. So he stood complaining against us without seeing God, because he is unclean.

Note that it is said that he came before the Lord, and it is not said that he saw the Lord. For he came to be seen, not to see. He was before the eyes of the Lord, and the Lord was not before his eyes, just as a blind man stands before the sun: he himself is immersed in the rays of light, but he sees nothing of the radiant light... For the power of God, by its gaze, pierces all things, so it sees the unclean spirit that he does not see. For even the very things that flee from the face of God cannot be hidden, for all is naked before the eyes of the Most High. So the absent Satan came to Him who is present.

* Who are those called sons of God but the chosen angels? And as we know of them, they look upon the eyes of His majesty. It is fitting for us to ask: From where did they come to present themselves before God? For it was said of them by the voice of the Truth, "In heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven" (Mt 10:18). And the prophet says of them, "Thousand thousands ministered unto him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him" (Dan 10:7). If they are always beholding and standing beside Him, we must carefully and exactly consider from where they came, for they never leave Him; but since Paul says of them, "Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?" (Heb 14:1), from this we learn that they are sent, and we discover from where they came...

They do not go in a way that deprives them of the sight of God, so that the joys of inward contemplation are taken from them; for if by being sent they lost the vision of their Creator, they could not raise up the fallen, nor declare the truth to those in ignorance, and they could never offer to the blind what they were deprived of by leaving the source of light.

The nature of the angels differs from the state of our present nature, where we are bound by place and limited by the blindness of ignorance; but the spirits of the angels, though limited by place, have a knowledge that rises far above ours, beyond any comparison, a knowledge extending outwardly and inwardly, for they contemplate the very Source of knowledge itself...

And just as their spirits themselves, when compared with our bodies, are spirits, so when they are compared with the sublime, incomprehensible Spirit they are counted as body. Therefore they are sent from Him, and also stand before Him, for in this they are bound to be sent, and at the same time are wholly present and never leave Him.

So at the same time they always see the face of the Father, and yet they come to us, being sent through the quality of inward contemplation. It can then be said, "The sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord," as they return there by the return of the spirit, to where they never left Him by any withdrawal of the mind from Him.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"And the LORD said unto Satan, Whence comest thou?
Then Satan answered the LORD, and said, From going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it" [7].

By saying, "From going to and fro in the earth," he indicates that he did not exceed his limits, for "that great dragon... was cast out into the earth" (Rev 12:9). Many of the early Fathers of the Church see that the earth in the Holy Bible points to the earthly, carnal man who is occupied only with earthly things, so the enemy of good roams as in his own possession. Heaven, by contrast, points to the spiritual man, who is occupied with eternal things. Satan cannot creep into the heart of the spiritual man, but he roams without restraint in the heart of the carnal man.
The enemy of good knows no idleness, for he does not rest night or day from going to and fro in the earth to seduce the children of God to leave the kingdom of light and be occupied with sins.

* "From going to and fro in the earth, and from walking up and down in it" [7]. You see that heaven is inaccessible to wicked Satan. If you say, "Well! Heaven is not open to him, but the world welcomes him." Yes, this is for your benefit, for if even with so vigilant an enemy you take no care to reform yourselves, what idle people you are...?
Listen to Paul as he says, "Whom I have delivered unto Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme" (1 Tim 20:1).

Do you wish to hear another text? Do you not see the tormentors who accompany the officials? So Paul uses the demons. But the good results are not the work of Satan, but of God's love for man, who uses Satan for this purpose.

* What then does it mean that Satan is asked, "Whence comest thou?" but that He may condemn his ways as though they were unknown. For the light of the Truth knows nothing of the darkness, which it rebukes, nor of the ways of Satan, which it condemns as a judge. It is fitting that he be asked about them as though they were unknown. And for this reason it was said to Adam in his sin, by the voice of his Creator, "Adam... where art thou?" (Gen 9:3), for the divine power did not ignore the hidden place to which His servant had fled in his disobedience, but He saw that the one who fell in his sin was hiding from the eyes of the Truth under sin...

He condemns Satan; therefore his way was examined, but the chosen angels do not need to be asked from where they came, since their ways are known to God. They are, as it were, representing His movement, for they are subject to His will alone, and they cannot be unknown to Him.

* The devil roams on the earth, since he scorned to dwell in peace in the heights of heaven. And as one who is reported as not having flown but walked, he shows the weight of sin that keeps him always below...

God speaks with the angels when His inward will is disclosed to them as the object of their perception, while the angels speak with the Lord when by this they contemplate what is above them, and stand before Him in amazement. And so God speaks with the souls of His saints in one way, and they speak with Him in another... We see them in the Revelation: "They cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?... And it was said unto them, that they should rest yet for a little season" (Rev 9:6-11).

God speaks with Satan in four ways: He condemns his unjust ways, He rebukes him by the righteousness of His saints, He permits him to test their innocence, and sometimes He stops him from tempting them...

He rebukes him by the righteousness of His chosen ones, when He says, "Hast thou considered my servant Job? for there is none like him in the earth (all)." He permitted him to put his righteousness to the test when He said to him, "Behold, all that he hath is in thy power" [12]. Again He prevented him from tempting him when He said, "Only upon himself put not forth thine hand" [12].
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"And the LORD said unto Satan,
Hast thou considered my servant Job,
that there is none like him in the earth,
a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil?" [8].

In God's speech with Satan He shows how much He esteems Job His servant, "for there is none like him in the earth" in uprightness and godliness. Through the relationship of mutual love between God and the true believer, the latter says, "Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods? who is like thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?" (Ex 15:11), "Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage?" (Mic 7:18). And at the same time God esteems His believers in their faith, as with Job (Job 1:8), and the centurion, and the Canaanite woman, and the wonder is that all of them were Gentiles.

* Patience was indeed in Job, which God knew, and to which He bore witness, but it became known to men through the test of temptation. What was hidden within and unseen like fruit appeared by what happened and came to be outwardly.
St. Augustine * Satan resolved to enter into a struggle, not with Job but with God, while the blessed Job was the subject of dispute between them...

Had God not known that Job would certainly continue in his uprightness, He would not have delivered him to Satan. He did not deliver him to him in order to destroy him by the temptation... And the fires of envy were kindled in the mind of the tempter because of God's praise of him.

When the ancient enemy fails to discover any evil of which he can accuse us, he turns to the good points to turn them into evil, and when he is defeated in deeds he looks to our words to find room for accusation.

He struggles to darken the intention of the heart, so that our good works do not issue from a good mind, and thus are not considered good in the eyes of the Judge. For even if he sees fruit on a green tree in the heat, he looks for a worm to spoil the roots.
* Notice the stupidity and cunning of Satan. God bears witness that Job is blameless, so do you wish (O Satan) to snatch away the testimony of God...?
When God says, "My servant Job," this is sufficient to define his virtue...
He (Satan) was immediately enraged when he heard God call Job His servant, for to him this was counted as a rebuke of himself, and it provoked him to attack.
You (O Satan) were formerly a servant... This is what Paul meant: "Know ye not that we shall judge angels? how much more things that pertain to this life?" (1 Cor 3:6).

Job reached this degree so that God added: "A perfect and an upright man, (and true), one that feareth God." "An upright man," but you, on the contrary, though you are not a man, did not persevere in virtue.

St. John Chrysostom * [Hast thou considered my servant Job?] [8]. At the same time it precisely means that the traitor (the devil) bears a malicious intent toward those whom he counts as sinners because of their vices, and as righteous through his deception.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem "Then Satan answered the LORD, and said,
Doth Job fear God for nought?" [9].

The enemy of good could not bear to hear a word of praise spoken of anyone other than himself, even though it came from God, who searches the hearts and knows the thoughts and all secrets. So King Saul could not bear the women praising the youth David, who had delivered him and all his army and his people from Goliath the giant and his army (1 Sam 18:6-9). And the chief priests and scribes could not bear the children praising the Lord Christ in the temple (Mt 21:15 etc.).

* Satan is called the slanderer because of his slanders, for he slanders man before God, saying, "Doth Job fear God for nought?"... and he slanders God before man, saying, "The fire of God is fallen from heaven, and hath burned up the sheep" (Job 16:1). He was eager to provoke him by saying that the calamity came down from heaven above, so as to set the servant at strife with the Master, and the Master with His servant. In fact he did not set them at strife, but he tried and was unable.

St. John Chrysostom * [He shall judge the poor of the people, he shall save the children of the needy, and shall break in pieces the oppressor] (Ps 72:4). Rightly is Satan called the "slanderer" (the oppressor), for he slandered God, claiming that God forbade taking from the tree (of the knowledge of good and evil) out of envy, and he slandered Job with lies, saying [Doth Job really fear God for nought?... Put forth thine hand now, and touch all that he hath, and he will curse thee to thy face] (Job 1:9, 11). In the eighth Psalm He gave him two names, "the enemy and the avenger," while here (Ps 72:4) He calls him a slanderer.

Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus * Certainly Satan is the one who brings accusation against the saints. He cannot, in the presence of such a Judge, ascribe a false accusation, for he knows with whom he is speaking. Therefore, since he knows his inability to bring a false charge against us, he resorts to saying something true. Therefore our adversary, who envies us for being in the kingdom of heaven and does not want us to be there, from where he was cast out, says: [Doth Job serve God for nought?] (Job 1:9)...
It is fitting for us to take care that our love for God is not for the sake of a reward. For what kind of reward is this that God gives you?

Whatever He gives you is less than Himself. Do not worship God in order to receive something from Him. Worship Him without hoping for anything in return, and then you will receive Him, for God keeps Himself for you to enjoy.

If you love what He created, how much more is the Creator of the world? Remove from your heart the love of creatures, that you may cleave to the Creator, and then you will say what is in the Psalm: [It is good for me to cleave to my God] (Ps 73:28).

Fr. Caesarius, Bishop of Arles * Satan says, "Doth Job fear God for nought?" Why do you marvel at Job? Why do you make extraordinary declarations about an upright man? For you yourself insist on his righteousness, and this only because of your gifts, which he received with great generosity in return for his virtue. He has abundance in everything; he is glutted with everything; he has no anxiety, nothing that makes him sin. His house is well built, full of good things. All his possessions are fenced with a hedge of blessings. His sons surround him like a crown that crowns him. Why should Job not be upright? Why should he not be godly? Which commandment is he bound to neglect? For he who has never tasted poverty, why should he steal?

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * With impudence he entered into an argument with God (Job 1:9). This is not the attitude of Satan alone, but of wicked men. Did not the one of whom it is said in the Gospel do the same: "I knew thee that thou art an hard man, reaping where thou hast not sown, and gathering where thou hast not strawed" (Mt 24:25)...

He was seeking to distort Job's motive... God always wishes to pronounce His judgment from the words of His enemies, so as to leave them no room for any excuse, as it is said in the passage: "Out of thine own mouth will I judge thee, thou wicked servant" (Lk 22:19)... By this deceit is always caught in its own net.
St. John Chrysostom "Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side?
Thou hast blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land!" [10].

Rabbi Yose b. Hanina concluded from (Job 1:10) that Job's goats were able to kill wolves. And R. Yohanan concluded from (Job 1:14) that God granted Job to taste paradisal life, so Satan envied him, and began to fight him, slandering him concerning his righteousness.

Satan puts the blame on God: "Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side?" Truly God had set a hedge around him for the protection of him and his house, and granted him success and wealth, and blessed his works, but He did not do this out of partiality, for Job was not characterized by dullness and slackness.
The speech of Satan reveals that he expended every effort to find a gap through which to enter Job's heart or mind in order to draw him into his kingdom, but he found none.

* "Because thou hast said, Thou, O Lord, art my refuge; thou hast made the most High thy habitation" (Ps 91:9). In order to enjoy this divine care he says: Experience hope in the Lord, and make Him a refuge for yourself... "There shall no evil befall thee, neither shall any plague come nigh thy dwelling" (Ps 91:10). You will stand firm before the darts of Satan, and they will not hurt you at all. Thus divine grace was set around Job's house, which the enemy bore witness to, crying out in a loud voice: "Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house?" And when He permitted him (to tempt him), He showed on the other side his wickedness, and the just Judge crowned the victorious wrestler.

Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus * "Hast not thou made an hedge about him?" Do you not notice that even Satan fully realizes that all of Job's security comes from God? He says, "Thou hast blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land." Do you not see that his wealth is a gift from God? Do you not see that it is not the fruit of injustice (or seizure)...?

"But put forth thine hand now, and touch all that he hath, and he will bless thee to thy face (that is, curse thee)" [11]. He wanted and desired to receive this authority from Him, but he did not dare to say it.

* What is God's own work, if not this: to do good to all humanity, by chastisements as well as by pleasures? Let us then give thanks not only when we are in prosperity, for this is nothing great. This too Satan knows well; therefore he said: "Doth Job fear God for nought? Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about all that he hath on every side?" (Job 1:9-10)

St. John Chrysostom * Blessed David knows that this temporary abandonment on God's part toward us is sometimes for our good, and in his prayer he asked that it not be continual (for he knows that God's abandoning man is harmful, since human nature is unable to walk toward perfection); therefore he besought that it be within certain limits, saying: "O forsake me not utterly" (Ps 8:119). In other words he says: I know that You forsake Your saints for their benefit, to test them... Therefore I do not ask You not to forsake me, for it is not beneficial for me not to feel my weakness [therefore he said, "It is good for me that I have been humbled" (Ps 119:71)], nor is it useful for me not to have the opportunity for battle. And this opportunity will certainly not be available to me as long as I am filled with the constant protection of God. For Satan does not dare to fight me as long as I rely on Your protection, so he comes forward objecting and complaining against me and against You: "Doth Job fear God for nought? Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side?" (Job 1:9-10). I ask You to forsake me, but "not utterly" (the Greek word is "not much"), because it is useful for me that You forsake me a little, so that the steadfastness of my love may be tested.
Fr. Daniel * Your words strike me hard in my chest, and make a hedge around me on every side.
St. Augustine "But put forth thine hand now, and touch all that he hath, and he will curse thee to thy face" [11].

In a discourse of Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus, on divine providence, he raised the objection of some: Why do the majority of the rich live a life marked by injustice? Why do they not seek justice? Perhaps he drew such an objection from Philo of Alexandria and from some of the Stoics. Theodoret answers: [Again, you forget that man has a free will. By this you deprive him of the glory that was given to him by his Maker. Besides this, evildoers would find a strong ground for defending themselves if the Judge distributed wealth to the righteous alone in the present life. They would say what their master said about Job: "Thou hast made a hedge about them and about their houses. Thou hast multiplied their crops and their vineyards. But put forth thine hand now and touch all that they have, and they will bless (that is, curse) thee to thy face." This is what hardened sinners would say if the practicers of virtue alone received the gift of wealth.]

St. Augustine sees that the true believer, like Job, is a stretched-out trumpet, and that trials are like beating with a hammer; when it strikes the trumpet it gives forth joyful sounds of praise. So the hammer that shatters the unbeliever reveals the peace and rejoicing of the believer, and so commends him before God.

* If it were in his power, would (Satan) not take vengeance for himself? But he is not permitted to do so. When he wished to tempt Job, he asked to receive authority to do so, and he was not able to do anything he had not received authority for. So why do you not worship God without fear, He without whom no one will harm you, and by whose permission you are disciplined but not defeated?
* (Satan) was able to envy the holy man (Job), but was he able to harm him?
He could accuse him, but was he able to condemn him?
Was he able to take anything from him or harm him, even the size of a fingernail or a hair of his head, without saying to God: "Put forth thine hand"?
Give me authority. It was given to him.
One tempted, and the other was tempted. But the one who was tempted conquered, and the one who tempted was defeated.
So God, who permitted Satan to take away all that he had, did not forsake him inwardly, as his servant. He made the very soul of His servant a sword by which Satan was defeated.

And what is the result? I think that it is for the benefit of humanity in general. The man who was defeated in paradise became a victor on the dunghill. In one place the devil defeated him through a woman, and in another place he conquered the devil and the woman together.
St. Augustine * Satan prepares the temptation; if he sees a person who is weak he attacks him, but if he sees him strong he stops.

St. John Chrysostom * This also we read of: that divine righteousness truly helped faithful Job in his wrestling, when Satan opposed him in a unique battle. But if Job had advanced against his enemy, not by his own strength but under the protection of God's grace, supported by divine help without exercising any endurance on his part, then in his submission to these many trials... Satan would have been able to speak with justice, slandering with what he had said before: "Doth Job fear God for nought? Hast not thou made an hedge about him... about all that he hath on every side? But put forth thine hand now," that is, permit me to fight him, "and he will curse thee to thy face" (Job 1:9-11).

But the slandering enemy could not make this protest after the battle, because he was defeated by the strength of Job and not by the strength of God; not in the sense that God's grace forsook Job, for it was what gave the tempter authority to tempt within the limits in which it saw that Job could resist, and at the same time grace did not protect him from the enemy's attacks in a way that removed his virtue and his striving, but rather helped him. That is, it does not permit that enemy, who is extremely cruel, to take away his mind or to drown him in his weakness by instilling thoughts beyond his strength, or to descend with him into a contest unequal to him.
Fr. Chaeremon * Divine providence often permits the believer to face afflictions, but this shows others the virtue hidden in him; so it was in the case of Job.
Fr. John of Damascus "And the LORD said unto Satan,
Behold, all that he hath is in thy power; only upon himself put not forth thine hand.
So Satan went forth from the presence of the LORD" [12].
God permitted Satan to tempt Job, as He permitted him to sift Peter the Apostle, but He took care that his faith should not fail (Lk 22:32), for trials turn to praise and honor and glory (1 Pet 1:7).

The permission that the Lord granted to Satan gives the believer reassurance and peace, for the enemy of good cannot touch a believer without the permission of his God, nor can he even approach his possessions without the permission of his God. God is the almighty, loving, wise Father, who gives permission to the extent that we can bear, and in a way that turns to our glory if we are faithful.

It is said of the enemy of good, "Satan went forth from the presence of the LORD," as it was said of Cain (Gen 4:16), since evil cannot bear to exist in the divine presence. But of the sons of God who stand before God it is not said that they went forth from the presence of the Lord. So believers remain in the presence of the Lord even in their moments of sleep!

God permitted Satan to receive authority to tempt righteous Job within the limits He set for him. Here Pope Gregory (the Great) distinguishes between Satan's will and his authority. As for his will, it is always evil; but his authority that is permitted him by God will contain no injustice, because it is by divine permission for our proving and edification. For this reason we do not wonder at what is stated in (1 Sam 10:18): "The evil spirit from God came violently upon Saul, and he raved in the midst of the house." He is an evil spirit, but the saying "from God" is because he could not have rushed upon Saul without receiving authority from the just God. St. Paul says: "There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able" (1 Cor 13:10). Therefore David the psalmist says: "Prove me, O Lord, and try me" (Ps 2:26).

St. Augustine sees that God permits Satan to bring afflictions upon them, either for their discipline, as He delivered His people to captivity by strangers; or for testing so that they may be proved, as He permitted Job to be tempted; or to send them forward to receive the crown, as He permitted martyrs to be persecuted.

*In truth, when Satan asked to be given authority against Job, his attack on him was the cause of Job's receiving double glory after his victory. His receiving twice what he lost in the present showed in truth that he will without doubt receive in the same way in the heavenly places. The Apostle says: "And if a man also strive for masteries, yet is he not crowned, except he strive lawfully" (2 Tim 2:5).
In truth, how can there be striving if there is no one to resist?
How great is the beauty and splendor of the light, which cannot be discerned unless the darkness of night stands against it.
Why are some praised for purity, if not because others are condemned for their impudence?
Why are the strong glorified, if not because there are cowards?
When you make use of what is bitter, then the sweet becomes all the more worthy of praise for you.

Origen * We read in the Book of Job how Satan himself, who appears to have all authority for a time, cannot do anything without permission. He received authority over lower things, and lost his authority over everything greater and higher. This authority of his is not like that of one who issues a penalty, but the penalty rests upon himself.

* God permitted the tempter, not that He might know what He already knows (about Job), but that we might know and imitate him. He delivered him to the tempter, and everything was taken away. And the man remained stripped of his possessions and of his family and of his children, but he was full of God.

* The tempter was permitted to tempt a holy man, Job. In one moment he took away all things, removed all that he possessed, took away the inheritance, and killed the heirs. This did not happen little by little, but all together, in one blow... He announced it all in a sudden announcement. When everything was removed, Job alone remained, but there remained in him the vows of praise which he offers to God.

* God granted (His people) their request, and gave them a king after their heart, as it is written, and not after His own heart. He also granted what Satan asked of Him, to tempt His servant that he might be proved.
St. Augustine * Do you not see the limits that were set in the test? Do you not notice that Satan could not even touch the flock if he had not received authority?

St. John Chrysostom * The tempter Satan is permitted to stir up war against the saints by every means of temptation, so that their love for God may be proved, and that it may be a witness. This is when things are taken away from them, or they are deprived, or become in want and destitute of sensible things, while they remain lovers of God, steadfast in His love, loving in truth. And while (Satan) tries to entice them, they remain undefeated, and do not change their love for God...

For the enemy strongly desires to tempt every man, if that were possible for him, and asks God on behalf of all to tempt them, as he asked on behalf of the righteous man Job... And when he received permission in a short time, Satan approached immediately according to the strength of the one he would tempt. So the evil one struggles with them according to his desire. By these means, those who are upright and steadfast in the love of God are proved when they scorn everything and count it as nothing beside their love for God.
St. Isaac the Syrian * Authority against us is given in two forms, either for punishment when we sin, or for glory when we are proved, as we see in the case of Job.

Cyprian the Martyr * "Behold, all that he hath is in thy power; only upon himself put not forth thine hand" [12], can have another meaning. The Lord truly knew that His soldier was courageous, and that victory was certain under all circumstances for this steadfast wrestler. And that the enemy would return to the Lord defeated from one struggle. Then He permits him another battle so that he may be defeated once more, and the one who follows Him faithfully becomes all the more incomparably victorious over the defeated enemy who has regained his strength for new wars.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
*What is written about Job is not without meaning, for it is clear from the Scripture that Satan asked for him and sought him. For Satan cannot do anything of himself without permission from God.

What does Satan say to the Lord? "Deliver him into my hand, for he will curse thee to thy face" (Job 1:11). And Job is still as he was until now, and so is God, and so also is Satan. Therefore, to that extent Satan seeks him and says to the Lord: [He serves You only because You help him and protect him and support him; but put forth Your hand now and deliver him to me, and he will curse You to Your face.]

In short, when a person has obtained consolation by grace, grace withdraws a little so that he may be delivered to trials. And Satan comes and brings with him thousands of evils as temptations for the man, such as despair, apostasy and evil thoughts, to torment the soul with them, in order to weaken it and separate it from hope in the Lord.

St. Macarius the Great *[Lead us not into temptation]. The prayer here is not that we may not be tried, but that we may not enter (be led) into temptation. For since every man must be tested by fire, he should pray not that the fire may not touch him, but that he may not perish. For vessels of clay are tested by the furnace, and man is tested by afflictions, trail of tribulation (Sir 27:6)(a).
Joseph was tested by the temptation of fornication, but he did not enter into temptation (Gen 7:39-12).
And Susanna was also tried without entering into temptation (Addition to Dan 13:22).
And many of both sexes were tried without entering into temptation.
But Job was the greatest of them, for he stood with wonderful steadfastness in the Lord his God.

St. Augustine * (The demons) have no authority nor power to exercise against anyone unless they receive permission from God according to His plan, such as what happened against Job (Job 1:12), and against the swine mentioned in the Gospels (Mk 5:13).

Fr. John of Damascus * The evil spirits have no authority to harm anyone; this is clearly shown in the case of the blessed Job, where the enemy did not dare to tempt him except as God permitted... The spirits themselves confessed this, as it is in the Gospel, for they said, "If thou cast us out, suffer us to go away into the herd of swine" (Mt 31:8). If they have no authority to enter the unclean dumb animals except by permission from God, how much less are they able to enter man, who is created in the image of God?!
Fr. Serenus

13 And there was a day when his sons and his daughters were eating and drinking wine in their eldest brother's house: 14 And there came a messenger unto Job, and said, The oxen were plowing, and the asses feeding beside them: 15 And the Sabeans fell upon them, and took them away; yea, they have slain the servants with the edge of the sword; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee. 16 While he was yet speaking, there came also another, and said, The fire of God is fallen from heaven, and hath burned up the sheep, and the servants, and consumed them; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee. 17 While he was yet speaking, there came also another, and said, The Chaldeans made out three bands, and fell upon the camels, and have carried them away, yea, and slain the servants with the edge of the sword; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee. 18 While he was yet speaking, there came also another, and said, Thy sons and thy daughters were eating and drinking wine in their eldest brother's house: 19 And, behold, there came a great wind from the wilderness, and smote the four corners of the house, and it fell upon the young men, and they are dead; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee.
"And there was a day when his sons and his daughters were eating and drinking wine in their eldest brother's house" [13].

* We must notice the timing at which the trials came. Satan chose the time of the temptation when the sons of blessed Job were occupied in a feast (Job 1:13). The adversary did not search only for what to do, but for when to do it. Although he had received permission, he sought the suitable time to carry out his destruction. And by God's arrangement the purpose was to record this for our benefit, for the enjoyment of complete pleasures is a preparation for the coming of calamities.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"And there came a messenger unto Job, and said,
The oxen were plowing, and the asses feeding beside them" [14].

In the Septuagint it says "the she asses with their young." With great cunning the enemy wanted to increase the bitterness of the calamity: the Sabeans carried off the useful oxen, since they were plowing the land, and the she asses that were fruitful, since their young were with them. By this the enemy wanted to strike violently, to make the wound in the soul of righteous Job more bitter. Besides this, the calamities fell one after another with extreme speed.
And the Sabeans fell upon them, and took them away; yea, they have slain the servants with the edge of the sword; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee [15].

When Satan took permission to tempt, he did not lack the will with which to carry out his plan, for the wicked fulfil the counsel of their wicked father. As the Lord Christ said to the Jews of His time: "Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do" (Jn 8:44). For he is "the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience" (Eph 2:2).

* Do you not see the swiftness of the blow...? Nothing like this had ever happened before, nor had anyone heard of such a thing. Add to this that it was no longer possible to plow the land, and in a moment Job was stripped of all his possessions. The sight of the destruction of a flock is always painful, especially if it happens at a time when a man depends entirely upon it... Add to that the occurrence of killing in the midst of the devastation, which makes the struggle unbearable, as brutality and savagery appear. It is a double calamity, killing and raiding expeditions, with the remaining emaciation added to the afflictions that befell him, so that it no longer left him ignorant of the dreadful nature of the calamity of the event.

St. John Chrysostom St. Ambrose affirms that many things that seem evil and wicked, and from which we suffer, become an opportunity for the growth of our virtues, as happened with Job in his many trials.
* Would (Job) not have been in a less blessed state if he had not suffered these things by which in truth he was proved?
St. Ambrose "While he was yet speaking, there came also another, and said,
The fire of God is fallen from heaven, and hath burned up the sheep, and the servants, and consumed them; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee" [16].

The calamities followed one another in moments and with extreme speed, and perhaps the enemy did so deliberately so as not to leave Job an opportunity for balanced thought, but with the successive disasters he would think that God's wrath had come down upon him and would not stop. The trials were like waves that never subside. "Deep calleth unto deep" (Ps 42:7).

What is remarkable about the messengers coming to Job is that they affirm that the oxen were plowing and the asses feeding. As though even the animals were doing their part, so that there is no blame on the sons, nor the servants, nor the animals, and as though all the blame falls on God alone and no one else. Satan's plan was extremely well devised, to strike Job's heart so as to turn all his feelings and thoughts toward blaspheming God.

While I was writing down this interpretation, a young man suddenly died, and his friend, who was very dear to him, began to blaspheme: "Why did God take the dearest friend I have?" and he refuses any consolation... and sometimes he even mutters: "Where is God? And if He exists, where is His mercy and His care?" As though the enemy of good in every generation expends every effort to turn the energies of humanity toward blaspheming God.

The enemy of good did not give Job the opportunity to think of waging war against the Sabeans and recovering his possessions, for the next news came announcing that a fire from heaven had come down from God and burned up the sheep and the servants and consumed them. If he wanted to fight the Sabeans, from where would he bring his men to fight, when a divine fire had burned them up? And then, would he fight God? And how could he reach Him...? It was as though nothing remained within Job's reach but his tongue to blaspheme God as a violent oppressor who knows no mercy.

St. John Chrysostom sees that by saying, "The fire of God is fallen from heaven," the enemy wanted to suggest to Job that what befell him was not human blows but from God, and directed against him alone and not the rest of those around him. Perhaps by this he wanted to distort the image of God in his eyes. For although he had committed no great sins and had not been negligent in worshipping God, yet God had come down in His wrath upon him and no one else, which stirs in him the motive to blaspheme God as unjust. Since God burned up the sheep, of which he had chosen the best to offer as burnt offerings to God, God appears as One who is not pleased with his burnt offerings and does not accept his worship, or as though "it is vain to serve God" (Mal 3:14).
Nothing had been heard of burning coming from heaven since the burning of Sodom and Gomorrah; therefore Job says: [For destruction from the LORD was a terror to me] (Job 31:23).
* Lest the loss of his possessions should not stir him to sufficient grief when he heard the news, he spurred on his feelings with the very words of the messenger.

Notice how cunningly it was said "the fire of God," as if to say that you are suffering from a visitation of the One whom you want to appease with so many sacrifices. Behold, you have fallen under the wrath of the One whose service you busy yourself with every day...
This is the aim: that he should recall to his memory his past services, and reckon that he had served in vain, as though he wanted to stir up in him the feeling of the Creator's injustice.

For the godly mind, finding itself facing the bearing of crosses at the hands of a man, seeks consolations from divine providence. And when it sees the storm of temptation drawing its strength from outside, it seeks to cover it with trust in the Lord, and takes refuge inwardly in the harbor of conscience. But that cunning adversary wanted at that very moment to break the heart of this brave saint, by blows directed from a man and by despair of God.

He came to him with news first of the Sabeans who had carried out the plunder, and immediately the report came of the fire of God that fell from heaven, so as to close the door completely to any means of consolation.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"While he was yet speaking, there came also another, and said,
The Chaldeans made out three bands, and fell upon the camels, and have carried them away, yea, and slain the servants with the edge of the sword; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee" [17].

The enemy did not leave him to think why the fire fell from heaven as though by divine command, for another messenger came to him telling him of a new blow by the deed of the Chaldeans. In this he wants to confuse Job's mind. For if the fire had come down from God, Job might think that it was a blow to discipline him, but when he finds that even men fall upon him, how will he justify this?

For the third time a grave calamity befalls him, and it came by way of three bands of Chaldeans, at a time when Job had lost every possibility of resistance. Perhaps the enemy wanted by this blow that Job should cry out in his heart: "Why does the Lord make the way of the wicked prosper?"
"While he was yet speaking, there came also another, and said,
Thy sons and thy daughters were eating and drinking wine in their eldest brother's house" [18].
"And, behold, there came a great wind from the wilderness, and smote the four corners of the house, and it fell upon the young men, and they are dead; and I only am escaped alone to tell thee" [19].

To increase the bitterness of the calamity, he sent him grave news, that nature too was in revolt against him, for a great wind shook the house and killed his sons and daughters, so that it would be hard for him to bring out their bodies whole! Their appearance would be extremely hideous. Besides this, to confuse Job's mind: how do heaven and earth join together against him, God and men and nature resisting him, why? What had he done to fall under these successive calamities from different sources?

This, the most grievous of the blows, the enemy left to the end, so as to aim a deadly arrow at Job's heart, for his sons and daughters all died in moments under the rubble. It is an extremely grave loss. When David's infant son fell ill, he could not bear the bitterness, but went to and fro crying out; what then of Job, who lost all his sons and daughters suddenly.
Job needed his children to comfort him in all that he had lost, but their death, especially in this way, surely made him forget all the previous trials and fall into unbearable bitterness.

St. John Chrysostom says that in the previous calamities there may be justification for the messenger's saying: "and I only am escaped alone," since he escaped what befell Job's animals; but that this last messenger should escape the fall of the house while all Job's sons and daughters die together is unnatural, so what is the secret? Chrysostom sees that this messenger was not a man but Satan himself, for how could one who served Job's sons and daughters escape without them, while he was with them in the same house that fell and destroyed those in it?
* Have you lost a child! Have you not lost him? Do not say this; he is asleep, not dead; he has moved and has not been destroyed; he is on a journey from a bad state to a better one.
Do not provoke God to anger, but entreat Him. For if you bear this nobly, the rest is doubled for the departed as well as for you. But if the opposite happens, you inflame God's wrath all the more...
Give thanks, for by this the cloud of grief is dispersed from you. Say with Job: [The LORD hath given, the LORD hath taken away] (Job 21:1).
St. John Chrysostom

20 Then Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head, and fell down upon the ground, and worshipped, 21 And said, Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD. 22 In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly.
"Then Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head, and fell down upon the ground, and worshipped" [20].

Had Job not behaved thus he would have been counted a man dull of feeling, rigid, unnatural and foolish, unmoved by the death of his sons and servants. By this behavior he revealed the bitterness of his soul without going beyond the bounds of propriety, in view of the multitude of the successive trials and their hideousness.
Besides this, what he did was in keeping with the customs followed at that time. His behavior does not mean that he lost his inner peace or his courage and patience and power of endurance.

Some commentators see that he had recourse to this because the enemy of good tried to instill thoughts of blasphemy against God. So the tearing of clothes and the shaving of the head are a sign of his insistence on rejecting these thoughts. For the tearing of clothes is a sign of the desire to reject blasphemy, as the high priest did when he thought that Jesus Christ had blasphemed.
His prostration to the ground is a sign of his sincerity with himself, as he felt that he was a sinner and that his soul had been brought down to the dust.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem sees that Job tore his clothes and shaved the hair of his head because of grief, but more so in order to strip himself of everything, even his garment and the hair of his head, so that the enemy of good would find nothing in which he could tempt him. And in humility before God he fell to the ground.

* He "worshipped" to convince the traitor that he slanders him in vain before God. For the one of whom he (Satan) said that he would blaspheme (Job 11:1; 5:2), behold, he worships. The person of whom he said that when his possessions were destroyed he would show ingratitude before God, behold, he gives thanks more than before.

* Some count it a high degree of the philosophy of steadfastness that when they fall under severe discipline they are dull in their feeling of the blows and in the pain of the scourgings. And some exaggerate their sensitivity to the pain of the blows...

The prophet says: "Thou hast stricken them, but they have not grieved; thou hast consumed them, but they have refused to receive correction" (Jer 3:5). In contrast to this, concerning the inward dialogue in the feeling of discipline, the psalmist says: "They shall not stand firm in the trial" (Ps 140:10) (Vulgate). For they stand firm in the trial if they bear it with patience.
* It was the custom in ancient times that each one kept up his personal appearance by letting his hair grow, to cut it in times of grief.

When the holy man lost everything in the time of his trial through the adversary, he realized that Satan has no authority to tempt him without the permission of the Lord; therefore he did not say: "The Lord gave, and Satan took away"... For it would be sad if what the Creator gives were taken away from him by the enemy. But the one who takes it is none other than the One who gave, who took back what was His and did not take what is ours. For everything we use in our present life comes from Him, so why should we grieve if we return to Him what we borrowed from Him through His generosity?
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* O the courage of Job, which surpasses all that is told! O the humility! O the love of God...!

Did the enemy think that Job did not care about the oxen, and was not concerned about the she asses, and counted the flock a thing of no value, and the camels as though they were nothing, and all his possessions things to be despised?
What about the grief over the death of his sons and daughters, how did it not cast him into terror...?
He who was the father of many children no longer had anyone to call him "my father."

He did not say to God: "What many sins has Job committed, that he should be counted unworthy to embrace his children at their death, and not be able to honor them by burying them in a tomb, nor be able to be comforted with tears as a fully natural custom, nor be able to lead a funeral procession, as fathers and friends usually do...?"
Then I wish you would not be angry when you are stripped of your possessions, and deprived of temporal honors, and separated from sons or fathers.
When you lose them according to the law of nature, do not be troubled...
For your true wealth, which is the praise of God, cannot be taken away from you, a thing that makes you strong to defy all events.
Does the servant bring an accusation when he is asked for the talents that his master entrusted to him? (Mt 19:25)
Or when he has taken a loan, is he troubled when he returns it...?
Yes, since we give what is not ours, let us come before God as One worthy of thanks, when He gives as when He takes.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * "Then Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head" [20]. Do not think, beloved, that this gesture is a sign of defeat; rather it is especially a sign of victory. For if he had not acted at all, he would have been thought to be in a state of stupor, but he truly showed himself wise and a godly father at the same time. For what a loss this was that befell him! He did not grieve only over the loss of his sons and also his animals, but over the way in which they died. Who is not shattered before these events? What man of iron is not moved by them?

Paul also had these feelings in the face of tears, for he says: "What mean ye to weep and to break mine heart?" (Acts 13:21) and by this he was an object of admiration! So Job is worthy of admiration, because despite the feelings that drove him to this movement, he expressed them in a way in which there was nothing unseemly at all...

Moses (the prophet) broke (the tablets of the Law), and Joshua tore his clothes (Ex 15:32-20; Josh 6:7); if Job had not torn his clothes it would have been said that God created him with an unfeeling (rigid) nature, but he accepted the sufferings that befall the righteous so that you may realize that he was bound to be wise even in his grief.

* "And fell down upon the ground, and worshipped" [20]. Lest you think that his tearing of his clothes means blasphemy, and that he is in a state of anger at the events, listen to what he says. He yielded his garment to Satan. The text says: "And shaved his head... and said, Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither." Again he speaks well. For from that time he faces the struggle, casting himself naked.
He fell to the ground and made Satan fall. He showed his feelings and made clear his godliness...
