Finally God asked them to ask Job to pray for them, and to offer a sacrifice for them; thus the Church does not cease to pray for the heretics that they may turn from resistance, and recover their membership in the Church, and enjoy the heavenly life of the Church.

* All these gestures are good and fitting for friends who reveal their sympathy with him, but what came afterwards was the opposite. It was not of the same kind, but quite the opposite and wicked. See what happened. It is unbelievable, they spoke as spiteful adversaries.

* When the soul is filled with despair immediately it is not inclined to hear anything of what is said. Therefore when Job's friends came and saw the catastrophe of his house, and the righteous man sitting in the mire, covered with sores, they tore their garments and sighed, and sat beside him in silence, showing that nothing is fitting to offer one who suffers thus but quiet and stillness. For the trial was far greater than to have a consolation.
St. John Chrysostom
Adam on the dunghill!
* Satan could not keep silent when he saw man in the garden of Eden enjoying You as his Paradise!
He approached him through the serpent, and dared to use the mouth of Eve.
And by his envy he drove Adam and Eve out of the garden, and by sin death reigned over them and over their offspring!
* Now that he has seen in every person the broken Adam.
He thought he could break Job as he broke his first father.
He did not speak with him through the serpent, but dared to accuse him before You, O Creator of all!
* In pride he declared that he was going about the earth and walking upon it, as though he were a king with authority!
Yes, remove our dust from us, that we may no longer remain earth, and he may not be able to walk about in our hearts!
He will see us as a second heaven, and will flee from before us.
You make us sit in the heavenly places, so he cannot creep in to us!
* How wonderful, You alone, the Holy One, praise us!
And the evil devil accuses us!
Is he jealous for holiness, that he accuses us of our weakness?
In his wickedness he wishes to destroy all, that they may share with him his blasphemy against You, O You who alone are holy!
* He aimed all his fiery darts at poor Job!
He who was the morning star stands before an unarmed man!
He had no rest until he struck his whole body!
With Your permission he killed all his sons and daughters, and left his wife to use against him.
He struck his whole body, and left him his tongue in the hope that he might blaspheme You!
With great cunning he spent all his effort to break the one who believes in You, and did not realize that his arrows turn back upon him!
* Adam in the garden inclined his ear to hear the enemy's counsel, through Eve his helper!
Job in the midst of the ashes opened his mouth to silence the satanic counsel!
Adam was silent with a sinful silence, and broke Your divine commandment.
And Job spoke good words, and rescued his wife from the satanic wiles!
Adam was stripped bare in the garden, and fig leaves could not cover him!
And Job put on a garment of worms, more splendidly beautiful than the garment of kings!
Adam and Eve were terrified when they heard Your voice!
And the heavenly ones stood in amazement before the praises of the one sitting in the midst of the ashes!
Adam supposed that his being forbidden to eat of the tree of knowledge was injustice and deprivation.
And Job reckoned that all that was taken from him was by Your permission for his good!
Amid all the blessings of the garden and its possibilities Adam's eyes were fixed on one tree!
Amid all the unbearable trials Job's eyes were fixed on You, O Maker of good things!
Adam opened his mouth to justify himself, and Job opened his mouth and did not sin with his lips!
* The friends came, each from his own place, and would that they had not come!
They wanted to comfort him with their human thoughts, and gave him bitterness!
They showed all feelings of tenderness and sharing in the sufferings, but they did not bring You to him, O heavenly Comforter!
* You are my heavenly Friend, carry me to You, to Your place, that I may rest in the bosom of Your Father!
You came down to me, and were tempted that You might help those who are tempted!
Be You the secret of my comfort, my peace and my true joy!

entries.section: 1. He curses the day of his birth and wishes he had not been born

paragraphs.text: 1 After this Job opened his mouth, and cursed his day. 2 And Job spake, and said: 3 Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said, There is a man child conceived. 4 Let that day be darkness; let not God regard it from above, neither let day shine upon it. 5 Let darkness and the shadow of death rule over it; let a cloud dwell upon it; let the blackness of the day terrify it. 6 As for that night, let darkness seize upon it; let it not rejoice among the days of the year, let it not come into the number of the months. 7 Lo, let that night be barren, let no shout be heard in it. 8 Let them curse it that curse the day, who are ready to rouse up the dragon. 9 Let the stars of the evening thereof be dark; let it look for light, but have none; neither let it see the eyelashes of the morning: 10 Because it shut not up the doors of my mother's womb, nor hid sorrow from mine eyes.
It was a weakness in his life that Job cursed his conception. Although he is described as upright, he cursed his day, yet he did not blaspheme against God.
After this Job opened his mouth, and Job cursed his day. [1]

Ezekiel sat in the land of captivity, and his soul was groaning because of the destruction and ruin to which the people and their city and the temple had come. He was silent seven days, astonished, and the word of the LORD came to him (Ezek 3:15-16). And Job sat among his friends, and his soul was groaning over what had befallen him, so he opened his mouth after the long silence to curse the day of his conception and the day of his birth and the days of his trial.

Both were silent, Ezekiel and Job. The first was occupied with what belongs to God and His people and His temple and His city, and the second with what concerns himself and what people think of him. The first enjoyed the surpassing word of God, and the second descended to despair and bitterness and cursed his life.

We need to sit in silence, but to rise above the ego, to be occupied with what belongs to God and people and not with ourselves and our dignity. Then the Holy Spirit of God lifts us up as if to heaven, and we hear the divine voice and discover the divine mysteries that grant living hope.

Sadly, Job looked at the day of his conception as the worst day in history, and reckoned it the starting point of his unbearable sufferings. He forgot the good things he had enjoyed. The lean years devoured the years filled with blessings. His mind became a prisoner of the bitterness in which he lives, so he looked at his whole life through an extremely gloomy lens.

What befell Job befalls many when their days of affliction are prolonged. So we hear the prophet Jeremiah cry out: “Woe is me, my mother, that thou hast borne me” (Jer 15:10); “Cursed be the day wherein I was born” (Jer 20:14).

When the day of our eternal meeting with our Christ on the clouds is hidden from our eyes even for moments, the world grows narrow upon us and we even reckon our creation to be in vain. [How long, LORD? wilt thou hide thyself for ever?... wherefore hast thou made all men in vain?] (Ps 89:46-47).

Here we pause a little before mankind's concern with birthday celebrations since ancient times. We find the wicked finding in this day the opportunity to express what is in their hearts of frivolity and earnest desire to dominate others, while the children of God stand in seriousness looking at their entering the path of sufferings. They reckon the day of their birth to be the day of their entering the valley of tears, but in a living, joyful hope that they are passing over to the new heavenly life.
* At birthday celebrations, where the desire for the domineering word rules over (the wicked), they dance to express by the movements of their bodies this word.

Someone noticed that the Book of Genesis speaks of Pharaoh's birthday (Gen 40:20), where it is said that the unruly man loves matters concerning birthdays. I have taken this quotation from him, for I have not found in the Holy Scripture any righteous man who made a birthday for himself. Herod was more unjust than this famous Pharaoh. For the latter killed the chief baker at the celebration of his birthday, while the former killed John.

Origen Origen expounded at length in his comment on the words of the prophet Jeremiah: “Woe is me, my mother, that thou hast borne me a man of strife” (Jer 15:10), which I have presented previously in the commentary on the Book of Jeremiah. Here I quote short passages:

* Who am I, that I was born only to be condemned, and to be quarreled with by men because of my reproof and blame of them, and because of my teachings which I teach to all the inhabitants of the earth.

Origen Truly, whoever has experienced the day of his second birth by water and the Spirit and has become a son of God does not curse even the day of his bodily birth, reckoning all his sufferings a crucifixion and burial with his Christ, and a narrow way by which he enters the open gates of heaven and the joy of the eternal resurrection.

Here we must not deny that despite the bitterness Job reached to the point of cursing the day of his conception, he did not blaspheme against God, nor did he regret his worship of Him. What he uttered reveals the bitterness of his soul, but he submitted to the will of God. He is under sufferings like us!

* What is understood by “After this”? After the arrival of his friends... for those who drew near did not greet him as a wrestler and did not ask him: How are you? They offered no remedies for the sores, nor did they stand upon the price Job had won for his treasure of virtues. They did not say to him: Do not lose heart, for your comforter is near you; do not fear, for your enemy is being defeated. Do not be ashamed, for the end is not far, and the victory is at the doors.

* “Let the day perish wherein I was born,” not the day on which he was created, but on which he was born... For God created me in goodness, but Eve who disobeyed bore me in troubles (Gen 3:16). David was not ignorant of this, but understood by the Spirit and said in a prophetic psalm: [In iniquities my mother conceived me, and in sin she bore me] (Ps 51:5).
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * O wonder that truly surpasses nature! Astounding events!

Death, once hated and execrated, is now surrounded with praises and considered blessed! After it used to bring mourning and grief and tears and dismal gloom, behold, it has appeared as a cause of joy and the center of a festive celebration!

For all the servants of God their death is declared a joy! For the end of their life alone gives them the assurance that they were received by God. Therefore their death is called blessed, because it seals their perfection and shows their blessedness, since the steadfastness of virtue prevails over them, as the saying of Inspiration: [Call no man happy before his death] (Sir 11:30). We do not apply this saying to you (O Mary), because your blessedness does not come from death, and your death did not complete your perfection... Not at your death, but from this very conception you are called blessed by all generations. No, it is never death that made you blessed, but you cast death down and dispelled its gloom and showed that it is joy (in Christ, born of you).

Fr. John of Damascus *Is it not shameful that you groan because of death, while Paul sighs because of the present life, writing to the Romans: [The whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together... but ourselves also, which have the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves] (Rom 8:22-23). He says this not to condemn present things, but out of longing for the things to come.

entries.section: 1. He curses the day of his birth and wishes he had not been born

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom And Job spake, and said: [2]
St. John Chrysostom sees that the friends' silence throughout the week reveals the dreadfulness of what had happened, and that they were unable to utter a word unless he began first to speak.
Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said,

entries.section: 1. He curses the day of his birth and wishes he had not been born

paragraphs.text: There is a man child conceived! [3]

Most likely Job was a king or a chief, and the day of his birth was a day the people prized, so he wished that this day be blotted out and cast into the sea of oblivion, where it becomes a sight of misery and wretchedness.

* Job knew that his birth was the beginning of all woes, so he longed that the day on which he was born would perish so that the root of all troubles might be removed. He desired that the day of his birth perish in order to receive the day of the resurrection. Solomon heard the saying of his father: “LORD, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is: that I may know how frail I am” (Ps 39:4). For David knew that what is perfect cannot be possessed here, therefore he was hastening toward the things to come. Now we know in part, but it will be possible to attain perfection when the truth, not the shadow, of the divine and eternal majesty begins to shine, and we see it with open face (1 Cor 13:12; 2 Cor 3:18).

* Bodily pleasure and enjoyment in this life have drawn us, and we have come to fear to complete this journey in which there will be more bitterness than pleasure. But the saints and the wise lamented the length of life in this journey, since they reckoned departure to be with Christ far more glorious (Phil 1:23). They did not curse the day of their birth as one of them did: “Let the day perish wherein I was born” (Job 3:3).
St. Ambrose * This is also what the Preacher (Ecclesiastes) said: “Wherefore I praised the dead which are already dead more than the living which are yet alive” (Eccl 4:2)...

These are words that announce a disheartened and deeply affected soul. For David also says: “I said in my consternation (my great fear)...” (Ps 31:22)... and in another passage: “And I said in my tranquility, I shall never be moved” (Ps 30:6). This is also what Job said in his sorrow. Do you not see, my beloved, that those who are hurt utter loud cries? Do you blame them? No, rather we excuse them! For if they did not express themselves in this way, it would seem as though they did not share in human nature. Do you not hear Moses say: “If thou deal thus with me, kill me, I pray thee, out of hand” (Num 11:15)...

Do not listen to the bare words, but search for the basis of the thought. You have heard that Job “did not sin... with his lips” (Job 2:10), and he did not sin even after he uttered those words. Behold, you hear God Himself saying again: “Do you think that I deal with you in any other way than to declare your righteousness?” (Job 40:3) LXX.
St. John Chrysostom * Perhaps you say that God is the creator and builder of the world (Heb 11:10) [so why do we not love the world?]

You speak truly. But the bearers of God despise the world, not the world that God created from the elements and that He fashioned, but the one we made by our conduct, a different, corrupt world, of which the deceiving enemy has been made the prince by us (Jn 12:31; 14:30; 16:11).

This is what the Lord affirms precisely, for He said this to His disciples: “the prince of this world cometh, and hath nothing in me” (Jn 14:30). It is not without reason that He says: “prince of this world,” but He said so lest you think He is speaking of this visible creation, for our enemy is not the prince of this world, and the traitor has no power at all over the elements.

In what sense does He say: “the prince of this world cometh,” except the world that we make not according to the will of God, and by which we give a basis for unbelief and disobedience and disorder and every kind of sins?

To this world Paul clearly refers in accordance with the word of the Lord, saying in his Epistle to the Ephesians: “And you who were dead in trespasses and sins, wherein in time past ye walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience” (Eph 2:1-2). Thus we have formed an evil world, and in this world we have made ourselves self-sufficient, needing no others, from corrupt sources...

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Let him say: “Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said... There is a man child conceived” [3], as though he said: Let the delight that hastens man to sin perish, and the weakness of his unrestrained mind, by which he becomes blind like one who has reached the darkness that consents to evil.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Let that day be darkness.

entries.section: 1. He curses the day of his birth and wishes he had not been born

paragraphs.text: Let not God regard it from above, neither let the day shine upon it [4].

He wished that the day of his birth had been darkness, because the light of his life had been extinguished and the sun had set upon him, and perhaps he wanted his whole life to be night, so that he would sleep and not rise.

Despite the godliness and uprightness and faith Job reached, the Book does not hide his human weaknesses, so we do not marvel if thoughts of despair passed through him, wishing he had not been born. The Fathers have warned us of the wrong fear that leads to despair.

* There is a contrition of heart that is spiritual and useful, and this touches the heart in its depths. And there is another contrition, harmful and disturbing, which leads it only to defeat (like despair).

St. Mark the Ascetic * If labor (in keeping good thoughts) wears us out, we fall into despair; therefore may we hasten to the rock of knowledge and recite the Psalms and know the virtues upon the strings of the harp of knowledge.
Fr. Evagrius the monk Let darkness and the shadow of death rule over it.
Let a cloud dwell upon it.

entries.section: 1. He curses the day of his birth and wishes he had not been born

paragraphs.text: Let the blackness (darkness) of the day terrify it [5].
* “Let darkness and the shadow of death rule over it,” since darkness is truly our enemy, just as Christ is the light (Jn 8:12; 9:5; 12:46). For this very reason (the traitor) is darkness.
And as Christ is righteousness (1 Cor 1:30), so (the traitor) is sin.
And as He is the source of life (Ps 36:9) and the image of His substance, so the traitor is “the shadow of death” (Heb 2:14-15).

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Is there anything more terrifying than Satan? Yes, for in resisting him we find no shield except faith (1 Pet 5:9), for it is a hidden shield against an unseen enemy, who shoots various arrows in the darkness of night (Ps 11:2) at the unwatchful. Since we have an unseen enemy we need faith as a mighty weapon of war, as the Apostle says: “Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked” (Eph 6:16). So when the devil aims the arrow of fiery, impure lust, faith presents the image of judgment, so the mind cools and the arrow is quenched.

entries.section: 1. He curses the day of his birth and wishes he had not been born

paragraphs.text: St. Cyril of Jerusalem As for that night, let darkness seize upon it; let it not rejoice among the days of the year, let it not come into the number of the months [6].

Fr. Hesychius distinguishes between two days: the day of disobedience that brought darkness upon us, and the day of the Savior in which He says: “This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears” (Lk 4:21). The first day brought darkness and grief upon mankind, and the second is the joyful day of salvation in which the prophecy of the prophet Isaiah was fulfilled (Isa 61:1-2). For when we meet the Savior our joyful days of the Gospel are no longer compared with the days of gripping darkness that corrupts life. Therefore Job asked that the day of his birth in sin be cursed and utterly excluded and not counted among his days in the Lord.

* May that day and night be cursed, and let darkness carry them away, let it not enter into the number of the days of the months... May this day, the day of disobedience, not be counted among the benefits given to us through the Savior. May the grief (of the darkness) that comes from the day not be mixed with the blessings the Savior grants us, nor the curse corrupt them.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Lo, let that night be barren!

entries.section: 1. He curses the day of his birth and wishes he had not been born

paragraphs.text: Let no shout be heard in it [7].
His ears could no longer bear the sound of music or shouting and rejoicing, because there is no place for joy in his depths. It is as though he had lost his hope for a time.

St. Augustine likens hope to an egg that carries within it a life which it presents through the warmth of tribulations and sufferings, for he says: [It is an egg, and not yet a (chick). It is covered with a shell, but do not look at it so; rather wait patiently, and put it in warmth and it will bring forth life. Press it.]
* Hope drives a person toward eternity, toward the future, in practical faith, and perseverance with joy and delight amid sufferings.
* Let us listen and rejoice in hope even if the present is a life not loved but endured, for you will have strength to bear all its trials.
* We rejoice in hope, looking to the coming rest; by this we walk with joy amid troubles.
St. Augustine * The person who does not look at what can be seen, but eagerly awaits what cannot be seen, rejoices in hope.
Origen * What is the hope of the Gospel but Christ? For He is our peace, who works all these things... and whoever does not believe in Christ loses everything.

* Hope is certainly like a strong rope let down from the heavens that helps our spirits, lifting whoever holds it firmly above this world and the trials of this evil life; but if a man is weak and lets go of this holy cord, he falls at once and is choked in the pit of evil.

* Nothing makes the soul so courageous and risk-loving as hope! And before our obtaining the things we hope for, it gives us a reward, which is: “patient in tribulation.” Before our obtaining the things to come, you enjoy in the present life a great good through trials, as you become a patient and proven man...

Love makes things easy, and the Spirit helps, and hope enlightens, and trials refine you, making you a proven one able to bear everything nobly; accompanying all this is a very great weapon, which is prayer.
St. John Chrysostom * Man's patience begets hope, and good hope glorifies man.

entries.section: 1. He curses the day of his birth and wishes he had not been born

paragraphs.text: St. Evagrius Let them curse it that curse the day, who are ready to rouse up the dragon [8].

Just as the mourning women attend funerals and lament with the family and friends of the dead, so he reckoned the day of his birth a bitter funeral, and asks the cursers to come forward and share with him in cursing this day.

Some see that certain crocodile hunters used to curse crocodiles with the bitterest curses, hoping that the crocodile would become weak through their curses and incantations and they would gain mastery over it.

The Jesuit translation reads “Leviathan” instead of “dragon,” and as we shall see in its description in chapter forty-one that it applies to the crocodile, what is meant here are the curses that sorcerers and astrologers use to stir up Satan.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus warns us against comparing matters according to their size or weight. So we do not marvel if the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove, and the Lord Christ was called a sheep [a lamb] (Isa 53:7) and a pearl (Mt 13:46) and dew [rain] (Ps 72:6), while the adversary was called a great mountain (Zech 4:7), and leviathan (Job 3:8; 40:20) and the king who lives in the waters (a). Let us not despise the Kingdom of Heaven because it was likened to a grain of mustard seed (Mt 13:31).
Let the stars of the evening thereof be dark.

entries.section: 1. He curses the day of his birth and wishes he had not been born

paragraphs.text: Let it look for light, but have none; neither let it see the eyelashes of the morning [9]

*“Let the stars of its evening (its dusk) be dark... and let not Lucifer be seen rising” (Job 3:9) LXX. The stars of night are mentioned here with poor light, referring to the demons. For they take the form of an angel of light, but at the rising of the true Light (Jn 1:9) they become dark, and continue in their perversion.
This is what the text says: “Let it remain dark.” But they do not come to the light, since they cannot recover their tyranny.

Moreover, they will not see Lucifer standing, he of whom Isaiah said: [Lucifer, who rose in the morning] (Isa 14:12). After that he says [he was crushed to the earth] to indicate that he can no longer rise and return to his former dignity.
By his fall from heaven to earth he wanted to destroy man, but God gives the one who is not deceived authority to crush the deceiver under his feet, and to shatter him piece by piece.
But why does Job curse him?
For a good reason which he does not hide (which is what appears in the two verses [10-11]).

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem St. Augustine tells us of the defeat of the wicked devil, whose false light was extinguished by his killing the Lord Christ according to the flesh, the true Light, the Righteous One who dispels the darkness. He thought he could dispel Him as he shattered the first Adam, but behold, he shattered himself.
* What could be more righteous than reaching even the death of the Cross for the sake of righteousness?
And what work is greater in authority than the resurrection from the dead, and the ascension into heaven in the same body in which He was killed?
First the Righteous One conquered Satan, and afterward received authority!
The Righteous One triumphs because there is no sin in Him, and He died unjustly at the hands of Satan!
He receives authority, because He lived again after death, and will die no more...
Satan was defeated by his own victory...
By deceiving the first man he slew him, and by slaying the last Man he lost the first man from his net!

St. Augustine * In Holy Scripture the title “stars” is sometimes used for the righteousness of the saints shining in the darkness of this life, and sometimes for the vain appearance of hypocrites, who do every good thing for the praise of men. For if doers of good were not luminaries, Paul would not have said to his disciple: “in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world” (Phil 2:15).

Again, if there were not among (the members of the Church) those who seem outwardly to be walking uprightly, there would not be some who by their conduct receive honor from men, and John would not have seen the stars falling from heaven, when he said: [And his tail drew the third part of the stars of heaven, and did cast them to the earth] (Rev 12:4).

* The eyelashes of the morning [the rising of the dawn] is the beginning of the Church in the light, where the wicked cannot be seen, for they are shut in and compelled to descend into darkness through the weight of their evil works, so that they do not see the just Judge. Thus it was truly said by the prophet: Let the wicked be taken away from the way, that he behold not the glory of God (Isa 26:10) LXX.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 1. He curses the day of his birth and wishes he had not been born

paragraphs.text: Because it shut not up the doors of my mother's womb, nor hid sorrow from mine eyes [10].

His wisdom failed him, so Job desired something extremely cruel, namely that his mother had given birth to him before the appointed time, so that her womb would open and he would come out a stillborn, and she herself would be exposed to danger and even death. A very painful picture because of complaining!

Pope Gregory (the Great) offers us a wonderful symbolic interpretation of this phrase, where he sees the believer returning to the first parents while in Paradise as in a mother's womb, and he wished to be born there and that the gates of Paradise not be opened to drive him out by the serpent. He says that the serpent opened the mouth of this womb for man to come out of the joyful garden, and to live in the valley of death. He desires that the door of the first Paradise had remained closed so that humanity would be born and multiply in heavenly, joyful gladness.

entries.section: 2. He wonders why he did not die and go to the grave as soon as he was born

paragraphs.text: He wished he had died immediately after his birth, for he believes that this would have been better for him, for he would then be with “kings and counselors of the earth,” in rest and quiet in the grave. For death is better than life.

entries.section: 3. The song of death and its sweetness

paragraphs.text: 11 Why died I not from the womb? why did I not give up the ghost when I came out of the belly? 12 Why did the knees prevent me? or why the breasts that I should suck? 13 For now should I have lain still and been quiet, I should have slept: then had I been at rest, 14 With kings and counsellors of the earth, which built pyramids for themselves; 15 Or with princes that had gold, who filled their houses with silver: 16 Or as an hidden untimely birth I had not been; as infants which never saw light. 17 There the wicked cease from troubling; and there the weary be at rest. 18 There the prisoners are at ease together; they hear not the voice of the taskmaster. 19 The small and great are there; and the servant is free from his master.

Offering a lament, desiring that he had died in the womb, he looked at his life with its pains and calamities and found death sweet, offering a poem about death that is sweeter than temporal life, so to speak. He saw in the abyss deliverance from what he suffers on earth.

Pope Gregory (the Great) offers us at length a symbolic interpretation of the song of death and its sweetness, seeing in Job that he desired to die in the womb, that is, with his parents Adam and Eve in Paradise before going out to the world that lies in the Evil One, as we saw. And he sees in his meeting in the grave with the kings and counselors of the earth a meeting with the giants of faith and the spiritual leaders, where all rest in one eternal life, in which there is no one groaning or suffering, nor any small one envying a great one [The prisoners are at ease, they hear not the voice of the taskmaster; the small and great are there, and the servant is free from his master] (Job 3:18-19).
Why died I not from the womb?
Why did I not give up the ghost when I came out of the belly? [11]

Perhaps Job realized his mistake when he desired that his mother be endangered by his coming out stillborn before the time of his birth; he returned to correct the matter, and desired that he had been born and died immediately after coming out of his mother's womb.

Job looked at life from his birth as a curse and calamity to him, and reckoned death the greatest blessing that could have come upon him. In contrast to this the prophet Jeremiah in the midst of his bitter lament offers a hymn of thanks to God for “the gift of life,” saying: [It is of the LORD's mercies that we did not die from the womb, and were not annihilated] (Lam 3:22).

It is told in a fable that an old man was very tired from carrying something heavy, so he threw the load on the ground, and in his despair he called upon Death. When Death came and asked him what he wanted, supposing he was asking to take his soul and die, he was surprised when he said: “I beg you to help me carry my heavy load.”

Job offered us a lament in which he sings of his love of early death from the moments of his birth and praises the grave in it. It is as though death and the grave had become his intimate friends. But when the Lord Christ came by His own will and authority to death and the grave, turning it into a joyful song, it is sung not by the despairing but by those full of hope in the heavenly things, who seek fellowship in eternal glory, and who long to meet their heavenly friends, sharing with them their praises.

Through Christ Jesus the Crucified, the Giver of resurrection, we sing: “For whether we live, we live unto the Lord; and whether we die, we die unto the Lord: whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's” (Rom 14:8).

entries.section: 3. The song of death and its sweetness

paragraphs.text: Why did the knees prevent me? or why the breasts that I should suck? [12]

Pope Gregory (the Great) rejects the literal interpretation of the two verses [11-12], looking at the blessed Job who was given such lofty spiritual knowledge, and offered praises to the Judge in his depths, and cannot desire to have died by miscarriage, or immediately at his birth. Rather he sees in these two verses the righteous Job lamenting either his committing sin in the heart or practicing it in deed. He says there are four ways of committing sin in the heart, and four similar ways of committing it in deed, and he desires that it had perished in its stages before reaching its full maturity. These four stages are:
A. Its conception in the womb: this is the first stage where it begins in the heart by the presentation of the suggestion, and in deed the practice takes place secretly.

B. Its coming out of the womb or its birth: this is the second stage, where the suggestion turns into delight in the heart, and in deed it turns from secret practice into open practice before the eyes of people without shame.

C. The knees' receiving it: the third stage, where it turns from delight of the heart into inward consent and acceptance. And in deed it turns from open practice into a habit to which the sinner is enslaved.

D. Suckling from the breast: the last stage, where it turns from acceptance of sin into defense of what the sinner commits, as though he had not sinned. And in deed it turns from habit into full maturity in the practice of sin.

The four stages: sin in the heart; sin in deed. (1) Conception in the womb: the suggestion of sin; committing it secretly. (2) Coming out of the womb or its birth: delight of the heart; committing it openly without shame. (3) The support of the knees: inward consent of the heart; turning it into a habit. (4) The nourishing of the child by the breasts or suckling: defense of the error; its growth and maturity. Pope Gregory concludes this discussion by saying:
[It is fitting for us also to know that the ways (the first three stages) can be corrected easily... but the fourth (stage) cannot be corrected except with difficulty.

Thus our Savior raised the girl in the house, and the young man outside the gate, but Lazarus He raised in the tomb. For he who commits sin secretly is like a dead person laid in the house. But he who commits sin openly has been carried outside the gate, committing sin shamelessly in the open. And he who commits sin once and many times under the pressure of habit has fallen into the heap of the tomb.

And yet the Savior in His mercy restores all of these to life, for grace often shines in this case with its light upon the dead, not only through hidden sins but also upon him who practices them openly, and who falls under the pressure of habit...

But our Savior does not raise those of the fourth way to life. Truly it is hard for the one who continues in his evil habit, holding fast to the tongues of flatterers (defending the error), to be healed of the death of the soul. Of this it was said: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Lk 9:60). For the dead bury their dead.]

Thus Pope Gregory sees in the fourth stage of sin, which is the defense of the error and covering it, its arrival at maturity and the impossibility of rising from its death until the sinner confesses his sin and does not justify his error or give himself an excuse as both Adam and Eve did.
For now should I have lain still and been quiet,

entries.section: 3. The song of death and its sweetness

paragraphs.text: Then I should have slept and been at rest [13]
Pope Gregory offers us a justification for the bitterness of Job's soul. He looks at what man could have attained had sin not entered into his life. He says:

[Man was placed in Paradise, and bonds of love were attached to him that he might follow his Creator in obedience; thus he could have been transferred one day to the heavenly city of the angels even without the death of the body. For he was created immortal in a manner by which he could die if he sinned, and so become mortal. But if he had not sinned he could have remained without death, and in full freedom receive the blessedness of a world in which there is no possibility of error or of death.

Since the time of redemption the elect are sent through the death of their bodies to the very place which the first parents ought to have reached without the death of the body had they remained steadfast in what they were created. Thus man would have remained “lying down and at rest,” reaching his eternal city in rest. He would have found in it a place of rest and quiet from the tumult of human weakness...

This quiet of peace man enjoyed when he was created and received freedom of will to face his enemy. But when he submitted to him by his own will, immediately human weakness was found settled in him. For although he was created by his Creator in a state of quiet full of peace, as soon as he bowed under his enemy by his will he fell under the tumult of war. The suggestions of the flesh itself became a kind of cry against the rest of the mind, something man did not know before the disobedience, because it did not exist, and he bound himself to his sins, so that it came to serve him in matters against his will, and he suffered from the tumult of thought, as the flesh wrestles against the spirit.]

*Rejoicing in God's creation is desirable; that a person become a man (mature) receiving the image of God, this is happiness. But loitering in defiled life, and being captivated for the sake of many people, this the righteous hate.

entries.section: 3. The song of death and its sweetness

paragraphs.text: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem With kings and counsellors of the earth, which built pyramids for themselves [14]

Job reckoned death a rest with the kings of the earth and their counselors, those who wanted to immortalize their memory by building the pyramids and huge, luxurious tombs, but no one is any longer able to distinguish between their dust. The pyramids and gold and silver and all they left behind no longer represent anything.

Pope Gregory sees that the kings here are the angelic spirits who devoted their energy to serving the Creator of all beings subject to them. They are also called counselors because they give counsel to the spiritual world, where they unite us to themselves as partners with them in the Kingdom.

entries.section: 3. The song of death and its sweetness

paragraphs.text: Or with princes that had gold, who filled their houses with silver [15]

It was the custom of kings and great men to place gold and silver in their tombs as a kind of honor even after death, and perhaps lest their corpses mingle with the corpses of the poor. But death does not distinguish between great and lowly, rich and poor, master and servant. As the wise man says: [The rich and poor meet together] (Prov 22:2).
Pope Gregory sees that the princes are the leaders of the holy Church who fill their houses with the word of God, the gold refined by fire (Ps 12:6).

entries.section: 3. The song of death and its sweetness

paragraphs.text: Or as an hidden untimely birth I had not been; as infants which never saw light [16].

In the grave after the dissolution of the body there is no one who can distinguish between the dust of a king or a great man or a buried stillborn who never came out to life in the world. Job sees that the fetuses that died before seeing the light of life are in a happier rest than he is in, for he desires sleep to rest and does not find it.

Job desired sleep even as a fetus that never saw the world, and did not realize that true rest is in Christ Jesus, in whom alone we sleep, that is, are buried with Him, to rise to eternal life in surpassing glory beyond expression.

Pope Gregory sees that the buried stillborn who rest are the elect from the beginning of the world who lived before salvation and yet died to the world, those who did not have the two tablets of the Law, so they died as in the womb, and feared God through the natural law. They believed that the Intercessor was coming, so they strove as they could; they mortified themselves to pleasures, and kept the concepts which the Law had not yet recorded. This period before the Law presented us our fathers dead for this life; they were like fetuses that died in the womb.
This Pope offered us examples of the stillborn:
A. Abel: of whom we do not read that he resisted his brother when he killed him.
B. Enoch: who was commended, and walked with God and was translated.
C. Noah: who by divine judgment became the only one (with his family) alive.
D. Abraham: a pilgrim in the world, because he is the friend of God.
E. Isaac: a pilgrim with his physical eyes weak from old age, he did not see present things, but was enlightened by the spirit of prophecy, to see the things to come with extraordinary insight.

F. Jacob: in humility he fled from the wrath of his brother, and by his gentleness conquered him. He was fruitful in his offspring, and more fruitful in the riches of the Spirit, so he bound his offspring with the bonds of prophecy.

entries.section: 3. The song of death and its sweetness

paragraphs.text: There the wicked cease from troubling; and there the weary be at rest [17].

Death puts a final end to the injustice of the wicked who do not cease to resist the truth and persecute the children of God, for death ended what Herod, persecutor of the Church, did (Acts 12:1-6, 23). And death grants true rest to those who bore persecution with thanksgiving for God's sake. “Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them” (Rev 14:13). “The righteous is taken away from the evil to come. He shall enter into peace: they shall rest in their beds” (Isa 57:1-2).

* Then comes praise to death, and thanks to it, for it takes some away from evil, and others are freed from their misery, those who find in it a refuge against their evils, and those who find in it an obstacle that restrains their malice.
St. John Chrysostom The prisoners are at ease together.

entries.section: 3. The song of death and its sweetness

paragraphs.text: They hear not the voice of the taskmaster [18].
Captives often desire death to rest from humiliation. Samson preferred to die with all those who mocked him rather than live grinding “in the prison house” (Judg 16:21).
* Death abolishes everything. Not only is there no longer a possibility of supporting evil, but not even the mere sound of evil reaches the ears anymore.

entries.section: 3. The song of death and its sweetness

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom The small and great are there; and the servant is free from his master [19].
By death the taskmaster and the one under forced labor become equal, the great with the small. All lie together in the grave which makes no distinction between this one and that.

* No one can escape its authority, neither slave nor free. All human things perish with death: wealth as well as honor. The inequality in this present life is enormous. Great is the freedom after our departure there.

St. John Chrysostom * I add: “and the servant is free from his master,” for it is written: “Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin” (Jn 8:34)... In this present life the servant indeed flees from his master, but he is not free from him... But there the servant is free from his master. There is no longer any doubt there about the forgiveness of sin, when the remembrance of sin no longer condemns the soul. The soul becomes secure, so the conscience is not terrified by a sense of guilt, but rejoices in forgiveness and its enjoyment of freedom, Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Death leads to itself slaves and their masters, and there the masters are not honored more than their servants.
St. Aphrahat

entries.section: 4. The riddle of the survival of those who desire death

paragraphs.text: 20 Wherefore is light given to him that is in misery, and life unto the bitter in soul; 21 Which long for death, but it cometh not; and dig for it more than for hid treasures; 22 Which rejoice exceedingly, and are glad, when they can find the grave? 23 To a man whose way is hid from him, and whom God hath hedged in? 24 For my sighing cometh like my bread, and my roarings are poured out like the waters. 25 For I was greatly terrified, and it came upon me, and that which I dreaded came upon me. 26 I was not in safety, neither had I rest, neither was I quiet; yet trouble came.
In astonishment Job looks at those who desire death and do not find it, for God hedges them about as with a fence, that they may live a life of pain without realizing God's plan for them.

When Job found that it did not help to wish that he had not been born, or had died as soon as he was born, we see him here complaining that his life continued remaining without being cut off; he cried out because of the long period of trial. He justified his intense desire for death with the following: 1- He felt constantly weary amid his severe afflictions, which seemed as though they would continue. 2- Even in the days of his former prosperity he was always afraid of troubles, and therefore never felt at rest, and therefore said [I was not in safety, nor quiet, nor had I rest].

With the testimony of James the Apostle to Job, “Ye have heard of the patience of Job” (Jas 5:11), and with his endurance of all these trials without sinning, and with what he saw on the faces of his friends of intense sorrow for his condition, he opened his mouth to speak. He began to complain that he was born, and that he did not die when he was born, and that his life was prolonged in his affliction. He had been patient for a long time, but he could no longer bear it. For however great a man's patience, let him realize that he is weak and liable to fall. It is as though the Book warns us with the Apostle Paul: [Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall] (1 Cor 10:12).
Wherefore is light given to him that is in misery, and life unto the bitter in soul? [20]

Job complains here that his life continued and did not cease. He hastens death, welcoming its coming. Although light is a good gift, in the midst of his bitterness he reckoned this light to increase his misery. The candle of his life was given to him so that he might see the misery he was in, and it would have been better for him to have no such light.

* All the righteous are in sorrows in this life (Ps 34:19), those of whom it was said: “we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:22). [They have eaten ashes like bread, and mingled their drink with weeping] (cf. Ps 102:9). They desire to pass through the trials here, giving thanks for these means. Thus they are in sorrow like David declaring with such phrases: “All the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears” (Ps 6:6).

As for the righteous desiring death, since they [dig for it as for treasures], Elijah confirms this to me in the words: "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers" (1 Kgs 4:19).

Paul also agreed with this when the disciples at Caesarea wanted to prevent him from going up to Jerusalem, for he said: "What mean ye to weep and to break mine heart? for I am ready not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem (Acts 13:21).
Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * Those who live in pleasures dread death, but the sorrowful beseech it that they may depart quickly.
The rich dread death, and the poor desire it that they may rest from their toils.
The strong tremble when they remember it, and the sick look to it in hope that they may rest from their pains.

Father Aphrahat * When the good are afflicted with evils and the wicked with good things, this is perhaps for the benefit of the good, that they may receive punishment (discipline) here if they have sinned in anything, so that they may be freed completely from eternal judgment. And the wicked find good things here that offer them deliverance in this life, so that they may be drawn on to the full torments to come. Therefore it was said to the rich man as he burned in hell: "Son, remember that thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things, and likewise Lazarus evil things" (Lk 16:25)... The saints walk in greater dread, fearing the luxury of this world more than its dangers.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* As for rest, what do we find in the world except constant war with Satan, and a struggle in an unceasing battle against his arrows and swords?! Our war is waged against the love of money, pride, anger and vainglory, and our struggle is constant against bodily lusts and the allurements of the world.

The mind of man is besieged by the enemy on every side, and the assaults of Satan close in upon it from every quarter. With effort the mind is able to defend itself, and scarcely can it resist in every spot. If it despises the love of money, lusts rise up within it. If it overcomes lusts, vainglory springs forth. If it triumphs over vainglory, anger and pride are kindled in it, and drunkenness with wine allures it, and envy tears apart its harmony with others, and jealousy corrupts its friendships.

Thus every day the soul suffers many persecutions such as these, and great dangers such as these distress the heart; and yet the heart still rejoices to remain here so long amid the wars of Satan! Though it would have been more fitting for our longings and desires to be set on hastening to go to Christ by way of a speedy death. For the Lord Himself taught us, saying: "Verily, verily, I say unto you, That ye shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice: and ye shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy" (Jn 20:16).
Which of us does not wish to be without sorrow?!
Which of us does not long to hasten to obtain joy?!

The Lord Himself also declared the time when our sorrow would be turned into joy, saying: [But I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man taketh from you] (Jn 20:16). Since our joy lies in seeing Christ... what blindness afflicts our mind, and what folly assails us, when we love the sorrows of the world, its tribulations and its tears more than hastening toward the joy that will not be taken from us?!
* What a benefit we gain by departing from this world!

The disciples grieved when Christ announced to them that He would depart, so He said to them: "If ye loved me, ye would rejoice, because I said, I go unto the Father" (Jn 28:14), teaching us to rejoice, and not to grieve, when one of our loved ones departs from this world, truly remembering the saying of the blessed Apostle Paul: "For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain" (Phil 21:1).

We count death the greatest gain, a thing we cannot acquire by the nets of this world or reap by the sins and vices of the flesh. For by death we leave painful toils and are delivered from the poisonous fangs of Satan, to go to Christ's calling of us, rejoicing in eternal salvation.

entries.section: 4. The riddle of the survival of those who desire death

paragraphs.text: St. Cyprian the Martyr Which wait for death, but it is not, and dig for it more than for hid treasures [21]
By saying, "dig for it more than for hid treasures," he reveals his readiness to spend every possibility in searching for death as one who searches for the greatest treasure he could possess.
Job never thought of suicide, despite his seeking death at any cost, for his life is in the hand of his God; it is not for him to end it himself.
*Those who seek mortification perfectly search for it like those who dig for hidden treasures; the nearer they come to their goal, the greater zeal they show in the work.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* The death of the righteous has become a sleep; rather, it has become life.

St. Basil the Great St. Gregory of Nazianzus looked to his elder sister, St. Gorgonia, as a living model of the Christian, and was deeply moved by her, being enamored of her piety and godliness. And he showed how she prepared for death without fear, but rather longed for it:
* Gorgonia's homeland was the Jerusalem above (Heb 22:12, 23)... where Christ dwells, and with Him the assembly and church of the firstborn, who are written in heaven...

* Everything she was able to wrest from the ruler of this world she deposited in faithful places. She left nothing behind her except her body. She parted with everything for the sake of the heavenly hope. The only wealth she left to her children is the imitation of her example, and that they enjoy what she deserved.

* Here I speak of her death and what distinguished her at that time, that I may give her her due... She longed greatly for the time of her dissolution, for she knew Him who had called her, and she preferred to be with Christ more than anything else on earth (Phil 23:1).

This saint yearned to be freed from the bonds of the body and to escape the mire of this world in which we live. And what is still more excellent, she had tasted the beauty of her Beloved, Christ, for she was constantly contemplating Him.
She knew beforehand the hour of her departure from this world, which doubled her joy. It seems that God informed her of it so that she might prepare and not be disturbed then.

She spent all her life washing herself from sin and striving to attain perfection. She received the gift of continual renewal by the Holy Spirit and became steadfast in it according to the merit of her earlier life..

Nor did she neglect to supplicate for her husband too, that he might attain perfection, and God answered her petition, for she wished that everything connected with her should be in the state of perfection that God desires of us, so that nothing on her part might be lacking before Christ.
And when the end came she delivered her testament to her husband, her children and her friends, as was to be expected from such a saint who loved all.

Her last day on earth was a day of solemn celebration; and we do not say that she died full of the days of the sons of men, for this was not her wish, since she knew that those days which are according to the flesh are evil days, and are nothing but dust and mirage. Rather she was full of the days of God... And so she was set free, or rather it is better to say that she was taken to her God, or fled, or changed her dwelling, or hastily delivered up her trust.
At the time of her repose a solemn silence fell, as though her death were a kind of religious ceremony.
Her body lay as though paralyzed after the spirit had left it, motionless.

But her spiritual father, who was watching her closely during this wonderful scene, sensed her murmuring and listened stealthily, and behold, he heard her reciting the words of the Psalmist: [I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep] (Ps 8:4). Blessed is he who falls asleep with these words in his mouth.

Thus you sang, O fairest among women, and the song became reality. You entered into sweet peace after suffering, and you reposed as befits a woman beloved of God, who lived and fell asleep amid words of goodness.
How precious is your portion! It surpasses what the eye can see, amid a host of angels and heavenly powers; it is full of splendor, purity and perfection!
Beyond all this is her vision of the Holy Trinity, which is no longer beyond comprehension and perception, which were formerly limited, held captive by the body.
I hope that your spirit will accept this praise from me, as I did for my brother Caesarius. For I was careful to pronounce eulogies for my brothers.
St. Gregory of Nazianzus * Death, for those who understand it, is immortality; but for the foolish who do not understand it, it is death.
We ought not to fear this death, but to fear the perishing of the soul, which is ignorance of God. This is what truly terrifies the soul!

* It is impossible for us to escape death by any means. Since the wise truly know this, they practice the virtues and think upon the love of God, and face death without sighs or fear or tears, considering that death is inevitable on the one hand, and on the other that it frees us from the sicknesses to which we are subject in this life.

entries.section: 4. The riddle of the survival of those who desire death

paragraphs.text: St. Anthony the Great Which rejoice exceedingly, and are glad, when they can find the grave? [22].

*Thus Paul regarded those disciples as dead and as buried in the tomb of contemplation, those to whom he said: "For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God" (Col 3:3). He who seeks death rejoices when he finds the grave, for he who desires mortification rejoices all the more when he finds the rest of contemplation; for in dying to the world he hides and conceals himself in the bosom of inner love from all the disturbances of outward things.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 4. The riddle of the survival of those who desire death

paragraphs.text: To a man whose way is hid, and whom God hath hedged in [23].

He had no hope of improving his state; he saw no door of escape, nor any road to walk, since God had hedged him in, so that he became as one in his place, unable to move. As it is said in Hosea: "Behold, I will hedge up thy way with thorns, and make a wall, that she shall not find her paths" (Hos 2:6). And as Jeremiah cried out: "He hath inclosed my ways with hewn stone, he hath made my paths crooked" (Lam 3:9).

* Even death entered as a fruit of sin, and yet the loftiness of God, His tenderness and His surpassing providence turned this to the benefit of our race. What burden does death carry, tell me? Is it not a freedom from troubles? Is not death a freedom from cares? Do you not hear Job praising it in the words: Death is a help for man, a hidden way.

St. John Chrysostom * "Whose way is hid" means that he will not know when or by what means his departure from here will be. For God hides this knowledge from him; that is, He does not permit him to know, so that men may await death all their days. And thus they prepare. God hides this for our great benefit, to give us the opportunity to fulfill what He commanded His disciples: "Watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come" (Mt 42:24).
Father Hesychius of Jerusalem *Dear beloved brethren... We must take into consideration that we are looking forward until God wills for us to leave the world, for we now live as guests and strangers.
Let us love the day appointed for us, on which we are freed from the snares of the world and return to Paradise and the Kingdom...

For what man placed in a foreign land does not wish to hasten his return to his own country? And which of those who hasten to return (by sea) to their friends does not long for a fair wind so that they may quickly meet those who are dear to them?!

We look to Paradise as our homeland... and to the Fathers (the Patriarchs) as our fathers; why then do we not hasten, nay run, to behold our city and greet our fathers?! For we have very many dear ones waiting for us. Therefore what happiness will flood us and them when we gather together?!
What joy there is in the heavenly Kingdom, where we no longer fear death?! And what sweet, lasting happiness in eternal life?!

There is the glorious fellowship with the Apostles; there is the choir of the rejoicing prophets; there are the countless multitudes of martyrs, crowned with victory in their struggle against the passions; there are the triumphant multitudes of virgins who conquered the lusts of the flesh by their chastity... there are the merciful, crowned, those who wrought righteousness by feeding the poor and helping them, and who kept the commandments of the Lord and turned their earthly possessions into heavenly treasures.
Then let us hasten to these beloved brethren with great longing. May we desire to be with them and hasten to come to Christ.

May God look upon our great longing, and may Christ the Lord look upon the aim of our mind and our faith, He who gives the great reward that is for His glory to those who have a great desire to honor Him.

entries.section: 4. The riddle of the survival of those who desire death

paragraphs.text: St. Cyprian the Martyr For my groaning comes like my bread, and like the waters my sighing is poured out [24]

Job's groaning became the necessary daily bread, without which he cannot live. His sorrows recur regularly, as if they were meals on which he feeds. His sighs became like a full river overflowing with sorrows without ceasing.

* If all creation is to be dissolved and the fashion of this world is to change, why should we marvel, being part of creation, that we feel a severe, general pain and are given over to sorrows that our God allows to come upon us according to the measure of our strength, and He does not suffer us to be tempted above that we are able, but with the temptation gives the way out, that we may be able to bear it?

* The Lord commands: [All things have measures and weights] (Wis 11:21), and He brings upon us trials that do not exceed our power of endurance; rather He tries with sorrow all who fight on the way of true religion, and does not allow them to be tried beyond what they can bear. He gives tears to drink in great measure (Ps 80:5) to all who ought to show that in the midst of their sorrows they keep their thanks to Him.
* I am convinced that if there is a voice that moves the good God, He will not make His mercy far off, but will give with the temptation the way out, that you may be able to bear it.

entries.section: 4. The riddle of the survival of those who desire death

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great For I greatly feared a fear and it came to me, and that which I dreaded came upon me [25].
It seems that in the days of his prosperity he feared that disasters would befall him, so he says: "I greatly feared a fear and it came to me, and that which I dreaded came upon me" [25].

* As long as I am here, as long as I am in this world, as long as I bear a mortal body, as long as I sigh amid the maladies of disobedience, as long as, while standing, I am "in fear lest I fall," as long as my goodness and my evils are threatened with instability, the whole life of man together is vanity.

St. Augustine * If the hope of Christians were confined to the limits of this life, our lot would truly be bitter, for it would be confined in the body before the time (the time of eternity); but if they have the love of God and their souls withdraw from the bonds of the body, they count that the beginning of true life. Why then do you grieve like those who have no hope? So take your rest and do not fall under your troubles, but show yourself higher than the troubles and exalted above them.
* Beloved, is the trial hard? Let us endure hardships, for no one who avoids the spears and the dust of the battle wins the crown. Is the enemy deceiving you, and is his war without profit...?

* These trials are wearying, because they serve the Lord. They are weak, because the Lord has mingled their evil with weakness. But let us beware of crying out loudly because of a little pain. By this we would be condemned. For you deprive yourselves of the eternal reward given to the righteous.

You are the sons of those who confessed Christ. You are the sons of the martyrs. They resisted unto blood against sin. Therefore keep such examples near and dear to you, that you may become courageous for the sake of your Christianity.

None among us has had his flesh cut by the lash... None of us has suffered the confiscation of his dwelling... We have not been driven into exile, we have not been imprisoned... Then how great is the suffering we have endured?... In truth perhaps we should regard the source of our pain as being that we have suffered nothing, and that we are unworthy of the sufferings of Christ.

entries.section: 4. The riddle of the survival of those who desire death

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great I was not at ease, nor did I dwell, nor did I rest, and the wrath (anger) has come [26].

He goes back in memory to before the trial to see that he was not at ease, for he feared that a disaster would befall him; yet this did not drive him to complacency or idleness, but he worked watchfully with earnestness.

* The unwary man who enjoys prosperity, rules over his enemies, and is praised and admired by them, needs pity more than any other man. In truth, since he expects no change, he cannot face even the problems of prosperity with propriety. So when hard times come upon him he is confused and discouraged because of his lack of caution and because he is impractical. Job, on the contrary, was not like this; even in his prosperity he expected hard times every day... Another says: "In the time of plenty think of the time of hunger: and in the days of riches think upon poverty and need." (Sir 18:25).

St. John Chrysostom * What Job grieved over was not the things his friends imagined; rather his soul was in another dread, not knowing whether the enemy was robbing him of his inner wealth, whether he had been able to plunder from him the good things, a stripping that is counted the greatest calamity. For this Job testified openly: [I was not at ease, nor did I dwell, nor did I rest, and the wrath has come upon me] [26]. He did not know peace, for he was troubled because of his children. [He was not in tranquility (quietness)], since he offered sacrifices for them every day (Job 5:1). The wrath (indignation) came upon him, for he lost his sons at one time, and his wealth and his bodily health. For even when the righteous man is very righteous, if he is pleasing to God in all things, it is impossible for him to live without coming to know the trials in this world (Jas 2:1). He cannot exist without knowing the sorrow of this world, even as the Lord said to His apostles (Jn 6:16-22). Paul himself says: "Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution" (2 Tim 12:3).. And Christ for His part said: "Be of good cheer; I have overcome the world" (Jn 33:16). Again He said: [He that endureth to the end shall live] (cf. Mt 22:10; 23:24), by the power of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem The desire for death no longer arises from fleeing tribulation and trials. For the true Christian, as a living member joined to the Head, Jesus Christ, receives the marks of the crucified Christ who accepted death by His own will, and so loves suffering, seeks it and desires it even unto death, not for the sake of suffering in itself, nor as an escape from the world, but because it is the sign of the fellowship of true love and the union between the suffering, crucified Bridegroom and His bride. Thus the cross, with suffering as with death, for the true believer has gone forth from being the sign of sin and the indication of man's veiling and deprivation from God, the source of happiness, to become a sign of love and fellowship. So the Apostle Paul says: "Always bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus" (2 Cor 10:4). And he affirms that these are the sufferings of Christ: "For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our consolation also aboundeth by Christ" (2 Cor 5:1).
* When He stretched out His hands on the cross He cast down the prince of the power of the air, that worketh in the children of disobedience (Eph 2:2), preparing for us the way to the heavens.
* When His body was lifted up on high, the things that are in heaven appeared.

* After the bodily resurrection of our Savior, there was no longer any reason to fear death. Those who believe in Christ trample on death as if it were nothing, preferring rather to die than to deny faith in Christ. For they are convinced that death does not mean destruction but life; through the resurrection they become incorruptible...

The clear proof of this is that before faith in Christ people looked on death as a terrifying matter, as something that made them cowards. But as soon as they received the faith and the teaching of Christ, they on the contrary came to count death a small thing which they trample on, and which makes them witnesses to the resurrection which the Savior accomplished against death.
St. Athanasius the Apostolic * After Christ came and died for the life of the world, death is no longer called death but sleep and repose.

* Do you not know how the cross has set right many errors? Did it not shatter death, wipe out sin, end the power of Satan, and satisfy the being of our good body? Has it not set right the whole world, and yet you do not trust in it?

*Who can utter the mighty acts of the LORD? (Ps 2:105) Out of death we have become immortal; have you understood the victory and the way it was reached? Learn how this victory was won without toil and sweat. Our weapons were not stained with blood, nor did we stand in the battle line, nor were we wounded, nor did we see the battle, yet we have won the battle. The struggle is that of our Christ, and the crown of victory is ours.

Since the victory is ours, it befits us as soldiers to chant today with joyful voices the hymns of victory. Let us praise our Lord, saying: [Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is thy victory? O grave, where is thy sting?] (1 Cor 54:15-55).
St. John Chrysostom
Let me die, that I may live with You!
* I see in every newborn child a living image of my own birth; he is born to cry out as he enters the world, as though he had come out into the valley of tears!
Who of mankind does not bear a yoke?
Righteous Job cursed the day of his birth, and Jeremiah cried out: "Woe is me, my mother, that thou hast borne me."
And the Psalmist groans, saying: [Wherefore hast thou made all men in vain?] (b)
If these were the cries of godly men of God, then what shall I say? And with what shall I speak?
* We were driven out of the joyful Paradise, and became as those in the darkness of a night that does not pass.
Our hope has been cut off that the light of day will dawn upon us.
Our days have become full of groaning.
We often cry out with righteous Job:
Why did we not die while still in the womb?
Why did we not give up the ghost as soon as we were born?
* Thank You, O wondrous Sun of Righteousness!
You rose upon those sitting in darkness.
Nay, You came down to our earth and shared our sufferings.
Now, while You Yourself are tempted, You help those who are tempted!
Let me bear the cross, since You have borne it!
Let me accept shame, and be cast out of the camp, that I may find You there crucified between two thieves, numbered among the transgressors, You who alone are the Holy One!
Sufferings delight me as long as You are with me, and the tomb becomes heaven for me, since You have dwelt in it!
* Let me die, that I may live with You.
Now in You my soul rests!
You are my happiness and the joy of my heart.
You are my joy, my peace and my treasure!
You are everything to me.

entries.section: 1. His asking Job's permission to speak

paragraphs.text: 1 Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: 2 "If one test a word with thee, wilt thou be offended? But who can refrain from speaking?
Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered: [1]

This introduction reveals that the three friends had conferred together and agreed to confront Job in a serious manner, for they supposed that he had deceived them and the people by the piety, worship and giving to others that he displayed. And that his outward appearance hid secret evils that no one knows but God.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem says that Eliphaz spoke to Job without shame, in an unbecoming spirit, as one who wished to overthrow this firm, strong and established tower. He observed that Job opened his mouth (Job 3:1), while Eliphaz answered (Job 4:1). The first spoke in innocence; he opened his mouth to utter words so that he might find in his friends comfort for what had befallen him; but Eliphaz answered as one who carried within him, he and his friends, a bitter struggle, desiring to crush him. Eliphaz's words came as an answer to questions in his own soul and a revolt within him!
If one test a word with thee, wilt thou be offended?

entries.section: 1. His asking Job's permission to speak

paragraphs.text: But who can refrain from speaking! [2]

It seems that the friends, despite their silence, carried within them a suppressed boiling in their hearts. They look at Job on the dunghill not with eyes of pity but with intense vexation that he had deceived them and all those around him; but the deception could not last, for God exposed him for his evils and his deceit.

When Job opened his mouth and murmured, they supposed that he had gone far beyond bounds, and they could keep silent no longer. They had endured him all week while he was silent, and had endured his deception. Now that he has murmured and cursed the day of his birth they regard themselves as men of God, defenders of God's justice and righteousness!
They supposed that Job's murmuring and his questions contained an insult to God's justice, so they had to answer his questions firmly.

He begins his speech by saying: If someone examines the matter and speaks to you a frank word, will you be offended? But even if you are offended, we cannot keep silent. He seems, like one in politeness and modesty, to ask permission for everyone to speak with him. And frankly he tells him that, although they feel his pains, they cannot flatter or cajole him. Perhaps Eliphaz wanted to ask Job not to misunderstand them and think that they are harsh with him, or that they do not care about what he suffers; they do not wish to add sorrows to his sorrows, but to find the right door for remedying the situation.
* By the words he utters, Eliphaz strikes as with a trumpet to proclaim war against Job.
Father Hesychius of Jerusalem *Not everyone is able to know how to minister to those in such trials. Many often add pains to pain, some through baseness, others through folly.

It is clear that those who undertook to offer words of comfort were inexperienced in this matter, like physicians who increase wounds. Therefore they rightly deserved to be called by Job evil physicians (cf. Job 13:4), those who inflamed the wound out of the spite within them.

It is a kind of baseness to show spite with a violent outburst, and to envy a man who was cast down on the ground, and to throw him into countless difficulties, one who deserved to be treated with gentleness.

Observe how their words were not only devoid of comfort but caused grave discouragement. They stirred up long discussions with renewed accusations.. Hence it was said: [Add not more troubles to a distressed heart] (Sir 4:3).

St. John Chrysostom The Septuagint reads: "Wilt thou speak much in grief?" St. John Chrysostom sees that "grief" here means "sin," as if he were saying to him: [Under thy tongue is toil and pain] (cf. Ps 10:7).

*Eliphaz did not say: Do you commit evil deeds? but said: "Will you speak?" because the fame of his life was radiant throughout the length and breadth of the earth, for everywhere there were testimonies to his virtue. He did not say to him: Do not say that your works are good, for sin sometimes springs from words.

*"Who can bear the violence of thy words?" (Septuagint)... What did Job say? He besought death and deliverance from the present life. Did he say: "So many evils have overtaken me despite my righteousness and my great virtues"? No, but he said this: I long to disappear with the wicked, with my servants, with the stillborn, that I may obtain the same as the wicked obtained. He did not say: I, who have such traits and such importance.
St. John Chrysostom
3 Behold, thou hast instructed many, and hast strengthened slack hands. 4 Thy words have raised up him that stumbled, and thou hast established the trembling knees!

Eliphaz began by praising Job for his teaching, his guidance and his giving to many, and he had to begin thus, because Job's practical life bears witness to this. On the one hand he wanted to show that he is a just man who does not distort reality, and on the other he wanted to use this praise to attack Job as a vain man.
At any rate, Eliphaz's words revealed to us Job's character as a living leader who bears a spirit of fatherhood in his concern to guide many, and in his generosity in giving.
Behold, thou hast instructed many, and hast strengthened slack hands [3].

He praises him as a practical teacher and guide, for he taught many and strengthened the slack hands so that they might work and serve. But he is as one saying to him: If you strengthened others with your wealth, why can you not strengthen yourself?

* Let us contemplate the towering height the man attained by guiding the ignorant, supporting the weak, and strengthening the slack, and this amid the cares of his house, his many obligations, his anxiety for his children, and the oversight of many affairs; for he had devoted himself to setting others on the straight path. But all heretics and wicked men, when they record the loftiness of the good, turn this loftiness into accusations.. Thus (Eliphaz) seeks an opportunity to revile the blessed Job from the very angle from which he recounts things praised in him.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Thanks be to Eliphaz who, though out of malice and not out of love, presented to us a wonderful aspect of Job's character. For as a king or ruler or chief of a tribe he was not a man who loved authority, commanding and forbidding, but in fatherhood he guided, advised and strengthened the slack hands.

For there are many guides, but they do not support the weak, nor do they bear a spirit of fatherhood. St. Paul says: "For though ye have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel" (1 Cor 15:4). The true spiritual guide bears the spirit of truth, the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of love, of whom the Lord Christ says: "Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth" (Jn 13:16). He who bears the spirit of truth offers practical help along with guidance, strengthening the slack hands, as the Apostle says: "comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men" (1 Thess 14:5).

St. Augustine sees that this is the way of him who offers the remedy to the citizens of the city of God during their journey on earth, that the Holy Spirit may work, granting healing to the sick souls so that they may enjoy reaching the heavenly homeland.

* If we hate the wicked and the disobedient, then we hate sinners. Thus, consequently, you will find that you have cut yourself off from most of your brethren, in truth from all, for there is no one without sin.
If we must hate the enemies of God as worse than ravening beasts, then we shall scorn everyone and swell with pride like the Pharisee.
