Paul commands us otherwise: "warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men" (1 Thess 5:14).

*"Though ye have ten thousand instructors... yet have ye not many fathers" (1 Cor 15:4)... Paul does not seek any honor here, but rather shows the depth of his love. Honor belongs to the instructor, and love is the mark of the father.
St. John Chrysostom Thy words have raised up him that stumbled, and thou hast established the trembling knees [4].

How much Job strengthened the slack hands for fitting work, took the hands of the stumbling and raised them from the dust, and strengthened their knees to bear them to walk in the way of life by the power of God. So Eliphaz praised him, so that when he rebuked him Job might not think that he was prejudiced against him, or ignoring his past with all its good deeds. Job comforted many, so he deserves to find one who comforts him.
Some commentators see that Eliphaz mentioned this to rebuke Job, as if saying to him:
[You who guided many, why do you not guide yourself?
And you strengthened slack hands, why did you not find rest for your weakness?
And if you helped the stumbling with words, why are you cast down on the ground in your body as in your soul?
If you established the trembling knees, why did you not encourage yourself, but are broken down before the diseases that have come upon you, walking as though paralyzed?

Is this not proof of your hypocrisy, that you offer the medicine to others and refuse to receive it yourself for healing of your sickness? You who taught others not to break down, do you break down? "Physician, heal thyself" (Lk 4:23).
See, your former talk was perhaps vain, and the good that you did contains folly!]
* Our neglect of our brethren is no light fault, but brings upon us great punishment and chastisement without mercy...
Persistent counsel and teaching make a man diligent and bring him to a better state, and in this I cite the common proverb that confirms this truth, that "constant drops of water split the rock."
What is softer than water?! And what is harder than rock?! Yet persistence in work continually overcomes nature. If this is so with nature, shall not human nature all the more be overcome...?!
What a large part of the body of the Church resembles the dead, without movement!!
You say: And what concerns us in this?

You have a very great capacity with regard to your brethren. For you are responsible if you do not counsel them, and ward off evil from them, and draw them here with power, and pull them out of their extreme slackness. For is it fitting for a man to be profitable to himself alone, and not profitable to himself and to many as well?
The Lord Christ made this clear when He called us [salt] (Mt 5:13), and "leaven" (Mt 13:33), and [light] (Mt 5:14), for these things are useful and beneficial to others.

For the lamp does not shine for itself but for those sitting in darkness. And you are a lamp, not to enjoy the light alone, but to bring back a man who has gone astray; for what benefit is a Christian who does not benefit others?! and who does not bring anyone back to virtue?!

Again, salt does not season itself but seasons food lest it spoil and perish... So God has made you spiritual salt, to bind together the corrupt members, that is, the lazy, slack brethren, and to strengthen them and rescue them from sloth as from corruption, and to bind them with the rest of the body of the Church.

And this is the reason why the Lord called us "leaven," for leaven too does not leaven itself, but though small it leavens the whole lump, however great. So do you also. For though you are few in number, be many and strong in faith and zeal toward God. And as leaven is not weak because of its smallness, since it has power and capacity by its nature... so you can, if you wish, draw to yourselves greater numbers than you, and they will have the same level of zeal...

For this reason do not gather here in vain. Rather I do not cease to beseech you with all zeal, as I used to do before, saying: "Come here with your brethren. Guide here. Guide the erring. Teach them by deeds, not by words only"...

May the God of peace and love, who removes from our spirits all rancor, bitterness and anger, condescend and grant us - through our being joined to one another in perfect unity as the members are joined to one another (Eph 4:16) - to offer Him with one accord, one mouth and one spirit the praise of our due thanksgiving.

St. John Chrysostom If we ignore Eliphaz's intention, we find a living testimony to a godly man who did not belong to Isaac the son of Abraham, a king and not a priest of any people, and yet he set in his godly heart the support of the stumbling and the strengthening of the trembling knees. He will judge many of God's servants and priests in the Old Testament as in the New. For there is no pastoral work greater than bending down toward those fallen to the ground to take their hands and rise with them. If the divine Word became incarnate and came down to our earth in humility, and carried us in Himself up to heaven, so it befits every servant, indeed every believer, to support and help so that all may enjoy fellowship with God.

By setting forth Job's traits, Eliphaz presented us with a living method of pastoral care, indeed of the life of faith, and of how every believer cares for the life of his brother through love, without ignoring his concern for the salvation of his own soul and the salvation of his household.

entries.section: 3. His rebuke for his lack of steadfastness

paragraphs.text: 5 But now it is come upon thee, and thou faintest; it toucheth thee, and thou art troubled. 6 Is not thy piety thy confidence, and thy hope the perfection of thy ways?
But now it is come upon thee, and thou faintest!
It toucheth thee, and thou art troubled! [5]

Eliphaz rebukes Job, saying to him that when his turn came to drink the cup of affliction he collapsed, fainted and was terrified. Here begins the attack to accuse him of hypocrisy. As if he were saying to him: When you were in prosperity you taught well, but when you fell into what others fall into, your weakness was exposed and your patience ran out.

* Minds fond of disputation attack the lives of the righteous in two ways: either by asserting that what they utter is wrong, or that they utter the truth which they do not observe in their conduct. Thus the blessed Job was rebuked by his friends over his manner of speaking. They encourage him because he speaks true things, but he does not keep them himself... Observe how they first praised him for his tongue, then complained of the weakness of his life. For the wicked, so as not to show themselves as wicked, sometimes say good things about the righteous, knowing that others know this about them.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

St. John Chrysostom justifies Job's distress and behavior, for it is a natural reaction to the multitude and severity of the calamities and the suddenness of their occurrence, besides the behavior of his friends and their provocative accusations against him.
We cannot ignore that it befits the leader, being in the position of leader, guide and father, not to be quickly disturbed before trials, so as to be a secret of strength and comfort for others.

* No one does more harm to the Church than those who have the appearance and title of holiness yet behave corruptly. And it is a grave error to entrust the place of pastoral care to a deficient person, since pastoral care is an example. A wrong choice of shepherd results in grave consequences, for while in sin he receives honor on account of the position he has taken. Let every unworthy man flee from the weight of this great iniquity and ponder, listening with the ears of his heart to this voice that says: "But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea" (Mt 18:6; Lk 17:2). Here the millstone signifies the whirlpool of life, and the depth of the sea points to eternal perdition. It is far better that a lay person who by himself put on the garment of holiness in outward show should perish alone than that this man should put on himself the garment of pastoral care and destroy others by his wicked example. And I am sure that the punishment of hell will be lighter if this man falls into it alone without being the cause of others' falling with him.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Although a man may keep himself pure from sin, even in lofty degrees, yet I know that one in this condition cannot lead others to virtue. For he who has received the care of a people, it is not enough for him to be free of sin... but he must rise in doing good, as the commandment says: "Depart from evil, and do good" (Ps 37:27).
So he must not only have the traces of vice wiped from his spirit, but also be furnished with virtues, so that he may surpass them in virtue rather more than his loftiness over them in honor.
He must know no limits to doing good or to spiritual growth, nor think it a great gain merely to excel over ordinary people.

He must not measure himself against others, whether wicked or somewhat advanced spiritually, but measure himself by the light of the commandments. Nor should he measure virtue on a small scale, since it flows from God the Greater, for "of him, and through him, and to him, are all things" (Rom 11:36).

entries.section: 3. His rebuke for his lack of steadfastness

paragraphs.text: St. Gregory of Nazianzus Is not thy piety thy confidence, and thy hope the perfection of thy ways? [6]

Here he rebukes him for the piety he showed during his prosperity: where is this piety? And where is your hope and the uprightness of your way? Are not all these vain pretensions with no roots in your depths?

Eliphaz carried out Satan's work and served his interests, for he wanted to stir Job up to blaspheme God by accusing him of hypocrisy, and that this piety, hope and uprightness of his were all vain appearances.

*"Is not thy piety founded on folly, and also thy hope and the perfection of thy way?" (LXX) By this he seeks to distort his former virtuous deeds... He is stabbing at Job's intention while he works. He means either that you did not work, or that your life is full of deceit, or that you did not fear God with an upright intention, but it was all mere talk. Your hope is without reason, it is full of folly... If your deeds were sincere and your life pure, you would not fear these evils...
You see how Eliphaz attacks him, wrestles with him, and makes every effort to prove that his folly brought these troubles upon him...

"By the commandments of the Lord they are destroyed" (9 LXX). Observe another thing.. He says: Do not think that demons and wicked men full of spite are responsible for what has befallen you. For God is chastening you, therefore the chastening is just, beyond dispute.

St. John Chrysostom Pope Gregory (the Great) comments on this phrase: [Where is your fear (piety), your strength, your patience, and the perfection of your ways?] that although he reviled him unjustly, he described precisely the ordering of the virtues and their ladder or degrees, which are the fear of the Lord, then trust in God, then patience, and finally the attainment of perfection:
a. The fear of the Lord, or piety, is the beginning of the way. "In the fear of the LORD is strong confidence" (Prov 14:26).
* Let us not count wealth a very good thing; for the great good is not to possess money, but to acquire the fear of the Lord and all the paths of godliness.
* Fear is no less than a wall, a protection and a mighty tower.
St. John Chrysostom b. Through the fear of the Lord we pass to strength, or "strong confidence in God," which appears only in trial.

* The fear of the Lord contains all those requirements (for continual joy). For the man who fears the Lord as is fitting, and trusts in Him, gathers all the sources of happiness and acquires the perfect fountain of delight. Just as a drop of water falling into a wide ocean quickly vanishes, so whatever befalls him who fears the Lord is dissipated and vanishes in the vast ocean of joy.

It is truly most wonderful that, even with causes of sorrow present, you find the man rejoicing. For since there is nothing at all that brings sorrow, this bitterness is of no value to him compared with his enjoyment of continual joy.

St. John Chrysostom c. Through trust in the Lord the believer enjoys patience. For a man is approved, in the true sense of the word, and grows in strength by bearing the faults of others. He who cannot face his opponent is wounded by the sword of cowardice.

* For four days we have been occupied in explaining the parable of Lazarus (and the rich man), presenting the treasure we find in a body covered with sores. A treasure not of gold and silver, but of wisdom and endurance, of patience and forbearance.
St. John Chrysostom d. Patience leads to perfection. For a man is truly perfect when he is long-suffering toward the weaknesses of others. [In your patience possess ye your souls] (Lk 21:19).

This is the ladder of perfection: the fear of the Lord and piety toward Him give us confidence in Him, and this gives us strength amid trials, this strength gives us patience in bearing others with their weaknesses, and by this patience we reach the ways of perfection.

* There are two forms of perfection, an ordinary one and a higher. One is acquired here, the other hereafter. One is according to human capacities, the other belongs to the perfection of the world to come; but God is just through all, wise above all, perfect in all.

St. Ambrose * The Apostle speaks of himself as perfect and imperfect. He counts himself imperfect, looking at how much righteousness he still lacks, yet perfect in that he is not ashamed to confess his imperfection and that he is advancing to attain perfection.
St. Augustine

7 Remember: who ever perished, being innocent? and where were the upright destroyed? 8 Even as I have seen, they that plow iniquity, and sow wickedness, reap the same. 9 By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his nostril are they consumed. 10 The roaring of the lion, and the voice of the roarer, and the teeth of the young lions, are broken. 11 The lion perisheth for lack of prey, and the whelps of the lioness are scattered abroad.
Remember: who ever perished, being innocent? and where were the upright destroyed? [7]

Eliphaz presents a practical proof of the accusation he directed at him. For - in Eliphaz's opinion - no righteous man has perished, and no upright man has been destroyed. He asks him for a single example, from Job's long experience throughout his whole life, of a righteous or upright man who suffered what Job has suffered.

This is a theological, moral principle that prevailed in many minds, for even after the Law David was astonished, reproaching the Lord, how the way of the wicked prospers and He allows afflictions to the righteous. But he soon discovers the truth, for the righteous will surely receive their heavenly reward, and the wicked who persist in their evil will fall under judgment. The Psalmist says: "Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity. For they shall soon be cut down like the grass, and wither as the green herb... I have seen the wicked in great power, and spreading himself like a green bay tree. Yet he passed away, and, lo, he was not: yea, I sought him, but he could not be found... But the salvation of the righteous is of the LORD: he is their strength in the time of trouble" (Ps 37).

Eliphaz's speech is true if by perishing and destruction he meant what is eternal, but to apply it to temporal calamities is not correct. Therefore his speech does not apply to Job, for he had not perished eternally.

The prophet says: "The righteous perisheth" (Isa 57:1). And the Wise Man says: "There is one event to the righteous and to the wicked" (Eccl 9:2), until temporal life ends and on the day of the Lord this one is separated from that.

* [What innocent man perishes? and where do the upright perish?] But it often happens in this life that the innocent perishes and the upright are utterly destroyed, yet in their perishing they are kept for eternal glory. If no innocent man perished, the prophet would not have said: "The righteous perisheth, and no man layeth it to heart" (Isa 57:1). If God in His providence did not destroy the upright, Wisdom would not have said of the righteous: [Yea, quickly was he taken away, lest wickedness should alter his understanding] (Wis 4:11).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* The wicked, unbelieving man, even if we suppose that he wraps himself in a heavenly body, remains naked because he does nothing to obtain the garment of the inner man.

St. Didymus the Blind * How beneficial are the trials and sufferings which some consider evil! The saints do not try to avoid them, but truly seek them with all their strength, enduring them courageously, and thus become friends of God, and obtain the crown of eternal life... And the blessed Apostle exults, saying: [I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ's sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong] (2 Cor 12:10).
Father Theodore Even as I have seen, they that plow iniquity and sow wickedness reap the same [8].
Eliphaz relies in his arguments on two main factors: his personal experience and observations: "as I have seen" [8], and "visions of the night" [13 etc.].

Eliphaz thought that through his observations he was presenting an exact theory, for he found through his statistics that calamities befall the wicked in proportion to their wickedness, that is, justly; but Job refuted this theory (Job 17:21 etc.).

It seems that Eliphaz did not react to the severity of the affliction that had befallen Job, and supposed that what befell him were light pains proportionate to his hidden wickedness, while his grave evil was his excess in murmuring against God.
Thus Eliphaz was hoping that Job would repent of his hidden evils so that the afflictions would be removed from him; but his cursing the day of his birth, this is what utterly crushes him!

This is fulfilled daily, for "whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap" (b), as the Apostle Paul wrote: "Seeing it is a righteous thing with God to recompense tribulation to them that trouble you" (2 Thess 1:6). And it is said: "He that leadeth into captivity shall go into captivity: he that killeth with the sword must be killed with the sword" (Rev 13:10). But God in His longsuffering waits for the repentance of the wicked, and in His love allows affliction to the righteous so that they may be approved.
Job's friends were pressing him, those who had come to comfort him! And like enemies they were troubling him with bitter words.

* The only comfort for those who find themselves in misery and grief is to be cleared of guilt, lest they appear to have borne their pains and misfortunes as punishment for sin. But his friends seemed to be trying to take away even this comfort from the holy Job, so that he would appear to be the cause of his own misery, as one who brought down the Lord's wrath by his grave iniquities, and that he endures these afflictions as the price of his wicked deeds! And they described the punishments of the wicked (cf. Job 8:4-9), who planted vices and reaped sorrows for themselves! These perished at God's command, for they were consumed by the breath of His wrath, which blew upon those dwelling in houses of clay, and they withered (cf. Job 19:4, 21) LXX, and God frustrates the plans of the crafty and shuts the mouth of the wicked (cf. Job 13:5, 16) LXX; and what the friends alleged was true as regards the power of the Lord, but untrue as regards the merits of that great righteous man.
St. Ambrose By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his nostril are they consumed [9].

All that the wicked devise and plan perishes by a breath from God, and all their wicked schemes fail. This is true: God is longsuffering with the wicked as He was longsuffering with Pharaoh of Egypt in the days of Moses the prophet, but when the cup of their evil is full He destroys them, that the rod of the wicked may not rest upon the righteous; so He destroyed Pharaoh and his army in the Red Sea. This does not apply to Job, because what befell him was for his approval and not for his destruction.

Eliphaz wanted to terrify Job that the bitter calamities that had befallen him were only the beginning, and that if he did not confess his hidden evils and put away his pride, his fate would be destruction and annihilation.

*(As if Eliphaz accuses him thus:) You are not as you suppose yourself to be in your pride, for you seek by deceit to make others consider you so. See what you have really done, as is plain from the corruption of your body. Your offspring also perished, and the best of your wealth, and all your property, and the crown of your inheritance. For in truth you are not pure, and in truth it is as you suppose. What a sick man you are in this matter... for it is not unjustly and without cause that these calamities have swallowed you up, but they are in harmony with justice, since God aimed them at you.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem At any rate, if both the righteous and the wicked are exposed to trials and afflictions, the soul of the former exults within him amid the sufferings because he receives the afflictions from the hands of God for his purification and approval. But the wicked groans within, and finds himself as one fallen into a net, and he may examine himself and return to the Lord his Savior, or may persist in folly and distress in his evil, and so fall into bitterness in this world as in the age to come.

*"The LORD trieth the righteous: but the wicked and him that loveth violence his soul hateth" (Ps 5:11)... He approves His righteous by testing them, but the wicked He hates. His soul loathes the wicked who love injustice...

He is the Judge of the righteous and the wicked; the wicked are judged because by their love of injustice they hate themselves... And as Solomon says in Proverbs: "He that refuseth instruction despiseth his own soul" (Prov 32:15). If he who loves injustice despises himself, then he who loves righteousness loves himself; and this agrees with the proverb: [He that getteth wisdom loveth his own soul] (cf. Prov 8:19)...

"Upon the wicked he shall rain snares" (Ps 6:11). Without doubt, for it is the Lord who sets snares for the sinners themselves, to catch those who have corrupted their freedom and must walk the straight way under His bridle, so He gives them the possibility of advancing through Him who said: "I am the way" (Jn 6:14).

*"How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts!" (Ps 1:84), in which a man's dwelling is changed from earth to heaven... The mind and heart filled with longing for the Lord's dwelling are fruitful and happy! When death comes upon the sinner, his thought is found occupied not with this dwelling but with punishments. He does not meditate on the Kingdom of Heaven, but on the terror of the flames of hell.

* [The ungodly are like the dust which the wind driveth away] (Ps 4:1). Scripture says that the wicked man will be wretched, not even like the dust of the earth. For dust seems to have no being, yet it surely has a kind of existence in itself... It is scattered here and there and has no single place, but the wind sweeps it away, and it has no power to resist. The same is true of the wicked. As soon as he denies God, the breath of Satan sweeps him away in error and throws him wherever it wishes.
* Wretched is the man who has masks of evil, and happy is the man who has many masks of goodness.
St. Jerome The roaring of the lion, and the voice of the roarer, and the teeth of the young lions, are broken [10].

He likens the unjust and cruel persecutors to roaring, howling lions. Through divine justice the sound of their roaring ceases, and their voice no longer terrifies in the wilderness or the forests. And their teeth are broken so that they cannot tear, that is, God takes their weapons from them, and they are no longer able to prey [11], so they die of hunger and leave no cubs to succeed them.

Perhaps Eliphaz wanted to accuse Job indirectly, declaring to him that he had been like a ravening lion, with none in the region who could stand before his might. His words were like the roar of the fearful lion, plundering and devouring in injustice and tyranny. But behold his might has vanished, his wealth is scattered and his family is lost, and not one son is left him like a cub to occupy his place.
Thus Eliphaz turned from praise to blame.
The lion perisheth for lack of prey, and the whelps of the lioness are scattered abroad [11].
*It is easier for a lion to be cowardly than for the righteous man to walk an easy life.

St. John Chrysostom * Eliphaz compares Job to a lion because of his kingly power, but he rightly adds: "the roar of the lioness" (Septuagint), alluding to the greatness of Job's virtue. He also added "the arrogance of dragons" since he wished to speak of his spirit, calling this beast (the dragon) king among reptiles. At any rate Eliphaz says that all this is broken; it tramples on the sufferings of the righteous...
Father Hesychius of Jerusalem

entries.section: 5. Supporting his opinion with a vision

paragraphs.text: 12 "Now a word was secretly brought to me, and mine ear received a murmur thereof. 13 In thoughts from the visions of the night, when deep sleep falleth on men, 14 fear and trembling came upon me, and all my bones shook. 15 Then a spirit passed before my face; the hair of my flesh stood up. 16 It stood still, but I could not discern the form thereof: an image was before mine eyes. I heard a low voice: 17 Shall man be more just than God? shall a man be more pure than his maker? 18 Behold, he putteth no trust in his servants, and his angels he chargeth with folly: 19 how much more them that dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, and who are crushed like the moth? 20 Between morning and evening they are destroyed. Without any regarding them they perish for ever. 21 Is not their tent-cord plucked up from them? They die without wisdom."
Now a word was secretly brought to me, and mine ear received a murmur (a whisper) thereof [12].

Here Eliphaz relates to Job a vision he saw, presenting it in order to condemn him. Some see that God gave Eliphaz this vision to calm his soul when he heard what had befallen Job. And that he saw this vision before meeting the tried Job.
This vision was presented to him secretly as a word that stole to him, like one whispering in his ears.
In humility Eliphaz confessed that he had received a small portion of the divine mystery and had not grasped the whole vision as he ought.

entries.section: 5. Supporting his opinion with a vision

paragraphs.text: In thoughts from the visions of the night, when deep sleep falleth on men [13].

In the middle of the night, when people were still and fell into deep sleep, that is, slept, Eliphaz was preoccupied with what lay behind what happened to Job, so God showed him this vision. The Psalmist David invites us to speak in our hearts with God, and to be silent until God speaks with us: "Commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still" (Ps 4:4). And as St. Mar Isaac the Syrian says: "Let your mouth be silent, and your heart will speak; and let your heart be silent, and God will speak."

It befits us at night to remember God and meditate on His law, and He will reveal to us His secrets and wisdom. "When I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches" (Ps 63:6).

entries.section: 5. Supporting his opinion with a vision

paragraphs.text: Fear and trembling came upon me, and all my bones shook [14].

It seems that before seeing the vision he felt a trembling shake all his bones. His heart was filled with the fear of the Lord, and he realized His greatness and felt that he was too small to reproach God. Thus he was prepared to receive the divine message. The Psalmist urges us: "Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling" (Ps 2:11).
Then a spirit passed before my face.

entries.section: 5. Supporting his opinion with a vision

paragraphs.text: The hair of my flesh stood up [15].

A spirit passed by Eliphaz, most likely an angel sent from God, to serve the Word. And the hair of his skin stood up, for the heavenly beings have been an object of terror to man since Adam's fall; he fears that a painful message will reach him and does not expect good news.

In ancient times the Levites were obliged to shave all the hair of their bodies (Num 8:6-7), since it represents unnecessary bodily matters. So Eliphaz, bearing evil toward Job, could not bear the spirit passing before his face; he lost his peace and his whole being was disturbed until the hair of his body stood up, a sign of the fullness of his disturbance even regarding what is superfluous in his body.
It stood still, but I could not discern the form thereof.

entries.section: 5. Supporting his opinion with a vision

paragraphs.text: An image was before mine eyes [16].
Eliphaz saw the angel clearly; he passed before him as an apparition, "an image before mine eyes," or as one who sees in a mirror, unable to describe him: "I could not discern the form thereof."
The voice came to him softly, for we do not hear the quiet voice of God amid the noise. Elijah did not meet God in the tempest, but in the quiet, gentle breeze (1 Kgs 19:11-13).

Eliphaz bore bitter carnal thoughts toward Job, therefore when the spirit passed by him he could not with his carnal mind see spiritual things, but saw what was more like phantoms, and could not distinguish the voice of the Spirit, which was low; his ears could not distinguish it. Thus Eliphaz confessed without knowing it that he had lost his peace, so the visions of the night became troubling imaginations. He could not sleep and rest while men were sleeping in deep sleep. His bones trembled, the hair of his body stood up, and his mind was confused with phantoms. This is the fruit of the corrupt man who turns truth into falsehood and slanders his brethren unjustly.
I heard a low voice: [16]

entries.section: 5. Supporting his opinion with a vision

paragraphs.text: Shall man be more just than God? shall a man be more pure than his maker? [17]
The message came to rebuke Job for his murmuring; he does not dare claim to be more righteous than God, nor purer than He.
"Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker!... Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou?" (Isa 45:9).
"Righteous art thou, O LORD, when I plead with thee" (Jer 1:12).
"And enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified" (Ps 2:143).
"Let God be true, but every man a liar; as it is written, That thou mightest be justified in thy sayings, and mightest overcome when thou art judged" (Rom 4:3).
"Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight" (Rom 20:3).

* For a man to be righteous he must keep the Law in everything, which human nature can hardly accomplish. Since every man is a liar, on that day when the Lord comes to judge mankind, He alone is justified in what He says, for His words are true in everything, they are words of truth.

Origen * I do not trust in myself, but I ask for the mercies of Thy truth and justice. "Enter not into judgment with thy servant" (Ps 2:143). How clearly the prophet declares his confidence in the tenderness of Christ, when he says: [Summon not thy servant to judgment before thee].
St. Jerome * If every man is a liar, and God alone is truth, what befits us, the servants of God and His bishops, but to cast away human errors and obey the Lord's commandments?

entries.section: 5. Supporting his opinion with a vision

paragraphs.text: St. Cyprian the Martyr Behold, he putteth no trust in his servants, and his angels he chargeth with folly [18].
St. John Chrysostom sees that he is speaking here of the heavenly powers, for God does not trust them, in the sense that their nature is not immune from error.
St. Basil says in his letter to Amphilochius that the heavenly powers have freedom of will and can incline to good or to evil, therefore they need the Spirit's help.

As he says in his third treatise against Eunomius that the authorities and principalities, etc., have holiness from their striving and continual contemplation of God, and are not holy by their own nature, and that, as they long for goodness, they receive holiness according to the degree of their pure love for God.

And in his treatise on the Trinity he says that these heavenly beings derive holiness from the Holy Spirit according to the rank of each. Thus it appears that they are not good by nature, but by the freedom that draws them to goodness and grace.

What keeps the angels from falling now is that their contemplation of God grows and increases, and secondly their awareness of the trial that befell the fallen angelic orders on account of their pride, this together with their continual resistance to the wicked angels increases their longing for goodness and their approval before God.

* The lilies represent the radiant beauty of the heavenly angels, whom God clothed with the splendor of His glory. They neither toiled nor spun, for they received from the beginning what they always are. And since at the resurrection men become like the angels, He wished us to hope for the beauty of the heavenly garment, so that we may be like the angels in splendor.
St. Hilary * Truly men and angels are accounted harsh if compared with You, for You alone are the King of all tenderness... We ask that You be the Judge, for You are tender toward all nations!

St. Jerome * The nature of an angel is rational, intelligent and free, subject to change, that is, of changeable will. For every created being is changeable, and only the uncreated does not change. And everything rational is free. Since its nature is rational and intelligent it is free, and since it is created it is changeable, having the capacity to remain and advance in goodness, and to turn to evil... And the angel is immortal not by nature but by grace.
Father John of Damascus It seems that the following statements are not part of the vision, but are Eliphaz's comment.

Even the angels, though they are holy beings, are not entrusted with the mysteries of God, but God reveals them to whom He wills. God is the good Shepherd who tends His vineyard Himself; He does not hand over His affairs entirely into the hands of those in heaven or on earth, however great their purity or holiness. For the angels, if compared with God, are counted foolish, and if compared with His wisdom, are counted ignorant.

* There is no need to tell how, when Moses and Aaron disobeyed the command of God at the waters of Meribah, they did not enter the Promised Land (Num 13:10); for the blessed Job relates that the angels and every creature can err [(Job 18:4) - the speaker is Eliphaz).

entries.section: 5. Supporting his opinion with a vision

paragraphs.text: St. Jerome How much less in them that dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, which are crushed like the moth? [19]
By comparing the wisdom of the angels with the wisdom of God, the former is counted folly, and by comparing the life of earthly man with the life of the angels, the latter is counted as a moth.

If this is so for the angels who dwell in heaven, what then of men, who dwell in houses of clay? Perhaps by houses he means here the bodies that were created from dust. The angels do not die, whereas men are crushed like the moth between the fingers of the hand, easily and quickly. If God does not entrust His angels who dwell with Him in heaven, pure and immortal spirits, would He entrust man, who dwells on the earth, created from dust, and who dies for the most trivial causes as the moth is crushed?

* We dwell in houses of clay, since we exist in earthly bodies. Paul, reflecting well on this, said: "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels," and also: "For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have in the heavens a building of God, an house not made with hands" (2 Cor 4:7; 5:1).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* It is clear that God does not entrust the righteous as you trust in yourself, for God knows their nature and the inclination of their bodies to fall. The fallen angels drive (God) to refuse trust, since He perceives their corruption in them. He stripped them of their original dignity and rank, and made them debased, because they thought evil against Him. If this is so for those who have this nature and dwelt on high among the virtuous powers, if this is the case with the angels, whose nature is higher than ours, what shall we say of the others, of men who are still sinners? Their nature is not only dust, and their dwellings among the creatures are made of clay (Gen 2:7); these easily corrupt as sinners, like a garment eaten by the moth (Jas 5:2).

entries.section: 5. Supporting his opinion with a vision

paragraphs.text: Father Hesychius of Jerusalem They are destroyed from morning to evening: they perish for ever without any regarding it [20].

Man has no right to boast against God, nor to think that he possesses knowledge, for perhaps between morning and evening, before the day passes, a man dies and is no longer found on the earth. Every day, indeed every minute, people die on the face of the earth, and yet no one thinks of his own death; there is none who heeds this truth, nor any who is admonished in earnest.

* The sinner is cut off from morning to evening, that is, from the beginning of his life to its end he is wounded by committing sin... On the contrary, Paul rightly urges us, saying: "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil" (Eph 16:5). We redeem the time if with tears we mend our past life, which we lost through carelessness.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Is not their tent-cord plucked up from them? (the ropes of their tents)

entries.section: 5. Supporting his opinion with a vision

paragraphs.text: They die, even without wisdom [21].
Their human wisdom, in which they take pride, is taken away from them, and they die, and with them die their wisdom and their foolish plans.
*Eliphaz brings an accusation against all sinners in general, and was not ashamed to number Job among them.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * As if he were saying: Those of whom you said, "without understanding they perish for ever" - these surely die without wisdom... Since the wicked look upon the chosen in a debased way, because they are walking toward an unseen life through visible death, it is therefore well said here: "They die without wisdom".. And because Eliphaz said these things, which are true in their meaning and are against the wicked, yet he was counted by the blessed Job as deserving of blame, and exalted himself in haughtiness over wisdom.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
This is what man reached because of sin, but the Incarnation of the divine Word and the offering of salvation changed the situation completely.

* We obtained this because of the "body" which the Lord offered; He offered to the Father the firstfruits of our nature. And because of the dignity of the One who offered and the perfection of the offering, the Father found the "gift" acceptable, received it with His hand, joined it to Himself, and said (to the incarnate Lord): "Sit thou at my right hand" (Ps 110:1).
Did not (the humanity united with the divinity) rise above the heavens?!
Is this not an honor beyond measure?!

Our nature (in the person of the incarnate God) has risen above the heavens, and has been exalted above the angels. It has passed over the archangels and the Cherubim, and soared above the Seraphim, higher than all the heavenly powers, and has rested in the true divine throne alone...

The conduct of our race was so evil in the past that it was in danger of the whole human race being wiped from the face of the earth. And now we, who were formerly counted unworthy to remain on the earth, have been raised to the heavens.
We, who were formerly unworthy of earthly glory, now ascend to the Kingdom of Heaven, and enter the heavens, and take our place before the divine throne.
This nature of ours, from which the Cherubim guarded the gates of Paradise, behold, today it is raised above the Cherubim!
How can we pass over so great an event (the Feast of the Ascension) so quickly?!
For we who have wronged such great mercies, so that we became unworthy of the very earth, and fell from all authority and dignity - by what merit are we raised to such a high honor?!
How did the conflict end?!
Why did God's wrath cease...?

For this is truly wonderful: that peace has come, not through any work done by those who provoked God's wrath... but He who was rightly angry with us Himself calls us to peace. For the Apostle says: "Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us" (2 Cor 20:5). And what does this mean? That although we have wronged Him, it is He who seeks us and calls us to peace. It is truly so, for since He is God, and the God who loves, He calls us to Himself.
St. John Chrysostom * He who knows the weakness of human nature gains experience of the power of God.

Father Maximus the Confessor * When you hear that the divine majesty is higher than the heavens, that its glory cannot be expressed, its beauty cannot be described, and its nature cannot be approached, do not despair of seeing what you desire. It is within your power, for within you is the capacity by which you can perceive divine things. For He who created you gave you at the same time this wonderful loftiness.
St. Gregory of Nyssa
Anoint my words with the anointing of love!
* Job's friends set it in their hearts to crush him!
They thought the bitter moments of his calamities a favorable opportunity to attack him!
But let the whole world attack him; what can harm him, as long as You are on his side!
What can dishonor him, as long as You bear witness to him!
* Often I think myself wise, and count my words true.
But what is the use of understanding and wisdom without love?
Anoint my lips with the anointing of Your Holy Spirit, and set a guard over my mouth, that I may speak only what my heart carries of the overflow of Your love!
That I may love You, and so love Your creation, and instead of biting criticism fill every soul with hope in You!
* Eliphaz saw in righteous Job a hypocritical man; the unbearable calamities that befell him are the natural fruit of his hidden sins.
Job was counted wise in the eyes of men, teaching others and guiding them, yet he sees him unable to guide himself.
He sees him as a man unable to carry out what he recommends!
* Grant me holy eyes, that I may not look with the eyes of Eliphaz, filled with malice and lying in wait for his righteous brother, to bring false accusations against him!
* Grant me eyes compassionate toward my brethren, that my heart may cry within me:
Who is weak, and I am not weak?
Who is offended, and I burn not?
* In tender fatherhood Job did not know authority, and was not the one who commands and forbids those under his authority, but in tender fatherhood he guided many.
Nothing occupied him all the days of his life but the salvation of every soul, even the members of his household!
He was a support for the weak, strengthening their slack hands, raising them from their fall, and making firm the trembling knees!
He bore Your image, O Lover of mankind!
And he refused to work except according to Your divine good pleasure!
* Trials surrounded him to swallow him up, and sudden disasters followed one another without mercy, and Job seemed as one who had lost everything, even his health!
But as a man he cried to You in bitter groans, yet his heart did not turn aside, and his lips did not utter a word of blasphemy.
He counted that he had lost nothing, for You are his treasure, and the source of his goodness and his good things!
He lost nothing, for he had gained You!
* Eliphaz found his opportunity, and displayed his wisdom and his theological understanding.
He said: No righteous man suffers what has befallen Job, nor is any upright man destroyed as he has been destroyed!
This is nothing but a divine testimony to Job's hidden wickedness!
And since what befell him has befallen no one in all of history, he is the most wicked of the wicked, and the chief of all sinners and hypocrites.
Look at Job, like a lion that used to prowl, terrifying and threatening, and behold, now he is dying of hunger, with no prey.
He lost all his sons; he no longer has a cub!
The lion became the mockery of children, and a plaything with no power!

* Eliphaz saw a heavenly vision, and instead of being restrained, he trembled and feared, and went back to affirm that Job is not more righteous than the angels, for God charges His angels with folly!
Who is Job, dust and ashes, that he should justify himself before God!
Behold, his tent has been plucked up, and his death has become a disgrace and shame before all!
* In longsuffering God left Eliphaz and his friends to mock, and in His heavenly wisdom permitted Job to be insulted by them.
But behold, the insult becomes for him a store of earthly and heavenly glory.
And every accusation against him is turned into an eternal crown!
Let the wicked accuse the children of God unjustly, but He will not allow their rod to rest upon His righteous ones!
* Truly, no creature will be justified before You!
You alone are the Holy One!
Before the light of Your splendor, all lights vanish!
Before Your righteousness, no creature will be justified!
* If You, the Judge, came to save and not to judge, how dare I judge my brother?
How shall I rob You of Your throne, O Searcher of hearts?
Grant me, along with wisdom, love, and along with my longing for the salvation of all, a compassionate heart!

entries.section: 1. The saints are witnesses to the wisdom of God

paragraphs.text: Call now, is there any that will answer thee?
And to which of the saints wilt thou turn? [1]

Eliphaz was very confident of his position, so he set before Job to choose the arbitrators. He says to him: "Call now, is there any that will answer thee?" meaning: search yourself throughout the whole world, is there anyone whom calamities have reached as they have reached you?
Is there a saint among all humanity to whom what befell you has befallen? God has not dealt with any saint in this way, so surely you are not one of them.
Is there among the saints one who cursed the day of his birth as you did?
Has any saint risen up in revolt as you did, and been so hasty in judgment?
"To which of the saints wilt thou turn?" They all agree with me in my opinion. All of them stand on my side, and support what I say.
Eliphaz spoke these words, counting Job deserving of blame. He was puffed up with the pride of wisdom.

* "And to which of the saints wilt thou turn?" He says this in mockery: you cannot secure the saints to support you in your affliction, those whom you did not want to be in your company when you were able.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* "Call now, is there any that will answer thee? and which of the holy angels dost thou behold?" (LXX) As if Eliphaz were saying: You amuse yourself when you think that God is a witness with you, while you are unable to enjoy a visit of an angel to you in your prayers. You met a deceiver who deceived you, and persuaded you that he was sent from God. He made you believe this, but it is clear that God has not given testimony to that for you.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem As for the effectiveness of the prayers of the saints, it is said in the Book of Acts that an angel appeared in a vision to St. Paul and said to him: "Fear not, Paul; thou must be brought before Caesar: and, lo, God hath given thee all them that sail with thee" (Acts 27:24).

* If here a ship in danger, suffering from foundering, was found, and the prisoners were saved for Paul's sake (Acts 27:24), consider what it will be for the holy person in his house; for many are the trials that assail us, trials more dangerous than the trials of nature, but God is able to grant us to be saved if only we obey the saints as those in the ship did, if we carry out what they command us. For they were not only saved, but also contributed to the faith of others.
While the saint was in chains he did greater works than those who are free.

Behold, the situation here is this: the free centurion needed his bound prisoner, the skilled captain of the ship was in want of one who was not a captain, but rather he was the true captain. For he steered, as a captain, a ship not of this kind (an earthly one) but the Church of the whole world, having learned from Him who is also the Lord of the sea. He steered it not by human skill, but by the wisdom of the Spirit. In this ship there are many shipwrecks, many waves, evil spirits, "without were fightings, within were fears" (2 Cor 7:5); and he was the true captain.
* Urge those who have friendly converse with God to offer more prayers, with greater perseverance, that the storm which is shattering the whole world may be calmed.
St. John Chrysostom * The world continues to exist only because of the prayers offered by Christians.
Aristides of Athens * Our prayers are common and public; when we pray we do not pray for one person, but for all the people, because we all, the whole people, are one.
* May the prayers for the brothers and sisters not cease in the presence of the Father's mercies.
St. Cyprian the Martyr

2 For wrath killeth the foolish man, and envy slayeth the silly one. 3 I have seen the foolish taking root: but suddenly I cursed his habitation. 4 His children are far from safety, and they are crushed in the gate, neither is there any to deliver them. 5 Whose harvest the hungry eateth up, and taketh it even out of the thorns, and the thirsty swalloweth up their substance.
For wrath killeth the foolish man, and envy slayeth the silly one [2].

Sinners are counted fools, since they do not accept God's wisdom. These are killed by anger, and envy corrupts their bones. Perhaps Eliphaz means by this that what befalls Job is the natural fruit of his foolishness, ascribing to him folly and stupidity.

He says that the deceiver deceived him and stirred up anger in him, and that he mocked him so that Job would kill himself. In this he wishes to justify himself, but his own stupidity has been revealed.

* [Wrath kills the fool, and envy slays the child] (cf. Job 2:5). It must be noted that he who is angry is a fool, and he who envies is counted a child. For the former is not without reason declared a fool, since he brings death upon himself by his own will, and lets himself be stirred up by anger. And the latter proves by his envy that he is an immature child, for when he is envious he testifies that the one he was able to torment is greater than he.

St. John Cassian * Nothing surpasses love, and consequently nothing is lower than anger. We must care for nothing, however useful and necessary it may seem, so as to avoid anger, which causes disturbance, and we must not be troubled by matters, even those we reckon to be non-essential, so that we may keep the calm of love and peace without lack, for we must realize that nothing is so destructive as anger and vexation, and nothing so profitable as love.
Father Joseph * Nothing is more dangerous than rage, nor harsher than anger!
* There is a drunkenness of anger more dangerous than the drunkenness of wine!
St. John Chrysostom * Let us consider how grave is the sin of anger (wrath), by which we are separated from tenderness, and the likeness to the image of the Most High is corrupted.

By anger wisdom is driven out, and we remain in folly in all that we do and are bound to do, as it is written: "Anger resteth in the bosom of fools" (Eccl 7:9). For with the withdrawal of the light of understanding, agitation corrupts the mind.
By anger life is lost, even wisdom appears held back. As it is written: [Wrath destroys the wise] (Prov 1:15) LXX...
By anger righteousness is nullified, as it is written: "For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God" (Jas 20:1)...
He who does not control his feelings with the prudence proper to man must live in solitude like an animal.
By anger harmony is destroyed, as it is written: "A wrathful man stirreth up strife: but he that is slow to anger appeaseth strife" (Prov 15:18)...

By anger the light of truth is lost. As it is written: "Let not the sun go down upon your wrath" (Eph 26:4). For anger brings the darkness of confusion. God hides from him the rays of the knowledge of Himself. By anger the radiance of the Holy Spirit is shut off. On the other hand, it is written according to an ancient translation: "On whom shall my Spirit rest, but on him who is humble and peaceable and who trembles at my words" (Isa 2:66).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* If a person is angry as a human being, he puts an end to anger as a Christian.

St. Jerome * Whoever is irascible is devoid of longsuffering and love; he is quickly troubled by trivial words, and stirs up strife over some slight, petty matter, and wherever there is no place for him he throws himself in... Who does not mourn for such a one? He is abhorred by God and men.

St. Ephrem the Syrian * The Holy Spirit is called the peace of the Spirit, and anger is called the disquiet of the soul, so we must conclude that nothing keeps away from us the presence (work) of the Spirit like anger.
St. John Climacus It is not strange that Eliphaz accuses Job of jealousy or envy, which are Eliphaz's own sins, for he projects his faults upon him, saying: "and envy slayeth the silly one" [2].

* The envious man does not count the calamities that befall him a trial; rather the trial for him is the good that befalls another, and conversely success for him is not that he himself be happy, but that trials befall another. The envious man grieves at seeing the good deeds of people, and rejoices in the calamities that befall them. It is said that the birds of prey that devour dead carcasses are destroyed by a sweet fragrance (perfume), for their nature agrees with what is evil and corrupt. And anyone who comes under the control of this disease (envy) is destroyed by the happiness of his relatives and neighbors, but if he sees an evil temptation he flies to it and puts his crooked beak into it and brings out the hidden calamities.
St. Gregory of Nyssa *Before all things it befits the man upon whom the yoke is laid to be steadfast in his faith... let him drive away from himself envy and anger, and remove deceitful lips.

St. Aphrahat the Persian Sage * The harm is trivial and the danger slight when the limbs are wounded by a sword, for the healing is easy so long as the wound is visible and the remedy is applied. The sore that is seen can be treated easily. But the wounds of the envious are hidden and secret, and admit no cure for their healing, so they shut in upon themselves hidden pains within the recesses of the conscience.

* Such people do not enjoy food or take pleasure in drink. They are constantly groaning, sighing and grieving, for as long as envy is not driven out their hearts are torn day and night without ceasing.

All evils have limits, and every sin ends in the commission of the crime. The adulterer's sin ends at the limit of committing the transgression, the thief's crime stops when he kills, the robber puts a limit to his greed, and the deceiver puts an end to his fraud, but envy has no limits.
It is an evil that works continually, and a sin that has no end.

St. Cyprian the Martyr * [Envy kills the weak (the lesser - little one)] (cf. Job 5:2). It is impossible for us to envy anyone except those whom we think better than ourselves in a certain respect. Therefore it is said that envy kills the "lesser." For the envious man bears witness against himself that he is less than another, since envy torments him on his account...
Such was Cain, who went down to kill his brother, for he went mad when his offering was rejected, because of the one whose offering God accepted and who was preferred over him (Gen 4)...
And so Esau was inflamed to persecute his brother, because he lost the blessing of the birthright, being deprived of it for a mess of lentils (vegetables) (Gen 27:38; 29:25)...

And so the brothers sold Joseph to the passing Ishmaelites, since the secret of the revelation was hidden from them, and they put themselves in a position of opposition to his advancement, lest he be a ruler over them (Gen 5:37-11).

And so Saul persecuted his servant David by throwing a spear at him, for he feared that the man would attain a stature greater than his own, since he perceived his daily growth in virtue (1 Sam 10:18-11).

So the one whom envy kills is the weak (the lesser), for if he did not feel that he is the lesser he would not grieve at the goodness of others. For envy corrupts the mind and kills everything it finds good. Solomon said: "A calm (peaceful) heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones" (Prov 30:14)...

So whoever longs to be perfect and whole, let him avoid the poison of envy, and concentrate his affections on the inheritance which is not diminished by the number of heirs, which is one inheritance for all, and complete for each one. And which shows itself a greater inheritance the more the number of those who are granted it increases... So when a person does not long for evil things, nothing stands in the way of love.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
I have seen the foolish taking root: but suddenly I cursed his habitation [3].

Eliphaz sees that Job had previously taken root and prospered, but since he is foolish his state did not last. And behold, he curses his habitation. It is as though Eliphaz brings a new accusation against Job, for besides accusing him of hypocrisy, and that behind his seemingly good works he hides hidden evils that none knows but God, for which reason calamities unheard of in the history of mankind have befallen him, he was a fool who ran after wealth and the love of the world. An accusation as far as can be from the life of this righteous man!

Perhaps this does not mean that Eliphaz desired Job's destruction, but since he discovered - according to his thinking - that what befell him was from God's anger against him as a wicked man, he realized that it was by God's justice that Job should fall under the curse, to uproot him from this world with all his wealth, because his heart was attached to it.

Scripture warns us against loving the world and clinging to it. "Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world. If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world" (1 Jn 2:15-16). "Ye adulterers and adulteresses, know ye not that the friendship of the world is enmity with God? whosoever therefore will be a friend of the world is the enemy of God" (Jas 4:4).

* The foolish takes root in the earth and clings to it, for he is attached to the love of the earth with all the desire of his heart. He exalts himself by his rooting, when he clings in this world to temporal goods, until he obtains what he desires, and submits to no authority, and rules over the weak without resistance, and resists those who exercise authority well, and reaches better circumstances by wicked means, so that by leaving the true life, he lives this present time in greater happiness.
But when the weak see that the wicked prosper, they become fearful and troubled within, because of the scope that sinners have, and the steps of their mind stagger.
In the same way the psalmist declared: "But as for me, my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped. For I was envious of the proud, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked" (Ps 2:73-3).

But when the strong see their glory, they immediately fix their minds on the punishment (discipline) that follows glory. And with deep inner thought of the heart they despise the things that swallow up the proud from outside with the increase of vain conceit. It is well said: "I have seen the foolish taking root, but suddenly I cursed his beauty." For to curse the beauty of the fool is to condemn his glory by a considered judgment, for the more he sinks into torments the more he exalts himself in sin. For his arrogance is temporary, but his punishment is permanent.

He who begins his way with honor ends with judgment. In any case, the more the wicked man finds a way for himself in this world, the more people he draws into destruction, therefore it is rightly said: "His children are far from safety." For the children of the fool are those who imitate him, born in the ambition of this world. They are far from safety, especially as regards their practice of evil if compared with their freedom from weakness.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* You want now to inherit the earth; beware lest the earth inherit you.
If you are meek you inherit it, or if hard, it inherits you...
You will truly inherit the earth when you cling to the Maker of heaven and earth!
St. Augustine * Who that has tasted the sweetness of the fruits of the tree of life wants to run toward the foul fruits of (love of) the world?
* As fire does not stay in water, so the knowledge of God does not stay in a heart entangled with the passions of the world.
* None has perfectly renounced the world but he in whom Your fire burns always, O Lord.

St. John Saba * The soul that is about to receive the Word, the Logos, ought to die to the world (Gal 14:6) and be buried in Christ (Rom 4:6; Col 12:2), so that it finds none but Christ, for this is the fitting reception that He asks for Himself from it.
St. Ambrose His children are far from safety, and they are crushed in the gate, neither is there any to deliver them [4].

Perhaps the gate was high and fell on Job's children and those at the feast who thought themselves in peace and safety. It fell with its weight and crushed them beneath it, and there was none to deliver. So Job's evil - in Eliphaz's opinion - came upon his sons and destroyed them.

* This means: why are you terrified at the death of your children? For the children of fools do not perish because of lack of deliverance, but are afflicted while still alive... and there is no one to deliver them, since God requited them justly. Also their gain which they obtained unjustly is taken from them by the righteous, since there is none to save them from evil, and all their strength is wasted in pleasures and is exhausted, perishing by God's command.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem Who are those who think they are safe, standing inside a house with a closed door, which none can break into to harm them? In Eliphaz's view, Job's sons and daughters, who in his opinion are wicked and hypocrites like their father, think themselves happy at the feast, and expect no harm to creep in upon them. They are safe, inside the gate, under the guard of their servants and slaves! But they are not safe; rather the gate, which is the source of their safety, falls on them and destroys them.

This saying bore a prophecy about the Lord Christ who said: "I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture" (Jn 9:10). Through this door the Gentiles believed and entered into the faith, and went out to the heavenly life, and found divine pasture. This same door became a stumbling block to those who thought they were safe, since they clung to the letter of the Law, and thought that they, rather than others, were inside the divine doors.

They rejected faith in the Lord Christ, so the door - the entrance of believers - became a stumbling block to them, for He says: "If I had not come and spoken unto them, they had not had sin: but now they have no cloak for their sin" (Jn 22:15)

* Let us not be confused, brethren, in understanding Him, as He bears likenesses both as the door and also the doorkeeper. For what is the door? The way of entrance. Who is the doorkeeper? He who opens the door. Who then is He who opens it, but He Himself, where He reveals Himself to be seen?
* This great sin is their unbelief in Christ, who came specially to renew their faith. Had He not come, they would have been free of this sin.

By His coming the life of unbelievers became all the more laden with destruction, as it became for the salvation of those who believe. For He is the head of the Apostles and their chief, He became as they declared: [To some the savour of life unto life, and to some the savour of death unto death] (2 Cor 2:16).

St. Augustine * "And they are crushed in the gate..." As the entrance of a city is called a gate, so on the day of judgment it is the gate of the Kingdom, through which all the elect enter into the glory of their heavenly city... "Neither is there any to deliver them" [4]. For the Truth saves from eternal woe those who in their temporary state have been afflicted by discipline. He who refuses distress is left at that time without any means of salvation. For they did not care to receive Him (the Savior) as their Father who trains them, therefore the wicked in their time of trial will not find Him a deliverer who helps them.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Now let us consider what the Gospels say in light of the promises of good things. And we must say: the good things that the Apostles proclaim in these Gospels are simply "Jesus."
One of the good things they proclaim is the resurrection. But the resurrection, in a certain sense, is Jesus, for He is the One who says: "I am the resurrection"...

As Isaiah says: [How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of those who bring good tidings of good] (Isa 7:52). He sees how beautiful and fitting is the proclamation of the Apostles who have walked (in Christ), and He is the One who says: "I am the way." He praises the feet of those walking in the way, those who think on Jesus Christ, and go through this door to God (the Father).
They proclaim the good things, the beautiful feet, that is, Jesus.
Origen Whose harvest the hungry eateth up, and taketh it even out of the thorns, and the thirsty swalloweth up their substance [5].
Job's and his sons' wealth became plunder for the Sabeans and the Chaldeans. They broke through the barriers made of thorns, and seized the wealth.

Perhaps he refers here to the thief who steals the whole crop, even that mixed with thorns, or to the custom to which Dr. Thomson referred in his explanation of this passage, where he says that the farmers, after threshing the grain, often place it beside the straw in a special place, and cover it with thick bushes full of thorns so that the animals do not approach it and eat it, and when thieves want to steal the grain they must first remove these thorny bushes.

It says in the Jesuit translation (Dar al-Mashriq, Beirut): "The hungry eats his harvest, snatching it from among the thorns, and the thirsty swallows his wealth." He who does not open his heart with true inner love to the hungry, the thirsty and the needy becomes plunder for others. The hungry breaks into his storehouses, and the harvest is seized from among the thorns, and many thirst for his wealth, and count it their right to swallow all he has and leave him nothing.

Thus Eliphaz looks at Job and his children as not having been generous in love, but they gave generously for the sake of appearance and vain glory, while their hearts were dry and hard, so they deserved to have their possessions plundered by the hungry and thirsty.

In bitterness Tobit cried to the Lord, saying: [For we have sinned against You, and have not obeyed Your commandments, so You delivered us to plunder, and exile, and death, and we became a byword and a laughingstock and a reproach among all the nations among whom You scattered us] (Tob 3:4). And the psalmist says: "Thou makest us to turn back from the enemy: and they which hate us spoil for themselves. Thou hast given us like sheep appointed for meat; and hast scattered us among the heathen. Thou sellest thy people for nought, and dost not increase thy wealth by their price... (Ps 10:44-14). And the Lord says: "Thy substance and thy treasures will I give to the spoil without price, and that for all thy sins, even in all thy borders" (Jer 13:15; cf. Jer 3:17; 6:30; 37:50; Ezek 21:7; 46:23; Isa 13:10).

* "Thy substance and thy treasures will I give to the spoil without price, but for all thy sins" (Jer 15:13). What are the riches of the sinners that God gives to the spoil in return for all their sins? Are they the riches that they gather on earth? Every man in fact lays up treasure for himself, either on earth if he is an evil man, or in heaven if he is a good man, as the Gospel tells us (Mt 19:6-20). Does He say to this people: because of your sins I give your treasures and riches to the spoil, meaning by those riches the prophets such as Jeremiah and Isaiah and Moses?! God has taken these treasures from this people, and said through the Lord Christ: "The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof" (Mt 43:21). This nation is we ourselves, for God has given the riches of this people (the prophets) to us.

They were first entrusted with the oracles of God (Rom 2:3), then we after them were entrusted with these oracles; they were taken from them and given to us. Likewise we can say that the statement: "The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof," which the Savior said, was fulfilled in Him. Not that Scripture was taken from them, but that they at present do not possess the Law nor the prophets, because they do not understand or grasp what is written in it. They have the books, therefore the kingdom of God that is taken from them is "the meaning of the Holy Scriptures." They do not care to know any exposition of the Law and the Prophets, but read it without understanding. And with the coming of the Lord the following prophecy was indeed fulfilled: "And he said, Go, and tell this people, Hear ye indeed, but understand not; and see ye indeed, but perceive not. Make the heart of this people fat" (Isa 9:6-10; Mt 14:13-15). The prophecy of Isaiah was also fulfilled: "For, behold, the Lord, the LORD of hosts, doth take away from Jerusalem and from Judah the stay and the staff, the whole stay of bread, and the whole stay of water, the mighty man, and the man of war, the judge, and the prophet, and the diviner, and the ancient, the captain of fifty, and the honourable man, and the counsellor, and the cunning artificer, and the skilful in enchantment" (Isa 1:3-3). All this God has taken from them, and given it to us who have come from the Gentiles...

He says: "Without price but for all thy sins, even in all thy borders," as though saying to this people: Your treasures and your riches I give to the spoil because of your sins that have filled all your borders, for there is no place among this people that is not filled with sin. How could all their borders not be filled with sins, they who killed the Truth, since the Lord Christ is the Truth, and killed Wisdom, since the Lord Christ is Wisdom, and killed Justice, since the Lord Christ is Justice? By judging the Son of God to death they lost all that truth, wisdom, and justice. And when the Lord of glory Jesus rose from the dead He never appeared to those who killed Him... but appeared only to those who believed in Him; He appeared to them alone when He rose from the dead.

"And I will make thee to pass with thine enemies (and subject thee to slavery in the midst of thine enemies) into a land which thou knowest not: for a fire is kindled in mine anger, which shall burn upon you"(a). This people has indeed been subjected to slavery in the midst of its enemies and in a land it did not know. And after these threatening words directed to the people, Jeremiah or the Lord Christ continues his prayer and adds to his previous words these words: "O LORD, thou knowest: remember me, and visit me, and revenge me of my persecutors; take me not away in thy longsuffering"(b) or [Be not longsuffering toward them](LXX).
Origen
6 For affliction cometh not forth of the dust, neither doth misery spring out of the ground, 7 but man is born unto toil, as the birds of prey to soar on the wing.
For affliction cometh not forth of the dust, neither doth misery spring out of the ground [6].
After Eliphaz demonstrated that all Job lost is a just punishment from God, he began as one who encourages him lest he fall into despair.

"Affliction cometh not forth of the dust, neither doth misery spring out of the ground." It is not like natural crops that sprout at certain times and come forth from the dust like grass, but all that happens is by divine providence. Or in other words: do not blame the soil when affliction appears, for it is not its doing, but yours, for the cause is within you. "If thou scornest, thou alone shalt bear it" (Prov 9:12).

As we do not expect trees to appear from soil without the planting of seeds, so it befits us not to think that afflictions come upon people without their having committed evils. What befell Job is not by chance, but is the harvest of evil planting.

This truth was revealed to us by our Lord Jesus, the Creator of the soul, who knows that the disease of the soul is in itself and not outside it. The human soul is like a single earthen vessel which differs only in the nature of what is inside it; if what is inside one is gasoline and inside another is water, the approach of a live coal will bring the first to burst into flames and explode, but the second will quench the coal.
St. John Chrysostom wrote more than one treatise affirming that no one and no circumstance can harm a person unless the person harms himself.
* Someone may say: Did not Satan harm Adam, since he corrupted his being, and made him lose Paradise?

For the cause here lies in the negligence of the one who was harmed, his lack of self-control, and his lack of striving. For Satan, who used various powerful schemes, could not subject Job to himself; how then could he, by lesser means, have dominated Adam, had Adam not been able by himself to master himself?!

What then? Does harm not befall one who is exposed to slanders and suffers the plundering of his property, so that he is deprived of his goods, driven out of his inheritance, and struggles in grievous poverty?

No, rather he benefits if he is dignified, for did these things harm the Apostles? Did they not always struggle with hunger, thirst and nakedness?! And because of these things they became glorified and renowned and gained for themselves more help from the Lord?!
And also what harm befell Lazarus because of his sickness and sores and poverty and having no one to shelter him? Were not these things weaving for him a crown of flowers of victory...?!
Joseph's brothers, for example, harmed Joseph, but Joseph himself was not harmed.
And Cain cast his nets for Abel, but Abel did not fall into them. And this is the reason for which disciplines and punishments exist.

For God does not lift the punishment from the one who devised the harm merely because of the good that the one who endured the harm enjoys, but confirms his punishment because of the evil of the doer of iniquity. For although those upon whom evil falls become more glorious at the expense of the plots devised against them, it was not in the intention of man that another should not harm him, but he gains great benefit at the hands of his adversaries.
St. John Chrysostom But man is born unto toil, as the birds of prey to soar on the wing [7].

Man was created to live in peace and rest and joy of heart, but by transgressing the commandment and turning his back on God, the source of his happiness, "man became born unto toil," for he was born in sin (Ps 51:5). And toil became as if an inseparable part of our being, or as if we were created to suffer it, as birds of prey were created to soar on their wings on high. It is not for us to be surprised at the affliction that befalls us as though a strange thing had happened to us (1 Pet 4:12). We must eat our bread in the sweat of our faces (Gen 3:19).

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that man's life is a continual striving with the enemy of good, entering a battle that does not stop, but these battles end in the victory of those who strive and their crown.

*He says: This despair springs from within people. Note how he was obliged once more to show that his words agree with nature, so that his speech would not be criticized. For human nature was created thus. For the earth produces nothing more pitiable than man, so it befits us not to be astonished or to wonder: we are born to cause pain and to suffer. This is also what the prophet said: "For all... the days of our years... yet is their strength labour and sorrow" (Ps 90:9-10). And Jacob said: [The days of the years of my life... few and evil] (Gen 9:47). "But man is born unto toil." He says that in our nature it is impossible to escape suffering. For he does not want anyone to object again that Job is righteous. He says: He is righteous, but human nature is usually created to endure evils. Note that he stepped out to nature to affirm that Job is not blameless.

St. John Chrysostom * We must not withdraw from our struggle of vigilance because of dangerous despair, for [now the kingdom of God suffereth violence, and the violent take it by force] (Mt 12:11). No virtue can be attained without struggle, and the mind cannot be restrained without deep sorrow of heart, for "man is born unto trouble." And in order to reach "unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ" (Eph 13:4), we must be always in great struggle with endless care.

Fr. Serenus * Let us have great caution and diligence regarding external circumstances when we are struck by the weight of sorrow, so that we may attain the hope of receiving the things above. The mind stands to receive the heavenly things through these outward disciplines.

* [Man is born unto trouble, as the bird for flying]... Since man enjoys reason, he perceives that it is impossible for him to pass the time of his pilgrimage without sorrow. Therefore when Paul enumerated his afflictions to his disciples, he rightly added: "For yourselves know that we are appointed thereunto" (1 Thess 3:3).

For when the body is struck with blows, the mind rises up, seeking the things above. Paul again bears witness to this, saying: "Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day" (2 Cor 16:4). Thus, [man is born unto trouble, as the bird for flying], for the mind flies freely toward the heights for the very reason that the body suffers from bending downward in heaviness.

The word "man" here represents life according to the flesh. So Paul says: "For whereas there is among you envying, and strife, and divisions, are ye not carnal" (1 Cor 3:3), and then he continues: [are ye not men?] (1 Cor 4:3) [Vulgate].
In this life [man is born unto trouble], for every carnal man, seeking temporal things, burdens his soul with the weight of his lusts.

It is a hard trouble to seek the glory of the present life, to acquire what one seeks, and to preserve it diligently when one prevails. It is a hard trouble, with endless pains, to hold on to things that you know will not last for a long time.
