paragraphs.text: 8 Oh that my request might come, and that God would grant me my hope! 9 That it would please God to crush me, and let loose his hand and cut me off. 10 Then my comfort and my rejoicing shall still be in torment that spareth not, for I have not denied the words of the Holy One. 11 What is my strength, that I should wait? and what is mine end, that I should be patient? 12 Is my strength the strength of stones? or is my flesh of brass? 13 Verily my help is not in me, and succour is driven quite from me!
Oh that my request might come, and that God would grant me my hope! [8]

Eliphaz rebuked Job harshly for seeking death, and instead of withdrawing what he had said, Job returned to repeat it more than before, and the Book has recorded his words for us, not that we may imitate him, but to warn us.
He asked God to fulfill his request and grant him his hope, not by bringing him through the trial, but by showing him mercy with death.

entries.section: 2. Death is the end of troubles

paragraphs.text: That it would please God to crush me, and let loose his hand and cut me off [9].

What Job hopes for in his distress is that God, who stretched out His hand against him so that he became poor and then bereaved and sick, would stretch out His hand all the more and crush him and take his life. Yet he never thought of suicide, unlike the philosopher Seneca, who encouraged suicide as a legitimate means to be rid of unbearable pains, which shows no respect for the law of God or the law of nature.
Job longed for the speed of his death, and turned this desire into a request he presented to God, but it was a prayer or request not according to God's will.

entries.section: 2. Death is the end of troubles

paragraphs.text: Then my comfort and my rejoicing shall still be in torment that spareth not, for I have not denied the words of the Holy One [10].

With his intense desire to be delivered from pain by death, Job's heart bore spiritual touches, so in faith he anticipates enjoying consolation and joy after his departure from the world. It is clear that Job had a good conscience and a living hope in eternity, though he expected a painful torment to overtake him before his death: "my rejoicing in torment that spareth not."
"That spareth not" or "let him not spare," as if he says: "I do not seek that God should spare me, but let Him allow the pains of death that put an end to my pains and bring me into rest.
In unseemly boldness Job challenges the Lord God and says: [Let him not spare!]

Job mixed his reproach - even if he transgressed the limits - with his faith and clinging to God's word, saying: "I have not denied (concealed) the words of the Holy One." He counted himself entrusted with the word of the holy God, perhaps having enjoyed divine visions. As if he says with the Apostle Paul that he did not receive the grace of God in vain (2 Cor 6:1). He was ready to enjoy the divine Word and to bear witness to it to others, that they might enjoy it with him.
The rule of his life is the word of the Holy One; he was not ashamed of it, nor slack in bearing witness to it.
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh sees that not even death can keep him from closing his mouth from witnessing and praising God.
* O Lord, I will not cease from praising You, even after my death.
He who lives for You and by You does not die; and the silence of death has no power to silence him.
Then let Him speak by my mouth, that it may be repeated after my death in the future.
* You are the Word who gives a word to those who speak; by You all who speak, speak for Your sake.
A ray, a radiance and a great light shone in me, that I may look upon You.
For by looking upon You the soul is enlightened, and so acquires goodness.
And when the soul draws away from You it is filled with darkness, and if it gazes upon You it puts on light to utter words of Your tidings...
Silence and speech stand over me demanding of me.
O Lord, order my life as You will.
If I am silent I am amazed, for I feel my insufficiency in (speech).
I am silent in amazement, and not in vain arrogance.
And if I speak, may my word be according to Your glory and for Your sake.

When the soul is filled with silence in amazement at You, this silence is speech full of every benefit. And if the soul is moved to glorify You with love... then in love I am moved, and I am moved to glorify You. And in amazement I am silent and do not cease from glorifying You.
Grant me, O Lord, amazement (in silence) and the word, that I may be enriched. Every day may I be amazed, and every day may I be moved to speak!

St. Mar Jacob of Serugh * He says: Surely I am not presenting to You anything contradictory. For I have no conscience drawn to resemble these things that You speak. In simplicity I say that I am enduring disciplines that exceed the limits of nature, for the trials that have befallen me exceed the capacity of the human body... He did not say: "I have passed through sufferings though I am righteous," but says that he cannot bear them, as David says: [Have mercy upon me, O LORD; for I am weak] (Ps 2:6).

St. John Chrysostom * "I have not denied the words of the Holy One." Often God's words to us are not sounds of words but works imposed on us. For He speaks to us by the things He does with us in silence. Therefore blessed Job would have denied the words of God if he had murmured at the blows upon him. But his feelings toward the one who smote him appear in his calling him "the Holy One," submissive to him who strikes him.

* "I do not deny the words of the Holy One." He never murmured at the injustice of him who smote him. For in the midst of his blows he calls the smiter "the Holy One." But we must realize that sometimes the adversary smites us with sorrows, and sometimes God does so...
By the blows of the adversary we steal away virtue, and when our evil habits are broken by the blows of the Lord we become strong in virtue.

The prophet foresaw this blow when he said: [Thou shalt shepherd them with a rod of iron, and like a potter's vessel thou shalt crush them] (Ps 9:2). For the Lord shepherds us and breaks us with a rod of iron, with the strong staff of righteousness according to His dispensation, while He gives us life from within, He grieves us from without. For He lowers the strength of the body and exalts the aim of the spirit.

Thus this blow is likened to a potter's vessel, as Paul says: [We have this treasure in earthen vessels] (2 Cor 4:7). And he describes the breaking together with the shepherding, saying: "Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day" (2 Cor 16:4). May the holy man who longs to draw near to God declare it powerfully in a spirit of humility even through the blows that befall him.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* He declares plainly: [I do not slander my holy God]. This means: I do not care for this life, I do not fear departure from this body, for I do not wish to be found a liar in relation to the testimonies that the holy God gave concerning me (Job 1:1; 2:3). For God does not bear witness to anyone's holiness except to those whom He finds practicing the works of the saints. He also said: [There is none like Job on the earth] (Job 1:8; 2:3). Therefore we must be careful during this corruptible life, since it is not possible for carnal men to receive such an important testimony from God and in the same character.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem What is my strength, that I should wait?

entries.section: 2. Death is the end of troubles

paragraphs.text: and what is mine end, that I should be patient? [11]

Job had no hope of seeing good days again, for his health had reached the bottom, and he came to a hopeless state. There is no longer any healing for his body, and he no longer has strength to wait. Job realized how weak he had become, and it was fitting for him to put his hope in Him who bears our weakness instead of longing for death out of despair.

* [What is my strength, that I should endure? and what is mine end, that my soul should be calm?] My life is short (Job 5:14); how many cycles of months and years does it contain? How should I not be troubled over this swiftly passing life?
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * The Lord (Christ) had pity on his (Adam's) weakness, and entered to accept shame in his place!
* O Light of Christ, who enlightens darkened eyes, let Your light shine on my weakness, that I may be enlightened by You.

St. Mar Jacob of Serugh * Let us put on our heads the helmet of salvation, that we may not be wounded and die in the battle. Let us gird our loins with truth, that we may not be found weak in the fight.
Let us rise and awaken Christ, that He may calm the waves for us.
Let us take the shield against the wicked one, as the preparation of the gospel of our Savior (Eph 6:15-16).
Let us receive from our Lord authority to tread on serpents and scorpions (Lk 10:19)...
Let us rejoice in our hope at all times (Rom 12:12), that He who is our hope and Savior may rejoice in us...
Let us take for ourselves weapons for the battle (Eph 6:16), which is the preparation for the gospel.
Let us knock at the door of heaven (Mt 7:7), and it will be opened before us and we shall enter it.
Let us ask for mercy diligently, and we shall receive what is necessary for us. Let us seek His kingdom and His righteousness (Mt 6:33).
Let us meditate on what is above, on the heavenly things, where Christ is ascended and glorified.
But let us forget the world, which is not ours, until we reach the goal to which we are called.
Let us lift up our eyes to the heights to see the light that is manifested.
Let us lift up our wings like eagles, to see where the body is (Mt 24:28)...

Our enemy is clever, my dear, and he who fights us is a deceiver. He prepares himself to attack the courageous victors, to make them weak. But the feeble ones who are his he does not fight, for they are captives delivered up to him.

Whoever has two wings flies away from him with them, so that the arrows he hurls at him do not reach him. The spiritual see him fighting, and his weapon does not prevail over their bodies. All the children of light do not fear him, for darkness flees before the light. The children of the Good One do not fear the evil one, for He gave them to tread upon him with their feet (Gen 3:15).
St. Aphrahat Is my strength the strength of stones?

entries.section: 2. Death is the end of troubles

paragraphs.text: or is my flesh of brass? [12]

* [Is my strength the strength of stones? or is my flesh of brass?] (Job 6:12) Even if my strength were like the strength of stones or brass, the torments issuing from the enemy would make it give way, for he [esteemeth iron as straw, and brass as rotten wood] (Job 41:27). If God says this of the enemy, then it is necessary that we seek departure from this body on every side.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * It is necessary to bear in mind that the "strength" of the righteous is of one kind, and the strength of the corrupt of another.

For the strength of the righteous is to subdue the body and resist our own will, and to destroy the pleasure of the present life, and to love the roughness of this world for the sake of eternal rewards, and to despise the enticements of prosperity, and to overcome the terror of trials in our hearts; but the strength of the corrupt is unbroken attachment to passing things, and continual demand for more vainglory, even at the cost of life, and the search for greater measures of evil, and the resisting of the life of the righteous, not only with words and conduct but also with arms, so that they may be self-assertive, and the committing of evil daily without any lessening of desire.

Therefore it was said to the elect by the psalmist: "Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all ye that wait for the LORD" (Ps 24:31). And it was proclaimed to the corrupt by the prophet: "Woe unto them that are mighty to drink wine, and men of strength to mingle strong drink" (Isa 22:5).

How well Isaiah perceived both kinds of strength in the words: "But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength" (Isa 31:40). For since he did not say "receive" but "change" (renew) strength, he clearly perceives that the strength they leave is of one kind and that which enters them is of another.

* What we indicate here by brass and stones, is it not the blows of the Most High, which have been softened by no blows of discipline? On the contrary, it was said to the elect by the prophet, with a promise from the Lord: "And I will take away the stony heart out of their flesh, and will give them an heart of flesh" (Ezek 19:11).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
It was not possible for Job to rely on his own strength, but he places his hope in our Lord Jesus, the Giver of strength.

* Among all those born who put on flesh there is one who is righteous, He is Jesus Christ, as He testifies of Himself, saying: "I have overcome the world" (Jn 16:33). And the prophet also testified of Him: "Because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth" (Isa 53:9). And the blessed Apostle said: "For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin" (2 Cor 5:21). How did He make Him sin? He bore sin without committing it, and nailed it to the Cross (Col 2:14). The Apostle also says: "Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize?" (1 Cor 9:24).

Add to this that none among men went down to the battle and was not wounded or struck, because sin has ruled since Adam transgressed the commandment (Rom 5:14), striking many, wounding many, and killing many. And none among the many killed it until our Savior came on His cross. It had a sting that pricked many, until the end came, and its sting was broken when it was nailed to the Cross.

entries.section: 2. Death is the end of troubles

paragraphs.text: St. Aphrahat Verily my help is not in me, and succour is driven quite from me! [13]

* [There is no help for me from myself] [13]. Blessed Job was rich in virtue, yet he was not self-reliant, so he spoke thus as one without strength... It is clear now that, as one whose mind was struck with regard to hope, he looks that he has no hope from himself. But since he declares that he is weak in himself, he adds also that his kinsmen have forsaken him. [My friends also have left me]. But note that he who is despised from without sits within on the judgment seat. For at the very moment in which he declares himself abandoned, he immediately breaks that by uttering judgment in the words: [He that withholdeth pity from his friend forsaketh the fear of the Lord](a).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Job groaned over his friends because they left him in his trial, but our Lord, the glorious Jesus, did not leave man whom He loved, but crossed over to him even to Hades to free him from it.

* When Jesus, the slayer of death, came, and clothed Himself with a body from the seed of Adam, and was crucified in His body, and tasted death, and when Death realized that He had come to it, it was terrified in its place, and was confounded when it saw Jesus. It had shut its gates and did not wish to meet Him. Then He burst open its gates, and entered it and spoiled it of its plunder.

And when the dead saw a light in the darkness, they lifted up their heads from the bondage of death, and looked and saw the exaltation of the Messiah the King. Then the powers of darkness sat in mourning, for the authority of death had been taken from them.

Death tasted the deadly medicine for it, and its hands fell, and it learned that the dead would rise and flee from its authority. And when (Jesus) struck Death by despoiling its possessions, it wailed and cried aloud in bitterness, saying: "Get away from my kingdom, do not enter it. Who is this living One who enters my world?"

And as Death cried out in terror (for it saw the darkness beginning to vanish, and some of the righteous who slept arose to ascend with Him) it realized that when He comes in the fullness of time, He will bring out all those imprisoned under its authority, and they will go to see the light.

Therefore when Jesus completed His ministry among the dead, Death cast Him out of its kingdom, and did not permit Him to remain in it. And it reckoned that its devouring Him like the rest of the dead was not pleasing, for it has no authority over the Holy One, and corruption cannot come upon Him...

Just as when a man takes poison in the food given for life, and realizes in himself that he has eaten poison in the food, he vomits the food mixed with poison from his belly, but the effect of the poison remains working in his members, until the structure of the body dissolves little by little and corrupts. So the death of Jesus abolished death, for by it life reigns and death is abolished, he to whom it is said: [O death, where is thy victory?] (1 Cor 55:15).
St. Aphrahat

entries.section: 3. His criticism of his friends' harshness

paragraphs.text: 14 The right of the sorrowful is known from his friend, though he forsake the fear of the Almighty. 15 My brethren have dealt deceitfully as a brook, as the stream of brooks they pass away; 16 Which are turbid with hail, and the snow is hid in them. 17 When they flow, they are cut off; when they grow hot, they dry up out of their place. 18 The caravans turn aside from their way; they go into the waste, and perish. 19 The caravans of Tema looked, the travellers of Sheba hoped for it. 20 They were ashamed because they had been confident; they came thither, and were abashed. 21 For now ye are become like it; ye see a blow, and are afraid. 22 Did I say, Give me something, or from your substance bribe on my behalf? 23 Or, Deliver me from the hand of the adversary, or redeem me from the hand of the tyrants? 24 Teach me, and I will hold my peace: and cause me to understand wherein I have erred. 25 How forcible are upright words! but what doth your reproof prove? 26 Do ye think to reprove words, when the speech of one in despair is for the wind? 27 Nay, ye fall upon the fatherless, and dig a pit for your friend. 28 Now therefore look upon me; for I will not lie to your faces. 29 Return, let there be no injustice; return again, my right is in it. 30 Is there injustice in my tongue? or cannot my palate discern perverse things?
The right of the sorrowful is known from his friend, though he forsake the fear of the Almighty [14].

Job rebukes his friends for their violence and harshness. Truly only Eliphaz spoke, but signs of acceptance and agreement appeared from the other two friends. Job feels that their harshness has become a new reason to wish for death, for what rest has he in this world if his friends who came to console him have become his tormentors?

It is the right of the sorrowing man that those who are at ease should show him sympathy, and display pure love to him, and cheer his heart, and listen to his complaint, and mingle his tears with their tears. This is what is fitting for them as members with the sorrowing one in the same one body.

He who does not show tenderness to the sufferer has forsaken the fear of the Almighty, that is, has lost the fear of the Lord, for how can the love of the Lord and His fear be established in one who does not care about the pains of his brother (1 Jn 3:17)?
Are trials the touchstone of friendship? They reveal true friends from those who claim friendship. [A brother is born for adversity] (Prov 17:17).

* There are two commandments of love: the love of God and the love of our neighbor. By the love of God the love of neighbor comes into being. And by the love of neighbor the love of God is strengthened. For he who truly does not care for the love of God knows nothing of how to love his neighbor, and when we advance in greater perfection in the love of God we suckle the milk of love toward our neighbor.

Because the love of God begets the love of neighbor, therefore when the Lord spoke with the voice of the Law and uttered the words "Thou shalt love thy neighbour," it was preceded by His saying: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God" (Mt 37:22; Deut 5:6, 10, 12)... Again the love of God is strengthened by love of our neighbor, and John testified to this, saying: "He that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?" (1 Jn 20:4)... By this a wise man rightly says: [A friend cannot be known in prosperity: and an enemy cannot be hid in adversity] (Sir 8:12).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* It is not enough to show mercy, but it is fitting for us to give it generously, with a bountiful spirit, and not only a bountiful spirit but a joyful, cheerful spirit...

And he stressed the same point strongly when he wrote to the Corinthians to urge them to generosity, saying: "He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully" (2 Cor 9:6). And to correct their disposition he says: "Not grudgingly, or of necessity" (2 Cor 9:7)... For if you grieve while you do mercy, you are harsh and violent.

If you are sad, how can you support those who are in sorrow...? This is the reason for saying "he that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness," for how can he who receives the Kingdom be sad of countenance?! Who remains gloomy of look while receiving the forgiveness of his sins? Therefore do not think of your spending of money (work of mercy), but of the overflow you receive through the spending. For if he who sows rejoices though he sows uncertain as to the harvest, how much more he who ploughs the heavens? For you give only little to receive much... By two mites the widow was reckoned to have surpassed those who offered many talents, and this because of her generous spirit.
* The strong is joined to the weak and supports him, and does not allow his perishing.

Again if he is joined to a slothful person he raises him up and urges him to work. It is said: "A brother helped by a brother is as a strong city." This is not surpassed by distance of space, nor heaven, nor earth, nor death, nor any other thing, but it is stronger and more effective than all things. This, though it proceeds from one soul, is able to embrace many at once.
Hear what Paul says: "Ye are not straitened in us, but ye are straitened in your own bowels... be ye also enlarged."
St. John Chrysostom * "A faithful friend is the medicine of life" (Sir 6:16).

There is no remedy as effective in healing pains as the sincere friend who comforts you in your afflictions, and manages you in your troubles, and rejoices in your success, and grieves in your calamities. He who has found such a friend has found a treasure. For the faithful friend has no equal, and the weight of gold and silver does not equal the goodness of his faithfulness (see Sir 6:14-15).
* Rightly may you have a friend whom you call "half of my soul."
* There is no true friendship unless you make it like a joint that welds souls, so they cleave together by the love poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit.
* There is no remedy as effective for healing pains as the sincere friend who comforts you in your afflictions.

entries.section: 3. His criticism of his friends' harshness

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine My brethren have dealt deceitfully as a brook, as the stream of brooks they pass away [15].

When they came together to console him, and remained seven days and seven nights silent, he expected from them a word of consolation that would quench the inner flame, but they pounced on him savagely like those who betray him, heaping false accusations on him, and pouring on his wound what inflames it, instead of offering oil to soothe its inflammation.

* [My nearest acquaintances did not support my needs]. Merely because God ignored him, his relatives made light of him amid such pains. For every time God draws away, man is deprived of his refuge, and all become against him as enemies. He says no one knew me in my trial. But this is in the seriousness that [all who used to honor me are now against me](c). It is exceedingly bad that a person should trample under his feet a man lying prostrate. It seems to me that he was alluding by this to his friends who were with him.

* Had he not been wicked he would not have become your enemy. So desire good for him, and his evil will end, and he will no longer be your enemy. He is your enemy not because of his human nature but because of his sin!

St. John Chrysostom Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that Job likens his friends to those who fear the ice that freezes from below and the snow falling upon them from above. They trample with their feet on those on whom temporal earthly trials have come, since they seek the glory of the world, and they do not realize that heavenly punishment will come upon them like snow falling upon them, from which they cannot escape.

* Let us follow Him while He is persecuted and fleeing from the distress caused by His opponents, so that we too may [go up into a mountain and sit with Him](d). Thus we rise to a glorious grace, higher than everything, and reign with Him. As He Himself said: [Ye which have followed me in my trials, when the Son of man shall sit in the throne of his glory, in the regeneration, ye also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel] (Mt 19:28; Lk 22:28).

entries.section: 3. His criticism of his friends' harshness

paragraphs.text: St. Cyril the Great Which are blackish by reason of the ice, and wherein the snow is hid [16].
They came in the appearance of a brook that offers water to the thirsty, yet they offered him water laden with mud, in which the ice is hid, and which cannot be drunk.

Job groans because of the muddy consolations of his friends, which are full of mire. For out of the dregs of their earthly hearts they offer mire, and out of the coldness of their love they offer snow. So it is with every soul that places its hope in the consolations of men: it receives nothing but mire and ice, which, instead of refreshing wounded souls, crush them by the earthly, temporal thinking and the spiritual coldness that they conceal.

But whoever receives the consolations of the Holy Spirit, which lift the soul up to heaven, free it from the mire of this world, and grant it the warmth of the Spirit, has his earthly heart changed by the water of the Spirit into a heavenly paradise. The Spirit removes from within him every love of earthly things, so that he sings, "[He] hath made us sit together in heavenly places." He scatters every coldness of the soul, bestowing a surpassing flame of love that all the waters of the world cannot quench.
* He (the Holy Spirit) is called the Comforter, because He comforts and gladdens those who are in tribulations.

St. Macarius the Great * The Holy Spirit whom He would send was called the Comforter, given this title because of His work. For He not only gives rest to those whom He finds worthy and delivers them from every grief and disturbance in the soul, but at the same time grants them a sure joy that never dissolves. An eternal joy dwells in their hearts, where the Holy Spirit dwells.
* It is impossible for anyone to receive the grace of God unless he has the Holy Spirit, in whom are all the gifts of God.

St. Didymus the Blind * When the soul is filled with the fruit of the Spirit, it is stripped entirely of gloom, distress and weariness, and puts on spaciousness, peace and joy in God, and opens in its heart the door of love for all people.

St. Isaac the Syrian * The kingdom of the pure soul is within his heart; the sun that shines in it is the light of the Holy Trinity; the air of its breeze is the Holy Spirit the Comforter; those who dwell there with him are the natures of the pure spiritual beings; and their life, joy and delight is Christ, the radiance of the Father...
* Whoever looks within himself to our Lord, and whose soul is mingled with His light, has his heart filled with joy.

entries.section: 3. His criticism of his friends' harshness

paragraphs.text: The Spiritual Elder What time they wax warm, they vanish: when it is hot, they are consumed out of their place [17].

Job likens his friends to a brook that has become dry because of the heat, with not a drop of water in it to drink. Travelers turn aside to it, hoping to quench their thirst and the thirst of their animals; they leave the road of their journey and go to it over great distances, almost losing their way, only to be surprised by its dryness, and so shame comes upon them.
It did not stop at there being mud in the waters of the brook; rather, it quickly dries up, and Job goes to it to drink, and finds a dry streambed.

What is meant by the word "wax warm"? Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that those on whom chastisements fall have their minds become hot, inflamed with the fires of fruitless remorse, because they do not think of eternal things but are occupied with temporal glory. Their remorse therefore crushes them all the more, and they melt away in their place.

* [You who are terrified before me, behold, they have cast me down like ice or thick snow, which, when it melts at the approach of the heat, can no longer be distinguished](e). He says: It is as though sorrows have pressed upon me from every side, and those subject to me and my companions have become against me. Not only has the law of love been annulled, but even the awe that leads to obedience has vanished. As for me, who wrestle with trials and violent passions, I have become like frozen snow, which, when the season of heat comes, dissolves and vanishes and no trace of it remains. It leaves no signs behind it, because the king, who is I, sits on a dunghill. The one who wore purple has become utterly naked outside the city. He sits outside to spend the night, he who formerly dwelt in splendid dwellings, whose houses were overlaid with gold and silver in abundance. He who was surrounded by many servants is now forsaken. He who had many sons and inherited crowns has suddenly come to ruin; he has lost all the wealth of his house.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * This garment that you put on within Baptism, O man, has light for its warp and Spirit for its weft, and it is flame. The Father prepared it for you, the Son wove it for you, and the Spirit fashioned it for you. You went down into the waters and put it on divinely. The Trinity gave fire in Baptism to burn up iniquity and that souls may live with God.

entries.section: 3. His criticism of his friends' harshness

paragraphs.text: St. Jacob of Sarug The paths of their way are turned aside (the caravans turn aside from their way); they go to nothing, and perish (they enter the wilderness and perish) [18].

The brook turned away from those in need of it, so that the thirsty find no water to drink. So the friends, with their consolations, moved far away from Job, and became like a stream of water that flees from the thirsty. But the Holy Spirit the Comforter waters the soul and satisfies it, so that it needs nothing.

* It is known, my brethren, that each of us seeks his rest and his joy, but he does not seek it as he ought, nor where it is to be found. Everything depends on distinguishing true joy from false joy; on the contrary, we are often deceived by the phantoms of vain joy and false good.

The miser, the arrogant, the glutton and the lustful each seeks joy, but one places his joy in amassing great wealth, another in the honor of ranks and dignities, another in delicious food and drink, and another in satisfying his unclean desires. None of them seeks his joy as he ought, nor where it is to be found; therefore none of them finds it, though all of them desire it.

Everything in the world cannot satisfy the soul and give it true joy. Why then do you weary yourself, foolish man, wandering in vain through many places, expecting to find good things with which to fill your soul and please your body?! Love one good that contains all goods, for in it alone you will find sufficiency.
Rest in the one great and universal Good, for in Him is sufficiency for everything.
And you, O my soul, bless the Lord, who satisfieth thy mouth with good things (Ps 103:2, 5).
St. Augustine The troops of Tema looked.

entries.section: 3. His criticism of his friends' harshness

paragraphs.text: The companies of Sheba waited for them (the processions of Sheba waited for them) [19].

The caravans of Tema and Sheba, the caravans of the merchants of those lands in the Arabian desert, looked to the waters and hoped to drink from them, but they were ashamed when the waters fled from them.

The blessed Job asks us to consider the paths of Tema and the ways of Sheba. Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that Tema is translated "south wind" and Sheba is translated "net." So the man who is not occupied with eternal things is like one upon whom the hot south wind blows, making his life dissolute as by the working of heat, and his feet become like those caught in a net or bound with the fetters of temporal things.
They were ashamed in that wherein they were confident.

entries.section: 3. His criticism of his friends' harshness

paragraphs.text: They came thither, and were ashamed [20].

When travelers in the wilderness head toward a well-known brook, they feel relieved because they are confident that they will find water to drink; but their confidence is utterly shattered when they find it dry. Such is Job's position toward his friends, in whom he thought he would find his consolations, only to find that they offer dry words and hearts without love, so that his hope in them is utterly disappointed.
His confidence was great that he would drink from the waters of the brook in the midst of the wilderness. But his assurance proved vain.
The friends came to Job and were ashamed, and as Pope Gregory (the Great) says, they were unable to shake the saint's mind with their harsh, bitter criticism.

These are the feelings of the blessed Job, that his friends have been put to shame, since with all their slanders they failed to bring him into despair, but they themselves became confused through the madness of their violent folly.

* [They are ashamed while I hope.] When the wicked direct their evils at the righteous, and see their inward hope shaken, they rejoice, because their deceit has borne fruit. They count the spreading of their errors the greatest gain they have acquired, rejoicing when their fellows perish. But when the hope of the righteous man is rooted within and is not shaken nor bowed to the earth by outward evils, the souls of the wicked are put to shame because they are unable to reach the depths of those in trial, and they are abashed, since their violence appears to have no purpose.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

In the opinion of Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem, Job says to them: "Look at your provinces subject to tribute, or at your neighbors, as at your roads. For you surely realize that, though they thought themselves more renowned than others, they are yet worthy of blame." Shame covers those who trust in their cities and their wealth, which Job had in abundance. When he was struck by trials, God removed all this from him; therefore their confidence in what is theirs is mistaken, and soon their pride will be annulled and their haughtiness will perish.
For now ye are like them.

entries.section: 3. His criticism of his friends' harshness

paragraphs.text: Ye see my casting down, and are afraid [21].

Job assures his friends that they have become like this deceptive brook, which waters no one and gives no consolation, but offers mirage and deceit... Such are the vain consolations of men; they are nothing at all!

"Ye see my casting down, and are afraid." It is as though he says: When I was in prosperity you flattered me, at a time when I did not need your flattery. And when the blow fell on me, you were afraid, and gave me bitterness instead of sweet words, and sharp criticism instead of consolations.

* [Now you have come and seen my blow, and you are afraid]... It is as though he says plainly: "I feared God when I was supported by prosperity and did not feel the wounds of the blow. But you did not fear God out of love; you were terrified of Him only through the blows of the rod.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. His criticism of his friends' harshness

paragraphs.text: Did I say, Bring unto me? or, Give a reward for me of your substance? [22]

Even though he had been reduced to a state of nothingness, he asked nothing from them, did not burden them in anything, did not ask for money, and did not put them to any expense. Why then do they take this painful attitude?

entries.section: 3. His criticism of his friends' harshness

paragraphs.text: Or, Deliver me from the enemy's hand? or, Redeem me from the hand of the mighty? [23]

He did not ask them to rescue him from an enemy or from the hand of the mighty, nor did he ask them to pay a ransom to deliver him. Thus Job was chaste in soul, even when he reached the bitterest condition of poverty.

entries.section: 3. His criticism of his friends' harshness

paragraphs.text: Teach me, and I will hold my tongue: and cause me to understand wherein I have erred [24].

Job differed with them in opinion, yet he was not stubborn, but was ready to accept the truth if he was in error, saying, "Teach me, and I will hold my tongue: and cause me to understand wherein I have erred."

In the midst of affliction, when someone rebukes us, especially if he is prejudiced against us, it is hard to listen to him or accept his counsel, as we fix our eyes on his evil prejudice and his exploitation of our distress to crush us. But Job, in the midst of affliction, declares to his friends that he is ready to listen and hear, and that if they point out a fault in his life he will correct himself.

What a wonderful picture of a soul that, though troubled by the bitterness of successive calamities, carries inner calm and a marvelous readiness to accept the counsel of his friends, whatever their intentions.

* "Teach me." Behold, you see Job listening to you in silence. In my sorrows, am I rebellious? Do I not feel the flood of the trial? I am not closed to accepting counsel. If you refute me because I am mistaken, you will see me hasten to correct the situation.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * This means: I asked nothing of you in the past, nor have I asked anything of you now, and you have come on your own initiative to find me and comfort me. Why then do you treat me as an enemy? [Teach me, and I will hold my tongue; if I am erring in anything, tell me.]
In any case, even under these circumstances I do not refuse to learn, as long as you speak what is profitable. And I will keep silent if you utter acceptable words.
Surely they cannot present clear accusations, but only guesses and conjectures.
Since a person's life was clearly full of virtues, it was fitting for them not to see in the chastisements what they say.

St. John Chrysostom God alone is absolutely perfect; He teaches the whole world and has no need to be taught. But we, as shepherds who serve by God who dwells in us, must always have an expanding heart, continuing to expand in order to receive from God, so that the fragrance of Christ may spread the more in us, for however great the expansion of our heart, it is only a tiny point in comparison with the depth of God's love and His infinite abundance.

A shepherd, even if he is a patriarch, if he is not always learning, his growth stops, his stagnation shows, and he stumbles his people in their spiritual growth. But to the extent that he bows low at the feet of the Lord, opens his heart to Him in prayer and in the study of the Holy Bible, and always listens with all his heart to learn the judgments of God in every matter, he grows in his fellowship with Him, and his flock grows with him as well.
* I cannot escape the work of teaching, since the priesthood has been laid upon my shoulders, though I tried to flee from it(f).
And I desire to strive in learning so that I may be able to teach.
For there is one Master (God) who alone does not learn what He teaches to all.
But men must learn before they teach, and receive from God their Teacher what they teach others.

St. Ambrose * Read the Holy Scriptures continually, and never lift the Holy Bible from your hand. Learn what you will teach others, holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that you may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers (1 Tim 3:4), "But continue thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of, knowing of whom thou hast learned them." [Be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you] (1 Pet 3:15).

entries.section: 3. His criticism of his friends' harshness

paragraphs.text: St. Jerome How forcible are right words! but what doth your arguing reprove? [25]

Job was not at ease with their manner of dealing with the matter; it was fitting for them to converse with him in a spirit of love and uprightness. But to use the method of criticism and rebuke based on groundless assumptions and conjectures is not for edification.

* [Well! The words of a true man seem to be worthless.] He says: It seems to me that I am unable to lead the battle, because my adversaries oppose me, and because when the truth is spoken and openly declared, there is no one to listen to it. For the words of the righteous man seem worthless to everyone.
St. John Chrysostom * [Since the words of a true man seem vain.] They are vain for those who are not truly so. But when I look at you, I do not know whom you are serving?!

entries.section: 3. His criticism of his friends' harshness

paragraphs.text: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Do ye imagine to reprove words, and the speeches of one that is desperate, which are as wind? [26]
Rebuking in a spirit of violence and with harshness will not bear fruit.

* [I ask of you neither a word nor strength, nor does your rebuke make me cease from speaking.] Yes, for even if it were fitting for you to judge my case according to the present circumstances, I do not entreat you... [for I do not seek strength from you]... I pay no heed to the sounds of this speech of yours, besides that you attack the fatherless and wrong one of your friends. He tells them that neither enmity nor friendship has any effect on you. In any case, if you wish, let me return to my saying: [I ask nothing.] For even if you take a stand of opposition, I repeat once more: my conscience does not rise up against me.

entries.section: 3. His criticism of his friends' harshness

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom Yea, ye overwhelm the fatherless, and ye dig a pit for your friend! [27]
As Job looks at their conduct toward the fatherless as toward their friends, he can repeat: [My conscience will not rebuke me by your words.]
He likens them, as they rebuke him while he is in a bitter state and in calamity, to one who humiliates an orphan unable to repel insults.

Job counted himself, having lost his children, like an orphan who has lost his parents, needing their tenderness so that they might be like God, since He is "a father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows" (Ps 68:5).
What grieves him is that they, being his friends, set a trap into which he falls, instead of supporting him to come out of the trap of successive trials.

* [Yes, you crush and exert yourselves to destroy me.] He shows how weak he is, for he calls himself [an orphan]. When love is wounded, it does not take away love; therefore he immediately complains that they are destroying him, and yet testifies that he is their friend.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Every monk (man) who seeks perfection and desires to strive lawfully in his spiritual combat must rid himself entirely of the sin of anger and wrath, and heed the warning addressed to him by the "chosen vessel," who says: "Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice" (Eph 31:4). And when he says: [Let all anger be put away from you], he excepts no one, whatever the necessity or what is profitable for us; and if need arises, any erring brother must be treated at once in a manner that will not make him like a person who went to treat a patient with a slight fever and entangled himself in his own anger and wrath, so that he lost his sight and insight. For he who wishes to heal another's wound must himself be sound and whole, suffering from no weakness, lest the saying of the Gospel be addressed to him: "Physician, heal thyself" (Lk 4:23), and lest, while he sees the mote that is in his brother's eye, he does not see the beam that is in his own eye. For how can he see well enough to cast the mote out of his brother's eye, he who has in his own eye the beam of anger? (Mt 7:3-5)

entries.section: 3. His criticism of his friends' harshness

paragraphs.text: St. John Cassian Now therefore be content, look upon me; for it is evident unto you if I lie [28].
Job was truthful with himself as with others; therefore he asked them to look closely at him and reconsider the matter, for he does not lie nor deceive anyone.

It is as though he says to them: Do not hunt for some of my words; look at my face, for even though I cursed the day of my conception and the day of my birth, which is what you are hunting for, I did not blaspheme my God.
Look closely at my sores, for they are unbearable, and what my tongue utters is not without reason. I am not contending with my God.
Return, I pray you, let it not be iniquity.

entries.section: 3. His criticism of his friends' harshness

paragraphs.text: Yea, return again, my righteousness is in it [29].

He returns and repeats, calling on them to think again; he asks them to return to themselves and not to be prejudiced against him, that they may see his right. For if he was not able to keep his calm, this does not mean that he lost his uprightness and nobility.

entries.section: 3. His criticism of his friends' harshness

paragraphs.text: Is there iniquity in my tongue? cannot my taste discern perverse things? [30]
He asks them whether he uttered with his tongue any word of blasphemy against God. What iniquity do they accuse him of? Is not what he uttered commensurate with the bitterness he suffers?
* When we expose our brother's sin, God exposes our sin, and when we tell people of our brother's crime, God does the same with us.

One of the Desert Fathers * Guard your tongues, by not speaking evil of your brethren. For he who speaks evil of his brother angers God who dwells in him. What each one does to his companion, he does to God.
St. Macarius the Great
Aim the arrows of Your love at my heart
* In the midst of the distress of this world my soul groans within me!
Does anyone perceive the weight of my cross?
Does anyone share the bitterness of my soul!
My troubles have flooded over my head, and my heart is greatly distressed.
* My Lord, expose my sin before my eyes; instead of crying out from the multitude of afflictions, let me sink into the depth of Your love, O Forgiver of sins and Deliverer of my soul from corruption!
I no longer see in my heart the enemy's arrows, aflame with fire.
Rather, in the midst of distress I see the arrows of Your love piercing my depths.
My whole being turns into a joyful wedding.
I sing and chant: I am wounded with love!
* I no longer look for comfort from men, nor do I feel any longer the triviality of my life!
Though my life has become like loathsome food without salt, by Your love I see You as the true salt who pours sweetness upon my depths.
In You I become the salt of the earth and the light of the world!
I no longer lament my weakness, for You are my strength and my help.
* In the midst of my distress the consolations of men have become a burden on my soul.
From their channels they offer muddy waters that hide ice within them.

But You, O heavenly Comforter, give me Your Spirit within me as a spring of living water, refreshing my soul and renewing my life; You remove all dust within me, and turn my desert into a heavenly garden.
There is no place for ice within me, for Your Spirit is a blazing flame of fire; who can quench it?
* My friends criticize me in order to justify themselves; they display their human wisdom without sincere love.
But You are the wonderful Teacher, You teach by the commandment full of love.
You speak with me that I may speak with You; You guide me and carry me in Yourself, and lift me up to the bosom of Your Father, justified in You!
* The rebukes of men often drive me to despair and crush my depths, so that I long for death.
Your rebukes carry a tender fatherhood: they wound and bind up, they uproot the tares from Your field, that You may plant Your paradise in my depths; Your firmness carries surpassing sweetness.
Your glances carry with the rebuke a surpassing tenderness!
* Be You my unique Friend; Your words are serious, full of sweetness!
Your glances grant hope, and crush my soul with love!
Meeting with You turns my heart into a temple for You.
Your touches set my whole being aflame that I may run to You!
Come and dwell in me, and I will dwell in You forever.

entries.section: 1. His days are like the days of a hireling, full of misery

paragraphs.text: 1 Is there not a struggle for man upon earth? and are not his days also like the days of an hireling? 2 As a servant earnestly desireth the shadow, and as an hireling looketh for the reward of his work: 3 So am I made to possess months of vanity, and wearisome nights are appointed to me. 4 When I lie down, I say, When shall I arise? the night is long, and I am full of tossings to and fro unto the dawning of the day. 5 My flesh is clothed with worms and clods of dust; my skin is broken, and become loathsome. 6 My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and are spent without hope.
Is not the life of man a struggle upon earth, and are not his days also like the days of an hireling? [1]

Job seeks an excuse for himself even in the extremity of his longing for death, supporting his opinion with the fact that the whole of man's life is toil, for he is "of few days, and full of trouble" (Job 14:1). Every man realizes that his days are few, and has justification for longing for death soon; therefore he wonders how they could regard him as having committed a heinous crime when he longed for it.

By saying "upon earth," which God has given to the children of men (Ps 115:16), he points to the lowliness of man, for his dwelling place is still below on earth, and not among the heavenly orders. Truly, he does not dwell in hell as the enemy of the good does, but for a time on earth. We live here temporarily, governed not by the fate of the Stoics nor the blind chance of the Epicureans, but by the counsel of God and His high, heavenly, divine plan.

As for the state of man here, it is "a struggle... like the days of an hireling," a state of continual striving, like soldiers in a battle that does not stop. Our enemies do not cease to oppose us, and they do not sleep at night. By death the battle is decided, either that we may be crowned eternally or be in shame and disgrace.

Our days are like the days of a hireling: we work all day long to give account at its end. Like a hireling who wishes the day to end quickly so that he may rest from the exhaustion of continual work. The hireling welcomes the passing of the day and the coming of night for rest, as the watchman rejoices at the passing of the night with the light of morning (Ps 130:6). The hireling longs for the end of the day, because "the sleep of a labouring man is sweet" (Eccl 5:12).

* Is not the life of man upon earth a struggle, and his life like the days of an hireling? Like the servant who lurks in the shadow for fear of his master, or like the hireling who looks for his wages? So also I wait for empty months and wearisome nights appointed to me. If I lie down I say, When will the day dawn? And if I arise I say again, When will evening come? I am full of pain from night until the dawn of morning. My body is putrid with the corruption of worms, and I have wetted the clods of the earth by scratching my sores, which discharge pus! My days are more trifling than empty talk, and are spent without hope. I say: [My bed will comfort me], but You [scare me with dreams, and terrify me through visions] (Job 1:7-6, 13-14) LXX.

* How wretched is the state of man! Like a hireling, he toils and labors for others while he himself is in want! And he cannot support himself except through the sympathy of others! Every day he endures a bitter bondage under the oppression of fear and dread. And lest his master seize him, he thinks he can hide from him in the shadow of this world, the wandering, roving, fleeing shadow! Think of the one of whom Sirach speaks in the book of the Wisdom of Sirach, Ecclesiasticus: [Every man sins on his bed, despising and saying to himself, Who sees me? Darkness is around me, and the walls hide me; whom do I fear?] (Sir 23:25-26). Do not think that such a man is a prodigal hireling...? Like the young man in the Gospel, of whom we read that he received his portion of the inheritance from his father, and when he came to be in want and in need, began to feed the flocks of others as a means of satisfying his hunger and paying his expenses with what he received (Lk 11:15-16); but he at least finally came to himself and repented, for he returned to his father, and did not conceal his sins but disclosed them.

But the man who thinks that God does not see him, He who sees everything, and that his iniquities can be hidden by darkness, lives in the shadow; yet he vainly thinks that he escapes observation, for the eye of the Lord, brighter than the sun, uncovers all secrets and hidden things, lights up every darkness, enters into the knowledge of the depth of the heart, and penetrates the heights and the depths (Jn 19:3-20; Sir 23:28). Therefore the man who thinks he is under the protection of darkness thinks in vain; for he cannot escape from the light that shines in the darkness, and the darkness comprehended it not (Jn 5:1).

Hence he is discovered as a fugitive and a wicked hireling, and is recognized before he can hide himself! For all things are known to the Lord before He examines them, not only with regard to past events, but future ones also.

* Whoever thinks that he hides his crime is lost in an empty hope, for that is mere feeble talk and not the truth. Truly, [the talk of sinners is empty and hateful] (Sir 27:14); it yields no fruit, only weeping! For [the talk of a fool is like a burden in the way] (Sir 21:19), and what is sin but a weight? It is a weight on the shoulders of the wayfarer in this world, so that he is weighed down with a heavy load of guilt! If he is unwilling to submit to the carrying of the burden, he must turn to the Lord who said: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Mt 28:11).

St. Ambrose * God is in His saints when they are tried, and holiness follows trial. It is impossible for anyone, even a saint, to pass through this world without trial. As Job says: [The life of man upon earth is a struggle (warfare)] (Job 7:1).

* We read in the book of Job how, while the first messenger of evil was yet speaking, there came also another (Job 1:16). And in the same book it is written: [Is there not here a trial?](a) and according to the better Hebrew text: "There is a warfare against man upon earth." We strive in this life that we may be crowned in the life to come, and for this purpose we risk our lives in the battle of this world (Mt 4:1-11)(b). Scripture testifies of Abraham that God tried him (Gen 22:1-19). For this reason also the Apostle says: [We glory in tribulations... knowing that tribulation worketh patience, and patience hope, and now hope maketh not ashamed] (cf. Rom 5:3-5). And in another place: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? As it is written, For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter" (Rom 8:35-36). The prophet Isaiah comforts such persons with the words: [You who are weaned from the milk, drawn from the breasts, behold trial upon trial, yea, and hope upon hope] (Isa 28:9-10) LXX. As the Apostle expressed it: "The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us" (Rom 8:18).

St. Jerome * When you flee from Egypt you come to very high ascents of work and faith. You face a tower, a sea and waves. The way of life is not traveled without the waves of trials. The Apostle says: "All that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution" (2 Tim 3:12). Job also declared no less than this: [Our life upon earth is a trial] (Job 7:1).

Origen * Job in turn repeated the saying of Eliphaz: Yet man is born unto trouble (Job 5:7). What does this mean for Job? He came to the final conclusion that this is not the only injustice, but that it springs from the very nature of man, which provokes these trials, as God decrees that the life of man must be painful. But Job added "upon earth," since it will no longer be so "in heaven."
St. John Chrysostom * What is this life but a fullness of snares?
We walk among snares (Sir 9:20); we live among many trials. [What is the life of man upon earth but a state of trial?] (Job 7:1) LXX.
He did well to add "upon earth," because there is one whose life is in heaven.
His life "upon earth" is the wages of a hireling, all toil and distress, feebler than vain tales (Job 7:1-2, 6) LXX, swimming in words and overflowing with words.
Its dwelling is in houses of clay, and life itself is mire. There is no steadiness of mind, nor endurance. By day man longs for night, and by night he seeks the day (cf. Job 7:4).

St. Ambrose * The evils that come upon you will pass, and he whom you await with patience will come. He will wipe away the sweat of toil. He will dry every tear, and there will be no more weeping. Here below we must groan amid trials, as Job asks: "[What is the life of man upon earth but a trial?"] (Job 7:1).
* My evil sorrows contend with my good joys, and on which side victory will be won I do not know.
Woe is me! Have mercy on me, O Lord!
Woe is me! Behold, I have not hidden my wounds!
You are the Physician, and I am sick.
You are merciful and I am wretched. [Is not the life of man upon earth a trial?]
Who desires sources of provocation and hardships? You command that we endure troubles, not that we love them.
You have commanded us to endure, not to love them. For there is no man who loves what he endures, though he must endure.

* Do not think that you are without sin while you are in this life, for we read of this in Holy Scripture: [Is not the life of man upon earth a trial?] Therefore, as long as we are in this body, you must say in prayer, as the Lord taught us: [Forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive them that trespass against us]. Remember to forgive quickly. If anyone sins against you and asks forgiveness, then you can pray sincerely and obtain forgiveness of your sins.

* [Human life upon earth is a trial] (Job 1:7) LXX; no one is ever in complete safety, nor ought he to be, until he comes to that city from which no friend departs and into which no enemy enters. Now, while we are in the very glory of the Church, we recognize the voices of our trials, and as members of Christ we submit to our Head in the bond of love, and support one another with a common spirit, and we say from the Psalms what we find in them about the martyrs who went before us, saying that trials are common to all men from the beginning to the end.
* The more (a person) loves his heavenly homeland, the more his earthly journey becomes in itself a great trial... In this trial, that is, in this life, whoever stands firm above it seeks God.
* You women indeed live in chastity, holiness, purity and virginity, and yet what is your life here? Are you not humbled when you hear: [What is human life upon earth but a trial?] (Job 7:1) LXX?
Does not the saying: [Woe unto the world because of offences!] (Mt 18:7) draw you away from self-reliance in pride?
Are you not afraid lest you be counted among the many whose love waxes cold because iniquity abounds (Mt 24:12)?
Do you not beat your breasts when you hear: "Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall" (1 Cor 10:12)?
Amid these divine warnings and human dangers, do we find it hard to urge holy virgins to humility?

* It is not fitting for any man to feel secure in this life, which in its entirety is called a trial (Job 1:7). For he who has been able to attain a better state than the evil he was in, let him not turn from the better to the worse. Our only hope, our only confidence and our only sure promise is Your mercies.
* I say: Oh! that I had wings like a dove! for then would I fly away, and be at rest!
Then I would wander far off and remain in the wilderness.
Yet even in the wilderness I shall perhaps have the same experience, for it is said: [I waited for him that saveth me from faintness and from the tempest] (Ps 55:8) LXX.
Truly, the life of man upon earth is a life of trial.

* No one is certain of that eternal life which God, who cannot lie, promises to the children of the promise before the times of eternity. No one is certain unless he completes his life, which is a state of trial upon earth (Job 7:1). For God urges us to persevere in it until the end of this life, as we say to Him every day: "Lead us not into temptation" (Mt 6:13).

* There is no man of whom men can say with complete assurance that he is righteous until he departs from this world. For in his life, which is a trial upon earth, he that standeth must take heed lest he fall (1 Cor 10:12).

* There we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is (1 Jn 3:1). But now, as long as the corruptible body presseth down the soul (Wis 9:15), and human life upon earth is wholly a trial (Job 7:1), in His sight shall no man living be justified (Ps 143:2).
* It has been shown sufficiently that in this life, which is wholly a trial, no one ought to boast as though he were free from all sins.

* Who but the proud man thinks he can live thus without needing to say to God: [Forgive us our debts]? Such a person is not a great man, but one puffed up with vanity, and an opponent of God, who giveth grace abundantly to the humble (Jas 4:6; 1 Pet 5:5).

St. Augustine * [Are not his days like the days of an hireling?]... So the days of man, when they are imbued with the knowledge of the truth and of eternal things, are compared to the days of a hireling, for he counts the present life as his road and not his city, a struggle and not the palms of victory. Seeing that he is far from his reward, he withdraws the more slowly to draw near to his goal...

Now it has been said by the voice of the Savior: "My kingdom is not of this world" (Jn 18:36). So all of us who have been given hope in heaven put on the troubles of the present life and busy ourselves with caring for others. For it often happens that even if we are compelled to serve the children of perdition, we oblige ourselves to render to the world what is the world's, and to care for what belongs to others, that we may receive the reward that is ours. So we busy ourselves faithfully with the affairs of others until we reach our reward. In contrast to this, the Truth says to some: [And if ye have not been faithful in that which is another man's, who shall give you that which is your own?] (Lk 16:12).

So the citizens of the upper land(c) say to their Creator the words of the Psalmist: [For thy sake we are killed all the day long] (Ps 44:22). And Paul says: [I die daily, brethren, for your glory] (cf. 1 Cor 15:31); and also: [For the which cause I also suffer these things: nevertheless I am not ashamed: for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day] (2 Tim 1:12)...

* We should notice that he did not say that trial attends the life of man, but described it as having itself become a trial. For since (man) had freedom of will, he turned aside from the upright form in which he was created and became subject to a base state of corruption. While the life of man brought forth harm to itself from itself, it became itself the very thing into which it had fallen... The life of man has in a certain way become a "trial." For even if we restrain ourselves so as not to sin, while we practice good works the remembrance of evil works overshadows us with a mist of the soul.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Pope Gregory (the Great) presents to us many examples of how the life of man, even in his spiritual striving, has become a "trial" from which he suffers.

For example, he mentions that when a man strives to abstain from a luxurious life carried to excess, this abstinence or asceticism can become a trial for him. By asceticism his face becomes pale, and when others notice his pale face they consider him worthy of honor and praise him, and through their praise vainglory creeps into the mind of the ascetic.

He gives us another example: a man may be granted knowledge of the divine Law, and he rejoices that he has received more understanding than others, and is lifted up with a joy that carries selfishness, and by his haughtiness spoils the gift of understanding he has received. On the day of judgment his state will be worse than that of others by the very thing in which he appeared more splendid than others in this life.

Thus he presents many examples of various virtues that turn to his destruction because of the corruption of his nature, so that what is for edification becomes the very cause of his perdition, because his life is a "trial."
St. Augustine asks, since it is said in the book of Job [Is not the life of man upon earth a trial?] (Job 1:7) LXX, why do we pray: "Lead us not into temptation"?

He answers that we must distinguish between two kinds of trials. The first kind is that in which there is an inducement to sin; of this it is said: "Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of God" (Jas 13:1). And there is a trial for proving, of which it is said: "For the Lord your God proveth (trieth) you, to know whether ye love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul" (Deut 3:13). God knows what is in the heart; what is meant here is "that we ourselves know" what is in our hearts.

* This I know, that the life of man upon earth is a trial (Job 1:7), and that there is a heavy yoke upon the sons of Adam (Sir 1:40). But what pleases me the more is to discuss the question concerning this building, when we say that we are sojourners or strangers on earth, since we have found our upper city, where we receive the earnest here, and when we reach it we shall not leave it.

entries.section: 1. His days are like the days of a hireling, full of misery

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine As a servant earnestly desireth the shadow, and as an hireling looketh for the reward of his work [2].
The servant who toils in the heat of the day longs for the shadow; so Job longs to depart from the day of this world by death, to find shade in the grave.

The lengthening of the shadow points to the end of the day with its toils, when the worker longs to end his day. In India time was measured by the length of a person's shadow. When a man was asked about the length of his working day, he was asked to stand in a sunny place and the length of his shadow was measured, and they would tell him the time. So the one who wishes to leave his work often says, How long is my coming shadow?

* "Deliver me, O Lord, from mine enemies: I flee unto thee to hide me" (Ps 9:143). I who once fled from You, now flee to You. Adam fled from the face of God and hid among the trees of paradise, and of him it is said in the book of Job: [As a servant fleeing from his master, and finds a shadow] (Job 2:7) LXX. He fled from the face of his master and found a shadow. Woe to him if he continues in the shadow, lest it be said afterward: [All those things are passed away like a shadow] (Wis 5:9).

St. Augustine * [Like a servant who eagerly longs for the shadow, and a hireling who looks for the end of his work, so I possess months of vanity, and number wearisome nights...](d) Paul runs panting to lay hold of this shadow, longing to depart and to be with Christ (Phil 1:23). This shadow is already possessed by those who say with all the desire of their hearts: "We have borne the burden and heat of the day" (Mt 20:12)... This is the reason why Paul is always lifted up with boldness in the face of calamities, for he is [like a hireling who looks for the end of his work]... for he declares that he was burdened above strength, saying: "We were pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life" (2 Cor 1:8). But how he wiped away from his soul the streams of this great toil with the towel of his reward, he tells us himself, saying: "For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us" (Rom 8:18). Thus, as a hireling looking for the end of his work, he is concerned to increase the reward.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 1. His days are like the days of a hireling, full of misery

paragraphs.text: So am I made to possess months of vanity, and wearisome nights are appointed to me [3].

In the midst of his suffering Job reckoned that his whole life had been wasted without profit, and thought that all the months of his life were evil and his nights misery. After the trial he was unable in his sickness to work, so he forgot all that he had done before in the days of his health and prosperity, but God will not forget them. He felt that his presence on earth was a burden on the community, for he was without work, and he did not realize how the Creator of heaven and earth cherishes him, and how many are blessed through him.

The believer longs for eternal rest as a shadow in which to take refuge after suffering the heat of the sun of trials and afflictions in this world. In this he realizes that his life is a short journey, not reaching a year or years, but counted months, vain months and cruel nights, nights of hardship and toil. It is a passing life, but toward a glorious eternity. The more we realize the shortness of time, the more we pass over rejoicing into eternity, indifferent to the heaviness of life and its troubles.

He counts our life as months of evil or months of vanity, and nights of evil or of hardship and toil, and they are counted and fixed, "appointed to us." He mentions the months that comprise the days, and does not forget the nights, for the believer cares about his salvation as a whole, or his life as one unit, as he cares about each night by itself. He cares about every small and great thing in his conduct, as about life as a whole.
When I lie down, I say, When shall I arise?

entries.section: 1. His days are like the days of a hireling, full of misery

paragraphs.text: The night is long, and I am full of tossings to and fro unto the dawning of the day [4].
His nights became exceedingly long, because sleep found no place in him, so that the minutes hardly pass, and at the same time he does not look forward to a day in which he may find rest.

Neither place nor time gives true rest to man, but the inner peace of the heart; whoever flees from pains by sleeping at night finds in his sleep anxiety and terrors perhaps more severe than what he suffers by day.

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees in these words the cries of the holy Church as long as she is in this life full of corruption; she laments, unsatisfied with the instability in which she is. She wishes to ascend by constant contemplation of God in order to find rest in Him, and to fortify herself in Him so as to serve her Creator with love, so that corruption cannot approach her and touch her. Sin corrupted the life of man and deprived him of stability, so that he is in constant struggle: if he rests, as at night, he seeks to work, and if he works, he seeks to rest. Since sin made him lose the possession of God, his mind no longer finds rest. His true rest is in God, the fountain of rest.
Pope Gregory has another interpretation, which is that sleep here indicates falling into sin, which brings corruption on man.

* This also can be understood in another sense. For sleep is lying prostrate in sin. If sleep were not a symbol of sin, Paul could not have said to his disciples: "Awake to righteousness, and sin not" (1 Cor 15:34). For the same reason he entrusts to his hearer the following: "Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light" (Eph 5:14). And also: "It is high time to awake out of sleep" (Rom 13:11).

By consenting to evil practices we perish by corruption, and by allowing images of evil deeds to arise in the heart we are defiled with the stains of dust; therefore he says: "My flesh is clothed with the filth of dust."
Pope Gregory (the Great)
My flesh is clothed with worms and clods of dust (clay).

entries.section: 1. His days are like the days of a hireling, full of misery

paragraphs.text: My skin is broken, and become loathsome (my skin is cracked and festered) [5].

His sores bred worms that filled his body, so that the worms around his body in his wounds were like a garment he wore, and he could not be rid of them. The scabs of the sores became like heaps of dust, and his skin shrank and was torn. Thus who can describe the sight of Job, who had become like a heap of dust loaded with worms, with an exceedingly foul smell, corruption creeping in it; whoever looks at him is utterly disgusted.
* The sores of his body were preparing for him the crown of heaven.

entries.section: 1. His days are like the days of a hireling, full of misery

paragraphs.text: St. Jerome My days are swifter than a weaver's shuttle, and are spent without hope [6].

If Job longs for the swiftness of death, it is because his condition reveals it. He believed that his state was hastening him to the end of his life on earth, that only a few days were left to him, for naturally his body cannot resist this disease. His life ends without hope of returning to his former prosperity.

entries.section: 2. Death puts an end to present misery

paragraphs.text: 7 O remember that my life is wind: mine eye shall no more see good. 8 The eye of him that hath seen me shall see me no more: thine eyes are upon me, and I am not. 9 As the cloud is consumed and vanisheth away: so he that goeth down to the grave shall come up no more. 10 He shall return no more to his house, neither shall his place know him any more.
O remember that my life is wind: mine eye shall no more see good [7].

Perhaps Job noticed that his friends, though they had not interrupted him in his speech, could no longer bear to look at him in his hideous appearance, nor to hear his voice; therefore he turned from speaking with them to speaking with God, for He alone is long-suffering, listens to wounded hearts, and does not scorn sick bodies however disfigured their appearance. He cried out to God, saying: "Remember that my life is wind." Thus Job wished to draw God's tenderness and compassion, as an exceedingly weak creature whose life passes swiftly without stopping, as the wind passes. As the Psalmist says: "Remember that they were but flesh; a wind that passeth away, and cometh not again" (Ps 78:38-39).

Thus Job kept before his eyes a plain truth about the shortness of life, and his certainty of his death and of not escaping it. This truth makes us not put our hope in the world, nor attach ourselves to visible things, nor be ruled by the things of the senses. For our happiness here consists in our realizing that we are strangers who must walk faithfully, and with a rejoicing spirit, until we pass over to our permanent dwelling.

* The eye of the dead sees good no more, for the soul no longer practices good works once it is stripped of the body. For this reason the rich man who was perishing in the fire of hell knew that he could not amend his state by good works, for he does not return again to practice what is for his good, but asked for his brothers whom he left behind: [I pray thee therefore, father Abraham, that thou wouldest send him to my father's house: for I have five brethren; that he may testify unto them, lest they also come into this place of torment] (Lk 16:27-28).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
The eye of him that hath seen me shall see me no more.

entries.section: 2. Death puts an end to present misery

paragraphs.text: Thine eyes are upon me, and I am not! [8]

Job noticed that his friends had surrounded him and sat around him seven days without speaking, but while looking at him they were like the blind, not seeing Job as he truly was; but the eyes of God look upon him in the midst of his trial, even though, because of the severity of the calamities, he appeared as one who does not exist, or who has lost his life and being!

Man needs the Lord's looking upon him, for He alone looks at the heart and is able to comfort him, and even to renew him. When our Lord Jesus, in the midst of His trial, looked at Simon Peter, he could not bear the eyes of the Master, and he went out and wept bitterly, until he met Him again after His resurrection, and He raised him from the tomb of his denial and restored him to his pastoral work!
Job in his trial realized that there is no way to complain about what had befallen him by God's permission except to lift his complaint to God Himself.
Time will pass quickly and those who now look at us will not see us; [we go hence, and are no more] (Ps 39:13); we leave what is visible to enjoy the invisible.

By saying "thine eyes are upon me, and I am not," the righteous Job reveals that he trusts in God's care and providence for him, and that He will send him to eternity to enjoy it, not by any merit on Job's part. Therefore he says: "I am not"; for my part I die, but who raises me up but You? And who brings me into glory but You?

* [The eye of man shall not see me] [8]. For the [eye of man] is the tenderness of the Savior, who softens the hardness of our dryness when He looks upon us. So the Gospel testifies, saying: "And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord... And Peter went out, and wept bitterly" (Lk 22:61-62). But when the soul is stripped of the body, the "eye of man" no longer turns, for it will not save a man after his death, if grace did not grant him forgiveness before his death. Therefore Paul says: "Behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation" (2 Cor 6:2). So the Psalmist says: [For his mercy is for the one who is present] (cf. Ps 118:1).

Whoever is not rescued by mercy now, in the present state, is handed over by justice alone to punishment. Solomon says: "And if the tree fall toward the south, or toward the north, in the place where the tree falleth, there it shall be" (Eccl 11:3). For at the moment of the fall of the human being, the Holy Spirit or the evil spirit receives the soul departing from the chambers of the body, and that spirit keeps it forever without change.
If it has been glorified, it is not cast into woes; nor, if it is cast into eternal woes, does it rise again to find a means of escape...

After the present life, man no longer "sees with the eye of man," therefore he adds at once: [Thine eyes are upon me, and I am not standing!] as though saying in plain words: When You come in sternness to judgment You do not look in order to save, but look in order to punish.
