The person to whom You have not turned in the present time with Your saving, compassionate care, You look upon afterward by the law of justice.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
As the cloud is consumed and vanisheth away.

entries.section: 2. Death puts an end to present misery

paragraphs.text: So he that goeth down to the grave shall come up no more [9].
In his speech with God, Job confesses that he is going to his last abode without return to this world; his life here on earth is like a cloud that moves and vanishes without return.

* When it is said: [The dead praise not thee, O Lord] (Ps 115:17), this shows that this life alone is the appointed time for repentance and forgiveness. [And he that goeth down to hell shall come up no more] [9]; those who take pleasure in this life are the ones who will praise God. But those who died in sins have no time left to praise after death like those who enjoy blessings. Rather they lament over themselves, for praise belongs to him who gives thanks, and wailing to him who is under punishment. Therefore the godly rise to praise, but those who died in sins have no time for confession (thanksgiving) afterward.

* Concerning the phrase: [So he that goeth down to the grave shall come up no more] (Job 7:9). Notice what follows, "He shall return no more to his house"; and since the whole world will come to an end, and every house will be laid waste, how shall he return again to his house when there shall be a new earth, different? But they ought to have heard Job say: "For there is hope of a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that the tender branch thereof will not cease. Though the root thereof wax old in the earth, and the stock thereof die in the ground; yet through the scent of water it will bud, and bring forth boughs like a plant. But man dieth, and wasteth away: yea, man giveth up the ghost, and where is he?"(e) He speaks with reproach and blame! He says, if the tree falls and lives again, shall not man live again, for whose sake all the trees exist? And lest you suppose that he sealed up the words, read what follows: and he says "If a man die, shall he live again?" (Job 14:14), and immediately adds: [I will wait till I rise]. And in another place: "And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet without my flesh shall I see God" (Job 26:19). And in Isaiah: "Thy dead men shall live, together with my dead body shall they arise" (Isa 26:19). And in Ezekiel: "Behold, O my people, I will open your graves, and cause you to come up out of your graves" (Ezek 37:12). And in Daniel: "And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt" (Dan 2:12).
St. Cyril of Jerusalem * It is as though he says plainly that whoever flies up on high (like the cloud) vanishes, for he boasts in himself, rushing to ruin.

* Rightly are the hearts of the despairing likened to clouds, for they become dark with the mist of error and dense with many sins, but when they vanish they pass away, for the flame of the last judgment shines upon them and they are scattered by the winds.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 2. Death puts an end to present misery

paragraphs.text: He shall return no more to his house, neither shall his place know him any more [10].

Job knows perfectly well that by his death he will no more return to his house in this world; he will own nothing, nor enjoy earthly things, nor carry on his temporal works. He leaves everything to the one who comes after him and takes his place.

"Neither shall his place know him any more": not only will Job not return to his place after his death, but the place and those who dwell in it will not know where Job is, for the connection between Job and those who live in his place is completely severed.
* Once a man is handed over to eternal punishments he is not called back again from there, where he could bind himself with love...
Pope Gregory (the Great)

When the Lord Christ healed the demoniac, "he said unto him, Go home" (Mk 5:19), that is, return to his inner depths, taking care not to sin again; but after death a man cannot return to his house to amend his inner depths so as not to sin.

* Man was created to contemplate his Creator, so that he may always seek to be in His likeness, and dwell in the delight of His love. But if he is driven out of himself by disobedience, he loses the foundation of his mind. He is left outside in the dark ways, wandering far from the dwelling of the true light.

* "Neither shall his place know him any more": for the place of man, not a local place, has become the Creator Himself, who created him to be in Him, as a place for man. But he left the place when he listened to the words of the deceiver, forsaking the love of the Creator... Yet there are very many who, after receiving the help of the Savior, have sunk into the darkness of despair and perished again in extreme despair, as they despise the medicines of mercy offered to them. And rightly is it said of him who is condemned to eternal perdition: "Neither shall his place know him any more." It is to be noticed in particular that he does not say, "and he knows his place no more," but, "neither shall his place know him any more." For the word "know" is ascribed not to the person but to the place, which with firmness says in the end to those who dwell in evil: "I know you not whence ye are" (Lk 13:25).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. A description of his wretched state

paragraphs.text: 11 Therefore I will not refrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul. 12 Am I a sea, or a whale, that thou settest a watch over me? 13 When I say, My bed shall comfort me, my couch shall ease my complaint; 14 Then thou scarest me with dreams, and terrifiest me through visions: 15 So that my soul chooseth strangling, and death rather than my life. 16 I loathe it; I would not live alway: let me alone; for my days are vanity.
Therefore I will not refrain my mouth;
I will speak in the anguish of my spirit;
I will complain in the bitterness of my soul [11].

When the prophet David perceived the vanity of temporal life he said: "I was dumb, I opened not my mouth" (Ps 39:9); but Job, knowing the same truth, did not stop speaking, but declared his complaint with bitterness in order to give his last testament to his friends and those around him.
It is fitting for us in our last breaths to confess our sins as we praise and thank God, that we may depart in the peace of God instead of complaint and murmuring.

* "I also will not refrain my mouth," for the man who is ashamed to confess the evil he has done [refrains his mouth]... Therefore the Psalmist says: [Let us come before his presence with confession] (Ps 95:2). We have received from Solomon: "He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy" (Prov 28:13). It is also written: [The righteous man is the first accuser of himself] (cf. Prov 18:17).

* [I will speak in the anguish of my spirit], for "the anguish of the spirit" prepares the tongue for speech, so that there is the voice of confession against the commission of evil. For it is fitting to keep in mind that the corrupt often confess sins, but they boast of them greatly and do not weep over them. But the elect express their bitter condemnation of themselves with tears, which disclose the words of confession. Therefore it is well that, after the blessed Job promised not to restrain his lips, he immediately added the anguish of the spirit.

[I will speak in the bitterness of my soul (spirit)]... The bitterness of the spirit has its own tongue in the heart of the righteous, and it speaks more precisely and is listened to more (than the bodily tongue). Therefore he did not say: "I speak in the bitterness of my spirit," but said: [I will speak (converse) with bitterness], since the power of grief takes each sin separately and stirs the mind, numbed, to lamentation.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* When you are occupied with some sin, be an accuser of yourself (Prov 18:17), and do not wait for others to bring the accusation. By this you become like a righteous man who accuses himself in the first speech he makes in court, or you are like Job, whom the multitude of the people in the city did not hinder from declaring his crime before all."
St. Basil the Great * The Father listens to you while you speak within yourself, and hastens to meet you. When you are still far off He sees you and runs.
He looks at what is in your heart, and hastens so that no one may delay you, and even embraces you.
His "meeting you" is His foreknowledge, and His "embracing you" is the declaration of His mercy and an expression of His fatherly love.
He falls on your neck to raise you, you who have fallen under the weight of sins, and to bring you back to heaven when you have turned toward the earth, that you may seek your Creator.
Christ falls on your neck, to deliver your neck from the yoke of bondage, and to make you bear His easy yoke (Mt 11:30)...
He falls on your neck by saying: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you" (Mt 11:28-29).
Thus the Lord embraces you when you repent.

entries.section: 3. A description of his wretched state

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose Am I a sea, or a whale, that thou settest a watch over me? [12]

David the Psalmist looked to God as he thought of his passing from the world, so he kept silent with his mouth in order that his heart might praise God and contemplate the glories God has prepared for him; but Job looked at himself and thought of his sufferings, and so was in a raging revolt, and gave himself an excuse by saying: "Am I a sea, or a whale?" [12]. Am I a raging sea without ceasing, that needs to be held to its limits? Or a dragon whose bridle must be held so that it does not devour all the fish of the sea?

* I am not in a strength like that of the sea, which You made great among creatures, and for its sake You placed sand around it as a guard, You who by Your command set the sea in its bounds and break its power...
Nor have I the malice of the dragon, for You set enmity between him and man.

You signified to him to keep himself far from man as his enemy, giving him a warning in this regard: "I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel" (Gen 3:15).

In any case: "Thou settest a watch over me" means that You set over me a malicious watcher, the traitor, who observes all my actions and all my words. He examines even my thoughts and betrays me in everything I do.

Moreover, he lays to my charge, in the form of an accusation, a matter that was not in my mind. I did not keep Your commandment in order to obtain passing happiness, but I love God for the sake of the life to come, as a faithful servant (Mt 24:25; 25:21, 23). The enemy made him a watcher over me; under his watch he was bound and fettered in a wretched state and with exceedingly cruel trials. And You stretched out the hand of Your help to him, and not to me, therefore the trials came upon me.

entries.section: 3. A description of his wretched state

paragraphs.text: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem When I say, My bed shall comfort me, my couch shall ease my complaint [13].
He hoped, as many people are accustomed to do, to find in sleep an escape from what had befallen him, and so he awaited the coming of night, that he might perhaps doze, if only for a while.

* In Holy Scripture the words "bed," "couch" or "cradle" made of the straw on which animals lie down are usually used to indicate the secrets of the depths of the heart. Therefore every single soul, pierced by the Bridegroom with the spears of holy love, says in the Song of Songs: "By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth" (Song 3:1)...

So the Truth says to those who love Him: "The kingdom of God is within you" (Lk 17:21). Again: "If I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you" (Jn 16:7), as though saying plainly: "If I do not withdraw My body from your attention concentrated on it, I will not lead you by the Comforter, the Spirit, and you will perceive the invisible." Therefore it is said by the Psalmist of the righteous: "Let the saints be joyful in glory: let them sing aloud upon their beds" (Ps 149:5), since, fleeing from harm to outward things, they are glorified in peace within the depths of their hearts.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* This resembles the angels, who do not sleep because they are always standing on guard. Therefore you speak the truth, and so you imitate the angels who do not sleep and who do not flee from facing the truth by means of unreal fantasies.

* A man sleeps after he enters into a state of absence, and during sleep the food is digested and the health of those who share in the table of the feast is preserved. Therefore the bride sleeps after the feast. This sleep is considered unusual, and differs from ordinary sleep, in which the person is not unaware of what is around him. The two are opposed to one another, for sleeping and waking follow each other. And we see in the bride a distinctive mixture of opposites: she says, "I sleep, but my heart waketh" (Song 2:5). What do we understand from this verse? This sleep resembles death, in which all the functions of sensation cease: there is no sight, hearing, smell, taste or sense of touch, but the blood pressure falls. A person forgets anxiety during sleep, the passion of fear is calmed, anger diminishes and anxiety over bitter trials lessens, and it makes the person unaware of evils. Therefore we learn from the bride that she was lifted up and boasts, saying: "I sleep, but my heart waketh."

St. Gregory of Nyssa * Cast off the sleep of heedlessness so that you may knock at the door of Christ. Paul asked that this door be opened to him to speak the mystery of Christ (Col 3:4); perhaps this is the door that John saw open: "After this I looked, and, behold, a door was opened in heaven: and the first voice which I heard was as it were of a trumpet talking with me; which said, Come up hither, and I will shew thee things which must be hereafter" (Rev 4:1). The door was opened to John and also to Paul, that they might receive for us loaves for our nourishment, because they persevered and knocked at the door in season and out of season (2 Tim 4:2), to restore life to the Gentiles who were weary and worn out from the way of the world with the abundance of heavenly food.

entries.section: 3. A description of his wretched state

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose Then thou scarest me with dreams, and terrifiest me through visions [14].
Night could not carry him away from weariness, nor sleep draw him out of distress; rather the dreams terrified him and the visions frightened him. The night became disturbing no less than the day.
We need the strong hand of God, who alone can keep us; behold our Keeper, who neither slumbers nor sleeps.
* What are we to understand here by dreams and visions but imaginings of the last examination at the judgment...
If dreams did not often bear deceptive images coming from our hidden enemy, the wise man would not refer to them by saying: [For dreams and vain imaginations have deceived many] (Sir 34:7).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. A description of his wretched state

paragraphs.text: So that my soul chooseth strangling, and death rather than my bones [15].
He did not care by what kind of death he died; what concerned him was that God would allow him to die. He does not seek deliverance from the affliction, but from temporal life as a whole.
I loathe it; I would not live alway.

entries.section: 3. A description of his wretched state

paragraphs.text: Let me alone; for my days are vanity! [16]

Besides the calamities that befell the blessed Job, whether concerning his possessions, the death of his sons, or his wife's opposition to him, St. John Chrysostom adds the following things, which made the trial exceedingly bitter:
[First: his lack of certain knowledge about the Kingdom of Heaven and the resurrection, of which he rightly spoke with sorrow: [I shall not live forever, so I must endure much] (Job 16:7) LXX.
Second: his sense that he had done many good works.
Third: his sense that he had done no evil.
Fourth: his supposition that what had befallen him came from God's hands; for if it had been from the hands of Satan, this would have lessened his distress.
Fifth: his hearing from his friends, who accuse him of evil, saying: "God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth" (Job 6:11).
Sixth: he sees those who live in evil in prosperity, and puffed up against him.
Seventh: he has no other before him to look to who has suffered such things.]

* [Let my life be freed from my spirit, and my soul from my body, and my bones from death. For I shall not live forever, so I am bound to endure patiently]... He had the desire to depart from here... until his body was dissolved. Job did not care about the stripping of his bones. Why is this? Because he says that the present life is quickly passing. "I shall not live alway." It is clear that Job is speaking of earthly life. How is he to be long-suffering in this matter? Only because the attainment of happiness requires long-suffering and patience, that is, the happiness to come... Job's speech clearly hints that material life is weak, corruptible, unstable, quickly passing, and does not bear the marks of eternal life.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem

entries.section: 4. A cry to God for his deliverance

paragraphs.text: 17 What is man, that thou shouldest magnify him? and that thou shouldest set thine heart upon him? 18 And that thou shouldest visit him every morning, and try him every moment? 19 How long wilt thou not depart from me, nor let me alone till I swallow down my spittle? 20 I have sinned; what shall I do unto thee, O thou preserver of men? why hast thou set me as a mark against thee, so that I am a burden to myself? 21 And why dost thou not pardon my transgression, and take away mine iniquity? for now shall I sleep in the dust; and thou shalt seek me in the morning, but I shall not be.
What is man, that thou shouldest magnify him? and that thou shouldest set thine heart upon him? [17]

In his distress Job felt that man is too trivial to be the object of God's regard, contention and testing. It is as though he says to God: Why do You occupy Yourself with so weak a creature? Why do You visit him from the morning and try him? He is too trivial to stand before You, utterly unable to enter the crucible of trials. The Psalmist says: "What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?" (Ps 8:4).
Perhaps Job stood amazed before God's surpassing care for man; for despite man's weakness and lowliness, God is occupied with him, testing him in order to prove him and glorify him.

Job marvels that God sets His heart upon man so that he is dear to Him, like a person to whom He is tender, and makes a place for him in His divine heart. He visits him every morning with new mercies, as a friend takes care for his friend's love for him, or as a physician asks every morning about the state of his patient. And every moment He tests him, like one who feels his pulse and is jealous over him.

In his discourse on the creation of man, St. Gregory of Nyssa sees that God created the world with all artistry as a great palace prepared for Adam and Eve as king and queen. And that God offered man every possibility of happiness and authority over the creation that God brought into being for his sake.

In his discourse on true greatness and false greatness, St. Jacob of Sarug spoke creatively, bringing out God's surpassing love for man. He adorned the heavens with stars and prepared the earth with beautiful creatures, and gave both to man to be under his authority. God willed for man to be possessor of glory and authority, but through the envy of the devil he fell into false greatness, and so lost his true greatness. Yet God allowed Adam to return to what he had been, dust, not to humiliate him, but that he might not live forever having lost his greatness; rather, by discovering his true nature he receives glory through the work of the Savior.

* God glorifies man by enriching him with an abundance of the gift of reason, visits him by the inspiration of grace, and glorifies him by the greatness of the gift of virtue; for although he is nothing in himself, through the generosity of God's compassionate love He grants him to be a partaker in the knowledge of God Himself. The Lord sets His heart upon man, and thus glorifies him, and then brings him to judgment after He has given him His gifts, weighs his merits with precision, and with firmness judges the burdens of life, and brings precise punishment after he has been given many advantages.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Which of the earthly creatures was created in the image of God except man?
And to whom was given authority over all nature and its creatures, to hold as his own?

It is an original honor that crowns his brow and exalts him to heaven, above the stars, loftier than the sun in majesty and dignity... And although he is lower in rank than the angels because of his attachment to a material body, he was granted power to understand and know his Lord and Creator.
St. Basil the Great * He stretched out the heavens, and set in them all the lights: the sun, the moon and all the stars, which move about in it.
The heavens did not ask, but He adorned them with fair sights that dazzle the eyes of beholders.
The sun has no mouth with which to ask for a great light to shine on all creation.
He adorned all kinds of birds and beasts with delightful and brilliant colors from the beginning.
He adorned creation, and in its perfection its adornment did not change.
He perfected the house of all creation, as it is said, and adorned it with beautiful forms.
The house stood, a building full of wonder.
He filled it all with beauty, with adornments that cannot be uttered.
And when He had perfected the house with all that is in it, the Maker sought to set in it one who is full of beauty.
He took dust and formed Adam, and breathed into his face the breath of life-giving life.
He perfected him, and he became a pattern full of wonder!
He made him in His likeness, and filled him with glory and splendor!
His light blazed, and the light of the sun went out before him because of the glory his Lord granted him when He created him.

St. Jacob of Sarug * Adam was not created to die, but to strive for immortality, and to show his trustworthiness. And to offer proof of it he added: [Who gave us the earnest of the Spirit](f)... And now He works through Baptism, and gives us a pledge that is not small: the Holy Spirit.

entries.section: 4. A cry to God for his deliverance

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom And that thou shouldest visit him every morning, and try him every moment! [18]

* With what did David sing in similar terms? [Lord, what is man, that thou takest knowledge of him? or the son of man, that thou makest account of him?] (Ps 144:3-4). Why did David say this about men, and what was his thought when he explained what follows: [Man is like to vanity: his days are as a shadow that passeth away](g). Why in all truth does God glorify this weak man, and give him regard in the present state of evil? The righteous ask God because of their ignorance... For He is [the maker of good things and the lover of mankind](h) (Wis 7:22), and visits often the one He has created and gives him great attention. Therefore David also adds: "Bow thy heavens, O Lord, and come down" (Ps 144:5; 18:9). By this he shows God's intense concern for men, for in bowing the heavens He Himself comes down to us, "the Word was made flesh" (Jn 1:14); He shared our condition, strengthening and fortifying our weakness. As for Job, he shows at length how much good comes to the man whom God remembers.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * [And that thou shouldest visit him every dawn (morning), and try him suddenly] [18]... Night turns to light when the darkness of our error is lit by the knowledge of the truth. Night turns to light when the splendor of righteousness lights our hearts, which the dense blindness of sin had covered. Paul saw the dawn appear in the minds of the disciples when he said: "The night is far spent, the day is at hand" (Rom 13:12).

But let us note that after God visits man at dawn, He tries him suddenly; for by His approach He lifts our hearts to the virtuous heights, and when He withdraws He allows him to be attacked by temptation. After receiving the gifts of the virtues, if the soul is not stirred by the assault of temptation it becomes puffed up, and thinks that what it has received is from itself...
So Elijah was visited at dawn, and he opened the doors of heaven with a word, but immediately he was tried, and fled to the wilderness as one without help, for fear of a lone woman (1 Kgs 19:1-3).

And so Paul, when he was caught up to the third heaven and penetrated the mysteries of paradise, received contemplation. Yet when he returned to himself he wrestled against the assaults of the flesh, and was subjected to another law in his members, and was grieved by its rebellion, seeing that the law of the Spirit was threatened (2 Cor 12:2 etc.).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 4. A cry to God for his deliverance

paragraphs.text: How long wilt thou not depart from me, nor let me alone till I swallow down my spittle? [19]
He asks God to lift His rod from him, if only for moments, that he may breathe.
St. John Chrysostom, in his treatise "Divine Providence," dealt with the problem of those who stumble in the love of God because of the afflictions that befall them:

* Let us then hasten to correct those who stumble because of affliction, forgetting God's providence and love, and spare them from falling under this penalty, making clear to them the cause of their sickness.
What is the cause of this great danger: disregard of God's providence?!

It is rashness and curiosity of thought. It is the desire to understand all the causes of the events that befall us, and the wish to contend against God's providence, which cannot be comprehended nor described, that providence which surpasses all examination and investigation! Yet man is not ashamed of this curious attitude, full of recklessness.

Who, then, surpassed Paul in wisdom? Tell me, was he not a chosen vessel? Did he not receive the surpassing grace of the Spirit, which cannot be uttered? Did not Christ speak in him? Did not God reveal to him things that cannot be uttered? Did he not hear what it is not lawful for a man to utter? Was he not caught up into paradise and lifted up to the third heaven?(i) Did he not traverse seas and land, drawing pagans to Christianity? Did he not receive the various gifts of the Spirit...? And with all this, this man, with his greatness, wisdom, power and fullness of the Spirit, since God favored him with these privileges, when he looks at God's providence, not in all its aspects but in one aspect of it, is overcome by the call, crushed, and quickly draws back, submitting to the incomprehensible God. For he did not search into God's providence for the angels, nor the archangels, or the Cherubim and Seraphim and all the invisible orders, nor into His care for the sun and the moon, the heaven, the earth and the sea, nor into His watchfulness over the whole human race and His concern for the irrational animals, the crops, the grass, the winds, the springs and the rivers... but God's special providence for the Jews and the Greeks, and he enlarged on the point, and explained how God called the Gentiles and rejected the Jews, and then showed how He accomplished salvation... And when he comprehended this, the Apostle discovered that he was before a vast ocean, and as he tried to examine the depths of this providence he trembled, realizing the impossibility of explaining its causes, and was awed before His infinite providence, which is unbounded, indescribable, unsearchable and incomprehensible, and he drew back in reverence, marveling, and saying: "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God!" (Rom 11:33).
He then showed how he touched its depths without succeeding in searching them out, saying: "How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!"

He did not say only that His judgments are unsearchable, but that they are also past finding out. Not only is man unable to understand them, but he has no right even to begin to search them out. It is impossible for him to grasp their end or even to discover the beginning of their design?!

And having said "How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out," he ended his discourse, filled with wonder and trembling, with a hymn of thanksgiving, saying: [For who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor? Or who hath first given to him, and it shall be recompensed unto him again? For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen].
St. John Chrysostom I have sinned;
what shall I do unto thee, O thou preserver of men?

entries.section: 4. A cry to God for his deliverance

paragraphs.text: Why hast thou set me as a mark against thee (why hast thou made me a target for thee), so that I am a burden to myself! [20]

God bore witness of Job that he was perfect and upright, but Job confesses that he is a sinner. He says "Have I sinned?" or "I have sinned." If before his friends he declares that he is innocent, and has not committed one of the heinous sins which the friends perhaps thought he had committed in secret, yet before God he declares that he will not be justified before Him, because he sins. How can he justify himself before God "the preserver of men," who knows what is in their hearts and thoughts and is concerned with their holiness and purity.

Job declares before God his inability to act: he has sinned, but what can he do for God? There is no one who can satisfy divine justice, but we ask for His mercies, and hide under the shadow of His wings, and prepare ourselves for the work of His grace, and so become the object of His good pleasure.

* He says: [If I have sinned, what shall I do, O You who perceive the mind of men?] [20] Are You not the one who called me [blameless, truly, righteous, godly, with no evil in me?] (Job 1:8; 2:3). You did not give this testimony out of ignorance, for You know man entirely, since You created what is within him and what is outside; but if those who revile and despise me, saying that I am a sinner, make light of my righteous deeds, which qualified me for Your testimony, what shall I do?
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * He says this not to accuse God personally, God forbid! but because what had befallen him gave rise to a great accusation against God.
Therefore he says: [You perceive the mind of men]. For even if they do not speak, You know their secret thoughts, all their personal reflections.
Such a man has endured much. For he did not say: "I am righteous," but said: They have a good idea of me. See, they bring an accusation against You because of my trials.
St. John Chrysostom And why dost thou not pardon my transgression, and take away mine iniquity? for now shall I sleep in the dust;

entries.section: 4. A cry to God for his deliverance

paragraphs.text: and thou shalt seek me in the morning, but I shall not be! [21]

In fervent prayer he cried out asking for forgiveness: "Why dost thou not pardon my transgression, and take away mine iniquity?" It is clear that he did not ask merely for temporal rest and for the trial to be lifted from him, but asks for God's favor, that his inner joy might be restored to him.
He asks for forgiveness now while he is in the world, because if he dies and lies in the dust there is no place for repentance, and his relation with God is cut off.

* By these very words, what does he declare but the desire for the expected Mediator, of whom John says: "Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world" (Jn 1:29). Or rather, sin is taken away completely from mankind when our corruption is changed into the glory of incorruption.

For we can never be freed from sin as long as we are held in the mortal body. Therefore the person longs for the grace of the Savior for the perfection of the resurrection, when the person looks upon evil as having utterly passed away. Therefore immediately after speaking of the punishment he deserved (through his inheritance from Adam) and the judgment he dreads because of his deeds, he continues: [Now I shall sleep in the dust, you will seek me in the morning, and I shall not be]. It was said to the first man when he sinned: "Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return" (Gen 3:19). Now in the morning, that is, in the revealing of souls, when thoughts become naked at the coming of the Judge, light comes in place of the darkness of night. The Psalmist said of this: [In the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up] (Ps 5:3).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* I, the sinner, always need healing.

* Whenever we receive it (in Communion) we proclaim the death of the Lord. By the death we proclaim the forgiveness of sins. If the shedding of blood is for the forgiveness of sins, it is fitting for me always to receive it, that it may always forgive my sins.
St. Ambrose * That you are called a man is the work of God, and that you are called a sinner is the work of man himself.
Blot out what you have done, that God may save what He has made.
It is fitting for you to hate your own work in you, and to love God's work in you.
When your own works do not please you, in this God's good works begin, since you find fault with your evil works.
The confession of evil works is the beginning of good works.

You do the truth and come to the light. How do you do the truth? You do not pamper yourself, nor humor yourself, nor flatter yourself, nor say: "I am righteous," while you are not righteous; thus you begin to do the truth.

You come to the light that your works may be made manifest, that they are wrought in God, because your sin, the very thing you hate, you cannot hate unless God shines in you and the truth shows it to you.

But whoever loves his sins even after being admonished, hates the light that admonishes him and flees from it, for the works he loves do not appear to him to be evil. He who does the truth accuses his evil works in himself and does not justify himself, and does not pardon himself until God forgives him.

So whoever wishes God to forgive him knows his sins himself and comes to the light, where he gives thanks for the showing of what he must hate in himself. He says to God: "Hide thy face from my sins." But with what face does he say this unless he adds: [For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me] (Ps 51:11)?
Let your iniquities be before you, you who do not wish them to be before God.
But if you put your sins behind you, God will push them forward and set them before your eyes, and this will happen at a time when there is no longer any fruit of repentance.
St. Augustine
Our days are an unceasing trial
* What do I see in my life upon earth?
An unbroken chain of trials.
I live like the hireling who awaits the end of the day, to rest from his toil and receive wages for his living.
* The day with all its hardship hands me over to the night, and the night with its terror hands me over to the day.
When shall I find my rest?
The months of my life hasten me to my departure.
The days of my sojourn pass quickly like vapor, they pass and are scattered without return!

* If I go down to Hades I do not return to life on earth, and my dwelling place on the face of the earth no longer knows me * In the midst of afflictions I cry out: Who am I, dust and ashes, that You should care for me and discipline me?
Who am I, a creature of dust, that You should visit me?
* You are my hope, my joy and my treasure!
In You I do not fear death; in You my wearisome journey is turned into a joyful passage!
Accompany me on the way of my sufferings, and my sorrows will turn into unceasing songs and praises!
Then answered Bildad the Shuhite, and said: [1]
How long wilt thou speak these things?
And shall the words in thee (thy words) be a strong wind! [2]

In sharp heat Bildad tries to silence Job's mouth and criticizes his emotional outburst. Bildad flared up and attacked Job: "How long wilt thou speak these things?" as though he were saying that the words of Eliphaz were entirely sufficient, and that Job ought to have kept silent and submitted. He likened Job's revolt to a violent, stormy wind, but it will not be able to stand before divine justice.

St. John Chrysostom sees that Bildad rushed headlong in his attack on righteous Job; for had he kept silent and been patient he would have realized that what Job said was nothing but a natural reaction to the severe sufferings and trials into which no one else had fallen. Moreover, even in his reproach of God, he did not deny that he was a sinner who asks His forgiveness. But Bildad's babbling, or his rashness in speech, made him fall into condemning the righteous man and into exaggerated criticism, so that he saw evil in the righteous man's good words. Bildad did not realize that a suffering man's expression of the weariness he sees is something that human nature necessarily requires.
* Did he (Job) say that he suffers injustice?

Behold, you (Job's friends) have not reached your goal in any way, for he never said this. But Job spoke of the weakness of his nature, saying, "Am I a sea, or a whale?" (Job 7:12), "Is my strength the strength of stones?" (Job 6:12) What is my life? [For I shall not live forever, that I may bear with patience] (Job 7:16). Besides this, he knew his sins: "Why dost thou not pardon my transgression?" (Job 7:21)...

After that, Bildad condemned himself in his babbling, for he failed to understand that those who actually experience pain find comfort in expressing themselves, since Job himself said: [I also will not restrain my mouth, for I am in distress] (Job 7:11). In any case, he says that these words with which I speak are required by necessity.

* The golden vessel is not used for base things because of its high price; how much more the mouth, which is more precious than gold and coral, so that we must not defile it with foul speech, cursing and the slander of others.

St. John Chrysostom * The words of the righteous are always grievous to the unjust, and what they hear for edification they carry as a burden on their shoulders. This is what Bildad the Shuhite plainly indicates about himself when he says: "How long wilt thou speak these things?" He who says "How long" shows that he is not yet able to bear words of edification.
The unjust boast greatly that they say what is right, and they find faults in good sayings...
When criticism is exaggerated, the discourse certainly loses its meaning...
The wicked blame good things, lest they themselves be seen not to know what is good.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Holy Scripture, like the Fathers, has warned us of the sin of Bildad: rash babbling in speech, which gave rise to condemnation and to exaggerated, biting criticism:
"In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise" (Prov 19:10).
"For a dream cometh through the multitude of business; and a fool's voice is known by multitude of words" (Eccl 3:5).
"For in the multitude of dreams and many words there are also divers vanities: but fear thou God" (Eccl 7:5).

* The Apostle did not say that there is no one who tames the tongue, but that no one (of men) can tame the tongue; even once it has been bridled, we confess that this is by the tenderness of God's grace and His help.
* A man can tame wild beasts, but his tongue he cannot bridle...!
A man can train everything except himself; he has no power over himself!
He is able to train everything that he fears, or ought to fear, but as for himself, whom he does not fear, he has no power over him!
Therefore let us take refuge in God, who is able to bridle it. You cannot persuade your tongues because you are men... Let us ask God to tame us, saying to Him: "Lord, Thou hast been our refuge."
Can (man), the image of God, tame the lion, while God is unable to tame His image?

Our hope lies in this Tamer, that we may submit to Him, seeking His mercy... Let us bear with Him until He tames us, and we become perfect, for He often allows us chastisements. If you use whips in taming wild animals, does not God use them to turn us, His wild beasts, into His children?
St. Augustine * Babbling is the throne of vanity, and from this throne appear the love of self-display, boasting and bragging.
Babbling is a sign of ignorance, the door of slander, a guide to jesting and laughter, and a servant of lies and hypocrisy.
* It is a proof of drowsiness and a scattering of memory; it removes watchfulness, cools fervor and weakens prayer.
St. John Climacus * Beware of the babbling tongue and of the two eager ears (for hearing news). Do not belittle others, and do not listen to one who belittles another.
St. Jerome * Do not be hasty with your tongue, for the mouth is a snare of death.

The so-called Barnabas * He who guards his tongue shall never be robbed of his treasure. The mouth of the silent man interprets the mysteries of God. And he who speaks hastily becomes distant from his Creator.
The Spiritual Elder * We must not use rebuke except rarely. And if we are compelled to use it, we must strive eagerly to serve God and not ourselves.

Let us have one aim, and let us do nothing with a double heart. Let us take out of our eyes the beam of envy or malice or pretence, so that we may be able to see and take the speck out of our brother's eyes. Let us look at the speck with the eyes of the dove, which belong to the bride of Christ (Song 1:4), whom God chose for Himself as a glorious Church without spot or wrinkle, that is, pure, without guile (Eph 27:5).

St. Augustine * Do not be a judge of your brother, that you may be made worthy of forgiveness; you may perhaps see him always in error, but you do not know with what end he will depart from the world. For the thief crucified with Jesus was a murderer and a shedder of blood, and Judas was a disciple of Christ and one of the intimates, since the money box was with him, yet in a short time they changed, so that the thief entered Paradise, while the disciple deserved the gallows and perished.
St. Anastasius

entries.section: 2. God is just in what befalls believers

paragraphs.text: 3 Doth God pervert judgment? or doth the Almighty pervert justice? 4 When thy children sinned against him, he delivered them into the hand of their transgression.
Doth God pervert judgment? or doth the Almighty pervert justice? [3]

Bildad reckoned that Job's revolt was an outburst against God, as though God perverts judgment and reverses the right. Far be it from anyone to think this. Man in his weakness may resort to reversing the right because of his fear, but God is "the Almighty"; He is neither unjust nor does He do what is false.

* The blessed Job did not deny this in his speech, nor was he ignorant of it when he held his tongue. But all the insolent speak well-known truths in grand words in order to show by this that they are learned.

They disdain to keep their peace in a spirit of humility, lest they be thought silent through ignorance. Yet it is well known that they praise the uprightness of God's justice when they themselves are safe from calamities and enjoy the prosperity of their lives while others suffer disasters.

They walk in evil, and yet they think themselves righteous. Being in prosperity, they imagine that this is by virtue of their merits, and conclude that God does no injustice... But if a power of correction (by discipline) touches their lives even to the slightest degree, they at once rush to attack the divine government, though a little before - since no harm had touched them - they were lavish in praise and admiration of the divine providence.

They refuse to admit that any judgment is just when it falls upon them... Well does the Psalmist speak against the confession of the wicked: [He will praise thee when thou doest good to him] (Ps 49:18)... For this reason we do not wonder that Bildad praises the justice of God so long as it does not touch him personally.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees in Job's friends a symbol of the heretics, for when they see the holy Church in tribulation for her edification, they reckon that what has befallen her is a matter of divine justice, and that the prosperity they enjoy is on account of their virtues.

Often the enemy of good supports the heretics in every age with material means and temporal honor, in order to ensnare the children of God from the bosom of the holy Bride, at one time by dazzling, deceptive philosophies, at another by material enticements, and a third time by keeping them from the tribulation that the Bride, the partner of the Crucified, endures.
This is the role of Bildad, who in his ignorance imagined wisdom, and reckoned Job a blasphemer against God the Almighty and a murmurer against divine justice.
* (The enemy of good) invented heresies and schisms in order to ruin the faith, corrupt the truth, and destroy unity.
And since he is unable to keep us in the dark ways of the new error, he draws us into a new maze of deception.

He catches people away from the Church herself, and while they think they have drawn near to the light and escaped the night of the world, he plunges them into a new darkness, of which they are unaware.

And although they do not hold to the Gospel and the order of Christ and His law, they claim to be in the light through the deceptive flatteries of the enemy, of whom the Apostle says that he transforms himself into an angel of light and adorns his servants as servants of righteousness.
They call night day, death salvation, despair hope, treachery faithfulness, and the antichrist Christ, and he thwarts the truth by deception, by presenting the truth in a false form.
This is what happens, my brethren, when we do not return to the fountain of truth, when we do not look to the Head and keep the teaching that comes from heaven.
St. Cyprian * It is the habit of the devil to imitate the things that belong to God. He raises up false apostles to oppose the true Apostles, and takes the form of an angel in order to deceive men.

Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus * There are philosophers who have skillful discussions about virtues and vices, distinguishing between them and giving definitions of them, and in the end offering a precise logical sequence, filling books, and protecting their wisdom with talkative speeches; these dare to say to people, follow us, join our party if you wish to live happily. But they do not enter by the door; these want to destroy, slaughter and kill.

* If we find these three persons, holy brethren, we find those whom it befits us to love, those whom we must bear with, and those of whom we must beware. The shepherd is loved, the hireling is borne with, and the thief is guarded against.

St. Augustine * "A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject; knowing that he that is such is subverted, and sinneth, being condemned of himself" (Titus 10:3-11). May we, like wise sailors, sail in our faith on the sound course so that we may cross most safely, and follow the coasts of the Holy Scriptures.

entries.section: 2. God is just in what befalls believers

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose When thy children sinned against him, he delivered them into the hand of their transgression [4].

Bildad tries to provoke Job by ascribing what befell Job's children to the fruit of their sin and evil, so that they received just recompense from God. What inflamed Job's wounds all the more was that Bildad reckoned the death of Job's children in this horrible manner to have no other explanation than that they disobeyed God, so He delivered them into the hand of their transgression. Job had confessed that he was a sinner, and he used to offer burnt offerings in the names of his children lest a sinful thought against God had crossed their thoughts. But it cannot be judged that what happened was the natural fruit of a disobedience they had committed.

5 If thou wouldest seek unto God betimes, and make thy supplication to the Almighty; 6 If thou wert pure and upright; surely now he would awake for thee, and make the habitation of thy righteousness prosperous. 7 Though thy beginning was small, yet thy latter end should greatly increase.
Yet if thou wouldest seek unto God betimes, and make thy supplication to the Almighty [5].

Bildad offers Job good advice, to hurry and rise early, asking and making supplication to God, but Bildad did not feel that Job deserved to obtain more than what he had. He advises him to pray and petition God so that He may restore to him manifold what he lost, if he is pure and upright.

How strange! Bildad offers Job destructive advice that reveals the ruin of Bildad's own heart. He asked him to pray early to the Almighty. This seems excellent scriptural advice, for the believer asks of the Almighty, asks and receives because he rises early to God, but he does not make prayer for the enjoyment of the Giver of gifts but for the acquiring of temporal gifts, reckoning that the answering of prayer by the enjoyment of temporal things is a sign of God's pleasure and of the holiness of the one who prays. It is a dangerous indicator that corrupts faith in God, who wants us to seek the Kingdom of God and His righteousness, and all these things are added to us.

Nothing prevents us from asking God as our Father for everything, even trivial matters, as a sign of our living fellowship with Him, but the answer, in the obtaining of what we ask, will not be a sign of our sanctification and of God's love for us.

Perhaps Bildad here was certain that Job would not recover what he had lost, which would be a sign of his wickedness, like his perishing sons. On the other hand, Bildad sets the measure of righteousness and uprightness as a person's enjoyment of temporal things. Pope Gregory (the Great) says: [Wicked people count temporary pleasures a special blessing of divine reward. What they themselves run after with great care and intense desire, they promise to others as a great thing.]
Prayer - in the mind of St. Augustine - is the language of the soul's longing for God. It is the interpreter of the heart's desire.
* Prayer is the reaching of the mind, filled with love, to God; it occupies mind and heart, thought and desire, knowledge and love. The whole life of the good Christian is a holy desire.
* Alas! It is easy to ask things of God and not to ask God Himself, as though the gift were better than the Giver.

* God does not forbid love of these things, but that we find our happiness in loving them. It befits us to make the love of our Creator the goal of our esteem for these things... The dowry is given to the betrothed so that through her dowry she may love him. So God gives you everything; therefore love the One who made them.
* What precious thing does he ask of God who holds his esteem of God Himself in contempt?!
* Ask nothing of God, but the gift of Himself to you.
* To hope for God from God - this is to love God, the Giver of grace.
* It is not right to love what comes from God if God Himself is forgotten because of it(a).
* You will find nothing that He offers you better than Himself, but if you find what is better than Him, ask for it by every means.
* Does God have no reward? There is none but the gift of Himself!

St. Augustine Father Aphrahat looks upon prayer as an inner meeting of the pure heart with the Holy God; prayer is the speech of the heart, which will not be an object of delight to the Holy God unless it is pure and clean.
* Prayer is beautiful and its works are upright; acceptable prayer makes a person feel rest. Prayer is heard when we feel forgiveness in it.
Beloved prayer is pure prayer, free of all guile. And prayer is strong when the power of God works in it.

My dear one, I wrote to you that when a person commits himself to fulfil the will of God, and it is the basic axis of his prayer, the person rises high in his prayer. I have told you this: do not neglect prayer.

You must long for prayer and not grow weary of it. As our Lord said and it is written: "that men ought always to pray, and not to faint" (Lk 18:1), you must yearn for vigil, and put away from you heedlessness and sleep. You must be awake at all times, by day and by night, and not grow slack.
St. Aphrahat * Did Job need this teaching of yours?
Was he not praying always throughout his whole life? And you say: [Rise early in prayer to the Lord Almighty].

Not only did he not cease to pray early to the Lord, but he offered it early (Job 1:5), and throughout the day and at every moment, he praised God seven times a day (Ps 119:97, 164), by day and by night; for this was not folly to him. The end of his trials shows this, the result of his struggles (which showed that he was a man of prayer)...
You have misjudged (O Bildad) and wronged the wrestler, for Job did not fail to see God, of whom you speak in order to criticize the righteous man, and not to glorify God.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem If thou wert pure and upright; surely now he would awake for thee, and make the habitation of thy righteousness prosperous [6].
Bildad thinks that if Job were pure and upright, this calamity would not have befallen him, and that if he had acted well at the first trial, the second trial would not have come upon him.

This is not right, for a good man may be tried more than once, and may even be exposed to a trial that extends through his whole life, which is counted as nothing when compared with the eternity he will enjoy.

Bildad pretended to advise Job to repent of his evil so that God might restore to him what he had been, and even more than he had been, but in his depths he wanted to assure him that he is wicked and a hypocrite.
Though thy beginning was small, yet thy latter end should greatly increase [7].

Bildad sees that Job is a wicked man; if he were upright and fell into a trial, his latter end would be better than he was before the trial. Indeed God wanted to prove to Bildad that Job is righteous and upright, so He made his latter end better than his beginning.

Job's latter end became more glorious than his children, but what he gained at the end of his life was nothing but a pledge of the glory prepared for him in the eternal life. He died an old man, full of days, but he rises to live eternally in the heavenly Jerusalem.

Many martyrs and saints suffered at the end of their lives, but these sufferings and torments are spiritual pearls and jewels whose greatness and splendor we shall recognize on the great Day of the Lord, when they take pride in the love they expressed by accepting sufferings with thanksgiving and joy!

entries.section: 4. The accusation of Job with hypocrisy

paragraphs.text: 8 "Enquire of the former age, and prepare thyself to the search of their fathers: 9 For we are but of yesterday, and know nothing, because our days upon earth are a shadow. 10 Shall not they teach thee, and tell thee, and utter words out of their heart, saying: 11 Can the rush grow up without mire? can the flag grow without water? 12 Whilst it is yet in his greenness, and not cut down, it withereth before any other herb. 13 So are the paths of all that forget God; and the hypocrite's hope shall perish: 14 Whose hope shall be cut off, and whose trust shall be a spider's web. 15 He shall lean upon his house, but it shall not stand: he shall hold it fast, but it shall not endure. 16 He is green before the sun, and his branch shooteth forth in his garden. 17 His roots are wrapped about the heap, and seeth the place of stones. 18 If he destroy him from his place, then it shall deny him, saying, I have not seen thee. 19 Behold, this is the joy of his way, and out of the earth shall others grow."
Enquire of the former age, and prepare thyself to the search of their fathers [8].

Bildad did not dare to declare to Job that what had befallen him - according to his personal experience - is nothing but a confirmation that he is wicked; rather he laid the foundation of this judgment on the experience of the ancient generations. If Eliphaz had relied on his personal experience, Bildad completes that by referring to the experience of the ancients.

In his comment on these phrases [8-10], Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem sees that what happened with Job resembles what happened with Abel. Cain looked at the corpse of his brother Abel, lying slain on the ground (Gen 4), and thought that this was the fruit of his deed, and that Cain was righteous, the earth having settled and rested so as to be in his hands while he was in tranquillity, and he did not discover the truth that the voice of his brother's blood cries out, having reached heaven.

As Cain looked at Abel, reckoning that what befell him was because of his evil, so Bildad and his companions looked at Job on the dunghill, and reckoned him wicked. And as God bore witness to the righteousness of the slain, declaring that the gates of heaven were open to receive his voice, so God bears witness to Job and listens to the cries of his heart. Cain wanted to trample his brother under his feet, and the friends wanted to crush Job's soul under their feet.

It befitted Job's friends themselves to ask the early ages and see that the injustice that befell Abel was not from an evil in him but because of his righteousness, and that his life did not end with earthly blessings and temporal goods, but with the opening of the gates of heaven to receive the cries of his blood shed on the earth.

Eliphaz said that God does not allow any of the upright to be destroyed thus (Job 4:7), whereas Bildad says here that God drives hypocritical wicked people to shame, disgrace and ruin in this world. If Eliphaz wanted to assert that Job is not upright, otherwise all this would not have befallen him, behold, Bildad directs to him an outright accusation that he is a wicked hypocrite.

He asks Job to resort to the early ages to make sure for himself that what he says is true, through the long practical experience of God's judgments concerning the wicked from the early ages until their own time.

entries.section: 4. The accusation of Job with hypocrisy

paragraphs.text: For we are but of yesterday, and know nothing, because our days upon earth are a shadow [9].

He asks him not to rely on his own experience, even if he is an old man, because the whole age is like a day, as though it had passed yesterday, and his knowledge is limited, and his experience is almost as fleeting as his life. This is what drives us to look to the experience of the ancient generations.

His words came close to what King David sang in his farewell prayer, saying: "For we are strangers before thee, and sojourners, as were all our fathers: our days on the earth are as a shadow, and there is no hope" (1 Chr 29:15), but his heart and mind were not like David's heart and mind. The words that Bildad uttered are useful, and could have been holy if his heart had been pure, clean, loving and holy.

entries.section: 4. The accusation of Job with hypocrisy

paragraphs.text: Shall not they teach thee, and tell thee, and utter words out of their heart, saying [10].
The early Fathers bear love toward their children and grandchildren, so along with their experience they offer us their wide hearts; therefore their words carry weight.

* Bildad set down words of wonderful truth against hypocrites, but in this speech he was pointing to himself. For had he not been pretending to righteousness in a feeble manner, he would not have dared to teach a good man with such great rashness... His words in truth carry wonderful power, but they should have been directed to the foolish and not to a wise man; to the wicked and not to a good man, for he who pours water into the river while his gardens are dry and thirsty shows that he is no less than a madman.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
I have previously spoken of the importance of the Fathers' heritage in the book "The Beginnings of Christian Patristic Literature", where it says:
[To what extent are we committed to what is found in the heritage of the Fathers?

The holy Fathers represent the mind of the universal Church, which she received from the Apostles by the action of the Holy Spirit, who works without ceasing in the life of the Church. St. Augustine speaks of them, saying: "They held fast to what they found in the Church, they practiced what they learned, and what they received from the Fathers they entrusted to the hands of the children", "He who despises the holy Fathers knows that he despises the whole Church".

This authority rests on two factors: a natural factor, since the Fathers were marked by a holy life and faithfulness in receiving the deposit of the living faith from the hands of the Apostles, and therefore they are better able to bear witness to the life of the Church in all its aspects, especially as they hold one mind, in spite of the differences of cultures, gifts and circumstances, with the great distance between the apostolic sees and the difficulty of communications at that time. And the second factor is divine, in that the Fathers lived enveloped by the Holy Spirit, the Church's leader and guide into all truth, who keeps her within the circle of the Cross of Christ.
This does not mean the infallibility of the Fathers as individuals; rather the universal Church as a whole lives preserved by the Spirit of the Lord...

The heritage of the Fathers occupied a distinguished place in the life and faith of the Church; St. Athanasius relied on it in his defense, as St. Basil relied on many ecclesiastical traditions through the sayings of the Fathers before him.

This tendency, that is, resorting to the sayings of the earlier Fathers, increased in the fourth century and grew greatly in the fifth. St. Cyril of Alexandria, for example, in his writings to the Egyptian monks in defense of the title of St. Mary Theotokos (qeotokoc) - to affirm that the One born is the Word of God incarnate, without separation of the divinity from the humanity - indicated to them that they should follow in the footsteps of the saints, since they kept the faith delivered to them from the Apostles, and taught Christians rightly. Once again he affirms that the correct teaching concerning the Holy Trinity was made clear "by the wisdom of the holy Fathers". And in his discourse against Nestorius he resorted to the teaching of the holy Church extending throughout the whole world and to the honored Fathers themselves, declaring that the Holy Spirit spoke in him. And to support his discourse about the Lord Christ he relied on some patristic excerpts from their polemical writings, which he presented to the Council of Ephesus.]

entries.section: 4. The accusation of Job with hypocrisy

paragraphs.text: Can the rush grow up without the mire (the marsh)? or can the flag grow without water? [11]
As Bildad accuses Job of hypocrisy, he presents painful images of the hypocrite in general, though he means Job in particular:
First: the papyrus, which grows only in waters full of mud, and the dry flag that has no water [11].

entries.section: 4. The accusation of Job with hypocrisy

paragraphs.text: Second: the spider, which relies on its house and thinks it is safe, though its house will not stand [14-15].

entries.section: 4. The accusation of Job with hypocrisy

paragraphs.text: Third: the grass that the sun burns and dries, though the sun is the secret of the life and growth of plants [16].
Fourth: one who stumbles on the stones in the road, and falls and perishes.
Fifth: the leafy, beautiful tree whose roots the axe strikes, so that it is uprooted and dies.

What is the experience of the early Fathers in this matter? The Fathers answer that the hopes and joys of hypocrites are like papyrus and flag. Both grow in the marsh amid mud or mire or slime, and with water. So the hypocrite does not achieve hope without a stagnant ground or an atmosphere other than mire. He relies on outward appearances of religiosity, piety and success, his appearances being deceptive, on his conceit of himself, on the words of praise directed to him; all these are nothing but mire, and their hopes are nothing but papyrus and flag.

If the papyrus points to the hypocritical man, who needs the holy waters of the Holy Spirit: in the midst of the waters the believer is born a son of God by the Holy Spirit, and by the waters of the Spirit he is refreshed and renewed, until he bears the icon of the Lord Christ, and so is made worthy to receive fellowship in eternal glory.

* By the papyrus and the flag he points to the life of the hypocrite, for he has the appearance of greenness, but without fruit useful for the service of man; though he is green, he has merely the color of holiness, always dry, practically fruitless...

Hypocrites are separated from the Giver of many blessings by the tendencies of the thought of their hearts; while receiving His gifts they seek their own praise, not the glory of the Giver. And while they glorify themselves by praising themselves for the blessings given them, they oppose the Maker of good things by the very gifts.

The hypocrite criticizes severely the life of the one who rebukes him. Longing to prove him wrong beyond all limits, so as to justify himself, not by what he practices of deeds but by highlighting the faults of others... Well was it said of Solomon: "Reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee" (Prov 9:8)...

Here we need to know that the loftiness of the righteous begins in the heart and grows to the end of the present life. But the practices of hypocrites, since they have no roots, often come to nothing before the end of the present life. They often devote their lives to holy studies, and since they do this not to lay up stores of virtues but to obtain praise and flattery, when they reach a phrase that gives them human praise, they are glad of temporal success. Therefore they are altogether empty of holy learning, and they show by their conduct afterward how they love temporal things, while as for eternal things, they go no further than speaking of them with their lips... They are witnesses against themselves that their goodness does not spring from the heart.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* For this end the Savior, who had no need of baptism, was baptized, to sanctify the water for those who would be born again.
St. Clement of Alexandria * Baptism is called "the washing of regeneration", since it is accompanied by the renewal of the Spirit who hovers over the waters.

* The Holy Spirit creates for Himself a new people, and renews the face of the earth, when people through Him put off [their old man with his deeds] (Col 9:3), [and walk in newness of life] (Rom 4:6).

* Everyone who is counted worthy of fellowship in the Holy Spirit, through knowing His unspeakable mysteries, will surely obtain rest and joy of heart. For when he has arrived, under the Spirit's guidance, at knowledge of all that happens - how and why it happens - his soul cannot be troubled or feel sorrow.
* Human nature is weak. And in order to become strong it needs the help of one who strengthens it. Whose help? The help of the Spirit.
That is, he who seeks true strength must become strong by the Spirit.

The majority become strong by the flesh and according to the flesh. But the soldiers of God (2 Tim 3:2) become strong by the Spirit, and therefore courageous in facing the fleshly mind [which is concerned with what belongs to the flesh] (Rom 7:8). The spirit is in a wrestling with the flesh, but the spirit of man, which that Spirit strengthens, will win the victory.
Origen * The Lord was baptized not to be cleansed but to cleanse the waters, so that when the waters were washed by His body, which did not know sin, they might be used in baptism.
St. Ambrose * Christ was baptized, I mean He purified the water by His baptism.
Tertullian Whilst it is yet in his greenness, and not cut down, it withereth before any other herb [12].
Quickly the papyrus appears with its beautiful green leaves, but it dries up and vanishes in a short time, even before it is plucked up (Ps 129:6).
So are the paths of all that forget God; and the hypocrite's hope shall perish [13].
The secret of hypocrisy is man's forgetting God, who searches hearts and knows the hidden secrets in thought.

* [So are the paths of all that forget God, and the hypocrite's hope shall perish]... The hope of the hypocrite cannot stand, for since he does not make eternity his goal, he loses all that he holds in his hand. The inclination of his mind is not fixed on the glory that has no end, but if he pants after passing praise, he loses what he labored to obtain. The "Truth" bears witness to this, saying: "Verily I say unto you, They have their reward" (Mt 6:2).
No one can bind himself to the perishing and remain himself imperishable. For he who embraces perishing things naturally descends to perishing. Let him say: "and the hypocrite's hope shall perish".
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Job, who was subjected once more to trial, praised God and blessed Him; truly he did not forget God. Therefore the end of the righteous is not compared with the grass that withers in the heat [12]. Since he is like a tree planted by streams of water, that yields its fruit in its season (Ps 1:3), keeping the fruit of virtues, he causes many plantings in the world to flourish.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * It is a source of joy and glory for men to have children who resemble them... How much more is the pleasure of God when a spiritual man proves in his works and his praises and declares the divine loftiness in his life.
St. Cyprian * O soul, He who created you can satisfy you. And if you seek anything else, it is to your misfortune.
St. Augustine Whose hope shall be cut off, and whose trust shall be a spider's web! [14]
Since the hypocrite does not rely on God, everything he hopes for, and even what he obtains, becomes like the house of the spider, which weaves its delights and consolation in a flimsy web.
This text appears in the writings of Pope Gregory (the Great) as "His folly does not satisfy him..."
* It is infinite folly for a man to labor with toil and run panting after a moment of praise, so that a person practices the heavenly commandments with great effort and seeks an earthly wage...

"And whose trust shall be a spider's web"... It may happen that the words of hypocrites last to the end of the present life itself, but since they do not seek the praise of their Creator, their works are not counted good in the eyes of God.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* [For the hope of the ungodly shall perish, his house shall be without an inhabitant, and his tent shall prove to be a spider's web] (LXX). Why do you say this to Job? Is it because you really know the end of the wrestler, and you have your own view concerning the dweller of his house and his tent as a spider's web?

But you think that his house is made of wood and stone, built for him by virtues (Mt 7:24). You imagine his tent made from this earth, and for this reason you think it will perish like a spider's web, whereas his dwelling is really in the heavens, as in the words of Paul: "For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this we groan, earnestly desiring to be clothed upon with our house which is from heaven" (2 Cor 5:1-2).
For this reason Job also groans, but you (O Bildad) look upon these lamentations as cowardice and blasphemy. He [supports his house] (his trust), not by visible things, but by what is invisible.
Therefore Scripture speaks with words of wisdom: [Wisdom hath builded her house for herself, she hath set up her seven pillars] (Prov 9:1)...

Job took this with patience, and did not renounce his confidence in his relationship with God; on the contrary, he bore the enemy courageously and repelled his vain attacks, so that he might have a bold face against all conflicts in new attacks.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Hypocrisy is hated by God and abhorred by man. It brings no reward and is altogether without benefit for the salvation of the soul, but rather is the cause of its perdition.

If hypocrisy is sometimes not exposed, it is only for a time, for it does not last long, but everything is revealed, and it brings calamity on its owner, and so it is like a woman ugly in appearance from whom her outward adornment, applied to her by artificial means, is stripped.

* Hypocrisy is foreign to the characteristics of the saints, for it is impossible for anything of what we do or say to escape the eyes of the Godhead, for "there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known". All our words and deeds will be revealed on the Day of Judgment. Therefore hypocrisy is wearisome and without benefit. It befits us to be approved as true worshippers who serve God with frank and clear features.

St. Cyril the Great * Everyone sees the thief "hypocrisy" carrying everything before his eyes and rejoicing in it! What a new kind of robbery, that draws people and delights them while they are being robbed!
St. John Chrysostom He shall lean upon his house, but it shall not stand:
he shall hold it fast, but it shall not endure [15].
The hypocrite boasts of his works and relies on them, as the spider holds fast to its flimsy house.

As the spider thinks it is fortified by its web, by which it catches its prey, and does not realize that its web can easily be swept away, so the hypocritical man fortifies himself in his formalities and outward appearances of piety and his resources, and behold, he loses everything.

* [He shall lean upon his house, but it shall not stand: he shall hold it up (with a prop), but it shall not endure] [15]. As the house of our outward life is the building in which the body lives, so the house of our thought is whatever the mind concentrates on... for everything we love is for us as though it were a dwelling that gives it rest. Therefore, since Paul set his heart on heavenly things, though he is still on the earth, he is a stranger to it. [Our conversation is in heaven] (Phil 3:20). But the mind of the hypocrite, in all that he does, thinks of nothing but his reputation and fame...
The empty soul, finding that it keeps nothing within itself in spite of all its labors, seeks testimony from outside...
The hypocrite leans on this house of flattery in vain, for on the Day of Judgment no human testimony will stand. The praise he received as testimony for him he receives as his wage.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

The Christian, while he walks on earth in a spirit of responsibility and commitment in all that he is entrusted with, bears a heavenly touch in his thoughts as in his feelings and emotions, translated into his words and outward conduct. Our life is a divine school in which we learn and train for the heavenly life, in all the directions of our life.
* I want you to keep your minds on these things always (Col 1:3). For our concern with them frees us from the earth and transports us to heaven.

St. John Chrysostom * It is right for us to be there in the presence of God in the heavens, we who learned the lesson while on earth, and went there to heaven in order to be in the love of God the Father, whom we came to know while on earth, and because God the Word, the Holy One, made everything and taught us and teaches us everything, and trains us in all good things.

St. Clement of Alexandria * When the will of God is accomplished by us who are on earth as it is accomplished by those in heaven, we become like the heavenly ones, as we bear like them the image of the heavenly (1 Cor 49:15) and inherit the Kingdom of Heaven (Mt 34:25). And those after us who are on earth come, praying that they may be like us when we are in heaven (Paradise).
Origen He is green before the sun, and his branch (his boughs) shooteth forth in his garden [16].

The incarnate Word of God came, the "Sun of righteousness", who rises on those sitting in darkness that they may enjoy the light of righteousness, and become children of light and children of the day. The sun that transfers us from the darkness of the tomb to the light of heaven dries up the grass. This is the work of the Lord Christ, who raised mankind from the death of sin and entered with it into the embrace of the Father, while the deniers who insist on not believing in Him dry up and become fit for the eternal fire.

* [He sees it green before the sun comes.] The Lord is often represented in Holy Scripture by the title "the Sun", as was said by the prophet: "But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise" (Mal 4:2). The wicked who are driven away at the judgment are described in the Book of Wisdom: [We have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness has not shone on us, and the sun has not risen on us] (Wis 5:6). Therefore before the sun the papyrus is seen to be green.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 4. The accusation of Job with hypocrisy

paragraphs.text: His roots are wrapped about the heap, and seeth the place of stones [17].
The cornerstone raises from us living stones built up in the house of the Lord, in the heavenly Temple. But the wicked stumble over the cornerstone, and fall and perish.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem uses the Septuagint (LXX), while Pope Gregory (the Great) refers to the Vulgate.

* [He falls upon a heap of stones, and lives among flint]... People are referred to in Holy Scripture by stones, as was said to the holy Church by Isaiah: "And I will make thy battlements of rubies, and thy gates of hewn stones (of carbuncle)" (Isa 54:12)...

Peter expressed this by offering the counsel: "Be ye also built up as living stones, a spiritual house" (1 Pet 2:5). Here, since he calls them stones, he by no means called them "living stones", but by the bare title of stones; he sets up the lost and the elect mingled together.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* [He sleeps on a heap of stones, and dwells among pebbles] These belong to those of whom Isaiah spoke: "Prepare ye the way of the people... clear it of stones" (Isa 62:10). And also: "Prepare the way, take up the stumblingblock out of the way of my people" (Isa 57:14; 1 Macc 5:4; Ps 140:6). He (the enemy) drains himself and wounds himself with an incurable death, when we clear our ways of snares and stumbling stones.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem If he destroy him from his place, then it shall deny him, saying:

entries.section: 4. The accusation of Job with hypocrisy

paragraphs.text: I have not seen thee [18].

He gives another likeness of the hypocrite, the beautiful, flourishing tree, which keeps its greenness in spite of the rays of the sun, and whose roots are firm in the rocky soil, unshaken by the winds. When the axe strikes this tree it is utterly uprooted, and no sign of it remains in the place where it was planted.

The hypocrite is like the tree that everyone desires to enjoy the sight of, but when hypocrisy, like the axe, strikes its roots, it loses its vitality and its fruit and its beauty.
