He becomes like the foolish virgins who have all the appearance of the wise virgins, but have no oil, so they do not carry light that comes out of their lamps. They remain in the darkness, unable to enter the bridal chamber of the heavenly Bridegroom, where darkness can have no place.

* [If God must destroy him, his place will deny him.] The hypocrite is destroyed from his place when he is removed from the praise of the present life by the intervention of death. But the inner witness denies him, and thus destroys him, and proves that God does not know him, since in justice He condemns the life of the pretender. The Truth does not know him, nor does He recognize the good works he practiced. For he did not practice them with a sound purpose in thought. Therefore when God comes to judgment He will say to the foolish virgins: [Verily I say unto you, I know you not] (Mt 25:12). For seeing the corruption of the thought, He condemns even the incorruption that is in the body.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* [If one is swallowed up, the place will deny him.] By swallowing up in Holy Scripture is meant what the prophet Isaiah said: [Death shall be swallowed up for ever, and the Lord God shall wipe away every tear from every face] (Isa 25:8). For this reason "his place shall deny him", because the swallowing by which death swallowed Adam (cf. Rom 5:17), which urged him to disobey the commands of God (Gen 2:17), swallows death itself to its destruction.
But "his place shall deny him". What place? Perhaps this concerns death, for the place of the traitor is death.

It can also be said: [He wipes away every tear from every face] (Isa 25:8). (The Lord Christ) made Adam glorious by His crucifixion, death and resurrection, and turned the craftiness of the accuser back upon the enemy. He saved Adam, and the curse was wrested away by the One to whom all that exists belongs.

entries.section: 4. The accusation of Job with hypocrisy

paragraphs.text: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem This is the joy of his way, and out of the earth shall another grow [19].
This is the fate of the wicked hypocrite, for he thought that his hope would turn into joy. Yet he is uprooted like the tree and another takes his place, in the same place.

20 "Behold, God will not cast away a perfect man, neither will he help the evil doers. 21 When he shall fill thy mouth with laughing, and thy lips with rejoicing, 22 They that hate thee shall be clothed with shame; and the dwelling place of the wicked shall come to nought."

After reviewing painful images of the hypocritical man, meaning by him "Job", he presents to us a joyful image of the perfect man, asking Job to leave his hypocrisy and walk the way of perfection. Perhaps while describing what the perfect man enjoys of God's good pleasure in him and in his sacrifices and offerings, and how his mouth is filled with joy and his lips with shouting, and how he enjoys victory over the enemies whom the Lord grieves, he set this before himself and his two friends Eliphaz and Zophar. It is as though he is calling Job to leave his hidden evil and follow the example of his three companions, who in Bildad's mind are perfect. Bildad sees that the tent of the wicked Job no longer exists, whereas they have their dwellings fortified by God. Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem sees that what Bildad said concerning those perfect in the Lord applies to Job, for while he accuses him of evil and calls him to perfection, behold, he defends him without knowing it.
Behold, God will not cast away a perfect man, neither will he help the evil doers [20].

In the conclusion of his speech Bildad summarizes his moral theological understanding, which is that God does not reject the perfect man, but answers his request even if it seems that He has rejected him. And He turns his mourning into dancing and joy, and fills his inner mouth with spiritual laughter. Then those who reproached him will be put to shame when they see that he has returned to his former prosperity and joy. Their clothing will be shame and disgrace when they see him crowned with glory. Corresponding to this, God does not support evildoers and destroys their tents. Perhaps he wanted here to hint at Job as being wicked, whose cries God did not hear, and whose dwelling He utterly destroyed together with his family.

This is Bildad's judgment on Job, whom he advises to turn back from his evil and repent, and whom he accuses of evil and hypocrisy. He judged him not knowing what is in his heart or in his mind, indeed not knowing what passed between God and Satan in heaven.
* In any case Job is not a wicked man, nor a wicked soldier. On the contrary, one can apply to him what Bildad added, unaware that while he accuses him, behold, he becomes his defender.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Certainly when the perfect one appears in the judgment, He at once lifts up the simple and despised from their condition and glorifies them, and shatters the greatness of those of evil mind and condemns them... So God does not stretch out His hand to the evil in mind, since all who seek earthly glory He leaves below, even if they have done good things, whatever their goodness, for He does not grant them the heavenly joys.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
When he shall fill thy mouth with laughing, and thy lips with rejoicing [21].

Bildad calls Job to leave evil and walk in the way of perfection, so that he may enjoy spiritual laughter and joy in the Lord. This is the joy which the true believer enjoys, bearing within him our Lord Jesus, who gladdens hearts.

Christianity is a call to enjoy the joy of heaven; for if our Christ came down from heaven incarnate, it was only to carry us to His heavens as a bride rejoicing in her Bridegroom; for this reason the Apostle Paul calls us while in prison: [Rejoice at all times, and I say, my brethren, rejoice](b).

St. Anba Antony sees that joy is the food of the soul; without it the soul hungers and dies. The inner heavenly joy supports the soul in its exile from its heavenly homeland, and prepares the body to bear a mark akin to the spiritual, so that it is prepared to become a spiritual body on the great Day of the Lord.

* As trees cannot grow if they do not drink water, so the soul, if it does not receive heavenly joy, cannot grow and ascend to the heights. But the souls that have received the Spirit and heavenly joy are those that can rise to the heights.. For the mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven were revealed to them while still in this body, and they found boldness before God in everything, and all their requests were fulfilled.
* The soul is always nurtured by this joy and made happy by it, and by it ascends to heaven, for like the body it has its spiritual food.
St. Antony the Great * He who looks in himself to our Lord, and whose soul is mingled with His light, is filled in his heart with joy.

The Spiritual Elder * It is not fitting for a man to laugh at all times and be like a laughing animal... [A fool lifteth up his voice with laughter] (Sir 21:23). But the wise man smiles in a way that does not attract notice...
On the other hand, it is fitting for a man not to be gloomy and sullen, but only serious. For it is better for one who has stern features to smile.
The smile is one of the principles of education and its subjects.
St. Clement of Alexandria * True joy is the joy of the other life, where the soul is not tormented and torn by desire.
St. John Chrysostom * "The kingdom of God is within you"(c) means the joy that the Holy Spirit plants in your hearts, being an icon and pledge of the eternal joy that the souls of the saints enjoy.

St. Gregory of Nyssa * [The mouths of the saved are filled with laughter, and their lips with gladness]. Take heed, O Bildad, and look quickly at the weight of your words... But it will not "be filled" in truth until afterward in the age to come, where grace awaits Job, in that he is a saved man. There too he will enjoy lips filled with the work of grace, that is, filled with thanksgiving to God.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Christ proclaimed the laughter that comes from joy and gladness, as Holy Scripture says in Job: [Truth fills the mouth with laughter] (Job 8:21). Perhaps for this reason one of the Fathers (the Patriarch Isaac) was named "Laughter", because the name means divine gladness.

Origen * "When he shall fill thy mouth with laughing, and thy lips with rejoicing" [21]. The mouth of the righteous will be filled with laughter when the tears of their journey are completed, and their hearts will be filled completely with the shout of eternal joy. Concerning this laughter the Truth says to His disciples: "Verily, verily, I say unto you, That ye shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice: and ye shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy" (Jn 16:20). Again: "But I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man taketh from you" (Jn 16:22). Concerning this laughter of the holy Church Solomon says: [She laughs in the last day] (Prov 31:25). It was also said that it will go well in the end with him who fears the Lord. There is no bodily laughter there, but the laughter of the heart...
Pope Gregory (the Great)
They that hate thee shall be clothed with shame; and the dwelling place of the wicked shall come to nought [22].

* [Thy adversaries shall be clothed with shame], whether visible or invisible... The Egyptian was clothed with shame when he saw Joseph (Gen 39:20-21). Jezebel was in the same state when she saw Elijah sharing in the position of the saints, him whom she had persecuted with tyranny (1 Kgs 19:2); likewise the adversaries of Job who were not victorious were also clothed with shame when they saw Job rejoicing among the angels.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * As they see before the eyes of their mind their past evil deeds flowing forth, iniquity clothes them on every side, and drags them down by its weight. Then they suffer from the memory of their evils while they are being punished.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Let me possess You, O Wisdom of God!
* Your love brought You down to us, O Wisdom of God, for You are my light and my treasure and the secret of my joy and my peace.
You drew near to me, and longed to dwell within me.
Enter and dwell in me, that I may possess You forever.
* Without You, who will restrain my tongue so that it is not babbling?
I can tame wild beasts, but who will tame my tongue but You?
You fill my depths with Your riches, so that I feel no emptiness.
I am filled with You, so I do not hunger for vain talk.
You fill me with the pledge of Your glory, so I judge no one!
I possess You, and so I possess divine love.
I keep silent, that I may speak with You about every human being.
I love, and so I desire the glory of every person.
* Let me possess You, for You are the Crucified; let me walk as a member of Your Church, the suffering Bride.
I find my delight and my riches and my joy in being crucified with You.
False philosophical enticements will not draw me away, nor will the enemy of good ensnare me by denying the Church, Your Bride.
Nor do I seek temporal rest and passing happiness at the expense of eternal glory.
You keep Your suffering Church bearing the spirit of victory.
You are in her midst, so she shall never be moved!
* Let me possess You, that I may present You to every wounded sinner.
I present You in the language of love and gentleness, in Your wisdom, not in the language of biting criticism and wounding.
You covered me; grant me to cover my brethren.
You lifted me from hell to Paradise; grant me to embrace in love those who fell with me.
Wonderful is Your salvation, and wonderful is Your wisdom!
Make me, through You, wise and wonderful in my love for my brethren!
* Teach me, O divine Wisdom, how to pray to You.
Inflame my heart with Your love, so that I will ask for nothing but to possess You, and that all humanity may possess You with me.
What do You offer me but Your dwelling in me.
What do I hope for but to be united with You.
What reward is there for me, except the enjoyment of You!
Grant me Your wisdom, that I may possess You, and through You possess everything, by Your indwelling within me!
* When will You come, O divine Wisdom, that I may enjoy a glorious end, and enjoy the fellowship of the heavenly glories.
You will carry me to the bosom of the Father, and my soul will rest there eternally.
My labors will turn into heavenly rest, and my sufferings into perpetual sweetness, and my daily deaths into the joy of the resurrection!
* Grant me, O Lord, that You shine upon me with Your light, that I may know Your surpassing mysteries.
Let me experience them richly by Your grace, let me taste them in my life as through the experience of my fathers.
Let Your wisdom work in me as in my fathers.
Not that I should hold to the words of my fathers without their life.
Grant me a holy heart that receives the holy deposit, and hands it on, not in literalisms and formalities, but in the spirit of truth and holiness.
* Let me drink of the waters of Your Holy Spirit, that I may be like an olive tree planted in Your house.
The enemy will not be able to approach it, nor will his trials make it lose its vitality and growth.
I drink in Your constant remembrance, and Your name will not depart from my lips.
And may Your image not be removed from my heart!
I remember You always and am filled with hope.
I hide in You, and find safety and peace.
Instead of the spider's house that I wove for myself, let me dwell in Your embrace, O fortress of my life.
* By You, O Wisdom of God, all hypocrisy departs from me.
So I will not be like the papyrus that grows in waters containing mud, but like a tree planted by the streams of Your Holy Spirit.
Nor will I be like the spider protected by a flimsy house, but I will dwell in You, O source of all safety.
I will not be like grass that the sun burns and dries, but I will enjoy Your light shining on my depths.
Nor will I stumble over stones in the road, but I will become a living stone in the heavenly Temple.
Nor will I be like a leafy tree whose roots the axe has struck, but an olive tree planted in Your holy house.
* In You my soul rejoices, in You I enjoy the pledge of the joy of heaven!
In You I become the wise, holy bride.

entries.section: 1. No one will be justified before God

paragraphs.text: Then Job answered and said: [1]
I know it is so of a truth.

entries.section: 1. No one will be justified before God

paragraphs.text: But how should man be just with God? [2]

Job did not defend himself against Bildad's accusation of speaking too much (Job 8:2). He also revealed to him that he agrees with him in the principle: [God does not pervert judgment, and the pious are kept by the care of God, and the wicked man perishes by his wickedness](a).

But he asked: "How should man be just with God?" This question does not carry a spirit of murmuring, nor does it carry a revolt against the severity of God, but he confessed the reality that if God dealt with us according to our deserts, all mankind would perish, for there is none righteous in the eyes of God, no, not one.

If Job looks at himself, comparing himself with those around him, he sees that he is righteous, but when he looks at God the Holy and Righteous, he finds himself not pure, and unable to be justified before Him. For even His holy angels will not be justified before Him. The Psalmist says: "And enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified" (Ps 2:143).
No one will be able to be justified before God except His eternal Word, who became man without sin alone; he who hides in Him bears His righteousness, and so is justified before the Lord.

The Apostle says: "But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption" (1 Cor 30:1), "And that ye put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness" (Eph 24:4).

* Look how Job also confesses his sins (Job 9:2-3, 19-20, 30; 13:26 - 14:5; 16:14, 17). He says that he is certain that there is no righteous man before the Lord. So he is certain of this also, that if we say that we have no sin, the truth is not in us. While God gives a lofty testimony about his righteousness in terms of the level of human conduct, Job himself knows the truth that it is so, where he says: "How should a mortal be just before the Lord? If he will contend with him, he cannot answer him."

St. Augustine * We see him, through his words, expressing himself in a wonderful manner as pious and virtuous, presenting his conduct as his offering to God, adapting his words for the sake of the glory of God. Even when he speaks from himself, or when his wife provoked him, and when his friends angered him, and even when the accuser (the devil) pulled at his throat to make him blaspheme, the righteous man did not cease to glorify God. "I will bless the Lord at all times" (Ps 34:1).

In a better way Job corrected the words of his companions who insulted him, turning everything they uttered against the wrestler in spite and contempt toward the excellent Job into a blessing for God's sake. If you say: How so? Learn this, for Bildad, with a spiteful intention in his statement, began with this introduction: [Doth the Lord pervert judgment, or doth the Maker of all things reverse the right?] (Job 8:3) What could Job say to this? How does he answer his adversary, turning in a wonderful way what was meant to throw him down? Let us listen: "Then Job answered and said: [True, I know that it is so. But how should mortal man be just with the Lord?] [1-2].
Why do you insult Job as one who is not righteous?

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Job answered them: "True, I know that it is so. But how should mortal man be just with God? For if he will contend with him, he will not hear him, nor will he answer him one word in a thousand, for he is wise in understanding and strong and great; who is hard enough to be able to stand before him? Who makes the mountains grow old, and they know not! And who overturns them in his anger. Who shakes the earth from its foundations, and its pillars tremble! He speaks to the sun, and it rises not, and sets his seal upon the stars. Who alone stretches out the heavens and walks upon the sea as on level ground, maker of the Bier (or Pleiades) and the Evening star and the Mighty (Great) Bear, Great Bear, and the chambers of the horses.

[Doer of great things past finding out, and wonders without number, glorious and without measure or number. If he passes over me I do not see him, and if he goes by me I do not perceive how?] (Job 2:9-11) LXX. How much stronger was his trumpet when he made him cry out concerning the power of the Lord! But in this strength the righteous man receives help, not destruction. Truly, while it seems that it is the power of the Lord that is described, in reality the mysteries of our redemption are being revealed!

St. Ambrose * It is the treasure that was given to them in this life to possess within their souls, who [of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption] (1 Cor 1:30). He who has found the treasure of the heavenly Spirit and possesses it fulfills by it all the righteousness of the commandment and all the fulfilling of virtues in purity and without blame, indeed easily and without compulsion.

Therefore let us entreat God, and ask and request of Him with a sense of need, that He may bestow on us the treasure of His Spirit, so that we may walk in all His commandments in purity and without blame, and fulfil all the righteousness of the Spirit in purity and perfection, by means of the heavenly treasure, who is Christ.

St. Macarius the Great * When a man submits to God he receives righteousness, but he who stands against Him loses righteousness. For he who compares himself with the source of all good things deprives himself of the goodness he has received. He who ascribes to himself the blessings given him by God wages war against God with the very gifts of God.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* The righteousness of God is Christ; the Apostle says: [who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption]; as it is written, [He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord].

The righteousness of God, which is the gift of grace without merits, is not known by those who want to establish their own righteousness, and so do not submit themselves to the righteousness of God, which is Christ.
In this righteousness we find the wealth of God's sweetness, of which the Psalm says: [Taste and see how sweet the Lord is] (Ps 34:8).
St. Augustine

3 If he will contend with him, he cannot answer him one of a thousand. 4 He is wise in heart, and mighty in strength: who hath hardened himself against him, and remained safe? 5 Which removeth the mountains, and they know not, which overturneth them in his anger. 6 Which shaketh the earth out of her place, and the pillars thereof tremble. 7 Which commandeth the sun, and it riseth not; and sealeth up the stars. 8 Which alone spreadeth out the heavens, and treadeth upon the waves of the sea. 9 Which maketh Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades, and the chambers of the south. 10 Which doeth great things past finding out; yea, and wonders without number. 11 "Lo, he goeth by me, and I see him not: he passeth on also, but I perceive him not. 12 Behold, he taketh away, who can hinder him? who will say unto him, What doest thou? 13 God will not withdraw his anger; the helpers of Rahab stoop under him."
If he will contend with him, he cannot answer him one of a thousand [3].

No man can compete with his Creator in discussion or in struggle. A man cannot answer one question out of the thousand questions that God puts to him. God spoke with Job and put several questions to him, and Job stood unable to answer any one of them (Job 38-39). Thus the wisdom of man stands silent in helplessness before the surpassing wisdom of God.

God directs a thousand accusations to man, and man finds no answer to justify what he does in even one matter of the thousand, for God does not err in His judgment. And He knows our depths more than we know ourselves. We have nothing to do but lay our hands on our mouths as Job did (Job 40:4-5).

* Did I not confess my transgressions to You, my God, and You took away the iniquity of my heart? I do not contend in judgment with You, for You are the Truth. I do not wish to deceive myself, lest my iniquity lie against itself. Therefore I do not dispute Your judgments, because "If thou, Lord, shouldest mark iniquities... who shall stand?" (Ps 130:3).

* I do not dispute in judgment with You, who are the Truth. I will not deceive myself, lest my iniquities stand against the Truth. Therefore I will not contend in judgment with You. For if You mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand before You? (Ps 3:130).
* God alone is righteous and the One who justifies; He gives man righteousness.

They seek to establish their own righteousness, meaning that they think that goodness is from themselves and not a divine gift. In this they have not "submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God" (Rom 10:3), because they are proud and think they are able to please God by themselves and not by what is God's.

St. Augustine * In Holy Scripture the number 1000 usually refers to "the sum total".... The Psalmist says: [the word which he commanded to a thousand generations] (Ps 105:8)... So it was said of John the Seer: [shall reign with him a thousand years] (Rev 20:6), because the reign of the holy Church is accomplished where it becomes perfect in its totality...

Now he who contends with God does not belong to Him, but ascribes to himself the glory of his goodness. May the holy man consider that whatever he has actually received, even the gifts greatest in importance, if he is glorified, it is only because of what he received as a gift... And let him say: "If he will contend with him, he cannot answer him one of a thousand." For he who contends with his Creator is unable to answer Him one in a thousand. For the man who places himself in the position of perfection proves that he lacks even the very beginning of the good life.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* [If thou, Lord, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?] (Ps 3:130). That is, everyone says: "I am a sinner, I am full of countless sins, I cannot approach God and pray and call upon Him"... It is impossible for anyone to give a precise account of his affairs, but he seeks mercy and compassion. We say this, not to draw souls into indifference, but to offer consolation to those who have fallen into despair. [Who can say, I have made my heart clean, I am pure from my sin?] (Prov 9:20) Let him remember: [Who trusts that he is free from sins?].
St. John Chrysostom He is wise in heart, and mighty in strength.
Who hath hardened himself against him, and remained safe? [4]

If anyone dares and persists in his stubbornness and rebellion against God, he certainly reaps the fruit of his folly. All who defied and did not repent were not safe, nor did they find peace in their depths, rest in their way, or success in their works. All resistance to God is like grass or thorns that defy the fire and are burned and perish (Isa 27:4; Ezek 28:24).

The angels who hardened themselves against God were not safe (2 Pet 2:4). And since the dragon fought against God, he was cast down to the earth (Rev 12:7-9). So rebellious sinners [treasure up unto themselves wrath against the day of wrath] (Rom 2:5).
It is utter madness for a man to stand up to resist God or to contend against the All-wise and All-powerful, who knows everything and is able to do everything.

He who wants true peace does not enter into strife with God, but receives the Lord Christ, who is our peace, who gives us reconciliation with God His Father, and with our souls and with our brethren, and even with nature itself.

* [For he is wise in heart, and mighty in strength.] What wonder if we call the Creator of the wise wise, He whom we know to be Wisdom itself? And what astonishment that he describes Him as "mighty", since He is Power itself? But the saint, in praising the Creator with these two words, conveys meaning to us as he calls us to tremble at our knowledge of ourselves. For God is called "wise" since He knows perfectly the secrets of our hearts, and he adds "mighty", since He is known to strike them with power. Therefore He is not deceived by us since He is wise, and we cannot flee from Him because He is strong...

[Who resists him and has peace?] For the Creator of all things wonderfully governs them Himself, so that having been created they work together in harmony. Therefore any resistance against God breaks the harmony together in peace, and these things cannot be governed well, since they lose the government from above. If these things submit to God they continue in peace, and if left to themselves they work in confusion... The first father of the human race, when he disobeyed the commandment of his Creator, was exposed to the arrogance of the flesh, and when he did not submit to his Creator in obedience to Him, he lowers himself until he loses the peace of the body...

Now it is said that we resist God when we oppose His providence. Not that our weakness resists His unchanging decrees, but what our weakness does has no strength to be accomplished. But if human weakness attempts it, it often knows the power of His providence, and yet aims at opposing it as far as it is able.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* He who seeks peace seeks Christ, for He is peace.
St. Basil the Great * He says: "(Christ) is our peace" (Eph 2:14). Elsewhere he calls Him a mediator. He of His own will mediates between two divided realms.

Souls born of the fountain of God's goodness were confined in the world. A barrier was found in the middle, a kind of fence. A barrier made by the deceptions of the flesh and worldly lusts. And Christ, by His mystery, by His Cross and passion and way of life, broke down this barrier. He conquered sin and taught that it must be broken down.
He took away the barrier from the midst. He overcame the enmity in His flesh. The work is not ours. We were not called to free ourselves.
Faith in Christ is our salvation.
Fr. Marius Victorinus Which removeth the mountains, and they know not, which overturneth them in his anger [5].

We often look at the mountains in nature and think them firm and settled, that no one can move or shift them, so they were called "the everlasting mountains" (Hab 3:6), and the sun and the world seem fixed by their laws, but when the Lord wills, heaven and earth pass away, and the mountains too are moved by a word from Him. Our God is "He who removeth the mountains, and they know not", that is, whether they wish it or not. He is the God of the impossible; before Him Mount Sinai trembled (Ps 68:8), the mountains skipped (Ps 114:4), and the everlasting mountains were broken or scattered (Hab 3:6).
"The mountains shall be moved from their foundations with the waters, the rocks shall melt as wax at thy presence" (Jdt 16:18).
"The earth shook and trembled; the foundations of the mountains trembled and were shaken, because he was wroth" (Ps 18:7).
"The mountains melted like wax before the Lord, before the Lord of the whole earth" (Ps 5:97)
"He toucheth the mountains, and they smoke" (Ps 32:104).
"The mountains skipped like rams, and the little hills like lambs" (Ps 4:114).
"Come down, touch the mountains, and they shall smoke" (Ps 5:144).

* What are the mountains that the Lord made grow old? They are Moses and Aaron and Joshua the son of Nun and Gideon and the prophets and all the men of the books of the Old Testament. The Lord Jesus came, and brought the New Testament, and what He had made (before) became old. The Christian was renewed and the Jew grew old; grace was renewed, and the letter grew old. The mountains were moved and removed. Yes, He moved the understanding according to the letter, and overthrew it, and established the perception according to the Spirit. Therefore the understanding of the Law according to the flesh has passed away and the Law became spiritual. Therefore the Apostle says: "For we know that the law is spiritual: but I am carnal" (Rom 7:14). But he himself who was carnal became spiritual, as the Apostle affirms, saying: "and I think also that I have the Spirit of God" (1 Cor 7:40). Thus Jesus made these mountains grow old and the Jews did not know it. Indeed had they known it they would not have crucified the Lord of glory, nor followed Jewish fables.

St. Ambrose * We say that the Jews, although they previously enjoyed God's favor, being loved by Him more than others, yet this divine dispensation and grace have passed to us, when Jesus transferred the authority working among the Jews to the believers from the Gentiles.

* When Jesus addressed the Jews, saying: "The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof" (Mt 21:43), what other dispensation was He, by His divine authority, about to present, except that He pushed the whole Jewish Scripture - which contained the mysteries of the Kingdom of God - into the circle of light.

* We who were transferred from the Law and the Prophets to the Gospel have been circumcised again (Josh 7:5) (by the rock) which is Christ (1 Cor 4:10), so the word of the Lord to Joshua was fulfilled in us, "This day have I rolled away the reproach of Egypt from off you" (Josh 9:5).

Origen * He says: The mountains do not know it. And as David said: "He toucheth the mountains, and they smoke" (Ps 104:32). In this phrase he speaks of the power of God, saying that He is able to do all things in the strength of His wrath. For Job gives testimony to His justice, as he also gives testimony to His power.

St. John Chrysostom * [He uses the mountains, and they know not, He who overturns them in His wrath.] [He uses] the visible mountains in truth when He wants to change the face of visible creation. But it is no wonder for these (mountains) that they do not know that they are "used", for they were not given a mind like human beings and living angels. Therefore Job calls the power of the arrogant demons mountains. Therefore the prophet Jeremiah calls the accuser (the devil) [a destroying mountain, which destroyeth all the earth] (Jer 51:25). For the corruption of the demons is base. Although they are full of deceit, they cannot reach the thoughts of God, since He wants to hide His thoughts from them, nor did they perceive the fall that befell them. What Paul says is an example of this: "Howbeit we speak wisdom among them that are perfect: yet not the wisdom of this world, nor of the princes of this world, that come to nought: But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom, which God ordained before the world unto our glory: Which none of the princes of this world knew: for had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory" (1 Cor 2:6-8).

He who uses these (powers) in the conflicts of the mystery of the Cross is the One who created them (Col 1:16), and destroyed them (Amos 3:14), and not only destroyed them but "in His anger" demolished their altars, scattered their temples, and ruined their statues. In victory, He stripped them of their glory (Col 2:15), for not only did the demons usurp glory (Rev 13:4-8), when they ought not to have done this, but they also corrupted humanity along with them. But when does true, just destruction befall them, as in complete wrath? When this visible world ends. In any case, if you say, how does He do this? You will learn it from the following: "Which shaketh the earth out of her place" [6].

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem God in His love for mankind raises up from His true believers holy, firm mountains, which are like Mount Sinai where the Lord appeared and gave His law to Moses, or like Mount Tabor where He was transfigured in the midst of His Church, which includes the men of the Old Testament, represented by Moses and Elijah, and the men of the New Testament, represented by Peter, James and John. On the other hand, the wicked who resist the Lord, who do not submit to Him, even if they think themselves to be firm mountains, their foundations tremble before the Lord in His wrath, and by His fury He makes them shake; He touches them with His wrath and they smoke. They skip like rams from before His face, and melt like wax before the fire.

* "The earth shook and trembled" (Ps 7:18). When the Son of Man was glorified thus, sinners shook and trembled. "The foundations of the mountains trembled" (Ps 7:18), for the hope of the proud who were in this life trembled. "And were shaken because he was wroth." This is the hope in temporal blessings, which is no longer founded in the hearts of men.

* "The hills melted like wax before the Lord" (Ps 5:97). Who are the hills? The proud. Everything that exalts itself against God, through Christ and the Christians, trembles and submits... Where is the haughtiness of the powers? Where is the cruelty of the unbelievers? The Lord was to them a fire, and they melted at His presence like wax. They were hard until the fire worked.
St. Augustine * "The mountains melted like wax" (Ps 5:97). To me the mountains seem to be the powers of the demons. Whether they are mountains or not, they are certainly the proud people.

This fire does not destroy those below (the humble) but destroys only the haughty. As a matter of fact, lightning rarely affects those in the valley, but those on high on the mountains will not escape it.

St. Jerome St. Ambrose presents to us a wonderful concept of the moving of the mountains while they know not, for when He came into the world He moved the holy mountains, as He moved our concepts of Moses the prophet who received the Law and of the prophets and the men of the Old Testament. He moved them from the literal Jewish mind that we might receive them in the Spirit through the Gospel. For although the Jews hold to the Law and the Fathers and the Prophets, they do not know the mystery of God and His hidden wisdom, because they still see them through the veil placed on the face of Moses(b). All this was moved to become our portion, so that we may understand and know the mystery of God's eternal plan and His surpassing wisdom and His dispensation for our salvation. This is what the Apostle Paul cherished after he met the Lord Christ and the mountains were moved for him, and he gained insight into the divine mystery, so that he could not keep silent.
"Whereby, when ye read, ye may understand my knowledge in the mystery of Christ" (Eph 4:3).
"That the Lord would open unto us a door... to speak the mystery of Christ" (Col 3:4).

"That their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the knowledge of the mystery of God the Father and of Christ" (Col 2:2).
"And to make all men see what is the fellowship of the mystery, which from the beginning of the ages hath been hid in God, who created all things by Jesus Christ" (Eph 9:3).
Which shaketh the earth out of her place, and the pillars thereof tremble [6].
If the earth seems to be settled on pillars that no one can shake, yet at the command of its Creator it is shaken, and there is nothing to support it.

In the symbolic sense, we saw that the mountains are moved in the sense that the haughty who dwell on the mountaintops are exposed to destruction through the divine lightnings. On the other hand, the Law and the Fathers and the Prophets are high holy mountains, that move from the hands of the Jews, literal in their understanding, to the sons of the New Testament, to whom the divine wisdom has been revealed, and who have come to know the hidden mystery of Christ. By the same logic, the earth points to the wicked who have become dust like their father the first Adam, to whom it was said: [Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return](c). Now that the Heavenly One has come down to our earth, and dwelt among us, and become as one of us, we enjoy the heavenly life, and we hear the divine voice: [Heaven thou art, and unto heaven shalt thou return].
And dwelt among us, and became as one of us, we enjoy the heavenly life, and we hear the divine voice: [Heaven thou art, and unto heaven shalt thou return].

* The stranger centurion knows, while the Levite who was of His own did not know. The Gentile worshiped Him, and the Hebrew denied Him. Therefore it is not unreasonable that the pillars of the world moved (Job 9:6) when the chief priests did not believe.

The pillars moved in order that new pillars might take their place. As though God Himself deemed it fitting to say: [I have set up the pillars of it] (Ps 75:3). Learn what pillars He set up: "James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship" (Gal 2:9).

St. Ambrose * With vessels and a bucket one measures the water that comes out of natural springs, but the water that flows from spiritual springs is measured by our understanding and our burning desire and our reverence, by which we draw near to them. He who walks in this order at once carries countless blessings, for the grace of God works in him invisibly, and lightens the burden of his conscience, and brings him to abundant safety, and then prepares him to withdraw from the shore of the earth and bear the anchor of heaven. For a man who still embraces his body can have nothing attached to the earth, but sets before his eyes all the delights of heaven and contemplates them without ceasing.
* I want you to keep your minds on these things always (Col 1:3). For our concern with them frees us from the earth and transports us to heaven.

St. John Chrysostom * It is right for us to be there in the presence of God in the heavens, we who learned the lesson while on earth, and went there to heaven in order to be in the love of God the Father, whom we came to know while on earth, and because God the Word, the Holy One, made everything and taught us and teaches us everything, and trains us in all good things.
St. Clement of Alexandria * Abraham left his city and his relatives by a divine command, but his migration suited him as a prophet, its aim being the seeking of the knowledge of God.
In truth it was not a bodily migration - as I think - but was preparing him for the knowledge of those things which the Spirit discovers.

By leaving his homeland, that is, by going out of himself, out of the circle of base and earthly thoughts, Abraham raised his mind as far as possible above the common limits of human nature, and let go of the soul's attachment to the senses.
Thus, since the attachments of the senses did not hinder him, his mind became pure, perceiving what is unseen, and hearing and sight no longer caused his mind to err because of appearances.

St. Gregory of Nyssa * When the will of God is accomplished by us who are on earth as it is accomplished by those in heaven, we become like the heavenly ones, as we bear like them the image of the heavenly (1 Cor 49:15) and inherit the Kingdom of Heaven (Mt 34:25). And those after us who are on earth come, praying that they may be like us when we are in heaven (Paradise).

Origen * You must long for heaven, and the things that are in heaven, indeed even before heaven, for we have been commanded to make the earth heaven, and to behave and speak in all things as though we were speaking there, while we are on earth. This also must be the aim of our prayer which we offer to the Lord. Nothing hinders our reaching the perfection of the heavenly powers because we dwell on earth; rather it is possible, even while we dwell here, to do everything as though we were already dwelling on high.
* Truly the Lord came to abolish the old things and to call us to a greater homeland.

He does everything to set us free from unnecessary things and from our affection for the earth. For this reason He also referred to the pagans, saying: "For after all these things do the Gentiles seek" (Mt 6:32); who devote all their labor to the present life, and have no care for the things to come, nor for any heavenly thought.
St. John Chrysostom Which commandeth the sun, and it riseth not; and sealeth up the stars [7].

No one expects that the sun will not rise at its appointed time, since the Lord set fixed laws for it. But if He wills, it does not rise. Once He commanded it to stand still to serve His people, and it stood still (Josh 10:12). What happened in the days of Joshua the son of Nun proclaims God's wonderful work through His servants, and as St. Athanasius the Apostolic says: [Though the sun stood still at Gibeon, and the moon in the valley of Ajalon, yet this work is not the work of the son of Nun, but the work of the Lord who heard the prayer, He who rebuked the sea, and on the Cross made the sun darken (Mt 27:45).]
Again God commanded the sun to go back, and it obeyed the divine command (2 Kgs 20:9). So also with the stars, He alone is able to seal them or hide them from our eyes.
God by His will preserves the order of the course of nature as an extension of the process of creation, and as a work of the divine providence.
Which alone spreadeth out the heavens, and treadeth upon the waves of the sea [8].

God, who created the universe, preserves the law of nature, so the heavens remain spread out, and without His providence their order would collapse. He treads the seas with His feet and prevents them from returning to "turn again to cover the earth" (Ps 104:9). He walks upon the raging waves, declaring that He alone calms all the waves of trials raging against us.

St. John Chrysostom sees that there is no point of comparison between what Moses the prophet did during the crossing of the Red Sea and the Lord Christ's walking on the water. What Moses did he did as a servant through prayer, but the Lord Christ did so with absolute authority. When the wind blew they crossed under Moses' leadership on dry ground in the midst of the sea (Ex 14:21), but the Lord Christ walked on the surface of the sea as upon a road, to bear witness to what is written in Scripture: [Who walks on the sea as on a pavement].

* "Which alone spreadeth out the heavens" [8] - by the heavens what does he indicate but the heavenly life itself of the preachers, of whom the psalmist said: [The heavens declare the glory of God] (Ps 19:1).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* The Gospel of the Lord teaches us that it was not the Father but the Son who walked on the sea when Peter asked Him, saying: "Lord, bid me come unto thee on the water" (Mt 28:14).
* It is the Lord who seals and numbers the host of the stars (Job 9:7)(g). He alone spreads out the heaven, and He walked on the sea as upon a pavement (Job 9:8; Mt 14:25).

When Peter saw Him walking, he said: "Lord... bid me come unto thee on the water" (Mt 14:28). The Lord commanded him, but he hesitated and nearly sank and perished among the waves, had the Lord not stretched out His right hand to him (Mt 14:29-31). The body staggered, and the right hand of the Lord rescued. And the Lord said to him: "O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?" (Mt 14:31) It was faith that walked in the person of the Apostle, not the body.
St. Ambrose * Who could walk on the sea if not the Creator of the world?
Truly the Holy Spirit, who spoke very anciently through the blessed Job, said of Him: [Who alone spreads out the heavens, and walks on the sea as on the earth].
It was said of Him in the person of Wisdom: [I dwelt in high places, and my throne was in a cloudy pillar] (Sir 24:7).

Likewise David declared in the Psalm: [Thy way is in the sea, and thy path in the great waters] (Ps 19:77) Note also Habakkuk: "The overflowing of the water passed by: the deep uttered his voice" (Hab 10:3).
Father Chromatius Which maketh Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades, and the chambers of the south [9].

He is the Creator of the groups of stars, and here three groups are mentioned on behalf of all: "Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades," and He still preserves them in existence and directs their movements, for the service of mankind.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus sees that when Scripture here mentions Arcturus, Orion and the Pleiades, it means all the stars and His divine providence over them. This is like when it refers to His care for the young ravens (Ps 147:9), it means all the birds.
"The chambers of the south," that is, the stars seen from the side of the South Pole and not seen by those in the northern hemisphere.

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees in these stars a symbolic meaning of the seven churches, which are the universal Church, which St. John the Beloved saw as seven lampstands. It enjoys the seven gifts of divine grace; its rays shine with the light of virtue issuing from the Truth.

* By Arcturus, Orion, Pleiades and the chambers of the south he indicates the whole group of the stars of the heavens and everything that is there... Job is surely speaking of every kind of miracle accomplished by God. In any case he speaks rather of the dispensations accomplished for our sake, for they are certainly divine, lofty dispensations that surpass nature. They are incomprehensible, because they are too high for a human spirit to reach. And they are profitable because God receives worship from the creatures here below, and from those who are on high, which are filled with wonderful works... John the Theologian has declared to us: "And there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written" (Jn 21:25). Not only because they are above all number, but because His works are lofty, and the ears of this world are unable to receive them.
Father Hesychius of Jerusalem Which doeth great things past finding out; yea, and wonders without number [10].
Here Job repeats literally what Eliphaz had said, [please refer to the commentary on Job 5:9].
Lo, he goeth by me, and I see him not: he passeth on also, but I perceive him not [11].

God's works are transcendent; He works with us and around us and within us without our seeing Him (Acts 17:23). Our limited perception is unable to know His movements for our sake, so it is difficult, indeed impossible, for us to evaluate His actions, even the apparent ones, because we do not perceive what is behind them. We have no right to comment on His actions, or to think that we are able to explain them.
* Since the human race was deprived of inner joy because of sin, it lost insight of mind, and cannot tell where these things are going.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* [When (God) rises above me I do not see Him, and when He passes by me I do not know this either]. God rises above each one of us, when He postpones the judgment upon us. And on the other hand He passes by us, that is, passes in our midst... In the first place we cannot see Him with the eyes of our body, and secondly we cannot reach Him with our spirit, for what constitutes Him is exceedingly subtle not only for the eyes but even for spirits.

* He passes through our minds, but it is clear that His passing was accomplished through our life, where He passed by way of the dispensation of His incarnation, His suffering on the Cross, and His glorious resurrection... And above all this, who can know how He was man and God (at the same time); how He suffered and destroyed suffering; how He tasted death as man, and as God subdued Hades and destroyed death (1 Cor 15:54; 2 Tim 1:10; 1 Pet 3:22).
He is the One who freed mankind from that curse and from the evil of sin (Rom 8:2), and no one could lighten the burdens that were upon us, from which He freed us.

No one can any more say to Him: "What doest thou?" or why do You justify sinners, and bring - under the blessing - him who was under the threat of the curse (Gal 3:13-14; Deut 21:23). He did this first as God, by the power that belongs to Him as God, working with authority, burying the debt of our sins in the earth (Col 2:14), therefore he adds: "He turns back His anger," that which was against us.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that this is the state of the person who feels isolated from God. He passed by him and granted him the experience of purity, but afterward he fell under the bitterness of the temptations of the flesh, which surround the mind and throng upon it, so that the inner eye becomes unclean, and consequently unable to see God. This is by God's permission so that the mind may be humbled and seek divine help.

* When the mind finds itself weak under temptation it turns to seek the help of the divine Being, and ceases entirely to depend on itself. And so it happens that He passes by, and the mind clings itself to God in the deepest way, by the very means by which it grieved over its fall and its distance from God.

Therefore God's entering and departing cannot be fully discovered by our faculties as long as the place of alternation of our state (from God's entering and departing) is hidden from our eyes. For example there is no definite assurance whether a particular trial is for testing virtue or is an instrument for our destruction.
As for gifts, we never perceive whether they are rewards for works we have done, or are support on man's way to his (heavenly) homeland.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* When the Apostle touched on the knowledge of divine matters - in his Epistle to the Corinthians - he affirmed that his knowledge - despite what he had received of it - is still limited and extremely scant. For he said: "And if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know" (1 Cor 8:2).

He assured us that now we know in part, but the greater part of it we shall know in the age to come: "For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away" (1 Cor 13:9-10).

And when he wished to clarify the difference between our knowledge here and our knowledge in the other life he resorted to this illustration: "When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things. For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face" (1 Cor 13:11-12).

Have you perceived the extent of the difference between them? It is like the difference between the knowledge of a little child and that of a mature man, and like the difference between seeing in a mirror and looking face to face, for the mirror indicates a deep expression but in obscurity...! Why then do we not believe Paul's words: "Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus?" (Rom 9:20).
Consider how it befits us to submit to God's will in silence!

He undoubtedly does not mean by this saying that he wishes to deprive us of our will. Far be it! But he affirms that the inquirer ought to keep silent, like clay in the hand of the potter, neither resisting nor disputing. He mentioned the potter and the clay to remind us of our nature, for they are on one level as regards their existence (since the potter is created from dust) and yet the clay submits to the potter; what forgiveness then can man hope for when he recklessly dares to dispute the will of God who formed him, though the difference between him and Being itself is infinite?!
Remember, O man: who are you?
Are you not clay and dust and ashes?
Are you not a vapor?
Are you not grass? Are you not the flower of the grass?

Thus the prophets compete in drawing pictures before our eyes to express the truth of our existence. But God, whom you want to subject to your reckless curiosity, is not subject to death or change. He is eternal, without beginning or end, incomprehensible, beyond all understanding and all reason, indescribable and invisible! These attributes cannot be grasped by me and you, or even by the Apostles and prophets, nor even by the heavenly powers - despite their invisible purity and spirituality and their continual dwelling in heaven.
St. John Chrysostom If he taketh away, who can hinder him? who will say unto him, What doest thou? [12]

God is the One with authority; no creature has the right to review what He does. We place our trust in Him, and accept His will, even when it seems bitter to us. "If he taketh away" even our souls, who can resist Him, or enter into discussion with Him? "Who will say unto him, What doest thou?" or why do You do so? (Dan 4:35).
* [If He wills to destroy, who can turn Him back, and who will say to Him: What doest thou?]
"Who can turn Him back?" that is, who will rescue us? No one can say: "What doest thou?" First, no one dares to, and no one would be there, because the results bear their own testimony.
Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * The works of our Creator must always be honored without examination, for they will not be unjust.
For he who searches for the cause of His secret counsel is counted as nothing but a man's resistance to His counsel in arrogance.

When man cannot discover the motive of God's works we must keep silent in humility, submitting to His works, because the bodily senses are not at a level that can penetrate the secrets of His majesty...
Later Paul adds: "Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus?" (Rom 9:20)
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Pope Gregory (the Great) comments on Job's saying: "Who will say unto him, What doest thou?" saying that no one can resist the wrath of God. Yet Scripture gives us several examples of some men of God standing before the wrath of God.

Moses the prophet resisted the wrath of God when he stood interceding for the fallen people, saying: "Yet now, if thou wilt forgive their sin; and if not, blot me, I pray thee, out of thy book which thou hast written" (Ex 32:32).

Also Moses asked Aaron to take a censer, and put fire in it from off the altar, and put on incense, and go quickly to the congregation, and make an atonement for them, "for there is wrath gone out from the LORD" (Num 16:46-48).

And Phinehas quenched the wrath of God when the people committed fornication with strange women, and he showed his zeal by thrusting the Israelite and the Midianite woman through the belly, so the plague was stayed from the children of Israel (Num 25:8).
And so David stood interceding for his people before the Lord to remove His wrath from them (2 Sam 24).
And the Truth demanded of us that we pray even for our enemies and persecutors (Mt 5:44).

Thus God shows the greatness of His surpassing love for man, for although no being can stand before the wrath of God, yet even in His wrath He declares His love, giving man an opportunity to break into the love of God by his humility and repentance and love for God and people and for the salvation of his soul; he asks mercy for himself and intercedes for his brethren.
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh presents us with a wonderful picture of resisting the wrath of God, namely by repentance:
* Jonah said: There is no means of nullifying the wrath, for iniquity has entrenched itself and the overthrow has come to destroy you...
Distress has drawn near, and the fall is at the door.
The Lord sent me, that Mighty One who bears creation, to proclaim the overthrow with a voice of terror upon your walls...

These voices struck the king of Nineveh, and he was terrified when he heard the dreadful news. He feared Jonah more than ranks of mighty men. And the dreaded king humbled himself before a lowly man. He rose from his splendid throne. And the dreaded king humbled himself before a lowly man. He rose from his splendid throne and cast the crown from him, and put on sackcloth, and prepared himself for repentance...

He realized that this battle was not like the usual battles, so he gathered his people and urged them to strive. He gathered his soldiers and lined them up for supplication, and supplied the ranks of soldiers with prayers to fence the gates. He made men and women and children hold to fasting, each according to his strength, to line up for battle against the wrath.
The king said to his soldiers words like these: Gather together for supplication, for a new fight we enter, contrary to custom...
No son of a single day ceases from striving. A fierce battle, in which you will see no weariness. Infants nursing on milk join us here in the ranks and support us before evil comes upon us.
In this battle the boys are stronger than the men, and the children strive more easily than the mighty.
The children who have not sinned in this battle go out by the thousands and join us, for through them the struggle becomes better.

Behold, the Hebrew asserts and threatens our destruction, let us work lest he rejoice if we are defeated. He has not ceased calling for wrath upon our corruption. And we will not cease until we call for mercies for our salvation. The man sought to establish his word because he is a prophet; let him preach, and let us ask his Lord...

We return to his Lord, the One with authority, that He may not destroy us. He is a messenger who speaks what was told him. It is within his authority to preach, not to destroy, so let us not grieve. If the matter were in his (the prophet's) hand, he would overturn the city. Let us not tire, for destruction is in the hand of the Lord. It is not in the hand of the prophet to build and tear down as he threatens... But against his voice we awaken voices of repentance, and call with weeping, so that we silence the man and quiet him. Let us not ask him, for he will not obey us and stop his speech. Let us send the voices of our sufferings to the Most High, and He will save us.
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh God will not withdraw his anger.
The helpers of Rahab stoop under him [13].

When He is angry no one can turn Him back from His anger except His mercy and love. He crushes the proud who resist Him. And as it says in the Book of Zechariah, [Be silent, O all flesh, before the LORD] (Zech 2:13). Repentance with its sighs and tears and humility turns back the divine wrath.

* Repentance is a fire that consumes all human weakness, removes negligence and laziness and heaviness of the body, and gives the soul a wing with which to fly toward heaven, and shows it from this high summit the vanity of this present life.

He who does not rise to the observation post cannot take a true picture of the earth and its contents. For many things darken the field of vision, deafen the ears, and make the tongue falter. Therefore it befits man to pull himself away from this noise, and keep far from the smoke, and enter into solitude to find deep peace and calm and stillness together with enlightenment.

When the eyes are fixed on the love of God, and the ear no longer hears except His words as though a sweet spiritual symphony, the soul becomes (God's) captive and feels a loathing for food and sleep.
Truly the clamor of the world and material concerns slide over the soul but do not enter into it, and by the soul's rising thus it no longer cares about the cracking of earthly storms.

And just as the dwellers of the mountains no longer hear the sounds of the city nor see what goes on in it, but count all this like vague noise, so those who have left the world by their own will and set off flying in the heights of philosophy (wisdom) no longer perceive anything of the conditions of the world, for all their senses are directed toward heaven.
Therefore let us seek not only the solitude of the wilderness, but the solitude of inner desire. Let us hide on the highest summit of the soul where nothing earthly dwells.
The power of repentance is like a wind that drives away the dust and sweeps away passions faster than smoke.
St. John Chrysostom * What sins can repentance fail to wash away? What deep-rooted stains can such tears not wash? By Peter's threefold confession he wiped out his threefold denial.
St. Jerome * Prolonged prayer and abundant tears draw God to mercy.
* Weeping alone leads to blessed laughter.
* Jesus wished to show in Himself all the beatitudes, for He said: [Blessed are those who weep], and He Himself wept in order to lay the foundation of this beatitude well.
Origen

entries.section: 3. His inability to contend with God

paragraphs.text: 14 How much less shall I answer him, and choose out my words with him? 15 For though I were justified, I would not answer, but would implore mercy of my judge. 16 If I had called, and he had answered me; yet would I not believe that he had hearkened unto my voice. 17 He who crusheth me with a tempest, and multiplieth my wounds without cause. 18 He will not suffer me to take my breath, but filleth me with bitterness. 19 If it be a matter of the strength of the strong, he saith: Here am I. And if it be a matter of judgment, he saith: Who will try me? 20 If I be justified, my mouth shall condemn me; and if I be perfect, he shall pronounce me guilty. 21 "I am perfect. I do not care for myself. I despise my life."
How much less shall I answer him, and choose out my words with him [14].

Job stands in contrition before God, confessing that he is unable to enter into dialogue with Him. But as many see it, Job fixed his gaze on his weakness, and slid toward despair, instead of looking to God's surpassing mercies and His love for mankind, and forgot that the almighty God longs to enter into dialogue with His creature, and did not prevent Satan from conversing with Him, as we saw in the first two chapters of the book (1, 2).

* It is worth noting that this saint (Job) passed over to judging himself so that when God's judgment comes it finds nothing in him to lay hold of. He looks at his weakness and says: "How much less shall I answer him, and choose out my words with him" [14]. For he does not rely on his own righteousness, but takes refuge in hope alone in appealing to God's compassion. Therefore he added: [Even if I had some righteousness I would not wish to answer, but would make supplication to my judge] [15]. And since he is aware of the appeal to God, he adds: [When I call He answers me, I believe that He does not hear my voice] [16]. Why does he diminish himself so... why is he terrified with such sorrowful doubt? His eyes are fixed on the dread of the Judge... and he shrinks before the power of the searching eye. For all that he does seems small to him.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. His inability to contend with God

paragraphs.text: For though I were justified, I would not answer, but would implore mercy of my judge [15].

Man may justify himself because he does not even know the truth of himself, and what is within him. He does not know the hidden faults that man himself may not perceive. This is what the Apostle Paul expressed by saying: "For I know nothing by myself," that is, he did not feel any evil dominating him, "yet am I not hereby justified" (1 Cor 4:4). So the Apostle feared that if he justified himself, hidden sins that he did not know would be revealed to him. This is what drove Job to ask mercy from the Judge, the Searcher of hearts, and to throw himself on His mercies and not on his own personal merits.

What occupies Job's mind is not to be justified in the eyes of people, for although they insult him and cast him to the ground, and crush him with their feet, the One who judges him is the merciful Judge, before whom he cannot be justified by himself, but seeks His mercy and divine tenderness.

* He says (Job to Bildad): You revile Job in vain. What do you gain by trampling the righteous with your feet? I postpone the judgment to God, taking refuge in His divine providence and tenderness. He does not listen to what is said about me without examining; He is not subject to what is said about me. God does not accuse Job as a sinner, nor does He even listen to it, for the following reason: even if I am righteous compared with those who are righteous, yet I need a kind of judgment of God concerning me and testimony from on high. If my life agrees with the divine truth of the Judge, then no one can nullify the power of this truth.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * All human righteousness is not counted as righteousness if examined by exact judgments... As if he says plainly: Even if I need to grow in the practice of virtue, I would be advancing in life, not by my own merit, but by the forgiving grace of God. Therefore we must be fervent in prayer when we walk uprightly, so that all the ways of righteousness we walk may be seasoned with humility.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. His inability to contend with God

paragraphs.text: If I had called, and he had answered me; yet would I not believe that he had hearkened unto my voice [16].

Some interpret this statement: that since he believed, his prayers were heard, not for the sake of his prayer itself, but for the sake of the holy name of God in which he believed. "Not for your sakes do I this, saith the Lord GOD, be it known unto you" (Ezek 36:32).

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees in Job's speech here a living picture of the continual struggle in the life of the believer, for by grace he calls on God and God answers him, as his heart is inflamed with love for divine things, but in the midst of this wonderful loftiness temporal thoughts invade the mind, and the believer finds himself as one who has fallen, and thinks that God does not hear his voice.

* Often the mind is inflamed with the fire of divine love, and rises to see the heavenly things and the hidden mysteries. The mind moves to the heights, and is wounded by perfect love, and becomes a stranger to lower things; but afterward when it is struck by a sudden temptation the soul which God supported with a clear purpose bows down, and is wounded by a temptation that assails it. It stands bewildered, wavering between good and evil practices, and cannot tell which side is stronger.

It often happens that it stands amazed how it possesses the heavenly truths while it wrestles with evil thoughts. Again it needs to know how evil thoughts creep into it while the zeal of the Holy Spirit powerfully carries it to lofty things. These alternating movements (between heavenly thoughts and evil ones) are rightly seen by the psalmist when he declares: "They mount up to the heaven, they go down again to the depths" (Ps 107:26)... The mind is terrified by these movements of its own, and by the things to which it is involuntarily subjected, until it thinks within itself that it is cast out and rejected.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. His inability to contend with God

paragraphs.text: He who crusheth me with a tempest, and multiplieth my wounds without cause [17].

Job felt that he had not committed extraordinary sins, yet extraordinary calamities befell him, for the storms of trial blew, not to disturb him but to crush him. The calamities wounded him abundantly without cause.

Some commentators see that Job attacked divine justice by saying "without cause," but some see that Job was bewildered because he had not fallen into a flagrant transgression, nor committed a sin that in the eyes of people is a great crime.

* "He who crusheth me with a tempest" [17]... It is rightly called a "tempest," because it is announced by the disturbance of the elements. And as the psalmist testifies by saying: [Our God shall come, and shall not keep silence: a fire shall devour before him, and it shall be very tempestuous round about him] (Ps 50:3). Another prophet also says: "The LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm" (Nah 1:3). In this whirlwind the righteous man will not be broken, because he always fears and is afraid lest he be broken.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Note in his words that he did not say: "He has never wounded me without cause," but "multiplieth my wounds without cause." For it is not because of the multitude of his sins that those many wounds came upon him, but to test his patience...

Again, he says: [His way have I kept, and not declined. From his commandments have I not departed] (Job 23:11-12). He keeps God's ways and did not turn aside from them, for he did not forget them, but was advancing running in them, although he is weak, and sometimes stumbles and falls. And yet he continues in the way, sinning less and less until he reaches the state of perfection, so that he no longer sins.

* He said this about the Jews who in their self-reliance despised grace, and did not believe in Christ, that he says that they wished to establish their own righteousness, this righteousness which is of the Law, not that they carry out the Law, but they establish their righteousness in the Law, when they reckon within themselves that they are able to carry out the Law by their own power, being ignorant of God's righteousness (Rom 10:3), not the righteousness that belongs to God but the righteousness that God grants to man.

entries.section: 3. His inability to contend with God

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine He will not suffer me to take my breath, but filleth me with bitterness [18].
Every person is exposed to sufferings from time to time, but sufferings did not leave Job to breathe, nor did bitterness depart from him. And in all this he did not know what the cause was.

* "He will not suffer me to take my breath, but filleth me with bitterness" [18]. Often He allows trials to befall me, so that I cannot take my breath. For often the enemy brings torments upon me, [I am filled with bitterness]. Also my wife and my friends are the ones who make me out a fool by their reviling me and speaking with me spitefully. Therefore I feel that this comes upon me from God, who permits it to come upon me, although He is able to prevent it from me. And yet I will not cease to bear witness to God's justice and power (Ps 71:19). By His divine providence He keeps all things in His hand. No man of sound mind dares to slander His judgments, for they proceed from the righteous Almighty.
Father Hesychius of Jerusalem If it be a matter of the strength of the strong, he saith: Here am I.
And if it be a matter of judgment, he saith:

entries.section: 3. His inability to contend with God

paragraphs.text: Who will try me? [19]

Job looks to God and sees Him, without dispute, as the Strong One, whom none can stand before. He speaks and it is done (Ezek 22:14). As for judgment, there is no higher authority, nor a supreme court that listens to the protest of a man; He is the Judge of all, above all creation.

* [Since He is strong, He judges; who then resists His judgment?] [19]... The sun proclaims Him as other creatures do, how great and mighty He is, and it cannot disobey His command (Ps 104:19). Likewise the moon proclaims Him as it grows (until the crescent becomes a full moon) and wanes (as it diminishes after its fullness) according to His law. The sea also proclaims Him, as it does not transgress the limits assigned to it, and the sand resists the violence of the waves.

This is the reason for which no one can resist His judgments and disobey them. In any case, if you are speaking of the judgments by which He judges mankind, who has the audacity to resist Him? If you speak of Abraham, he said of himself: "I am but dust and ashes" (Gen 18:27). And David in the same spirit said: "Mine iniquities are gone over mine head: as an heavy burden they are too heavy for me" (Ps 38:4).

entries.section: 3. His inability to contend with God

paragraphs.text: He does not cease to sing with his harp what the famous Isaiah proclaims: [Woe is me, for I am a wretched man, of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people] who keep defiled teachings (cf. Isa 6:5). Therefore the wrestler adds: [If I appear righteous my mouth will be defiled] [20] How can this be? Listen: it is not easy for a person to be without blame in deeds and words. Therefore he rightly adds: [And if I appear perfect, I am surely a fool].

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * Someone may say: What shall I do? How can I be light, when here I live in evils and iniquities?! And thereby despair and grief creep upon him, since we have no salvation without fellowship with God, and God is light and in Him is no darkness at all, and sin is darkness, so how am I to be cleansed from it?! The Apostle continues, saying: "and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin." How great is this assurance that He has given us! By virtue of our being in this world in the midst of trials a man may stumble after his sins have been forgiven in Baptism, therefore we must do what we can, confessing our state as it is so that the Lord Christ may heal us by His blood.
St. Augustine If I be justified, my mouth shall condemn me?
And if I be perfect, he shall pronounce me guilty [20].

As for Job, if he justifies himself, his defense turns into iniquity, and he is judged by his words, for God knows the hidden things of the heart that man himself may not know. "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." If Job counts himself perfect, he counts this an accusation against God, and a guilt that he commits as a proud man ignorant of his depths.

* I glory that I am being saved, not because I am without sins, but because sins have been forgiven. I do not glory because I am useful or because someone is useful to me, but because Christ is my advocate (lawyer) before the Father, because the blood of Christ was shed for me.
St. Ambrose I am perfect. I do not care for myself.

entries.section: 3. His inability to contend with God

paragraphs.text: I despise my life [21].

Job looks to his old age and sees in himself that he is an old man who has no profit from the long years he has lived, for they have produced nothing! They are despised, fruitless years. These are the feelings of the man who looks at his life outside the circle of God's love and His grace, the Giver of fruit!

entries.section: 4. We do not judge by appearance

paragraphs.text: 22 It is one. Therefore I said, He destroyeth the perfect and the wicked. 23 If the scourge slay suddenly, he will laugh at the trial of the innocent. 24 The earth is given into the hand of the wicked: he covereth the faces of the judges thereof; and if it be not he, then who?
It is one.
Therefore I said, He destroyeth the perfect and the wicked [22].

Job's friends insist that the righteous prosper in this world and are protected from trials, and if trials reach them they are soon removed from them. But the wicked fail, trials surround them in this world and crush them, and there is none to deliver. But Job affirms the opposite: some of the wicked may prosper and flourish in this world, while the righteous are exposed to successive trials. This is the main point of dispute in all the discussions between Job and his friends, whose aim is for the friends to affirm that Job is a wicked hypocrite, who bears the appearance of godliness and hides evils that anger God.
Job affirms here that temporal events are not the measure by which to recognize the truth of a man, whether righteous or wicked.

"It is one": calamities may befall the wicked as well as the righteous, and death comes upon these and those. "The sword devoureth one as well as another" (2 Sam 11:25). It devours Josiah the good king as it devours Ahab the wicked king. Thus we see that "He destroyeth the perfect and the wicked." The good and the wicked were sent together into the Babylonian captivity (Jer 24:5, 9).

* [It is one; I said, He destroyeth the perfect and the wicked] [22]. This can be clarified in the following words: I said these words about myself, that even if I am perfect I do not appear perfect if examined closely, nor if I am wicked do I appear so if I remain hidden, withdrawn from the exact piercing examination. But the strict Judge, He perceives all things, and pierces the devices of the wicked in a wonderful way. In order to attain what is better He judges each according to his inclination.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Are these not the utterances of the citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem:
[My tears have been my meat day and night] (Ps 42:3).
[All the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears] (Ps 6:6).
"My groaning is not hid from thee" (Ps 38:9).
[My sorrow was stirred] (Ps 39:2)?

Do not the children of God who groan, being burdened, not wish to be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life? Do not even those who have the firstfruits of the Spirit groan within themselves, waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body? (Rom 23:8).

Did not the Apostle Paul himself, a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem, have all this when he was burdened and in continual sorrow of heart for his brethren the Israelites? But there will be no death in the City except when it is said: [O death, where is thy struggle? O death, where is thy sting? for the sting of death is sin].

entries.section: 4. We do not judge by appearance

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine If the scourge slay suddenly, he will laugh at the trial of the innocent [23].

As the sword suddenly stretched out kills this one and that one; the wicked to his destruction, and the righteous for the proving of his faith. [That the proving of faith, though it is tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory] (1 Pet 1:7). For the innocent make light of death because it is a passing over into glory!
