Pope Gregory (the Great) comments on the phrase: [He laughs at the trial of the righteous] saying: [If He uses the expression "laughter" of God to mean His joy, it is said that He laughs at the trial of the righteous, since they seek Him zealously (in time of trial) and He rejoices in us tenderly, for our pain causes Him a kind of joy when we have holy desires to discipline ourselves out of our love for Him.]

* Paul says (2 Cor 4:17) that our present sorrows are light since they occur within the limits of a certain time and a particular place. In return for this light labor we acquire glory beyond all measure.
Ambrosiaster * Every trial is either a punishment for the wicked or a testing of the righteous... So peace and calm in times of contention can benefit the good while corrupting the wicked.
St. Augustine The earth is given into the hand of the wicked:
He covereth the faces of the judges thereof.

entries.section: 4. We do not judge by appearance

paragraphs.text: And if it be not he, then who? [24]

Often God allows the wicked to escape and even to rule over the earth; on the one hand the enemy does not complain that the righteous worship the Lord and fear Him to obtain temporal blessings and earthly success, and on the other hand God leaves the wicked in his freedom in case he repents of his deed if he touches God's love, or the cup of his evil is filled if he persists in his rebellion and stubbornness.
If the wicked enemy is called "the god of this world," we should not wonder if the wicked take over the earth and think they are successful and kings.
The earth is given into the hands of the wicked, and the righteous enjoy heaven, because the Heavenly One dwells in them.

[He covers the faces of the judges of the earth] while the righteous are subjected to injustice on earth and the wicked put on masks, so they appear as judges of the earth, as those who judge justly, though it is not so.

Despite presenting this truth, many see that Job's style carries a kind of murmuring: how does the Lord leave the wicked to prosper and dominate the earth, and appear as judges who judge the innocent.

With the presentation of an important principle with wisdom, Job's words could have comforted him inwardly, so that he would not care about his friends' accusations. But it seems that inner murmuring - as a human weakness - stirred up bitter feelings in him. For he saw that his days of prosperity had passed quickly, had fled from him, and no trace of them remained, so that he became as one who had never tasted good.

St. Augustine sees that the earth here indicates the body, for God may permit the body to be delivered for discipline into the hand of the wicked, or for testing and proving, but the soul of the righteous the enemy cannot approach.

What does the saying "The earth is given into the hand of the wicked" (Job 24:9) mean but that, since the body was created from dust, God may permit our earthly bodies to be delivered to the wicked, but they have no authority over them except over the dust that is in them, but since it bears the new nature which is in the image of its Creator, and puts on the image of the second Adam who is from heaven, none of them has authority over it. St. Augustine sees that the divine Word Himself, when He became incarnate, took this earthly body and permitted it to be delivered to the wicked for trial and killing, so that we should not fear the wicked, but share with our Christ His sufferings and death in order to experience His resurrection and its glories.

* Often the righteous man is delivered into the hand of the wicked, not to honor the latter, but that the former may be tested, and although the wicked man comes to a stately death as it is written (Job 23:9), yet in the present time the righteous is an object of mockery, while the goodness of God and the great stores laid up for each are hidden.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus * What is the meaning of "The earth is given into the hand of the wicked" (Job 9:24)? The body is delivered into the hands of persecutors, but God does not leave His righteous one there. From the captive body He brings out the soul that is not conquered.

* "The wicked watcheth the righteous, and seeketh to slay him. The LORD will not leave him in his hand" (Ps 32:37-33). Why then did He leave the martyrs in the hands of the wicked? Why did they do to them whatever they wished (Mt 12:17)? They slaughtered some with the sword, and crucified some, and threw some to the beasts, and burned some with fire, and led some in chains, and destroyed them by ruinous schemes. Surely [the Lord did not forsake His saints](d) He does not leave them in their hands. Finally why did He leave His only-begotten Son in the hands of the wicked...? Hear what another book says prophesying about the sufferings of our Lord to come at the hands of the wicked: [The earth was given into the hands of the wicked] (Job 24:9)... He is speaking of the delivering of the body into the hands of the persecutors. But God did not leave "His chosen one" (Ps 10:16) there, for through the body that was captured, He led the soul that was not defeated.

* "Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance shall be ours" (Mk 12:7). How foolish you are! How will the inheritance be yours? Is it because you killed him? Yes, you killed him, but the inheritance will not be yours... When you boasted that you had killed him, he had only fallen asleep, for he said in another psalm, "I laid me down and slept."
They plotted and wanted to kill me, and I slept; had I not willed it, I would not have slept.
I slept, for [I have power to lay down (my life), and I have power to take it again] (Jn 10:18).
[I laid me down and slept; I awaked] (Ps 3:5).

Rage, you Jews! Let the earth be given into the hands of the wicked, that is, let the body be left in the hands of the persecutors, that they may hang it on a tree, fasten it with nails, and pierce it with a spear.
Did not the One who sleeps add that He also rises?.. When was Eve created? When Adam slept! When did the sacraments of the Church come forth from the side of Christ? When He slept on the Cross.

* Let the persecutors rage! Let the earth be given into the hand of the wicked (Job 10:17)! Let the body be nailed to the tree with nails, and pierced with a spear. For He who lies down and sleeps says, [I shall rise again](ح).
St. Augustine

entries.section: 5. The terror of his troubles and his perplexity

paragraphs.text: 25 Now my days are swifter than a post: they flee away, they see no good. 26 They are passed away as the swift ships: as the eagle that hasteth to the prey. 27 If I say, I will forget my complaint, I will leave off my heaviness, and comfort myself: 28 I am afraid of all my sorrows, I know that thou wilt not hold me innocent. 29 If I be wicked, why then labour I in vain? 30 If I wash myself with snow water, and make my hands never so clean; 31 Yet shalt thou plunge me in the ditch, and mine own clothes shall abhor me.
"Now my days are swifter than a post: they flee away, they see no good" [25].
The speed of runners (who run before the chariot) was often used in ancient times to carry urgent messages. The kings kept some of these runners for the service of the royal palace.

When King Hezekiah sent an invitation to all Israel and Judah to celebrate the Passover in Jerusalem, "the posts went with the letters from the king and his princes throughout all Israel and Judah" (2 Chr 30:6). In the days of Jeremiah it seems that this service had become established and organized, for in his prophecy about the destruction of Babylon it was said: "One post shall run to meet another, and one messenger to meet another, to shew the king of Babylon that his city is taken at one end" (Jer 51:31). The Persians likewise used swift messengers. They were used when the order was issued to kill all the Jews in the empire (Esth 3:13, 15), and also when the order was issued to take vengeance on their enemies: "So the posts that rode upon mules and camels went out, being hastened and pressed on by the king's commandment" (Esth 8:14).
* Tell me, what is steadfast in this world? Is it wealth, which often does not remain even until evening? Or is it glory? Listen to what a righteous man says: "My life is swifter than a runner."

St. John Chrysostom. Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that God created man to see good, that is, to see God, the supreme Good. But once sin entered his life, he lost his inner sight and no longer beheld the divine light nor saw good, and so he doubts the dealings of God.

* Man was created for this purpose, to see good, which is God. But since he did not wish to stand in the light, he fled from the light and lost his eyes. On the same level he committed himself to bodily things through sin. So he became subject to blindness and unable to see the inner light...

But when we think about such matters, doubting continually (about God as the maker of good things), hard questions press upon us as we keep silent: "Why does God create a person whom He foresaw would perish? Why, being the greatest in power and goodness, did He not intend to create man unable to perish?"

And while the mind questions thus in its silence, man fears that in his rashness through these questions he will fall into pride, and so he draws back toward humility, which restrains the thoughts of the heart.

entries.section: 5. The terror of his troubles and his perplexity

paragraphs.text: And the more he came into severe trials, in the midst of troubles, the more he suffered over the interpretation of the hidden meaning of events. Therefore he continues: [If I say, I will not speak in this way, I change the look of my face and am struck with grief] [27].
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"They are passed away as the swift ships."
"As the eagle that hasteth to the prey" (his catch) [26].

The days of his prosperity have departed like a ship hastening to its safe harbor, and like the eagle that swoops down on its prey in the twinkling of an eye. As no trace remains of the ship after it has passed, nor of the eagle in the air after it has swooped on its prey, so the days of prosperity have passed and no trace of them is left. Behold, time hurries man as though to vanishing; soon it carries us over into eternity, and time will have no place in our eternity.

* "Our life is swifter than a runner; it passes and nothing is seen. It is like the passage of a ship, or like a flying eagle seeking food" (Job 9:25-26) LXX; so passes the life of man. What we say we forget, and no sign of our passing remains visible except that it is filled with sorrow and grief. "I am smitten in all my limbs. Is there a mediator between us, to reprove and decide between us?" (Job 9:28, 33) LXX.

St. Ambrose. * As the sea leaves no traces of ships, and there are no traces in the air of the eagle swooping on its prey (Wis 5:10-11), so it is with the wealth of the world when it passes: it will not leave a particle of the traces of happiness. For wealth and what comes from it is cast into oblivion. For this reason Job, as an example, despised every influence of that life and its instability, and he advises us not to be attached to it.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem. "If I say, I will forget my complaint, I will leave off my heaviness (my face), and comfort myself (and smile)" [27].

It seems that Job began to look beyond time and to find that his distress would one day be dissolved and cease to exist, when his soul departs from this world and all his life becomes like a shadow that has passed, leaving no trace. He said to himself that he would forget the distress he was in, leave his cares, and be comforted or rejoice (laugh).

Even if righteous Job wanted not to speak in the midst of his affliction, and resolved in his heart to ignore what had befallen him, the look on his face bears witness to the violence of the trial and speaks of the harshness and fury of the storm, without his uttering a word.

* The evils that come upon you will pass, and He whom you await with patience will come. He will wipe away the sweat of weariness. He will dry every tear, and there will be weeping no more. Here below we must groan in the midst of trials, as Job asks: [What is the life of man on earth but a trial?] (Job 7:1).

entries.section: 5. The terror of his troubles and his perplexity

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine. "I am afraid of all my sorrows, I know that thou wilt not hold me innocent" [28].

Job sees that if he were to enter even into a dialogue with himself about his sufferings, he might sin against God; therefore he fears to think about them, since he cannot be justified. He feared to reproach God for permitting him these sufferings, because he knows that by this God would not acquit him, but it would be against him.
* [I was afraid of all my works, knowing that you would not acquit me when I am guilty] [28-29].

What works the blessed Job practiced, this holy history has made plain. For he had learned to propitiate his Creator by offering many burnt offerings. According to the number of his sons, as it is written, he rose up early in the morning and offered burnt offerings for each one of them, cleansing them not only from unclean deeds but also from evil thoughts. He recorded for us, with the testimony of the Holy Bible: "For Job said, It may be that my sons have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts" (Job 1:5).

He practiced compassion, as he declared of himself when his friends troubled him: "Did not I weep for him that was in trouble?" (Job 30:25). He undertook the role of tenderness, for he says: "I was eyes to the blind, and feet was I to the lame" (Job 29:15).
He kept the purity of chastity in his heart; in this he reveals himself most clearly and with dignity: "If mine heart have been deceived by a woman" (Job 31:9).
He reached the highest summit of humility from the depths of his heart, for he says: [If I did despise the cause of my manservant or of my maidservant, when they contended with me] (Job 31:13).

He gave with great generosity, saying: "Or have eaten my morsel myself alone, and the fatherless hath not eaten thereof?" (Job 31:17)... He practiced hospitality, saying: "The stranger did not lodge in the street: but I opened my doors to the traveller" (Job 31:32).

And in the midst of all these things, to complete his virtues by the highest way of love, he loved his very enemies. He says of this: "If I rejoiced at the destruction of him that hated me, or lifted up myself when evil found him: neither have I suffered my mouth to sin by wishing a curse to his soul" (Job 31:29-30).

Why then was the saint afraid of his works (Job 9:28), when he had always practiced works that make God yield before disobedience? How is this? How could he fear even these wonderful works in dread, saying: [I am afraid of all my works] [28]? Unless we conclude from the works and words of the saint that, if we truly wish to please God after overcoming evil habits, we must fear the very good works we practice. For there are especially two things that we must seriously dread in the practice of good works, namely: slackness and deceit. It was said by the prophet according to the old translation: [Cursed be he that doeth the work of the Lord deceitfully and slackly] (Jer 48:10).

A man commits the crime of deceit in the work of the Lord when he loves himself excessively for the good works he has done, and exerts all his effort to turn good works into a reward. Likewise it is fitting for us to bear in mind that there are three ways in which deceit is practiced: its aim is either to win the secret feelings of one's fellow creatures, or to seek praise, or to obtain an external (material) benefit. In contrast, it was said by the prophet of the upright man: [Blessed is he that shaketh his hands from holding of bribes] (cf. Isa 33:15)... that is, if he does not aim at vainglory from his fellows, nor flattery from their lips, nor gifts from their hands...
For this reason, good works themselves cannot escape the sin that lurks in them unless they are guarded by great fear. Therefore the saint rightly said in this place: [I was afraid of all my works].
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 5. The terror of his troubles and his perplexity

paragraphs.text: "If I be wicked, why then labour I in vain?" [29]
Job sees that he wearies himself in vain to be cleared before God.
* He who knows the weakness of human nature experiences the power of God.
Fr. Maximus the Confessor. * He says: I know that I am weak before the infinite justice of God; but before men I am righteous according to your testimony (Job 1:1, 8; 2:3).

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem. * Because these men beheld the greatness of God, the smallness of their own persons appeared to them. They looked upon the waves of His splendor, the purity of His nature, the wonder of His eternity, the glory of His majesty, the power of His limitlessness, the sublime beauty of His holiness, and upon these things that exist naturally from Him, and upon Him, and for Him, and through Him. So their thoughts were enlightened to see their own souls and to contemplate their persons, as it is written. They were also on guard lest the answer of iniquity be found in their hearts, or the thought that leads to supposing that the goodness of their persons was merited by their virtues, so as to reach the summit of God's greatness.

* My soul cannot stand firm in true humility, see its own smallness, and consider the poverty of its nature, unless the hidden riches of God dazzle it and the loftiness of His sight moves it. Poverty is left behind through riches, and darkness is hated through the shining of light. And the humility of the soul is felt from the wondrous loftiness of God; he who has sensed the greatness of God sees his own smallness.

entries.section: 5. The terror of his troubles and his perplexity

paragraphs.text: St. Jacob of Serugh. "If I wash myself with snow water, and make my hands never so clean" [30].

* Snow is the tears of humility, in which all the other virtues are exalted in the eyes of the strict Judge... For some grieve, but not in humility; when they grieve they weep, yet they offer these very tears while despising the lives of their brethren, or in arrogance against the dispensation of their Creator. These have water but not snow water, and they cannot wash, because they do not wash with the tears of humility. But he who washes and is cleansed from sin by snow is the one who says in assurance: [A broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise] (Ps 51:17).

* "Snow" can also be understood in another sense. Water comes from a spring and from a stream flowing out of the earth, but snow falls from heaven. Very many grieve, lamenting over earthly things... They wound themselves with pain in their prayers, but because of their joy in temporal pleasures they do not wash with snow, for their tears flow from below...

But those who grieve because they long for rewards on high are washed and cleansed with snow, for heavenly compunction overflows upon them. For they seek eternity with tears and sorrow, with longing for it kindled in them, and by this they receive from on high the means by which they are cleansed.
* What is meant by the hands but "works"? The prophet said to certain persons: [Your hands are full of blood] (Isa 1:15), meaning "your works are full of cruelty."
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* In this great battle, since man lives under grace and it helps him, and therefore he fights well and rejoices in the Lord with fear, he does not need mighty fighters or fierce destroyers to put to death the deeds of the flesh; rather we can be healed of some wounds of sin by this daily saying: "And forgive us our debts" (Mt 6:12), striving with this prayer against the vices and against Satan, the chief of vice, with very great care and exceeding skill, nullifying his deadly counsels, which he offers, namely that man should not condemn himself and should offer excuses with which to justify his sins.
These (satanic) counsels not only leave the wounds unhealed, but drive them to grave and deadly harm.

And here appears the need for a chastity full of watchfulness, so as to restrain the lust of human pride, in which man is pleased with himself and does not wish to see in himself that he is worthy of blame. So when he sins he disdains to confess his sin, and instead of accusing himself with healing humility, he looks for an excuse to offer with deadly arrogance.

And to restrain this pride, we find him who asked chastity from God with the words "Set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips. Incline not my heart to any evil thing," fearing lest he "practise wicked works." For this "excusing" is more than evil speech..

For the wicked man denies that he is wicked, in spite of committing the evil that he cannot deny. Since he cannot hide the doing of evil, because it is plain that he has committed it, he looks for a way to ascribe the evil to another, thinking by this that he keeps himself far from what he deserves.

And since he does not wish in himself to be a criminal, he adds to his fault another fault by offering justifications. And instead of accusing himself of his sins, he offers excuses, not knowing that by this he removes from himself pardon, not punishment.

entries.section: 5. The terror of his troubles and his perplexity

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine. "Yet shalt thou plunge me in the ditch, and mine own clothes shall abhor me" [31].

In ancient times it was thought that snow water had the property of cleansing the skin. They thought that the skin became white by means of snow water, and that it prevented sweat. And some thought that a black person could make his skin white by washing in snow.

There is no way to be acquitted before God: snow is unable to clean his skin, nor lye (soap or cleanser) his hands. There is no use in it, for the more man tries to clear himself, the more he finds himself plunged into the mire (the ditch), until he hates his clothes and loathes to touch himself.

Perhaps Job sees that not only is it vain to clear himself before those around him, but with every attempt at acquittal God uncovers his hidden weaknesses, and he sees himself sunk in the mire, loathsome in the sight of men. Job did not dare to dispute with God as though He were a man like himself, for the pot has no right to argue with the potter.

* It is clear that men are called righteous and are said to be without faults, but if negligence creeps in on them they fall. Man always occupies the middle place: he can slip from the height of virtue into vice, and he can rise from vice to virtue. He will not be safe, but must fear the wreck of his ship even in fair weather; therefore no man can be without sin. Solomon says: "For there is not a just man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not" (Eccl 7:20). Likewise in the book of Kings: "There is no man that sinneth not" (1 Kgs 8:46; 2 Chr 6:36). Likewise the blessed David says: [Who can understand his errors? cleanse thou me from secret faults. Keep back thy servant also from presumptuous sins] (Ps 19:12-13). And again: "Enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified" (Ps 143:2). And the Holy Bible is full of such statements.

St. Jerome. Pope Gregory (the Great) sees in Job's words here the cries of repentance, for he feels that although he is righteous in the sight of men, he is guilty in the eyes of God, and so he asks for pardon. Thus Job lived all his life seeking repentance, and so his life became blessed.

* In one day, my brother, you can acquire all eternity, and in one day you can lose it. Thousands of days have been given to you on earth to be used for your eternal salvation or your eternal judgment. Blessed a hundred times is the day on which you repent of all your evil works and defiled words and thoughts, and return to God with a cry asking for mercy. This day is better for you than a thousand other days!

What is this blessed day? It is the day of man's condemnation of himself. When the dawn of that day breaks, the man who until then had condemned the whole world, when he looks at himself, sees that he is the greatest sinner on God's earth. He feels shame before God, before every man, and before everything that God has created on earth. This shame is kindled in him like a fire; then he knows and confesses: "I am the greatest sinner on God's earth, all other men are better than I... Lord, have mercy on me, Lord, I am the sinner, and wash me from the mire of my sins, that I may begin to be like Your creation."
Do not expect, my brother, that the blessed day of repentance will come of itself, but lay hold of it on the first day it meets you, and say: "You are the blessed day on which I buy eternal life."

Bishop Nikolai Velimirovich. * What is meant by "clothes" but the earthly body, in which the soul is wrapped and covered...? It is said that our clothes abhor us, since they make us hated. He who said: "But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members" (Rom 7:23) felt the hatred of the clothes. These very clothes, in which he was never able to find final delight, he longed with all zeal to cast aside, that he might one day receive them back in a far better state, saying: "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?"
Pope Gregory (the Great)

32 For he is not a man, as I am, that I should answer him, and we should come together in judgment. 33 Neither is there any daysman betwixt us, that might lay his hand upon us both. 34 Let him take his rod away from me, and let not his fear terrify me: 35 Then would I speak, and not fear him; but it is not so with me.
"For he is not a man, as I am, that I should answer him, and we should come together in judgment" [32].

* What does this mean, approximately? If the one who punishes me were a man, his punishments would not entirely condemn the one who falls under them. I could stand trial before him and prove to him that he is unjust, but because You are God, this is impossible.
St. John Chrysostom. "Neither is there any daysman betwixt us, that might lay his hand upon us both!" [33]

Job's complaint represents the cry of humanity since its fall, for it is in need of a mediator to whom it can resort, to bring man back into the divine embrace. Who is the one who has the power to stretch out his hand in love to join man to God? Who has such boldness, except the Word of God incarnate, who is one with the Father in the same essence, and equal to Him, and who became one with the sons of men, becoming the second Adam?
Since our Lord Jesus Christ alone is the Intercessor without sin, He is able to do the work of reconciliation between the Father and man.

* Do you not see how Job proclaimed the coming of Christ, prophesying under the appearance of this prayer the mystery of the mediator of our life? For this reason Paul also said: "For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Tim 2:5). For what would happen if Christ had become incarnate and repeated what Isaiah said in rebuking the people? "Wash you, make you clean; put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes; cease to do evil; Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow. Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow" (Isa 1:16-18).

Why is Christ called "the Mediator"? Because He took the form of man and of God (Phil 2:6). It is necessary for the mediator to be able to lead enemies to reconciliation (Rom 5:10), to bear the face of both; for by this he achieves agreement and reconciliation. And since Christ wanted to reconcile man with his Father (2 Cor 5:18), being God and becoming man (Phil 2:7), He took the form of both.

Indeed He went further than this; for He declares to men what He does in the matter of their judgment, how He is the Judge and yet the One who loves them, and how the Judge appears as the doer of good and the compassionate; for He describes washing, bearing witness to the washing of Baptism.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem. * "We have peace with God" (Rom 5:1), through our Lord Jesus Christ, who reconciled us with God through the sacrifice of His blood...
Christ came to destroy the enemies, to make peace, and to reconcile us with God, from whom we were separated by the barrier of evil that we erected by our sins.

* He appeared in His bodily form and gave Himself as a body, drawing to Himself the carnal, that He might first transform them into the likeness of the Word who became flesh, and then afterward into what He was before He became flesh.
Origen. "Let him take his rod away from me, and let not his fear terrify me" [34].

* Who can take away the rod of God, that is, His divine wrath, so that man is no longer terrified of it? It is our Lord Jesus Christ, who laid our iniquity upon Himself, and brought us into the divine love, so that by His Holy Spirit we became sons of God, with boldness toward Him.

"Let him take his rod away from me" [34], for since He became incarnate and became like us, He does not strike us with the rod nor with fear, on condition that we flee to His grace and to faith, flee to Him who rose from the dead. The angel said to the women: [Fear not ye] (Mt 28:5, 10). And when He appeared to the disciples He used the same language again. In this sense Job continued: "Then would I speak, and not fear him" [35]. For He has done away with fear for us, and established the law of love (Mt 22:37-39). This is what John the Theologian wrote: [Perfect love casteth out our fear] (cf. 1 Jn 4:18).
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem. "Then would I speak, and not fear him."
"But it is not so with me" [35].
Through the Mediator we enter in to the Father with the boldness of sonship, enjoy His love, and rejoice in union with Him.

* Under the Law God held the rod, saying: [If a man does this or that, let him die the death](ه). But in His incarnation He took away His rod, showing the way of life by gentle means. For it was said to Him by the Psalmist: [Ride on and reign and rejoice, because of truth and meekness and righteousness](و). For He does not think to frighten as God, but dwells in our hearts as a loving Father. As Paul clearly teaches us: "For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father" (Rom 8:15). Therefore it was fitting to add here: "Then would I speak, and not fear him" [35], for when the saint saw the Savior of the world coming in meekness, he did not wrap himself in fear, but by the grace of adoption ascended to love. John says: "There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear" (1 Jn 4:18). And Zacharias says: "That we, being delivered out of the hand of our enemies, might serve him" (Lk 1:74).

Fear has no power to raise us from the death of sin, but the grace of meekness poured out raises us to the throne of life. This was indicated by Elisha, for when he sent his servant with the staff, he did not at all bring life back to the dead boy. But when he came in person and stretched himself upon the dead body, and joined himself to its members, and walked to and fro, and breathed into the mouth of the dead body seven times, he restored it to the light of new life through the ministry of tenderness... So God, when He presented the terror of the Law by Moses, was like one who sent the staff by the servant. But when He came in His own person and stretched Himself in humility upon the dead body, He made Himself joined to the members of the dead body". Who, "being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men: And being found in fashion as a man..." (Phil 2:6-8).

He breathed into the dead body seven times, by declaring the divine grace, granting the Spirit of sevenfold grace to those cast down in the death of sin. After this he arose alive, in that boy whom the staff of terror could not raise, but who received life by the Spirit of love.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Why are you afraid, O Christians?
Christ speaks: "It is I; be not afraid."
Why are you troubled by these things? Why are you afraid?
I told you beforehand that these things would surely happen... "It is I; be not afraid. Then they willingly received him into the ship."

When they knew Him and rejoiced, they were freed from their fears. "And immediately the ship was at the land whither they went." An end was found at the land, from the watery region to the solid region, from disturbance to steadiness, from the way to the goal.
St. Augustine. * It is God's will not to deliver you from fears, but to urge you to despise them, for this is greater than being delivered from them.
St. John Chrysostom
Grant me eternal reconciliation!
* Who is justified before You, O Holy One?
If You judge, it is You who are justified!
If You declare my sins, my grief is without measure.
If You bring a thousand accusations, I cannot answer with a word!
You are the searcher of hearts and reins; my thoughts and my hidden weaknesses are not hidden from You.
I confess to You that I am a sinner.
* I cannot stand before You in dispute, for You are Wisdom itself and Power.
Before You the firm mountains are moved, and they know it not.
Before You the proud souls collapse, and the human mountains melt like wax before the fire.
Let all pride within me be moved.
And let all corruption in my depths melt away.
And let Your holy mountains arise, Your steadfast word, in place of my proud, failing mountains!
* The Jews thought that they were the owners of the high mountains, since they received the Law, and from them came the fathers and the prophets.
These mountains were moved away from them, and You transferred them to us, that we may enjoy them in the Spirit and not the letter.
You unveiled to us the inner mysteries of the Law, and You declared to us the prophecies fulfilled by Your coming.
And You shone upon us with the truth in place of the shadows!
Glory to You, who set up Your mountains in our depths!
* How can I enter into judgment with You, O mighty Creator?
You command the sun and it does not rise, and the stars and they do not move.
Let the sun stand still, and my inner darkness appear; let the stars stop, that I may find no glimmer of inner light!
In place of the visible sun, rise upon me, O Sun of righteousness, for I need You, since I sit in darkness.
Shine upon me with the light of Your righteousness, and raise up from me a star that bears the splendor of Your glory.
Instead of justifying myself before You, let me possess You and be justified.
* How can I appear before You as in a court of justice, when You stretch out the heavens and walk on the heights of the sea?
Let a heaven arise from my earth, that I may become a dwelling for You.
Pass through the inside of my soul as over a raging sea.
Your presence silences the waves and calms the winds and the storms.
I am in need of the riches of Your grace, for You pass by me and I do not see You, You go by and I do not perceive You.
Who can say to the Creator, Why have You done so?
I keep silent in the midst of the storm, and await Your presence, for You are the Physician of my soul, who heal me of my many deadly wounds!
I want to see You!
I want to hear Your voice!
* Why is my soul disturbed when the earth is given into the hand of the wicked?
Behold, the devil has become the ruler of this evil world!
Let him reign, but the earth will pass away, and he will descend into Hades!
Why does my soul groan, when You, the Holy One, became man!
The devil aimed the arrows of death at You, and did not realize that You are the resurrection and eternal life.
By Your own will You gave Your body over to death for a time.
That You might destroy death and kill it in its own house.
I no longer fear the wicked one, for he will no longer find in me an earth to receive.
You have turned my earth into heaven, so there is no place for the enemy of good within me!
* I look forward to my departure with joy and gladness of heart!
My life is counted as a ship on the sea, leaving no trace on the waters.
And I fly like an eagle in the sky, leaving no trace of my journey in the air.
By Your Holy Spirit I fly to You, and rest in the bosom of Your heavenly Father.
I boast of nothing but Your Cross and the riches of Your grace that covers my weaknesses and my evils!
* I will not justify myself! No, I have nothing with which to be justified.
Grant me eternal reconciliation.
You alone take away the enmity, and bring me into the bosom of Your Father.
You speak by Your blood, so I am filled with hope and love!
In You alone and through You I enjoy the eternal glories.

1 "My soul is weary of my life; I will leave my complaint upon myself; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul. 2 I will say unto God, Do not condemn me; shew me wherefore thou contendest with me. 3 Is it good unto thee that thou shouldest oppress, that thou shouldest despise the work of thine hands, and shine upon the counsel of the wicked? 4 Hast thou eyes of flesh? or seest thou as man seeth? 5 Are thy days as the days of man? are thy years as man's days, 6 That thou enquirest after mine iniquity, and searchest after my sin? 7 Thou knowest that I am not wicked; and there is none that can deliver out of thine hand.
"My soul is weary of my life."
"I will leave my complaint upon myself; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul" [1].

With some courage Job stands before the Judge to raise his complaint to the One who passed sentence on him to enter into bitter afflictions. Job the tempted man realized that there is no way to complain about what had befallen him, by God's permission, except to raise it to God Himself.
Job was unable to defend himself before God, for he feared His greatness and found no one to reconcile him to Him. Then he cried out: "My soul is weary of my life." In despair he longed for death.

Job let loose his complaint against himself; he does not accuse God of injustice and cruelty, but accuses himself of ignorance, not knowing the basis of the dispute, for Job supposed that the fault was in him, yet he does not know it.
He did not want to utter a word, lest he sin, but the bitterness within him burst forth and spoke. As the Apostle says, "sin that dwelleth in me" (Rom 7:20).

* [My soul is anxious concerning my life] [1]. Now that the present life has begun to become tasteless and the love of the Creator to become sweet, the soul is kindled against itself, and accuses itself of the sins that it formerly justified, as it was ignorant of heavenly things. Therefore he continues: [I will let loose my words against myself] [1].
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Let your sufferings be books that counsel you.

St. Ephrem the Syrian. Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that righteous Job, in the midst of severe trials, lifted his heart toward heavenly things, and his heart was kindled with love toward God. Then the sins that he had not felt before, or had regarded as trivial or justified, became clear to him; therefore he loathed what his life had been, and became the accuser of himself, allowing himself to utter his complaint against himself.

Job became a judge of himself, so as not to fall under condemnation on the great day of the Lord, which would find him guilty. He prefers to condemn himself before God condemns him, even in this world, lest his enemies mock him when God hands him over to them for his discipline. Truly, how sweet it is for a man to lay the blame on himself!

Thus affliction is turned from a weight that embitters the soul into an enjoyment of the weight of eternal glories, which we experience in the midst of sufferings. Therefore the Apostle Paul says: "For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory" (2 Cor 4:17).

* "I will speak in the bitterness of my soul." He who tells of his sins, loathing them, must speak in the bitterness of his soul, so that the bitterness itself may punish the accusations of his tongue in justifying his conscience. But we must keep in mind that it brings a kind of security from the pains of compunction, which deals a blow to itself, and then it rises with greater confidence to face the interrogation of the heavenly Judge.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* The soul does not return to God unless it is torn away from the world, and nothing rightly tears it away but toil and pain.

St. Augustine. * The nature of the Apostle Paul was not different from our nature; nor was his soul different from our souls; nor did he live in another world, but dwelt in the same world and city and was subject to the same laws and customs, yet he surpassed in virtue all men, past and present. Now where are those who object to the difficulty of virtue and the ease of sin? This man condemns them by his words: "For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory" (2 Cor 4:17). If his afflictions were bearable and light, how much more ours, which, if you compare them, become nothing or mere pleasures...?

Paul embraced sufferings with love and without reward, and bore with all joy the difficulties and obstacles he met on the road of virtue. He was not troubled by weakness of the body, or the pressures of responsibility, or the tyranny of habits, or anything else. Moreover, his responsibilities surpassed all the tasks of leaders and kings, yet he grew in virtue daily. The increase of dangers became a cause for his zeal to be kindled all the more, and he said: "Forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before" (Phil 3:13).

When death drew near to him, he called everyone to share this joy with him, saying: "For the same cause also do ye joy, and rejoice with me" (Phil 2:18). He exulted with joy in affliction and pain and in every humiliation. He wrote to the Corinthians: [Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ's sake] (2 Cor 12:10). And he called these the weapons of righteousness, showing that they are a fruitful source of benefit to him, so that he became invincible before his enemies. And in spite of beatings, persecution, and insults, he was like one at a joyful wedding, correcting many concepts of victory, rejoicing, giving thanks to God, saying: "Now thanks be unto God, which always causeth us to triumph in Christ" (2 Cor 2:14).
* How glorious are sufferings! By them we are made like His death!

As the refiner of gold casts the piece of gold into the furnace to endure the fire for a time until he sees that it has been purified, so God permits humanity to be tested by afflictions until it is purified and gains great benefit... Let us not be troubled or despair when trials come upon us. For just as the refiner of gold knows the time when the gold should be left in the furnace, and brings it out at the appointed time, and does not leave it any longer in the fire lest it be spoiled and burned, how much more does God know this. So when He sees that we have been purified all the more, He frees us from our trials lest we be cast down and cast out because of the increase of our evils.

When something happens to us that we did not expect, let us not murmur nor let our hearts faint, but let us endure God, who knows these things exactly, so that He may test our hearts with fire as it pleases Him, since He does this with the aim of benefiting those who are tried. Therefore the wise man commands us to submit to God in all things, because He knows perfectly when to bring us out of the furnace of evil. (Sir 1:1, 2)
Let us submit to Him always, and thank Him continually, enduring everything with contentment, whether He grants us blessings or offers us chastenings. For the latter are a kind of blessing.
For the physician is not only one who allows us to bathe (in the baths)... or to go to pleasant gardens, but also when he uses the scalpel and the knife he is a physician!
And a father is not only when he caresses his son, but also when he disciplines and punishes him... he is a father!

And since we know that God is more compassionate than all physicians, we are not to inquire into His dealings, nor demand an account from Him of them, but let Him do what is good in His eyes. We do not distinguish whether He frees us from the trial or disciplines us, because by both ways He desires to restore us to health and make us partners with Him; and He knows our different needs, and what suits each one of us, and how and in what way we must be saved.
Let us follow Him wherever He commands us, and not think much whether He commands us to walk an easy and smooth road or a hard and rough one.
St. John Chrysostom. "I will say unto God, Do not condemn me."
"Shew me wherefore thou contendest with me" [2].

Despite what appears in Job as murmuring, he declares his ignorance of the secret of the dispute and condemns himself, although he does not know what his offense is. Therefore in humility he asks: "Do not condemn me," that is, do not separate me from You.
Since You have permitted me to bear sufferings, do not permit sin, the cause of my weariness, to settle within me.
Since You have permitted me the rod of discipline, do not permit my destruction.
Discipline me, but do not judge me worthy of condemnation. As the Apostle says: "But when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world" (1 Cor 11:32).
What Job desired was fulfilled in Christ Jesus: "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit" (Rom 8:1).
God permits trials so that the believer may cry out, asking for knowledge and the discovery of the mysteries of God: [Make me understand; do not contend with me].

Through affliction righteous Job realized that he was a sinner, but this is not enough for him; he wants God to grant him understanding to realize what his sin is, so that he may confess it to God and flee from it through divine grace.
* Great is faith, and great is the power of conscience, that a man should call God as a witness to the fulfillment of his aim.
Job did not reject what befell him through his human condition, but rejects what comes from unholiness, confessing that it befalls him out of weakness.
That a man sins is from his human condition, for no one is exempt from falling.
But that he should act in an unholy way is not from his human condition; it is the poison of unbelief through the evil heart.
It is not fitting for the righteous man to do this.
Forgiveness for man depends on the mercies of God, not on the power of man.

St. Ambrose. * [Saying to God: Do not condemn me, make me understand why You contend with me?] [2]. In declaring himself a sinner, [in the bitterness of his soul], what does he say to God except that he asks not to be condemned, since the bitterness of his present compunction removes the pains of wrath from his sins?

God judges man in this life in two ways: by recognizing that through present troubles he has already begun to bring upon himself the torments to come, or else by lifting the torments to come through the present blows...
Discipline delivers from woe only those who change. But those who are not reformed by present troubles enter into other troubles as a result.

If some present punishments did not preserve from eternal woe, Paul would not say: "But when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world" (1 Cor 11:32). As it was said to John by the voice of the angel: "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten" (Rev 3:19), as it is written: "For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth" (Heb 12:6)...

Rightly it is said here: [Make me understand, why do You judge me?] [2]. As though he were saying plainly: You have exercised Your judgment upon me by Your blows upon me, so that by these blows You may make me secure from condemnation.

This statement can also be understood in another sense. Often the righteous man receives the blows of trial, and as he examines his life with the skillful eye that questions him, he cannot determine precisely for what sin he was struck, even though he feels in himself that he is a sinner. He is all the more terrified under the rod because of his ignorance of the true reason for the blows. He prays to the Judge to show him the purpose of His striking him, so that he may be disciplined by weeping over his sin. For he is fully certain that the righteous Avenger will not grieve anyone unjustly. And that he has been placed under the scourges as a grave warning, and yet he could not discover of himself what he ought to grieve over.
"Is it good unto thee that thou shouldest oppress, that thou shouldest despise the work of thine hands, and shine upon the counsel of the wicked?" [3]
Job returned to reproach God like one who feels wronged, since He lets the wicked carry out their evil counsel in the lives of His believers, who are the work of His hands.

It is clear throughout the whole book that Job did not ascribe injustice to God, but he was in great perplexity, for he did not know how to interpret the events, in spite of his awareness and certainty of God's providence.

When man in his weakness concentrates on the afflictions that have come upon him, he wonders how God leaves the wicked to carry out their evil counsels against the children of God. Man thinks as though God had forgotten that he is the work of His hands and the object of His care, and that He has left the wicked to do what they want.

But when the believer lifts his eyes to God, he realizes that He is the good heavenly Physician who turns the counsels of the wicked into the edification and glory of His children. He permits them to inflict affliction, but He gives His children the power of patience and endurance. God will not permit a trial beyond the strength and capacities of His believers! Rightly we sing, saying: "The LORD hath broken the staff of the wicked, and the sceptre of the rulers" (Isa 14:5).

* The Lord did not [shine upon the counsel of the wicked] in a way that would restrain the soul of the righteous, even when he hands over his body to the arts of their testing of him... But the sharpness of their counsel becomes nothing, since the Creator adjusts the blows according to our ability to endure...

Paul said well: "But God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it" (1 Cor 10:13). If the merciful God allowed trials beyond our power, certainly there would be no man able to stand before the cunning schemes of the evil spirits without falling to the ground.
* He fittingly adds: "the work of thine hands," as though saying frankly: You will not press with hard cruelty on one whom You remember You created by Your grace.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* He did not say: "Why do You disown the righteous man, the virtuous man," but "the work of thine hands."
St. John Chrysostom. * [You shine upon the counsel of the wicked]; if it is because of my sins (that You discipline me), how do You regard their counsel?

* Truly the righteous suffer at the present time within certain limits, and at the present time the wicked oppress the righteous. How? Sometimes the wicked reach worldly positions, and become judges or kings. God does this to discipline His flock, to discipline His people... But He does not leave the rod thus. For the rod of the wicked is left for a time upon the lot of the righteous, but it is not left forever.

St. Augustine. * "As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people from henceforth even for ever" (Ps 125:2)... He says: if even mountains fortify it, it still needs fortification from the Lord to be impregnable... It is not for her to trust in a chain of mountains.

What makes it fortified, see this: [For the rod of the wicked shall not rest upon the lot of the righteous] (Ps 125:3). He points to a fitting reason for obtaining the Lord's help, so as to encourage them to trust in Him. What is it? The Psalmist says: He would not bear that the goodness of the righteous be in the hands of sinners...
He does not permit them to gain authority over the inheritance of the righteous; and if He permits it, it is only for a time, for their correction, counsel, and discipline.
St. John Chrysostom. "Hast thou eyes of flesh? or seest thou as man seeth?" [4]

Job was confident that God's eyes are not like the bodily eyes of men; He sees in the dark and knows hidden things; His eyes are in every place (Prov 15:3), and run to and fro throughout the whole earth (2 Chr 16:9). Everything is open before God. Therefore the Apostle says: "But we are sure that the judgment of God is according to truth" (Rom 2:2).

Since God is aware of the secrets of Job's heart, and knows his love for Him and the purity of his heart, He has no need to permit the enemy to tempt him in order that he may be proved before the Lord.

Truly God had no need to hand Job over to temptation in order to examine his depths; rather He permitted it to put the enemy of good to shame, and that Job might be proved all the more through his patience and endurance with thanksgiving, without blaspheming God.

In plain reproach Job tells God that His eyes are not like the eyes of men; they search the depths of man without limit, and know even what he will do in the future, so what need is there to examine him? He asks Him not to hand him over to the wicked one, lest he press upon him and he sin.

* "Hast thou eyes of flesh? or seest thou as man seeth?" [4]... The eyes of the flesh cannot look at the works of the ages except within a certain limit of time; moreover the days and years of men differ from the days and years of eternity. Our life begins in time and ends in time, while eternity is without limits...
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* "Or seest thou as man seeth?" These words mean... You have no need to examine Job and look closely at him to see whether he is as the enemy claims, for as You are God You know him beforehand. You do not look as a mortal looks, so why was I handed over to the enemy so that he might force me to commit iniquity?
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem. "Are thy days as the days of man? are thy years as man's days" [5].

As God is unlimited, His days are unlimited; He is the Creator of time. The days of man, as Jacob said to Pharaoh, are [few and evil], subject to change. Therefore God's view of things and His judgments differ from man's view. For God the past is as the present and the future; all is present before Him.
"That thou enquirest after mine iniquity, and searchest after my sin?" [6]

Job sees that God is too great to enquire after his sin or search after his iniquity, or that Job in his own eyes is too insignificant for God to be occupied with him to search out his sins. It is as though he says with the prophet Jeremiah: "We acknowledge, O LORD, our wickedness, and the iniquity of our fathers: for we have sinned against thee. Do not abhor us, for thy name's sake, do not disgrace the throne of thy glory" (Jer 14:20-21).

* It is as though he says, questioning in humility: Why do You examine me by blows in time, when even before time existed You knew me fully within Yourself? Why do You hold an inquiry about my sins through blows, when by the power of Your eternity You knew me before You created me?
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"Thou knowest that I am not wicked; and there is none that can deliver out of thine hand" [7].
He had already confessed that he is a sinner, but he is not a wicked obstinate man who resists God and His commandment, nor a hypocrite. Therefore he says: "Thou knowest that I am not wicked."
So it is fitting for us to confess that we are sinners, yet by grace we declare to Him with the Apostle: "Thou knowest that I love thee" (Jn 21:17).
Although I confess that I am wicked, there is none to deliver me out of Your hand but You! To You I flee, so do not be angry with me!

* [There is none that can escape out of Your hand]; it is as though he says plainly: What is left for You but to forgive, You whose power no man can resist? For just as there is no one who enjoys Your visitation by his own merit and loftiness, so it is Your compassion that allows the obtaining of forgiveness.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Even if You bear witness for me, I cannot be saved by my righteousness, and when You wish to strike me I cannot save myself, because [who can deliver me out of Your hands?] All creation is in the right hand of Him who has eternal glory.
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem

entries.section: 2. His life in the hand of God

paragraphs.text: 8 "Thine hands have made me and fashioned me together round about; yet thou dost destroy me. 9 Remember, I beseech thee, that thou hast made me as the clay; and wilt thou bring me into dust again? 10 Hast thou not poured me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese? 11 Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews. 12 Thou hast granted me life and favour, and thy visitation hath preserved my spirit. 13 And these things hast thou hid in thine heart: I know that this is with thee:
"Thine hands have made me and fashioned me together round about."
"Yet thou dost destroy me" [8]?
Man owes his existence to God, but when a trial comes upon him he sees as though God wants to swallow him up.

Many of the Church Fathers used this passage to answer the followers of Mani and others who claimed that the human body is an element of darkness, and that it is corrupt by nature and must be gotten rid of.

St. Jacob of Serugh sees that the body cannot live alone, nor can the soul live alone. [The body was not granted permanent life without the soul, and the soul was not granted sensation without the body. The life of the soul is lifeless without the body, and the body laid in the dust remains without life.]

Many Fathers of the Church pointed out that one of the blessings of the divine Incarnation is that God restored dignity to the body which He created, for the eternal Word of God did not disdain to bear a true human body and to perform bodily acts.

* Because the Word came down and came to be flesh with those of flesh, He walked in the way of all who are born, and remained in the world thirty years in humility. Then He began to act with the power of His might.
It is wonderful that He dwelt in the carpenter's house, mingled with them, and lived according to their custom...
The wonder is that the heavens are full of His glorification, and He was content with a small house in which to be brought up...!

He became a child and nursed milk and did not tire... He became a boy and measured the markets with His steps... He became a youth and worshiped in the carpenter's house. He became a man and bowed His head before John, and with the penitents He went down to be baptized in His humility...

Let us believe that He came and became flesh, not in appearance but in truth. He became man so that the world might feel that the second Adam had shown Himself to renew the world in place of the first, whom the serpent bit.

Had He begun to perform mighty works from His youth, they would have wronged Him, saying that He had not truly become incarnate, and that His body was an illusion and was not a body. For this reason our Lord waited thirty years, and then began to walk in the way of mighty works, so that in the body He might be a perfect man like Adam. For He went out to contend with the enemy (Satan) in place of Adam.

St. Jacob of Serugh. * We do not want to be rid of the body, but of the corruption in it. Our body is a burden to us, not because it is a body, but because it is corrupt and subject to pain. But when the new life comes, it removes this corruption; I say this corruption, not the body itself.

* If you wish to learn what kind of body God made at first, let us go to Paradise and look for the man who was created in the beginning. That body was neither corrupt nor dead. Rather it was like a golden statue coming out of the furnace shining with splendor, its frame free from all corruption. Work did not make it weary; no sweat poured from it. Nothing plotted against it, nor was anything of the kind found to trouble it.

St. John Chrysostom. * How great was this saint's grief for the common weakness of all men! How severe is the providence that God made man with His hands! Iniquity may be excused on the plea of (human) weakness, and grace declares its eternal work in us through the tenderness of heavenly protection.

St. Ambrose. * [Thy hands have made me and fashioned me together round about; yet thou dost suddenly cast me down] [8]. It is as though he says to Him in humility: Even if what I do is unfit to satisfy You if it is subjected to a just examination, remember Your mercy, lest the work of Your hands perish... Why do You thus slight me, when You created me in such circumstances of honor?
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* [You have struck me] not as a judge, but as a father who corrects me!
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem. What does he mean by the hands of God?

* Since we read that the Holy Spirit is the finger of God (Lk 11:20), we reckon that the fingers refer to the Son and the Spirit. Finally, to indicate that he holds sanctification from both the Son and the Spirit, a certain saint says: "Thine hands have made me and fashioned me" (Job 10:8).
St. Ambrose. * [Thy hands have made me and formed me]. It refers to the divine providence that works after our creation.
Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus. "Remember, I beseech thee, that thou hast made me as the clay."

entries.section: 2. His life in the hand of God

paragraphs.text: "And wilt thou bring me into dust again?" [9]
Job resorts to God's surpassing love for man. God raised him from clay and gave him all these surpassing capacities; will God turn back from His love and return man to what he was?
Man must not boast because he was formed from clay, and at the same time he must not belittle himself or despise his life, for he is the work of God, who created him in His image and likeness.
* Job seems to say: Remember the weakness of the flesh, and forgive my iniquity.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Why do You forget Your work? Why do You forget Your visitation?
Yes, why do You forget my weakness?
For what is man but Your visiting him? (Ps 8:4; Heb 2:6).

Therefore do not forget him who is weak. Remember, O Lord, that You created me weak; remember that You formed me as the clay (Ps 103:14; Job 10:9). How can I stand unless Your providence continually directs me to strengthen this clay, so that my strength comes forth from Your face? [Thou hidest thy face, they are troubled] (Ps 104:29).

* The needs of the body generate concerns and bring us into pursuits that hinder the soul's strength and prevent its concentration. Saint Job explained this well: [Remember that you have made me of clay] (Job 10:9). If the body is clay, then surely it defiles us and does not cleanse us. It corrupts the soul and defiles it by excess in satisfying passion. "Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews" (Job 10:11). Thus our souls are bound and tormented by the sinews of the body, and at times become hardened, often when they bow down. "Do not release me from my sin. If I am wicked, woe is me! If I am righteous, I dare not lift up my head, for I am full of dishonor. You bring tortures against me" (Job 10:14-15, 17) LXX.

St. Ambrose. * (Man) is placed in the hand of God (Ps 31:6), who is a safe harbor (Ps 107:30) and a strong tower (Ps 61:3); by nature He is merciful, rescuing and saving. God takes care of those whom He made from clay with surpassing providence... He set up a royal form clothed in glory (Ps 8:6), an image worthy of honor; He gave him features after the likeness of the Creator, since He willed it. Therefore it befits each one of us to keep this image at all times, and especially in time of trial... So now Job depicts precisely the whole history of Adam, giving us a brief teaching, which Moses explained at length.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem. * Jonah was distressed after his flight and the reconciliation of the people of Nineveh with God... suffering and agitated in a human way, full of sorrow. So God commanded the earth to cause a gourd to grow for Jonah to shelter his head, then commanded the sun to increase its heat and scorch it. Jonah was angry at its perishing, but when the Lord comforted him and then tried him, hear what He says to him: [Thou hast had pity on the gourd, for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it grow; which came up in a night, and perished in a night: And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand?] (Jon 4:10-11).

This is what He wanted to say: Did you not rejoice in the shade of the gourd? How much more ought I to rejoice at the salvation of the people of Nineveh! Were you not pained at its perishing? So the perishing of humanity pains me...

He did not say to him: "You had pity on the gourd" and stop... but continued: "for the which thou hast not laboured, neither madest it grow." For just as the gardener has pity on the tree over which he has labored more than over others, so God wanted to establish His love for mankind through this love. It is as though He says to him: You defend strongly the work of another, in which you did not labor; how much more is it fitting for me to defend the work of my hands! Then He lessens the sharpness of the charge brought against them by saying: "that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand," that is, they sinned without knowledge...

And He reproaches those who groan that they are forsaken, saying: "Concerning my sons, and concerning the work of my hands command ye me" (Isa 45:11), as though saying: Who reminds a father of his son or urges him to think of him? Or who reminds the artist not to spoil his art?!
St. John Chrysostom. Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the earthy man bears an earthy mind that inclines to temporal earthly things, but the Holy Spirit lifts him up to heavenly things.

It is out of God's love that He withdraws the grace of His Holy Spirit from him, as it were, for a time, until he discovers his true state and cries out: "Wilt thou bring me into dust again?" [9]. Man feels his weakness and realizes that without the intervention of the breath of heavenly grace he is dry dust.

entries.section: 2. His life in the hand of God

paragraphs.text: "Hast thou not poured me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese?" [10]
A wonderful comparison: as a simple person can pour milk or make cheese, so with ease and simplicity God made man.

* When the Lord took a body He was not ashamed of it, since He is the Former of bodies. But who told us this? The Lord says to Jeremiah: "Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee" (Jer 1:5). If He was not ashamed of creating the body of man, would He be ashamed of the body in which He hid His divinity, He who creates infants in the womb, as Job wrote: "Hast thou not poured me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese? Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews?"

St. Cyril of Jerusalem. Again, when the grace of the Holy Spirit works in it, our mind is drawn away from what it was, and our understanding becomes like poured milk, and is formed by the Holy Spirit anew into tenderness and gentleness, and becomes like a piece of cheese.

* The immortal rational nature is hidden in our worn-out body, and suggests by all its acts in it and through it. And so, since you have this body, which has become an altar on which incense is offered, place upon it all your thoughts and evil counsels before the face of the Lord, lifting up your minds and hearts to Him, beseeching Him to send His holy fire to burn up all that is on this altar and purify it; then your adversaries (the demons and sins), the priests of Baal, will fear you and perish at your hands, as happened with Elijah the prophet (1 Kgs 18:25 ff.). Then you will behold the Holy Comforter in the divine water (Baptism) that rains upon you a spiritual rain.

entries.section: 2. His life in the hand of God

paragraphs.text: St. Anthony the Great. "Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews" [11].

When God created man, He did not create him naked, for He clothed him with skin; nor did He make him weak, for He knit him with bones and sinews. Thus our inner organs are clothed with skin and fortified with bones and nerves. Man could have lived in dignity and strength had sin not stripped him and weakened his power.

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the inner man is clothed with skin and flesh, because while rising toward heavenly things he finds at the same time an obstacle, being besieged by bodily movements that hinder him.

And St. John Chrysostom sees that Job touches upon the surpassing providence of God, who created him out of nothing and gave him skin and body, bones and sinews; how then could this Creator, so inventive in His love, care, and powers, fail to care for man, His beloved?

* He means: Are You not the One to whom he gives assurance of the greatness of love toward man and the greatness of this wisdom? If Job refers to the formation of man in some detail, it is only to prove that, after He created him out of nothing, He would deny this great providence of God and His surpassing wisdom? And he has shown that man (in himself) is nothing.
St. John Chrysostom. * He is a wise Maker indeed; who prepared the womb to bear the fetus?!
Who gives life to the lifeless things within you?!
Who bound us with muscles and bones, and clothed us with skin and flesh, and as soon as the child is born the milk overflows from the breasts?!
How does the child grow to be a boy, then a youth, then a man, and remain so until he passes into old age, without anyone noticing this subtle change from day to day?!

entries.section: 2. His life in the hand of God

paragraphs.text: St. Cyril of Jerusalem. "Thou hast granted me life and favour, and thy visitation hath preserved my spirit" [12].

If we have anything to complain about, even of what comes from God, we resort to Him. He permits affliction so that we may learn to resort to Him, for He is the One who created us that we might enjoy Him, not that we might murmur.

Along with the gift of the body in the splendor of its creation and its visible and hidden capacities, God gave us something greater, namely the breath of life from the mouth of God. He granted us life and mercy, and gave us the grace of reason and thought along with heart and emotions.
He established the soul hidden in the body, but what keeps it is not the body with its powers and energies, but the providence of God.

* How powerful is this holy man's lament for the common weakness of all men! How heavy was the charge that God made man with His hands, and yet man offers an excuse for committing sin on the plea that he is weak, while grace declares the eternal work in us through the tenderness of heavenly protection.

St. Ambrose. * "And thy visitation hath preserved my spirit" [12]. It is not enough that you have this by nature, but it requires Your divine providence over us. He says: Throughout all my life I rely on Your divine providence.

* If you doubt God's providence, ask the earth and the heavens and the sun and the moon, ask the irrational creatures and the plants... Ask the rocks and the mountains, the sand dunes and the hills. Ask the night and the day. For God's providence is clearer than the sun and its rays. In every place, in the wilderness and in inhabited cities, on the earth and in the seas... wherever you go you hear a speaking testimony of this crying providence...
In every place voices rise resounding, clearer than the voices of rational men, proclaiming to everyone who wants to hear the watchful love of God!
And when the prophet wished to record the power of these voices he said: [Their line is gone out through all the earth, and their words to the end of the world] (Ps 19:4).
Our own language is understood only by the people of our tongue, but creation speaks a language that all peoples understand!
St. John Chrysostom. "And these things hast thou hid in thine heart."

entries.section: 2. His life in the hand of God

paragraphs.text: "I know that this is with thee" [13].

Job was in a struggle between these free divine graces and God's surpassing care to preserve the body as well as the soul, and the unbearable troubles he was permitted to suffer. Therefore he says: "And these things hast thou hid in thine heart," that is, the two agree together through Your will hidden within You, whose depths none of us can fathom. He is certain both of God's providence and of God's permitting him to suffer: "I know that this is with thee."

* [Since You have hidden these in Yourself, I know that You can do all things, and nothing is impossible for You](أ). Do you not see that the possibility of knowing God is revealed in His creation (Rev 1:19); it is enough for my creation to show me God's existence and power, without need of heaven? For since we were created thus, to exist from a seed, and to be under this help, and not to be allowed to fall into dangers, all this suffices to show God's power and authority. Likewise in the fact of the sinner's being preserved and not punished (here), and in the righteous man's being disciplined and punished.
St. John Chrysostom. * How could such a thing (granting life and mercy) not belong to such a Creator?
What could be impossible for Him?

If You made the clay in the image of God (Gen 2:7), and made the dust pass to the rank of a rational being, if You give earthly beings a happiness equal to that of heavenly beings, how could You not work a miracle for me?
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem

14 If I sin, then thou markest me, and thou wilt not acquit me from mine iniquity. 15 If I be wicked, woe unto me; and if I be righteous, yet will I not lift up my head. I am full of confusion; therefore see thou mine affliction; 16 For it increaseth. Thou huntest me as a fierce lion: and again thou shewest thyself marvellous upon me. 17 Thou renewest thy witnesses against me, and increasest thine indignation upon me; changes and war are against me.
"If I sin, then thou markest me, and thou wilt not acquit me from mine iniquity" [14].

Job does not deny that he is mistaken, and that God knows his sins and marks them, and by this Job will not be justified before Him. "If thou, LORD, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?" (Ps 130:3)

* If I sin, You mark me, lest I fall into the pit (Ps 28:1), into the utmost sin, and be utterly lost, and lest I stray from the flock (Jn 10:1) and go to the den of wolves. According to the law of justice You do not find me righteous, but find me blameworthy under the stroke of the inherited curse (Gen 3:17).

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem. Job realized that he could not be justified by himself, but needs the One who grants it. Like all the fathers of the Old Testament he was longing for the coming of the Messiah, the Savior.
* The Lord Christ suffered at the time when Pontius Pilate was acting as governor and judge...
Who suffered? Our Lord, the only-begotten Son of God!
And what happened to Him? He was crucified, died, and was buried!
And for whom? For the wicked and sinners!
How great is this condescension! How great is the grace!
"What shall I render unto the LORD for all his benefits toward me?" (Ps 116:12).

St. Augustine. * Christ appears to each one according to his need. To those who need joy He comes as a vine; to those who need to be in the presence of the Father He comes as a door; those who need someone to offer their prayers find Him the Intercessor, the High Priest within them; and to sinners He is the Lamb (slain) for their sanctification.

He is all things to everyone without His nature changing, but remains as He is. He remains, and the work of His sonship will not change, but He adapts Himself to our weakness, being an excellent physician or a teacher full of tenderness. He is the Lord Himself; He did not receive lordship by advancement, but the work of His sonship is natural.

* The word "Jesus" means "Savior," and in Greek it means "the Healer," for He is the physician of souls and bodies, the healer of spirits; He opened the eyes of the man born blind, and led minds to the light. He heals the visibly lame, and leads sinners in the way of repentance. He says to the paralytic: "Sin no more," and also: "Take up thy bed, and walk" (Jn 5:14, 8), because the body was paralyzed by the sin of the soul. He ministered to the soul first so that healing might extend to the body.
Therefore if any of you is suffering in his soul from sins, you will find Him a physician for you. And if any of you is of little faith, let him say to Him: "Help thou mine unbelief" (Mk 9:24).
And if bodily pains afflict any of you, let him not be unbelieving but draw near, for Jesus heals such diseases, and let him know that Jesus is the Christ.
St. Cyril of Jerusalem. * Often the mind is disturbed in its depths at the remembrance of sin, and so urges its practice in a worse form than it had when it was first committed.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* "If I sin, then thou markest me" (Job 10:14). Confess your sins, O man, that you may obtain forgiveness: "Declare thou thy iniquities first, that thou mayest be justified" (Isa 43:26) LXX.
Why are you ashamed to confess them, when you were born in them? (Ps 51:5). He who denies his guilt and does not confess it in truth denies his birth.

But do you want to keep what you have received? Why do you think you possess what you have not received? Therefore let the sinner and the unholy confess, and let the righteous not exalt himself nor be proud, lest he lose the reward of his righteousness through pride (Job 10:15).
St. Ambrose. "If I be wicked, woe unto me."
"And if I be righteous, yet will I not lift up my head."
"I am full of confusion; therefore see thou mine affliction" [15].

Without repentance we fall into this woe to which Job refers here. For nothing can rescue me from it, neither moral loftiness nor my worship, whatever it may be, as long as it is without repentance. This is what Job means by saying: "If I be righteous," that is, if I rely on my self-righteousness or on my conduct or service, all this will not lift up my head before my God.
The Holy Bible warns us against sin of any kind, for it brings shame and dishonor: "I am full of confusion; therefore see thou mine affliction" [15].
"Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people" (Prov 14:34).
"Have mercy upon us, O LORD, have mercy upon us: for we are exceedingly filled with contempt" (Ps 123:3).
"The wise shall inherit glory: but shame shall be the promotion of fools" (Prov 3:35).
"When pride cometh, then cometh shame: but with the lowly is wisdom" (Prov 11:2).
"Poverty and shame shall be to him that refuseth instruction: but he that regardeth reproof shall be honoured" (Prov 13:18).
"When the wicked cometh, then cometh also contempt, and with ignominy reproach" (Prov 18:3).
