It is as though he were saying in plain words: for this reason Your corruptible creature is able to be held fast in incorruption, because he is lifted up by the hands of Your authority and kept by the grace of Your care. For the human creature, by this alone, being a creature, inherits in himself a collapse downward from what he is, but man receives from his Creator that he is bound to be lifted up to what is higher than himself by contemplation, and to hold fast incorruption in himself. He is lifted up to firmness in unchangeableness by the right hand of his Creator.

Who can estimate the generosity of the divine mercy, that it brings man after sin to the height of such glory? God takes into account the evil things we do, but in His compassion He forgives them in mercy. And so it is added: [For now thou numberest my steps, and passest over my sins] [16].
Pope Gregory (the Great)

16 For now thou numberest my steps: dost thou not watch over my sin? 17 My transgression is sealed up in a bag, and thou sewest up mine iniquity. 18 "And surely the mountain falling cometh to nought, and the rock is removed out of his place. 19 The waters wear the stones: thou washest away the things which grow out of the dust of the earth; and thou destroyest the hope of man. 20 Thou prevailest for ever against him, and he passeth: thou changest his countenance, and sendest him away. 21 His sons come to honour, and he knoweth it not; and they are brought low, but he perceiveth it not of them. 22 But his flesh upon him shall have pain, and his soul within him shall mourn."
For now thou numberest my steps!
Dost thou not watch over my sin [16]?
The wise man says: "For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD, and he pondereth all his goings" (Prov 5:21).

* [You number my steps, not one of my sins escapes You] [16]. He says: I want to be saved, because I am the work of Your hands, and not because I am righteous in any way, nor because I demand justice from You, nor that You should forget my iniquities, for it is not possible for any offense to escape You.
St. John Chrysostom My transgression is sealed up in a bag, and thou sewest up mine iniquity [17].
The Lord says: "Is not this laid up in store with me, and sealed up among my treasures?" (Deut 32:34).

This is about the joyful day of judgment, but now it seems to Job that God numbers his steps and seals up his transgressions as in a bag, as the papers of accusation are sealed against the accused. Job feels as though God scrutinizes every act Job performs and records all his sins against him, and all his iniquities are reckoned against him.

* [You seal up my transgressions, as if in a bag, but You heal my iniquities] [17]. Our transgressions are sealed up as in a bag, since whatever we do by outward conduct, if we do not wash it away by repentance, is kept in the secrecy of God's judgments as in a hidden place, until one day it appears from the bag of secrecy into the openness of judgment. It was also said by Moses: [Is not this laid up in store with me, and sealed up among my treasures? In the day of vengeance I will repay for them] (Deut 32:34). But if we are crushed by the blow of discipline for the evils we do, and grieve over them with repentance, then He "seals up" and "heals" our iniquities, so that He leaves nothing here for which we are not punished, nor is anything kept for which we shall be punished in the judgment...

So with the iniquity of His persecutor (Saul of Tarsus), whom He cast to the ground, He did this to him: He sealed and healed, saying of him to Ananias: [he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel: for I will shew him how great things he must suffer for my name's sake] (Acts 9:15).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
And surely the mountain falling cometh to nought, and the rock is removed out of his place [18].

While the three friends reproach Job because, instead of repenting and returning to God, he accuses God of injustice in their eyes, Job makes clear that if weakness has come upon him, and he seems like one who has lost his hope, it is from the weight of the blow. He is like the mountain, which in spite of its firmness crumbles, and like the rock, which does not move, but under stress is removed from its place, and like the stones which successive drops of rain wear away and which the floods sweep off. So he likens himself to the mountain, the rock and the stones... But the trial is exceedingly severe!
The waters wear the stones: thou washest away the things which grow out of the dust of the earth [19].

In the midst of his sufferings Job wrestles between his inability to bear the pain and his hope of enjoying the eternal reward. He has revealed his hope of an exchange and change even of his body, but he fears that this hope may be shifted by the length of the affliction. For we see that with the passing of time some mountains crumble, the rock is removed from its place, and the stones are worn by the water that falls on them continually and are swept away by the floods like the dust of the earth. He cries out that his patience may not last.
* He likens the ruin of man in this way... There are two kinds of trials:

One kind passes through the mind, even of a good man, and happens suddenly. He is tried suddenly, so that, not expecting what happens, he is seized with dizziness and falls to the ground and does not see his fall.

And there is another kind that comes little by little in the mind, and with good suggestions corrupts the resisting soul, not by its excessive extremity but by its insistence it corrupts the powers of righteousness.

When the first kind of trial is present, which makes a sudden attack and often brings the good man to the ground, it is said: [And surely the mountains fall to nothing, and the rock is moved from its place] [18], meaning the mind whose place was righteousness, and which by a sudden impulse is moved to sin.

Again, since there is another kind of trial, which pours itself quietly into the heart of man and wearies him, corrupting all the firmness of his steadfastness, it is said: [The waters wear the stones]. In this way, the soft flattery of the lust which is not forgiven absorbs the firmness of the soul, and the slow creeping in of the evil habit damages the steadfast and strong aim of the mind. Therefore it was added: [and by the washing the earth is eaten away little by little]. For just as by the overflowing of the waters the earth is eaten away little by little, so the evil habit creeps in by slight degrees, and even the strong mind is swallowed up. Rightly it was said: "and in the same way thou destroyest the hope of man"...

Let us see how David, "the high mountain," who was able to contemplate the great mysteries of God in the spirit of prophecy, collapsed in a sudden fall, when he desired and took another man's wife, and killed her husband at the cost of his army. Then the mountain fell in a sudden fall, when this mind, which was accustomed to dwell with the heavenly mysteries, was overcome by a sudden trial, and descended into such a terrible corruption...

Let us also see [the waters wearing the stones, and by the washing the earth eaten away little by little], in Solomon, who by his excess in relations with women and his association with them slipped down this road until he built a temple for idols, he who had earlier built a temple for God...

Thus the blessed Job sets forth both kinds of trial, whether that which happens suddenly in excess, or that which enters quietly and by a long way. Let him contemplate the falls of his fellows of creation (the mountains, rocks and earth), from which what happens outside can find a key for his meditations.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
And thou destroyest the hope of man [19].
Thou prevailest for ever against him, and he passeth.
Thou changest (disfigurest) his countenance, and sendest him away [20].
Job asks for divine intervention before the hour of his death comes while he is in hopeless murmuring.

At the moments of death the face of man changes, either because of sickness or the state of emaciation that comes upon a man shortly before his death. Man loses his beauty, splendor and greatness, so that his relatives find that burying him is an honor to him. As Abraham says: [Give me a possession of a buryingplace with you, that I may bury my dead out of my sight] (Gen 23:4, 8).

[You have shattered the hope of man]... Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem says that this is the reason David says: [Revive me, O God, for the waters have come to my soul] (Ps 69:1). For when our first parents Adam and Eve fell into disobedience they were driven out of Paradise and the sentence was pronounced: [Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return](i), and the earth brought forth thorns and thistles; what hope did Adam have after such a curse had come? Therefore Job continues his speech: [You have rejected him forever, and he is gone!]
His sons come to honour, and he knoweth it not; and they are brought low, but he perceiveth it not of them [21].

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem sees that Job is looking at his father Adam, who has passed over to hell, so that he no longer knows what has befallen his children, that is, humanity, which is his offspring. "For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?" (Mt 16:26).

* If the Lord's journey in the flesh had not taken place, the Savior would not have paid a price to death. He would not have destroyed the power of death by His might. If the body that was subject to death were one thing and the body that the Lord took another, then death could not have been stopped from carrying out its works, and the sufferings of the incarnate God would have been of no benefit; we who died in Adam could not have lived in Christ.

St. Basil the Great * We know Him as the firstborn of those who have rested, the firstborn from the dead. Without any dispute the firstfruit is of the same characteristics and nature as the rest of the fruits... Therefore as the firstfruit of death was in Adam, so the firstfruit of the resurrection is in Christ.

St. Ambrose Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that this is the position of the souls that have not enjoyed salvation, but as for the souls of the righteous, or [the holy souls, since they see the splendor of Almighty God within them, they cannot imagine for a moment that something outside is unknown to them. But carnal persons, since they concentrate all their care on their children (on temporal matters), therefore Job declares that afterward they are ignorant of the things they love here with all their hearts, so that even if "their children are in honor or in disgrace, they do not know."]
But his flesh upon him shall have pain, and his soul within him shall mourn [22].
With his wonderful longing for death to escape the severe affliction, he fears the hour of death because it is dreadful, so that his soul seems to lament over the body that it is leaving.

* It was well said: [his soul within him shall mourn for him], for everyone who wants to rejoice in himself afterward comes, for the same reason, into woe, when he passes from the source of his true joy. For the true joy of the soul is the Creator. Therefore it is fitting for man to remain in eternal sorrow within himself because of leaving his Creator and seeking joy in himself.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
To You I cry in the midst of my bitterness,

1 Then answered Eliphaz the Temanite, and said, 2 "Should a wise man utter vain knowledge, and fill his belly with the east wind? 3 Should he reason with unprofitable talk? or with speeches wherewith he can do no good? 4 As for thee, thou opposest the fear of God, and contradictest godliness before Him. 5 For thy mouth uttereth thine iniquity, and thou choosest the tongue of the crafty. 6 Thine own mouth condemneth thee, and not I: yea, thine own lips testify against thee. 7 "Art thou the first man that was born? or wast thou made before the hills? 8 Hast thou listened in the council of God? and dost thou restrain wisdom to thyself? 9 What knowest thou, that we know not? what understandest thou, which is not in us? 10 With us are both the grayheaded and very aged men, much elder than thy father. 11 Are the consolations of God small with thee? and the word spoken gently with thee? 12 "Why doth thine heart carry thee away? and why do thine eyes wink, 13 That thou turnest against God, and lettest such words go out of thy mouth?
"Then answered Eliphaz the Temanite, and said,
Should a wise man utter vain knowledge, and fill his belly with the east wind? Should he reason with unprofitable talk? or with speeches wherewith he can do no good?" [1-3]

Eliphaz begins the second round by accusing Job of being deceitful, for he had gained great fame as a wise man. He bore this title, but he did not bear true wisdom; his knowledge is vain and hollow, and his learning false; he fills the air with talk that is of no use, indeed he fills it with destructive talk.

By the belly he means here his inner depths, his heart and his thought. As it is written in the Book of Proverbs: "The words of a talebearer are as dainty morsels, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly" (Prov 18:8).

He accuses him of pretending to wisdom, while his depths are full of an east wind, which the people living east of the Mediterranean know as a wind full of storms and whirlwinds, dry and hot, destroying the fields (Isa 27:8). It is like the wind that the Greeks call "Euroclydon" (Acts 27:14).

Whenever people think a man wise, it is fitting that he be all the more reserved, lest he believe the praise of men. He should be silent, so as to enjoy the wisdom of the Spirit of God who dwells in him, not the spirit of the world or its empty wind, especially the violent and useless east winds.

So Eliphaz and his two companions see righteous Job as a man who destroys the fields. This is not strange, for the heretics will not cease to level accusations against the Church of Christ, that she carries a destructive east wind, and that her teachings are of no use.

* We have often said that the blessed Job is a type of the holy catholic Church, and that his friends bear a likeness to the heretics, who seem to defend the Lord and so find the opportunity to utter foolish words. They launch words of abuse against the righteous, and for them everything the faithful think provokes their displeasure, and they reckon it as words in the wind.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Whoever cries to God with the voice of true humility and the right confession of faith is a lamb, but whoever utters blasphemies against the truth and enmity against God is a wolf.

St. John Chrysostom * They corrupt the teachings of God, and set themselves up as wicked interpreters of the good word of revelation; they destroy the faith of many by snatching them away from the faith under the cover of knowledge... They deceive the simple with embellished words and fair appearance, destroying them with insipidness.
St. Irenaeus It is fitting for us to profit from Eliphaz's accusation of righteous Job, for although it is an accusation with no foundation in truth, it often applies to us.

Let us cry to our God, and He will give us the light of divine knowledge, shining upon our depths, enlightening our interior with heavenly light, so that our conduct becomes a living witness to our words, and our thoughts are in harmony with our words and our actions.

Truly, when the Holy Spirit who dwells in us breathes upon us, the dry winds of the evil enemy, which destroy the fields, cannot turn toward us. The Spirit of God breathes, and turns our wilderness into a joyful garden, and the enemy has nothing in us to destroy, for it is the fruit of the Spirit!
"As for thee, thou opposest the fear of God, and contradictest godliness before Him" [4].
Some Jewish scholars see that Eliphaz here means: "If God created the one who leads astray, He also brought into being the Torah by which man can subdue the one who leads astray.

After attacking him as a man who appeared to many to be wise, although in his depths there is a wind destroying the fields of the Lord and ruinous to souls, he now attacks him also as a religious person who worships God. For his worship - in the opinion of Eliphaz and his two companions - is vain worship, because it is devoid of godliness or the fear of the Lord.

What a grave accusation! He does not have the fear of the Lord, and has no sincere godliness in the eyes of God; that is, his worship is not accepted. If "the fear of the Lord is the head of wisdom"(a), then whoever is without fear is ignorant and foolish, and his worship is not accepted, however many attractive formalities it carries.
* The fear of the Lord urges the soul to keep the commandments, and through keeping the commandments the house of the soul is built.

* Therefore let us fear the Lord and build houses for ourselves, so that we may find shelter in the winter, where there is rain and thunder, for whoever has no house suffers great dangers in the time of winter.

Fr. Dorotheus * If anyone wants to obtain the love of God, let the fear of the Lord be in him, for fear begets weeping, and weeping begets strength. And when all these are perfected in the soul, the soul begins to bear fruit in everything. And when God sees these good fruits in the soul, He smells them as the fragrance of sweet incense, and He and His angels rejoice in it, and He fills it with joy, and keeps it in all its ways until it reaches its place of rest without being harmed.
When Satan sees the great heavenly Guardian surrounding the soul, he is afraid to approach it or attack it because of this great power.
Therefore, acquire this power so that the demons tremble before you, and your works become easy, and you delight in the divine work, for the sweetness of the love of God is sweeter than honey.

Truly, many monks and virgins in the communities have not tasted this divine sweetness and have not acquired the divine power, thinking they have received it although they have not striven. But whoever strives for it will certainly receive it through the divine mercies, for God is no respecter of persons.

Whoever wants to have the light of God and His power must despise the honors of this world and its defilement, hate all the things of the world and the pleasure of the flesh, and purify his heart of all evil thoughts. And he must offer to God fasting and tears night and day without relenting as pure prayers; then God will pour out that power upon him.
Strive to receive this power, so that you do all your works with ease and facility, and have great boldness before God, and He grants you all that you ask.

St. Abba Anthony the Great The fear of the Lord is the steering wheel of the soul, given to us by the Spirit of the holy God, who alone is able to bring us from glory to glory, and to grant us grace upon grace, through our fellowship with the Lord of glory, the holy Jesus. The fear of the Lord brings us into the royal road, so that we do not swerve toward sin, nor toward self-righteousness. He keeps us from blows on the left and on the right, until we enter into the bosom of the holy heavenly Father.
"For thy mouth uttereth thine iniquity, and thou choosest the tongue of the crafty" [5].
Eliphaz reckoned Job's defense of himself as an iniquity that he cannot justify.

* This is the reason why he declares that he is [guilty in words] because of his insolence before God - but it is not for the sake of truth that Eliphaz slanders him in this way, nor does he speak out of zeal for God, but for his own sake and for the sake of his friends, since they saw themselves rebuked openly.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * [For thine iniquity teacheth thy mouth, and thou followest the tongue of the crafty] [5]... as though he were saying to him: the evil you utter you have learned rather from your evil life.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that what Eliphaz uttered against Job signifies what the heretics utter against the holy Church. As Eliphaz accused Job of insulting God, of not having the fear of God, of not walking in godliness, and of his mouth proclaiming the evil his life carries, so the heretics who deny that the Lord Christ took a true body, and that He truly died, attack the holy Church, thinking that her faith that the Word became true flesh and truly died in the body is an insult and contempt toward God.
"Thine own mouth condemneth thee, and not I: yea, thine own lips testify against thee" [6].

It is as though Eliphaz says to him: I am not judging you by your conduct before the trials, but behold, your mouth after the trials have come is itself a witness to your iniquity, and your lips pronounce the judgment on you, and not I.

The three friends had provoked him, and when he was stirred they did not consider that they had provoked him in the midst of his affliction, and they reckoned his agitation, as they interpret it, as testimony against him.
"Art thou the first man that was born? or wast thou made before the hills?" [7]
He rebukes him with a question: "Art thou the first man that was born?" as though he were saying to him:
Are you the first man to have been created, so that you have become more able than others to understand the judgments of God?
Did you live in the days of creation, and treasure up within you the wisdom of past ages, so that you speak with pride and boasting and in the confidence of certainty?
Were you formed before Adam? Adam sinned, and yet he did not suffer what you suffer, and still do you not want to confess your sins?

"Or wast thou made before the hills?" If Wisdom itself is like the lofty mountains (Prov 8:23-25; Ps 36:6), are you greater than Wisdom itself? Is it not fitting for you to bow before her, to draw from her instead of being proud of your own wisdom?

Wisdom says: "Before the mountains were settled, before the hills was I brought forth" (Prov 8:25). It is as though Eliphaz, in mockery, asks Job: Are you perhaps Wisdom itself, which began before the hills, and has become personified, or become a person?

* Job did not say this, nor any word by which he claimed glory for himself; he did not say that he was created before all humanity... but in one phrase he spoke of what happened to humanity at the beginning (Job 13:26), and so put himself in the place of all. But Eliphaz wanted to accuse Job of holding lofty thoughts about God; listen to what he added: [Hast thou heard the judgments of God? or hast thou restrained wisdom to thyself?] [8].
Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Hast thou listened in the council of God? (hast thou given ear in the council of God?)
Or dost thou restrain wisdom to thyself?" [8]
He saw God, in His love for mankind, as holding something like a heavenly council, and meeting with His godly ones as His beloved. So the Psalmist says:
"While the king is in his council, my spikenard sendeth forth the smell thereof" (Song 1:12).
"For who hath stood in the counsel of the LORD, and hath perceived and heard his word? who hath marked his word, and heard it?" (Jer 23:18)
"But if they had stood in my counsel, and had caused my people to hear my words, then they should have turned them from their evil way, and from the evil of their doings" (Jer 23:22).
"God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods" (Ps 82:1).
"The secret of the LORD is with them that fear him; and he will shew them his covenant" (Ps 25:14).
In mockery he says to him: Do you think you are the one carrying out the works of God in His council?

Do you claim to be the keeper of the secrets of heaven? Or that you are more able than others to know God's dealings? As though you were unique on earth in your knowledge of what goes on in heaven, and of what the God of heaven is planning? Do you know God and we do not know Him?
"Dost thou restrain wisdom to thyself?" Is there no wise man besides you? Have you monopolized wisdom to the exclusion of all others?
* It is as though he says in plain words: "You who speak of the Eternal, remember that you were created in time; you who argue about wisdom, remember that you do not know His counsel."
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* It cannot be denied that God exists spiritually and not bodily, as befits His nature. He is present with creatures in a wonderful way, which only a very few understand... Rightly it was said that God stands in the assembly of men in an invisible way, as He Himself affirms through the mouth of the prophet (Jer 23:24).

St. Augustine If Eliphaz mocks righteous Job, claiming that he possesses a unique wisdom that qualified him to sit in the council of God, then although Job did not make that claim, our Christ truly desires us to enjoy the honor of the divine presence. So it is no wonder that He said to His disciples that they would judge the tribes of Israel, and the Apostle Paul said that we shall judge angels, that is, we bear witness against the devil and his angels, by our enjoyment of the surpassing riches of God's grace.
"What knowest thou, that we know not?
what understandest thou, which is not in us?" [9]
They look at him in order to answer his saying, [What ye know, the same do I know also] (Job 13:2), by saying: "What knowest thou, that we know not?"

Perhaps the words of Eliphaz seem logical, for he answers Job with what Job had already answered them. But how far apart are the thought of Job and the thought of Eliphaz! Job defended himself because they had heaped many accusations on him and considered him foolish, without wisdom or knowledge, so he affirmed to them that what they uttered is known to every man by nature, and contains nothing new.
Eliphaz said this only in defense of himself, and at the same time he belittles the person of Job, his knowledge and his wisdom.
"With us are both the grayheaded and very aged men, much elder than thy father" [10].

They thought that he was proud because of his old age and experience, so they boast to him that on their side are those who are greyer than he and than his father, and they agree with us in what we say to you. Perhaps one of these friends was older than Job.

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the heretics went out from the Church, which represents the wise elder, while they are without true heavenly wisdom. Yet the heretics claim to be the Church that has experience and wisdom, as though the Church were the intruder and they the elders possessing knowledge.
* John testifies that all the heretics went out from the holy catholic Church, when he said: "They went out from us, but they were not of us" (1 Jn 2:19).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"Are the consolations of God small with thee? and the word spoken gently with thee?" [11]

Eliphaz reckoned that Job's rejection of their counsel was a rejection of the consolations of God Himself, and that what they uttered, in spite of the harshness and bitter rebuke in it, is to be counted as gentleness, because he deserves more.

The phrase "and the word spoken gently with thee" is sometimes translated "Is there any secret thing with thee?", meaning: is there in your heart a secret sin that hinders your enjoying the consolations of God? For those who hide their lusts within them do not profit from the consolations of God.
"Why doth thine heart carry thee away? and why do thine eyes wink? [12]

Why does your heart draw you into resisting itself, and resisting the one who discloses to you the secrets of God's dealings? Why do your eyes wink? That is, you pride yourself with your eyes, as though you mock our counsel and care nothing about what we tell you. Truly it is fitting for the believer to clothe himself with humility, for the proud heart is the enemy of itself. But the humble man profits from many, and God speaks with him through his guides. He sees God manifested in the Church, and bows in his depths to continual learning in the Lord.
* Because I was ignorant of these things, I mocked Your holy children and servants, but I gained nothing from this except that You scorned me.
St. Augustine * Whoever receives from him (the bishop) receives from Christ, and whoever does not receive from him does not receive from Christ...
He said: He who obeys you obeys me, and he who opposes you opposes me. And he who opposes me opposes Him who sent me (Lk 10:16).

The Didascalia * We ought to receive any man whom the master of the house (God) has sent to be head over the house, inasmuch as it is we who asked Him to send him. It is clear, then, that we ought to look upon the bishop as upon the Lord Himself.

* It is fitting for you to obey your bishop without hypocrisy, in honor of God, who wills that we do so. Whoever does not do this does not in truth deceive the visible bishop but mocks the invisible God. For this action does not concern a man but God, who knows all secrets.
St. Ignatius Theophorus "That thou turnest against God, and lettest such words go out of thy mouth?" [13]

"That thou turnest against God," that is, that you stir yourself up against God, for they reckoned his rebellion against them to be a rebellion against God Himself. And they counted his longing for death as resistance to the divine plan and an inner rebellion against His judgments, so that he entered into enmity with God. As though he had turned aside to the side of the devil, who is forever in rebellion against God.
Pope Gregory (the Great) says that Job's friends judged him to be an opponent of God, quoting some phrases he uttered without regard for what was in his heart.

It is difficult to judge a man by the words he utters without knowing what is in his heart. What Peter the Apostle said about the Lord Christ: "Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God" (Mt 16:16) are the same words that Satan and his hosts uttered in more than one place when they said: [We know thee... thou art the Holy One of God] (Mk 1:24). The first the Lord Christ blessed, and the others He rebuked and drove out.

It would have been fitting for Job's friends to ask him to clarify and explain what he says, and not to give an understanding of his words according to what their envious hearts desired, which spared no effort to catch his errors!

* [Why doth thine heart swell against God, that thou allowest such words to go out of thy mouth?] Often when the righteous are struck with many woes, they are bound to confess their deeds, as Job did. After living a righteous life he fell under the pressure of the blows of the rod. And when the wicked hear their words, they think that they speak out of self-importance and not out of truth. For they weigh the words of the righteous by their own feelings, and do not think that good words can be uttered in a humble spirit. For just as it is reckoned a great sin for a man to ascribe to himself what is not his, so it is not at all a sin in him to speak in humility of the good things he has done. Therefore there are often words in common that the righteous and the wicked utter, but the heart is always completely different!

So when the Pharisee entered the temple he said: "I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess" (Lk 18:12), but the tax collector went out justified rather than he. King Hezekiah too, when he was struck with sickness in his body and came to the last moments of his life, prayed with a wounded heart: "Remember now, O LORD, I beseech thee, how I have walked before thee in truth and with a perfect heart" (Isa 38:3). The Lord did not overlook this confession in its fullness, nor did He reject it, but immediately answered his prayers. You see that the Pharisee justified himself by deed, and Hezekiah affirmed that he was righteous in thought also, and by the same act one became guilty and the other pleased God. Why is this, except that Almighty God weighed the words of each according to his inner thought, and these words were not proud in the ears of God because they were spoken with a humble heart...

The heretics are accustomed to mix some true points with statements that carry false persuasions. All the companions of the blessed Job were deceived by their rebuke of Job, even though they uttered true things they had learned through their contact with Job. Such words were all contradictory. Otherwise the Apostle Paul would not say: "He taketh the wise in their own craftiness" (1 Cor 3:19)...
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 2. The need for humility before God

paragraphs.text: 14 What is man, that he should be clean? and he which is born of a woman, that he should be righteous? 15 Behold, he putteth no trust in his saints; yea, the heavens are not clean in his sight. 16 How much more abominable and filthy is man, which drinketh iniquity like water!
"What is man, that he should be clean?
and he which is born of a woman, that he should be righteous? [14]

It is true that no man is clean before God, and no one born of a woman is righteous in His eyes, because of the corruption of human nature. As he said before: "Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?" (Job 14:4). But what Eliphaz aims at is to affirm that Job is an evil hypocrite. So he applies this truth to Job and does not apply it to himself and his companions.

* He said this, perhaps because Job said: [Withdraw thine hand far from me: and let not thy dread make me afraid] (Job 13:21)... Eliphaz exaggerated greatly to increase the defamation of Job and the accusations leveled against him; his anger became of no use to him.

And while he was defaming Job, Eliphaz found himself sinking into him, for he reviled righteousness with his anger, and in his madness he failed to perceive the circumstances in which Job uttered these things. Consider what he added: "What is the mortal (man), that he should be clean? or he which is born of a woman, that he should be righteous?" [14]. And Job had uttered the very same words plainly: [Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one! even if his life is one day] (Job 14:4-5).

Job was not ignorant of the weakness of our race; on the contrary, since he knew it he did not hide the matter, but proclaimed it aloud, as you hear. For Job had already said before what Eliphaz boasts of. He said it with propriety, declaring our weakness with wisdom and calm. Therefore he did not deserve to be a target of accusation, but of praise.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * [What is man, that he should be pure?] For by the very fact of being called man he is described as earthly and weak, for the word man (in Hebrew) is called earth (adamah). How can he be freed from stain who was created from the earth, and by his own will fell into weakness?
It was added: [and one born of a woman, how can he be righteous?] For the woman presented the first piece of evil to man in Paradise. So how can one born of her who presented evil appear righteous?
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 2. The need for humility before God

paragraphs.text: "Behold, he putteth no trust in his saints; yea, the heavens are not clean in his sight" [15]

God uses His saints and His angels, but He does not entrust them with the salvation of man, since they are not sufficient to accomplish salvation. If the stars are counted as not shining beside the sun, what are the heavens beside their Creator?

* No one can be found clean from defilement in the eyes of God, no one, however short his days (see Job 14:4-5). "The heavens are not clean in his sight" (Job 15:15), "his angels he charged with folly" (Job 4:18). Why do I say all this? If the heavens are not clean, and even His angels are not without fault, how much more is evil in the thoughts of men? Where are those who say: [Stand by thyself, come not near to me; for I am holier than thou] [(see Isa 65:5) LXX; (Lk 5:8)]. We know that day by day we suffer from what is in our thoughts, so that we are ashamed and feel embarrassed to declare them. Many have not committed grave sins, and others have never sinned with their tongue, but there is none among men who has not sinned in thought, therefore the Psalmist says: "For the thought of man shall confess to thee"(b).

* "And hath put all things under his feet" (Eph 1:22)... Why all things? Why is it said that the angels, principalities, powers and all other powers, who never opposed the Lord, are put under His feet? The matter seems obscure. But the answer is that there is never anyone who is without sin. [The very stars are not clean in his sight] [15], and all creation trembles at the coming of the Lord... There is another explanation, which is that "all" does not refer to everyone but to those who are the subject of the dispute. Just as someone says: "All the citizens cried out," he does not mean by this that there was never anyone silent, but this is said of the majority that overwhelms the minority.

St. Jerome * [Behold, among his saints there is none unchangeable, and the heavens are not clean in his sight]. He repeats the name "the heavens," which is indicated by the title [saints]. It is written of these same saints: "The heavens declare the glory of God" (Ps 19:1). These are by nature subject to change. But when they earnestly desire to cleave always to the unchangeable Truth, by cleaving to Him they come to the crossing over (the heavenly life) to become unchangeable...

For what is this change but a kind of death? For it changes a thing into something else, and so it kills what it was in order to become what it was not. It is said of the Creator of all things: "Who only hath immortality" (1 Tim 6:16), as He alone is unchangeable in Himself. It is written of Him in James: "with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning" (Jas 1:17). For change itself is a shadow...

It was well said here: "the heavens are not clean in his sight," for in themselves, before the exact knowledge of God, even the preachers of purity cannot be perfect. As John testifies who says: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us" (1 Jn 1:8). If among the saints there is none who is unchangeable, and the heavens are not clean in His sight, who then claims for himself that he practices righteousness?
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 2. The need for humility before God

paragraphs.text: "How much more abominable and filthy is man, which drinketh iniquity like water!" [16]

If God does not entrust the saints with some of His works, such as salvation, how much more is the state of corrupt sinners who drink iniquity like water. Man finds his delight in iniquity as a thirsty man delights as he drinks water. And the wicked man reckons evil an integral part of his being, which he cannot do without, as a man needs water and cannot live without it.

* [How much more abominable and unprofitable is man, which drinketh iniquity like water!]... "Abominable" because of his uncleanness and stain, and "unprofitable" because of the evil of his imperfect life. "Abominable and unprofitable" can also be understood in another sense. Often the wicked man does something upright, but by practicing wrong things even the things he did uprightly become nothing...
What is eaten needs first to be chewed in order to be swallowed, but what is drunk has no obstacle before it... So the fool practices sin without drawing back, "drinking iniquity like water."
Pope Gregory (the Great)

17 "I will shew thee, hear me; and that which I have seen I will declare; 18 Which wise men have told from their fathers, and have not hid it: 19 Unto whom alone the earth was given, and no stranger passed among them. 20 The wicked man travaileth with pain all his days, and the number of years is hidden to the oppressor. 21 A dreadful sound is in his ears: in prosperity the destroyer shall come upon him. 22 He believeth not that he shall return out of darkness, and he is waited for of the sword. 23 He wandereth abroad for bread, saying, Where is it? he knoweth that the day of darkness is ready at his hand. 24 Trouble and anguish shall make him afraid; they shall prevail against him, as a king ready to the battle. 25 For he stretcheth out his hand against God, and strengtheneth himself against the Almighty. 26 He runneth upon him, even on his neck, upon the thick bosses of his bucklers: 27 Because he covereth his face with his fatness, and maketh collops of fat on his flanks. 28 And he dwelleth in desolate cities, and in houses which no man inhabiteth, which are ready to become heaps. 29 He shall not be rich, neither shall his substance continue, neither shall he prolong the perfection thereof upon the earth. 30 He shall not depart out of darkness; the flame shall dry up his branches, and by the breath of his mouth shall he go away. 31 Let not him that is deceived trust in vanity: for vanity shall be his recompence. 32 It shall be accomplished before his time, and his branch shall not be green. 33 He shall shake off his unripe grape as the vine, and shall cast off his flower as the olive. 34 For the congregation of hypocrites shall be desolate, and fire shall consume the tabernacles of bribery. 35 They conceive mischief, and bring forth vanity, and their belly prepareth deceit."
"I will shew thee,
hear me; and that which I have seen I will declare" [17].

After belittling the person of Job, his conduct and his wisdom, he asked him to listen to him without protest on his part. He says to him: "I will shew thee," that is, I will explain to you what deserves to be heard, and I will present to you truths that I saw with my eyes and touched myself.

Since sin blinds the eyes of the wicked man, he thinks himself wise, and that there is none who can guide others like him. He is amazed how people do not profit from his wisdom, so he imposes himself on them as a teacher, and in conceit wants to teach all the time. Therefore James the Apostle says: "Be not many masters, my brethren" (Jas 3:1); rather it is fitting even for the teacher and all men of the priesthood to be lovers of continual learning.

[I will shew it to thee, hear me, and I will declare to thee what I have seen]. All the arrogant have this trait: when they have a sound concept, even a trifling one, they twist it to serve their pride. Instead of working to raise themselves on high in understanding, they fall into the pit of self-glorification, swallowed up by pride, and reckon themselves more learned than the learned. They seize for themselves esteem from those who approve of them, and use this to teach with authority those who are holier than they.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* In teaching others I desire to be able to learn, because there is one Master (God) who does not learn from what He teaches all. But men must learn before they teach, and receive from God their Teacher what they teach others.
As for me, I came from the judge's seat to the priesthood... and I had no opportunity to learn, therefore I had to learn and teach at the same time.
St. Ambrose "Which wise men have told from their fathers, and have not hid it." [18]

If the wise learn through the experience of their fathers without limiting themselves to their personal experiences, and so learn from the forebears through successive generations, and do not hide these experiences, then Eliphaz, who claims to be wise, presents these experiences to Job, even if they conflict with Job's experience or his personal understanding.
To what extent are we bound by what is found in the tradition of the Fathers?

The holy Fathers represent the mind of the catholic Church, which she received from the Apostles by the working of the Holy Spirit, who works without ceasing in the life of the Church. St. Augustine speaks of them, saying: [They held fast to what they found in the Church, they practiced what they had learned, and what they received from the Fathers they deposited in the hands of the children], [whoever despises the holy Fathers knows that he is despising the whole Church].

This authority rests on two factors: a natural factor, since the Fathers were characterized by a holy life and faithfulness in receiving the deposit of the living faith from the hands of the Apostles, therefore they are better able to bear witness to the life of the Church in all its aspects, especially since they hold one mind, in spite of the differences of cultures, gifts and circumstances, with the great distance between the apostolic sees and the difficulty of communications at that time. And the second factor is divine, for the Fathers lived led by the Holy Spirit, the Leader of the Church and her guide into all truth, who keeps her within the circle of the cross of Christ.
This does not mean the infallibility of the Fathers as individuals, but the catholic Church as a whole lives preserved by the Spirit of the Lord.
"Unto whom alone the earth was given, and no stranger passed among them." [19]

The wisdom that Eliphaz presents, which he received from his fathers, is the experience of trustworthy people in high positions, better able than others to manage the affairs of the earth, with whom no ignorant man, a stranger to the spirit of wisdom, shares. While Job said: "The earth is given into the hand of the wicked" (Job 9:24), Eliphaz says to him: [The earth is given into the hand of wise, holy, trustworthy men], and so it will remain in their hand, and not be given into the hand of a stranger to them. Here perhaps he hints that Job is neither wise nor holy nor a trustworthy person, otherwise the Sabeans and the Chaldeans, who are strangers, would not have plundered his wealth. And on the other hand, since Job lost his possessions, like one driven out of his distinguished position as a king or the chief of a tribe, he is not worthy to be among the wise to whom alone the earth was given.

Perhaps he refers here to the Church on earth, for those who manage her are the wise who walk in the spirit of the early Fathers, under the leadership of the Spirit of the holy God. And it is not fitting for there to be a stranger among them who does not have the true evangelical, ecclesial, spiritual spirit.
"The wicked man travaileth with pain all his days, and the number of years is hidden to the oppressor." [20]

Eliphaz almost says frankly and boldly that Job is a wicked man to whom the saying applies: "The wicked man travaileth with pain all his days, and the number of years is hidden to the oppressor." Thus he accuses Job of injustice and violence, so he has become worthy to writhe with harsh afflictions and trials; what he did has returned upon his head, so there is no longer time to pretend to be other than what he is within, for his days will not be long.

*Eliphaz the king of the Temanites, Bildad the tyrant of the Shuhites, and Zophar the king of the Minaeans (Mineans) rebuked Job violently on the ground that he suffered such punishments because of his sins. In their trivial outlook they did not perceive that the Lord had delivered him to be tried, so that he might be formed by the trials and receive a greater crown like a wrestler for Christ. Therefore they did not see this great mystery of wisdom. Their narrow hearts were afraid lest they should appear to be accusing God of injustice if they allowed that punishments could come upon a righteous man. They threw the responsibility on righteous Job for the punishments that had come upon him, saying: the whole life of the wicked passes in anxiety, and [the rich who gathers by injustice is vomited out] (Job 20:15). They claimed that he suffered all the sorrows, as a man suffering on earth because of his sins.

St. Ambrose * This saying is misleading, for we see many of the wicked living in prosperity and peace. Even if this does not last through all their lives, at least it occupies a large part of their lives (Jer 12:1). In any case Eliphaz wanted to correct the words of Job, who mocks the prosperity of the wicked. He also wanted at the same time to show that he himself was not wicked in living in prosperity.

[The years that are given to the oppressor are many]. In this too Eliphaz does not speak faithfully, for when God wills it He puts an end to the power of the oppressor; it is not bound by a number of years, nor limited by any time. He said this because Job said: [The just and blameless man is laughed to scorn, for at the appointed time he is made ready to die by the blows of the stranger, and sees his house destroyed by the wicked] (Job 12:4-5). Job wanted to speak of the time during which God allows sinners to torment the wicked (Wis 2:10) according to their ability (1 Cor 10:13), intending that each be tried according to his measure, declaring that they fight for virtue until they are crowned.

As for Eliphaz, he uttered these words against Job: [He gives many years to the strong], but this too is a misleading statement, like the following one. [And his terror is in his ears] (21): how can terror be in the ears of one who does not keep the law of God in his heart, and how does he not open his ears to those who could teach him the fear of God (Ps 37:31; 40:8; 34:12)?

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * [And the number of the years of his injustice is uncertain]... It is known that every proud man practices tyranny according to his measure. What one practices in a state by virtue of his high position that suits him; another in a province, another in a city, another in his family, and another hides his evil and practices it on himself in the thought of his heart. For God is not concerned with the amount of evil that a man can practice, but the amount that is in his mind to practice. And when a man has no authority outwardly he is counted a tyrant inwardly, and iniquity rules him within. For although he does not oppress his relatives outwardly, inwardly he searches for an opportunity and authority to oppress others. For God looks at the hearts of men, so in God's eyes the wicked man is counted to have already practiced what he imagines.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"A dreadful sound is in his ears:
in prosperity (in an hour of peace) the destroyer shall come upon him." [21]

Eliphaz sees that Job should not be astonished that the sound of terrors does not leave his ears, for heaven and earth are requiting what he did before. He has no way to escape distress, for the sound of his evils pursues his ears, so he is like Cain, who believed that everyone who found him would slay him (Gen 4:14).

We do not deny that "there is no peace, saith the LORD, unto the wicked" (Isa 48:22). But the phrase here refers to the inner peace that sin takes away by isolating man from the source of his peace, while afflictions and troubles may intensify upon the saints to prove and sanctify them by the Spirit of the Lord, as they may intensify upon the wicked so that perhaps they may return to God by repentance.

As for outward peace and prosperity, we are not surprised if the Psalmist is astonished at the peace of the wicked, saying: "For I was envious of the proud, when I saw the peace of the wicked" (Ps 73:3). It is not true peace, for the writer of the Book of Wisdom says: "Moreover it was not enough for them that they erred in the knowledge of God; but they plunged into the great war of ignorance, and those so great evils they call peace" (Wis 14:22).
The Lord Christ came as Savior of the world, granting true inner peace to His believers.

"For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace" (Isa 9:6)

"How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!" (Isa 52:7)
"But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed" (Isa 53:5)

"For the mountains shall depart, and the hills be removed; but my kindness shall not depart from thee, neither shall the covenant of my peace be removed, saith the LORD that hath mercy on thee" (Isa 54:10)
"And I will make with them a covenant of peace, and will cause the evil beasts to cease out of the land: and they shall dwell safely in the wilderness, and sleep in the woods" (Ezek 34:25).

"Moreover I will make a covenant of peace with them; it shall be an everlasting covenant with them: and I will place them, and multiply them, and will set my sanctuary in the midst of them for evermore" (Ezek 37:26).

"Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace! O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts, perform thy vows: for the wicked shall no more pass through thee; he is utterly cut off" (Nah 1:15).
"To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace" (Lk 1:79).
"Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men" (Lk 2:14).
"Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid" (Jn 14:27).
"These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world" (Jn 16:33).

* [A terrifying sound is always in his ears, and when there is peace he expects plots] [21]. But there is nothing happier than simplicity of heart... and nothing is terrifying in meeting with others. For simplicity is like a fortress of strength, and there is no doubt in passing through what has no remembrance of itself, therefore Solomon said well: "In the fear of the LORD is strong confidence," as he also says: [A secure mind is like a continual feast] (Prov 14:26; 15:15). For mere rest in safety is like a continual refreshment. On the other hand the evil mind is always in pains and toils, either because it struggles with trials that may come upon it, or fears that they may come upon it through others. Since it contrives plots against its relatives, the mind fears the plans that its relatives contrive against it... and when there is peace it dreads the occurrence of plots, since it always deals craftily, putting in its mind that no one deals simply with it. It is written: [When the wicked falls into the presence of the wicked he condemns] (Prov 18:3), for the darkness of his evil surrounds him, and consequently he despairs of there being light. Therefore it was said afterward: [He believeth not that he shall return out of darkness, but the sword awaits him] [22].
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, Lord, only makest me dwell in safety" (Ps 4:8).
"The Lord will give strength unto his people; the Lord will bless his people with peace" (Ps 29:11).
"Let them shout for joy, and be glad, that favour my righteous cause: yea, let them say continually, Let the Lord be magnified, which hath pleasure in the prosperity of his servant" (Ps 35:27).
"But the meek shall inherit the earth; and shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace" (Ps 37:11).
"Mark the perfect man, and behold the upright: for the end of that man is peace" (Ps 37:37).
"He hath delivered my soul in peace from the battle that was against me: for there were many with me" (Ps 55:18).
"The mountains shall bring peace to the people, and the little hills, by righteousness" (Ps 72:3).
"In his days shall the righteous flourish; and abundance of peace so long as the moon endureth" (Ps 72:7).
"Great peace have they which love thy law: and nothing shall offend them" (Ps 119:165).
"He maketh peace in thy borders, and filleth thee with the finest of the wheat" (Ps 147:14).
"For length of days, and long life, and peace, shall they add to thee" (Prov 3:2).
"Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace" (Prov 3:17).
"The fear of the Lord is the crown of wisdom, making peace and perfect health to flourish" (Sir 1:22).
"For if thou hadst walked in the way of God, thou shouldest have dwelled in peace for ever" (Bar 3:13).
"Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom 5:1).
"For to be carnally minded is death; but to be spiritually minded is life and peace" (Rom 8:6).
"And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!" (Rom 10:15).
"For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit" (Rom 14:17).
"Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another" (Rom 14:19).
"Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that ye may abound in hope, through the power of the Holy Spirit" (Rom 15:13).
"Now the God of peace be with you all. Amen" (Rom 15:33).
"And the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly" (Rom 16:20).
"Grace be to you and peace from God our Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Cor 1:3).
"But God hath called us to peace" (1 Cor 7:15).
"For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints" (1 Cor 14:33).
"And your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace" (Eph 6:15).
"He believeth not that he shall return out of darkness, and he is waited for of the sword." [22]

The wicked man is pursued by his evils; he loses all hope of coming out of the darkness that surrounds him. He lives in terror, as though the sword were poised over his neck, expecting to be killed from one moment to the next. For in the depths of his being he knows that "he that killeth with the sword must be killed with the sword" (Rev 13:10).
"They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace" (Jer 6:14; 8:11).
"We looked for peace, but no good came; and for a time of health, and behold trouble!" (Jer 8:15)

"Hast thou utterly rejected Judah? hath thy soul lothed Zion? why hast thou smitten us, and there is no healing for us? we looked for peace, and there is no good; and for the time of healing, and behold trouble!" (Jer 14:19)
"There is no soundness in my flesh because of thine anger; neither is there any rest in my bones because of my sin" (Ps 38:3).
"And the way of peace have they not known" (Rom 3:17).
"And the peaceable habitations are cut down because of the fierce anger of the Lord" (Jer 25:37).
"He wandereth abroad for bread, wherever he may find it, and knoweth that the day of darkness is ready at his hand." [23]

The wicked man lives in wandering and emptiness, like one hungry for a crust of bread, unlike the righteous (Ps 37:23-25). And the day of darkness, or the day of judgment, is at the door, hastening toward him, and there is no postponement. The day of the Lord is light for the faithful believers, and darkness for the wicked, for they will be sentenced to the everlasting, outer, eternal darkness.
* When a man practices unlawful things, he fears what he has done!
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Because the rebel, our adversary, wages war with pride, and wants to conquer by arrogant exaltation, our victorious King gave us the weapon of humility.
Without the unconquerable power of humility, no one is victorious.
By humility the pride of the deceiver is bowed down, and he becomes a footstool for the feet of the meek and peaceable.
See how our mighty fathers opened the way for us: they put on humility, the garment of Christ, and overcame the wolf and bound him with the chains of darkness.
* The demons prepared for me a temptation that makes all who hear of it tremble...
In their impudence they return and show their cruelty toward me, threatening me.
And when I make before them the sign of the Cross, our life, they return to the darkness that is their portion, and their fire is quenched.
The Spiritual Elder (John the Dalyatha)
"Trouble and anguish shall make him afraid.
They shall prevail against him, as a king ready to the battle." [24]

The wicked man is frightened by inward harm and distress of soul more than by outward trials. As the Apostle Paul says: "Indignation and wrath, tribulation and anguish, upon every soul of man that doeth evil" (Rom 2:8-9). For whoever loses his attachment to God, the doors of an unbearable hell open within him. The wicked man may think that he has rid himself of his inner fears, but these fears reign over his heart, his mind, and his inner powers, and enslave him, so that with his whole being he becomes a captive, as to a cruel king ready with mighty, unconquerable armies. Whoever wants to regain his freedom should begin with inner freedom in Christ Jesus our Liberator, or with freedom through divine righteousness against evil.

* [Distress makes him afraid, and troubles besiege him, like a king preparing for battle.] In all that the wicked man does, the fence around him is made of affliction, calamity, and troubles, so that his soul is troubled with anxiety and misgivings. A man who secretly longs to keep the good things of others from them by force wearies and distresses himself with the thoughts of his heart, hoping that it will not be discovered. Another, having abandoned the truth, sets his mind to lie so as to deceive the minds of his hearers. But the greatest labor is to defend himself with enough caution that his deception may not be found out... For the way of truth is smooth, but the way of falsehood is rough. Therefore it was said through the prophet: [They teach their tongue to speak lies, and weary themselves to commit iniquity] (Jer 9:5).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* When a bird is caught, it is not necessary for its whole body to enter the net; it is enough that the net seizes only its foot, for this does not lessen the hunter's control over it.

So it is with Satan: if he wants to bring us into his snare, it is not necessary for him to control all of our conduct and our faith; it is enough for him to begin to control our conduct. "Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth... And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you."
* Satan is called strong, not because he is so by nature, but in reference to the authority that has come to him because of our weakness.

* What degradation is greater than that of Satan, who was puffed up? And what exaltation is greater than that of the man who wants to be humble? The first has come to crawl on the earth beneath our feet, and the second has been raised on high with the angels.

St. John Chrysostom * Now, my beloved, Satan has been slain, that tyrant who is against the whole world... Death no longer reigns, but life rules in the place of death, for the Lord says: "I am... the life" (Jn 6:14), so that everything has been filled with joy and gladness, as it is written: [The Lord reigneth; let the earth rejoice] (ج)... Now that death has been abolished and the kingdom of Satan has been destroyed, all things are filled with joy and gladness.
St. Athanasius the Apostolic "For he stretcheth out his hand against God, and strengtheneth himself against the Almighty." [25]
"Running upon him (rushing upon him), stiffnecked, with the supports of his shields arrayed (with his thick bucklers)." [26]
"Because he hath covered his face with fatness, and made collops of fat on his kidneys." [27]
When the wicked man stretches out his hand against God and exerts himself against the Almighty, he crushes himself by himself.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem says that Eliphaz likens Job to the Accuser (Satan), who was a great commander, holding the first rank among the heavenly beings, and fell (Rev 12:7-9). He raised his hand against the Lord, and lost his mind by resisting God. Delusion swallowed him, that is, he was filled with pride. And he took a hostile stand toward God through haughtiness. He is like Satan, who strikes in battle and hides, putting his shield on his shoulders, bearing a hard heart, covering his face with its fat, that is, with prosperity; and since he stuffs his belly with the evil of sinners, he cannot lift up his face before the Creator. He lays two layers of fat on his thigh, that is, he exercises his power through two things: greed and indulgence in pleasures. But Eliphaz tried in vain to compare the righteous Job with the Accuser, Satan.

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that these expressions apply to the Antichrist, the very chief of the wicked, who, when he raises his hand against God, is said to "prevail," but only for a time, since he is permitted to be exalted and glorified, and is then punished without mercy forever. He stretches out his hand against God, meaning that he persists in doing evil, unconcerned about the judgments of God. As for his running against God with a thick neck, it means that he commits shameful deeds that anger the Creator. For such a man is said to run in doing evil with no enemy to hinder him. And the thickness of his neck is the wealth of pride, supported by storehouses that overflow as though they came from the flesh.

These expressions also apply, in the view of Pope Gregory (the Great), to the wicked man who arms himself with authority, exalts himself against God, and takes a stand against the commandments of the truth. He disregards the riches of God and arms himself with the vain riches of temporal things. He covers his face with fat, seeking the fat of temporal goods without having the fear of the Lord in him; he oppresses the poor and exalts himself with the power of temporal glory.
* All the proud carry haughty necks; they not only practice evils, but refuse to count them as evils. And when they are rebuked, they justify themselves.

* The wicked wage war against God, and the earthen vessels are shattered and become fragments; so men puff themselves up, depending on their own strength. This is the shield of which Job speaks concerning the wicked man. [He runs against God, on the stiff neck of his shield.] What is "the stiff neck of his shield"? It is the man who depends most of all on his own self-protection.
St. Augustine "And he dwelleth in desolate cities, and in houses which no man inhabiteth, which are ready to become heaps." [28]

"And he shall dwell in deserted communities and ruined houses that have become ruins" (v. 28 LXX). We may be surprised at the expression "deserted communities," because the word "community" comes from people gathering together, so how can it be deserted? Wherever there is a great crowd of the wicked, each of them feels isolated, because sin corrupts a man's relationship with his brethren and removes love from them. Each one feels as though there is no one to share his feelings, and no one who understands his depths.

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the inhabitants of the house are the thoughts; for the wicked, their thoughts will find no rest, so that they feel that they are wreckage and ruins with no one dwelling in them.
"He shall not be rich, neither shall his substance continue, neither shall he prolong the perfection thereof upon the earth." [29]

The wicked man does not know the feeling of satisfaction and contentment; he is not enriched, but remains poor continually, with nothing to fill his inner emptiness, even if he possesses much outward wealth.

The wealth he gathered by evil passes away by another evil. All his riches dwindle until they vanish: "which came up in a night, and perished in a night" (Jon 4:10). [Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished] (Prov 13:11).
When the wicked man loses his sons and dies, strangers inherit from him.

"Neither shall he prolong the perfection thereof upon the earth," that is, the time of his enjoyment of his wealth will not be long. He exerts all his effort to leave his wealth to his sons after him, but he fails to accomplish that.
Pope Gregory (the Great) says that the wicked man suffers from inner emptiness and will never feel satisfied; even his being appears like a passer-by without fruit.
"The darkness shall not depart from him.
The flame shall dry up his branches, and by the breath of his mouth shall he go away." [30]
He lives as one in perpetual darkness, and he corrupts his children as children of darkness, so that they are like the branches of a tree that has dried up and been burned.

The text in the Septuagint reads something like this: "He shall not be able to escape from the darkness by any means: let the wind blow upon his flower, and it shall fall." It is as though it says: the wicked man falls into a darkness from which he cannot be delivered, while upon his offspring, or his flower, the wind blows and makes it fall without its turning into fruit.
What the Septuagint says about his flower appears in the Hebrew text as his "branches," which the hot winds dry up, the scorching wind that burns the crops.

By the breath of his mouth the wicked man passes away, for he dies suddenly. As it was said: "This night thy soul shall be required of thee" (Lk 12:20), and also: "The wicked is driven away in his wickedness" (Prov 14:32). And the love of the world passes away with the passing of the world.
* If the proud man wants to turn back from sin to righteousness, he must depart from the darkness. But since he does not seek the light of righteousness, he does not depart from the darkness.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"Let not him that is deceived trust in vanity:
he goeth astray.
For vanity shall be his recompence." [31]
A man often thinks that deceit and the ways of evil can save him. At the beginning they lead him astray, but he soon drinks from the cup of evil that he himself filled.
"Let this be the reward of mine adversaries from the Lord, and of them that speak evil against my soul" (Ps 109:20).
"The wicked worketh a deceitful work: but to him that soweth righteousness shall be a sure reward" (Prov 11:18).
"For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord" (Rom 6:23).
"It shall be accomplished before his time, and his branch shall not be green." [32]
Not only does he lose his wealth, but he quickly loses his life, like one who dies before his appointed time.

It is true that the wicked may live to old age, and holy, righteous people may die in early childhood. But the years of the wicked man are counted as nothing, for the years of his life are like ashes, while one day of the days of the saints is counted in the eyes of God as a thousand years.
"For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night" (Ps 90:4).
"But, beloved, be not ignorant of this one thing, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day" (2 Pet 3:8).
Even his children, whom he thought would be among the great ones of this age, become dry branches that are "not green."

What is the branch that is not green but the spiritual fruit of the believer? If he walks in evil, the fruit of the Spirit of the Holy God dries up in him, and becomes a cause of judgment instead of a support.

* Job was hoping for this: that because of his sufferings and his patience he would receive from God the reward of his inheritance. Eliphaz says that his "cup," or harvest, will perish before its time (of harvest), surely meaning that he will perish before the time of reward. [And his branch (on the tree) shall not flourish]... Thus Eliphaz declares that Job, who is expecting very great benefits, awaiting them as though they were in his hands, will be disappointed and will obtain nothing of what he expected.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * [Before his days are fulfilled he shall perish, and his hands shall be withered] [32]... Probably the wicked man, in God's hidden foreknowledge, is not assigned a long life by God; for since he wants to live according to the flesh, he imagines that he lives many days. And since he cannot reach the age he seeks for himself, he appears as one who perishes before his days are fulfilled.

This statement can also be understood in another sense. We commonly see people who walk in evil and yet reach a very advanced old age. How then can it be said: [Before his days are fulfilled he shall perish], when we see among them people whose limbs tremble with old age, and yet their passions do not cease to bring their evils upon them? There are some who, after losing the way of life, turned back, and their conscience began to torment them, so they left their shameless ways, changed their deeds, resisted their old evils, fled from earthly things, and followed heavenly aims; but before they were established in these holy aims and in the mortification of the mind, they returned to what they were at the beginning, and fell into their evil habits that they had resolved to leave... For unless the heart is first established in heavenly desires by continual seeking and continual conversion, when it turns back to carry out outward things, it is uprooted from its steadfastness in good work.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"He shall shake off his unripe grape as the vine, and shall cast off his flower as the olive." [33]

His children will be like the bitter unripe grapes that fall from the vine before they grow and ripen, and like the olive blossom that falls and does not turn into fruit. His children die in the dawn of their lives and do not attain what he desired for them.

* [His cluster is spoiled like a vine at the beginning of its blossoming, and like an olive tree casting its flower. For the company of hypocrites shall be barren.] Let us consider how the hypocrite is spoiled like a vine at the beginning of its blossoming, or like an olive tree casting its flower.

If a vine, when it puts forth its blossoms and a severe cold touches it through a sudden change of weather, loses all its moisture and greenness, so there are some who, after passing periods in evil, long for the ways of holiness; but before good desires are established in them, as we have said, a kind of prosperity in the present life comes upon them, and they are entangled by it in outward concerns, and as their mind is drawn away from the warmth of inward love, it is as though a cold came upon them, and everything that had begun to appear in them of the shoots of virtue is killed. For through earthly occupations the mind becomes exceedingly cold unless it is established within...

[And he shall be like an olive tree casting its flowers]: when the olive tree has blossomed and comes into contact with a thick fog, it is stripped of the fullness of its fruit. So also many who enter upon good works are greatly praised by those who see them, and when they find pleasure in their praise, a fog descends upon their thoughts, and they no longer distinguish with what intention they do this, and so they lose the fruit of their work through the fog of the love of praise.

It was well said by Solomon: [Let us rise early to the vineyards, to see whether the vines have blossomed, and the flowers have borne fruit] (Song 7:12). The vines blossom when the minds of believers offer good works, but they bear no fruit if in their aim they cannot overcome their sinful practice.
* Hypocrites seem fruitful and green in the eyes of their fellow creatures, but in the sight of the hidden Judge they appear fruitless and withered.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"For the congregation of hypocrites shall be desolate, and fire shall consume the tabernacles of bribery." [34]
* Fire burns the tents when the heat of greed corrupts the thoughts.

The hypocrite's mind will not rest from thinking of evil; for as he pursues earthly things or the love of praise, he murmurs against what belongs to others, and runs panting that it may be his, and strives to show others to be wicked by comparison with himself, since he wants to appear holier than the whole world.

By making others despised, he tries to appear at all times worthy of honor. Therefore, seeking praise from his neighbor, he spreads the nets of his tongue in judging his fellow creatures, so that he may catch a good opinion of himself among those whom he seeks to please.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"They conceive mischief, and bring forth vanity, and their belly prepareth deceit." [35]

* [He conceives sorrows.] And what is the fruit of this? [Vanity comes upon him, and his belly bears deceit.] Or rather, "he will bear" from what comes of "deceit"; he bears deceit itself, by bearing things that are of no use and do not profit him at all.

If Eliphaz were thinking about all these things realistically, and if he had met deceivers here, he would not have thought in a truthful and sincere way, because the judgment of many deceivers is reserved for the ages to come. And if he is speaking of rewards to come, he wrongs Job in vain. In vain he was condemning him for his sorrows. For the splendor of this life often falls upon the slaves of greed, and the miseries of life upon the righteous. God did not decree this wrongly, but altogether rightly. For He does not grant the righteous man the splendor of this life, whose fullness is leaves of trees, whose strength is shadow, whose wealth is straw, and whose glory is smoke; but the righteous man is made worthy of the Kingdom of Heaven, of incorruption, of immortality, and of heavenly glory, in which a person rejoices with the angels. This is why, even if they wear themselves out with sweat and meet with many hardships, they do not blame the Judge, knowing that through these slight afflictions they receive the glory to come (2 Cor 4:17), which shall be revealed to us (Rom 8:18) from the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * [They conceive woe and bring forth iniquity, and their womb prepares deceit.] A man conceives woe when he plans evil things, and brings forth iniquity when he begins to carry out what he planned.
By indulging in envy he conceives woe, and by uttering slanders he brings forth iniquity.
It is a great evil when the wicked man strives to show others to be wicked, so that he himself may appear holy, by showing others to be unclean.

We must bear in mind that the Holy Bible uses the term "belly" or "womb" for the "mind." It was said by Solomon: [The lamp of the Lord is the ways of men, searching all the inward parts of the mind] (Prov 20:27). By the term "womb" the mind is rightly understood, for as offspring are conceived in the womb, so thought is generated in the mind. And as flesh is found in the belly, so thoughts are in the mind. The womb of the hypocrite prepares deceits, for he is always conceiving in his mind great evils against his relatives, in keeping with his aim for himself of appearing innocent before all men.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Let me profit from the reproaches of those who reproach me!
* Unjustly did Eliphaz and his two friends accuse the righteous Job!
They measured out bitter accusations to him, and they became a cause of glory for him!
As for me, in my weakness allow me to profit from their accusations!
* They claimed that he is hiding behind wisdom, but wisdom is innocent of him, for his knowledge is vain, and his depths carry destructive winds!

Grant me, O Lord, knowledge from You; shine with Your light upon my depths, that my life may become a living witness, that I may speak only what I live by You and in You. Grant that Your Holy Spirit may blow within me, that the destructive evil spirits may not be able to slip into me!
Let every word be anointed with the anointing of the Spirit.
And let my life be salt to the earth!
* Grant me, O Lord, that Your fear may take the steering wheel.
My soul walks in the royal road.
I enjoy fellowship with the Bridegroom of my soul, the Way, the Truth, and the Life!
I turn neither to the right nor to the left!
For the steering wheel is in the hand of an almighty, wise, and loving Father!
