* Be, O Lord, the keeper of my mouth, and set a strong door before my lips, that nothing may come out of it but what pleases You. Grant that my words may be in harmony with my depths and my conduct,
so that they may not be a witness against my iniquity and a cause of my condemnation!
* I return in my thought to Your wonderful works.
You created everything for my sake.
And You gave my father Adam mind and wisdom.
You wanted his offspring to be truly wise, that they might be counted Your children, imitating You!
Grant me the Wisdom who sits at Your right hand.
Give to me not according to my merit, but according to Your love!
* You long to gather together all Your believers, and that Your believers be gathered to You.
You long to shine with the light of Your wisdom upon all.
You want all to be as those who are in Your council.
You reveal Your surpassing mysteries to those who fear You.
* Grant me, O Lord, the spirit of wisdom that is from You.
Then I will not exalt myself with knowledge that is not from me, nor claim wisdom as if it were unique and lofty.
Let me honor every human being, and appreciate the gifts God has given him!
* That I may profit from every sincere counsel, grant me humility, that I may profit from the wisdom of all, if possible.
But I do not seek human consolations, for You are the heavenly Physician, the giver of true consolations.
I listen to Your voice through Your Church, and You are revealed before my eyes, and I enjoy the joy of Your mysteries!
I see You revealed in Your servants, and I receive Your gifts from Your hands through them!
You are the giver of gifts to humble hearts!
* I look at myself, and I perceive the truth of my weakness.
Who can be justified before You, O Holy One?
No one born of woman is accounted pure before You, even if he is but one day old!
Your saints confess their weaknesses!
And the heavenly ones are not pure before You!
Do not entrust anyone with my salvation but Yourself!
* I confess to You that I drink iniquity like water.
But You are the forgiver of sins, You are the rescuer of souls from corruption!
* Now, O Lord, look upon Your holy Church.
Grant to all, priests and people, to be kindled with love of continual learning.
May all walk, led by Your Holy Spirit, in the footsteps of the early holy Fathers.
Let there be no stranger among us, with a perverted mind.
But may all be one flock under one Shepherd, enjoying Your fruitful pastures!
May all enjoy the spirit of simplicity, so that there be no proud or hypocrite among them!
* Grant me not to judge anyone, for You alone are the searcher of hearts.
I often suppose of one who falls under the weight of trials that it is the fruit of his hidden evils.
Who can comprehend Your wisdom, O Savior, Lover of mankind?
Not everyone who suffers is a saint or a wicked man.
You alone allow prosperity or distress, and in both cases You seek nothing but our salvation and our glory!
* Our hidden glances at those who tempt crush them, but Your divine hand provides what is for the edification of those who believe in You.
* My God, You are the source of my peace, indeed You are peace itself; whoever possesses You, no terror and no anxiety will enter his life!
He fears neither the darkness nor the sword!
There is nothing to terrify him as long as You dwell in his depths!
But whoever runs after evil runs after a destructive mirage; he gains vanity and loses the truth, wandering and emptiness come upon him, and he comes to need a crust of bread.
Distress comes upon him, and the enemy of good reigns over him.
Let me flee to Your Cross, and I will see You tearing up the bond that is against me, freeing me from the slavery of the devil, and bringing him beneath my feet.
In humiliation that tyrant falls and is made a public spectacle!
* Yes, let me draw near to You, O wonderful Crucified One, and be united with You, and pride will find no place in me.
Pride is shattered, which shattered my soul, turned my paradise into a wilderness, and made my dwelling a ruin!
Deceit flees, and the ways of evil are closed before me.
There is no more famine in my soul, nor bloodshed surrounding me.
My vine is filled with clusters of Your love!
And my olive tree bears fruit, to overflow with the oil of Your grace!
My soul knows poverty no more, but bears, by Your Holy Spirit, joyful heavenly fruits.
The destructive fire of evil does not approach my tent, but it is kindled with the holy fire of Your Holy Spirit.
My whole being becomes glorified in You.
I become like the heavenly ones, Your servants, the flames of fire!

entries.section: 1. Job rebukes his friends for their harshness

paragraphs.text: 1 Then Job answered and said, 2 "I have heard many such things: miserable comforters are ye all. 3 Shall vain words have an end? or what emboldeneth thee that thou answerest? 4 I also could speak as ye do: if your soul were in my soul's stead, I could heap up words against you, and shake mine head at you. 5 But I would strengthen you with my mouth, and the moving of my lips should asswage your grief.
Then Job answered and said: "I have heard many such things.
Miserable comforters are ye all!" [1-2]

The debate grew sharp in a painful way, until Job's ears wearied of listening to his friends, and he cried out: "I have heard many such things: miserable comforters are ye all." This is what Job's soul had come to. The wise man says: "The beginning of strife is as when one letteth out water: therefore leave off contention, before it be meddled with" (Prov 17:14).

Even if they speak words of comfort, they are painful, because they come from hearts that do not share his sufferings and do not feel his feelings. As the wise man says: [They sing songs to a heavy heart] (Prov 25:20), to no profit.

In the introduction of Father Hesychius of Jerusalem there is a wonderful discourse on Job's patience, especially in facing his friends who opposed him and mocked him, and he praised the virtue of patience, or longsuffering.
* A person can discover, through deep discernment, that patience is the foundation of the virtues.
Through patience Abraham became the father of nations (Gen 17:5; Sir 44:20; Rom 4:17), and the friend of God (Jas 2:23).
By patience Isaac, in the likeness of the only-begotten Son, became a sacrifice (Gen 22:2).
And by patience also Jacob carried a staff like a cross (Gen 32:10; Heb 11:21); and he who fled (Gen 27:43), patience made him return full of riches (Gen 32:22-23).

With such patience Job also struggled and raised the banner of victory, although his adversaries were many and powerful. And although he was entirely naked, he appeared as an armed man, awe-inspiring before those who wrestled with him. Job found himself cast on the ground, and those who wished to create obstacles (the demons) were circling around him in the air (Eph 2:2). Those who reviled him were clothed in purple, but he was clothed in sores. Yet the powers of the heavens counted him splendid...
The poor glorify him; the rich serve him, and all generations fixed their gaze on Job as a reflection of righteousness.
What need is there of many words about him? Do you want to learn the power of the patience that was in Job?

There were three friends who reviled him; they were healthy in body, full of vitality because of the abundance of their temporal blessings. And when they grew weary of speaking, each of them rested in turn. As for Job, he alone had his body covered with sores and his soul grieved. By his endurance he overcame these strong men, and by his patience he quieted the inflamed, chattering talk of those who insulted him, relying in vain on their chatter.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * The Church repeats the words of the psalmist David: [The sinners plowed upon my back] (Ps 129:3). By this is meant that while the Church bears patiently with heretics or the lost of every kind, those whom she is able to correct, she carries on her back the works of those who commit iniquity. So when the blessed Job saw his friend Eliphaz bringing many complaints against him, accusing him of hypocrisy, he was crushed in the bitterness of the criticism, showing him to be a false comforter. By his longsuffering Job became a symbol of the Church, which in general bears such things...

Now by this answer the blessed Job points to the age of the Church, when she is seen, because of the pressure of her adversaries, to have been cast on the ground by their temporary power. Therefore it was said: "Miserable comforters are ye all" (Job 16:2), whether they are heretics or wicked men, as she looks to the good labors in the trial. When they intend to comfort her, they stir up wrong things in their minds.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Drink mockery eagerly (willingly) as though it were the water of life. Drink it from every person, whoever he may be, as from one who wants to give you a purifying medicine that will save you from fornication. Then a star of deep purity will rise in your soul, and the lamp of God will no longer be put out in your heart.
St. John Climacus "Shall vain words have an end?

entries.section: 1. Job rebukes his friends for their harshness

paragraphs.text: or what emboldeneth thee that thou answerest?" [3]

Job felt that they were going round in an empty circle, for they had nothing but a multitude of words without a clear aim, with nothing new and useful in them. Perhaps he counted their speech a calamity like the other calamities that had befallen him, if not worse than all the previous calamities. He felt that his friends were stirring up against him without cause, and wronging him with no benefit to themselves.
* "Shall vain words have an end?" Vain words are those that serve temporary vanity, and whose aim is not righteousness.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

When a man loses true love, his heart suffers emptiness, so that he does not practice sincere friendship, but behaves in complete passivity, ignoring his suffering friends, or finding many pretexts to accuse them of evil, and instead of comforting them he disparages their persons and their conduct. Such were Job's friends in their silence as in their words!

The loss of love deprives a person of the sanctification of the two gifts, silence and speech. If he is silent, his silence carries not love but disregard for those around him, and if he speaks, he utters falsehood, and destroys himself and the souls of others.

The Holy Bible warns us against vain talk as against vain silence, so that when we are sanctified our silence is sanctified as well as our speech, and there is a time for speaking and a time for keeping silence, and both work for the edification of man and the comfort of his brethren, as for the glory of God.
"A tale out of season is as music in mourning" (Sir 22:6).
"In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise" (Prov 10:19).
"A fool also multiplieth words: a man cannot tell what shall be; and what shall be after him, who can tell him?" (Eccl 10:14).
"He that useth many words shall be abhorred; and he that taketh authority unjustly shall be hated" (Sir 20:8).
"Accustom not thy mouth to coarse speech, for therein is no lack of sin" (Sir 23:17).
"Honour and shame is in talk: and the tongue of man is his fall" (Sir 5:15).
"A wise man shall be renowned by his words: and a prudent man pleaseth great men" (Sir 20:29).
"Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones" (Prov 16:24).
"Refrain not to speak in the time of salvation, and hide not thy wisdom when it is fitting to display it" (Sir 4:28).
"Make not many words with a fool, and go not to him that hath no understanding" (Sir 22:14).
* The wise man is he who strives to please God, and is much in silence, and if he speaks, he speaks little, uttering what is necessary and pleasing to God.

* In silence you see your mind, but when you use your mind, you speak within yourself. For during silence the mind gives birth to the word, and the word of thanksgiving offered to God is the salvation of man.
* He who speaks foolishly has no mind, for he speaks without thinking about all things. Therefore examine what is profitable for you, for the sake of the salvation of your soul, in order to do it.
St. Anthony the Great * The mind cannot be freed from (natural) change in all things unless it goes out of the circle of itself and makes for itself a place in silence, which is higher than thought.
* The mind cannot be silent unless the body is silent, and the wall that separates them cannot be broken down except by silence and prayer.

St. Mark the Ascetic In a letter of Mar Philoxenus to the monks of Amid, which he wrote from his exile, urging them to strive for the right faith and not to be silent in bearing witness to the truth, it says:
[The monk who keeps silent about the faith out of hypocrisy does not know God.
The monk who grows lukewarm in zeal out of shame before authority does not know Christ.
The monk who is like everyone he is with (changing his colors and going along with each one) out of hypocrisy wears the face of a devil.
The monk who puts on Christ and is silent about the truth, his garment is the leprosy of Gehazi.
The monk whom grace visits and who is silent about the faith, his mouth will be stopped on the last day like the legion of demons.]

entries.section: 1. Job rebukes his friends for their harshness

paragraphs.text: "I also could speak as ye do: if your soul were in my soul's stead, I could heap up words against you, and shake (move) mine head at you." [4]

What does the righteous Job desire for his friends? Did he bear hatred and enmity, and in the distress of his soul ask that what had befallen him should befall them, and that he should take the position of the comforter?
Does he desire to mock them in their trials, and shake his head at them in contempt, since shaking the head in the East is a sign of scorn (Isa 22:37; Jer 16:18; Mt 39:27)?

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that what Job says is a prayer that comes from a loving man, who knows that they will not learn practical love except by entering into the experience of distress and trials. The motive is not to destroy them, but that through outward distress their hearts and inner depths may be set right.

But as for his heaping up words in the air (in vain) and mocking them by shaking his head, this is what Job does not accept, nor did he do it when they returned to him asking for prayer and for sacrifices to be offered on their behalf. What he says here is only to rebuke them and make them review themselves, that they may realize that they are uttering hollow words and mocking a suffering man! It is as though he were saying to them: it is fitting for you to do what you want others to do to you.

Moreover, since Job represents the suffering Church, she, in her love for the salvation of the wicked, asks that the Lord's rod be stretched out for discipline and not for vengeance, so that they may learn from sorrows outside how to enjoy love within.

* He says: [Oh, that your souls were in my soul's stead! And that I might comfort you with words, and shake my head at you, and move my lips for your relief] (Job 16:4-5). Sometimes it is necessary for wicked minds that cannot be corrected by the preaching of a man to be struck by God. This is what the preacher (Job) asks for them, out of tenderness toward them. For since this happens out of a great zeal of love, it is clear that he does not ask it for them as a punishment, but for the correction of the erring, so that it is a prayer for them, and not a curse against them.

The blessed Job shows in these words that he aims at this: his friends, who did not know how to sympathize with him in love in his grief, must learn by experience how they ought to be tender in the sorrows of others, and in this way live in a better inward state, understanding something about outward weakness...

Now we comfort the wicked in their falling under the rod when we point to outward sorrow for the building up of inward health in them. And we shake our heads when our mind, the leading part in us, inclines toward compassion. And we support them amid the blows of trials when we lessen the force of their sorrow with gentle words.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
It is fitting for the Church, who loves all men, to practice rebuke at times, and to ask the Lord for discipline for the salvation of the fallen, and not for their destruction.
* God bears with all the weaknesses of men, but He will not allow the man who continually murmurs to be left without discipline.

* A friend who rebukes another in secret is a wise physician, but he who wants to heal before the eyes of many is in truth an abuser... The righteous man imitates God; he will not discipline a person to take revenge and vengeance for his evil, but to correct him or that others may fear.
St. Mar Isaac the Syrian "For the commandment is a lamp; and the law is light; and reproofs of instruction are the way of life" (Prov 6:23).
"Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish" (Prov 12:1).
"Poverty and shame shall be to him that refuseth instruction: but he that regardeth reproof shall be honoured" (Prov 13:18).
"A fool despiseth his father's instruction: but he that regardeth reproof is made shrewd" (Prov 15:5).
"The ear that heareth the reproof of life abideth among the wise" (Prov 15:31).
"He that refuseth instruction despiseth his own soul: but he that heareth reproof getteth understanding" (Prov 15:32).
"Open rebuke is better than secret love" (Prov 27:5).
"The rod and reproof give wisdom: but a child left to himself bringeth his mother to shame" (Prov 29:15).
"He that hateth to be reproved is in the footsteps of the sinner: but he that feareth the Lord will repent in his heart" (Sir 21:7).
"A sinful man will not be reproved, but findeth excuses according to his desire" (Sir 32:21).

entries.section: 1. Job rebukes his friends for their harshness

paragraphs.text: "But I would strengthen you with my mouth, and the moving of my lips should asswage your grief." [5]

Job spoke frankly with his friends: that even on the ordinary social level they had not observed the simplest rules of friendship. And that if the positions were exchanged, he could do with them what they had done with him, namely offer comforts with the mouth and tongue and pretend to words of wisdom without sharing sincere feelings. It is as though he were demanding that they exchange positions with him, even for a moment, so that they might feel the arrows they aim against him with empty words of comfort.

It was fitting for them to bind up his broken bones with their gentle words and a loving heart, not to break his bones with the violence of their hearts. The prophet Isaiah says: "The Lord God hath given me the tongue of the learned, that I should know how to succour him that is weary with a word" (Isa 50:4). For one who has collapsed and become very sick needs a good ointment to support him, not stinging words that break him down all the more.

6 "Though I speak, my grief is not asswaged: and though I forbear, what am I eased? 7 But now he hath made me weary: thou hast made desolate all my company. 8 And thou hast taken hold of me, and a witness is found; my leanness rising up in me beareth witness to my face. 9 His wrath hath torn me and persecuted me; he gnasheth upon me with his teeth; mine enemy sharpeneth his eyes upon me. 10 They have gaped upon me with their mouth; they have smitten me upon the cheek reproachfully; they have gathered themselves together against me. 11 God hath delivered me to the ungodly, and turned me over into the hands of the wicked. 12 I was at ease, but he hath broken me asunder: he hath also taken me by my neck, and shaken me to pieces, and set me up for his mark. 13 His archers compass me round about, he cleaveth my reins asunder, and doth not spare; he poureth out my gall upon the ground. 14 He breaketh me with breach upon breach, he runneth upon me like a giant. 15 I have sewed sackcloth upon my skin, and thrust my horn into the dust. 16 My face is red with weeping, and on my eyelids is the shadow of death.

I have already pointed out that his lament over his condition carried wonderful prophecies about the suffering Lord Christ as Mediator and propitiatory Intercessor for us before the Father. At the same time he represents the suffering Church, which shares with her Christ His sufferings and crucifixion at the hands of those outside, as well as of the heretics who resist the divine truth.
"Though I speak, my grief is not asswaged:
and though I forbear, what am I eased?" [6]

Job was in perplexity: if he speaks, what use are his words with hard men who have no regard for his feelings; and if he is silent, does silence do away with the bitterness of his soul? If he pours out his complaint, he is accused of murmuring and misunderstood, and his grief increases. And if he is silent, he is accused of gloom. If he defends himself, they count him as clinging to self-righteousness, and if he keeps silent, they count him a wicked man who deserves greater chastisement!

The man who is earnest in his life and seeks the salvation of his soul profits from the words of the children of God, as he profits from their silence. If they speak, he receives the words in the Spirit of God for his edification, and if they are silent, he touches their inward contemplations and their enjoyment of the heavenly life. But he who in carelessness or in stubbornness seeks neither the truth nor eternal life stumbles at the words of the righteous, and also at their silence.

Job expressed the position of the Lord Christ, who, if He spoke the divine truth, was accused of being a blasphemer (Mt 26:65), and if He kept silent on the Cross, they said: "He saved others; himself he cannot save" (Mt 27:42). His soul was sorrowful unto death, not because of the pain, but for the bitterness of the sin which He bore for us in order to kill it by His death.

If the soul of the Lord Christ was sorrowful, the Church, His bride, remains groaning all the days of her sojourn until the elect complete their struggle, and the believers enjoy the fellowship of glories at the Lord's final coming.

* [What shall I do? If I speak, my grief is not taken from me, and if I bear it (in silence), it does not leave me]... No one is ignorant that this applies to the person of the blessed Job. But as for the universal Church, when she speaks, [her grief does not cease], since she does not see the wicked corrected by her words. And if she is silent, her very position of silence grieves her all the more, for while she is silent she sees the sin of the wicked increasing and exalting itself.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Persecution is good for you, for the love of the Cross is rich in you. Torments are dear to you, for the fire of love of Him who cast His fire into the world (Lk 12:49) is ablaze in you. Your struggle is wonderful, because your persecutors are wicked. Your battle is full of wonder, because your enemies are fierce. If the pagans were persecuting you, it would be a justification for your sufferings and a relief for your torments, but now the Jews, the enemies of the Cross, line up against you. Your sufferings are higher than any sufferings, and your crown is more triumphant than any crown...

Great is the beauty of him whose sufferings are many. So the crown becomes beautiful in proportion to the severity of the affliction. The Comforter Spirit who makes you wise knows how to speak in you, and says: "For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us" (Rom 8:18). The affliction of a short time brings you near to keeping the everlasting life that has no end, and when you die to the world you show by death the life with Christ.
Who does not long to reap eternal life from the afflictions of time?

The world dissolves and its beauty fades, and it leaves its riches, its authority passes away and its splendor is despised, its rank is nullified and its life comes to an end, its forms change, and it is scattered like roses, and withers like flowers, and flees like a shadow, and is rolled up and hurries like a wheel, and with it pass away all the things that run in it, whether comfort or torment, honor or insult; all its properties remain with it and like it. Its afflictions do not last long, and its comfort is not real.
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh "But now he hath made me weary.
Thou hast made desolate all my company." [7]

When Job felt the insincerity of his friends' intention, in bitterness he declared his perplexity to them, for he knows that what has befallen him is by God's permission, and so he became weary and perplexed.

He was weary of his inability to make the right decision: whether to speak or to keep silent? And Job was weary of his friends as of his very life. What added sorrows to him was the desolation of all his company. His sons and servants died, those who worked with him were scattered, and his friends became his opponents, gloating over his misfortune.
"Thou hast taken hold of me.
A witness is found.
My leanness rising up in me beareth witness to my face." [8]

Some of the Fathers see that Job, who is a type of the Lord Christ, sees in all that befell him only shadows of what would befall the Lord Christ. If they gathered against Job to destroy him, the powers of darkness joined together against the Lord Christ, and the sons of darkness seized Him to crucify Him, and sadly one of His disciples betrayed Him.

Job became like one seized in bitter captivity, and he became extremely lean, since his flesh wasted away because of the sores that covered his whole body; his leanness became a subject of talk proclaimed on his face, meaning that his features bore witness to the leanness he had reached.

Some translate this phrase: [Thou hast filled me with wrinkles, and this is a witness against me, and my leanness rose up against me to bear witness to my face]. His whole face became wrinkled, not because of advancing age, but because of the severity of his diseases. The sight of his face bears witness that he did not complain for nothing and without cause.

* Job proves that he gained great profit from the attack of the combatant (Satan), since the latter did not know that Job was being crowned by the very means by which he thought he was deceiving him. Therefore Job says: [Since thou hast taken hold of me, thou hast become a witness against me] (Job 16:8). For the enemy did not seize only Job's goods and his sons and daughters, but also seized Job in his own person, since the accuser took hold of him to wrestle with him and take possession of him (أ).

This is a testimony against the righteous man, accurately borne by the enemies. And so, a short time after these battles, God presented these thoughts to Job: You think that I am speaking with you in another way... but I will show forth your righteousness, you will appear as one who bears God. In every case these evils also bear testimony in Job's favor.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem What happened to Job as a symbol was fulfilled in the person of the Lord Christ. And what happened with the Lord Christ opened the door for His Church to share His sufferings and crucifixion. The traitor Judas betrayed his Lord, but as for the Church, the false Antichrist remains attacking her secretly until he appears at the end of the ages to oppose her openly to her face.

It is a perpetual war between God and the devil, or between the kingdom of darkness and the kingdom of light. In ancient times Job's friends represented the kingdom of darkness, and in the days of the Lord Christ its hideousness appeared in the traitor disciple who joined with the opponents, and after the ascension of the Lord Christ into heaven the many enemies of Christ oppose her until the day when the Antichrist appears openly in a decisive and bitter battle.

* "My leanness (my falsehood) rose up against me." Job speaks of Judas, for he was the Lord's disciple (Lk 14:26-27, 33) and His apostle, but was found a liar [vain] (Jn 12:6), and a traitor (Lk 6:16).

* "It answers (challenges) to my face." When I said to my disciples: "Verily, verily, I say unto you, that one of you shall betray me" (Jn 13:21), he dared to say to my face without shame: "Master, is it I?" (Mt 26:25)

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * Satan, our enemy and adversary, will make war to keep us in his grasp. Who will escape from him? He who understands what was said of the poor and needy: [The Lord will deliver him in the day of evil] (Ps 1:41).

St. Jerome * The enemy does not kindle war against us directly and openly, but through his tricks. What are the devil's tricks? They lie in trying sometimes to capture us by short ways, but he always uses deceit... The enemy does not set temptations out in the open before us. He does not openly proclaim the worship of idols, but through his military deceits he presents opportunities for idol worship, and by enticing with words, using his skills.

St. John Chrysostom * In ordinary battles the commanders do not arm women or children or old men, but our Commander, the Lord Christ, distributes this royal weapon (which is the possession of Christ Himself) to all equally. Then He teaches them the military tricks of the devil.
Father Theodoret * Every story (of the battles of the Old Testament) contains a kind of victory and triumph over the spiritual powers of Satan.

Origen * [The liar has risen up against me, he resists me to my face.] Even in her time of peace the holy Church is subject to the liar, for many do not believe the promise of eternal life, and falsely claim to be believers. And since they cannot oppose her preaching openly, she is exposed to the liar from her back and not before her face. And when the time of evil breaks out (the days of the Antichrist), he who now makes light of the Church will stand in full awareness opposing her to her face, using plain statements with words that he borrows from the true faith.

But we must realize that when we face such things from the hands of carnal men, those who kill us violently, they are not in the violence of the evil spirit who rules their minds, as Paul says: "For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world" (Eph 6:12).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* The great Savior was beaten with rods, and by the sentence passed by the governor He went out to be crucified!
He came to His own, and His own received Him not, but cast Him out from among them with scorn!
He went out to die with the wicked without any fault, then Judas repented, the lamp that was put out among his companions, and was ashamed of the evil deed he had done.

He who betrayed Him returned the silver to those who had seized Him, scorning himself, and confessed that he had betrayed Him in wickedness... And the crucifiers also fled as though they were not near, and said: What is it to us? See thou to that.
The innocent blood cast terror on those who shed it, and they began to be terrified and tremble at it before they spilled it!
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh "His wrath hath torn me and persecuted me.
He gnasheth upon me with his teeth.
Mine enemy sharpeneth his eyes upon me." [9]

Who is this enemy who tears him in his wrath against him? Is it Eliphaz and those with him, who crushed him by their accusations against him unjustly? Or is it Satan, who will not rest at the rest of a man who worships God in truth, so he stirs up the wicked against him?

Some see that in his weakness he sees his enemy to be God Himself, who permitted him the harsh trials, the cause of which Job does not know. If "the wrath of a king is as messengers of death" (Prov 16:14), what then would be the wrath of the King of kings? But it is clear from the context of the discourse that this is not what is meant.

* "He gathered his wrath against me, and threatened me, and gnashed his teeth upon me; mine enemy looked upon me with terrible eyes" (Job 16:9) LXX. Who are the wicked but the members of Satan? Therefore he works through them by what he puts in their hearts and they are bound to carry out. For Satan until now harbors wrath against the holy Church, but his wrath is scattered, so he places his hidden temptations through the stewardship of his members...

The teeth of this enemy are the persecutors and the executors of torments upon the righteous, who disfigure the members of the Church when they pour trials upon her elect through their persecutions of them. And the eyes of this enemy are those who plan what is to her harm for execution, and by their counsel they shed light on the cruelty of her persecutors. Therefore her ancient enemy gnashes his teeth upon her, as long as he hunts through the cruel sons of perdition the life of the righteous in her. He looks upon her with terrible eyes, through the counsels of the wicked. So he does not cease to devise trials in order to torment her more and more. And just as the incarnate Truth (the Lord Christ), in His preaching, chose poor and simple persons from the common people, so on the other side the apostate angel, the accursed man, will choose at the end of the world to preach his falsehood cunning and crooked men who have the knowledge of this world.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Look how the Jewish nation was an adulteress!

She despised her Father and hated Him from Sinai, and when His Son became incarnate for her salvation, she seized Him and put Him on the Cross, and stood dancing and laughing and scorning and mocking.
Come, O Moses, look at the bride whom you brought out of Egypt, what she does to her pure Bridegroom!

Come, look at the feast she set before Him. She brought myrrh, she mixed vinegar, she drew the sword. Instead of manna she gave Him vinegar. Instead of the bitter waters that He made sweet for her, she put gall in the sweet waters for Him.
The chosen vine produced bad grapes.
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh "They have gaped upon me with their mouth.
They have smitten me upon the cheek reproachfully.
They have gathered themselves together against me." [10]

As for the Lord Christ, against whom all the powers of evil joined together, it was said of Him: "They gaped upon me with their mouths" (Ps 22:13), and it was said: "They shall smite the judge of Israel with a rod upon the cheek" (Mic 5:1), and this was fulfilled literally (Mt 26:27).
* [They smote me upon my cheek, they filled up the full measure of my punishments] (Job 16:10)... Thus the wicked smite the cheek of the holy Church when they persecute the righteous preachers.
The lost sinners think they are doing a great work when they put an end to the lives of the preachers.

After the smiting on the cheek it was fitting to say: [They filled up the full measure of my punishments], for these punishments complete their satiety, these that discipline the mind of the Church in a particular way.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* They covered His eyes and mocked Him, and struck Him with their fists, and said to Him: Prophesy to us, who is it that smote thee!
They struck with the reed the exalted Head, and the angels were terrified!
With these corrupt and evil things they repaid Him with madness...!
They became mad to veil the face of the Sun of Righteousness, lest He shine forth and the world see their corruption.
The foolish bride veiled the Bridegroom, lest He see her wickedness and corruption.
They veiled the Physician, lest He bind up their wounds and heal them!
Look at Christ, how much did He endure from the wicked?!
How did that fool dare to spit in His face!
How did you dare, O tongue, to sprinkle spittle...?!
How did you endure, O earth, the mockery of the Son...?!
A fearful sight, full of amazement, that a man should see the wax standing and spit in the face of the flame...
And this also happened for the sake of Adam, because he deserved to be spat upon for he had erred! And in place of the servant the Master rose up to receive all things!
He offered His face to receive the spittle, for He promised in Isaiah that He would not turn away His face from enduring the shame of spitting...!
The Master had pity on his weakness (Adam's), and entered Himself to receive the shame in his stead!
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh "God hath delivered me to the ungodly, and turned me over into the hands of the wicked." [11]

The wicked had no authority over our Lord Jesus Christ, but since He accepted to be a sacrifice for sin for the world, out of love for mankind and obedience to the Father, the Lover of mankind, He gave them authority from above (Jn 19:11).

Such were the outlooks of the righteous Job; he counted all his life to be in the hand of the Lord, even what befell him from the wicked was by God's permission, so he says: "God hath delivered me to the ungodly." In the same spirit, when Shimei cursed the prophet David, he counted it as coming from God (2 Sam 16:5-13).
God uses even the wicked, while they enjoy their full freedom, to be a sword against their wicked brethren, or to discipline His children (Isa 10:5) or to prove them.

* Job says that this is done by "God." It is clear that he means the Father, for the only-begotten Son submitted to these (sufferings) not only of His own full will but also according to the will of His Father, for the will of the Father and the Son is one, since He wishes to complete His wonderful work for us, and to suffer for our salvation. Well then! Let us compare Job's words here with the words of the Savior...

[The Lord delivered me to the ungodly], that is, to Caiaphas, who questioned Him saying: "I adjure thee by the living God, that thou tell us whether thou be the Christ, the Son of God" (Mt 26:63). And he received an answer he did not deserve, but because he adjured Him he heard this answer to his question: "Hereafter shall ye see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven" (Mt 26:64), and Caiaphas rent his clothes as though he were before a blasphemer.

"And turned me over into the hands of the wicked," that is, in the presence of Caiaphas and the other leaders of the Jews. For how could they not be wicked, those who cried out to Pilate: [Away with this man (to death), and release unto us Barabbas, who for a certain sedition made in the city, and for murder, was cast into prison] (Lk 13:18-19).
Father Hesychius of Jerusalem "I was at ease, but he hath broken me asunder: he hath also taken me by my neck, and shaken me to pieces, and set me up for his mark (target)." [12]

Job was at ease in his enjoyment of the Lord's temporal goods given to him before the trial, but in the midst of the trial he felt that all that happened to him was not haphazard, nor were they chance events. It was as though God had shaken him and taken hold of his neck, as a father holds his son in his rage. As though He had chosen him out of all mankind to set him up as a mark or target at which He directs all His arrows, as though God had set him apart for this target.

* "When I was at ease he shook me, and took hold of my hair and plucked it out" (LXX). It can rightly be said that the Lord Christ calls His apostles "His hair," since they are the adornment of the head, for He was with them in peace. But when they left Christ because of the sufferings, the disciples were scattered, and therefore Job said this phrase. How was this fulfilled? Christ Himself said to His disciples: "All ye shall be offended because of me this night" (Mt 26:31)... Jesus added afterward: "For it is written, I will smite the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered abroad" (Mt 26:31; Zech 13:7).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* We look and marvel at the Victor who stood in the court. The Son of the free who was smitten on His cheek, the Sun who embraced the pillar (around which the Lord was bound to be scourged), the Fire that is scourged with whips (Mt 27:26), the Light that is despised by darkness (Jn 8:12; 1:5), the Lord of Gabriel whom Caiaphas' servant struck (Jn 18:22), the lion's whelp whom the contemptible foxes tear (Hos 5:14).
The great Sea judged by dust.
The Fearful One who rode upon the Cherubim climbed the tree of the Cross.
The Giver of glory to the lily, and of diverse colors to the roses (Mt 6:28), hung naked in shame.
The Planter of Paradise is given vinegar and gall (Gen 2:8; Mt 27:34).
The Flame is pierced with the spear (Jn 19:34).
The Crowner of the sun with rays had a crown of thorns placed on His head (Mt 27:29).
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh "His archers (the archers of his arrows) compass me round about.
He cleaveth my reins asunder, and doth not spare.
He poureth out my gall upon the ground." [13]

Job counted those who contributed to the coming of his calamities as like special archers of God, to whom the divine command was issued to aim their arrows at him. And the arrows came true; they reached Job's kidneys and cleaved them asunder without mercy, as though the aim of the arrows was to kill him without pity.

"He poureth out my gall upon the ground." He took this comparison from what hunters do when they hunt a wild beast and slaughter it: they throw its gall on the ground in disgust. He counted himself as already slain, a target.
"He breaketh me with breach upon breach.
He runneth (rusheth) upon me like a giant." [14]

Job was not struck by one deadly blow, so that he might die and be at rest, but he was struck by successive blows, one blow after another, and wound upon wound. So he did not rest by dying, nor did he take breath between one blow and another, but he came to expect more, with no hope of an end to his troubles, or even of a halt at the point he had reached.

Perhaps he felt as though God were storming him like a mighty one, as cruel kings, when they conquer, bring the members of the defeated royal family, and throw them on the ground, and the king sets his foot on their necks, as a kind of enslavement, humiliation, and public disgrace.

Father Gregory (the Great) sees that Job is speaking of the enemy of good, who will not cease to storm the Church to seize the weak members as captives under his authority, and he attacks the Church like a mighty giant. The enemy wages war on the Church as a body, and also on every member in her by every possible means, in order to destroy many, if possible.

* "He breaketh me with breach upon breach." The holy Church is broken, breach upon breach, through her weak members, when sin is added to sin, until iniquity reaches a dangerous degree. This applies to one whom greed drives to theft, and theft to deceit, and he defends sin with lies...

"He meets him like a giant" (LXX). The enemy can be easily resisted if a person does not agree with him, whether in turning away from the faith or continuing in it. But if the soul has become accustomed to submit to his persuasions, then in so far as it submits to them, it becomes very hard for it to struggle against him in little or much.

Our wicked enemy "like a giant" wages war against her when she is overcome by an evil habit. But the holy Church often brings the minds of believers back to repentance, even after the commission of sins, and washes them from the practice of sins by the effectiveness of a man's disciplining himself by his own choice.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

St. Mar Jacob of Serugh presented to us in his letter (19), which he sent to the Monastery of Mar Isaac Giyula, a vivid picture of the devil's resistance to mankind. He says that he began his war with lying (Jn 8:44) and wishes to end it with error.
In the first generation in the Garden of Eden, he cast enmity between God and His image (Adam and Eve).
And in the seventh generation he taught man fornication, and defiled the children of God (the children of pure Seth) with the daughters of Cain the outcast and their embroidered beauty.
And in the tenth generation the earth was filled with the wicked. God sent the divine Law, stretching out the hand of Moses like a lamp, to enlighten the earth that had grown dark.

And in the fourteenth generation the earth was filled with the worship of idols, and God was forgotten even in the midst of His people. So God sent Elijah the prophet, the second Moses, to declare his zeal for the glory of God against error.

And in the last times God sent His Son incarnate, and He became one of us, to make us with Him and like Him, and He gave us Himself to take us to His Father, and He descended to the bottom of the depth to raise us to the power of the height, and humbled Himself to the utmost humility in order to put to shame by his humility the wicked one who wished to become god by robbery.

* The enemy wages war to bring a man out from one form (of life) to another. And when he has brought him out of that form, he begins to make him blame himself with thoughts of gloom which Satan casts into his mind, so he thinks that he behaved badly on the day he changed his work and joined another.
He troubles him at every opportunity, and in all that he does, in order to win him over, drawing him to his cunning and contrary counsels.
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh "I have sewed sackcloth upon my skin, and thrust my horn into the dust." [15]

His splendid clothes no longer suited his body full of sores, nor were they fitting for one in such distress, so he sewed sackcloth for himself; he sewed the sackcloth himself, for there was no one to take pity on him and sew it for him in the midst of his severe sufferings.

The "horn" indicated authority and strength; so he himself thrust his horn into the dust, a sign of his complete rejection of any honor or exaltation. Job counted the dust to be the best place, not only to sit in the midst of, but also to bury in it his honor and authority.
* What is meant by sackcloth and ashes but repentance, and by skin and flesh but the sins of the flesh?
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"My face is red with weeping, and on my eyelids is the shadow of death." [16]

Job not only lost joy, but the time became fitting to shed tears for his sins, and for the Lord's chastisements of him, and the harshness of his friends toward him, so his face became red with weeping, and his eyes bore the marks of death.

It is remarkable that Job's whole face became red, and not only his eyes, with the abundance of tears, but he did not fear death, for it had become without authority over him. He saw it as a passing shadow after Christ Himself drove the chariot of death to destroy death itself by it, and to give us the power of His resurrection. This is what the Church sings, praising the One who rose from the dead: "By His death He trampled death!"

* [On my eyelids is the shadow of death] (Job 16:16). Not death, but [the shadow of death], because the Savior is asleep. Therefore Father Jacob prophesied of the death of the Savior for our sake, uttering the following words in his blessing: [From my seed, my son, thou art gone up, thou liest down as a lion and like a whelp, and who then shall rouse him up?] (cf. Gen 49:9). For He has no need of anyone to wake Him, He who raises all mankind. He rose by Himself of His own will.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * "My eyelids are darkened" (LXX): Rightly they called by the name of eyelids those who are entrusted with guarding the safety of the paths of the feet. But the ruling guardians cannot understand the secret judgments of God; the "eyelids" of the holy Church "are darkened."
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Life made light of death, saying: [O death, where is thy sting? O Hades, where is thy victory?] (1 Cor 15:54-55).

On the day of Sunday the door of heaven was opened to them, which had been shut on Friday in the faces of the angels lest they go down to Golgotha, and they hastened to descend in their white garments, to receive our King who had saved the captives and returned to His Father.
The new tomb became the house of the wedding, built in the garden for the slain Bridegroom, who brought back the bride from the war of the enemies.

The angels in their white garments gathered and came to the Beautiful Gate, and the women disciples with their spices (Lk 23:56). Simon and John ran because of the glad tidings (Jn 20:3-8). Cleopas and his brother (Simon) had their eyes opened by the bread of blessing to see the resurrection openly. The friends uncover their faces, and the haters bow their heads.
Annas is ashamed, and Caiaphas cannot speak.
Judas is hanged, and the chiefs of the synagogue strike their faces.
The door of Hades is shut, and the door of Baptism is opened.
The Cross is set up in the watercourses.
The rational flock came to be refreshed by the waters that flowed from the Cross.
He looked at him as he was clothed with light and standing at the spring, and he conceived and gave birth in the likeness of the appearance of his beautiful light.
He put on a white garment shining like light, and made him white as snow...
The whole flock is white, for the whole Cross is clothed with light.
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh * After Christ came and died for the life of the world, death was no longer called death, but sleep and repose.

* Do you not know how the Cross corrected many errors? Did it not destroy death, and wipe away sin, and put an end to the power of Satan, and satisfy the being of our good body? Did it not set right the whole world, and yet you do not trust in it?

* Who can utter the mighty acts of the Lord? (Ps 2:105) From death we have become immortal. Have you understood the victory and the way it was reached? Learn how this triumph was acquired without toil and sweat. Our weapons were not stained with blood, we did not stand in the battle line, we were not wounded, we did not even see the battle, yet we have won the battle. The striving is (our enjoyment) of our Christ, and the crown of victory is ours.

Since the victory is ours, it is fitting for us as soldiers to chant today with joyful voices the hymns of triumph. Let us praise our Master, saying: [Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is thy victory? O grave, where is thy sting?] (1 Cor 54:15-55).
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 3. His recourse to the just God

paragraphs.text: 17 Although there is no injustice in my hands, and my prayer is pure. 18 "O earth, cover not thou my blood, and let my cry have no place. 19 Also now, behold, my witness is in heaven, and my record is on high. 20 My friends scorn me: mine eye poureth out tears unto God. 21 That he might judge a man with God, as a son of man with his neighbor.
"Although there is no injustice in my hands, and my prayer is pure." [17]

The testimony of his conscience remained upright and never left him, for he did not mention that he had committed injustice against any person, nor offered a prayer for temporal things, nor spread out his hands in prayer after defiling them with some injustice.

* [There was no injustice in his hand] (Job 16:17). It is said of the Savior in the divinely inspired Holy Scripture: [He had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth] (Isa 53:9), [My prayer was pure], for the Savior was pure even from anger and wrath. It was plain to the Jews who crucified Him that He prayed: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do" (Lk 23:34). Therefore Job was a prophet and a God-bearer, who by certain words was able to see the sufferings of Christ as though they were before him. For this reason he spoke about his own person with the aim of showing the sufferings to the forefathers of the Jewish people, so that people might be able to understand them well, and afterward He presented to us the very event itself.
He did not offer his righteous speech out of boasting, but to lead his friends, and all the generations after them, to follow his example.
In his speech he left us a good seal, his pure prayers.

They comfort and help the righteous toward purity of prayer, as they are made worthy of faith. They keep prayer pure in the same way that Paul also understands it: [I will therefore that men pray every where, lifting up holy hands, without wrath and doubting] (1 Tim 2:8). For prayer is pure when the hands are pure from covetousness and from every blemish. Let us know this: how can a man be righteous unless it is by reason of his inner man (Rom 7:22), freed from malice, and not falling into doubt when he prays? For we speak with God Himself, and we draw near to the great King, who washes me thoroughly from mine iniquity and cleanses me from my sin (Ps 51:3).

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * As I remember, I said that the blessed Job, who bears a symbol of the Holy Church, uses at times the voice of the body (the Church), and at other times the voice of the Head (the Lord Christ). And while he speaks of her members, suddenly he speaks with the words of her Head. Therefore he adds here: "I suffered this without iniquity of my hand, while offering my pure prayers to God" (LXX). He suffered without iniquity in his hand, [who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth] (1 Pet 2:22). Yet he endured the pain of the Cross for our salvation. He alone above all others made pure prayers to God, for in enduring the distress of His sufferings He prayed for His persecutors, saying: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do" (Lk 23:34). How can the purity of prayer be described more than this? Who can understand it more than this?

He grants the tenderness of His intercession even to those whose hands practiced the suffering, for the very blood of our Savior, which His persecutors shed in their rage, they came to drink after they believed in Him, declaring that He is the Son of God.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* The purity of his prayer arises from these circumstances: it is not unseemly for him to ask for forgiveness in his prayer, since in truth he himself grants pardon to others.
St. Augustine * Be moved by prayer, ask for tenderness with humility, and take from the Giver of good things...
He is the one who receives all prayers and petitions; no prayer enters to His Father without Him, and no gift comes out from Him except by His hands...
He received the prayer of Hannah in the temple of the sanctuary, and went out to her with mercies from His Father's house.
He listened to the prayer of Jonah in the belly of the whale, and brought it in to His Father as an offering.
He listened to the Pharisee and the publican in the temple of the sanctuary, when they stood up to pray, and heard the petition...
He hears the whole world, and does not forget to present its prayers just as they were rendered...
* Pure prayer finds its way to God; it speaks to Him, listens to Him and trusts in Him.
* Do not grow weary in your asking. Do not think that your petition returns empty.
Do not say: I have asked much and have not found, and perhaps I shall never find.

entries.section: 3. His recourse to the just God

paragraphs.text: St. Mar Jacob of Sarug "O earth, cover not thou my blood, and let my cry have no place." [18]

Some interpret this phrase as meaning that he sees his friends to have shed his innocent blood by pouring false accusations against him, so he asks the earth to witness for him against them, and not to confine his cries in any place, but to let them rise to God on high.

If his friends have accused him of evil and hypocrisy, then he calls the earth to witness: if he has shed innocent blood or committed some crime, let it uncover it and make it known (Gen 4:10-11; Isa 26), and let it not conceal his soul so that it does not cry out.

* "Cover not"; may the struggles of Job not be forgotten, may the very sweat of my distress, which pours forth in the practice of virtue, not be taken away, I who have put on every kind of works of patience. May the sores of the righteous man be uncovered to the eyes of the public, so that they may purify themselves by the desire to imitate him.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * Remember his pure conscience and his blameless prayer: "O earth, cover not the blood of my body" (Job 16:18) LXX, so that his prayer may be directed like incense toward the Lord (Ps 141:2), and not be deposited in the earth.

The prayer of the saint pierces the clouds (Sir 35:17), but the earth opens its mouth and hides the prayer of the sinner in the blood of the flesh, as God said to Cain the murderer: [Now art thou cursed from the earth, which hath opened her mouth to receive thy brother's blood from thy hand; when thou tillest the ground] (see Gen 4:11-12).

St. Ambrose * "O earth, cover not the blood of my body, and let my cry find no place in which to hide in thee" (18 LXX). It was said to man when he committed sin: [Dust thou art (earth), and unto dust shalt thou return] (Gen 3:19). [This earth] does not cover the blood of our Savior, where every sinner takes for himself the price of his salvation, and confesses, praises and proclaims it to all his kinsmen as far as he can. Moreover, the earth did not cover His blood, since the Holy Church has preached the mystery of His salvation in all parts of the world.

Observe what he adds: [Let my cry find no place in which to hide in thee]. For the very blood of salvation which is received is itself the cry of our Redeemer. Paul says: [The blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel] (Heb 12:24). It was said of the blood of Abel: [The voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground] (Gen 4:10). But the blood of Jesus speaks better things than the blood of Abel, for the blood of Abel brought about the death of his brother, whereas the blood of the Lord gained life for His persecutors. Therefore the mystery of our Lord's passion is not without profit in us, but we are bound to imitate what we receive and to preach what we worship.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. His recourse to the just God

paragraphs.text: "Also now, behold, my witness is in heaven, and my record is on high." [19]
Lest he be accused anew of being proud and ascribing to himself a self-righteousness, he asks heaven to bear witness for him, and the One who dwells in it to declare his uprightness.
* If you ask: And where was witness borne to Him? I answer you: At the Jordan, saying: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (Mt 3:17)...
He made clear that there is no voice in God, and no form for Him, but He is higher than all forms and tones of this kind.

St. John Chrysostom * [My witness in heaven] not because of his wealth, for God has no need of a reward, He who does not fear works of enmity, and is not occupied with the love of the world (Mt 6:19-20).
[And my advocate on high], He who knows best the works and the words and the movements of thoughts, He who gives us the unforgettable memory of Job preserved in the divine Scriptures.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * [Also behold my witness is in heaven, and the fellowship of my heart on high] (Job 16:19) LXX. For when the Son came down to earth He had a witness in heaven, for the Father is witness to the Son, of whom He said in the Gospel: "The Father himself, which hath sent me, hath borne witness of me" (Jn 5:37). Rightly also He was called "the fellowship of my heart," since they have one will and one counsel, the Father working always in union with the Son...
This can also apply to the voice of His body, the Holy Church, which bears the tragedies of this life for the sake of the heavenly grace that leads her toward the eternal rewards.

She despises bodily death, as she aims toward the glory of the resurrection. What she suffers is temporary, and what she expects is eternal. She has no doubt concerning these eternal blessings. For she sees with the mind the resurrection of His body, and is greatly strengthened to have hope, and reckons that what she has seen has passed through her Head. And she hopes without doubt that it will be fulfilled in His body, that is, in her...

So may the believing people, when they suffer from opposition, when they are troubled by bitter afflictions, lift up their mind to the hope of the glory to come, and trust in the resurrection of the Redeemer, saying: "Even now I see my witness in heaven, and the fellowship of my heart on high."
Rightly He called Him "fellowship," since He has known our nature not only by creating it, but also by taking it to Himself. His knowledge was fulfilled by taking what is ours...

But this voice can apply to each one of us along with the blessed Job, for every man who aims in what he does at human praise seeks a witness on earth. But he who longs by his deeds for the good pleasure of Almighty God thinks that he has a witness in heaven.
It often happens that the good works themselves in us are reckoned sinful by rash people, but he who has a witness in heaven has no need to fear the reproaches of men.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* When the wise obtain good things, they send a part of them ahead of them, as Job said: [My witnesses in heaven] (Job 16:19). And also: [My brothers and my beloved are with God] (Job 16:20). And our Lord commands those who gain possessions to make for themselves friends in heaven out of them, and to lay up for themselves treasures there.
St. Aphrahat "My friends scorn me:

entries.section: 3. His recourse to the just God

paragraphs.text: mine eye poureth out tears unto God." [20]

His friends did not stop at opposing him, but began to defame him and conspire against him. He expects from them neither kindness nor comfort, but pours out his tears before God alone, the source of all comfort, offering Him the sacrifice of a broken and contrite heart, which He does not despise! The friends mocked his cries, so he offered his tears as a pure offering to God, in hope of relief for the weary.

* [Let my petitions come before the Lord]. For if my prayer reaches on high, my enemies perish (Ps 91:2); the righteous stands firm (Wis 5:1), the snare is broken, and the bird, set free, flies in liberty (Ps 124:7); and the persecutors bow their heads, while the persecuted rejoice (Mt 5:10-12).

* [And let mine eyes weep before him]. He said deliberately [before him], that is, before God. Job added this fittingly, for weeping before men is of no benefit at all to those who pray. For even if they adorn themselves with wise thoughts, it is madness for us to receive glory from men.

But let us pour out our tears before Him (Ps 56:8), for as much as we let our tears overflow in prayer before the Lord, the deceitful flee and are dissolved (Ps 5:6), while the King is clothed with tenderness.
For tears wash souls and bodies, and cleanse every defilement, and wholly purge every blemish, and make those who weep appear whiter than snow (Ps 51:7-9).

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem * "My friends are full of words, but mine eye poureth out tears unto God" (LXX). What does he mean by the eye but the intention of the heart? "If therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light" (Mt 6:22).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. His recourse to the just God

paragraphs.text: "That he might judge a man with God, as a son of man with his neighbor." [21]

Job knows that there is no man who can judge in his favor, but he stands before God, the searcher of hearts, who knows the thoughts and intentions; He alone can judge him and so justify him through His rich grace.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem sees that the man referred to here is the Son of Man, the Son who became incarnate for our sake (Jn 1:12; Rom 3; 1 Jn 4:2; 2 Jn 7), who sits at the right hand of the Father (Ps 110:1). He intercedes for us as equal to the Father in royal honor, and refutes the accusations of the devil who slanders us.
"When a few years are come, then I shall go the way whence I shall not return." [22]
Job felt that death was at the doors; a few years would pass, and he would enter his eternal home, and would no longer return to this world.
* [My years are numbered, and their end is coming] (Job 16:22), meaning that I do not ask this in vain, but because the end of my life has been reached, and the collapse of that life is near...!
[I am going the way of no return], of which David said: [I go the way of all the earth] (1 Kgs 2:2).

To return here, that is, below, is impossible for man. The prophet David himself testifies concerning his son who died, saying: "I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me" (2 Sam 12:23). On the other hand, since we are going on a road after which it is impossible to return here, let us hasten and prepare provision for the journey, that is, the virtues. On this road we shall neither hunger nor thirst, nor be stripped nor lose the glory of life.

Father Hesychius of Jerusalem Job realized that the Messiah would not come in his time. The life of Abbot Sisoes the Great tells how the true believer rejoices at the moments of his soul's departure from this world, even though, in his sense of weakness, he asks for a chance to remain for repentance. It was said of him that when he was about to leave the world he said: "Behold, Father Anthony is coming." After a little he murmured, saying: "Behold, the ranks of the prophets have come," then he said: "The ranks of the apostles are coming." And each time his face shone more brightly. At one moment he seemed to be speaking with someone, and those present asked him: "Who is it that speaks with you, Father?" He said: "Behold, I see the angels who have come to receive my soul. But I entreated them to give me a little time that I might repent." The elders said to him: "You have no need of repentance, Father." The old man said to them: "In truth, I do not think that I have even begun yet." Then all were convinced that he was at a very high stature of holiness and perfection. His face shone like the sun, and those present were afraid, but he declared to them: "Behold, the Lord has come, and He says: Bring me the vessel of the wilderness." And at once he gave up his spirit, and there was in the place something like lightning, and the whole house was filled with a sweet fragrance."

Since the Lord has broken the power of death and has shone upon us with the splendor of His resurrection, the believers weep, not for fear of death for themselves or for their loved ones, but rather they weep over their sins, as they weep out of longing to depart and be with the Lord Christ.
* As, according to the natural order, we weep for the dead, so it is fitting for us to weep for our salvation, in a manner that cannot be surpassed.
Let us weep with such longing and courage that everything may serve us... Let us remember salvation.
Those who lose their children and wives think of nothing but those they have lost, while we who have lost a heavenly kingdom think of anything but this.

There is no man who loses his father (or his mother or one of his relatives) who is ashamed to submit to the law of mourning, even if he is of royal descent. For he falls to the ground and weeps bitterly, and changes his garments, and of his own will does all the things that befit such a time.

This is not done as a result of training, nor out of weakness belonging to such grief, but he does all this without any difficulty... But we who grieve, not for a wife, nor for a child, but for a soul, not for another, but for our own souls, make an excuse for ourselves on the plea of poor health or of our being people of high learning...
Yet we neglect even what requires no bodily effort.

I ask: what effort do we need in order to practice contrition of heart, vigil in prayer, and reflection on our sins...? These are the things that make God merciful toward us. But we do not do such things.
St. John Chrysostom The author of the life of St. Ephrem the Syrian, ascribed to St. Gregory of Nyssa, depicts for us how he was concerned to shed tears in order to enjoy eternal salvation.
[When I began to recall the flood of his tears, I myself began to weep, for it was very difficult to pass with dry eyes through the ocean of his tears.
There was never a day or a night, or a part of the day or the night, or any moment, however short, in which his watchful eyes were not seen swimming in tears.

And as he said, at times he wept for the misery and folly of all in general, and at times he wept for certain vices. You would find him weeping and lamenting not only when he spoke of repentance, ethics and the disciplining of life, but even during the prayers of praise.]
* The soul is dead through sin. This calls for grief, weeping and tears, mourning and lamentation over the iniquity that brought it down to destruction.
Crying, weeping and lamenting bring it back to God...
God grieves over the image that was lost (because of our sins). The soul is much dearer to God than all His creation. Through sin it has become dead, and you, O sinner, do you not care...?!
Pour out tears and raise it up!
Offer God this joy; He rejoices that you are raising up your soul.
St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian * Let us have pity on ourselves, and open a way to the righteous tenderness of the Father! Let us sow in tears, that we may reap in joy!
* Tears are the flood that falls upon sins, and they cleanse the world.
St. Gregory of Nazianzus
Miserable comforters are ye all!
* Often I long to hear a word of comfort from a man.
But I have realized that they are all miserable comforters.
There is none who can enter my depths, and share my feelings, and groan with my groanings, except You, O Lover of every human soul!
They may utter sweet words with their lips, but do they have a heart wide enough to bear my weaknesses?
And even if they speak gentle words, the eyes of man criticize, whereas Your eyes behold all that is good and beautiful in me!
* Grant me not to lean on human consolations; You are my reliance, my comfort and the joy of my heart.
Even if You wound me, Your wounds carry a medicine for my healing.
With Your chastenings I feel the surpassing sweetness of Your love!
* Grant me, in the midst of my sufferings, not to be preoccupied with the looks of people or their words.
But let me look to You, O Source of all comfort!
* Let the sons of men make light of me, for in their mockery I see a useful medicine for my depths!
Let me bear all mockery, for You alone shine upon me, and scatter my darkness, O Sun of Righteousness.
* I marvel: if people are silent, I feel their neglect of me.
And if they speak, they pierce my heart with their words as with deadly arrows!
But You, in Your silence, carry me to the vision of Your glories, and in Your words, You kindle my heart with Your love!
Teach me how to be silent, and how to speak!
Let the law of Your love be the guide of my silence and my words!
* Let me carry You in my depths, and present You to my brethren, present You to them by my prayers for them, and by my words that carry the sweetness of Your love!
Let me present to them not the arrows of criticism that tears down, but the arrows of Your love, which, though they wound, heal!
* Your comforts to me are the declaration of Your presence within me!
I see You, O Crucified One, and I find the pain sweet even unto death!
I see You destroying by the Cross the power of the devil, and I realize that the opposition of the enemy of good is only for my victory.
Let him strike with all his might, for I am hidden in You.
In You I enjoy a crown of glory that does not fade!
* My enemy who bears witness against me opens for me the door of victory over him!
It is a war that does not cease, but what can the devil do to You, O my Savior?
Can darkness put out the light?
Can the antichrist usurp Your Kingdom?
What a petty enemy he is!
He is deceitful and malicious, but You are the Truth that cannot be resisted!
* In the midst of my affliction let me open my eyes and see You, and if You allow chastening, You are a Father.
And if the affliction becomes extremely severe, Your eyes have pity on me!
The devil has no authority over me!
He may distort my image and press me hard!
But You are the secret of my eternal splendor and my heavenly rest!
* The enemy of good wants to strike me on my cheek, so that I may not utter a word of witness for You.
But Your word in my mouth is a blazing fire.
The enemy will not be able to quench its flame, nor can he silence it!
* Truly the enemy of good is like a dangerous giant; he will not despair of warring against the Church as a whole, and against every member in her.
He began his war with the first man in Paradise, and he continues to wage war in all generations in various ways, and will not stop until the end of the ages.
He works with all his might through the antichrist!
He works with all deceit and cunning, seizing every opportunity to destroy us!
He turns our life into hell, so that we lose hope of our salvation!
He darkens our eyes with despair, and we think that death has taken us captive forever!
But Your death has granted us the resurrection, and Your ascension has opened the gates of heaven before us!
The devil will no longer be able to imprison us in Hades, where there is eternal darkness!
We shall no longer fear him, for You, O Redeemer, are our victory!
You are our resurrection and our crown!
* Let the enemy strike with all his might, for the earth itself cries out.
The earth will not accept to drink innocent blood, but cries out to You.
The earth could not hold You in the tomb, for You are the Heavenly One.
Let me be united with You, so that I may no longer return to the dust of the earth, but in You become heavenly, and enjoy the fellowship of the heavenly glories.
* In the midst of my sufferings I see You as a witness for me in heaven!
You bear witness for me by Your death, Your resurrection and Your ascension, for as I share Your sufferings, I enjoy the fellowship of Your glories!
* In the midst of my sufferings my tears pour forth, not before people, but before You.
For men are miserable comforters, but You cherish my tears!
* In the midst of my sufferings I await my passing over to You.
My years are few, and the end of my earthly life is coming.
I am going the way of all the earth!
But not alone, for You are with me!
And to You I go to rest forever!
My spirit is corrupt.
My days are extinguished.
Surely the graves are mine [1].

Job reached a bitter state, and he counted himself as one dead. In the previous passage he looked at his remaining life as a short journey, a few years and then he would pass from this world without return. Here, in the midst of his bitterness, he counted that his spirit had become corrupt, that the light of his life had been extinguished, and that, while on the dunghill, he had become like one who dwells in the graves.

He did not say, "Surely the grave is mine," but "the graves." It is as though the graves of his fathers, which received them, were preparing to receive him also. The graves open their doors to snatch up humanity, and it is fitting for the believer, for his part, to prepare to enter as a victor and conqueror.

* No one can go from here to there as long as God has not called him. If God is the One who bound soul and body together, man does not loose them so that they may be joined in a new way. The soul does not separate itself from the body. Job said this, not because the common enemy was threatening him with death, but because he had been struck with his sickness. This is the reason for his asking in his prayer to leave the world.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * The spirit is crushed by fear of the judgment. The more the chosen feel the final judgment drawing near, the more they are terrified in their minds with fear, as they discover themselves. When they find in themselves any carnal thought, their souls are crushed by the zeal of their repentance... They judge themselves and discipline themselves more strictly, for they await the stern Judge coming at the doors. Therefore they always look to their departure as near.
But as for the minds of the lost, they suppose that they will live here for a long time, and so they practice many evil things.
Therefore the spirit of the righteous is crushed, and the spirit of the wicked grows fat...

["My days are shortened, and the grave alone is left for me."] For he who contemplates what he will be in death is always in fear, because from now on he lives as one who lives according to what he sees, indeed truly lives as in the eyes of his Creator...

Perfect life is attained by thinking of death, where the righteous man strives to escape from the snares of sin. Therefore it is written: ["Whatsoever thou takest in hand, remember the end, and thou shalt never do amiss"] (Sir 7:40).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

One of the chief exercises in the life of the Desert Fathers, as in the life of those who are earnest about their salvation, is remembering the hour of death, or the last day of the Lord's coming, not out of fear of judgment, but in preparation to enjoy the eternal glories, and for deliverance from the fate of the wicked.
* When you approach your bed, say to it: "This very night perhaps you will be my grave, O bed, for I do not know whether this night, instead of my temporary sleep, I shall have the permanent sleep."
So, while you have two feet, hasten to work, before you are bound with that chain which, once placed, is never loosed again.
While you have two hands, stretch them toward heaven in prayer, before the arms fall from their joints, so that when you desire to draw them back you will not be able.
While you have fingers, sign yourself with the cross, before death comes, which looses the proper strength of their nerves.

While you have two eyes, fill them with tears, before the hour comes when dust covers your black garments, and your eyes are fixed in one direction with a gaze that you neither grasp nor know. No, rather fill your eyes with tears while your heart is governed by the power of discernment, before your soul is shaken by its departure from it, and leaves the heart a house abandoned by its dweller.
O wise man, do not be deceived by expecting a long life!

* When the merchant finishes his work he hurries to his house. As long as the monk (the person) has not yet completed his part in the righteous struggle, he feels bitterness when he thinks of his departure from his body. But when he perceives in himself that he has redeemed the time (Eph 5:16) and has received his earnest, he desires to see the life to come. The merchant at sea fears inwardly lest the waves rise against him and scatter the hope of his work. So the monk (the person), as long as he is in this world, is governed by fear lest a sudden storm arise against him and shatter the work in which he has striven from his youth to old age. The merchant fixes his eye on the shore, and the monk (the person) fixes his eye on the hour of his death.

St. Isaac the Syrian * There was a brother who was fervent in prayer, and while his brother was performing the service, tears overcame him and at times he forgot passages of the Psalm. The brother begged him one day to tell him what he was thinking about during the service that made him weep so bitterly. He said to him: "Forgive me, my brother, for I always meditate during the service on the Judge, and my standing before Him, for I am a guilty criminal under interrogation. And since I find no justification for myself, I stand terrified, and my mouth is shut, and a verse of the Psalm slips past me. Forgive me for troubling you; let us each perform the service alone." The brother answered: "No, father, for I live without compunction, and at least when I see you I am ashamed." And when God saw his humility, He granted him the compunction that his brother had. Let us also keep our eyes on this gift, so that we may have the same benefit as this brother.
From the sayings of the Desert Fathers

entries.section: 2. A cry for help from the Lord
