And he said, This will I do: I will pull down my barns, and build greater] (Lk 12:17-18). So this man, who was in straits with abundance of goods, said: "What shall I do?" He was in care, as though the multitude of food pressed upon him.

* "He is burned with the heat, and every woe falls upon him" [22]. After acquiring gifts of wealth, he achieves what he desired, and another disturbance comes to him. Fear and anxiety come upon him to keep safe what it cost him boundless troubles to obtain. On every side he is terrified of conspirators, and fears lest what he did to others be done to him. He fears lest he be subjected to violence by someone stronger than he. When he sees a poor man he looks at him as a thief. He fears the very things he has stored up, lest through the weakness of his inherited nature they be lost through neglect. In all these matters, because of the very fear of punishment, the wretched man suffers severely from fear of what he may suffer.
But it is a wonderful security for the heart that does not seek what is not ours, but is content with what it receives day by day.
Fr. Gregory (the Great)

* "When he reckons himself satisfied, he falls into anxiety" [22 LXX]. This means that fruit rots when it ripens. But as we have said many times, what Job's friends said was not to abase the wicked and the ungodly, but rather to shake Job's patience.

And since the wrestler bore the sorrows that had come upon him with a great soul, confident in the benefits that patience brings, he (Zophar) threatened him that the future would be worse than the past.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem *Truly, a man's life does not consist in his possessions, through the abundance he has; rather, he is counted blessed and possessed of a glorious hope who is rich toward God.
St. Cyril of Alexandria * When we gain a farthing we are filled with joy, and when we lose half a farthing we sink into sorrow.
St. Jerome When he is about to fill his belly, God shall cast the fury of his wrath upon him, and shall rain it upon him while he is eating [23].

Nothing stirs up the fury of God's wrath against a man like his wronging his brother. While he thinks that he is filling his belly by wronging his brother, the fury of divine wrath rains fire and brimstone upon him. "Upon the wicked he shall rain... fire and brimstone" (Ps 11:6).
It takes him by surprise in the moments of his enjoyment of feasts, as he takes his food. Perhaps Zophar is pointing here to the death of Job's sons and daughters while a feast was being held.

He also points here to what happened in the days of the Flood, and to the destruction that came upon Sodom and Gomorrah, as the Lord Christ says: "They did eat, they drank, they married wives, they were given in marriage, until the day that Noah entered into the ark, and the flood came, and destroyed them all. Likewise also as it was in the days of Lot; they did eat, they drank, they bought, they sold, they planted, they builded; but the same day that Lot went out of Sodom it rained fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroyed them all" (Lk 17:27-29).

* [To fill his belly, so that God casts his wrath upon him, and rains his war upon him] [23]... [The rain of God's war] is the striking of hearts that exalt themselves against Him, and the wounding of the hateful soul with the arrows of His judgment... Whereas it would have been fitting for (the covetous man) to remind himself how he coveted what was not his, and with a greater evil set it in himself to gather the things he desired. And at another time he will grieve that he will be parted from the things he gathered.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
He shall flee from the iron weapon,
and the bow of steel shall strike him through [24].

Their destruction will be certain, without any possibility of escaping it. "He shall flee from the iron weapon." Fleeing points to iniquity, for the wicked man does not think of confessing his sins in humility before God to be reconciled with Him, but all he thinks of is escaping the vengeance that pursues him, yet in vain. For if he escapes the sword, "the bow of steel shall strike him through," or a bow of tempered steel. It is as though God uses the sword for those who think that they fight against Him by their own strength, and the bow for those who think that they are able to flee from Him by their cunning. For whoever thinks that he is able to escape one punishment finds another punishment pursuing him.

* This means that He (God) will overwhelm him with sufferings... But what are these sufferings? Let us pay attention. "Let him flee by any means from the power of the sword, and let the bow of bronze wound him. And let the arrow pierce his body, let the stars be against his dwelling, and let terrors come upon him" [24-25 LXX]. Job did not fall under these blows, for God forbade the Accuser (Satan) to kill him; therefore neither iron nor bronze nor any spear could approach him from among Satan's hired soldiers. Even as much as they brought upon him... no fire was kindled against him, that is, the fire whose source is not the earth. For Satan has no authority to stir up the terror of the heavens against him.

Zophar threatened Job with these things, wishing to terrify the wrestler with fear on every side. As for Job, he did not say how or from where these things come upon him, for he was confident in his righteousness.

Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * [He will flee from iron weapons, and rush toward the bow of bronze] [24]. We must know that covetousness sometimes creeps in upon people through pride, and sometimes through fear. Therefore some aim at appearing with greater authority, and burn to obtain what belongs to others. Likewise there are people who fear lest they come to be in need of the necessities of life, and so give over their minds to covetousness to seek what belongs to others, imagining that what they have does not suffice them. Now, the expression "iron" is suited to all "necessities." For it troubles the life of the needy with wounds of sorrow. It is an expression of the need for necessities, which leads to a painful life... [The iron entered into his soul] (Ps 105:18). What then are the iron weapons but the necessities of the present life that press upon the life of the needy with harshness? Iron is destroyed by rust, but bronze is destroyed by it with greater difficulty. Therefore iron signifies the present, temporary necessities, while bronze signifies the eternal destiny.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Do you wish to build your city well? [A little with the fear of the Lord is better than a great treasure without the fear] (cf. Prov 15:16). A man's wealth must work for the salvation of his soul, not its destruction. Wealth is for salvation if one uses it well, and thus it is a snare if one does not know how to use it (Prov 13:8). For what profit is a man's money if it does not support him on his journey?
St. Ambrose It is drawn, and cometh out of the body; yea, the glittering sword cometh out of his gall:
terrors are upon him [25].

The destruction will be complete when the bow pierces him and comes out of his gall, and terrors and very violent dread come upon him, and the pains of his death are exceedingly painful. Thus death falls upon the wicked man, pouncing on him and making him taste bitterness.

* [The terrifying ones come and fall upon him] [25]. Who are those here called the terrifying ones but the evil spirits, whom pious minds must fear and avoid? It is thought that these same evil spirits each cling to particular vices. When this wicked man leaves one group of faults for a moment and begins to commit another group, then surely [the terrifying ones come and fall upon him], so that when the soul of the wicked leaves one group of evil habits, another group takes it captive. Often you see a wicked man with earthly authority stirred by tumultuous passions, and he carries out all that his anger suggests to him. And when his anger subsides, lust stirs his soul. And when lust ceases for a time, self-importance at once occupies his heart on the ground that he is violent, and in order to show others that he is fearsome he aims at making himself an object of dread... Thus it is truly said of him whose mind's vice seizes the place of another vice: "The terrifying ones come and fall upon him."
Pope Gregory (the Great)
All darkness shall be hid in his secret places:
a fire not blown shall consume him;
it shall go ill with him that is left in his tabernacle [26].

The darkness in which the wicked man wraps himself is hidden; it is a thick darkness that not a single ray of light pierces. An inward darkness that passes through to him where he thinks he is safe, hidden in a place no one can reach. Perhaps by the hiding place he means his conscience, for the wicked man suffers from the darkness that falls in his depths, to find himself in gloom and bewilderment, from which none can save him except his returning in repentance to the true light, the Giver of peace.

A destroying fire that has not been blown is kindled within him, that is, no sound of it is heard. All see the wicked man's ruin and burning without being able to know the cause. Just as Jonah saw the gourd withered, but did not see the worm that caused it to wither (Jon 4:7).

And by his saying [a fire not blown] he indicates that the destroying fire of sin has fuel that burns very quickly and needs no blowing. "All the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up" (Mal 4:1).
"It feeds on the remnant in his tent": his evil creeps into his tent, or into his family, and becomes a cause of the destruction of many of his household.

* "All darkness is hidden in his secret places" [26]... It is said that all "darkness is hidden in his secret places," because he does not display all the evils that are in him, but he must bring them all down upon his fellow creatures.

[A fire not kindled shall consume him]; these few words declare the fire of Gehenna in a most astonishing manner. For material fire, in order to be fire, needs material fuel. And to continue, it must be supplied with the wood that is heaped upon it, as we know. It does not exist unless it is kindled, and does not continue unless it is served with fuel. Contrary to this, the fire of Gehenna, while it is a fire that destroys the sons of perdition who are cast into it bodily, is not kindled by human effort, nor does it continue by wood being cast into it. But once it exists, it remains unquenchable, and needs no kindling, and its heat does not diminish... The justice of the Almighty, since it foreknew the coming events, created from the beginning of the world the fire of Gehenna, which was to begin for the punishment of the wicked, and its heat will never cease, and it needs no fuel...

It was said by the Psalmist: [Thou shalt make them as a fiery oven in the time of thine anger: the LORD shall swallow them up in his wrath, and the fire shall devour them] (Ps 21:9). Thus Holy Scripture shows that the lost are burned inwardly and outwardly. It testifies that they are devoured by fire, and at the same time become a fiery furnace; so by fire they are tormented in the body, and by sorrow they burn in the spirit.
[Being left in his tent, it will be with him in the trial], for since he placed all delight in bodily life [he dwells in the tent of the body].
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Why did (Satan) not enter the blessed Peter, James and John, or any of the rest of the apostles?
Why did he enter Judas Iscariot?
What did Satan find in him?

Satan could not approach any of those we have mentioned, because their hearts were upright and their love for Christ steadfast. In the betrayer there was room for Satan. The malignant disease, covetousness, which the blessed Paul said is the root of all evils (1 Tim 6:10), had gained mastery over him. Satan is cunning in doing evil. When he gains possession of a person's soul, he does not fight him with a common vice, but rather seeks for the person he has mastered a means by which to make him his prey.

St. Cyril the Great * Three men came to Abraham (Gen 18:1-2) in the heat of the day; but in the case of Sodom two angels came in the evening (Gen 19:1). Good things are likened to light, and evil things to evening, until the Sun of righteousness shall arise upon them (Mal 4:2). For the punishment of the wicked is night and darkness, but the righteous shall shine as the light (Prov 4:18; Mt 13:43).

Fr. Theodore, Bishop of Mopsuestia * To the others He said: "Depart from me, ye cursed" (Mt 25:41). He did not say that they are cursed by the Father, for the Father did not cast the curse upon them, but their own works do that. He did not say that the eternal fire is prepared for them alone, but "for the devil and his angels." For concerning the Kingdom, indeed, when He said: "Come... inherit the kingdom," He added, prepared for you from the foundation of the world (Mt 25:34). But concerning the fire He did not say this, but "prepared for the devil." I prepared the Kingdom for you, but the fire I did not prepare for you but for the devil and his angels; yet you cast yourselves into it. You have attributed it to yourselves.
St. John Chrysostom The heaven shall reveal his iniquity; and the earth shall rise up against him [27].

The God of heaven, who sees hidden things, declares the evils of the wicked who persist in their evil, and the earth uncovers their iniquities and takes vengeance on them. [The earth shall disclose her blood] (Isa 26:21). For heaven cannot endure iniquity, and the earth rises up against it, and the wicked find no place for themselves here or there, but settle in Gehenna.

* "The heavens reveal his iniquity, and the earth rises up against him" [27]. What do we understand by the heavens but the righteous, and by the earth the sinners? So in the Lord's Prayer it is prayed: [Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven], to mean that the will of our Creator, as it is fulfilled in the righteous, may it be fulfilled in all sinners also. Moreover it is said of the righteous: [The heavens declare the glory of God] (Ps 19:1). And to man, when he sinned, the sentence was declared: [Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return]. And so when the wicked man is dragged to the dreadful judgment, it is said: "The heavens reveal his iniquity, and the earth rises up against him," for the man who here had no pity on the good or the wicked, at his dreadful interrogation, the life of the righteous and of sinners bears witness against him...

But it is also possible that "the earth" signifies not the sinful, condemned life, but those who are occupied with earthly matters, and through almsgiving and with tears obtain eternal life. Of these the Psalmist speaks when it was announced that the Lord is coming for judgment: "He shall call to the heavens from above, and to the earth, that he may judge his people" (Ps 50:4). For He calls the heavens from above, when those leave all that they have and hold fast to the inclination toward the heavenly life, they are called to sit with Him in judgment, and to come with Him as judges...

Nothing that the wicked man has done will be hidden from the insight of the time of judgment, though truly many deeds are now hidden, through deceit, from his fellow creatures; in the day of judgment they will appear in the light.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

If the heavens declare the iniquity of the wicked, and the earth exposes and opposes him, then it is fitting for the Church to ask the faithful to flee from the wicked who are determined on evil, and not from sinners who need someone to witness before them to the Gospel of forgiveness.

St. Cyprian emphasizes not only the severe divine punishments that come upon the wicked who oppose the truth, but also demands that God's children separate themselves from them so that God's wrath may not come upon them. [We find this plainly in the Book of Numbers, when Korah, Dathan and Abiram claimed the right to offer sacrifices in opposition to Aaron the priest. For the Lord teaches through Moses that the people are bound to separate from them lest they be joined to the same iniquity of the guilty and defile themselves with the same crime. "And he spake unto the congregation, saying, Depart, I pray you, from the tents of these wicked men, and touch nothing of theirs, lest ye be consumed in all their sins" (Num 16:26).]
* Do what you can to remove the wicked person, for as soon as he goes out Christ will dwell in you.
Origen * You despise gold; another loves it.
You scorn wealth; he runs after it with eagerness.
You love quietness, weakness and a hidden, private life, but he finds pleasure in speaking shamelessly in public squares, as in the streets and public places...

Do not be under one roof with him. Do not rely on your former chastity. You are no holier than David nor wiser than Solomon... If in your priestly work you are obliged to visit a widow or a virgin, do not enter the house alone. Do not let your companions think lightly of you... Do not sit alone with a woman in secret without a witness with you. If she wishes to disclose some private and secret matter, she has a nurse or a housekeeper or a virgin or a maiden or a wife. She cannot be without friends other than you, so that she must pour out her private secrets to you.
St. Jerome The increase of his house shall depart, and his goods shall flow away in the day of his wrath [28].
His offspring, which is the increase of his house, will be uprooted, as death comes upon them untimely, or they are forced to flee from their land and so are scattered and uprooted.
As wealth flows to the wicked man swiftly through injustice and deceit, so it is also dissipated with the same swiftness when divine wrath comes upon him.

* When the wrath of the Judge is declared, (the wicked man) is handed over to the fires of wrath, and is removed from the sight of (the Judge). For he who in life would not raise his mind to the heavenly things, since his sins drag him downward, will fall from before the face of the Judge into the depths of punishment. Now the Judge sees and bears with the sinner in his sins, because it is the day of gentleness, not the day of wrath, for He waits expectantly for everyone's conversion. Now is the day of gentleness, and while the hypocrite remains motionless, not stirred, practicing many evils and not disciplined by scourges, he will be driven out on the day of wrath, when he is carried to the punishment of vengeance; he is cut off from the face of the eternal Judge.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
This is the portion of a wicked man from God, and the heritage appointed unto him by God [29].
What the wicked man gathers for himself is not the wealth he acquired for a time, but the wrath that comes upon him. This is his permanent portion, and his eternal inheritance in the fire of Gehenna.

This is Zophar's speech, and it carried something of the truth, but he was mistaken in thinking that all this must come upon every wicked man while he is in this world, and that whoever has affliction come upon him in this life, that is a sign of the evil of the one who has fallen under it.

Zophar gave a sound interpretation of the working of evil in the life of the wicked man, but he erred in applying this doctrine, and he did not present the thought purely, but it was tainted with an evil inclination toward Job and an attempt to affirm that he is a hypocrite.
Truly evil is terrifying and sin is exceedingly sinful, but it is not for us to judge and condemn others according to our human outlook.

* If, when he was in this life, he had been careful to act uprightly, his portion would have been fellowship with the Lord in the Kingdom of Heaven. But since he chose to submit to evil lusts, his portion from the Lord is to be found in torment, since he did not seek to obtain fellowship in the grace of this Lord...
Now the saints do not desire to obtain a portion from the Lord, but to obtain the Lord Himself as their portion. For this the prophet prays, saying: "God is my portion for ever" (Ps 73:26).

But the wicked man, since he did not strive for the Lord Himself to be his portion, finds fire his portion, not the Lord. And being removed from the face of God, because he did not seek to find joy in Him, he is tormented, being unworthy of God.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Those who consent to iniquity will have no portion among the immortals.

St. Anthony the Great * Let us see next what God commands us to do, for He says: "Give glory to the LORD your God, before he cause darkness, and before your feet stumble upon the dark mountains, and, while ye look for light" (Jer 13:16). For He wants whoever gives the Lord glory to give Him glory while the light exists, because the glory of the Lord cannot be proclaimed when darkness comes. When then does darkness come, and when does it not? [Work while the light is in you](ح). For the light is in fact in you, as long as you carry within you the Lord Christ, who said of Himself: "I am the light of the world." And as long as this light is in you, give glory to the Lord; but know that darkness can come, so you must not wait for this darkness to fall, but give glory to the Lord before its coming.

* Perhaps we can clearly understand this matter if we use the words of the Lord Christ: [Work while it is day. Night comes when no one can work](ط); by day He means our present time, and by darkness and night, the end of the world and its passing away because of the punishment of the wicked. And Amos the prophet says: "Woe unto you that desire the day of the LORD! to what end is it for you? the day of the LORD is darkness, and not light" (Amos 5:18). If you know how great the sorrow and misery will be at the destruction of the world, grief will strike nearly most of the human race, who are punished for their sins, and then you will know that the atmosphere will become so dark and gloomy that no one will be able to glorify God, because even the righteous God has commanded, saying: [Go, my people, enter into your house, and shut your door upon you; hide for a little or for much, until the heat of my wrath is ended](ي).
* As what God has prepared for those who love Him surpasses the mind, so also the torments He has prepared for the wicked surpass the mind.

* Each one of us brings upon himself punishment for sin, the size of the punishment according to the kind and nature of the transgression... The debt collector comes to complete his work, and I resist him. I know that if I am not in debt at all, he has no authority over me. If I have a debt, the debt collector will send me to prison.
Origen
Your voice cuts through the flame of my evils!
*My soul groans within me:
Who can quench the flame of my evils, and who will pour the waters of Your righteousness within me, Your sweet voice!
* Since the fall of Adam we have learned that the tree of evil must be uprooted, that the tree of Your righteousness may be planted in us.
Let the temple of the devil with its abominations be uprooted, that by Your Holy Spirit You may establish in us Your holy temple.
Cut off, destroy and pull down what in me is not Yours, and plant and establish what is Yours, that I may become Your holy garden and Your holy temple.
* Pull down, O Lord, every strange leprous building, let its stones be taken down and cast out.
Let no defiled stone remain within me, for I am Your holy city.
Remove from my heart every thorn and plant in me Your garden, that I may become Your vineyard, exceedingly beloved to You.
I offer You of what is Yours, of the fruit of Your Holy Spirit.
That You may call Your heavenly friends, saying:
"Eat, O friends; drink, yea, drink abundantly, O beloved" (Song 5:1).
Come, O Lord Jesus, and dwell in my depths, where Your joyful garden is, and the temple of Your holiness!
*I know that the enemy of good offers pleasures and delights, but they are full of poison.
The joys of the ruler of this world will not last!
The sufferings we receive with thanksgiving from Your hands are sweeter than all the delights of the world!
*My sins crush me! At times in pride I do not care what I do, and at others in discouragement, so that despair reigns over my whole being.
I know that my sins have created enmity with Your word and Your commandment.
But Your word in the sweetness of its love disciplines, not to destroy me, but to bring me back to You, that I may enjoy Your salvation!
* My evils have shattered all goodness in me, and their defiled odor has spread within me!
I live as in a dream; all the delights my evils offer me pass away; I awake to find myself having gathered wind, and having clung to a shadow and a phantom!
My evils take my peace from me, for I have no peace except in Your divine embrace.
My evils have corrupted my soul, more than the worms do to my body.
* Why do I hoard my evils like a precious treasure, why do I hide them as one who has pity on them?
When they are the cause of my eternal destruction?
They pour out their poisons in my bowels, and store up for me eternal bitterness!
* My evils have become deadly food for me, instead of enjoying the heavenly manna, Your Body and Blood, which grant eternal life.
My evils have taken from me the sweetness of the true life.
Let me return to You, O Forgiver of sins, and enjoy You, for You are the Life.
You bring me back, not to the Garden of Eden nor to the Promised Land, but to the divine embrace.
That I may be satisfied with the sweetness of Your love, and rejoice in unity with the heavenly ones!
* You are all love. You desire the salvation of all, but it is my evils that condemn me!
You are greater than every evil.
You grant me Your righteousness, that I may live with You. I live to You and with You.
I meet You on the clouds, and enjoy the glory You prepared for me from the foundation of the world.

entries.section: 1. A gentle address to his friends

paragraphs.text: 1 But Job answered and said, 2 Hear diligently my speech, and let this be your consolations. 3 Suffer me that I may speak; and after that I have spoken, mock on. 4 As for me, is my complaint to man? and if it were so, why should not my spirit be troubled? 5 Mark me, and be astonished, and lay your hand upon your mouth.
And Job said: [1]

entries.section: 1. A gentle address to his friends

paragraphs.text: Hear diligently my speech, and let this be your consolations [2].

Job begs his friends to listen to him in a spirit of love, and to set their minds on understanding his intentions instead of judging him hastily. He now speaks in the language of friendship and calm, considering that their consolation of him in the midst of his sufferings is their listening to him with a good spirit. Perhaps he also means that as they listen to him thus, he finds rest, and so they are comforted, and by his consolation they are comforted and find rest. As though their listening had a double benefit, for him and for them.

Truly, listening to the words of the suffering benefits both sides. On one side the sufferer feels the tenderness of his brethren and their sharing with him, even if only by listening. On the other side, when the sufferer finds rest, his brethren are comforted by his rest, at least to certain degrees.

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the suffering Church, in the person of Job, calls the heretics and the people of the world to listen to her words, for she is able, through her crucified Christ, to offer them, through sufferings borne with thanksgiving, surpassing divine consolations. St. Paul directs the eyes of the suffering to the cross of the Lord of glory Jesus, not only that they may be filled with consolation, but that they may become a source of consolation to others. He says: "Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God" (2 Cor 1:4), and also: "As ye are partakers of the sufferings, so shall ye be also of the consolation" (2 Cor 1:7).

The suffering Church imitates our crucified Christ, for having suffered, being tempted, He is able to succour them that are tempted (Heb 2:18). And as we abide in Him we enjoy the fellowship of His sufferings, and are crucified with Him, that we may become through Him a source of unceasing consolations.
* Paul rejoices in his sufferings, seeing the wonderful fruits that sufferings bring about in the people, such as the Christians of Corinth.

entries.section: 1. A gentle address to his friends

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom Suffer me that I may speak; and after that I have spoken, mock on! [3]

He asked them not to interrupt him in his speech and to bear with his words; then, if they wish, let them mock him as they please. He says this hoping that their listening with a sincere intention will make them receive his words and be convinced by his arguments, and so change their tone.

What occupied Job's mind was not his friends' mockery of him, but that they should listen to him and bear with his words for their salvation, edification and consolation. So also the Church is not occupied with her temporal honor or with justifying herself, but what occupies her is the salvation of every soul, even of her opponents and persecutors. For love does not seek its own, but what belongs to others.

* It is clear that when someone counsels another and at the same time suffers more than the one he rebukes, he does this not to cause grief to the other, but to offer him deep love. Whereas he who reproves another without this feeling in fact tramples with his feet on his brother's feelings.

Fr. Ambrosiaster * Here (2 Cor 1:4) Paul shows that he suffers no less than those who sinned, but more than they. It is very hard for him to bear the pain of the error of the Corinthians that has overtaken him.
St. John Chrysostom * The mark of the Church, like her Bridegroom, is true, practical love, whereby she desires, if possible, that the whole world enjoy fellowship in eternal glory.

The mockery of people cannot crush the believer or harm the mockers themselves; yet in a spirit of humility Job speaks, asking them to bear with him, that he may win them for God, and they turn back from harming themselves.

The Psalmist bore the mockery of the proud, which could not shake his depths so that he turned aside from the law of God, for he says: "The proud have had me greatly in derision: yet have I not declined from thy law" (Ps 119:51). Wisdom cries out saying: "How long, ye simple ones, will ye love simplicity? and the scorners delight in their scorning, and fools hate knowledge?" (Prov 1:22). So she joined the foolish with the scorners and the fools in one class, since all of them acquire destruction for themselves. And the wise man affirms: "If thou be wise, thou shalt be wise for thyself: but if thou scornest, thou alone shalt bear it" (Prov 9:12).

And it is wonderful that in the midst of their rebellion against him he speaks in a spirit of meekness and humility, begging them to bear with his words; for his part, he will accept every mockery directed at him, but for the benefit of both sides he asks them to keep calm.

*As though he says: "Consider me wicked. But I have gained nothing from these remarks, and I know that you mock me. In any case, I do not give in." He says: "Why? Does a man mock me?" This means that no man can rebuke me, for I am not wrestling with a man!

St. John Chrysostom Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that Job's begging his friends to bear with his words is because when he speaks he utters what is for his benefit as well as theirs, if they are willing. He does not speak from the teacher's chair, but from the midst of the dunghill, perhaps to find benefit for himself while he speaks in a quiet spirit in an atmosphere of calm!

*When the righteous speak, they observe two things in their speech: that it be for their own benefit and that of their hearers, or for their own alone if it cannot be for the benefit of the hearers. When the good things they utter are heard with a good aim, they and their hearers benefit by them; but if their hearers mock them, they themselves benefit because they have avoided the sin of silence (in the face of error)... And so if his friends wish to be taught, let them listen, and if they are ready to mock, let them bear what is said, for teaching offered in humility to a proud mind has a grave and heavy weight.

* He says: [I ask you], showing how he speaks with humility, for he entreats persons whom pride swallows up against him, in order to bring them back to think on the teaching of the saving truth. The saints who are in the fold of the catholic Church are ready not only to teach what is true, but also to bear what is practiced against them, and they do not fear being mocked.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Humility draws God's grace to the soul... and this frees it from these two grave pains (anger at others or the anger of others at us), for what is graver than to be angry with your brother or to anger him?! But what do I say: does humility free the soul from these two pains only? No, it frees it also from every pain (passion) and every temptation.
When St. Anthony saw the snares of Satan spread, he sighed and asked God, saying: "Who can escape them?" And God answered him: "The humble escape them... indeed they cannot even approach him."

Do you see the power of this virtue?! Truly there is nothing greater than humility, for there is nothing that can overcome it. For if some sorrows come upon a humble person, at once he blames himself that he deserves them, and does not blame others or rebuke them. And so he bears all that may surround him with complete calm, without being troubled or grieved. Thus he is not angry with anyone and angers no one.

Fr. Dorotheus If Job was not concerned that they mock him, saying: "and after I have spoken, mock on," the Apostle Paul saw his Master accept mockery and derision with joy for the salvation of the world (Lk 23:35; Heb 13:13). As he also says of Moses the prophet: "By faith Moses, when he was come to years, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter... Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt" (Heb 11:24, 26). And he speaks of the apostles: "as it were appointed to death: for we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men" (1 Cor 4:9). "Being defamed, we intreat: we are made as the filth of the world, and are the offscouring of all things unto this day" (1 Cor 4:13).
* Christ commands us to bear insults with meekness, that we may grow in virtue and put our opponents to shame (Mt 5:10-12). This is accomplished not by rebuking them but by silence.

* Paul says that the main point is not that he and his fellow apostles suffer, for this is common to all. But what is more in the apostles is that they suffer without despair or anger, but on the contrary they are filled with joy, and thereby affirm that the evils that come upon them turn to good.
St. John Chrysostom * Those who love Christ are not fools as the world thinks them (1 Cor 4:10).
Fr. Ambrosiaster As for me, is my complaint to man?

entries.section: 1. A gentle address to his friends

paragraphs.text: and if it were so, why should not my spirit be troubled? [4]

He assures them that he does not present his complaint to a man, because this is of no avail. Rather he presents his complaint to God, and to Him he appeals the judgment. He is the Judge and Arbiter, the searcher of hearts and reins, before whom every human being stands on an equal footing, who listens to all and cares for all.

He assures them that if his complaint were presented to a man, his spirit within him would be troubled, for a man may not care about his brother, and not perceive what is in his heart and intention, and so pass an unjust judgment. But God is longsuffering and hears man and deals with him tenderly. So the believer lifts his complaint to God, not to take vengeance on his opponents, but to please God and not men. David the prophet says: "Let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight, O LORD, my strength, and my redeemer" (Ps 19:14). And the Apostle Paul says: "For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Gal 1:10).

* "For do I now persuade men, or God...? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Gal 1:10)... Let us not think that the Apostle teaches us, by following his example, to make light of the judgments of others... But if it happens that we can please both others and God, let us please others... But by saying "now," he has included it here particularly to show that men are pleased or not pleased according to circumstances (and not according to the truth).
St. Jerome * When someone pleases others for the sake of the truth, it is the truth that is pleased, not the one who proclaimed it.

St. Augustine Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that in his rebuke of his friends, that the dialogue with them grieved his heart, so that his spirit was troubled, is a tacit confession of his human weakness. For whoever fixes his eyes on God, grief cannot creep into his heart, nor distress into his spirit. For God, the source of joy, lifts the heart above sorrows whatever their source, and grants the spirit spaciousness.

*He who seeks to please God has no ground for grief in man's displeasure with him. If, in pleasing man, he does not please God, or thinks that he does not please both God and man together, grief does not come upon him, because he has confirmed that he is a stranger to the loftiness of wisdom. Now the blessed Job confesses that he did not please God in the midst of his blows, and therefore his mind returned to grief.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 1. A gentle address to his friends

paragraphs.text: Mark me, and be astonished, and lay your hand upon your mouth [5].

Whenever Job thought about his case he stood in amazement and trembling. Whenever he recalled the events that followed one another with unnatural swiftness, and the blows that came upon him from every side, trembling overtook him. He is bewildered, unable to explain what has befallen him.

*Consider what I do, and marvel at the blows I suffer. After that he says: [Put your finger on your mouth]. As though he says plainly: Since you know the good things that I practice, and see the sufferings under which I fall, take care not to sin with words because of my blows, but fear for your own wounds... Carefulness befits the fingers. Therefore it was said by the Psalmist: [Blessed be the Lord my God, who teacheth my hands to war, and my fingers to fight] (Ps 144:1). By the hands he points to work, and by the fingers to prudence.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

The Church asks the people of the world to look intently at her, and not to judge her hastily, but it behooves them to think with deliberation and prudence. They see behind the Church's severe distress and the persecutions poured upon her the surpassing peace of God that fills her being, God's wonderful plan toward her, and God's work through her sufferings to fulfil her mission and her witness to His joyful Gospel. The Church asks those outside to put their hands on their mouths in amazement before the astonishing truth: God's surpassing work in His suffering Church.

* Paul says: since he is held captive by these wounds, [I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus] (cf. Gal 6:17). He willingly submitted to his weaknesses in all these troubles, where the power of Christ is made perfect in virtue (cf. 2 Cor 4:10; 12:9).
St. Gregory of Nyssa * Beautiful are Paul's chains!

* He suffered for his enemies. This is the sweet-smelling offering, the acceptable sacrifice. And if you suffer for your enemies as a sweet-smelling offering, you become an acceptable sacrifice, even if you die. This is what he means by saying, be ye followers of God (Eph 5:1).

St. John Chrysostom The Fathers expanded greatly on the work of bearing sufferings, insults and mockery with joy, not only in the life of the sufferer but also in the life of the mockers themselves. St. John Chrysostom applied this to the relation of a man to his wife when she causes him sufferings, saying: [Even if it is necessary to give your life for her, do not refuse. And if it is necessary that countless troubles come upon you for her sake, and you endure all kinds of pains and troubles, do not refuse. For even if you bear all this, you have still not done what Christ did for the Church... And if you see her looking at you with disdain, constantly complaining and despising you, you can win her by your great love and tenderness toward her.]

6 Even when I remember I am afraid, and trembling taketh hold on my flesh. 7 Wherefore do the wicked live, become old, yea, are mighty in power? 8 Their seed is established in their sight with them, and their offspring before their eyes. 9 Their houses are safe from fear, neither is the rod of God upon them. 10 Their bull gendereth, and faileth not; their cow calveth, and casteth not her calf. 11 They send forth their little ones like a flock, and their children dance. 12 They take the timbrel and harp, and rejoice at the sound of the organ. 13 They spend their days in wealth, and in a moment go down to the grave.
Even when I remember I am afraid, and trembling taketh hold on my flesh (my body was seized with trembling) [6].
Wherefore do the wicked live, become old,
yea, are mighty in power [7].

The three friends expatiated on the calamities and misery that befall the wicked, but Job is amazed, and his body is seized with trembling, at what he sometimes sees of the wicked enjoying good things until they reach old age, and at the strength and authority they obtain while they are overbearing and harsh toward others.

Job does not deny that this happens to the wicked at times. They live in peace (1 Sam 25:6), and their life even extends to old age, and they have sons and grandsons, and gather huge fortunes, so that we hear in the Book of Isaiah, "the sinner being an hundred years old shall be accursed" (Isa 65:20). Not only may their lives extend to old age, but they are "mighty in power," that is, they rise to positions of authority and leadership.

Some of the wicked misunderstand God's longsuffering toward them, and Holy Scripture warns us of this: "Say not, I have sinned, and what harm hath happened unto me? for the Lord is longsuffering" (Sir 5:4). "Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?" (Rom 2:4).

* If we do not fall under discipline and continue in our same conduct, let us use the Apostle's word that enchants us: "The goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance; but after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath" (Rom 2:4-5).

* "Not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance; but after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath" (Rom 2:4-5). Your heart has hardened like Pharaoh's heart, because your punishment has been postponed and you were not struck at once! The ten plagues were sent upon Pharaoh not as from an angry God but as from a father who warns, and the day of tenderness toward him was prolonged until he turned back from his repentance (after each plague). But punishment came upon him when he followed the people into the wilderness, and in his zeal entered the sea itself after them. This was the way by which he learned the lesson that he ought to have feared God, whom even the elements of nature obey.

St. Jerome St. Jerome uses this phrase (Rom 2:4) in reply to the followers of Pelagius to affirm God's holiness and His care for the freedom of the human will; for although God knows beforehand of the wicked man who despises His longsuffering and kindness, yet He offers him great tenderness and mercy in a longsuffering that gives him the opportunity to repent; so when the wicked man despises this, the cause is not God's foreknowledge of his contempt, but the wicked man's persistence in his wickedness.

St. Ambrose asks us not to judge people according to the good things offered them from God's mercies, who truly cares for all; for this does not mean that God does not care about their conduct, or that He does not know what they do in secret, or does not perceive what is in their consciences, but what it affirms is that with the abundance of good things granted to the wicked, they are nevertheless wretched and do not know happiness.
Their seed is established in their sight with them, and their offspring before their eyes [8].
Job points to some sinners who enjoy seeing their offspring multiply.

Often believers, and even unbelievers, are occupied with the question: Why does God allow the wicked health, long life and wealth, and also the enjoyment of power and positions of leadership? And this while they enjoy seeing their offspring share with them all these temporal blessings. For man, because of the shortness of his life, thinks that God's justice must be fulfilled in this world, and finds it hard to wait for the great day of the Lord to see divine justice fulfilled. Moreover, it is hard for the human mind to accept God's surpassing longsuffering, who waits for the wicked to turn from their wickedness and return to the divine embrace.

*Job makes this declaration to his friends: [If I suffer in this way because of my sins, why do the wicked live? They grow old in wealth also, their offspring according to their pleasure, their seed before their eyes, their houses in prosperity, no fear is in them, the rod of God does not fall upon them].
St. Ambrose Their houses are safe from fear, neither is the rod of God upon them [9].

Although Zophar pointed to the constant fears of sinners and their perpetual disquiet, Job points to some sinners who have houses safe from dangers and fears, and upon whom God does not stretch out His rod.

Since the hearts of the wicked are occupied with houses made of clay and stones, and the furnishings they hold, and the treasures stored in them, the Lord gives them the desire of their hearts, granting them temporal, transient peace, and no one approaches their possessions and treasures. But what occupies the righteous is the heavenly house and the dwellings above, and the Lord also gives them the desire of their hearts. The former receive an abundance of temporal blessings and passing security, while the latter receive an eternal inheritance that does not corrupt or perish, and an immortal heavenly glory. They rejoice, as they hear the divine voice: "I go to prepare a place for you. And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and receive you unto myself; that where I am, there ye may be also" (Jn 14:2-3). Therefore the Psalmist says: "He (the Lord) shall give thee the desires of thine heart" (Ps 37:4). "Thou hast given him his heart's desire, and hast not withholden the request of his lips. Selah" (Ps 21:2).
Their bull gendereth, and faileth not; their cow calveth, and casteth not her calf [10].

Some sinners are rich and their possessions increase, so that even their bulls succeed in impregnating cows so that they conceive and bear abundantly, and their animals multiply and do not die quickly of sudden diseases.

The desire of the wicked man's heart is that his animals bear many, and that there be not one miscarriage among them. But the desire of the hearts of God's children is to enjoy many children in the Lord, and that none among them be lost. They look for the day of the Lord to sing: "Behold, I and the children whom the LORD hath given me" (Isa 8:18).

Among God's children there is no barren one, but all bear twins, that is, give birth to many. For in the Apostle Peter's address on the day of Pentecost about three thousand joined the Church, who received the faith, offered repentance, and enjoyed new birth through Baptism. In one day the Apostle Peter had thousands of children whom he begot by the Gospel of Christ. And what shall we say of the Apostle Paul, who almost every day brought many into the fold of faith through his preaching with a fiery, burning heart. He does not cease to beget even in the midst of chains, so that he says of the runaway slave, the thief Onesimus: "whom I have begotten in my bonds" (Phlm 10).
If animals in Holy Scripture often point to the body, then what occupies the people of the world is bodily matters, not spiritual.

The wicked man is occupied with the birth of animals, while the true believer is occupied with the spiritual birth of human beings that they may become children of the holy God, even if the cost be chains and prison or death.
* Onesimus deserved great honor, for he was born in the very struggles of Paul, in affliction for the sake of Christ.

* Observe the burning of Paul's heart. He preached the Gospel while bound and under the lash. Oh, how blessed are the chains, how they worked with great effort in that night, and how they begot children! Truly he says of them: [I have begotten them in my bonds](أ).
Observe how Paul is glorified! He has come to have children through this way who are counted in great renown.
O the inexpressible glory of these chains, for they bestow splendor not only on those he begot, but also on those who were begotten through him in these circumstances.
St. John Chrysostom They send forth their little ones like a flock, and their children dance [11].
They take the timbrel and harp, and rejoice at the sound of the organ [12].

They live, they and their sons; the number of little children increases until they go among their neighbors like countless sheep, and the children spend their time in dancing and merriment. The elders play on musical instruments and the little ones dance. The fathers are not concerned with their children's walking in the way of the Lord, as Abraham commanded his children (Gen 18:19), nor do they urge them to worship God, but all that concerns them is amusement, revelry and the enjoyment of temporal pleasures.

St. John Chrysostom often warned parents against neglect in the upbringing of their children, showing how grave this sin is, which he reckons one of the extremely grave sins, so that he did not hesitate to call it child-murder.

* The corruption of children does not come from nothing, but from the madness that seizes fathers regarding earthly concerns. Concern for earthly things alone, and counting everything else of no value, drives them involuntarily to neglect the souls of their children. I say, these fathers (and let no one think that these words arise in me from anger) are worse than murderers of children. The first separates the body from the soul, but the other casts both together into the fires of Gehenna. Death is inevitable according to the natural order, but the second fate parents could avoid if the parents' neglect did not lead to it. Bodily death can end in a moment by the resurrection when it comes, but there is no reward awaiting the lost soul. It does not enjoy the resurrection, but suffers eternal pains. This means that it is not unjust to call these fathers worse than murderers of children. It is not as cruel to sharpen a sword and hold it in the right hand to plunge it into a child's heart as it is to destroy and humiliate the soul, for there is nothing equal to the soul.

St. John Chrysostom The wicked think that they enjoy life because of the multitude of their children, without caring about their conduct and inner life and enjoyment of eternal glory. But the righteous feel that they, with their families, are surrounded by the saints like a light heavenly cloud, having fellowship with the Fathers, prophets, apostles, martyrs and all believers, whether those who have departed or their contemporaries, and even having fellowship with the heavenly orders. Their life is an unceasing heavenly feast and a joyful festival on a surpassing level! Their hearts and thoughts become strings of spiritual harps, upon which the Holy Spirit of God plays, so that heaven rejoices, and the heavenly ones rejoice with songs of spiritual joy.
They spend their days in wealth,
and in a moment go down to the grave [13].
With all this they are prosperous, spending their days in the ease of life; poverty has no place among them.

As for the fruit of their wickedness, in a moment they go down to the grave, without warning. Perhaps he means that at times in their death they do not suffer from incurable diseases and pains, but in a moment they die and go down to the tomb. As the Psalmist says: "For yet a little while, and the wicked shall not be: yea, thou shalt diligently consider his place, and it shall not be" (Ps 37:10). As the wise man says: "As the whirlwind passeth, so is the wicked no more: but the righteous is an everlasting foundation" (Prov 10:25).

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the speech here does not necessarily mean the falling of the wicked in a moment, and their collapse, and the loss of their temporal goods, but it may mean that what they enjoy in this world, however long their life, they enjoy as for a moment, where the whole of life passes in a moment, and they find themselves before the Judge, having prepared for themselves the way of Hades or eternal Gehenna.

*Yes, blessed one, you have described their delights at length. How do you now declare that in a moment they go down to the grave, except because all this long time of their present life is known to be but a moment when it reaches its end.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. The wicked's misuse of good things

paragraphs.text: 14 Therefore they say unto God, Depart from us; for we desire not the knowledge of thy ways. 15 What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? and what profit should we have, if we pray unto him? 16 Lo, their good is not in their hand: the counsel of the wicked is far from me.
Therefore they say unto God, Depart from us;
for we desire not the knowledge of thy ways [14].

The wicked misuse all that has been given them of wealth, authority or success, and it reaches the point of their challenging God Himself and rejecting the commandment. They are terrified at the presence of God. "They say to God: Depart from us." They do not wish to trouble themselves with being under His eyes, and do not want fear of Him to turn them aside from their thinking. They feel that they have no need of Him, and reject His knowledge in which they find no pleasure, for His knowledge rebukes them for their rebellion, and as the Lord Christ says: "And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil. For every one that doeth evil hateth the light, neither cometh to the light, lest his deeds should be reproved" (Jn 3:19-20). And on the day of the Lord, the Lord gives them the desire of their hearts, saying to them: [Depart from me... for I know you not] (Mt 25:41). For whoever cannot bear to see God by faith here in this world will not be able to bear seeing Him on the day of judgment. [They shall say to the mountains, Fall on us; and to the hills, Cover us from the face of him that sitteth on the throne] (Hos 10:8; Lk 23:30). "They shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him" (Zech 12:10).

The whole being of the true believer rejoices at seeing the One he longed to meet face to face (1 Cor 13:12), but the wicked man cannot bear to stay before God, but his works bring him out to the outer darkness.

The wicked are not pleased with the knowledge of God's ways, and God is not pleased with the ways of the wicked. For darkness cannot endure light, and light takes no pleasure in darkness. As the Apostle Paul says: "For what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?" (2 Cor 6:14)

* "They say to God: Depart from us!" Even fools do not dare to say this in words, and yet all the wicked say to God by their conduct, not by their words: "Depart from us." For those who practice works that God the Almighty forbids, what do they do but shut themselves against the Almighty? As thinking on His commandments is God's entering into man, so resisting His commandments is keeping God from dwelling in the heart...
[For we desire not the knowledge of thy ways], thus it is: they do not care to seek His knowledge.

The Truth says: [And that servant, which knew his lord's will, and prepared not himself, neither did according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes. But he that knew not, and did commit things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes] (Lk 12:47-48). Some choose not to know what they ought to do, and think they will be beaten less if they are ignorant of what they ought to do.

But not to know something is one thing, and for a man to choose not to know is another thing. For some wish to know but are unable; these do not know. But he who turns his ear away from the voice of truth lest he know, such a one is not in ignorance but is a despiser.

Now God's "way" is peace, God's way is humility, God's way is longsuffering. But the wicked care for none of this, and say: "We desire not the knowledge of thy ways." They exalt themselves in pride in this life. They are swallowed up in honors, that they may possess them, for they covet them. They ignore God's ways in the thoughts of their hearts.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* He who sits in darkness at night does not run after the light of the sun as long as he does not see it. But when dawn comes and the splendor of the sun begins to shine upon him, at once he follows its light.

St. John Chrysostom * "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face" (1 Cor 13:12). This is what the angels, who are called our angels, actually see. They are our angels in the sense that as soon as we are delivered from the power of darkness, we receive the earnest of the Spirit and are translated into the kingdom of Christ, and begin to be related to the angels.

entries.section: 3. The wicked's misuse of good things

paragraphs.text: St. Augustine What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? and what profit should we have, if we pray unto him? [15].

With unseemly boldness they protest against Him saying: "What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? and what profit should we have, if we pray unto him?" They imitate Pharaoh who said: "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice?" (Ex 5:2) They see in God an unknown personage to whom some ascribe power though in their view he is of no use, so they do not want him to have anything to do with them, nor do they want anything to do with him.

They look at worship as a duty hard to bear, or as a kind of grievous servitude, as they ask: "that we should serve him?" They see themselves as strong, mighty masters who do not accept submission to God: "Wherefore say my people, We are lords; we will come no more unto thee?" (Jer 2:31).

They say: "It is vain to serve God: and what profit is it that we have kept his ordinance..." (Mal 3:13-14), so there is no need to resort to God, for prayer in their view is of no use, but is a waste of time and energy.

The wicked may perceive in their minds God's power, and know the possibility of His working in the lives of men, but through their enjoyment of bodily pleasures and their preoccupation with the delights of the world they quiet their consciences by claiming that God ignores mankind and does not perceive their true needs, so that He appears as one in weakness and powerless to support them. Moreover, time is precious to them for gathering wealth and obtaining temporal honors, the object of their love. All worship of God, in their view, is a waste of time. And they murmur because God often postpones answering their requests until He grants them what, according to His divine mind, they are to possess, He who is the Creator of all gifts and good things.

* When man's mind turns miserably outward, he is immersed in the pleasures of bodily things, and does not return to his depths, nor can he think of the Invisible One... So it is written: "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God" (Ps 14:1; 53:1)...

It often happens that people make it their aim to serve their fellow creatures whom they see with the bodily eye rather than to serve God whom they do not see. For in all they do they reach out as far as their eyes reach, and since they cannot reach God with their eyes, they either make light of rendering allegiance to Him, or if they begin to do so they are filled with anxiety...

But when what is visible is withdrawn from before them... the eyes of the body are indeed open but they cannot see or perceive... The sense of patience departs from them, because the One who dwelt in them has left them, and the house of the body remained empty. The invisible spirit that was accustomed to see through the windows of the body has departed.

Therefore the invisible things are better than the visible. It befits all the carnal to come to a decision for themselves, and by the ladder of contemplation to ascend to God. He is God in that He remains invisible, and the Most High continues where He cannot be comprehended. But there are some who do not doubt that God exists and that He cannot be comprehended, but they ask things of Him and do not seek Him, but seek His external gifts.

[And what profit shall we have if we pray to Him]. During prayer, if God Himself is not the object of our petition, the mind is at once disturbed in prayer... God longs to be Himself the beloved more than the things He created, and for eternal things to be sought, not temporary ones. As it is written: "But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you" (Mt 6:33).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Lo, their good is not in their hand:

entries.section: 3. The wicked's misuse of good things

paragraphs.text: the counsel of the wicked is far from me [16].

They will not accept the belief that what is in their hands is God's gift to them, but think it made by their hands, the fruit of their toil, intelligence and planning. Thus they close their hearts to their needy brethren, reckoning that giving to them is a plundering of their possessions and a squandering of what they labored for. They hold fast to what they have lest they lose the goods from their hands.

*The rich man usually imagines that he commits no sin as long as he does not rob the poor materially. But the sin of the rich lies in his not sharing his wealth with the poor. The rich man's keeping all his wealth means in fact committing a kind of theft. The real reason is that all riches are from God, so it belongs to all equally... And the proof of this surrounds us everywhere.
Look at the fresh fruit that the trees and thickets produce.
Look at the fertile soil that gives every year an abundant harvest like this.
Look at the sweet grapes on the clusters that give us wine to drink...

Perhaps the rich claim that they own much land where fruits and grain grow, but it is God who makes the seed sprout and ripen. So it is the duty of the rich to share every harvest of their land with all who work in it, and with all who have need.
St. John Chrysostom They pass this spirit on to their offspring and their friends, who walk in the same direction, but Job declares: "the counsel of the wicked is far from me."

17 How oft is the candle of the wicked put out! and how oft cometh their destruction upon them! God distributeth sorrows in his anger. 18 They are as stubble before the wind, and as chaff that the storm carrieth away. 19 God layeth up his iniquity for his children: he rewardeth him, and he shall know it. 20 His eyes shall see his destruction, and he shall drink of the wrath of the Almighty. 21 For what pleasure hath he in his house after him, when the number of his months is cut off in the midst?
How oft is the candle of the wicked put out! and how oft cometh their destruction upon them! God distributeth sorrows in his anger [17].

Since Job spoke at length of the wicked's success in this world, he returns to ask: [How oft is the candle of the wicked put out?] Do you not see it often burning until the wick has burned out, and after that going out of itself?
How often do you see that [their destruction comes upon them, or that God distributes sorrows to them in His anger?] Do you not see that often their joys and luxury continued to the end?

* The righteous dies in the strength of his simplicity, and in full mastery of his will, having a soul full as if of meadows. But the sinner, though in luxurious living, with sweet perfumes rising from him, closes his life in the bitterness of his soul, and passes his last day without taking anything of the good things he once enjoyed, carrying nothing but the wages of his wickedness.

*The holy Job answers: Do not think that you are happy while immersed in pleasures because God's blows have not come upon you in this life. [The candle of the wicked is put out]. It gives light for a time, but does not bear eternal light. And although the world favors such people because they practice the will of the ruler of the world(ب) (Jn 14:30), yet generally there comes a moment of turning in events, when sorrows come from the wrath and displeasure of heaven, when the wicked are sifted "as stubble before the wind." The unjust are sifted as chaff, and the righteous as wheat. Look to the Lord who said to Peter: "Behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat: but I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not" (Lk 22:31-32).

St. Ambrose The believer cherishes the word of God as the lamp that lights his way, through which he passes into the Father's bosom to enjoy glories on an eternal level. But the wicked man sees in wealth or authority or the enjoyment of bodily pleasures his lamp that drives him not to the kingdom of light but is a lamp that leads him astray and brings him into the kingdom of darkness. And as the Apostle Paul says that even Satan is transformed into an angel of light, to deceive believers, perhaps to hold them captive under his authority, so that they become children of darkness.
But the deceptions of the enemy of good will not stand before men of faith but are dispersed, as a lamp is put out!
*The wicked man often thinks that earthly resources are to him like a great lamp is to light, but when destruction comes upon him he loses the wealth he loved more than himself.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
They are as stubble before the wind, and as chaff that the storm carrieth away [18].

Job holds that his speaking of the wicked's success does not mean that they are truly successful, for they are as stubble before the wind, and as chaff that the storm carrieth away. They are trifling, losing all value, prepared for destruction, and are exposed to it at the height of their glory and might.

*When the wicked man is seen in strength, and when he is like one who has no restraint or opponent to his violent deeds, the weak count him as ballast (a weight used to balance a ship or a balloon), and as rooted in this world. But when the firm judgment comes from the Judge, [the wicked shall be as stubble before the wind]... [and as ashes that the whirlwind scatters]. The life of the wicked man in the eyes of the Almighty is like ashes, which may seem green for a moment, but is seen as having been scattered by the divine judgment, left aside for eternal burning. These ashes the whirlwind scatters. In this "our God shall come, and shall not keep silence: a fire shall devour before him, and it shall be very tempestuous round about him" (Ps 50:3).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

The wind, without which trees cannot deepen their roots and multiply their fruits, is the very same that scatters the stubble and strews the chaff, so that it has no place of rest. What builds the believer shatters the wicked.

If the wind points to the Holy Spirit, then the Holy Spirit by whom the birth of believers as children of God is accomplished in the waters of Baptism, and by whom they are renewed until they truly become the icon of Christ, is the same fiery Holy Spirit before whom the thorns of sin cannot stand, but are burned!
God layeth up his iniquity for his children:
he rewardeth him, and he shall know it [19].
At times God lets the wicked prosper, but they bequeath failure to their offspring. So the sons inherit, with the wealth that arose from injustice and iniquity, the curse and destruction.
Perhaps some ask: What is the fault of the sons that they should inherit from their fathers grievous evils?

First: God is not unjust, and does not punish sons for the evils of their fathers. For the soul that sinneth, it shall die. Rather, God wanted the fathers' repentance, that they might lay up divine righteousness for their children. We do not deny the effect of the fathers' lives on their children, but the children of some of the wicked were saints, and the crowns of their sons became great, because they did not fill up the measure of their fathers in evil, but received God as their Father, walking by His Holy Spirit. And there were also wicked sons of holy fathers, so that the holiness of their fathers' life became a cause of greater judgment.

Second: God threatens the wicked with what will befall their children because of their evils, for often a man cares little about what will befall himself, but grieves intensely over what befalls his children. As though the aim of this threat is the repentance of the fathers for fear of the destruction of their children.

* We know that it is written: "visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, and upon the children's children, unto the third and to the fourth generation" (Ex 34:7). And it is also written: "What mean ye, that ye use this proverb concerning the land of Israel, saying, The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge? As I live, saith the Lord GOD, ye shall not have occasion any more to use this proverb in Israel. Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die" (Ezek 18:2-4). Thus in these two passages, despite the difference in meaning, the mind of the hearer must learn to search with the utmost care the way of discernment. We have inherited ancestral sin from our parents, and if we are not released from it by the grace of baptism, we carry with us the very sins of our fathers, seeing that we are still one with them...

In any case this can be understood in another way also: that whoever imitates the way of evil of his wicked father is bound to his sins also. But he who does not follow his father's evil will not bear the weight of his disobedience. Thus the wicked son of a wicked father is bound not only to the sins that he himself added, but also to the sins of his father, since he practiced his father's evil works, which he knows God is angry at. Since he did not fear to add to them his own evils... Therefore it is rightly said: [unto the third and fourth generation]. For up to the third and fourth generation the children can witness the lives of their fathers and imitate them, so that vengeance extends even to those who witness what they imitate to their harm.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
His eyes shall see his destruction, and he shall drink of the wrath of the Almighty [20].
The wicked man has deliberately closed his eyes so as not to see God's grace, and his insight was not opened to God's mercies, so he filled his cup with his rebellion and disobedience.

Often the wicked man shuts his eyes to what will befall him or his offspring because of his evils, but surely he will open his eyes on the day of the Lord to see his eternal destruction come upon him. He will drink of the wrath of the Almighty. This is the portion of his cup that he filled in the days of his sojourn in the world.

* If man, while in this life, wished to open his eyes to his sin, he would not afterwards [drink of the wrath of the Almighty]. But whoever turns his eyes away here from seeing his iniquity cannot avoid the sentence of judgment.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

God calls us by every means to enjoy the illumination of the Holy Spirit, that our eyes may be opened to see the evils that have corrupted our being, at the same time as we enjoy seeing God's surpassing work for the forgiveness of our sins and for the enjoyment of union with Him.

If we see our destruction while we are still in this world, we flee to God Himself, who alone is able to keep us from the eternal wrath. But he who does not want to realize the truth of his evils fills his cup with divine wrath, to drink of it on the great day of the Lord.
For what pleasure hath he in his house after him, when the number of his months is cut off in the midst? [21]

Though Job has dwelt at length on the prosperity and success of some of the wicked, he makes clear what this success is, even if it extends through all the days of the wicked man's life, which are but a few months, so that he opens his eyes suddenly and finds himself falling under divine wrath.

In the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, the Lord Christ showed us how he was troubled for his household while in Hades when he realized that all the good things he enjoyed in the days of his life on earth were unable to moisten his tongue. And his sorrow was doubled as he realized that his five brothers would follow him (Lk 16:25-28).

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the wicked man does not forget his house even in the world to come, for the Lord Himself told us of the rich man who lifted up his eyes in Hades asking for his five brothers (Lk 16:28). But this request no longer benefits his household, since the opportunity was lost to him.

Our work, as bearers of the Lord Jesus, the Fountain of joy, within us, is to rejoice and exult and be a cause of delight to our households. For if we rejoice here in our Christ who dwells in us, heaven rejoices in us, and many rejoice, so that we are as members of an almost heavenly family whose mark is true joy. Then even when we depart from the world we do not cease to ask for the delight of our households. This is what we touch in practice where we see saints in Paradise interceding for the joy of the whole world through its return to God and its enjoyment of divine joy.

22 Shall any teach God knowledge? seeing he judgeth those that are high. 23 One dieth in his full strength, being wholly at ease and quiet. 24 His breasts are full of milk, and his bones are moistened with marrow. 25 And another dieth in the bitterness of his soul, and never eateth with pleasure. 26 They shall lie down alike in the dust, and the worms shall cover them.
Shall any teach God knowledge? seeing he judgeth those that are high? [22]

No man can comprehend the knowledge of God, Judge of heaven and earth, who will judge the fallen angels and men on the day of judgment. His judgments are unsearchable and His ways past finding out. He alone decides whether a certain wicked man prospers here, even if his prosperity extends through all the days of his life, or fails. By His divine wisdom He directs what no man can comprehend. Since we are unable to comprehend God's knowledge, wisdom and plan, it is not for us to judge a person as righteous or wicked by what befalls him of troubles or what he enjoys of temporal blessings. Instead of judging our brethren, let us love them and pray for them for their spiritual edification and growth, and also for their repentance, that God may grant us with them true repentance and genuine spiritual growth.

*The judgments of God the Almighty upon us are exceedingly hidden and are not unjust. But when we lift the eyes of our minds to the heavenly things we see with our (inner) eyes that we have nothing to complain of regarding justice. For God the Almighty distinguishes the merits of the angels; some of them He established to dwell in eternal light without falling, while the others fell by their own will from steadfastness in their height, and descended to the wrath of eternal judgment... He does wonderful things above our level, and it is certainly clear that He orders all that concerns us with knowledge.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
One dieth in his full strength,
being wholly at ease and quiet [23].

God alone determines whether a man dies in temporal peace and vain glory despite his persistence in his sins, and another dies in bitter pains and misery and wretchedness, though both meet together in the outer darkness.

A wicked man may die in his full strength, or in the fullness of his power, his strength not weakened by sickness or old age, "wholly at ease and quiet." In his entirety he is in rest and peace, not fearing death because he does not think of it or await it.

The Word of God came incarnate and dwelt among us to give us His true peace and the earnest of the glory He prepared for us from the foundation of the world. This peace and this glory alone satisfy the soul. But the false peace of the world and its vain glory deceive man, but only for a moment, and then pass away.
Here it behooves us to ask for the illumination of the Holy Spirit so that we may distinguish the kind of peace we are in, for there are many kinds of peace.

A. The peace that deceives the wicked, who drink iniquity like water, and in recklessness say: There is no God, no judgment and no eternity. [Let us eat and drink; for to morrow we die] (1 Cor 15:32).

B. The peace that springs from friendships and sharing with others, such as our sharing with our loved ones in their joyful and sorrowful occasions, but we are not concerned with the salvation of their souls and ours. This peace is temporary. Of this peace the Lord Christ says: "Peace I leave with you" (Jn 14:27). As though He says: This peace of yours I do not take away from you, but leave it to you that it may be sanctified by My peace which I give you.

C. The divine peace which the Lord Christ promised us: [My peace I give unto you] (Jn 14:27). This peace, which is a divine gift, we enjoy through our fellowship with Him, His dwelling in our midst, and His constant accompaniment throughout the journey of our life. [Lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world] (Mt 28:20).
His breasts are full of milk, and his bones are moistened with marrow [24].

Some translate it "his breasts are full of milk, and his bones are moist with marrow." And in the Jesuits' translation it is "fatness clothes his forehead, and waters the marrow of his bones." Meaning that he is in good health, strong in build, caring for nothing but to live long years in joy and gladness. His hopes are broad in this life until death surprises him suddenly! Perhaps they defy death within them, as though it were not their portion.

Job's friends look at him as a man who has lost all he possessed of wealth and honor, and count this a sure sign of his wickedness, thinking he is in severe inward want and an emptiness that will not be filled. But he sees many wicked who are rich and possessed of authority and temporal honor, who reckon their breasts (udders) full of milk, that is, like a mother with a nursing infant in her arms offering him of her milk, and that their bones are full of vitality that dryness will never reach. These feelings that control such wicked men come from temporary wealth and vain honor, but only for a moment, when the Judge comes and they discover that they were in a dream that has vanished.
