For if Job had been accustomed to offer sacrifices for his children, in case they had sinned even in thought against God (Job 1:5), reckoning himself and the members of his household more righteous than others, then God did not hear him, and did not deliver him or rescue his children, and this is a sign of his wickedness. The man who returns to God asks even for others who are not innocent, and He delivers them, for the sake of the cleanness of the hands of the righteous man who lifts his hands in prayer. It is as though he were making light of Job, saying to him: If your hands were clean your prayers and your sacrifices for yourself and your family would have been accepted, but because they are evil they have brought evil upon all!
Truly the godly man does not enjoy God's work in him alone, but as he prays for others with a wide heart God answers him, as the Apostle Paul did when he was in the ship (Acts 27:24).
Eliphaz did not realize that what he said would actually be fulfilled, when Job prayed for him and for his two companions (Job 42:8).
Perhaps Eliphaz prophesies, without knowing it, about the Lord Christ, the Intercessor and Atoning One. Who is this one with clean hands but the Lord Christ, who alone is without sin?

He stretched out His hands on the Cross, asking: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" He rose by His power, granting guilty humanity the possibility of salvation and victory over death, and deliverance!
Truly our Christ alone, by His blood, delivers the man who is not innocent, by the power of His blood shed on the Cross.
Let me return to You by repentance,

1 Then Job answered and said, 2 "Even to day is my complaint rebellion: my stroke is heavier than my groaning. 3 Oh that I knew where I might find him! that I might come even to his seat! 4 I would order my cause before him, and fill my mouth with arguments. 5 I would know the words which he would answer me, and understand what he would say unto me."
Then Job answered and said [1]:
"Even to day is my complaint rebellion: my stroke is heavier than my groaning" [2].

Job says that his complaint is bitter. His friends reckoned it rebellion against God, but Job gives a justification for his complaint, which is that however much he groans, the groanings of his heart cannot express how heavy his calamities are. The wounds of his body and soul are exceedingly severe, and they justify his complaint.

* The pains of the afflicted man ought to be healed by the comfort of his friends, but because their comfort carried deceit, the pains of the stricken man became harsher than they were. Eliphaz did not hide his intention, as he promises better things if he repents; this was like a poisoned remedy, and the wound grew worse.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* "A faithful friend is the medicine of life" (Sir 6:16).

There is no remedy so effective in healing pains as the sincere friend who comforts you in your afflictions, manages your problems, rejoices in your success and grieves in your calamities. Whoever has found such a friend has found a treasure. For a faithful friend has no equal, and no weight of gold and silver can balance the goodness of his faithfulness (see Sir 6:14-15).

* Nothing establishes love so strongly as sharing in joy and pain. Do not, because you are far from troubles, isolate yourself also from sharing with others. When your neighbor is in distress, reckon the distress as your own. Share his tears to support his crushed spirit, and share his joy so that the joy in him becomes deep and rooted.

Establish love, for by this you serve yourself more than you serve him. By your tears you become merciful, and by feelings of gladness you purify your soul from envy and gloom... If you cannot remove evils from him, share them with him by your tears, and you will remove half the evil from him; and if you cannot increase his goods, share his joy and you will add something great to him.

St. John Chrysostom "My stroke is heavier than my groaning"; and in Pope Gregory (the Great) it came: "The hand of my stroke is heavier than my groaning." Here he means the blow that struck him at the hands of his friends who opposed him, for it is more violent than the trials that came upon him and drove him to groan. It is as though his friends, instead of comforting him to calm his groanings, inflamed the wounds, for their hands came more violently than what had befallen him. The son of Sirach says: "There is a companion who rejoices with his friend in prosperity, and in adversity becomes his enemy" (Sir 37:4).
"Oh that I knew where I might find him! that I might come even to his seat!" [3]

Job was confident of God's justice and longed to stand before His throne to complain to Him, for He would surely do him justice and would not crush him as his friends had done. As David the prophet says: "I am in a great strait: let us fall now into the hand of the LORD; for his mercies are great: and let me not fall into the hand of man" (2 Sam 24:14).

Perhaps Job felt that sin had separated him from God and that his weaknesses had spoiled his relationship with God, so he wanted to restore this relationship and enjoy his love for God. Therefore he cries out: "Oh that I knew where I might find him!" As the human soul says: "Saw ye him whom my soul loveth?" (Song 3:3) Who will grant me to find Him? Who will open for me the way to Him?

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that Job longed to stand before God and His servants of the heavenly orders, where he would taste love and mercy, instead of what he suffered from men of his own kind. Therefore he says: "that I might come even to his seat!"

* What is the "seat" of God but the angelic spirits, whom the Holy Bible testifies are called "thrones"? Who desires to come to the seat of God but he who longs to be among the angelic spirits... so that he is lifted up to dwell in glory by contemplating eternity... For when he sees with the eyes of faith the Creator of all things ruling the angelic spirits, then he comes to His seat.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

When the believer enjoys fellowship with the heavenly beings, he feels that his relationship with them is no less than his relationship with his brethren in humanity, if it does not exceed it in tenderness, mercy and love. They rejoice at his salvation, and in the name of humanity they sing the hymns of salvation, as though the salvation were their own.

* Today the King of glory is glorified on earth, as the prophet says, and makes us who dwell on earth partakers in the heavenly feast, to show that He is Lord of both (of the heavenly and the earthly). So He is praised with common hymns from both.
Therefore the heavenly orders sang, proclaiming salvation on earth: [Holy, holy, holy, Lord of Sabaoth, His glory fills all the earth](a).
And those below, as they share in the joyful hymns of heaven in harmony with them, cry out: "Hosanna in the highest, Hosanna to the Son of David."
Fr. Methodius "I would order my cause before him, and fill my mouth with arguments" [4].

Job longs to present his case to God, for He will surely give him the opportunity to defend himself. Since Job represents the persecuted Church, though the world troubles her, she can in Christ Jesus stand before the throne with boldness and confidence, since she bears His divine righteousness, as the Apostle says.

Pope Gregory (the Great) translates this verse: "I would order my cause before God, and fill my mouth with reproofs." For the believer finds it good to stand before God and bring his case, where the soul discovers itself and comes to know itself more precisely, and trembles.

How different is man's attack upon the believer to crush him from the Spirit of God's disclosing to man to expose him before himself, to reprove him and to give him true repentance as a way to enjoy the Kingdom of God. We have "boldness to enter into the holiest" (Heb 10:19), and we stand before the throne of divine grace.

In open conversation with God, man accuses himself, and so is justified in God's eyes. The Lord Himself says: "Put me in remembrance: let us plead together: declare thou, that thou mayest be justified" (Isa 43:26). And the text came in the Septuagint: "Declare first your transgressions, that you may be justified" (Isa 43:26) LXX.

* God opens to us many ways to accomplish this. For He says: "Declare first your transgressions, that you may be justified" (Isa 43:26) LXX. He also says: [I said, I will tell my iniquity to You, and You take away the iniquity of my heart] (see Ps 32:5). For the constant accusation of ourselves, or the remembering of sins, contributes not a little to lessening their guilt.

* There is another way that gives us this remedy, which is to judge ourselves for our faults, because: "Declare first your transgressions, that you may be justified" (Isa 43:26) LXX. Whoever is in afflictions and gives thanks has his sins loosed, and also by almsgiving, which is greater than everything.
St. John Chrysostom "I would know the words which he would answer me, and understand what he would say unto me" [5].

Job's friends misunderstood his questions about the reason for his falling under successive bitter trials. They counted them as a complaint against God, even as practical atheism. And they counted his questions about the success of the wicked as an attack on divine justice. But Job was confident that if he entered into judgment with God, God's answers to his questions would surely be entirely comforting and not provoking. Therefore he longed for dialogue with Him, and to submit to His judgments with complete submission. Dialogue with God is easier and sweeter than with men.

Perhaps Job is saying to his friends: I do not care much about your opinion of me, I only want to talk with God, for what concerns me is what God says about me and how He answers my questions. As the Apostle Paul says: "But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged of you, or of man's judgment: yea, I judge not mine own self... but he that judgeth me is the Lord" (1 Cor 4:3-4).

* Paul does not mean here (1 Cor 4:4) that he is without blame, but wants to stop the mouths of those who blame him without discernment. God is our Judge, and He alone knows for certain what goes on in our hearts.
St. John Chrysostom
"Will he plead against me with his great power? No;
but he would give heed to me" [6].

Truly, who can enter into a dispute with God, when it is written: "the weakness of God is stronger than men" (1 Cor 1:25)? And yet dialogue with Him is better than dialogue with the sons of men, because He cares for the one who complains and listens to him as a tender father to his son. Though He is firm, with firmness He declares His tender fatherhood to the son wounded by trials and afflictions.

Job believed that Almighty God would not terrify him, and that even in his judgment and conversation with him He would not display the perfection of His majesty and greatness, but would condescend and show him as much as he could bear, so that he could converse with Him. He would not be violent with him, for He is not like the sons of men. He is longsuffering, and listens to the one who cries to Him, and strengthens and encourages him. He gives him strength, and enters with him into a struggle not to defeat him but to give him victory, as was said of our father Jacob: "by his strength he had power with God: yea, he had power over the angel, and prevailed: he wept, and made supplication unto him: he found him in Bethel, and there he spake with us" (Hos 12:3-4).

Truly, whoever has tasted true companionship with God does not cease to meet with Him, for he perceives His tenderness, His longsuffering and His condescension for the sake of His beloved man, saying with righteous Job: "Will he plead against me with his great power? No; but he would give heed to me" (Job 23:6).

* They thought that my light burden was very heavy, but I bowed down to them, leaving the Kingdom of Heaven, to eat with them, taking the human form. Rather, I gave them my body as food: I was food for them and a partner with them at the table.
St. Jerome

entries.section: 3. His assurance of victory by the Cross

paragraphs.text: "There the righteous might dispute with him; so should I be delivered for ever from my judge" [7].

Job believed that the divine judgment is issued with uprightness, and that He would deliver him on an eternal level. By taking refuge in Him we escape eternal judgment. As St. Augustine says, we flee from divine justice by taking refuge in God Himself.

Pope Gregory (the Great) translates this verse thus: "Let Him do justice against me, and my judgment will come to victory." And he sees in this cry the Church asking God the Word to accomplish justice by the Cross, to come down to her and redeem her; then, as she enters into the judgment, she enjoys victory on an eternal level. She asks for the Word to come to reprove her, for by His Incarnation and His reproof of her the gates of divine grace open before her, and she is justified before the divine throne.

* "Let Him do justice against me, and my judgment will come to victory"... To reprove my ways let the incarnate Son be sent... For if the only-begotten Son of God had remained unseen in the power of His divinity (that is, had not become incarnate) and had not taken anything of our weakness (our humanity), how could weak men have found the means to obtain divine grace? For the weight of His majesty, if it be considered, would in fact be against us and not for our help. But the Mighty One, who is above all, came as one weak among us, and by equaling Himself to us, taking our weakness, He raises us to His power. For it was not possible for us to perceive the loftiness of His divine nature, we ourselves being unfit for it, but He bowed down to man through His humanity, and it became possible for us to ascend, as it were, to Him who came down. He rose, and we were raised.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Flee to God Himself, if you want to flee from Him.
Flee by confession, not by hiding.
Say to Him: [You are a refuge to me](b).
So let the love that alone gives life grow within you.
* Joyful is the face of the Lord; once it is seen, man finds his delight in nothing else.
St. Augustine

entries.section: 4. His failure to comprehend the mystery of God

paragraphs.text: "Behold, I go forward, but he is not there; and backward, but I cannot perceive him [8]. On the left hand, where he doth work, but I cannot behold him:

entries.section: 4. His failure to comprehend the mystery of God

paragraphs.text: he turneth himself to the right hand, that I cannot see him" [9].

Job expressed the bewilderment in which he was, as one who searches for God and does not find Him in the east, nor perceive Him in the west. Eliphaz had earlier commanded him to get acquainted with God (Job 22:12), and Job answers him that this is the desire of his heart, for he longs to appear before Him.

Job undoubtedly believed that God is present in every place, but here he complains of his inability to fix his thoughts on God and on His wisdom amid their pursuit of him with useless and provoking arguments. Though he believed in God's existence, it was as though something like a veil covered his inner sight, so that he was unable to recognize the reasons for his troubles that God permitted. He knew of no particular sin he had committed that he should repent of. He did not realize what God's purpose was in allowing him these calamities. And finally he did not know what the end of these calamities would be, whether God would deliver him from them. When? And how would this be accomplished?
Pope Gregory (the Great) offers us more than one interpretation of the east, west, north (or left) and south (or right) in this passage.

The first interpretation: God is everywhere, and He is indivisible, filling all, seeing man and knowing all that is in his depths, but man does not see Him and cannot distinguish Him by the senses. He is awesome though unseen.

The second interpretation: if we look to the east, that is, if we think of His majesty, since He rises from the east, we cannot comprehend His nature with our mortal mind. And if we look to the west, that is, if the sight of the heart fails because of the abundance of His splendor, He cannot be understood. And if we walk toward the left, where there is falling into sins, we do not perceive Him. And if we walk toward the right, where there are the right-hand blows of pride, hypocrisy and self-righteousness, we do not see Him.

* "Behold, if I go to the east, He does not appear; and if I go to the west, I do not understand Him. If I go to the north, what shall I do? I do not perceive Him; and if I turn to the right (south), I do not see Him" [8-9]. The Creator of all things is indivisible, and He is in every place... For the incomprehensible Spirit contains everything in Himself, He who at the same time fills and contains...

It is as though he were saying plainly: I cannot look upon the One who sees me, the One who looks upon me with all exactness; I have no power to look at Him... Our Creator, who is wholly perfect in every place and distinguishes everything, cannot be distinguished (by the senses), and He is the more awesome in that He remains unseen, and the outcome of our actions hangs in the balance, and their time is unknown.

These words can also be understood in another sense: we go east when we lift up our minds by thinking of His majesty, but He "does not appear," since He cannot be seen in His nature by a mortal mind. [If I go to the west, I do not understand Him](c); we go west when the eye of the heart that was lifted up in God draws back because of the abundance of light...

To go to the left (north) is man's submission to the pleasures of his sins. It is certainly clear that the person who still pleases his sins and throws himself toward the left cannot comprehend God...
A person goes toward the right (south) who is exalted over virtuous achievements.

But God cannot be seen by the one who is pleased to enjoy his good works selfishly, for he lowers the eye of the heart by the vanity of pride. Therefore it is well said everywhere: [Thou shalt not decline... to the right hand, nor to the left] (see Deut 17:11)...
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* You cannot see God, but you have the right to see Him by your love for your neighbor. And by looking to the source of that love you see God as far as you are able.
St. Augustine

entries.section: 5. His assurance that God purifies him by fire

paragraphs.text: 10 "But he knoweth the way that I take: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold. 11 My foot hath held his steps, his way have I kept, and not declined. 12 Neither have I gone back from the commandment of his lips; I have esteemed the words of his mouth more than my necessary food. 13 But he is alone, and who can turn him? and what his soul desireth, even that he doeth."
"But he knoweth the way that I take:
when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold" [10].

Job acknowledged the surpassing perfection of God, who fills all and knows all. He sees even the depths, and man does not see Him. Wherever man goes, whether east or west, north or south, he cannot see God, nor comprehend His divine mysteries and His plan for every man, but he knows one thing: that in God's eyes he is reckoned precious gold that needs purifying by the fire of trials to grow in purity and splendor. For despite the extreme bewilderment that came upon Job and his not perceiving what lay behind the events in the mind of God, he knows that God knows his way, and that He will bring him out of the trial pure like gold refined by fire; and that his trial is to test or prove his faith (1 Pet 1:7).

* "And He will test me like gold that passes through the fire." Gold in the furnace advances in the splendor of its nature, while it loses the dross. So as gold passes through the fire, the souls of the righteous are tried... By the fire of trial, again and again, their faults are removed, and their virtues increase.

It is not in pride that the saint compares himself to gold tested by trials... when he thinks of himself that he has been purified by the pain of trial, even if there was nothing found in him to be purified from.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* When God wants to give victory to a man and magnify him, He first delivers him to evil (trials) to be tested and examined, and then his beauty appears to the world by the good things that God does with him.

When God wanted to give Joseph victory and make him lord over Egypt..., what was the beginning of His work to lead to a good end? First his brothers seized him, insulted him, mocked him, stripped his garments, left him in the pit, cut off his hope, and sold him to merchants, and he became a slave serving masters, and the handsome son of free men who had committed no wrong was enslaved.

Whoever saw this evil work could not have thought that all these evils were being committed for Joseph's good. But God, who knew what He wanted to do for him, did not spare him when he was being crushed under all these evils, but let him fall into the pit, be sold to the merchants, and be thrown into prison unjustly. After all these things his beauty shone like the sun, his right appeared like gold, his evils vanished like smoke, and he mounted to the top of the chariot like a king, and rose up in the greatness for which God had set him, so that by humbling himself he might be exalted.

St. Mar Jacob of Serugh * As the refiner of gold throws the piece of gold into the furnace to endure the fire for a time, until he sees that it has been purified, so God permits the testing of human souls with afflictions until they are purified and gain great benefit...

May we not be disturbed or despair when trials come upon us. For just as the refiner of gold knows the time for which the gold must be left in the furnace, and brings it out at the appointed time and does not leave it any longer in the fire lest it be spoiled and burned, how much more does God know this. So when He sees that we have been purified the more, He frees us from our trials so that we are not cast down and driven out because of the increase of our evils.

When something happens to us that we did not expect, let us not murmur nor let our hearts faint, but receive it from God, who knows these things exactly, so that He may test our hearts by fire as it pleases Him, since this is done for the benefit of those who are tried. Therefore the wise man commands us to submit to God in all things, because He knows perfectly when to bring us out of the furnace of evil (Sir 1:1-2).

It is fitting for us to submit to Him always, and to thank Him continually, bearing everything willingly, whether He grants us blessings or offers us chastenings. For the latter are a kind of blessing.
The physician is not only one who lets us bathe (in the baths)... or go to pleasant gardens, but also when he uses the scalpel and the knife he is a physician!
And the father is not only when he caresses his son, but also when he disciplines and punishes him... he is a father!

And since we know that God is more tender than all physicians, it is not for us to investigate His dealings, nor to demand an account from Him of them, but what is good in His eyes He does. So we do not distinguish whether He frees us from trial or disciplines us, because by both ways He wants to restore us to health and make us partners with Him, and He knows our different needs, and what suits each one of us, and how, and in what way we must be saved...
Let us follow Him wherever He commands us, and not think much whether He commands us to walk an easy, smooth road or a hard, rough one.

St. John Chrysostom * As gold is tried by fire and becomes useful, so you who live in the world are tried by it. So you who are in the fire pass through the flame and are purified. And as the dross is cast off from the gold, so you will cast off every sorrow and trial, and become pure and useful for the building of the tower.
Hermas "My foot hath held his steps,

entries.section: 5. His assurance that God purifies him by fire

paragraphs.text: his way have I kept, and not declined" [11].

While Job acknowledges that he needs the dross to be removed from him, he returns and declares that he has set it in his heart to walk according to God's purposes and plans, committing himself to walk in the divine way step by step. He does not want to turn aside from the way to the right or to the left.

On one hand Job rejects what his friends claim, that these trials are the fruit of his evils, his hypocrisy and his secret opposition to God, but are a crucible to purify his depths so that he comes forth as gold refined by fire; and on the other hand he declares that he walks in the way of the Lord, keeps the Lord's commandments and does not turn aside from them.

* "My foot holds fast to His steps," for the works of God that we see are a kind of traces of His steps. By these works the good and the bad are judged, the righteous and the wicked are placed in their ranks... The Truth commands us to imitate the traces of the steps of His Father, saying: pray for them which persecute you and falsely accuse you, that ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven (Mt 5:44-45)... Peter says of these His steps: [because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps] (1 Pet 2:21)...

"His way have I kept, and not declined": whoever practices what his mind has resolved keeps the way and does not turn aside from it. For he who "keeps" what he has resolved does not turn aside from it in his practical conduct. This is what occupies the righteous: that they are committed to test their conduct by the ways of truth day by day, and reckon them a rule for themselves, binding them not to turn aside from their straight path.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Christ taught you to suffer, and He did this by suffering Himself. Words are not enough unless a practical example is added to them. What precious teaching He gave us, brothers and sisters! He was hung on the Cross, and the Jews were raging... He was hanging there, and at the same time He was healing them.
St. Augustine "Neither have I gone back from the commandment of his lips;

entries.section: 5. His assurance that God purifies him by fire

paragraphs.text: I have esteemed the words of his mouth more than my appointed portion" [12].
Job declares that he did not turn back from the divine commandment issued from the divine mouth, but advances according to it and always strives toward the goal.
He held fast to the commandment, counting it better than his necessary food, for he cannot live without it; it is the food and drink of his soul.

Job looks upon the divine commandment as issuing from the lips of God and as the word of His mouth, so it is not mere orders by which he is bound to direct his conduct, but a sweet and precious gift issuing from the mouth of that Lover! Therefore it is not a burden that he wants to flee from, but in sweetness he does not depart from it, and in longing he lays it up in his depths. As the Psalmist says: "I have rejoiced in the way of thy testimonies, as much as in all riches. I will meditate in thy precepts, and have respect unto thy ways. I will delight myself in thy statutes: I will not forget thy word... The law of thy mouth is better unto me than thousands of gold and silver... O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day. Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path. Thy testimonies have I taken as an heritage for ever: for they are the rejoicing of my heart. My tongue shall speak of thy word: for all thy commandments are righteousness" (Ps 119:14-16, 72, 97, 105, 111, 172)

* If Job had set for himself a rule, which was to walk as is fitting for him as a man, yet more precious than this rule is the divine commandment, as his treasure which he possesses and guards and keeps in his heart. [I hid the words of His mouth in the bosom of my heart]. For we hide the words in the bosom of our hearts when we hear His commandments, not in a passing way, but fulfill them in practice. It is written of the Virgin Mother herself: [But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart] (Lk 2:19).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Truly, whoever obtains material wealth rejoices because of this wealth, not when he has a part of the wealth, but when he obtains "all riches," all the fixed and circulating assets, that is, real estate and money. So also whoever desires spiritual wealth rejoices and is glad when he obtains complete wealth, by virtue of his progress in the testimonies of the Lord and his practice of the virtues. It is as though he were saying: Let Your testimonies be what makes me need nothing else, let them be my joy and my wealth.

Origen * Those whose citizenship is in heaven (Phil 3:19-20), as long as they dwell here occupied (with the heavenly things), are truly strangers. Let them pray that God's commandments may not be hidden from them, by which they are set free during their temporary journey, by their love for God with whom they will dwell eternally; and by their love for their neighbor so that he too may go to where they will be (that is, in heaven).
St. Augustine "But he is alone, and who can turn him?

entries.section: 5. His assurance that God purifies him by fire

paragraphs.text: and what his soul desireth, even that he doeth" [13].

With Job's sense of his human weakness, and at the same time being unable to ignore his faithfulness and earnestness in keeping the Lord's commandments and his surpassing esteem for them, he wanted to enter into dialogue with God to learn His divine purposes behind what had befallen him.

But Job realizes his limits, that he is a weak creature who does not reproach in order to change God's plan, and does not expect to oppose God. He knows that God is the Almighty, the Wise, the Father; what He wants is for good, and He is able to do it. It is as though Job wanted, in his dialogue, God to open his insight further so that he might swim in God's surpassing love even if afflictions pursued him from every side. By this dialogue Job benefits, so that his faith and love increase and he rises above words.

God is the absolute Truth; His counsel does not change, no one shares counsel with Him, there is none to change His will and purposes. Truly He pardons upon repentance, but His purposes do not change: "all his works are known unto the Lord from the beginning of the world."

He is almighty; what He desires He accomplishes. He is not like men who desire many things which they do not do, or cannot do, or do not dare to do, for He is all-powerful. "Whatsoever the LORD pleased, that did he" (Ps 135:6).

* "If He is judged, who is this that opposes Him? For He wills a thing and accomplishes it." Knowledge is kept within the limits of nature by all its ways, but faith makes its journey above nature... The man who follows faith becomes at once free and ruler of himself, and as a son subjects all the natures of creation as though he were a god, for by faith authority in the likeness of God is realized, to establish a new creation. He says: "You do what You will, and all things are present before You." And many times faith can bring everything out of nothing.

St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian Pope Gregory (the Great) comments on the expression [He alone], as though there were no being other than He, saying that it is fitting to distinguish between the self-existent, unchangeable Creator and the creatures that came into being from nothing and cannot subsist by themselves.

* "But He is Himself alone, and no man can change His mind"... Since there is a multitude of things in the circle of nature, why is it said by the voice of the blessed man: [He alone]? There is a difference between what exists and what exists originally, between what is subject to change and existence and what is independent of change. For all these things exist, but they do not subsist by themselves; if they were not upheld by the hand of Him who governs them they could never exist at all. For all things subsist in Him who made them, and they do not owe their life to themselves, nor have those who move and do not live come to have motion according to their whims. Rather it is (God) who moves all things, He who gives life to some, granting them life, while the other beings that are without life He preserves, lodging them in a wonderful way as lesser and lower beings.

All things were created out of nothing, and their existence ends in nothing, unless the Creator of things holds them with the hand of His providence. So all created things cannot by themselves subsist, nor move, but must submit to their Former, and only in this way do they move...
In any case, even if there is opposition against us from outside (that is, afflictions), it is fitting for us to realize that God works in us from within...

So in all cases God is regarded as the One who alone is, He who exists from the beginning and who said to Moses: [I AM THAT I AM: thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you] (Ex 3:14). So when we are chastened by the things that we see, we must fear Him whom we do not see...

Concerning His immutability, he added in a direct and fitting way: "no man can change His mind," for since He is by nature unchangeable, He is unchangeable in will. "No one can change His mind," for no man has authority to resist His hidden judgments... So it is written: "He issues a decree that does not change." And also: "Heaven and earth shall pass away: but my words shall not pass away" (Mk 13:31). Also: "For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways" (Isa 55:8)...

For even those things that seem to be done against His will and contrary to it, let us look to this: that what He has not commanded is sometimes permitted to be done so that it may serve what He has commanded and accomplish it with greater certainty. For the will of the opposing angel is evil, but God commands in a wonderful way so that God uses his very deceitful devices for the good of the righteous who are purified through their struggle. Therefore [whatever His soul desires, He does], using the very source that may seem to oppose His will to accomplish His will by it...
Pope Gregory (the Great)

14 "For he performeth the thing that is appointed for me: and many such things are with him. 15 Therefore am I troubled at his presence: when I consider, I am afraid of him. 16 For God maketh my heart soft, and the Almighty troubleth me: 17 Because I was not cut off before the darkness, neither hath he covered the darkness from my face."
"For he performeth the thing that is appointed for me: and many such things are with him" [14].

Job looks to God, the One, the only Almighty, existing by Himself, as the source of his life and the mover of all things by His surpassing providence, and therefore he sees that all that happens is for his benefit and good.

But in spite of this certainty, his human nature, which fears the calamities and pains that come upon him, will not be taken from him. Perhaps this fear or dread is not terror of what will befall him, but the holy fear of the Lord. For he stands in awe before the surpassing majesty and glory of God. He rejoices in the divine presence, but not in negligence or carelessness, rather in reverence and honor toward God.

* But you rightly put a question amid these words and say: [O blessed Job, why do you still tremble at sorrows in the midst of such blows? Sorrows have already gazed upon you; you have already been troubled by countless disasters]... But notice how the saint answers our question, adding: "For when He accomplishes His will in me, there are many other things with Him" [14]... With his sight of the incomprehensible power of authority that dwells in Him, the righteous man feels that he is not safe from the blow that comes upon him, and so his fear increases the more.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"Therefore am I troubled at his presence:
when I consider, I am afraid of him" [15].

Job had already declared that he does not tremble before God, because he has boldness toward Him. But here he mentions that he meditates on God's providence and works and fear comes over him, which is the fear of honor and esteem for the Lord, like the fear of a son toward his father.

Perhaps what terrifies him is his inner struggle, for in his distress at his friends' accusations against him he finds it good to converse with God and be judged before Him, as though he were saying with David the prophet: "let us fall now into the hand of the LORD; for his mercies are great: and let me not fall into the hand of man" (2 Sam 24:14). And at the same time Job knows that he is not worthy to converse with God and enter into judgment with Him.

* "Therefore I am troubled at His presence, when I consider that I am afraid of Him" [15]. He is truly troubled at the presence of the Lord, who sets before his eyes the dread of His majesty and is completely confounded by the awe of His righteousness, seeing that he is not worthy to answer if he is judged strictly...

As for blessed Job, we know that he was devoted to offering various sacrifices to God, and gave himself to works of generous giving and to supplying the needs of the poor, and was humble even before those subject to him, gentle with his opponents, and yet such countless disasters befell him... So what shall we say, we wretched creatures? What shall we say, we sinners, if the one who did all this was so afraid?
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Nothing is higher than the fear of God, because it rules over everything, and by the fear of God everyone turns away from all evils. Let us acquire this fear for ourselves and turn away from everything that God does not want, and prove all that pleases Him and keep it and do nothing that grieves Him, and know that everything we do He looks at, and nothing is hidden from Him.
St. Macarius the Great "For God maketh my heart soft, and the Almighty troubleth me" [16].

Although righteous Job had boldness even to enter into judgment with God, he holds to the holy fear, for he perceives the greatness of God and His majesty. Holy love casts out the fear of slaves, but it brings the fear of the Lord, so that the righteous wrap themselves in it before the Holy One. We do not wonder at Job's daring, courage and boldness before God, and at the same time his heart's growing faint and being terrified before the Almighty. This is the way of the children of God: they long with the Apostle Paul to depart and be with Christ and cry out, asking: "Even so, come, Lord Jesus," and at the same time they remember the day of judgment and weep over their sins.

* "For God has made my heart faint, and the Almighty has terrified me." It is said that the heart of the righteous man by divine gift becomes faint, as the fear of the coming judgment from the Most High pervades it. What is faint can easily be pierced, and what is hard cannot be pierced. Therefore Solomon says: [Happy is the man that feareth alway: but he that hardeneth his heart shall fall into mischief] (Prov 28:14)...

The hearts of the righteous are not secure but troubled, as they think of the great weight of the coming reckoning, and seek to enjoy rest here. They cut off their assurance by thinking of the inner severity. Yet such persons, amid the very chastenings of fear, often remember the gifts, and so they rejoice amid the fears and reconsider the gifts they received to support their hope so that fear subsides.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* If you keep in mind the Lord's judgment of the whole earth (Ps 9:7-8), as the Holy Bible says, then every event teaches you the knowledge of God.
St. Mark the Ascetic * Remember continually the hour of your departure, and do not forget the eternal judgment, and no sin will be found in your soul.
* How do we please God? There are five works that help to bring about God's gift:
The first: pure prayer.
The second: praise with the Psalms.
The third: reading the holy Scriptures.
The fourth: man's remembering his sins, death and the fearful judgment.
The fifth: work of the hands.
St. Mar Evagrius of Pontus "Because I was not cut off before the darkness, neither hath he covered the darkness from my face" [17].

Again, although the believer's heart grows faint and is filled with awe, he knows that in the abundance of God's grace he will not perish, and that darkness cannot cover his face as long as he has put his hand in God's hand. By faith the believer sees the gates of heaven open before him, and in watchfulness he fears as he stands, lest he fall, as the Apostle Paul said (1 Cor 10:12).

* "But I shall not perish because of the darkness that threatens me, and the darkness will not cover my face"... For the blows that come upon the righteous either remove the evils they practiced, or make them avoid the coming blows that may fall. But blessed Job, when he fell under the rod, was not purified from sins he had committed nor was he fortified against what threatened him. Rather the rod increased his goodness the more while he was under the blow, and so he says with certainty: "For I shall not perish from the darkness that threatens me, and the darkness will not cover my face."
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Your silence amid my pains is sweeter than the consolations of men!
* In the midst of the bitterness of my soul I complained; my pains are heavier than every groan or sigh. He who sees me thinks that I murmur against You.
I trust in You, in Your love and Your righteousness.
I want to meet You, for You alone search my heart. Why are You silent, O Lover of mankind?
Judge me, but according to Your mercy!
I want to converse with You, for I know that by Your Cross I am delivered forever.
* Why are You silent, O You who are wonderful in Your love?
I want to flee from divine justice by taking refuge in Your love.
I confess my sins to You, for who has pity on my weakness as You do?
* If I look to the east, I see Your greatness.
So I fall silent before Your splendor.
And if I look to the west, where I draw back before You, my understanding freezes completely!
If I walk on the left, where sins are, I cannot comprehend You.
And if I walk on the right, where the blows of self-righteousness are, I deprive myself of seeing You.
Tell me, how shall I see You and speak with You, for You are my only refuge.
* You are in every place, You are in my depths, and in my folly I did not know how to meet You!
You see me and search my depths, and because of my blindness I do not see You, nor comprehend Your mysteries!
Your plan for me is surpassing.
* You want me to be gold refined by fire, without dross; You permit trials for me, and You work in me without ceasing, even if You are silent.
Amid my bitter cries, You see my soul being purified as by fire.
You see me coming to You in glories that are the work of Your grace in me!
In Your silence You seem as one who does not care for my bitter cries, but You, the wise Potter, know when to bring me out of the furnace of trials.
You look upon me, the clay, and see me changed into a vessel of honor!
You will not leave me in the fire until I am burned, and You will not bring me out before the time lest I be spoiled!
* I see You, the heavenly Physician, in Your silence holding the scalpel.
Strike my body with it, and remove its sores.
I see You as the Father who, though silent, has His eyes upon His beloved son.
Now let me walk according to Your incomprehensible purposes.
With thanksgiving I receive Your plan for me, however bitter it may seem.
Let me keep Your way by Your grace.
For You have promised me that I shall be a son of the heavenly Father!
* In the midst of the depth of Your love I realize that You alone are the Almighty.
Who can understand the depths of Your wisdom?
Work in me, even if my soul grows bitter, for all that You do is for my sure edification.
I am the weak clay submitting to its mighty Former.
Even if I am distressed for a time, Your wonderful majesty captivates my whole being.
* You have fixed Your fear within me; it is my fortress and my refuge from the enemy's warfare.
In it I take shelter, and by it I walk as is fitting for a son of Yours!
In Him I am filled with hope, but in a spirit of reverence and godliness!
In Him I remember the day of Your coming, and cry out:
My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready!
Come, O Lord Jesus, for You are the Judge, and You are the Comforter and the Intercessor for me.

entries.section: 1. The indifference of the wicked toward the Judge

paragraphs.text: Why, seeing times are not hidden from the Almighty, do they that know him not see his days? [1]

As Job looks toward the day of judgment, he is filled with awe, or the fear of the Lord, for there he meets the One who is above time (Job 15:17-23). Job is amazed at the wicked, that although they are subject to time, living for a while and then departing, they do not fear God, who embraces all times and from whom no time escapes. Job sees that every man appears at a certain time and then disappears by his death, and does not know the day of the Lord's coming to judge him. It would therefore have been fitting for him not to practice injustice against his brother; perhaps by this he turns the accusation directed against him toward his friends, who do not fear God and do not care about their friend Job, but practice cruelty against him.

The times are not hidden from the Almighty. Past times are not hidden from His judgment (Eccl 3:15), present times are not hidden from the ordering of His providence (Mt 10:29), and future times are not hidden from His foreknowledge (Acts 15:18). Therefore it is fitting that the wicked should not think they escape the divine justice, since the past, like the present and the future, is before the presence of God. They have no right to say: "The LORD seeth us not; the LORD hath forsaken the earth" (Ezek 8:12; 9:9). The wicked have no right to say that wicked men lived in the past and spent all their lives in ease, prosperity and success, for even if they died, they will rise to be judged before the Judge from whom nothing is hidden. The Lord has hidden the day of His coming from men so that all may cease from their evils, lest He come upon them suddenly. The general day of judgment is called the day of the Lord (Ps 37:13); it is surely coming, but we do not know it.

* "The times are not hidden from the Almighty" [1]... We are hidden within the divisions of time, since we are created beings. But God, the Creator of all things, embraces our times... And concerning eternity, we have such thoughts as these: we do not yet know the appointed time of eternity.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Since we do not know the day of the Lord's coming for judgment, while all times are open before Him, the discipline of earnestly awaiting the Lord's coming, with a person examining himself daily in a spirit of hope in Christ, the Savior of sinners, and in the work of the Holy Spirit, was vital in the early Church, especially in monastic communities.

* Every one must draw out from himself each day the story of his deeds by night and by day. If he has sinned, let him cease from sin; if he has not sinned, he must not boast, but hold fast to what is good without neglect, and not judge his brethren or justify himself [until the Lord comes, who reveals the hidden things] (1 Cor 4:5; Rom 2:16), as the blessed Apostle Paul says. For often we have unwittingly done things that we do not know, but the Lord sees everything. Therefore, since we commit the judgment to Him, let us be kind to one another, let us bear one another's burdens (Gal 6:2), but let us examine ourselves and hasten to fill up what is lacking in us.

* My son, do not rebuke anyone quickly, for this is a fall for you. Rather, remember your departure from this body at all times, and do not forget the eternal judgment, for if you do so you will not sin again. For our spiritual fathers said: solitude is the study (that is, the meditation) in the remembrance of death and the flight from all the things of the body.
St. Abba Anthony the Great

entries.section: 2. Their work of plunder and seizure

paragraphs.text: Some remove the landmarks.
They violently take away flocks, and feed thereof [2].

Job looks at those around him and sees them indifferent to the just Judge. They remove the landmarks, that is, they seize the fields and lands of others, placing the boundaries of their own land (their landmarks) inside the land of another, and they seize their sheep and shepherd them as though they were theirs by right.
Here he begins with the first and gravest kind of evils, those which the Holy One cannot bear, namely the practice of injustice.

Nothing grieves the heart of God like injustice taking the place of love and truth. Man was created to be an icon of love, but [I saw under the sun... in the place of truth, there was injustice] (Eccl 3:16). There is none who cares for the tears of the oppressed, while their oppressors are arrogant (Eccl 4:1).

This practice was forbidden (Deut 19:14), and whoever violates the Law deserves the curse (Deut 27:17). As for seizing the flock, the prophet David judged the man who slaughtered the poor man's ewe lamb to be worthy of death (2 Sam 12:4-5), not realizing that he was judging himself, since he had seized the wife of Uriah the Hittite.

* "O Lord, why do the wicked flee from their hour, transgress the boundaries, and carry off the flock together with the shepherd?" Once more there is doubt, and he asks: Why do the wicked prosper...? Just as we do not know why one man falls under such sufferings unjustly while another brings them upon him, so naturally these injustices cause disturbance and affect one party as well as the other (the unjust and the wronged).

entries.section: 2. Their work of plunder and seizure

paragraphs.text: "They go forth like wild asses in a field" [6], meaning that they have despised the whole world, since they treat everyone lightly, thinking that there is no one who wrongs them and no one who does evil to them.
"But He (God) has not yet visited them." He will do so later, but He will scrutinize their faults and will not let them pass!

St. John Chrysostom says: The Preacher (Solomon the Wise) says: "And moreover I saw under the sun the place of truth, that injustice was there; and the place of justice, that wrong was there. I said in mine heart, God shall judge the righteous and the wicked: for there is a time there for every purpose and for every work" (Eccl 3:16-17). For the good God has made everything beautiful in its time, and the corruption that has come upon the world is not from the nature of the world itself, but through man's injustice and wrong toward his fellow man. And what testimony to the vanity of the world is like injustice occupying the place of truth, and wrong the place of justice? Corruption spreads into the depths of the courts of justice! But the Preacher believes in the just judgment of God. The corruption of the world does not mean that things proceed in a random manner without restraint; rather, God awaits the proper time to judge the righteous and the wicked. "For there is a time there for every purpose and for every work." In other words, if man by his corruption has wronged the world, since he has not put everything in its proper time and place, so that injustice has taken the place of justice... God intervenes to set the situation right, but also in His own time.
Perhaps among the gravest vices which the Holy Bible attacks, in both Testaments, is man's injustice toward his brother.

In His longsuffering God awaits our return to Him, that we may practice His love and righteousness; but the wicked insist on practicing violence and injustice. On the day of judgment, it seems as though God does not point out the details of their evils, but calls all their evils injustice, as if there were nothing that grieves the heart of God like man's injustice toward his fellow man. He addresses the wicked, saying: "I tell you, I know you not whence ye are; depart from me, all ye workers of injustice" (Lk 13:27). "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear! even cry out unto thee of injustice, and thou wilt not save!" (Hab 1:2).
The Holy Bible warns us against a man practicing injustice against his brother, affirming the gravity of injustice:
A. There is no refuge from injustice other than taking refuge in God Himself.
"Deliver me, O LORD, from the evil man; preserve me from the man of injustice" (Ps 140:1).
"Keep me, O LORD, from the hands of the wicked; preserve me from the man of injustice; who have purposed to overthrow my goings" (Ps 140:4).
B. The injustice that a man practices he only stores up for himself, and the injustice returns upon him to his destruction; he drinks from the very cup that he filled for his brother.
"Let not an evil speaker be established in the earth: evil shall hunt the man of injustice to his destruction" (Ps 140:11).

C. Injustice makes man lose wisdom and prudence, so that folly rules over him, and it deprives him of entering into a covenant with God, who is altogether just. For there is no fellowship between injustice and justice.
"Surely oppression maketh a wise man mad; and a gift destroyeth the heart" (Eccl 7:7).
"Wherefore thus saith the Holy One of Israel, Because ye despise this word, and trust in oppression and perverseness, and stay thereon" (Isa 30:12).
"For I the LORD love justice, I hate robbery by injustice; and I will make their reward faithful, and I will make an everlasting covenant with them" (Isa 61:8).
D. Injustice corrupts the spirit of shepherding, and makes leaders and rulers lose their pastoral work.
"Thus saith the Lord GOD; Let it suffice you, O princes of Israel: remove violence and robbery, and execute justice and righteousness, take away injustice from my people" (Ezek 45:9).

E. Every injustice enters, as into the storehouses of the palaces of those who think they are great and above the law, and there it settles; it will not go out without repentance and returning to You.
"For they know not to do right, saith the LORD, who store up injustice and robbery in their palaces" (Amos 3:10).
"Ye that put far away the evil day, and cause the seat of injustice to come near" (Amos 6:3).
"But let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and cry mightily unto God: yea, let them turn every one from his evil way, and from the injustice that is in their hands" (Jon 3:8).
F. Injustice corrupts the heart, the city of God Jerusalem, and the inner temple.
"They build up Zion with blood, and Jerusalem with injustice" (Mic 3:10).

"For he hateth divorce, saith the LORD, the God of Israel, and that one cover injustice with his garment, saith the LORD of hosts: therefore take heed to your spirit, that ye deal not treacherously" (Mal 2:16).

The psalmist sets the word "injustice" as though it were equal to the devil himself, placing injustice over against God, the object of our trust and our hope, and he warns us: "Trust not in injustice," as though there were before us one of two choices: God or injustice.
* "Trust not in injustice" (Ps 62:10). For my hope is in God... I have leapt up and placed my hope in God; can there be, in any way, injustice in God?
St. Augustine G. The outcome of injustice is vanity; it has no value.
"Trust not in injustice, and become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them" (Ps 62:10).
God has not promised His believers to remove injustice and persecutions from them, but He permits this for their glory and for His own glory in them, as a Savior who turns evils into good.

The psalmist says: "He shall redeem their soul from injustice and robbery: and precious shall their blood be in his sight" (Ps 72:14). Or, as it appears in some translations: "His name shall be honored in their presence."

* If Christians appear despised in this world, their name is honored in the presence of God. He no longer remembers the names with which they were formerly associated (and the labors) through Gentile (pagan) trifles, nor does He refer to the names that attached to them through their evil conduct before they became Christians. For they have received the name of Christians in the presence of God, the name that appears despised among their enemies.

St. Augustine In St. Augustine's commentary on Psalm 140, where the psalmist prays that God would keep him from the man of injustice, he sees that the psalmist gives us a living example of prayer against the unjust, in saying: "From the man of injustice deliver me... The proud have hid a snare for me, and cords; they have spread a net by the wayside; they have set gins for me" (Ps 140:4-5). For the prayer is not against the unjust man himself, but against evil and injustice, that God may remove the nets set against us.

* Many pray unskillfully against the wicked... It is fitting for you to pray against such nets, lest you lose your heavenly inheritance, lest you lose Christ, with whom you have a share in the inheritance; it has been appointed for you to live with Him forever, He who has made you an heir. For you have become an heir not by means of one whom you succeed after his death (the father according to the flesh), but by means of Him who lives with him forever.

St. Augustine True injustice, in the mind of St. Augustine, is not that which causes you material or temporal losses, such as seizing your inheritance or your possessions, but rather the setting of a snare for the soul so that it is deprived of fellowship with the Lord Christ in the eternal inheritance.

When the unjust man sets nets to catch the righteous, they themselves fall into their own snares and destroy their eternity. As the psalmist says: "Evil shall hunt the man of injustice to his destruction" (Ps 140:11).

* Evils come, but the wicked man does not endure; therefore he says: [it hunts him to his destruction]. For many of the good and righteous have been struck by evils, yet through the evils they were found (and did not perish). When evils pursued the good, that is, our martyrs, and seized them, they hunted them, but not to destruction. Their bodies were pressed, but the spirit was crowned. The spirit was taken from the body, but nothing befalls the body, which is hidden away for the future.

Let the body be burned and scourged and disfigured; is it taken away from its Creator because it was delivered into the hand of its persecutors? Will not He who created it out of nothing restore it in a better form than it had?

St. Augustine Pope Gregory (the Great) sees in Job's friends, who symbolize the heretics, that they constantly use every means, whether by enticement or deceit, to enlarge their borders and to plunder souls, by removing the marks that the Fathers set, that is, the evangelical, ecclesial and patristic concepts, so that they draw some away and turn them aside from the divine field. They take the gentle flock of Christ and count it as their own flock, and claim the right to shepherd this flock outside the Church of Christ.

* "Others remove the landmarks, and violently take away flocks and feed them" [2]. Whom does he indicate under the title "others" but the heretics, since they are strangers to the bosom of the holy Church? They remove the landmarks in order to overstep the ordinances of the Fathers by walking in a crooked way. Concerning these ordinances it is written: [Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set] (Prov 28:22).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
They drive away the ass of the fatherless, they take the widow's ox for a pledge [3].

He gives another example of injustice, which is that a man seizes the donkey of a poor orphan to profit from it materially, and the poor man cannot contend with the one who seized it. Or one who takes as a pledge the ox of a widow who uses it in her small field, for one reason or another, such as in payment of a small debt or of overdue rent. The wicked do not cease taking what is not theirs, so they covet the use of the orphans' donkey and take the widow's ox as a pledge.

God regards the injustice that falls upon an orphan or a widow as directed to Himself personally, for He is "a father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows" (Ps 68:5); "He doth execute the judgment of the fatherless and widow, and loveth the stranger, in giving him food and raiment" (Deut 10:18). "The LORD preserveth the strangers; he relieveth the fatherless and widow: but the way of the wicked he maketh crooked" (Ps 146:9). "He will not despise the supplication of the fatherless; nor the widow, if she pour out her complaint" (Sir 35:17). God has laid down many commandments concerning care for the orphan and the widow, of which we mention the following:
"Thou shalt not pervert the judgment of the stranger, nor of the fatherless; nor take a widow's raiment to pledge" (Deut 24:17).

"When thou cuttest down thine harvest in thy field, and hast forgot a sheaf in the field, thou shalt not go again to fetch it: it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow: that the LORD thy God may bless thee in all the work of thine hands" (Deut 24:19).
"When thou beatest thine olive tree, thou shalt not go over the boughs again: it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow" (Deut 24:20).
"When thou gatherest the grapes of thy vineyard, thou shalt not glean it afterward: it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow" (Deut 24:21).

"When thou hast made an end of tithing all the tithes of thine increase the third year, which is the year of tithing, and hast given it unto the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow, that they may eat within thy gates, and be filled" (Deut 26:12).
"Cursed be he that perverteth the judgment of the stranger, fatherless, and widow. And all the people shall say, Amen" (Deut 27:19).

"Thus saith the LORD; Execute ye judgment and righteousness, and deliver the spoiled out of the hand of the oppressor: and the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow, do not oppress, nor wrong, neither shed innocent blood in this place" (Jer 22:3).
"And oppress not the widow, nor the fatherless, the stranger, nor the poor; and let none of you imagine evil against his brother in your heart" (Zech 7:10).

"And I will come near to you to judgment; and I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, and against the adulterers, and against false swearers, and against those that oppress the hireling in his wages, the widow and the fatherless, and that turn aside the stranger from his right, and fear not me, saith the LORD of hosts" (Mal 3:5).

* Flee also, O bishop, from him who oppresses the widow, and from him who is strong against the orphan, and from him who is also cruel to his servants with blows or famine or evil dominion; their offerings are hated, and you are not to accept them.

The Didascalia * Priests ought to be compassionate and merciful toward all, bringing back those who have strayed, visiting the sick, and not neglecting the widow, the orphan and the poor, but always [taking care of good things before the Lord and men] (cf. Rom 12:17; 2 Cor 8:21), refraining from all anger, from partiality toward men, and from issuing an unjust judgment, fleeing from every love of money, not hasty in judging against anyone, not harsh in judgment, knowing that we are all debtors through sin.

Polycarp, Bishop of Smyrna * Your ministry will shine with greater brilliance if you resist the distress that befalls the widow and the poor at the hands of a man in authority, with the help of the Church, showing that the commandment of the Lord carries greater weight with you than courtesy to the rich.

St. Ambrose Perhaps among the most important forms of injustice that the Fathers of the early Church took care to warn the people against is usury, and the exploitation of their poor brothers by the rich, who lend to them at interest that causes them countless troubles. We have already spoken about usury in our book "Social Thought among the Fathers of the Church."
St. John Chrysostom presents to us a bitter picture of the rich exploiting poor families, lending to them at exorbitant interest that destroys these families.

* When a family becomes poor, it is driven to borrow in order to survive. But if the creditor demands interest on the debt, then this family falls even deeper into the pit. It is obliged not only to repay the debt but also the interest that accumulates on it. The creditor may claim, even to himself, that he is acting with propriety, but in fact he is acting with great cunning behind the appearance of giving, deliberately harming another.
He trades at the expense of the misfortunes of others, and profits from their calamity.

He seeks to gain material things under the guise of an act of mercy, and thus turns giving into theft. He appears to moor the poor family in a harbor of safety, but in truth he drives the ship toward the rocks. The creditor may ask: Why must I lend money to others when it is useful to me, and not ask for a reward for it? And the answer is that you will receive a reward: in return for the gold you lent on earth, you will receive gold in heaven at a rate of interest far greater than you can imagine.

St. John Chrysostom If we take the symbolic interpretation, the donkey of the orphan which the wicked heretics use signifies the plundering of simple souls from the bosom of the Church and their exploitation, as they bind them with the burden of the error of their faith and their beliefs. He calls him an orphan because he has not realized his sonship to God his Father and to the Church his mother, so he is an orphan of father and mother, and does not enjoy the peace of God and the joy of the Church his mother. The taking of the widow's ox as a pledge signifies the soul that does not perceive the Church as a joyful bride, and so walks in great sorrow like a widow. Such souls the heretics seize with temporary enticements, while they rob them even of their one ox, so that they are inwardly in want and need!

* "They drive away the ass of the fatherless, and take the widow's ox for a pledge" [3]... The ass is used to carry people's burdens. So he is like a kind of ass among the elect, submitting himself to bear earthly matters, bearing burdens for the benefit of men. Often when heretics seduce such a person and draw him away from the bosom of the Church, he is like one whose orphan's ass has been driven away, for they bind him to accept the error of their faith. They draw him away from his inclination toward what is good.

What is understood by the "widow" but the holy Church, which is deprived, for a time, of seeing her slain Bridegroom? Now the ox of this widow is each preacher individually. Rightly he adds here "for a pledge," for when the pledge is taken away, something truly remains in our hands while the other is sought.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
They turn the needy out of the way.
The poor of the earth hide themselves together [4].

The injustice of the wicked does not stop at seizing the possessions of others, lands and fields and flocks, and exploiting the little that the needy and the destitute have; rather, they think that the world was created for them, and that the poor have no right to live. So they spend all their effort to remove them from the earth, until the poor are compelled to flee and hide from their faces.

The unjust find their pleasure when they block the ways of escape before the poor, and threaten them that they will take vengeance on them as vagabonds; and when the poor hide in order to slip out of their hands, they mock them.

* "They turn the needy out of the way, and the meek of the earth are pressed together" [4]. Humility is often indicated by the expression "need" (poverty), and very many who appear meek and humble, if they do not hold fast to discernment, fall by imitating others.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

God Himself inclines His ears to hear the sighs of the simple and the meek whom no one cares about. The psalmist says: "LORD, thou hast heard the groaning of the meek; thou wilt establish their heart, thou wilt incline thine ear to do justice for the fatherless and the crushed, that the man of the earth may no more terrify them" (Ps 10:17-18).

* "His eyes watch the poor" (Ps 10:8), for he persecutes in particular the righteous, of whom it is said: [Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven](a), [He lieth in wait secretly as a lion in his den] (Ps 10:9). By the lion in a pit he means a violent man whose work is deceit... He draws him to himself by violence, with every torment that he can bring upon him... "LORD, thou hast heard the groaning of the meek" (Ps 10:17), this groaning that comes forth while they are burning, since, in the afflictions and troubles of this world, they long for the coming of the day of the Lord... [to do justice for the fatherless and the crushed, that he may no more terrify them] (Ps 10:18), and not for the sake of those who are conformed to the world nor for the proud.
St. Augustine

entries.section: 5. They think they are above the law

paragraphs.text: Behold, as wild asses in the wilderness, they go forth to their work; they rise early for food.
The wilderness yieldeth bread for them and for their children [5].

Job likens the wicked to the wild asses that range in the wilderness with no law to govern them. They rise early in the morning to eat, and look to the wilderness to provide food for their young. So the wicked count themselves above the law, with no work except eating and drinking and pleasures, and providing every pleasure for their children.

"In the wilderness": the wicked wish that the whole earth would be turned into wilderness, where there is no room for laws that govern society, and so injustice can be practiced on a wider scale. The wilderness is the most suitable place for savage people like these; yet there is no wilderness that hides a man from God or places him beyond His reach.

"They go forth to their work," which is robbery, for they have made plunder and the practice of injustice their constant occupation, from which they gain great profits. In their eyes they practice this profession with energy and zeal, for they "rise early for food" with prey. They go forth as to their work, as a man goeth forth unto his work (Ps 104:23), and as the righteous rise early to the Lord and glorify Him, the wicked go forth to the practice of injustice as a task to which they are committed. Thus the wicked rise early to practice their work. They spend the night planning evil, and when the morning dawns they hasten to carry out in practice what is in their hearts. As it was said of Ephraim: "He is like the Canaanite, the balances of deceit are in his hand: he loveth to oppress. And Ephraim said, Yet I am become rich, I have found me out wealth" (Hos 12:7-8).

"The wilderness yieldeth bread for them and for their children," for they provide for themselves and for their children from the plunder that they practice on the roads of the wilderness, instead of providing by honorable means.

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the heretics behave in this way, since they live in a barren wilderness, where they leave the Church, the house of God and His holy vineyard. They are unrestrained; what occupies them is pleasures and temporal goods, and they do not want any restraint or submission to any ordering such as fasting, prayer, prostrations (metanoias), etc., and if divine discipline comes upon them they do not care. Thus they live in a barren wilderness without fruit of the Spirit. They resemble Ishmael, of whom it was said: he will be a wild man; his hand will be against every man, and every man's hand against him (Gen 16:11-12).

* "Others, like wild asses (onagers) in the wilderness, go forth to their work" [5]. For the onager is a wild ass. Here the heretics are rightly likened to wild asses, since they are unrestrained in their pleasures and are strangers to the bonds of faith and sober-mindedness. Therefore it is written: [A wild ass used to the wilderness, that snuffeth up the wind at her pleasure] (Jer 24:2). A person is a wild ass used to the wilderness when he does not till the soil of his heart with the loftiness of discipline, and so dwells where there is no fruit... This is not the work of God, but their own work, that they do not follow sound teachings but follow their lusts. For it is written: [He that walketh in a perfect way, he shall serve me] (Ps 6:101).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* I know that what I am saying is painful, but how much benefit it contains! If the rich man had found someone to give him such advice, instead of flattering him and saying what he wanted to hear and drawing him into sliding into a life of extravagance, he would not have fallen into that abyss. He would not have come under that unbearable torment, repenting too late, seeking comfort; but everyone was working to give him pleasure, handing him over to the hell of fire.

I wish that we would preach and speak always and continually on this subject, for the Holy Bible says: "In all thy works remember thy latter end, and thou shalt never do amiss" (Sir 7:40), and likewise it says: [Prepare your work for your departure, and make everything ready for the road] (cf. Prov 24:27).

St. John Chrysostom * However green the wicked may be, they will perish, for they have been kept for the fire... These flourish in the happiness of the world, and perish by the power of God. They do not perish in the same way as they flourish; they flourish for a time, and perish eternally. They flourish in what is not truly good, and perish in real torments.

St. Augustine The psalmist was looking at the wicked living in peace in this world and in prosperity, like those who are in happiness, and he envied them and was jealous of them; therefore he confessed, saying: "But as for me, my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped. For I was envious at the proud (sinners), when I saw the prosperity of the wicked. For there are no bands in their death, and their body is fat. They are not in trouble as other men; neither are they plagued with other men. Therefore pride compasseth them about as a chain; they put on their injustice as a garment" (Ps 73:2-6).

* I observed the sinners and saw them in peace. What peace? A temporal, temporary, earthly and fallen peace, and yet this (peace) I ask from God. I saw that those who do not serve God have what I desired in order that I might serve God, so my feet slipped, and my steps slipped. But why do the wicked have this...? They cannot avoid their death, and their punishment is perpetual... Now I knew why they have peace and prosper on the earth. For death surely awaits them eternally; they do not avoid these things and will not be able to be saved from them... for their punishment will not be temporary but fixed and eternal.
St. Augustine

entries.section: 6. They want evil, and the Lord wants good

paragraphs.text: 6 They reap their fodder in the field, and they glean the vineyard of the wicked. 7 They cause the naked to lodge without clothing, that they have no covering in the cold. 8 They are wet with the showers of the mountains, and embrace the rock for want of a shelter. 9 "They pluck the fatherless from the breast, and take a pledge of the poor. 10 They cause him to go naked without clothing, and being hungry they carry the sheaves. 11 They make oil within their walls, and tread their winepresses, and suffer thirst.
They reap their fodder in the field, and they glean the vineyard of the wicked [6].

Since they feel that they are above the law, they reap the fields of others and offer their produce as fodder for their animals. It is as though they count their animals better than the owners of the fields, so they do not care about the hunger of the owners of the seized fields, even though the produce is offered not to men but to animals.
Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the field here and the vineyard refer to the Holy Bible. For the heretics pick passages from it and distort their meanings in service of their own passions.

* "They reap a field that is not theirs, and they gather by violence the vineyard of him whom they oppress" [6]. The field refers to the wide realm of Holy Scripture, which the heretics reap as though it were not theirs, for they pick from it passages to bear meanings quite far from what they mean. This is also described by the title "vineyard," which offers clusters of virtues through the words of truth. They are like those who press upon the owner of the vineyard, the author of Holy Scripture, with violence, for they distort by violence the meanings of the words of Holy Scripture. As (the Lord) said: [Thou hast made me to serve with thy sins, thou hast wearied me with thine iniquities] (Isa 24:43). And they gather the wine of that vineyard, for they gather together clusters of passages from it after turning them aside to their own notions.

The field or the vineyard can also be understood as the universal Church, which the corrupt preachers reap, and they press upon her Creator in His members, "gathering the wine together," by gaining control of persons who seem to be righteous.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Origen believes that the heretics first receive the deposit of faith, and later turn aside from it. [Heretics begin with faith, and then later turn aside from the way of faith and from the truth of the Church's teaching.] In their pride, the heretics search the divine Scripture not to discover the truth, but to confirm their own doctrines. Henri de Lubac says in his book on Origen:

[One must receive the faith in God in the Spirit in which the Church teaches us, and not behave like the heretics who search the Scripture merely to find what confirms their own doctrines. Their pride lifts them "higher than the cedars of Lebanon." Their sophistry is full of deceit. It is of no use for them to claim that they have a tradition descending to them from the Apostles, for they are masters of error.

While the faithful Christian never strays from the great tradition, in order to confirm their lies they wish to make us worship a "Christ" whom they have invented in a "wilderness," whereas our true Christ reveals Himself "inside the house." They distort those vessels of gold and silver, which are the holy texts, in order to fashion them in accordance with their passions. They are thieves and fornicators, who lay hands on the divine words with one purpose, namely to distort them with their perverse interpretations. They are counterfeiters, for they have coined their doctrines outside the Church. False teachers and false prophets, they spin out of the daughters of their own thoughts what they propose. They are the liars of whom Ezekiel spoke, who by their deceitful trickery daub their idols, which are their hollow doctrines, with sweetness for the one who listens to them, to make their deviation more certain. All of them claim that Jesus is their teacher and embrace Him. But their kiss is the kiss of Judas.]
They cause the naked to lodge without clothing, that they have no covering in the cold [7].
Again, since they are subject to no law, they strip others of their clothes and drive them out, so these spend the night without coverings to protect them from the bitter cold.
