Thus the heretics spend all their effort to strip the believers of their garments, that is, the true fellowship with the Lord Christ, of whom the Apostle Paul says: "Ye have put on Christ" (Gal 3:27), "and have put on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him" (Col 3:10). He also says:
"And that ye put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness" (Eph 4:24).
"Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil" (Eph 6:11).
"Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering" (Col 3:12).
"And above all these things put on love, which is the bond of perfectness" (Col 3:14).

* "They drive out the naked, and take their garments, those who have no covering in the cold" [7]. As garments cover the body, so good works do for the soul. Therefore it was said: [Blessed is he that watcheth, and keepeth his garments, lest he walk naked, and they see his shame] (Rev 15:16). When the heretics shatter the good works in someone's mind, they clearly strip off his garments. It was well said: "They have no covering in the cold," for the covering is related to righteousness, and the cold to sin.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* "Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth" (1 Cor 8:5).
And as we put off the old man and his deeds, we put on the new man, created after God (Eph 22:4, 24), and meditate in the law of God day and night, with a humble mind and a pure conscience.
Let us cast off from us all hypocrisy and deceit, keeping far from all hypocrisy and cunning.
May we pledge ourselves to the love of God and love of neighbor, that we may become a new creation, partaking of new wine...
Therefore let us keep the feast as we ought.

* We need to put on the Lord Jesus in order that we may be able to celebrate the feast with Him. Now we put Him on when we love virtue and are enemies of evil... when we love righteousness and not injustice, and honor contentment and have strength of mind, and do not forget the poor but open our doors to all men, and do not forget humility of mind and hate pride.
Pope Abba Athanasius the Apostolic * If the garment of your soul is "covetousness," put on another instead of it, and come, take off your old garment and do not put it on again.
I beg you to take off fornication and uncleanness, and to put on the shining garment of purity.
I command you this before the Bridegroom Jesus enters and looks at your garment.
I leave you a long time for repentance. It is an ample opportunity for you to take off, wash, put on, and enter!
St. Cyril of Jerusalem They are wet with the showers of the mountains, and embrace the rock for want of a shelter [8].

As the wicked work to rob the believers of their faith in the Lord Christ, to deprive them of the divine garments and the heavenly covering, these poor people become naked, suffering from the rains of the mountains, where they have no shelter in which to take cover from the rain, and they look for stones to embrace, or some rock that might cover them from the rain.

* "They are wet with the rains of the mountains, and embrace the stones for want of a garment" [8]. The rains of the mountains are the words of the teachers. Of these same mountains it was said in the voice of the holy Church: [I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills] (Ps 1:121). These persons are drenched by the rains of the mountains, those who are filled to the end with the streams of the holy Fathers. And the garment that we receive as a covering is good conduct, with which a man is covered so that the filth of his corruption may be covered in the eyes of Almighty God. So it is written: [Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered] (Ps 1:32). Who are those whom we understand by the title "stones" but the strong ones within the borders of the holy Church, those to whom it is proclaimed by the Shepherd: [Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house] (1 Pet 2:5). So also those who, on the basis of their practical conduct, have no complacency in them, fly to the protection of the holy martyrs, and practice tears and supplications at their holy relics in order to obtain forgiveness through their intercession. What then are these doing by such abasement but embracing stones, since they lack the covering of good practice?
Pope Gregory (the Great)
They pluck the fatherless from the breast, and take a pledge of the poor [9].

In their violence the wicked snatch the orphan while he is nursing at his mother's breasts, and seek out the poor to use them as pledges. They have no pity on the nursing infant that he is deprived of his mother, nor on the mother that she is deprived of her infant also. They choose a critical time, snatching the infant while he is nursing, and they care nothing for his cries and his hunger!
Pharaoh killed the children of the Hebrews, and so did Herod in order to kill the child King; these snatched the children and infants from their mothers' breasts with the sword.

Some think that the unjust, after they kill the fathers, snatch the infants in order to deprive them of their mothers. Others think that they snatch the infants as slaves, as happened in the days of Nehemiah (Neh 5:5).

* "They use violence in preying upon the fatherless, and ruin the common flock of the poor" [9]... The heretics use violence in preying upon the orphans, for they attack with violence the weak minds of the believers by words and deeds.

As for "the common flock of the poor," they are the uneducated multitudes, who, if they had received the wealth of true knowledge, would not have had the covering of their faith taken from them. For the original teachers are like a kind of nobles (senators) within the borders of the holy Church, multiplying knowledge in the heart and increasing the true wealth that is in them, whereas the heretics ruin the common flock of the poor, taking the covering of faith from the uneducated, making them naked through their poisonous preaching, while they are not able to do this with the educated.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
They cause him to go naked without clothing, and being hungry they carry the sheaves [10].

* "They take away the ears of wheat from the naked, and from those who walk without covering, and from the hungry" [10]. He says "naked" and then repeats "those who walk without covering," for there is a difference between being naked and walking naked. Everyone who does neither what is good nor what is evil is naked and trifling. But he who does evil "walks naked," for since he lacks the covering of good practice, he walks in the way of evil.

But some know the evil of their misery, and hasten to be satisfied with the bread of righteousness, and hunger to receive the sayings of Holy Scripture. When these change in mind, the sayings of the Fathers, for the reform of their minds, become as though they carried ears of wheat from a good harvest. And so the heretics take the ears of wheat from the naked, and from those who walk without covering, and from the hungry.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
They make oil within their walls.
They tread their winepresses, and suffer thirst [11].

The wicked do not cease from trampling upon the children of God in order to humiliate and crush them. But they do not know that as they tread upon them with their feet, the believers are turned into perfume, and into joyful spiritual wine.

What does he mean by saying: "within their walls"? The wicked wish to humiliate the believers and trample them inside the walls of the city, that is, they break into their places and insult them in their homes. But God turns the city into a holy winepress, that the believers may share in their crucified Christ, who says: [I have trodden the winepress alone] (Isa 63:3). The wicked tread the winepress, and the winepress overflows with wine that rejoices the heart of God and in which the heavenly ones take pride, while the wicked come out of the winepress in a state of thirst, obtaining nothing from their violence but emptiness.

* "They rest at midday among the heaps (threshing floors), thirsting for the winepress of trodden wine" [11]. All who persecute the holy Church, what do they do but tread the winepress? This is permitted through the divine dispensation, so that the clusters of the soul may overflow with spiritual wine, since they are stripped of the corruptible body, and so flow in the heavenly places as in a vessel. For while the wicked tread upon the righteous, they are like those who place clusters of grapes under their feet.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* The cluster does not become wine, nor the olive oil, unless the stone of the press passes over them.
* The soul does not return to God unless it is torn away from the world, and nothing truly tears it away but toil and pain.
St. Augustine

entries.section: 7. They think that God does not pay attention!

paragraphs.text: 12 From the pain men groan, and the soul of the wounded crieth out, yet God payeth no attention to injustice. 13 "They are among those that rebel against the light; they know not the ways thereof, nor abide in the paths thereof.
From the pain men groan, and the soul of the wounded crieth out, yet God payeth no attention to injustice [12].

Surely God hears the groans of the sufferers and the cry of the wounded, but since He turns the evil of the wicked into good for the sufferers, He seems like One who pays no attention to injustice. These are our feelings when injustice rules and wounds the believers, and we think that God is busy elsewhere than with His Church, and does not care about her wounds and the injustice that has fallen upon her! Perhaps Job means here that while the sufferers groan and the wounded cry out, the wicked mock them and go further in their evils, looking at God as if, in His heavens, He does not care about the injustice that falls upon men, whoever they may be!
The Jesuit translation has: "And in the cities men groan," so injustice does not stop at the villages but extends also to the cities.

"God does not pay attention to injustice," that is, He does not judge them quickly, but gives them time, that perhaps they may repent, returning to Him. He prolongs His longsuffering toward them, and may leave them all their life on earth, and not expose their folly here, until their souls are required, and they are counted fools and silly. As it was said to the rich man shortly before his soul was required: "Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee" (Lk 12:20). And as it was said of the rich man who gathers wealth by injustice: "He that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end shall be a fool" (Jer 17:11).

* [They cause men to groan from out of the cities] [12]. Cities are so called from the people who live together, and so the churches of the true faith are not improperly expressed by the cities... For this harmony among the people who live together was established by the Lord in the Gospels, even when He distinguished between places, when He wished to feed the people with five loaves. He commanded them to sit down by fifties or by hundreds in orderly arrangement, so that the multitudes of the believers might take their food in separate places but united together... But the heretics often shatter the united life and harmony of the good by attaching themselves to those in authority among the wicked of this world; therefore it was rightly said in this place: [they cause men to groan from out of the cities].
[The soul of the wounded crieth out]... for the soul of the righteous is wounded when the faith of the weak is shaken... But God does not allow him (the wicked) to pass without punishment.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
They are among those that rebel against the light.

entries.section: 7. They think that God does not pay attention!

paragraphs.text: They know not the ways thereof, nor abide in the paths thereof [13].

Since the wicked think that God does not care about His believers, and does not move in the face of the injustice that falls upon them, they rebel against God, the true Light. And they lose insight and are struck with blindness, so they do not know the ways of God, nor walk in His paths.

Some see that those who sin against the light of the divine commandment, while confessing that they know God, the true Light, are nevertheless rebels against this knowledge that they have received, for they do not wish to walk according to it.

Others interpret this phrase literally. Although they have the light of day, they choose the night that suits their evils; for this reason evils are called "the works of darkness" (Eph 5:11): "For every one that doeth evil hateth the light, neither cometh to the light, lest his deeds should be reproved. But he that doeth truth cometh to the light, that his deeds may be made manifest, that they are wrought in God" (Jn 3:20-21).

* For those who first rebelled while knowing afterward became blind and no longer know, as it is written: [Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful] (Rom 21:1, 28). It is added concerning them a little later: [God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not convenient]. For since they did not wish to glorify Him whom they knew, they were given a sense of rejection, and were left to this fate, that they no longer know how to appreciate the evils that they have done... Now those who do not care to do the plain good works no longer receive understanding of what is purer.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Thus, when the Lord Jesus saw the heavy burdens of the sinner, He wept. For He did not allow the Church alone to weep, but we see Him also having compassion on His beloved, and saying to the dead man, "Come forth" (Jn 11:43). That is, you who were cast into the darkness of conscience and the captivity of your sins and the prison of your crimes, come forth. Show your sins and you will be justified, for "with the mouth confession is made unto salvation" (Rom 10:10)...

Grant me, O Lord, that You come to my tomb and pour out tears over me, for my eyes have dried up and are no longer able to pour out such tears for my transgressions. If You weep, O Lord, over me (as over Lazarus), I shall be rescued... You call me from this tomb of my body, saying: "Come forth," so that my thinking may no longer be confined within the limits of this narrow body of mine, but go out toward Christ and live in the light, and I no longer think of the works of darkness but of the works of light.
St. Ambrose

14 The murderer riseth with the light, he killeth the poor and needy, and in the night he is as a thief. 15 The eye also of the adulterer waiteth for the evening, saying, No eye shall watch me: and he putteth a covering on his face. 16 In the dark they dig through houses; in the daytime they shut themselves up. They know not the light. 17 For the morning is to them the same as the shadow of death: for they know the terrors of the shadow of death.
The murderer riseth with the light.
He killeth the poor and needy, and in the night he is as a thief [14].
Job presents to us three kinds of wicked men who flee from the light: the murderer, who even if he kills in the daytime flees from the light like a thief hiding in the midst of the darkness.

And the adulterer, who waits for the coming of evening to practice his evil, thinking that the darkness hides his evil from the eyes of men; and the one who digs through houses, who shuts himself up in the daytime and sees that the night makes it easy for him to attack houses and escape.

When the wicked man rebels and defies God, and rises against the believers to kill them, he is like the murderer who in boldness kills openly in the midst of the day, aware that there is no one who can stand before him and stop him. He kills the poor and needy, not caring about the Father of the poor. Since he does this in defiance of God, the true Light, the darkness of his wicked deeds comes upon him, and he is like the thief who works in the darkness of the night. He is called a thief working by night after having been a bold murderer killing in the midst of the light of day. For after a man practices his evils with violence, without fear even of God, sin robs him of his strength and courage, and he becomes feeble and fears even his own shadow, so he is like a thief who is afraid lest someone catch him.

* "And in the night he is as a thief" [14]. For in the night of his temptations, although without strength, he shows a hand of cruelty. He advises those whom he sees as having authority with evil counsels, and goes here and there and seeks by all he can to do harm to the righteous. Rightly he is called "as a thief," because in all his evil counsels he fears lest someone catch him.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Our enemy is skilled, my dear, and a deceiver is he who fights us. He prepares himself to attack the brave victors, to make them weak. But the feeble ones who are his he does not fight, for they are captives delivered over to him.

Who has two wings to fly from him with, so that the arrows he hurls toward him do not reach him? The spiritual see him fighting, and his weapon does not prevail over their bodies. All the sons of light do not fear him, for darkness flees from before the light. The sons of the Good One do not fear the evil one, for He has given them to tread upon him with their feet (Gen 3:15).
St. Aphrahat The eye also of the adulterer waiteth for the evening.
Saying, No eye shall watch me.
And he putteth a covering on his face [15].

After comparing the wicked man to the murderer who kills in the daytime, he returned and compared him to the thief who fears the light and sneaks in by night lest someone catch him. Now he compares him to the adulterer who awaits the coming of night and the descent of darkness in order to practice his lusts far from the watching of any eye.

The adulterer practices his evil by night, so that no eye may watch him, hiding his face lest the husband of the woman with whom he commits adultery discover him and take vengeance on him, for "jealousy is the rage of a man: therefore he will not spare in the day of vengeance" (Prov 6:34-35).
He spends every effort to plan adultery so that no one may see him; therefore the Apostle Paul commands us: "Put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh" (Rom 13:14).

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the adulterer practices the bodily relation deceitfully, not seeking children for himself but the satisfaction of his vain lusts. So the heretics adulterate the word of God, seeking not spiritual offspring, the children of God, but the display of their eloquence and their knowledge, and so they are rightly counted adulterers!

* "The eye of the adulterer also watches for the waning of the light, saying: No eye sees me" [15]. There is nothing that hinders him. Let this be understood later, looking to the fact that he who wishes to commit adultery seeks darkness.

But since this passage was said against the heretics, it is fitting that this matter be understood in a mystical sense. Paul says: [For we are not as many, which corrupt (falsify, adulterate) the word of God] (2 Cor 17:2). For the adulterer does not seek offspring for himself, but seeks pleasure in the bodily intercourse, and so every wicked man, and whoever is rightly enslaved to vainglory, is said to falsify the word of God. For he does not seek to beget children for God by means of the holy word of proclamation, but seeks to display his knowledge. For whoever is drawn to speech through the desire for glory endures his pains for the sake of appearance more than for the begetting of children.

Rightly he added here: "No eye sees me," for adultery that is committed inside is truly very hard for the eye of a man to penetrate. This is committed by the (woman) who is bold and very much at ease, who does not fear that any man might see her in a way that would make him blush with shame.

Besides this, it must be known that just as the one who commits adultery binds himself unlawfully to the body of another man's wife, so all the heretics, when they push a believing soul into their error, are like those who push another man's wife into this way. The soul that has been married spiritually to God and united with Him as in the bridal chamber of love, when it is led into the corruption of teachings by the instigation of the wicked, is like another's wife who has been defiled by the corrupter.

Well was it said: [and he disguises his face with a mask]. The adulterer hides his face so that he may not be known. Now every man who lives by evil, whether in thought or in action, puts a mask on his face, for since he sinks to this through corruption of teaching or corruption of conduct, he does so to avoid being known in the judgment by Almighty God. Therefore the Lord will say to such persons in the end: [I know you not: depart from me, ye that work evil] (Mt 23:7). And what is the "face" of the human heart but its resemblance after the likeness of God?
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* The thoughts of these people do not trouble us much if we look at their behavior. They reject (God) as judge over them, He whom nothing deceives. They do not accept that He knows hidden things, for they fear that their hidden matters will be exposed by the light. But since the Lord knows their deeds, He hands them over to darkness. It was said: [In the night he is as a thief, and the eye of the adulterer waiteth for the darkness, saying, No eye shall watch me: and he putteth a covering on his face] (Job 14:24-15). Everyone who avoids the light loves darkness, seeking to hide, although he is not hidden from God, who knows not only what goes on in matters, but what is in thought, what is in the depths of men and in their minds. In Ben Sirach it says: [Who seeth me? Darkness is round about me, and the walls cover me, and nobody seeth me; what need I to fear?] (Sir 23:26). Though he lies upon his bed thinking thus, he is seized when he does not expect it (Sir 23:30-31). It was said: [It will be a reproach to him, for he knew not the fear of the Lord].

St. Ambrose * Pride begets apostasy, so the soul walks in darkness, and as it misuses the freedom of its will it falls into other sins, corrupting its being with the adulterers; he who was created as a companion of the angels becomes a keeper of swine.

* O bride... He knows the uncleanness of your heart and the defilement of your thoughts; therefore He has granted you that your old man be crucified with Him, so that you no longer live under the authority of darkness, but in the freedom of the children of God.
St. Augustine In the dark they dig through houses.
In the daytime they shut themselves up.
They know not the light [16].

By night it is easy to attack houses, and therefore the Lord Christ demands of us to watch: "If the goodman of the house had known what hour the thief would come, he would have watched, and not have suffered his house to be broken through" (Lk 12:39).

What are the houses that the wicked dig through but their inner man? For in the midst of the darkness of the evil will they corrupt their minds, their hearts, their consciences and their depths, so that evil may occupy the seat of command in them.

* [In the dark they dig through their houses, which they had marked for themselves in the daytime: they know not the light]. What does he indicate here by the title "houses" but the consciences in which we dwell when we practice something or occupy ourselves? Therefore it is said to the one who is healed: [Return to thine own house, and shew how great things God hath done unto thee] (Lk 39:8). That is, from now on guard against the habit of evil sin, and return to your conscience, and use the voice of preaching... So "in the dark they dig through their houses," for they seek to corrupt the minds of the good... The wicked man who fears correction ends in the darkness of grief.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* No one can enlighten himself, for all light comes from heaven, from "the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father" (Jn 15:26). By Him we see the Son, the Word, as we see the Father; indeed, by Him we see the truth of ourselves, for He enlightens our insight so that we uncover our weakness and feel our need of salvation. By Him shines for us "the illumination of the gospel of the glory of Christ... For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor 4:4-6).

* As it is written: [In thy light shall we see light](b), that is, by the illumination of the Holy Spirit [That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world](c)... So the glory of the Only-Begotten Son appears, and He grants the knowledge of God to the true worshippers.

* From Him came forth that saying from His sweet, saving lips: "They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick... I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance" (Mt 9:12-13). What excuse have you then? What excuse has any man, since the Lord has said this? He wishes to cleanse you of your weakness and to show you the light after the darkness.

* "They looked unto him, and were lightened: and their faces were not ashamed"(d). Blessed is he who bears this light that reveals sins without being ashamed of a conscience defiled by evil deeds... on the day of judgment. When the Lord comes, who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of the hearts (1 Cor 4:5), sinners also will rise to shame and disgrace... They will see in their souls the ugliness of sin and its marks, which are more dreadful than the darkness of the eternal fire, and the wicked will be ashamed forever, as the marks of sin are drawn before their eyes, having left their mark on their bodies... like an engraving that does not vanish, they remember it continually within their souls.
St. Basil the Great For the morning is to them the same as the shadow of death.
For they know the terrors of the shadow of death [17].
The Jesuit translation has: "For the morning and the shadow of death are one and the same to them."

The rising of the sun with the beginning of the day is welcomed by the righteous who seek the light of the Sun of righteousness, and welcome the work of the Lord Christ in their lives. But the wicked are troubled by the morning, and curse the sun because it exposes them, not only before others but even before their own depths, so they know the terrors of the shadow of death, and feel shame. They are confused and terrified, and fear of men, not of God, comes upon them, and dread even takes control of them.

The wicked wish that the morning would not come, but that their life would remain a night without interruption, for it is in harmony with the darkness of their consciences. But the righteous rejoice in the morning so that they may enjoy the light of the Sun of righteousness in them, and their life becomes an uninterrupted light, in harmony in their inner depths. The Apostle says: "But ye, brethren, are not in darkness, that that day should overtake you as a thief. Ye are all the children of light, and the children of the day: we are not of the night, nor of darkness" (1 Thess 5:4-5).

* "If the morning appears suddenly, they think it the shadow of death" [17]. For the "morning" is the mind of the righteous man which removes the darkness of his sins, which are dispelled by the light of eternity. It was said in a similar way of the holy Church: [Who is she that looketh forth as the morning?] (Song 10:6). By the same measure every righteous person who shines with the light of righteousness is at present built up to the heights with honors. In the same way, by the same measure, the darkness of death comes before the eyes of the wicked, so that those who remember that they have practiced evil deeds fear lest their condition be set right.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* "The rich man also died, and was buried" (Lk 16:22)... Do not pass lightly over this phrase... my beloved. For the tables inlaid with silver, the couches, the carpets, the splendid clothing and the other various kinds of furnishings, the perfumed oils and ointments, the great quantities of aged wine, the large amounts of food, the splendid tableware, the flatterers, the guards and the servants, and all the displays of boasting and show, fade and wither... All things are dust and ashes, mournful tunes and mourning, for no one can offer help after it is too late, or bring back the soul that has departed. Then the power of gold and excessive wealth is tested, for from among the crowd of those present he was taken naked and alone, and could take with him nothing of his abundance, but he was taken without companion or helper, and none of those who used to serve him could rescue him from the punishment and retribution, but he departed far from his retinue; he was taken away alone to bear the unbearable torment. "All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field: The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: because the spirit of the LORD bloweth upon it: surely the people is grass. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever" (Isa 6:40-8).

Truly death came and extinguished all this luxury and led him away as a captive with bowed head, groaning with shame, unable to speak, trembling with fear, as though his enjoyment of all this luxury had been a dream.
St. John Chrysostom

18 He is light upon the face of the waters; their portion is cursed in the earth; he turneth not toward the way of the vineyards. 19 Drought and heat consume the snow waters: so doth the grave those which have sinned. 20 The womb forgetteth him; the worm feedeth sweetly on him; he shall be no more remembered; and the wicked shall be broken as a tree.
He is light upon the face of the waters.
Their portion is cursed in the earth.
He turneth not toward the way of the vineyards [18].

After presenting the wicked who practice murder, adultery and theft as sons of darkness, who seek the night and fear the morning, Job moves us to the extension of their work not over the whole earth only but even in the seas. It is as though the earth has become small in their eyes, and they go off to the seas.

Some think that the robbers of the seas use light ships on the face of the waters so that they can move quickly from one channel to another, attacking one ship to catch up with another, plundering and looting; whereas working the land, especially tilling the land and planting vineyards, is a demeaning profession that does not bring benefits like plunder and looting.

We can also say that Job looks upon the wicked, the murderers, the adulterers and the housebreakers, as appearing like terrifying tyrants, but in reality they are in great weakness, like those who travel on the face of the waters as light ships amid stormy winds and violent waves. The earth curses them, so they find no shelter even under the vines, and they flee toward the seas hoping to hide, but the storms destroy them. But the righteous are a blessing on the earth, walking in the way of the vineyards, that is, the way of the spiritual wine that fills souls with joy and rejoicing.

* "He is light upon the face of the waters" [18]... The mind of the wicked man is "lighter than the surface of the water," so that any breath of some temptation that touches it draws it without any delay and resistance. If we imagine the unstable heart of any wicked man, what do we find in it but the surface of water facing a wind? At one time any breath of anger draws it, at another a breeze of pride, a breeze of lust, envy and vanity; all these breaths drive it and move it. Thus it is light on the surface of the water, every wind drawing it into error before it when error comes....

[Let their portion be cursed in the earth, and let him not walk in the way of the vineyards] [18]. He who does what is upright in the present life and faces calamities is truly seen to be in travail in his affliction; he is perfect, but for the sake of the eternal inheritance. But he who does what is evil..., and does not restrain himself from evil works because of the abundance of (temporal) blessings that he receives, is seen to be truly in luxury, but is bound with the bond of the eternal curse. Therefore it is rightly said here: "Let their portion be cursed in the earth"...

"The way of the vineyards" is the uprightness of the churches. Let us understand that the heretic or any carnal man leaves the uprightness of the churches or the way of the vineyards when he does not hold fast to the right faith or the right ordering of the life of the righteous... Therefore [walking in the way of the vineyards] is holding fast to the Fathers of the holy Church like hanging clusters of a vine, where one becomes drunk with their words in the love of eternity.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Drought and heat consume the snow waters: so doth the grave those which have sinned [19].

When the wicked try to escape the curse of the earth upon them by going off to the seas, destruction besieges them there. So they are like pieces of ice that melt before the heat and the intense burning. They suffer from spiritual drought, and sink down toward the abyss.
The womb forgetteth him; the worm feedeth sweetly on him.
He shall be no more remembered; and the wicked shall be broken as a tree [20].
"The womb forgetteth him": the wicked man thinks that everyone fears him and that everyone remembers him, but soon the mother who bore him forgets him.

Truly the Church does not forget all humanity, but groans for every soul that perishes. She cries out with her heavenly Bridegroom: "Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee" (Isa 49:15). But whoever insists on his evil and his ingratitude, the Church does not compel him to salvation, but by his isolating himself from Christ, the Giver of salvation, he hears the divine voice: "I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity" (Mt 7:23), and the Church says to him that she has forgotten him and no longer remembers him!

And "the worm feedeth sweetly on him" means that God does not condemn him to the death of being hung on the walls to be eaten by the birds of the air or being thrown to wild beasts, but leaves the wicked man to die and be buried in the grave, and the worm finds him sweet! He dies like all men, lies down in quiet until he stands before the Judge, and his evil judges him, and his fate is with the devil and his angels.

In ancient times they believed that worms exist in the skin and in all parts of the body, and that it is they that destroy the body. Roberts, in his book Oriental Illustrations, quoted from an ancient Indian medical work that there are 18 kinds of worms in the different parts of the body. The sick in India used to say: [Ah, my body has become a nest for worms, creeping through my whole frame]. [Behold, the worm eats my body without ceasing].

"He shall be no more remembered; and the wicked shall be broken as a tree": by his death he has no further remembrance, but men forget him, counting him as a tree that has been broken! Indeed God also forgets him, if the expression is right, so as to say to him on the day of judgment that He does not know him (Lk 13:27). God no longer remembers him, that is, He does not grant him His mercies and His grace, so he is as one forgotten by God.

* "May he have no remembrance, may he be crushed like an unfruitful stump" [20]. He who remains to the end of his life subject to evil habits will no longer have remembrance with his Creator, that is, the remembrance of the important matters on high for such a (wicked) man, which could make him turn back from his evil. For he realizes that he deserves to be completely blotted out from the remembrance of his Creator.

But let us bear in mind that God cannot be said "to remember" in a precise manner, for He who cannot forget, in what manner can He remember? Rather this is our way: to remember those whom we embrace, and to forget those from whom we keep ourselves far; for it is said of God that He remembers when He gives gifts, using human language, and that He forgets when He abandons one who is in transgression...

Thus it is written: [The eyes of the LORD are in every place, beholding the wicked and the good] (Prov 3:15). And the psalmist says: [The face of the LORD is against them that do evil, to cut off the remembrance of them from the earth] (Ps 16:34). Therefore He looks upon the person whom He punishes, but He counts as though He did not previously know these persons. For He will say to some in the end: [I know you not whence ye are; depart from me, all ye workers of evil] (Lk 27:13). Thus He sees and forgets the life of the wicked in a wonderful manner, in that He issues a harsh sentence, and forgets the remembrance of mercy.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Tell me and inform me, if you saw the leader of a gang roaming the roads, lying in wait at the crossroads for passersby, robbing the farmer and hiding gold and silver in caves and crevices, storing the stolen goods in hiding places, and acquiring many clothes and slaves from plunder and theft, tell me, would you consider this person happy because of his wealth and riches, or would you consider him wretched because of the punishment that awaits him? True, he has not yet been arrested, nor handed over to the judge, nor thrown into prison, there is no accusation against him, and the truth of his affair is not yet known or spread, but he eats and drinks lavishly and indulges in many pleasures; and yet we do not consider him happy because of the evident present possessions that he has, but we consider him wretched because of the torment that awaits him.

You must think in the same way about these greedy rich men, for they are a kind of robbers, lying in wait on the roads and robbing passersby, and hiding their goods in their houses as in caves and crevices. Therefore we do not consider them happy for what they have, but wretched for what awaits them, and because of the terrible trial and the merciless divine judgment and the outer darkness that await them.
True, robbers often escape from the hands of men, and yet, with this knowledge of ours, we pray for ourselves and for our enemies that we may avoid that life with its hateful wealth.

But with God we cannot say that, for no one will escape His judgment; rather all who live by theft and fraud will bring upon themselves an eternal punishment without end, like this rich man (in the parable of Lazarus and the rich man).

Beloved, if we recall all these thoughts in our minds, we shall no longer consider the happy man to be the rich man but the good man, and we shall not consider the wretched man to be the poor man but the wicked man. "Do not take into account what is present, but what is to come."
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 10. Their rod does not rest upon the righteous

paragraphs.text: 21 He wrongeth the barren that beareth not, and doeth not good to the widow. 22 He draweth the mighty by his power: he riseth up, and no man is sure of life. 23 He giveth him safety, and he trusteth; yet his eyes are upon their ways. 24 They are exalted for a little while, but are gone, and brought low; they are gathered as all, and cut off as the tops of the ears of corn. 25 And if it be not so now, who will make me a liar, and make my speech nothing worth?
He wrongeth the barren that beareth not, and doeth not good to the widow [21].
Evil is unable to wrong the fruitful mother, but wrongs the barren who has not borne; and as it is unable not to do good to the bride rejoicing in her bridegroom, but does not do good to the widow.
Who is the barren one here? And who is the widow?

The soul that does not enjoy the work of God's grace, and so cannot bear witness to the Gospel of Christ and have sons for the Lord, is counted barren. It was said of the Church that there is none barren in her, but all bear twins (Song 4:2; 6:6). Such souls, fruitful by the Holy Spirit, no wicked man can touch; rather his resistance and his attacks against them are turned into continual victories, and they enjoy crowns of glory.

What the wicked man practices against the bride united with her heavenly Bridegroom is counted only as good to her, for her splendor increases all the more, and she enjoys fellowship in the Cross with her Bridegroom; but she who is widowed by leaving her Bridegroom as one dead and not existing in her heart and mind, the wicked man does not do good to her, but destroys her by his evil.
Pope Gregory (the Great) also offers the following symbolic interpretation of this passage.

* "He feeds the barren, her who does not bear, and does no good to the widow" [21]. Who is she that is indicated by the barren, but the flesh that seeks temporal things alone, being unable to bring forth good thoughts? And who is counted a widow but the soul? The Creator wished to unite it with Himself; the marriage came in the bridal chamber of the fleshly womb, and as the psalmist testifies, saying: [as a bridegroom coming out of his chamber] (Ps 5:19).

Rightly she is called a widow, since her husband submitted to death for her, and now lives in another place in heaven, hidden from her eyes. Therefore the wicked man feeds the barren, and despises doing good to the widow, because he does not care for the soul and its life, while he obeys the lusts of the flesh.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
He draweth the mighty by his power.

entries.section: 10. Their rod does not rest upon the righteous

paragraphs.text: He riseth up, and no man is sure of life [22].

Job sees that the wicked man in his pride and self-esteem troubles even the great ones on earth, and the strongest of the strong cannot stand before him. And when he rages, in his fury he strikes down all those around him, no one is sure of his life, and at the same time he himself is not sure of his life, for "his hand will be against every man, and every man's hand against him" (Gen 16:12).

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the wicked is the heretic man who in the pride of his heart thinks that he is more skilled than all, despising others. He is puffed up with his learning and knowledge, although his knowledge is not true, because all that concerns him is his own glory and honor. Therefore, as the Apostle Paul says: [God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty] (1 Cor 1:27).

* John says: [He that saith, I know him, and keepeth not his commandments, is a liar] (1 Jn 4:2). And so Paul says: [They profess that they know God; but in works they deny him] (Titus 1:16). And so James says: "Faith without works is dead" (Jas 20:2, 26).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 10. Their rod does not rest upon the righteous

paragraphs.text: He giveth him safety, and he trusteth; yet his eyes are upon their ways [23].

Despite the troubles that the wicked man causes even to the great, he destroys himself, stretching out his hand against others, while they stretch out their hands against him. Yet God prolongs His longsuffering toward him, and allows him, despite his arrogance, to succeed in this world, and to live in prosperity and temporary comfort, and even to end his life in peace, as happened with Ishmael, who was marked by violence, for he lived and died before all his brethren (Gen 16:12; 25:18). Here Job says: "He giveth him safety, and he trusteth" (23). He appears as one under the special protection of divine providence, so that a man wonders how the wicked man lives in the world successfully, and how he escapes even the many dangers that he brings upon himself.

Since God prolongs His longsuffering toward the wicked man, he exploits this situation, thinking that no harm will touch him, and so becomes complacent. [Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily] (Eccl 8:11). They think that God does not care about their evils and will not call them to judgment. His success and his temporal safety make him complacent.
The wicked man thinks that he is beloved of God, better than all who are on the earth, and that he is the object of His divine care because of his own righteousness.

The eyes of the wicked man err in looking, seeing that his evil life is the way of truth, so he increases in pride and haughtiness; and yet the eyes of the Lord are on the way of the wicked man, longing that the wicked man abandon the pride of his heart and walk the way of the Cross in humility.

* Paul says: [Knowest thou not that the longsuffering of God leadeth thee to repentance? But after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God] (Rom 4:2-5)...

[For his eyes are upon their ways]; since the sinner cares for his ways, and relies on his mind alone, his eyes look toward the things profitable to him only temporarily. (The Lord Christ) showed the truth to the eyes of those who followed these ways, when He asked the swollen hearts of His disciples to seek true glory... saying: "Are ye able to drink of the cup that I drink of?"... And thus the cup of sufferings was set before their eyes as a thing to imitate, that they might first find the way of humility, if they seek the delights of greatness.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
They are exalted for a little while, but are gone, and brought low.

entries.section: 10. Their rod does not rest upon the righteous

paragraphs.text: They are gathered as all, and cut off as the tops of the ears of corn [24].

The wicked seem as though they are beloved of heaven, and think that they have been raised in honor, with no danger touching them, and suddenly they collapse and are as though they did not exist. Their pride is brought down and laid in the dust, and death comes upon them like all men; they are cut off like an ear of grain, and all vain honor vanishes.

* "They are glorified for a time, but they do not continue" [24]. The glory of the wicked, even if it lasts for a number of years, is counted by the minds of the weak to last a long time and to be established. But when it vanishes in a sudden end, it proves clearly that it lasts for a short time... The (temporal) glory has a limit that makes it a passing and trivial glory.

Man's glorifying of himself cannot continue, because it is separated from the firm foundation of the eternal substance, and falls under ruin, for by self-glorification he falls into himself. The psalmist says: [Thou castedst them down when they were lifted up] (Ps 18:73), for they fall inwardly... He says again: [For yet a little while, and the wicked shall not be] (Ps 10:37). Therefore James says: "For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time" (Jas 14:4). Therefore when the prophet expresses the brevity of fleshly glory he says: [All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the straw] (Isa 6:40)...
"Like the tops of the ears of wheat they are crushed." Certainly the haughtiness of the proud is shattered under the pressure of the final winnowing, while the life of the elect is glorified.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* A brother asked Abba Pambo: "Why do the demons hinder me from doing good to my neighbor?" He said to him: "Do not speak thus, or you make God a liar. Rather you should say: I utterly refuse to show mercy, for God, before this objection of yours, has already said: 'Behold, I give unto you power to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy' (Lk 10:19). So why do you not also crush the unclean spirits?"

entries.section: 10. Their rod does not rest upon the righteous

paragraphs.text: The Garden of the Monks And if it be not so now, who will make me a liar, and make my speech nothing worth? [25].
Job concludes his speech with a bold challenge to all those around him, to prove false what he has said, if they can.

* The righteous man, even if he utters something wrongly, is far from being condemned by the wicked who walk in an evil life... For those persons who still live on deceitful principles lose the boldness to rebuke deceit.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
May I fall into the hand of God and not fall into the hand of man!
* To fall into the hand of the Almighty is better than to fall into the hand of man.
Man, with his weakness and helplessness and his lack of awareness of the times, is harsh toward his fellow man.
And God, with His power and His knowledge of the secrets of the heart and His awareness of the times, is full of tenderness toward our weakness!
May I fall into Your hands, O wonderful Judge, and not fall into the hand of a man who shares my weakness and helplessness!
* I do not condemn my brothers for their harshness toward me, for I in turn am harsh toward my fellow in humanity.
I am with him under the same judgment; in my folly I cast my sins upon him instead of being gentle with him.
* You, the Judge, are gentle with me, to support my weakness.
And my brother, my partner in weakness, robs me of my humanity, invades my life, not robbing me of what I have, but robbing me of my very being!
* You cannot bear my tears, O Holy One, while my brother sees my tears and ascribes to me deceit and crookedness.
He goes about me without restraint, not to set right, but to wrong and to crush my depths.
* You created the world to be an icon of heaven, but corruption entered into us, and the beautiful world has become one whose law is injustice.
Wrong has taken the place in our human life of justice mixed with love.
The courts of justice have turned into centers of corruption.
And in Your longsuffering You await a return to the divine truth.
* I am not afraid of man's injustice toward me, but I fear my own injustice toward my fellow man.
For he takes refuge in You, and his depths cry out to You against me; what I do to my brother returns to me in a measure pressed down and shaken together.
Remove from me violence and harshness and injustice, so that I may enter with You into an eternal covenant.
Grant me gentleness toward those whom I lead, and let me bear a spirit of tender shepherding.
* My depths cry out, for all that I have done to my brothers lies hidden within them; who will deliver me from my evils but You?
Remove it from the storehouses of my heart, and let Your righteousness dwell in me.
Remove it from my depths, that they may become Your holy temple.
Take it away from me, for its outcome is deceit and vanity of no value.
Take it away, for I cannot bear Your wrath, O Righteous One who hates injustice!
* My God, Your grace removes the spirit of injustice from my eyes and from my brothers.
Without Your grace man loses inward tenderness.
He justifies to himself the plundering of orphans and widows.
He becomes like a beast, preying on the poor and the needy.
He counts the whole world as belonging to him and to his offspring.
He robs and plunders without restraint.
He does not care about the sufferings of his brothers, nor pay heed to their tears.
He snatches the orphan from his mother's breast, and takes the poor man captive, and counts him his slave.
He thinks that there is no law to restrain him, and no God to judge him!
He loves darkness, to kill and steal and commit adultery, counting that there is no one who sees, and no one who calls to account.
* Wretched is this unjust man.
God prolongs His longsuffering toward him that perhaps he may return and repent.
The curse falls upon him; he is in inward hunger and drought.
The abyss is prepared for him to swallow him.
The worm counts him a delicious feast.
His remembrance vanishes from the world, and he is broken like a tree from its roots.
In the midst of his wealth and pride he falls.
* Keep me, O Lord, in You, that I may not practice injustice, nor fear the injustice of men toward me, for You are my only refuge.

entries.section: 1. God, the Possessor of authority and the Giver of peace in heaven

paragraphs.text: 1 Then answered Bildad the Shuhite, and said, 2 "Dominion and fear are with him, he maketh peace in his high places. 3 Is there any number of his armies? and upon whom doth not his light arise?
Then answered Bildad the Shuhite, and said: [1]

entries.section: 1. God, the Possessor of authority and the Giver of peace in heaven

paragraphs.text: "Dominion and fear are with him." [2]

What Bildad uttered is a truth befitting God and us, namely that it is fitting for us to humble ourselves greatly before the exalted and awesome God, and that the distance between Him and us is vast. But Bildad erred in applying this to Job, since he did not bear toward him a spirit of love.

God, as the Creator of heaven and earth, the Creator of all and the Giver of life, has the absolute right to lay down laws and to govern the universe with absolute authority. As Nebuchadnezzar said when he returned to his senses and blessed the Most High: "His dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom is from generation to generation: and all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing: and he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou?" (Dan 4:34-35).
With the great boldness that the men of God had toward Him, they confessed that He is the great, mighty, awesome and fearful God.
"Let them praise thy great and terrible name; for it is holy" (Ps 99:3).

"And I prayed unto the Lord my God, and made my confession, and said, O Lord, the great and dreadful God, keeping the covenant and mercy to them that love him, and to them that keep his commandments" (Dan 9:4).
"And said, I beseech thee, O Lord God of heaven, the great and terrible God, that keepeth covenant and mercy for them that love him and observe his commandments" (Neh 1:5).

"Now therefore, our God, the great, the mighty, and the terrible God, who keepest covenant and mercy, let not all the trouble seem little before thee, that hath come upon us, on our kings, on our princes, and on our priests, and on our prophets, and on our fathers, and on all thy people, since the time of the kings of Assyria unto this day" (Neh 9:32).

Commenting on Psalm 99, which speaks of God sitting between the cherubim, the awesome One before whom the peoples tremble and the earth is moved, St. Augustine sees Him seated upon the human soul, enthroned there as upon His holy throne.

* The Cherubim is the seat of God, as Holy Scripture shows us, a high heavenly throne that we do not see, but the Word of God knows it; He knows it as His seat... God does not sit as man sits. But if you wish God to sit in you, then if you become good you become a seat for God... The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom. For a throne in our language is called a seat... Because God is exalted above all knowledge, it is said of Him that He sits upon the fullness of knowledge. Let there be in you the fullness of knowledge, and you will become the throne of God... And when you have the fullness of knowledge and have love, you become the throne of God, and you become a heaven. For the heaven that we look at with these eyes of ours is not very precious to God. Holy souls are the heaven of God, the minds of the angels, and all the minds of His servants are the heaven of God.
St. Augustine "He maketh peace in his high places" [2].

If men in their stubbornness or wickedness resist God, they only resist themselves, for they lose the surpassing peace of God. But the heavenly ones enjoy His peace in the heights, since they love Him and submit to Him and obey Him with perfect obedience. They bear the divine love and imitate His humility, so they do not exalt themselves over one another, nor envy, nor quarrel, nor murmur. It is God's surpassing gift to them, as those who love Him, to live in wondrous peace.

As for the inhabitants of the earth, they need obedience to God, so that they may enjoy His work as the Giver of peace, as the psalmist says: "He maketh the storm a calm, so that the waves thereof are still" (Ps 107:29; 65:7).

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that God, as the Creator of all things, reigns over them and has authority, striking awe into the hearts of mortal creation. On earth creation lacks peace, and confusion and anxiety come upon them; but in the heights, or in the heavenly world, God unites the elect with the orders of angels, and all are at peace.

In the Lord we are transformed from earthly dust into heavens, and are reckoned His high places, where He dwells in us and establishes our peace within us. As the Apostle says: "For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us" (Eph 2:14).
* Since Christ, the Son of God, is peace, He came to gather together those who are His, and to separate them from the wicked.

St. Augustine * "Peace I leave with you" (Jn 14:27). He says: "What harm can the troubles of the world do you, so long as you are at peace with me? For this peace is not of the same kind as that (which is of the world). That is an outward peace, often harmful and of no profit, with no advantage to those who possess it. But I give them a peace of the kind by which you are at peace with one another, and which makes you stronger."

St. John Chrysostom * "Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord": the King against the tyrant, who came not by showing that He is almighty and all-wise, but by what was reckoned as the foolishness of the Cross, by which He rescued those who are His from the captives held by the serpent, wise in evil.

"Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord": the Truth against the liar, the Savior against the destroyer, the Prince of Peace against the instigator of wars, the Lover of mankind against the hater of humanity.
"Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord," the Lord who comes to have mercy on the creature, the work of His hands.

"Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord," the Lord who comes to save man who had gone astray in error, to remove error from him, to give light to those who are in darkness, to abolish the deceit of idols and put in its place the knowledge of God, the Giver of salvation, so that the world may be sanctified. He removes the abominations and the misery that belong to the worship of false gods.
Father Methodius ascribes the high heavens to Himself, for the heavens are the Lord's (Ps 115:16), and Bildad calls them "his high places."

When the people are sanctified, the Lord ascribes the people and their feasts to Himself, so that it is called "the people of God," "my sabbaths," etc.; and when it rebels, He calls it "the people," "your feasts," "your sabbaths," etc.

entries.section: 1. God, the Possessor of authority and the Giver of peace in heaven

paragraphs.text: "Is there any number of his armies? and upon whom doth not his light arise?" [3]

The peace that dwells in the Lord's heights or heavens is not because the number of the heavenly ones is small, so that agreement and harmony might be reached among them, for "is there any number of his armies?" Rather, the secret of their peace in the Lord is that He shines with His light upon all of them. If the light of the sun reaches the whole earth, the light of God shines upon all the heavenly ones [and upon whom doth not his light arise?]

Thus He who shines with His light upon all the heavenly ones makes His sun to rise on the evil and the good (Mt 5:45), that all may seek the light of His surpassing grace and be enlightened, and bear His righteousness and His peace! He hides His light from no one, and does not begrudge His creation His knowledge, but He does not compel anyone to accept His grace.

The Lord Christ calls us to be children of God, saying: "That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust" (Mt 5:45). He wants all to be children of light. "For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor 4:6).

* "For ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord" (Eph 5:8). He did not say "by your virtue," but by the grace of God working in you. That is, you deserved punishments, and now you are no longer so. Therefore walk as children of light... in all goodness.

St. John Chrysostom * Those who were born again were children of night and became children of day; they were darkness and became light. Now Jesus entrusts Himself to them, and they come to Him not by night like Nicodemus (Jn 3:2), nor do they seek Him in the dark but in the day.

St. Augustine * By the Holy Spirit our return to Paradise is accomplished, our ascent to the Kingdom of Heaven, our return to adoption as sons, our freedom by which we call God our Father, our fellowship in the grace of Christ, our calling children of light, our fellowship in eternal glory, and in short our attaining to the state of the fullness of blessing.
St. Basil the Great

entries.section: 2. How can man be justified with God?

paragraphs.text: "How then can man be justified with God? or how can he be clean that is born of a woman?" [4]

However much the righteousness and holiness of man may rise, it cannot be compared with the loftiness of the righteousness and holiness of God (Ps 89:6). And if man enters into judgment with God, God is justified and man is condemned, as the psalmist says: "And enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified" (Ps 143:2). There is no error in the judgments of God, and no one can object to them or appeal against them.

* [Can a man be justified when compared with God? or can one born of a woman be found clean?] [4] This statement was spoken before by the blessed Job... since every man is righteous through being enlightened by God, not by comparison with God. For the righteousness of man, when compared with the Creator, is not reckoned righteousness; for even if man holds fast to his state in creation, the creature cannot be equal to the Creator.

In any case, this creature came to carry heavy burdens, and because of his weakness sin piled up upon him, that sin which the serpent brought into him by deceit, and the woman proved her weakness sufficiently. Now, since man is born through a woman subject to sin, he inherited the weakness of the first sin by procreation, not because the branch of the human race was corrupted at its root and did not receive the vitality proper to its creation; therefore it is rightly said now: "Can a man be justified, being born of a woman?"
As if he said plainly: Let no man think proudly against his Creator; let him consider from where he came to this place, and understand what he is.

But observe that there are those who have received help by the gift of the Spirit against the frailty of their flesh, and have built themselves up, and shone in the virtues. Yes! They shine in wondrous and astonishing signs. Yet there is no man who passes through life without sin, so long as he bears the corruptible flesh.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Who are those who desire to enter into judgment with Him but those who are ignorant of God's righteousness, and wish to establish their own righteousness...? "In thy sight shall no man living be justified." "Every man living" here means one who lives in the flesh, who lives expecting death. He is born as a man, received his life from a man, came from Adam... He can be justified before himself, but not before You. How is he justified before himself? By pleasing himself and not pleasing You. Enter not into judgment with me, O Lord my God. However upright I may seem to myself, when You bring out a standard from Your storehouses by which I measure myself, I find myself crooked.

* [Thou art justified in thy sayings, and overcomest when thou art judged] (Ps 51:4). You overcome all men, all judges; whoever thinks himself righteous before You is not righteous. You alone judge justly, and You are judged unjustly... You overcome all men, because You are above all men, and they were created by You.
St. Augustine

entries.section: 3. The stars are not pure in his sight

paragraphs.text: 5 "Behold even the moon, and it shineth not; and the stars are not pure in his sight. 6 How much less man, that is rottenness, and the son of man, which is a worm?"
"Behold even the moon, and it shineth not; and the stars are not pure in his sight" [5].

Despite the beauty of the moon and all the stars, in reality they are stones that carry neither light nor beauty in themselves, were the rays of the sun not reflected upon them. So it is with the Church, that is, the moon, and the believers also, that is, the stars: they have no beauty except by the shining of the Sun of Righteousness upon them, to scatter every trace of darkness and reflect His splendor upon them. It is said of the true believers and preachers: "And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever" (Dan 12:3).

Apart from the grace of God the moon becomes dark, unable to give light, and the stars are reckoned impure. As the prophet Isaiah says: "Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the Lord of hosts shall reign in mount Zion, and in Jerusalem" (Isa 24:23).
Origen sees that the moon and the stars here refer to rational beings to whom the Lord issues commandments (Isa 12:45), who are capable of advancing as well as of falling.

* What does he mean by the moon but the whole Church together, and what does he mean by the stars but the souls of the many who live uprightly? In the midst of the practices of wicked men they stand out by their rare virtues, as though shining in the darkness of the night. So Paul also says to his disciples: [Among whom ye shine as lights in the world] (Phil 15:2). And by the title "stars" he means the elect; Paul tells us this again when he says: [One star differeth from another star in glory] (1 Cor 41:15). So "the moon shineth not, and the stars are not pure in his sight." The Holy Church does not by her own power shine in so many wonders, unless the showers of strengthening grace fall upon her, nor are the minds of the many who live uprightly pure from the defilement of sinful practices, if they were judged apart from (divine) tenderness. For in the eyes of the strict Judge every individual is defiled through his inclination to corruption, unless the grace of (God) removes man day by day from this fall.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Let your ears listen from now to the glorious voice with which the angels will sing because of your salvation, saying: "Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered." This is when you enter as the shining stars of the Church, radiant in body and bright in soul.

Great is the baptism that is granted to you, for it is the release of captives, the forgiveness of transgressions, the death of sin, the new birth of the soul, a garment of light, a holy seal that cannot be broken, a chariot to the heavens, the delight of Paradise, a welcome into the Kingdom, the gift of adoption! But beware, for there is a serpent outside watching those who pass by. Be careful lest it bite you with the bites of unbelief.
When it sees many receiving salvation, it seeks to swallow it from them (1 Pet 5:8).

St. Cyril of Jerusalem * There is never one who is without sin. [The stars themselves are not pure in his sight], and every creature trembles at the coming of the Lord... There is another interpretation, which is that "all" does not refer to everyone but to those who are the subject of the dispute. It is as when someone says: "All the citizens cried out"; he does not mean by this that there was never anyone silent, but this was said of the majority that prevails over the minority.

St. Jerome * No man is without sin, whether his life is one day or he lives many years. If the stars themselves are not pure in the eyes of God, how much more the worm and corruption, which is what those have become who were subject to the sin of Adam's disobedience?

St. Augustine * Is He not good who lifted the earth to a heaven, so that the shining stars that accompany Him reflect His glory in heaven as in a mirror, just as the ranks of the apostles, the martyrs and the priests shine like glorious stars, and give light to the world?
St. Ambrose

entries.section: 3. The stars are not pure in his sight

paragraphs.text: "How much less man, that is rottenness, and the son of man, which is a worm." [6]

If man returns to his origin before creation and withdraws from God his Creator, he goes as dust and ashes, rottenness and a worm! And the wonder is that the divine Word in His incarnation humbled Himself greatly, and said by the mouth of the prophet: [I am a worm, and no man] (Ps 22:6).

* All men are born of flesh; what are they but worms? Out of this worm God makes angels. If the Lord Himself says: "But I am a worm, and no man" (Ps 6:22), who will hesitate to utter what is written in Job: "How much less man, that is rottenness, and the son of man, which is a worm" [6]. He said first "man is rottenness," and then "the son of man is a worm," for the worm comes out of rottenness... Behold what He wished to become for your sake, He who "in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (Jn 1:1).

St. Augustine * "How much more is man corruption, and the son of man a worm?" [6] As if he said plainly: If these very persons cannot avoid the contagion, who in the darkness of the present life shine with the splendor of the acquisition of virtues, how great then is the evil of those bound to life according to the flesh? If these persons cannot be freed from sin, who are already walking in the way of heavenly desires, what of those who still lie under the burdens of evil habits, who are abandoned to the pleasures of their bodies and still bear the yoke of corruption? Therefore Peter says: [If the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?] (1 Pet 18:4). Isaiah says: [Upon the land of my people shall come up thorns and briers; yea, upon all the houses of joy in the joyous city] (Isa 13:32)... The joyous city is the mind of the wicked, who does not care about the punishments to come, for the sake of the pleasure of the flesh, and when the mind goes out of its own being it plays in false merriment.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Pope Gregory observes that the first man is called corruption, since death came upon him through sin and he was corrupted. But the son of man is called a worm, since corruption breeds worms in the dead body.
Let the light of Your righteousness shine upon me
* You shine with the light of Your love upon all creation.
By You the heavenly orders are enlightened, and without You heaven appears impure.
By You the heavenly ones live in peace, and without You there is no peace even in heaven. * How shall I be justified before You, when corruption has come upon my depths?
Who removes corruption from me but You?
Let Your grace work in me, O All-Good!

1 But Job answered and said, 2 "How hast thou helped him that is without power? how savest thou the arm that hath no strength? 3 How hast thou counselled him that hath no wisdom? and how hast thou plentifully declared the thing as it is? 4 To whom hast thou uttered words? and whose spirit came from thee?"
But Job answered and said: [1]
How hast thou helped him that is without power? how savest thou the arm that hath no strength? [2]

Job addresses Bildad in an eloquent and splendid style, with humility and contrition. Job counts himself as one with "no power," and his arm as one with "no strength," and in mockery he says to Bildad: What a helper you are of him who has no power, and a strengthener of the arms that have no strength! While confessing his own extreme weakness, he rebukes Bildad, who thinks himself wise, a guide and a helper, yet is in fact crushing the spirit of him who has no power and of him whose arm has no strength.

Here Job exposes Bildad, showing that, like his two companions, he has spoken eloquent words and sincere truths of faith, but what he has offered is talk without love and dialogue without action. What he has offered does not help him who has no power, nor does it support an arm that has no strength.

* (Job says) But I do not blame you for defending the role of God, for this is needed. In any case, you ought not to condemn me, although, in truth, it should have been possible to defend the grace of God without subjecting Job to so many accusations.

St. John Chrysostom Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that it was fitting for Bildad (and his two companions) to work with God to support broken souls in a spirit of humility, not of haughtiness; for God asks His servants to work with Him (1 Cor 3:9) and to bear a spirit of humility, ascribing the fruit to God who works in them (1 Cor 3:7).

* Job answered and said: To whom do you give help? Is it to one who has no power? Or do you support the arm of one who is not strong? Here we need to know that we help even God, who is certainly not "without power," when we work in humility. Paul said: "We are labourers together with God" (1 Cor 9:3). If we contribute a voice of counsel to persons upon whom an inward grace is poured, we pass through with them by the Holy Spirit... We urge them toward perfection only when God is in the heart as a helper. Here too he says: "Neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase" (1 Cor 7:3). For he who plants or waters only helps, but the service is in vain unless God gives the increase in the heart.

But those who have haughty thoughts about the power of their own minds will not be helpers of God in humility, for they reckon themselves useful to God, and so make themselves strangers to profitable fruit.

* When pastors try to correct an erring flock, they must be adorned with humility, so that they do not stray in the use of their authority, and must feel that they are equal to the brethren whom they correct. And we pastors must train ourselves in silence and contemplation, and prefer the persons whose faults are being corrected to ourselves, because their sins have been corrected through us by hard training, whereas no one has rebuked us pastors for our own sins, even with a word. For this reason we pastors are judged before the Lord in proportion as we are released from punishment before men. And all the more is the flock freed from the divine judgment, because it is judged for its faults here in this world.

* Let the flock be assured that the pastors are inwardly humble before themselves. Thus the flock must understand what it ought to fear in authority and what it ought to imitate within the sphere of humility.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* It is plain that when one counsels another and at the same time suffers more than the one he rebukes, he does this not to cause grief to the other, but to offer him deep love. But he who rebukes another without this feeling in fact tramples with his feet upon his brother's feelings.

Father Ambrosiaster * Do not let the rank of the priesthood make you conceited, but rather let it make you humble, for dissolution and shame are born of haughtiness. The nearer you draw to the high ranks of the holy priestly order, the more it becomes you to be humble, remembering with fear the example of the sons of Aaron (Lev 10). The knowledge of the holy life is the knowledge of meekness and humility. Humility is the imitation of Christ. Arrogance, presumption and impudence are the imitation of Satan. Be an imitator of Christ, not of the antichrist; of God, not of the adversary of God; of the Master, not of the runaway slave; of the merciful, not of the merciless; of the Lover of mankind, not of its enemy; of your partner in the bridal chamber, not of the dweller in darkness. Do not be eager to exploit authority over the congregation, lest you place upon your neck the burdens of the sins of others.
St. Basil the Great How hast thou counselled him that hath no wisdom? and how hast thou plentifully declared the thing as it is? [3]

Job rebukes Bildad because he offered theoretical philosophies, like one speaking to a child who has no wisdom, and displayed his understanding and knowledge with an abundance of words without action. He presented what is true, but he did not take the circumstances into account, so that the truth came out of place and out of season.

* "To whom hast thou given counsel? Perhaps to him that hath no wisdom?" [3] To give counsel to an ignorant man is a work of love; to give it to a wise man is boasting; but to give it to Wisdom Himself is a perversion of the mind.

* The shepherd of souls must discern wisely and carefully between the virtues and the vices, lest avarice take hold of his heart while he is excessive in appearing to be a good manager, or he boast of his generosity as though it were a virtue when he is in truth a squanderer and a waster; or he overlooks what he ought to criticize severely, and so brings eternal punishment upon his flock, or he punishes faults without mercy and so sins a greater sin, or he spoils what could have been done with dignity and uprightness by his hasty and reckless expectations. Likewise, postponing a good deed may turn it into an evil one.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
To whom hast thou uttered words? and whose spirit came from thee? [4]

He says to him: [You have uttered words] out of place, for it was fitting for you to offer God's consolations to the tempted, not to terrify them with dreadful terrors. "And whose spirit came from thee?" That is, by what spirit are you animated to offer such talk to crush the wounded soul? It was fitting for you to seek wisdom and understanding from Him who gave you life and breath.
It was fitting for Bildad to say with the prophet Isaiah: "The Lord GOD hath given me the tongue of the learned, that I should know how to speak a word in season to him that is weary" (Isa 50:4).

* "Whom do you wish to teach? Is it not He who made the way of the breath? By the breath we live, and by understanding we are wise. But we must first live, and afterward be dyed with wisdom, for in order that we may have the power to be wise, we must first possess Him who gave us life; He Himself, without doubt, grants us understanding also.
* Treatment at the wrong time makes wounds more painful. And if the medicines are unsuitable, they are certainly not fit for the purpose of healing.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* (The Apostle Paul) presented three marks of the preaching of the word: a burning, venturesome zeal; a soul ready to endure any dangers that may befall; and knowledge and wisdom joined together. For his love of venturing (in his preaching), and his blameless life, would have profited him nothing had he not received the power of the Spirit. Look at him as it appears in him first, or rather hear his words: "That the ministry be not blamed"(a).
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 2. God's authority over the depths of the seas

paragraphs.text: The shades tremble beneath the waters and their inhabitants [5].
