By the shades he means the huge, mighty creatures such as whales and sharks, which, though they live in the waters, fear God, as though God's care extends to the mighty, fierce creatures in the waters of the seas and oceans, over which He seems to have no authority. As it is said by the prophet Jeremiah: "Fear ye not me? saith the LORD: will ye not tremble at my presence, which have placed the sand for the bound of the sea by a perpetual decree, that it cannot pass it: and though the waves thereof toss themselves, yet can they not prevail; though they roar, yet can they not pass over it?" (Jer 5:22).

Some think that the shades, or giants, here means those who in the days of Noah made light of him and thought that no evil would befall them, and who became as dwellers beneath the waters of the Flood that came upon them, and so were in trembling, but after it was too late!

* "Behold, the giants groan under the water" [5]. If by "giants" are meant those who hold power in this world, then the waters signify the multitudes, as John testifies by saying: [The waters which thou sawest are peoples] (Rev 15:17).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Do you not see this sea, with its many waves and violent winds, and yet this vast, great sea, raging so, is held back by weak sand! Observe also the wisdom of God: He has allowed it no rest and no calm, lest you suppose that its good order is by a natural arrangement, and yet it keeps within its bounds. It lifts its voice high with its turmoil, its roaring, and its waves amazing in their height. But when they reach the shores, the sands hold them back and break them, and they return of themselves, in order that you may learn from all these things that it is not the work of mere nature that the sea stays within its bounds, but the work of Him who by His authority checks it! For this reason He made the barrier weak, and did not encircle the shores with timbers and stones and mountains, lest you ascribe the order of the elements to such things. Therefore God Himself trained the Jews in these very circumstances, saying: "Fear ye not me? saith the LORD... which have placed the sand for the bound of the sea by a perpetual decree, that it cannot pass it" (Jer 5:22).
St. John Chrysostom * A grain of sand, the weakest of things, holds back the violence of the ocean.
St. Basil the Great
Hell is naked before him, and destruction hath no covering [6].

Job highlights the surpassing authority of God, that He is the Controller of all: He has authority over the huge, fierce creatures in the midst of the seas, and even over the devil and his angels who dwell in hell, for they are unable to do anything without His permission or leave.

Sheol is far from our sight, and the destruction that comes upon the demons and the wicked we have not yet seen, but everything is uncovered before the eyes of God, and He reveals it to whom He wills, such as His holy angels. It is said of him who worships the beast and his image and receives his mark on his forehead or on his hand: "The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb" (Rev 14:10).

Some think that Job is speaking of the wicked who have become sons of the devil and dwell with him in Sheol; these supposed that God did not see them, but they are exposed before the eyes of God. The Apostle says: "Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do" (Heb 4:13).

* [Hell is naked before him, and destruction hath no covering] [6] Paul says something like it: [All things are naked and opened unto his eyes] (Heb 13:4). By hell and destruction he means Satan and all who are bound up with his judgment.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Is it possible for God not to know such things, when there is no matter that escapes His care? "Hell is naked before his sight, and there is no covering for the wicked themselves," for they cannot hide.

St. Ambrose * (The word of God judges) the thoughts and intents of the heart, and there is no creature that is not manifest in his sight (Heb 4:12-13). With these words he terrifies them... He judges the inner heart, for in passing into it he punishes and searches it out. He says: And why do I speak of men? For even if you speak of the angels, and of the archangels, the Cherubim and Seraphim, or of any creature whatever, all is uncovered before that eye, all is plain and manifest, and nothing can escape from it.

* "All things are naked and opened" (Heb 4:13) to Him who judges us, and we are bound to give an account not only of words but also of thoughts, for this Judge quickly discerns the thoughts and intents of the heart.

* The righteous will shine forth as the sun, and even more than the sun, at that time; but the wicked will suffer all painful things to the utmost degree. There is no need there for records and proofs and witnesses, for the One who judges is everything: the witness, the proof and the judge, since He knows everything exactly: [All things are naked and opened unto his eyes].

St. John Chrysostom * "All things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do" (Heb 4:13). By this he means that He is other than all these (not a creature). Therefore it is He who judges, and each one of these is bound to give an account before Him.
Pope Athanasius the Apostolic

7 He stretcheth out the north over the empty place, and hangeth the earth upon nothing. 8 He bindeth up the waters in his thick clouds; and the cloud is not rent under them. 9 He holdeth back the face of his throne, and spreadeth his cloud upon it. 10 He hath compassed the waters with bounds, until the day and night come to an end. 11 The pillars of heaven tremble and are astonished at his reproof. 12 He divideth the sea with his power, and by his understanding he smiteth through the proud.
He stretcheth out the north over the empty place, and hangeth the earth upon nothing [7].

Holy Scripture likens God the Creator to one who spreads out the heavens and the earth, and who remains in His care for His creation, spreading out both until the times come to an end and He folds them up. The psalmist says: "Who stretchest out the heavens like a curtain"(b). And as it is written in the Book of Revelation: "The heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together" (Rev 6:14). As for his choosing "the north," it is because Job lives in the northern hemisphere, and so sees God spreading out the earth as over an empty place, that is, as though it were empty or as nothing when compared with the other world. The psalmist says: "The north and the south thou hast created them" (Ps 89:12).
Pope Gregory (the Great) holds that the north signifies Satan, whose kingdom is empty of God's grace. Even the kingdom of the devil is not hidden from God.
* The Lord gave the earth stability, and it will remain so as long as God wills it.

Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus * Who ought not to be amazed and perplexed at these things, declaring with certainty that they are not the work of nature, but of the divine providence that surpasses nature? For one says: [Who hangeth the earth upon nothing] (Job 7:26). And another: [In his hand are the deep places of the earth] (Ps 4:95).

St. John Chrysostom * "He stretcheth out the north over the empty place" [7]. "The north" is used in Holy Scripture to signify Satan... for he (Satan) reigns over those whose hearts are not filled with the grace of the love of God. But Almighty God is able to fill even the vessels of Satan, empty of every virtue, with the gift of His grace, and to place the fear of God in those persons whom He sees established in no conduct of righteousness. Therefore he rightly added: "And hangeth the earth upon nothing." For what does he mean by the earth, if not the Holy Church? It receives the words of preaching and brings forth the fruit of good works. Moses said of it: [Hear, O earth, the words of my mouth... let my speech distil as the rain] (Deut 32:1-2). And what is "nothing," if not the many peoples of the Gentiles, of whom the prophet says: [All nations before him are as nothing; and they are counted to him less than nothing] (cf. Isa 17:40).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

"He hangeth the earth upon nothing." He created the earth and set it up without pillars. There is nothing that a man can hang upon nothing, but God established the whole earth upon nothing. And as the Apostle says: "Upholding all things by the word of his power" (Heb 1:3). He who set up the globe of the earth and established it, that man might walk on it and live, can He not by the word of His power order the whole life of man?
* You set up the heaven for me as a roof, and You established the earth for me to walk upon.
For my sake You bridled the sea, for my sake You showed forth the nature of the animals, You put everything under my feet. You did not leave me lacking in any of the works of Your honor.
The Liturgy of St. Gregory the Theologian He bindeth up the waters in his thick clouds; and the cloud is not rent under them [8].

God keeps the waters of which it was said that they are "above the firmament" (Gen 1:7), so that they are not poured out in a single flood to drown the world, as happened in the days of Noah. They are kept (bound up) by divine wisdom. He lets them fall as rains by a well-ordered divine arrangement and in a set measure, so that, with all the weight of these waters that have become clouds, the clouds beneath them are not rent so that they fall all at once, for the benefit of those who dwell on the earth, men and animals and crops.

St. John Chrysostom stands amazed before God's surpassing providence, in that He allows the water (in the clouds) to be carried up above the air, and God seals it with the air, so that it runs to many places to water the earth.

* Who is it that "bindeth up the waters in the clouds"? It is a wonder that He places something that by its nature overflows so that it stays in the cloud, holding it fast by His word. But He pours out a part of it upon the face of the earth, letting it fall in drops at the proper time. He does not let loose the whole store of waters, but is content with the cleansing that was accomplished in the days of Noah. God remains true to His covenant.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus Pope Gregory (the Great) offers us a symbolic interpretation, seeing in the waters a symbol of knowledge, and in the thick cloud the company of the preachers, for it is God who grants the preachers heavenly knowledge.

If Bildad and his two companions claim wisdom and knowledge, it is fitting for them to be like the light cloud that flies in the sky and rises above dust and earthly things, so that they may enjoy heavenly wisdom and divine knowledge.

God in His surpassing providence grants us by His grace to become a cloud, or a divine chariot, as the prophet Isaiah said: "Behold, the LORD rideth upon a swift (bright) cloud, and shall come into Egypt" (Isa 19:1). By dwelling in us He fills us with His knowledge, His wisdom and His love, and flies with us as though to Egypt, that is, to the heart of every man, that we may present to them the One who dwells in us, God, the true Love!

* "He bindeth up the waters in his thick cloud, so that they burst not downward" [8]. What does he signify by the waters in this place but knowledge, and by the cloud but the preachers? For water in Holy Scripture is sometimes used to signify knowledge, as Solomon teaches us, bearing witness to it. He says: [The words of a man's mouth are as deep waters, and the wellspring of wisdom as a flowing brook] (Prov 4:18). And the prophet David bears witness that waters signify knowledge, saying that the dark waters are in the clouds of the sky, and the hidden mysteries, since they carried within them boundless mysteries, whose meanings are obscure in the eyes of those who behold them.

And what does the name "cloud" signify in this passage but the holy preachers, that is, the Apostles, who were sent out in every direction to the ends of the world, who know how to rain with words and to flash lightning with miracles? Isaiah looked upon them long ago and said: [Who are these that fly as a cloud?] (Isa 8:60).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* "His lightnings enlightened the world" (Ps 97:4). This is great joy... His lightnings shine over all the world: His enemies sit upon fire and are burned... How do the lightnings shine? By the world's believing. Where do the lightnings come from? From the cloud. And what is the cloud of God? The preachers of the truth... Our Lord Jesus Christ sent His Apostles out as preachers like clouds. They were seen as men and were despised, and yet they appeared as clouds.

St. Augustine * Virtue is a thing bright and joyful, and those who live in its way fly like a cloud, as Isaiah says: [And as the doves to their windows] (Isa 60:8). But sin is like something heavy and sitting still, as another prophet says: "a talent of lead" (Zech 5:8).

St. Gregory of Nyssa St. Basil the Great sees that all men are like clouds, ever in motion, moving as the winds direct them. He whom the wind of the Lord moves goes forth toward heaven, but he who leaves himself to the winds of the world and the passions moves toward hell for his destruction.
* Men are like clouds, moving here and there in the sky according to the changes of the winds.
St. Basil the Great He holdeth back the face of his throne, and spreadeth his cloud upon it [9].

It is out of God's love for us and His wonderful care that He veils the face of His throne, so that we do not see Him as He is, because, as He said: "There shall no man see me, and live" (Ex 33:20). He spreads cloud and mist over it, so that He appears as in obscurity, since our eyes are unable to behold Him, and we live by faith and not by sight, until we meet Him face to face on the great day of the Lord, as much as we are able to bear.

* The face of his throne is veiled, which means that we do not perceive the glory of His kingdom in this life. For while His greatness is within, He spreads His cloud, because the glory of the heavenly kingdom is not seen as it is. For [the corruptible body presseth down the soul, and the earthly tabernacle weigheth down the mind that museth upon many things] (Wis 15:9). So the mist is spread over us, and we do not see His glory, being darkened by the cloud of our ignorance. Rightly does the psalmist say: [Darkness was under his feet. And he rode upon a cherub, and did fly: yea, he did fly upon the wings of the wind. He made darkness his secret place] (cf. Ps 9:18-11)...

But if we reckon His throne to be the angelic powers, since He sits upon these very powers as upon a royal throne, He turns the face of His throne away from us, for as long as we have the mortal body we do not perceive the wonder of the ministry of the angels, nor how it is carried out.

"And spreadeth his cloud upon it," since He lifts up our heart to search; and the heart passes through in a hidden way, so that for all its endless searching it is turned back. So it is written: [The deep uttered his voice, and lifted up his hands on high] (Hab 10:3).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* [He bowed the heavens also, and came down: and darkness was under his feet] (Ps 18:9). This is the humility of the Righteous One, who bowed down because of the weakness of men.

"And darkness was under his feet." Those whose wickedness has blinded their eyes; these wicked, who care only for earthly things, cannot know Him, for the earth falls under His feet, bound to the footstool.
St. Augustine * Every mind, according to the measure of its stature, is enlightened with a limited quantity of light.

Mar Isaac the Syrian * The face of God is the impress of His substance (Heb 3:1). He who desires the face of God with all his heart, so that he is able to contemplate it with a pure heart and to fix his gaze upon it, shall be shown mercy, according to the Lord's saying. Such a man is able to utter the words that are before us.
How great is he who sees the face of God! Let the Lord Jesus teach you his greatness, as He says: "Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God" (Mt 8:5).
St. Didymus the Blind He hath compassed the waters with bounds, until the day and night come to an end [10].

Job looks upon the vast seas and sees the rivers pouring into them, and yet their waters do not increase so as to overflow the land; rather, the sands, small grains as they are, stand as a barrier that holds them back. Thus God granted the seas to respect the earth, so that they do not overflow the earth with their waters.

If the waters of the seas know their limits and do not pass them, it is fitting for the peoples and nations (the many waters) to respect others, so that no nation oppresses another, and no man another.

* As for the sea, if I am not astonished at its greatness, I must be astonished at its nobility: What bounds it? How does it rise and then grow calm at the end, like one who respects his neighbor "the earth"? How does it receive into itself all the rivers, and remain as it is, in spite of the overflowing of its huge being, if one may say so...? How is its limit set by an element such as sand alone...? "He hath set a bound upon the face of the waters by his commandment" (Job 10:26) LXX.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus * "He setteth bounds to the waters until the light and the darkness come to an end" [10]. As we said before, the peoples are signified in Holy Scripture by the waters. The Lord sets bounds to the waters when He deals with human knowledge, so that it does not attain perfectly to the knowledge of the inner splendor until the succession of changing seasons has passed away.

If we understand by the light the righteous, and by the darkness sinners, Paul says: [Ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light] (Eph 8:5), then nothing prevents us from understanding that the perfect knowledge of eternity is given to no one until the course of the righteous and the course of the wicked comes to an end.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
The pillars of heaven tremble and are astonished at his reproof [11].

* What are the pillars of heaven but the holy angels, the chief preachers of the Church, upon whom the whole heavenly world of the spiritual edifice, rising without ceasing, is established, as Holy Scripture says in another place: "Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God" (Rev 3:12). For he who is firmly established, with a sound aim in his mind, in the work of God stands as a pillar in the building of the spiritual edifice. Being set in this temple, which is the Church, he becomes both a use and an adornment. But Job calls those "pillars of heaven" whom the Apostle calls pillars of the Church, saying: [Peter and James and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave to me the right hand of fellowship] (Gal 9:2).

It is not unfitting to interpret the "pillars of heaven" as the churches themselves. For though they are many in number, they constitute one catholic (universal) Church spread over all the face of the earth. So also the Apostle John writes to the seven churches, meaning the one catholic Church supplied with the Spirit, whose grace is sevenfold...

Now the very powers of the heavenly world, who see Him without ceasing and for whom He is the object of contemplation, have become filled with dread. But it is not the dread of woe, since it is not the dread of fear, but the dread of wonder. For having brought such great dread by His wondrous work, He now recounts to us the dispensation of our salvation.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
He divideth the sea with his power, and by his understanding he smiteth through Rahab [12].

Some scholars, who reckon that Job lived in the days of the prophet Moses or after him, think that he is speaking here of God's work with His people, in that by His power He divided the Red Sea, and by His understanding He crushed Egypt, since the word "Rahab" is often used to express Egypt (Ps 87:4; Isa 51:9).

* "By his power the seas were gathered together suddenly, and his wisdom shook the proud" [12]. What does the sea signify but the present world, in which the hearts of men seek earthly things and are swollen with the surges of conflicting thoughts? For being stirred up by the arrogance of pride, and opposing one another in the passage of the waves, they shatter themselves together against the currents. But "by his power the seas were gathered together," for when the Lord became incarnate, the opposing hearts of worldly men believed and came into agreement...

Who is he who is here called the proud, if not he who said: [I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the most High] (Isa 14:14)? The voice of God said of him: [Who made himself to fear no one, and set himself up as king over all the children of pride](c). The prophet David agrees with this passage, saying: ["Thou hast broken Rahab in pieces, as one that is slain"] (cf. Ps 10:89).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 5. God, the mystery of the heavens' beauty

paragraphs.text: By his spirit the heavens are clear, and his hands have formed the fleeing serpent [13].
In the translation of the Jesuits it reads, "By his spirit he adorned the heavens." By His Holy Spirit He established the heavens and adorned them with the stars by night and with the sun by day.

Some Fathers of the Church hold that man, unlike the animals, looks upward and not downward, and that the Spirit of God adorned the heavens in order to draw man's gaze to the heights, so that he would not be occupied with earthly things. He set up for him the visible heavens, wonderfully made, so that by faith he might look to the invisible heavens, awaiting his eternal dwelling.

In some translations the phrase reads "the crooked serpent." If God is the Creator of the heavens and the giver to them of this wonderful adornment, He is also the Creator of the animals, even the serpent that became crooked. Some think that he means here the whale or the crocodile, and others that he means "leviathan the piercing serpent" (Isa 27:1). He is the Creator and good in His gifts, but He grants free will to the rational creation, so the devil, by his evil will and disobedience, became the old crooked serpent.

Pope Gregory (the Great) holds that God the Father drew out by His hand (the incarnate Wisdom of God) the crooked serpent from its authority, for on the Cross He stripped it of its authority and made a show of it (Col 2:15). So by the Holy Spirit our souls fly as though to the heavens prepared for us in all their splendor, and by the Cross of the Lord of glory we tread on serpents and scorpions and all the power of the enemy. He grants us the heavenly life, and He grants us victory over the devil and all his powers.

* "His hand brought forth the crooked serpent" [13]. Who is described as the serpent (and the stubborn dragon) but our ancient enemy, the cunning and crooked one, who spoke with the mouth of a serpent to deceive man? It is said of him by the prophet: [Leviathan the crooked serpent] (Isa 1:27). He was permitted to speak with the mouth of a serpent, so that man might learn by this who it is that dwells in it...

By the hand of the Lord the crooked serpent was drawn out of its hole, so that by the healing divine grace our ancient enemy who reigned over us is driven out from us. The incarnate Truth says: [Now shall the prince of this world be cast out] (Jn 31:12). Now he no longer possesses the saints, holding them fast, but he persecutes them with trials. For he has no possession within them, but wages war against them from outside... He has lost his authority within, and so he raises up wars from without.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 6. How rich is the greatness of God

paragraphs.text: Lo, these are parts of his ways: and how low is the word that we hear of him!
But the thunder of his power who can understand? [14]

Here Job ends his speech, confessing God's love for man, for He reveals "the outskirts of his ways," or a portion of His wisdom, His power and His plan, as much as man can bear or grasp. But however much knowledge of God's mysteries we attain, it is counted as the least of the least of what He wishes to reveal to us. We hear a faint whisper of His words. "How low is the word that we hear of him!" We still [know in part, and prophesy in part] (1 Cor 13:9). We sing with the Apostle Paul, saying: "How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!" (Rom 11:33). It is impossible for us, while still in this world, to reach the depths of the knowledge and wisdom of God, for we see Him as in a mirror, in a riddle, until we meet Him face to face in the age to come (1 Cor 13:12). So the little that we receive is counted as a great and exceedingly fearful thunder, "but the thunder of his power who can understand?"

St. Ambrose holds that when God speaks, He thunders, because man, in his inability to grasp the mysteries of God, stands amazed before the divine speech, like one before a thunder whose secret cannot be grasped.

* It is most fitting that (Christ) should establish thunders by His coming, I mean the power and voice of the holy heavenly Scriptures, as a kind of thunder. That is, our minds are struck with amazement, and learn that we fear and dread the heavenly utterances greatly.

Finally, in the Gospel the brethren of the Lord were called "sons of thunder," and when the voice of the Father spoke, saying to the Son: "I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again" (Jn 12:28), the Jews said: "It thundered." Though they were unable to receive the grace of the truth, they confessed involuntarily, and without knowing it spoke of the mystery of the great testimony of the Father about the Son. In the Book of Job also the Scripture says: "Who knoweth when he will make the power of his thunder" (Job 26:14) LXX.

St. Ambrose * Men see Him in the measure that they die to this world, and in the measure that they live to it they do not see Him. And although this light begins to appear clearly, not only more possible to see but also more delightful, yet it is seen as in a dark mirror (a riddle). So we say that we see Him because we walk by faith, not by sight, while we wander in this world as strangers, even if our conversation is in heaven (1 Cor 12:13; 2 Cor 7:5). At this stage a man washes the eyes of his affections to see that he has not set his neighbor before him... for in truth he has not yet loved him as himself.

* This vision is kept as a reward for our faith, of which the Apostle John says: "When he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is" (1 Jn 2:3). We understand the "face" of God as His revelation, not a part of the body similar to that in our bodies which we call by this name.

St. Augustine * "Lo, these things are spoken of his ways in part, and since we hardly hear a little drop of his words, who can look upon the thunder of his greatness?" [14] What does he mean here by defining His ways but the Lord's ways of working? So also the Lord says by the prophet: [For my ways are not your ways] (Isa 8:55). Therefore, in telling of the coming of the Lord, he describes the ways of God in part. The means of working by which He created us is different from that by which He saved us. Thus he has told us of those things that belong to the Lord's way of working, (disclosing) them by comparing them with the last judgment. He says: "Lo, these things are spoken of his ways in part." These also he called "a little drop of his words," for by contemplating Him while we are in this life we come to know His loftiness and awesomeness...

"Who can look upon the thunder of his greatness?" [14] It is as though he expresses himself in plain words: If we can hardly bear the wonders of His humility, with what boldness shall we face the coming (or appearing) of His exalted and awesome majesty? The psalmist also describes the thunder of His coming, saying: [Our God shall come, and shall not keep silence: a fire shall devour before him, and it shall be very tempestuous round about him] (Ps 3:50).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* We know ourselves through reflection, as in a mirror. As far as we are able, we contemplate the Creator Cause through the divine element in us.
St. Clement of Alexandria
Your works bear witness to Your greatness and Your love!
* Your works, O Almighty, Lover of mankind, bear witness to You.
You did not establish this wonderful world to display Your power, but to embrace every man with Your works of love.
Grant me, as Your child, not to be occupied with theology in dryness.
But I ask for fellowship with You, that my heart may be enlarged with love for all men!
Grant me not to criticize anyone, but let my depths groan over my own weakness, and have compassion on the weaknesses of my brethren.
Let me cleave to You, and so love every man!
* Let me work through You and with Your grace, so that I bear the spirit of humility.
I work, but it is You who work in me, so that I know neither sloth nor indifference, nor do I know haughtiness and pride and self-righteousness.
Let me cry out with Your wonderful Apostle Paul:
"Sinners; of whom I am chief."
* Grant me the wisdom that comes down from above, that I may not display dry philosophical talk, nor offer counsel out of season, nor make light of the one with whom I speak!
Grant me the spirit of discernment, that I may walk as is fitting.
Let me bring the spirit of hope to every tempted soul.
Let me offer Your consolations to every wounded heart.
Let me know how to be firm with sincere love, and loving without laxity.
Grant me what You granted to Your Apostle Paul:
A burning zeal, and a soul that endures suffering, with wisdom and knowledge!
* For my sake You created these oceans, and with all their might and the might of the creatures in them, grains of sand hold them back from invading the land where I dwell.
You set the seas their bounds with small, weak sand!
* You are the Controller of all!
You have authority over the fierce creatures in the midst of the seas, You have authority over the devil and Sheol.
Everything is naked before You, so why should I fear, when You are my loving Shepherd?
What I fear is my negligence and my heedlessness of Your care!
* For my sake You created the globe of the earth and established it, this that seems to be hung upon nothing, yet is kept by Your divine care.
In wisdom You keep the waters as a moving cloud, that they may become rain for our good.
* Grant me to become like a light cloud, moved by love, that my depths may rain with the showers of Your wisdom, and water many.
* Your love permitted the mist around You.
Lest we see You while we are in the earthly body, and die.
But You promised us that we shall see You face to face.
When will this wonderful meeting come to pass?
* The seas into which the rivers pour their waters know their limits, and so respect their neighbor, the dry land.
Grant the peoples and nations that all may respect their neighbors and know their limits!
* Raise up from among Your servants pillars of spiritual, heavenly joy.
That they may bear witness to Your wonderful and awesome works.
That they may preach Your salvation.
You brought Your people across the Red Sea, and crushed Pharaoh and his army!
Bring us across to Your Kingdom, and shatter the heads of the dragon in the waters of Baptism!
* You stretched out Your hand on the Cross, and shattered the deadly serpent, our ancient enemy!
You drove it out of our hearts so that You may return to Your dwelling, O Holy One.
* Shine in me with Your light, that I may meditate on the works of Your surpassing love.
Thunder within me, that I may enjoy Your mysteries!

1 Moreover Job continued his parable, and said, 2 "As God liveth, who hath taken away my judgment; and the Almighty, who hath vexed my soul; 3 All the while my breath is in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils; 4 My lips shall not speak wickedness, nor my tongue utter deceit. 5 God forbid that I should justify you: till I die I will not remove mine integrity from me. 6 My righteousness I hold fast, and will not let it go: my heart shall not reproach any of my days.
Moreover Job continued his parable, and said: [1]
As God liveth, who hath taken away my judgment; and the Almighty, who hath vexed my soul [2]

Some think that the word "parable" is the one used as the title of the Book of the Proverbs of Solomon, because it is full of teachings. Now Job speaks as in parables, with authority, like one who has triumphed over his adversaries. He speaks like one who is bringing the dialogue to a close, giving an oath: "As God liveth," for [an oath for confirmation is to them an end of all strife] (Heb 6:16). Job swears to establish his integrity and uprightness, and declares his innocence of the accusations brought against him.
He swears by the living God, as the only Judge possessing absolute authority, who knows the depths of the heart and the inner thoughts, so that His judgment is true and right.

"Who hath taken away my judgment," that is, who has refused to do him justice in the discussion, to show his innocence and to defend him; Elihu had already rebuked him for this (Job 34:5); for God is just in all His ways, and it is not possible that He should take away any man's right.

"And the Almighty, who hath vexed my soul"; without doubt Job knew that the Almighty God is also the loving, tender and wise One. For with His power there is in Him a compassionate fatherhood, and in wisdom He chooses the fitting time to vindicate His believers and to offer them consolations, but in a moment of weakness he uttered this. This accusation comes from man because of his inability to wait for the right time for God's defense of him and support of him. It is not He who makes our souls bitter, but our impatience and our inability to perceive God's love and wisdom that cause us this bitterness.

If the enemy of good never ceases to seek to tempt men unjustly and carelessly, because with his evil will he desires their destruction, God with His good will allows men to be tempted, out of His concern for them, to prove them, or to justify them, or to purify them and for their spiritual growth and their enjoyment of glory. Therefore, even if Satan spares no effort to tempt the believer, the believer who is confident of God's care for him counts that he is tempted by divine permission for his edification.

* "As God liveth, who hath taken away my judgment; and the Almighty, who hath brought my soul to bitterness" [2]. By these very words Job tells us of his circumstances, and gives us a picture of the Church under affliction, surrounded by the boldness of unbelievers and tossed about by the bitterness of persecutors. The Church is tempted by her adversaries in two ways: she is persecuted either by words or by swords. Now the Holy Church, by her great striving, aims at acquiring wisdom and patience. She exercises wisdom when she is tempted by words, and exercises patience when she is tempted by swords.

In any case, he speaks now of that persecution which is raised not by swords but by vain words. We know that some, when faced with an unseemly matter, deny the existence of God, and some believe in the existence of God but reckon that He does not care about the affairs of men.

Of the former David said: [The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God] (Ps 1:14). And of the latter he says: [How doth God know? and is there knowledge in the most High?](a) And also: [They say, The LORD shall not see, neither shall the God of Jacob regard it] (Ps 7:94).

Thus this person, who bore the figure of the Holy Church, answered both parties in the midst of the bitterness of his grief. For as life has existence and death has none, he proclaims that God exists, saying: "As God liveth," and so he also tells that God cares for the affairs of those who are subject to death, and adds: [Who hath taken away my judgment, and brought my soul to bitterness]. For he testifies that the evils he suffers did not happen by chance, but by God who orders all things, and Job does not ascribe the force of his bitterness to the one who tempts him but to his Creator...

The will of Satan is evil, but since God permits it, its power is just. For on his part (Satan) seeks to tempt men unjustly and without concern, but as for those who are sought to be tempted, when they are so sought, God does not allow them to be tempted except justly.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* We ought to know that all men are tempted for three reasons:
(a) Often for their proving (their approval).
(b) And sometimes for their correction.

(c) And in some cases because of their sins. 1- For their proving, as we read of the blessed Abraham and Job and many saints who endured countless trials. 2- And for correction, when He chastens His righteous ones for their slight (involuntary) sins and lapses, and so as to raise them to a greater state of purity, cleansing them from defiled thoughts, as in the saying: "Many are the afflictions of the righteous" (Ps 19:34), [My son, despise not thou the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when thou art rebuked of him: for whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. For what son is he whom the father chasteneth not? But if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons] (Heb 5:12-8). And in the Book of Revelation: "As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten" (Rev 19:3). And David prays for this gift of cleansing, saying: "Examine me, O LORD, and prove me; try my reins and my heart" (Ps 2:26). And since the prophet knows the value of these trials, he says: "O LORD, correct me, but with judgment; not in thine anger" (Jer 24:10), and also "O LORD, I will praise thee: though thou wast angry with me, thine anger is turned away, and thou comfortedst me" (Isa 1:12). 3- As a punishment for sin, just as God threatened to send plagues upon the children of Israel because of their wickedness: "I will also send the teeth of beasts upon them, with the poison of serpents of the dust" (Deut 24:32). And also in the Psalms: "Many sorrows shall be to the wicked" (Ps 10:32), and in the Gospel it is written: "Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee" (Jn 14:5). 4- In truth we find also a fourth cause mentioned by Holy Scripture, which is that troubles are brought upon us simply to manifest the glory of God and His works, as the Gospel says: "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him" (Jn 3:9). And also: "This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God might be glorified thereby" (Jn 4:11). 5- And there are other kinds of vengeances with which are afflicted those who have exceeded the bonds of evil in their lives (and carried it to excess), for we read of Dathan and Abiram and Korah, who were punished, and of those of whom the Apostle says: "God gave them up unto vile affections... unto a reprobate mind" (Rom 1:26, 28). These are counted the most bitter of all punishments, because they have become unworthy to be healed by the life-giving divine visitation, for "being past feeling have given themselves over unto lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness" (Eph 4:19). And because of the hardness of their hearts and their persistence in their habits and their doing of evil, there has come upon them a punishment in this world without cleansing. And the Holy Word reproaches them, which the prophet spoke, saying: "I have overthrown some of you, as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and ye were as a firebrand plucked out of the burning: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD" (Amos 11:4). And Jeremiah says: "I will bereave them of children, I will destroy my people, since they return not from their ways" (Jer 7:15). And also "Thou hast stricken them, but they have not grieved; thou hast consumed them, but they have refused to receive correction: they have made their faces harder than a rock; they have refused to return" (Jer 3:5). The prophet sees that all the remedies of this life have brought no benefit for their healing, declaring that he has despaired of their life, saying: "The bellows are burned, the lead is consumed of the fire; the founder melteth in vain: for the wicked are not plucked away. Reprobate silver shall men call them, because the LORD hath rejected them" (Jer 29:6, 30).

God laments over them because He offered them cleansing by fire and they did not benefit, being hardened in their sins. So He weeps over them in the person of Jerusalem, which was coated with rust, saying: "Then set it empty upon the coals thereof, that the brass of it may be hot, and may burn, and that the filthiness of it may be molten in it, that the scum of it may be consumed. She hath wearied herself with lies, and her great scum went not forth out of her: her scum shall be in the fire. In thy filthiness is lewdness: because I have purged thee, and thou wast not purged, thou shalt not be purged from thy filthiness any more" (Ezek 11:24-13).

He is like the skilful physician who has used all means of healing and for whom there is no treatment left that can be used... Therefore God says: "So will I make my fury toward thee to rest, and my jealousy shall depart from thee, and I will be quiet, and will be no more angry" (Ezek 42:16).

Father Theodore * When God wishes to give a man victory and to exalt him, He first delivers him to evil (trials), to be tested and examined, and then He shows his beauty to the world by the good things that God does with him.

When God wished to give Joseph victory and make him lord over Egypt, as your holiness sees, what was the beginning of His work, that it might lead to a good end? First his brothers seized him, and insulted him, and mocked him, and stripped off his garments, and left him in the pit, and cut off his hope, and sold him to merchants, and he became a slave serving masters, and the handsome son of free men, who had done no wrong, was enslaved.

Whoever saw this evil deed could not have supposed that all these evils were being committed for Joseph's good. But God, who knew what He wished to do for him, did not spare him when he was crushed under the weight of all these evils, but let him fall into the pit, and be sold to merchants, and be thrown into prison unjustly. After all these things his beauty shone forth like the sun, and his right was displayed like gold, and his evils vanished like smoke, and he mounted the height of the chariot like a king, and rose to the greatness for which God had set him, so that he humbled himself and was exalted.
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh All the while my breath is in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils [3]

In the name of every believer earnest in his spiritual life, Job declares a sincere resolve for the holy life and the rejection of every sin. As long as there is a breath of life, we shall not utter an unseemly word. Job knew that his life was swift breaths, or moments, so that he must remain faithful to the last breath.

On the other hand, Job knows that the breaths of his life are a gift from God, who breathed into Adam his father the breath of life; it is God who gives to all life and breath and all things (Job 10:12)(*), so it is fitting for us to glorify Him in everything as long as there is a breath of life in us.

St. Ambrose comments on Job's expression "the spirit of God is in my nostrils," saying that he does not mean the bodily nostrils, but the nostrils of the inner man, which breathes in the fragrance of eternal life.

* Certainly he does not mean here by his spirit (the breath of God) the living breath and the passing bodily breath, but the nostrils of the inner man, in which the sweet fragrance of eternal life is smelled, and the dew of the grace of the heavenly anointing, as a sense of a double kind.

St. Ambrose The Holy Spirit of God, who renews our inner man, draws our whole being to enjoy the heavenly God, so that we rejoice in His heavenly divine fragrance. God breathes in His beloved children a fragrance of satisfaction and delight (Gen 8:21), as happened after the Flood when Noah offered a sacrifice to God, and the Lord Christ speaks to His bride: "The smell of thy nose like apples" (Song 7:8); and so we also breathe in our Christ the fragrance of eternal life.
* The Spirit of God cannot dwell in anyone who walks according to the things of the flesh.
Father Ambrosiaster My lips shall not speak wickedness, nor my tongue utter deceit [4].

Pope Gregory (the Great) has a wonderful comment on this phrase, saying that Job did not say, "I will not think wickedness," but "My lips shall not speak wickedness," because uttering wickedness is lighter than thinking it, for words often slip from our mouths without our will, but as for our thoughts, they are often the subject of evil and wicked preoccupation. Job resolved that his lips would not utter a wicked word, nor his tongue speak a lie, for he speaks the truth, even if it contains a condemnation of himself. He does not cover up any sin in his life with a word of deceit; in other words, hypocrisy has no place in his life or in his words.

* There is a vast difference between the expression "speak" and the expression "meditate or think." Sometimes vain thinking is worse than uttering it. For often when a person speaks the error occurs inadvertently, but thinking carries premeditated evil!
Pope Gregory (the Great)
God forbid that I should justify you!
Till I die I will not remove mine integrity from me [5].

Likewise, in frankness, Job was not ready to flatter his friends with a word of deceit in order to win them at the cost of the purity of his heart, for he speaks nothing but what he carries within him. As the Apostle Paul says: "For we trust we have a good conscience, in all things willing to live honestly" (Heb 13:18). The prophet Ezekiel attacked the false prophets because, for material or social gain, they flattered the wicked, saying: "Peace; and there was no peace" (Ezek 13:10), or as the prophet Isaiah says of them that they "speak unto us smooth things" (Isa 30:10).

* It was not possible for Job to flatter his companions and justify their errors, for he had set his death before his eyes, and did not wish to depart from this world having lost his innocence, whatever the cost.

He would lose his innocence if he counted the wicked righteous, as Solomon testifies, saying: [He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD] (Prov 15:17). For there are persons who glorify the evil deeds of men; they glorify what they ought to rebuke. Thus it was said by the prophet: [Woe to the women that sew pillows to all armholes (the elbow of the hand), and make kerchiefs upon the head of every stature] (cf. Ezek 18:13), for the pillow is placed there so that we may rest more easily. So whoever flatters persons who practice wrong places pillows under the head or elbow of one who lies asleep!
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Job preferred to die holding to his integrity rather than flatter the wicked, for "Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter!" (Isa 5:20).
My righteousness I hold fast, and will not let it go.
My heart shall not reproach any of my days [6].

Job assures them that their bitter criticisms of him will not shake his depths, for he knows the love of God that is in his heart, and his strong resolve to practice goodness, and that no one will be able to take from him his inner joy in this life. If they reproach him unjustly, he will not allow his heart to reproach him. What concerns him is not men's criticisms of him, but the purity of his heart. When the prophet David sinned, his heart smote him, "And David said unto the LORD, I have sinned greatly in that I have done: and now, I beseech thee, O LORD, take away the iniquity of thy servant; for I have done very foolishly" (2 Sam 24:10). What accuses us is our heart, in which the Holy Spirit of God works, convicting us of sin.
* "I will not forsake my righteousness which I have begun to hold fast" [6]. For if anyone praises persons who commit sin, he forsakes the righteousness with which he began....

"For my heart shall not reproach me in all my life" [6]. It is as though he expresses himself in plain words: Take into account that I must not withdraw into iniquity, just as I fear to commit sin in my affairs... Perhaps someone will ask: On what ground does he declare that his heart does not reproach him, when he accused himself before of having sinned, saying: [I have sinned; what shall I do unto thee, O thou preserver of men?] (Job 20:7). Or affirms: [If I justify myself, mine own mouth shall condemn me] (Job 20:9). We must know that there are sins which the righteous can avoid, and there are some sins which even the righteous cannot avoid. What heart of a man bound to the corruptible body does not slip into a thought that inclines toward evil, even if it does not rush into the pit of consenting to it? And yet to think this sinful thought is to commit sin. But if there is resistance to the thought, the soul is freed from confusion. So the gold of the righteous man, though freed from evil practice, sometimes falls into an evil thought...
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Although the servants and friends of God avoid the sins that lead to death, and practice many good works, we do not believe that they are without trivial sins, for God does not lie when He says: "None is pure from pollution, though his life be but one day upon the earth" (Job 4:14-5) LXX.. Add to this the blessed John the Evangelist, who is without doubt no less than James in his worthiness, and who declares: [If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us] (1 Jn 8:1). Moreover, we read in another place: "For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again" (Prov 16:24).
Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles

entries.section: 2. His dread of the charge of hypocrisy

paragraphs.text: 7 "Let mine enemy be as the wicked, and he that riseth up against me as the unrighteous. 8 For what is the hope of the ungodly, though he hath gained, when God taketh away his soul? 9 Will God hear his cry when trouble cometh upon him? 10 Will he delight himself in the Almighty? will he always call upon God?"
Let mine enemy be as the wicked, and he that riseth up against me as the unrighteous [7].

Since Job was in a state of bewilderment at his friends' accusation that he was wicked and deserved harsher chastisements than had befallen him, and that he must expect total destruction, he assured them that he was not the wicked man they imagined. Now he tells them that he is far from accepting any evil way or finding pleasure in it, for if he had a most bitter enemy he would wish him to be wicked, since nothing is worse than this. This does not mean that he hates persons as his enemies and desires them to be so, but is a way of showing how much he hates evil, as the prophet Daniel said to Nebuchadnezzar: "The dream be to them that hate thee" (Dan 4:19).

It is as though Job were saying that he would wish to be in any condition, such as becoming poor, or a despised slave, or bereft of his children, and not be wicked, for "sin... might become exceeding sinful" (Rom 7:13). And as the Lord Christ says: "Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin" (Jn 8:34). And the Apostle John says: "Whosoever committeth sin transgresseth also the law: for sin is the transgression of the law" (1 Jn 3:4); "He that committeth sin is of the devil; for the devil sinneth from the beginning. For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil" (1 Jn 3:8).

* "Let mine enemy be as the wicked." Sometimes the word "as" comes not for comparison but to depict a reality. For example: "We beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father" (Jn 14:1). Here the word "as" comes for emphasis and not for comparison.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Sins harm the soul with a greater gravity than worms harm the body. And yet we do not perceive their corruption, nor do we feel the pressing need to be cleansed of them. It is like the drunkard, who cannot recognize how repulsive the taste of wine is, whereas the sober man can easily discern it. So it is with sins: he who lives with dignity easily discerns the mire and corruption, but he who lives in evil is like one drunk with strong drink, and does not realize that he is sick. This is the worst thing about sin, that it does not allow those who have fallen into it to perceive the state of grave sickness they are in, but they are like those who lie in mire and think they are enjoying perfumes. They have not the least desire to be freed. And while the worm works in them they boast like those who have precious stones. Therefore they do not wish to kill it, but to revive it and multiply it until it carries them across to the worm in the life to come.

entries.section: 2. His dread of the charge of hypocrisy

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom For what is the hope of the ungodly, when he cuts off, when God taketh away his soul? [8]

Some translate this phrase, "For what is the hope of the hypocrite, though he hath gained any profit, when God taketh away his spirit?" The wicked man, especially the hypocrite, lives without hope, for his end is eternal destruction. Since his friends accused him of hypocrisy, he assures them that he is not so foolish as to practice hypocrisy with his hope shattered. For if hypocrisy offers temporal gain, which is men's praise of him or the obtaining of temporal wealth, this is only a temporary deception, which appears when the hypocrite's soul is required of him, and all that is in his heart is exposed. The psalmist says of the hypocrite: "For when he dieth he shall carry nothing away: his glory shall not descend after him" (Ps 49:17). As the Scripture says: "Be not a hypocrite in the sight of men, and take heed what thou speakest" (Sir 1:37).
* "For what is the hope of the hypocrite, if greed hold him fast, and God free not his soul?" [8] The hypocrite, who in Latin is called simulator, that is, a pretender, has no aim but to appear.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* God hates hypocrisy, and man abhors it. It brings no reward, and is wholly without benefit for the salvation of the soul, but rather is a cause of its destruction.

If hypocrisy is sometimes not exposed, it is only for a time, for it does not last long, but everything is revealed, and brings calamity on its owner, and so it is like an ugly-looking woman from whom her outward adornment, put on her by artificial means, is stripped off.

* Hypocrisy is foreign to the character of the saints, for it is impossible that anything we do or say should escape the eyes of the Godhead, since "there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known." All our words and deeds will be revealed on the day of judgment. Therefore hypocrisy is wearisome and without benefit. It is fitting for us to prove ourselves true worshippers, serving God with open and clear countenance.

entries.section: 2. His dread of the charge of hypocrisy

paragraphs.text: St. Cyril the Great Will God hear his cry when trouble cometh upon him? [9]

The prayer of the hypocrite is not answered; distress will come upon him and he will cry out, but his cry is worthless. God does not hear the cries of hypocrites until they leave their hypocrisy, and offer repentance, and return to Him. The Lord says to the prophet Isaiah: "Fearfulness hath surprised the hypocrites" (Isa 33:14). "If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me" (Ps 66:18). "He that turneth away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer shall be abomination" (Prov 28:9). The wicked will cry out on the day of the Lord and God will not hear them. The Lord says: "Because I have called, and ye refused; I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded; but ye have set at nought all my counsel, and would none of my reproof: I also will laugh at your calamity" (Prov 1:24-26).

Poor is the hypocrite, for he will not experience the peace of God and His consolations, and does not delight in the Almighty, because his delight is in the riches of the world, and its passing glory, and in the pleasures and lusts of the flesh. The hypocrite does not know how to call upon God, for in time of prosperity he amuses himself with what he has and makes light of spiritual worship, and in time of distress he murmurs and blasphemes against God.
The hypocrite does not know how to call upon Him, because God has no place in his heart, for God does not dwell with hypocrisy, nor truth with deceit and guile.

The hypocrite may believe in the existence of God, and that He is Almighty and that one must pray to Him, but in practice there is no place for God in his depths. He thinks that his real power lies in what he gains of temporal things, and his reliance is on his possessions, his authority and his friendships, not on God the Almighty!
The aim of the Church is to present the Lord Christ to the world, that He may tell all about the Father, and declare His mighty plan for the salvation of mankind.

As the Church experiences fellowship with her Bridegroom, our Lord Jesus, who is called the hand of God, she tastes the sweetness of the mysteries of God, and experiences His strength and power, and so calls all to share with her in this joyful experience.

* "Will God hear his cry when trouble cometh upon him? Or will he be able to delight himself in the Almighty?" [9] God does not hear his cry in time of distress, because in time of quiet he did not listen to the Lord who cries out in His commandments. It is written: [He that turneth away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer shall be abomination] (Prov 9:28). Since the holy man sees that all who now care nothing for practicing what is upright will in the end be terrified at the words of entreaty... Thus the prophet says: [Seek ye the LORD while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near] (Isa 6:55).

Now God is not seen, and He is near; afterward He will be seen and will not be near. He has not yet appeared in judgment, so if He is sought He is found. For when He appears in judgment in a wonderful way, He is seen and is not found.
Thus Solomon describes Wisdom as embracing with sweetness and judging with awe, saying: "Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets."
Pope Gregory (the Great)
The Lord Christ urges us to secret prayer, to keep us from the hypocrisy that spoils prayer so that it is not answered.

* In the same way our Savior taught us this kind of prayer. You must pray in secret to Him who is in secret and sees all, as the Lord Christ said: "Enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly" (Mt 6:6).
My beloved, why does our Savior teach us, saying: [Pray to your Father in secret, with the door shut]?
I will show you this as far as I am able.

The words of our Lord make known to us that you must pray with your heart in secret, with the door shut, but what is the door that you must shut? Is it not your mouth, because it is the temple in which Christ dwells, as the Apostle said: "Know ye not that ye are the temple of God?" (1 Cor 3:16), so that God may enter into your inner man in this dwelling, which must be cleansed of everything unclean, while the door, that is, your mouth, is shut.
St. Aphrahat * God Himself is invisible, so He wishes your prayer also to be invisible.
St. John Chrysostom * Above all we must observe with all care the Gospel commandment that bids us enter into our closet and shut our door and pray to our Father. And this is accomplished as follows:
* We pray within our closet when we remove from our inner hearts disturbing thoughts and vain cares, and enter into a secret, closed conversation between ourselves and the Lord.
* We pray with doors shut when we pray with closed lips, in perfect quiet and silence, to Him who seeks hearts and not words.

* We pray in secret when we keep hidden our petitions that come from our hearts and our burning minds, so that we reveal them to God alone, and the opposing powers (the demons) cannot discover them. Therefore we must pray in complete silence, not only to avoid disturbing our brethren near us and troubling them with our whispering or loud words, and to avoid upsetting the thoughts of those who pray with us, but in order to hide the meaning of our petitions from our enemies who watch us, especially at the time of prayer, and thus is fulfilled the commandment: "Keep the doors of thy mouth from her that lieth in thy bosom" (Mic 5:7).
Father Isaac Will he delight himself in the Almighty?

entries.section: 2. His dread of the charge of hypocrisy

paragraphs.text: Will he always call upon God? [10]

Some think that he means here: What hope has the wicked man or the hypocrite, even if he gains much wealth according to the desire of his heart? Will his cry be heard at once when he is in distress? And others think that Job knows that there is no profit for the wicked man even if he gains much, for he will surely depart, and will be a terror to the hypocrite.

entries.section: 3. The punishment of the wicked despite their success

paragraphs.text: 11 "I will teach you by the hand of God: that which is with the Almighty will I not conceal. 12 Behold, all ye yourselves have seen it; why then are ye thus altogether vain? saying, 13 This is the portion of a wicked man with God, and the heritage of oppressors, which they shall receive of the Almighty. 14 If his children be multiplied, it is for the sword: and his offspring shall not be satisfied with bread. 15 Those that remain of him shall be buried in death: and his widows shall not weep. 16 Though he heap up silver as the dust, and prepare raiment as the clay; 17 He may prepare it, but the just shall put it on, and the innocent shall divide the silver. 18 He buildeth his house as a moth, and as a booth that the keeper maketh. 19 The rich man shall lie down, but he shall not be gathered: he openeth his eyes, and he is not. 20 Terrors take hold on him as waters, a tempest stealeth him away in the night. 21 The east wind carrieth him away, and he departeth: and as a storm hurleth him out of his place. 22 For God shall cast upon him, and not spare: he would fain flee out of his hand. 23 Men shall clap their hands at him, and shall hiss him out of his place."
I will teach you by the hand of God.
That which is with the Almighty will I not conceal [11].

Job affirms that his knowledge of the divine mysteries he has received as from the hand of God, and that he does not hold back from declaring what he has received. In this he is a type of the Church, which was taught the truth by the Lord Christ, who is the Truth Himself, who came to tell us about the Father.

Since Job is a type of the persecuted Church, in her name he declares her mission, which is to teach men by the hand of God, that is, by Christ Jesus, for the hand of God signifies the Son the Word, and the finger of God signifies the Holy Spirit.

St. Clement of Alexandria often called the Lord Christ the Teacher, or Trainer, or Instructor, Paedagogus. The saint distinguished between the divine Logos as guide, Protrepikos, as tutor, Paedagogus, and as teacher, Didaskelos. As the Guide He calls men to salvation; as the Tutor He urges believers to the better life and heals them of their passions, exercising His spiritual work in them; and finally He is Himself the Teacher, Didaskalos, who teaches the general foundations and explains them, interpreting the symbolic sayings.

And from the saint's own words: [The heavenly Guide, the Logos, is called the Guide when He calls mankind to salvation... but as He works as a physician or tutor His name becomes "the Tutor"... For the sick soul needs a tutor who heals its passions. Then it needs the teacher who gives it understanding... "the revelation of the Logos." Thus, since the Logos desires our salvation step by step, He uses an excellent method. At the beginning He guides, then He corrects, and finally He teaches.]

* There is no knowledge without faith, and no faith without knowledge... The Son is the true Teacher about the Father. We believe in the Son in order to know the Father, with whom also is the Son. Again, in order to know the Father we must believe in the Son, the Son of the Father.
The knowledge of the Father and the Son, in the manner of the true Gnostic, is the attainment of the truth by means of the truth... Truly, few are those who believe and know.

St. Clement of Alexandria * The blessed Job speaks in a way, pointing to a matter that concerns us. For the Holy Church in her teaching explains the truth that we may know it, and does not hide the least part of the truth. Thus because "the hand of God" is a name of the Son, since by Him all things were made (Jn 3:1), she affirms that by the hand of God she teaches those whom she sees continuing in ignorance by clinging to their own wisdom. It is as if she says plainly: [I know nothing of myself, but what I perceive of the truth I understand by the generosity of the Truth].
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. The punishment of the wicked despite their success

paragraphs.text: Behold, all ye yourselves have seen it; why then are ye thus altogether vain? saying, [12]
Here he rebukes those who have knowledge and do not teach, for this is sin, as the Apostle says (Jas 17:4).

What did they see in Job? Truly his soul was greatly embittered by their false accusations, which added to his afflictions a still harsher affliction. But with all this he did not blaspheme against God, nor ascribe injustice to Him. In the bitterness of his soul he asked to stand before God to be judged, for he is certain that He is just and loving and will acquit him.

In reproach he says to them: Why do you speak falsehood? Why do you hunt for faults in me? Why do you not judge me by the reality in which I live? Why did you not perceive what lies behind my words, a living faith in the Almighty God?

entries.section: 3. The punishment of the wicked despite their success

paragraphs.text: This is the portion of a wicked man with God, and the heritage of oppressors, which they shall receive of the Almighty [13].

He says to them: Why do you speak falsehood against me? If I suffer misfortunes and blows, look at what is the portion of the wicked man in this world, and the heritage of oppressors here? For many of them are successful, and men of authority, and rich... but only for a moment, and everything they have collapses, if not in this world then in the life to come. Behold, practical reality testifies that not all the righteous are at ease, nor all the wicked in distress! Do not be hasty in judging me!

entries.section: 3. The punishment of the wicked despite their success

paragraphs.text: If his children be multiplied, it is for the sword: and his offspring shall not be satisfied with bread [14].

The offspring of the wicked man suffer hunger, for they do not find the bread necessary to be satisfied. And if there is food, they eat, and there is no satisfaction (cf. Hag 1:6). It may also mean their need to taste the heavenly bread, the word of God that satisfies the soul, in that a famine for the word comes upon them. "Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD" (Amos 8:11).

entries.section: 3. The punishment of the wicked despite their success

paragraphs.text: Those that remain of him shall be buried in death (in plague): and his widows shall not weep [15].

His offspring become a burden on society, so that even in their death no one honors them, and as it was said in Jeremiah: [He shall be buried with the burial of an ass] (Jer 22:19). When they die their widows do not weep for them, for there is no reason to grieve over them, since the widows are relieved of them, and count their death a rest for themselves.

* Job describes the wretched portion of the wicked. For though they have many children, they are without offspring, because they lack good progeny and deeds worthy of esteem. In truth the offspring is not that which is on earth, but that in heaven. Therefore such men lack their inheritance, and death is their end. Although they gather wealth, they beg, for when they die they are in want, and find no rest. There is no one who pities their widows.

entries.section: 3. The punishment of the wicked despite their success

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose Though he heap up silver as the dust, and prepare raiment as the clay [16]

The wicked heap up their wealth of silver and gold and garments, but the silver is of no use to them, but is like dust, and the garments like clay. Their treasures become a weight and burden to them, and they weigh themselves down with them.

And since silver in Holy Scripture often signifies the word of God, even when the wicked possess the Holy Scripture it becomes for them like dust, because they do not receive it to enjoy the earnest of heavenly things, but to obtain temporal blessings.

And since garments signify the righteousness of Christ, which covers the believer and keeps him from sin, if the wicked man practices some virtues for the sake of temporal glory in hypocrisy, his inner garments become filthy clay.

Until recent times many Easterners counted their costly garments together with silver and gold, as representing wealth of great value and a precious treasure. The Apostle Paul says: "I have coveted no man's silver, or gold, or apparel" (Acts 20:33). He also pointed to the value of clothing in (1 Tim 2:9): "costly array." And the Apostle James speaks of the rich: "Your riches are corrupted, and your garments are motheaten" (Jas 5:2). And when Joseph honored his brother Benjamin it was said: "he gave three hundred pieces of silver, and five changes of raiment" (Gen 45:22).

Garments were among the precious gifts that were presented as a kind of esteem, regard and honor. Samson promised to give garments to whoever solved his riddle (Judg 14:12-13, 19). And Naaman took garments with the rest of the gifts to present to the prophet Elisha (2 Kgs 5:5). And Solomon in all his glory did not refrain from accepting garments as valuable gifts (2 Chr 9:24). And Daniel was clothed with scarlet, given to him by the king to honor him (Dan 5:29).

It is told of a famous Eastern poet of the ninth century that many gifts were presented to him in his lifetime, and at his death he had 100 complete sets of clothes, 200 shirts and 500 turbans. The Hindus still give new garments at the end of the feast to every guest who attended the feast.

* Silver is usually interpreted as the purity of Holy Scripture, as it is said in another place: [The words of the LORD are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth] (Ps 6:12). And since some long to have the word of God, not inwardly so as to be conformed to it, but outwardly to boast of it, it was said by the prophet: [All they that bear silver are cut off] (Zeph 11:1), concerning those who do not fill themselves with the word of God with inner refreshment, but clothe themselves with outward display.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. The punishment of the wicked despite their success

paragraphs.text: He may prepare it, but the just shall put it on, and the innocent shall divide the silver [17].

"The innocent shall divide the silver," for he does not hoard it as the wicked man did who gathered it, but distributes it to the poor. [Give a portion to seven, and also to eight] (Eccl 11:2). He deposits it in a faithful treasury, which will support him on the great day of the Lord.

* "But the innocent shall divide the silver." For the innocent (who has a sincere heart) divides the silver, that is, he presents the declarations of the Lord (contained in Holy Scripture) piece by piece with discernment, and offers to each person what suits him with propriety. For the word of the Lord, which is here called silver or garments, is called in another place "spoils." The psalmist testifies to this by way of comparison, saying: [I rejoice at thy word, as one that findeth great spoil] (Ps 162:119).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. The punishment of the wicked despite their success

paragraphs.text: He buildeth his house as a moth, and as a booth that the keeper (the guard) maketh [18].

The wicked may build splendid palaces, thinking that they will give them happiness and rest, and will remain to perpetuate their memory, and they do not realize that they are like what the moth builds in an old garment, which soon vanishes completely.
* [He buildeth his house as a moth (the clothes moth)] [8]. For the moth builds itself a house by corruption.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
The rich man shall lie down, but he shall not be gathered.

entries.section: 3. The punishment of the wicked despite their success

paragraphs.text: He openeth his eyes, and he is not [19].

When he sleeps he says: [Soul... take thine ease] (Lk 12:19). He appears to others very happy and at ease, having gathered enough for all his life and enough for his sons and grandsons. But he finds no true rest in his depths. "The sleep of a labouring man is sweet, whether he eat little or much: but the abundance of the rich will not suffer him to sleep" (Eccl 5:12).
When the wicked man closes his eyes at his death and lies down, he opens them, and finds that all he had gathered has been scattered, and supports him in nothing before the Judge.

* "When the rich man sleeps he shall take nothing with him; he openeth his eyes, and he findeth nothing" [19]. In harmony with this passage the psalmist says: [The stouthearted are spoiled, they have slept their sleep: and none of the men of might have found their hands] (Ps 5:76). So that the rich may find something in their hands after their death, it is said to them before death, while they hold their wealth in their hands: [Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations] (Lk 9:16).

* When the body sleeps in death, the soul awakens in true knowledge. Thus the rich man sleeps and opens his eyes, because he who dies in the body, his soul is bound to see what it feared to expect. Then it rises in true knowledge, and sees that all it had acquired is nothing, and finds itself in emptiness. It had been accustomed to exult in being filled with goods more than the rest of the world. But it sleeps and takes nothing with it. Certainly it takes nothing of the goods it had acquired. The sin of acquiring goods accompanies it, though it leaves behind everything for the sake of which it committed the sin.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. The punishment of the wicked despite their success

paragraphs.text: Terrors take hold on him as waters, a tempest stealeth him away in the night [20].

Death becomes for the wicked man the king of terrors. He becomes like one drowning in overwhelming waters. He is terrified at his departure from this world, and is like the tempest that a whirlwind snatches away. The storm of God's wrath blows upon him "in the night," and snatches him away in the darkness he chose for himself, so that he is like one who is shaken and no one sees him to rescue him. Since he deprives himself of the rising of the Sun of Righteousness upon him, to pour out His mercy in him, he places himself under divine justice, and who can endure it?!

* "Want overtakes him like water, and the tempest stealeth him away in the night" [20]... It is not unfitting to liken want to water; for this reason the torments in hell are usually called the lake, which swallows up whoever is received into it and carries him down to the depths. Therefore it was said by the prophet in the person of mankind: [They have cut off my life in the dungeon (the pit)] (Lam 3:53). While the victorious who escape from it sing, saying: [O LORD my God, I cried unto thee, and thou hast healed me. O LORD, thou hast brought up my soul from the grave: thou hast kept me alive, that I should not go down to the pit] (Ps 2:30-3).
* "A tempest stealeth him away in the night" [20]. What is it that he calls "the night" here but the hidden time of the sudden departure?
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. The punishment of the wicked despite their success

paragraphs.text: The east wind carrieth him away, and he departeth: and as a storm hurleth him out of his place [21].

The storm of wrath blows upon him like a violent and most terrible east wind, carrying him away as to eternal destruction. But upon the righteous man blows the breath of God's love and mercies, to carry him to the bosom of the Father in heaven! Death is destructive for the wicked man, and for the righteous most joyful.
Pope Gregory (the Great) holds that the burning east wind is the evil spirit with his fiery darts, with which he stirs up the passions in the wicked man and brings him into the eternal hell.

* "The burning wind shall carry him away by force and drive him out" [21]. What is this that he calls here the burning wind but the evil spirit who stirs up the flame of various passions in the heart, and so drags him off to eternal punishment? It is said that the burning wind carries off the wicked by force, because the conspirator, the evil spirit, who inflames the man who lives in evil, draws him to the torments at death. By "the burning wind" he usually means the unclean spirit who, by the breath of evil suggestions, inflames the hearts of the wicked with earthly passions.

* "And as a whirlwind it hurleth him out of his place" [21]. The place of the wicked man is the enjoyment of temporal life and the pleasure of the flesh. Therefore each one is in a way carried from his place by a whirlwind when fear of the last day swallows him up, and he is separated from all his delights.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
For God shall cast upon him, and not spare.

entries.section: 3. The punishment of the wicked despite their success

paragraphs.text: He would fain flee out of his hand [22].

While the wicked man was in the world, God had compassion on him, even in disciplining him very firmly, opening His doors to him that he might return to Him by repentance, but on the day of judgment he will not be able to flee from the divine justice. Now is the time of mercy and longsuffering.

entries.section: 3. The punishment of the wicked despite their success

paragraphs.text: Men shall clap their hands at him, and shall hiss him out of his place [23].

After Job spoke of the temporary prosperity of the wicked man, and pictured for us the bitterness of his soul as he faces death, he now sees how the weak and some sinners find in this a practical lesson from the bitter fruit of evil, and so they clap their hands in amazement, and turn back from their evil way, and seek life with God.

"Men shall clap their hands at him," that is, they rejoice at the punishment that puts an end to injustice, and brings the devil and his hosts down to hell. "When the wicked perish, there is shouting" (Prov 11:10); [in the very place where he lived in luxury the righteous shall laugh at him] (Ps 52:6), [they shall be ashes under the soles of the feet of the godly] (Mal 4:3).
