* When the sinner dies, those who witness his death shut their mouths while they hiss (like the sound of a serpent), and so they turn to those spiritual words which they had made light of, and so they begin to believe, and learn what they had not believed before, when they supposed that the wicked man lived in prosperity. Solomon says: [When the scorner is punished, the simple is made wise] (Prov 11:21)

* Every stroke from God is either to cleanse the present life in us, or as the beginning of a punishment to come... But as for the persons for whom the strokes are a curse and not a chastening, it is said of them: [Thou hast stricken them, but they have not grieved; thou hast consumed them, but they have refused to receive correction] (Jer 3:5). For these their strokes begin in this life, and continue in eternal strokes. The Lord says by Moses: [For a fire is kindled in mine anger, and shall burn unto the lowest hell] (Deut 22:32).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Who supports me in my trials but You?
* You alone are the Almighty, and You became tempted that You might help me.
Grant me wisdom when a trial of false accusations comes upon me.
And grant me patience when a bitter affliction comes upon me!
I believe that You are living, caring for all my affairs!
You permit bitterness to come to me, and You turn my bitterness into sweetness.
* Let affliction be for my spiritual growth.
So that my tongue may not rush into an unseemly word, nor my thoughts fall into ingratitude.
Let me not flatter the wicked at the cost of the purity of my heart, but act with a good conscience in all things!
For my death is lighter than my flattering of the wicked!
* Take away from me all evil, for it is deadly to my soul.
Take away from me all hypocrisy, for it deceives me.
* Teach me how to enter my closet and speak with You, O heavenly Father.
I have nothing greater than to possess You!
* You are the Guide, leading me to the way of salvation.
You are the Tutor, bearing me and training me by Your grace.
You are the Teacher, giving me Yourself, O divine Wisdom!
* Why should I fear the wicked man?
Even if he prospers, it is for a time; eternal punishment awaits him.
If his children are many, they suffer even from hunger.
His offspring become a burden on society, and at their death no one honors them; even their widows do not grieve for them.
And if they grow rich in silver and garments,
what use is silver to them without the pure silver word of God?
And what use are garments to them unless they are covered by the blood of Christ?
They build palaces to perpetuate their memory, and these are like an old garment that the moth has reached.
They gather wealth, and in a moment their souls are required of them.
The tempest of death blows upon them as in the midst of the darkness of night; their eyes are opened to see the lake blazing with fire before them.
The enemy of good draws them to dwell with him eternally.

1 "Surely there is a vein for the silver, and a place for gold where they fine it. 2 Iron is taken out of the earth, and brass is molten out of the stone. 3 He setteth an end to darkness, and searcheth out all perfection: the stones of darkness, and the shadow of death. 4 He hath dug a mine far from the inhabitants; without a foothold, hanging far from men, they dangle. 5 As for the earth, out of it cometh bread: and under it is turned up as it were fire. 6 The stones of it are the place of sapphires: and it hath dust of gold."
Surely there is a vein for the silver, and a place for gold where they fine it [1].

Men strive to know the secrets of nature, such as discovering precious metals, gold and silver, and they have been able to. For the sake of wealth man strives in these things and the like, yet in his folly he does not care to become acquainted with the mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven. For temporal wealth and curiosity he searches for what is buried in the earth, and does not search for the salvation of his soul and his eternal glory.

* "For there is a place from which silver comes, and a place for gold where they fine it; iron is taken out of the earth, and brass is molten like stone" [cf. 1-2 LXX]. By this he means that if God has set an order for general matters, how much more does He set an order concerning human affairs... He foresees things beforehand and cares for them Himself, and nothing happens by chance. Or rather he means that the gathering of (natural) facts is a matter clearly visible, while the plan of God Himself is invisible. Silver and brass have their known place, but the place of wisdom no one knows, but God alone knows it. (God) says to man: [The fear of the Lord, that is wisdom](a), and to depart from evil is understanding.

St. John Chrysostom * As silver is often refined, so the righteous man is tried, and becomes the Lord's coin, receiving the royal image. Solomon also calls [the tongue of the just choice silver, refined with fire] (cf. Prov 20:10), showing that the teaching which is tested and its wisdom proved is praised and accepted, where it is refined on earth when the soul of the Gnostic (the spiritual man possessing knowledge) is sanctified in various ways, withdrawing from earthly fires. As for the body in which (this soul) dwells, it is purified and gains the purity fitting for a holy temple.

St. Clement of Alexandria Pope Gregory (the Great) offers us a symbolic interpretation of this phrase: if man searches for silver and gold to extract them from the stones, it is fitting for the preachers to work without ceasing that they may have spiritual silver, that is, the word of God purified seven times in the fire like silver (Ps 12:6). And that they may have gold, which signifies the splendid, wise, heavenly life.

And the Pope distinguishes between the sincere preaching that presents pure silver and gold from the Holy Scriptures, interpreting them according to the mind of the Fathers, as the early Church lived them, and the heretics. For the latter do not present silver and gold refined by fire, but teachings of their own, for their own honor and for their human glory.

* "Silver has its beginning in veins (in the stones), and gold has a place where they fine it" [1]. Silver signifies the power of speech, and gold the splendor of life or the splendor of wisdom... It is as though he says plainly: he who prepares himself for words of sincere preaching must draw the sources of his presentation (of subjects) from the Holy Scriptures, and so base everything he utters on a divine foundation, for the benefit of those to whom he speaks.
Heretics often seek, in support of the false things they present out of their own heads, to extract things that certainly have no support from the pages of the Holy Scriptures.

For this reason the great preacher counsels his disciple, saying: "O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called" (1 Tim 20:6). For the heretics, longing to be glorified as though they were skilled in thought, present new things that did not occur in the ancient books of the ancient Fathers, and so they cast the seeds of ignorance to the wretched who listen to them, desiring to appear wise.

It is as though he says plainly: The true wisdom of the believers has a place in the catholic Church, and it suffers troubles that come from you and from your persecution of it, but it is purified from every impurity of sins by the fire of your persecution. So it is written: [Gold is tried in the fire, and acceptable men in the furnace of adversity] (Sir 2:5)...

The Apostle Paul teaches us when he says: "Though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing" (1 Cor 3:13). For some have wrong thoughts about God, and others have right thoughts about the Creator, but do not keep unity with their brethren. The former are cut off because of their error in the faith, and the latter because of their schism. For this reason the first part of the Ten Commandments forbade the sin of both parties, for it was said with the divine voice: [Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might]. And at once he added [Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself] (Deut 5:6; Mk 30:12-31). For he who believes what is wrong concerning God certainly does not love God, and he who has right conceptions of God and rends the unity of the Holy Church obviously does not love his neighbor, since he refuses to take him as his companion.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* The words of the Lord are pure words (Ps 12:6)... He says "pure," without the dross of false appearance. For many preach the truth in impurity, selling it in order to receive a bribe for temporal gain.

St. Augustine * (Schism) is the weapon of Satan, turning everything upside down. As long as the body is united together Satan cannot find an entrance, but the stumbling comes because of division. Where does schism come from? From opinions contrary to the teachings of the Apostles. And where do these opinions come from? From men's slavery to the belly and other passions... This is what he said when he wrote to the Philippians: "Whose God is their belly" (Phil 3:19).

St. John Chrysostom It is fitting for the preacher of the truth, indeed for every believer, to present silver and gold from God, that is, His surpassing heavenly peace, not the peace of this passing world; he presents God the Savior, who is the true peace.
* Peace will be your gold; peace is your silver; peace is your land. Peace is your life, your God is peace. You will have peace in everything you desire!
St. Augustine Iron is taken out of the earth, and brass is molten out of the stone [2].

Although the extraction of silver and gold requires greater effort than the extraction of iron and brass, the latter two metals are more useful to man, and because of their abundance their price is much lower than that of silver and gold. A man can live without silver and gold, though with great difficulty, but at present it is impossible for him to live without iron and brass. It is the surpassing wisdom of God that made what is necessary for man more abundant and its extraction easier, while what is for luxury is less in quantity and harder to extract.

Pope Gregory (the Great) holds that the extraction of all these metals, silver and gold and iron and brass, from dust and stones is a sign of the holy men of God (despite the difference in their spiritual level and their role in the work of preaching and witness for God), but all are extracted from dust and stones. We were dust and stones, occupied with temporal things, hard of heart. But the grace of God raised up from us people who are witnesses for God, who enjoy fellowship in the divine nature, in love and tenderness and meekness and humility and purity and holiness, and so on. All these are not from ourselves, but are the free gifts of God to believers who earnestly seek the salvation of their own souls and the salvation of their brethren in humanity.

* "Iron is taken out of the earth" [2]. It is as though he says plainly: Men of strength whose tongues are sharper than swords have become iron in this violent battle in defense of the faith, those who were at one time "earth," in the sphere of low works. When a man sins, it is said to him: [Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return](b). But [iron is taken out of the earth] when the stern warrior of the Church is separated from earthly conduct...

Was he not taken out even of the earth, who, occupied with earthly matters, served in the collecting of tribute (like Zacchaeus the tax collector)? But being taken out of the earth, he was strengthened with the strength of iron, the Lord bound him to the Gospel, tearing the hearts of unbelievers with his tongue as with a sharp sword. He who was formerly weak and entangled in earthly works afterward became strong in heavenly preaching.

"And the stone is molten by heat, and becomes brass." The stone dissolves by heat when the hard and cold heart is touched by the fire of divine love and is poured out in the blazing fire of the Spirit. Then it has a life glowing with heat in work. To the extent that it was hard before in its love of the world, it becomes strong in its love of God.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
St. Gregory of Nazianzus holds that the mind of the devout believer is like iron extracted from flint or stones.
* They are like iron extracted from flint, radiating fire from the fertile gold fit for light, for a small spark can quickly form the flame of truth within.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus When St. Cyril of Jerusalem speaks of the resurrection of the body he says that it becomes like iron heated by fire. It is the same body that we have in this life, but with a fiery nature fitting for eternity.

* This was recorded specially, how Paul says plainly: "For this corruptible must put on incorruption" (1 Cor 15:53). So this body will rise and put on incorruption and be fashioned anew. And as iron mingles with fire and becomes fire, or rather as the Lord who raises us knows: this body will rise, but it will not remain as it is now.

It is an eternal body. It needs no nourishment for its life as it does now, nor steps for its ascent, for it will be spiritual. It is a wonderful matter that we are not worthy to speak of, for it is said in the Gospel of St. Matthew the Evangelist: "Then shall the righteous shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father" (Mt 13:43), [and as the moon and as the brightness of the firmament] (Dan 12:3).
St. Cyril of Jerusalem He setteth an end to darkness, and searcheth out all perfection.
The stones of darkness, and the shadow of death [3].

When Job speaks of extracting metals from the belly of the earth, that is, from the dark mines, man in order to obtain them enters the mines to examine what is in them, using torches to set an end to the darkness so that it does not hinder him from determining his goal. He risks his life, and enters the rough places in order to extract the metals.

He who has no knowledge of the art of mining mocks those who search for the metals. He looks at them as people who expose themselves to dangers and death without purpose. So God extracts from our dust and stones metals precious in His eyes. But many are ignorant of God's plan and reckon Him as one who enters into darkness and examines things of no value. In other words, it is fitting for us to trust in God's plan and His providence and His work for us. He offers us salvation, whatever its cost, for in His foreknowledge He sees the glories we shall enjoy. He sees us as gold and silver and brass and iron extracted from earth and stones! He extracts from us, who were darkness, light. And as the Apostle says: "For ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord" (Eph 5:8).

* He says "He hath set a place for the darkness" [3] as if to say that the mind also has a place, for the darkness knows how to retrace its steps and efface itself (before the break of day)... He urges us not to demand an accounting (from God). He says: "Why is there darkness? Do you not know God to be the Almighty, who does everything with wisdom?"

St. John Chrysostom * [He hath set a time for the darkness, and He Himself searcheth out all things, and every one] [3]. He Himself has set a time for the darkness, that is, He has set an end to the wicked, where they cease to be wicked. Thus it is said to them by the Apostle: "For ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord" (Eph 8:5). The same great Apostle says to other disciples: "The night is far spent, the day is at hand: let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armour of light. Let us walk honestly, as in the day" (Rom 12:13-13). For this reason it is said in the Song of Songs concerning the coming of the Church: "Who is she that looketh forth as the morning?" (Song 10:6). The Church is likened to the morning, that is, to the knowledge of the faith, turning from the darkness of sins to the splendor of the light of righteousness...

Since God does what is good, and carries out the dispensation, and does not do evil, He controls the things that the wicked do so that matters do not go on to what is bad, but He searches out the end of all things and the end of every one, and bears all things in longsuffering, and sees the end of the elect, for evil turns to good for them...
God saw the end to which Saul would come even while he was persecuting (the Church); He sees him fall to the ground and say: "Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?" (Acts 6:9)...
He saw the people of Nineveh disobeying, but He looked to the end of their disobedience in their practicing reform (repentance).
He also saw the end of disobedient Sodom, and looked to the end of the burning of lust in the fire of hell.
He saw the end of the world of the Gentiles, while it was occupied in the darkness of evils, how one day it would shine with the light of faith.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

God the Creator, wonderful in His works, created the earth and brought forth upon it the creeping things and the beasts, and also created man from its dust. He still (creates) a new nature fitting for eternal life.
* From one earth come forth creeping things and beasts of prey and the flock, and upon it trees are set, and foods are found, and gold and silver and brass and iron and stone!
St. Cyril of Jerusalem He hath dug a mine far from the inhabitants.
Without a foothold.
Hanging far from men, they dangle [4].
The text appears in the writings of Pope Gregory (the Great) as "the stone of darkness also, and the shadow of the (sweeping) valley, is divided from the people on a journey."

When some dig in rocky ground uninhabited by people, others hear of them or see them doing so, and mock them. They suppose that they want to draw water from within the earth, but why do they choose stony regions far from the inhabited places? They are like those who dangle their feet in a pit of no use. So some mock God's plan and His saving work, just as the Jews mocked the Apostles and disciples who went out to preach among the pagan nations, like those who dig mines in a rocky, waterless land, without aim or hope!

* "The stone of darkness also, and the shadow of the (sweeping) valley, is divided from the people on a journey" [3-4]. What was that Jewish people, hardened in unbelief, who refused to receive the faith that had been announced to them beforehand through the prophecies by the Giver of life, but the stone of darkness? This is brought about by the hardness of their violence and their wrapping themselves in unbelief....

Perhaps by the sweeping torrent he points to being watered by the holy preaching, as it was said by Solomon: [The eye that mocketh at his father, and despiseth to obey his mother, the ravens of the valley (the torrent) shall pick it out] (Prov 17:30). For the wicked, finding fault with God's judgments, mock their father, and heretics of every kind, who despise the preaching of the Holy Church and scoff at its fruit, are they not despisers of the pain of their mother? It is not unseemly to call her their mother also, for those who speak against her came out of her, as John testifies, saying: "They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us" (1 Jn 19:2). But "the ravens of the valley" come when the true preachers go forth to defend the Holy Church from the streams of the Holy Scriptures.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
As for the earth, out of it cometh bread: and under it is turned up as it were fire [5].

Some hold that the earth that brings forth wheat for us to eat also brings forth fuel (petroleum) for the fire to feed on. By the wisdom given to us by the Creator we find what satisfies us from the very earth from which we bring out what we use as fuel.

Others hold that Job points to Sodom and Gomorrah, the land marked as exceedingly fertile, producing wheat in abundance on which many fed, which was turned because of the wickedness of its inhabitants into a furnace of fire, as God sent down upon it fire and brimstone.

Still others hold that in speaking of man's concern to extract precious metals from mines under the earth, he means that they turned the earth that overflows to them with food into mines, in which many perish because of the dangers to which they are exposed, so that it became like a furnace of fire under the earth.

* Pope Gregory (the Great) sees here a prophecy about Judaism, which at the coming of the Lord ought to have borne witness to Him and preached, presenting to the world Christ the bread of life, but through the envy of the Jewish leaders it was turned into a hidden fire destroying souls. [The earth, out of it cometh bread, is turned up in its place as it were fire] [5]. What occupied Judaism was to give bread, for it was accustomed to set out the words of the Law before the people. The sons of perdition were no longer able to interpret this very Law, as the prophet Jeremiah laments in his Lamentations, saying: "The young children ask bread, and no man breaketh it unto them" (Lam 4:4). But this [earth is turned up in its place as it were fire], for it destroys itself with the coal of envy when it sees the miracles of the believers... Was it not inflamed with the flame of the coals of its envy when it saw the miracles of our Savior, so that some of its men said: "What do we? for this man doeth many miracles" (Jn 47:11)? Or "Perceive ye how ye prevail nothing? behold, the world is gone after him" (Jn 19:12)
Pope Gregory (the Great)
The stones of it are the place of sapphires: and it hath dust of gold [6].

It was fitting for the men of Judaism or its religious leaders to present Christ the bread of life, and so become living stones in the temple of the Lord, of sapphire, that is, bearing the heavenly mark, so that the dust is turned to gold, in that the earthly are turned into the heavenly, if one may say so.

Some hold that God in His surpassing wisdom made many precious things, such as silver and gold and petroleum, hidden under the earth, or in the stones, so that man would not fix his eyes on these things, but lift his eyes to heaven. He treads them under foot, making light of them, so that his whole heart may be fastened to God.
The sapphire is counted in value next to the diamond, and is one of the most precious gems; it may be red, blue or yellow, but it is most often blue in color.

* "The stones of it are the place of sapphires, and it hath dust of gold" [6]. To the declaration of the glory mentioned before is added the iniquity of the sin that follows it. For the fall of each one is a wicked, criminal deed, since before the fall he was able to attain to a greater height... The stones signify the minds of the strong, when Peter said to the saints: "As lively stones, a spiritual house, an holy priesthood" (1 Pet 5:2). And the Lord promises the Church this when she comes, saying by the prophet: [Behold, I will lay thy stones with fair colours, and lay thy foundations with sapphires. And I will make thy windows of agates, and thy gates of carbuncles, and all thy borders of pleasant stones. And all thy children shall be taught of the LORD] (Isa 11:54-13). For He sets stones in her in order, distinguishing the holy souls in her according to the difference of their merits. "He lays her foundations with sapphires," for these stones bear in themselves the likeness of the color of heaven, and so the strength of the Church is founded in the souls that seek heavenly things...

And because she shines through faith in the splendor of the surpassing life and wisdom, there was added: "dust of gold"... But this gold was afterward dimmed by the darkness of unbelief. The prophet Jeremiah lamented its blackness, saying: "How is the gold become dim! how is the most fine gold changed!" (Lam 1:4) For the gold became dim, and the ancient splendor of faith and innocence itself grew dark with the night of evil, as unbelief came upon them.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

7 "There is a path which no bird of prey knoweth, and which the falcon's eye hath not seen: 8 The lion's whelps have not trodden it, nor the visitor passed by it. 9 He putteth forth his hand upon the flint; he overturneth the mountains by the roots. 10 He cutteth out a tunnel among the rocks; and his eye seeth every precious thing. 11 He restraineth the trickling of the rivers, and the things that are hid bringeth he forth to light."
There is a path which no bird of prey knoweth, and which the falcon's eye hath not seen [7].

Though it is within man's power to exploit the earth, so that it yields wheat and crops for his food, and to extract from its belly and from its rocks silver and gold and petroleum and precious stones, there is another wisdom that is not given except to him who seeks it, namely the possibility of knowing the divine mysteries, especially the mystery of the divine Incarnation and the mystery of salvation. However sharp a sight man may enjoy, like the sight of eagles and other birds of keen vision, he will not be able to see divine things by himself.

He chose birds of prey, because they fly to very great distances in search of food, and can see their prey from a great height, swoop down upon it and then return to their nest without losing the way, or mistaking it, even if it resembles their own nest.

The Chaldean Targum gives as an interpretation of this phrase that Satan, flying like a bird, did not see the tree of life nor recognize it, and neither did the eyes of Eve look upon it, nor did the sons of men walk toward it, nor did the serpent turn toward it.

Some hold that one who is concerned with extracting metals has eyes surpassing those of the eagle, with which he looks to great distances under the earth, and so knows the places of the precious metals, and digs and extracts them.

For the sake of riches and the acquiring of wealth it is not hard for man to penetrate the layers of the earth by the craft of mining to obtain an abundance of precious metals. And for the desire for food it is not hard for the ravening lions to recognize the paths among the forests and the wilds to hunt prey for themselves and their young; nor is prey hidden from the sight of birds of prey at lofty distances, yet the mysteries of divine wisdom remain hidden from man without the surpassing grace of God.

Human wisdom is a natural gift that God gives to man in degrees fitting for each one, as a talent by which one person is distinguished from another, but divine wisdom is a gift offered to him who seeks it sincerely and desires it.

* The wisdom of this world is not the wisdom of God. The wisdom of God is real, and nothing that corrupts it touches it. The wisdom of the world is foolish, though the simplicity of God's wisdom makes whoever receives it seem foolish in the eyes of the world. Believers receive this divine wisdom, and so are counted fools by the world.
Origen * Paul says that the wisdom of God is taught in harmony with the Lord, which shows that true wisdom is given through the Son.
St. Clement of Alexandria The lion's whelps have not trodden it, nor the visitor passed by it (nor has the lion walked in it) [8].

The young lion or lion's whelp walks among the forests and wilds as king of the beasts. It is as though he knows all the hidden paths, and no animal can hide from him. When he is hungry he knows how to reach his prey, as though he were acquainted with all the secrets of the region. So he who works in mining penetrates paths that he makes under the earth, which no lion's whelp has trodden, nor any lion walked in. And he who wishes to acquire the wisdom of God [the surpassing mystery of Christ] walks by the Holy Spirit a unique path that no creature can reach by himself, even if he be a great king possessing authority and surpassing strength and power!
Our Christ is the way, for as we walk in Him we become like spiritual lions, kings and priests unto God His Father (Rom 1:6).

* Paul enumerates two or three kinds of wisdom (1 Cor 1:20-25). First there is the wisdom which the world calls foolishness, and it is a greater wisdom than the other two. There is also the wisdom granted to men, by which we reason and act, and by which we advance and invent, and by which we know God. Finally there is a third kind of wisdom, in which there is contemplation of creation. The wisdom which the world counts foolishness is given to us through the Savior, so that the people who know God by natural wisdom and who are led to Him by contemplating the order of creation can receive salvation, which cannot be obtained by the two former kinds of wisdom, for they cannot rescue them from error.
Father Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus * The teaching of the Savior is sufficient in itself, without need of additional help, for He is the power of God and the wisdom of God.
St. Clement of Alexandria He putteth forth his hand upon the flint.
He overturneth the mountains by the roots [9].

When Job speaks of the surpassing mystery of Christ, as the wisdom of God, he saw a wonder. He saw the Lord Christ, in His love, power and wisdom, stretch out His hand on the Cross to embrace the Gentiles who had become like hard flint, and raise up from the stones children to Abraham, or children of faith. The roots of the lofty mountains, that is, those who hold temporal authority, do not stand before Him.

By the simplicity of the Cross, the wisdom of God, which the pagan world counts foolishness and the Jews count a stumblingblock, the Lord caught the philosophers and those in authority. And as the Apostle Paul says: "God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty; and base things of the world, and things which are despised, hath God chosen, yea, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are" (1 Cor 1:27-28).

* The philosophers could not accomplish what a few unlettered men accomplished, namely the conversion of the whole world. The philosophers spoke of trifles and persuaded only a very few. And the Apostles spoke of God and righteousness and judgment and converted great numbers.
* In human terms it is impossible for fishermen to catch philosophers, but this is what happened by the power of God's grace.

St. John Chrysostom * "He putteth forth his hand upon the flint, He overturneth the mountains by the roots" [9]. He puts forth his hand upon the flint, as He stretches out the arm of His preaching to the hardness of the Gentiles. So the blessed Job himself felt beforehand, presenting the history of the Gentiles, that they would know Him, and says: [Oh that they were graven with an iron pen and lead in the rock for ever!] (Job 24:19).

But what do we understand here by the mountains but those in authority in this world, who are puffed up in greatness because of their earthly standing? The psalmist says of them: "Touch the mountains, and they shall smoke" (Ps 5:144).

The roots of the mountains are their thoughts deep in pride. The mountains fall from their roots, because the worship of God brings the rulers of the world down to the earth, shattering their base thoughts.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* The Song lifts the bride to the highest summit of glory, bestowing on her the name of a fountain of living waters flowing from Lebanon. We have learned from Holy Scripture of the life-giving nature of God as a prophecy from the person of God saying: "They have forsaken me the fountain of living waters" (Jer 13:2). Then the Lord Christ says to the Samaritan woman: "Jesus answered and said unto her, If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water" (Jn 10:4). Then He said: "If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink. He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water. (But this spake he of the Spirit, which they that believe on him should receive)" (Jn 37:7-39).

Each of these passages says that the living water is the holy nature, so the Song may rightly call the bride truly a well of living waters flowing from Lebanon. This is in fact contrary to what is known, for wells usually contain still water, whereas the bride has running water in a deep well, and her waters flow continually.

Who is able and worthy to understand the wonders granted to the bride? It is clear that she has reached the utmost of her hopes, for she has been compared with the eternal Beauty from which all beauty arose. And in her spring she is exactly like the spring of her Bridegroom, her life like His life, her water like His water. His word is living, and by it every soul that receives Him lives.
These waters flow from God, as the fountain of living waters says: "For I proceeded forth and came from God" (Jn 42:8).

The bride keeps the overflow of His living water in the well of her soul, and becomes a house that treasures these living waters that flow from Lebanon, that is, that form streams from Lebanon, as the text says.

We have come into fellowship with God by possessing this well, so that we may fulfil the commandment of Wisdom (Proverbs 17:5, 18), and drink waters from our own well, and not from another's well. We enjoy this in Christ our Lord, to whom be glory and majesty forever, Amen.
St. Gregory of Nyssa He cutteth out a tunnel among the rocks; and his eye seeth every precious thing [10].

Job stands amazed at the power of the Savior and His love, for it is He who grants that in man, who has become like a rock, springs of living water burst forth within him, and at the same time looks upon man not with contempt, nor to condemn him for his heart of stone, but as His own living icon, most precious in His eyes. He removes from man the hardness of his heart of stone, and raises from him a heart full of love.
Some hold that in the craft of mining they cut channels for water in the rocks, and so the veins of metals which they are extracting are revealed to them.
* "He cutteth out channels (waters) among the rocks." He cuts rivers of preaching in the hard hearts of the Gentiles.

In the same way the prophet speaks of the watering of the wildernesses of the Gentiles: [He turneth the wilderness into a standing water, and dry ground into watersprings] (Ps 35:107). Likewise the Lord promises in the Gospel: "He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water" (Jn 38:7). What we heard as a promise has now been fulfilled.

Do you not see how the holy preachers overflowed like a spring from Judaism through the catholic Church spread over the whole world as channels of the heavenly commandments, flowing abundantly from the mouths of the Gentiles. This is because He has cut channels in the rocks; He has made the river of holy preaching flow from hard hearts.

"And his eye seeth every precious thing" [10]. It is a matter that must especially be kept in mind, that each individual soul is counted all the more precious in God's sight, the more it despises itself out of its love of the truth. "When thou wast little in thine own sight, wast thou not made the head of the tribes of Israel?" (1 Sam 17:15)... And on the contrary, he who counts himself most precious becomes very small with God... [He beholdeth the humble, but the proud he knoweth afar off] (Ps 6:138). Therefore [his eye seeth every precious thing]. In Holy Scripture the expression "God sees" is used in place of "God chooses," as in the Gospel: "for He chooses the humble. God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty" (1 Cor 27:1). He "saw what was precious" when He visited the human soul as it held itself in contempt, enjoying the enlightenment of His grace. It is said of this soul by the prophet: [If thou take forth the precious from the vile, thou shalt be as my mouth] (Jer 19:15). For the present world is vile in God's sight, but the soul of man is precious to Him. He who separates the precious from the vile is called "as the mouth of God," for God gives His words to this man.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* The Holy Spirit is the river that flows, according to the Hebrews, from Christ to the lands. And we have received this as the mouth of Isaiah prophesied (Isa 12:66). This great river flows continually and will not cease; it is not only a river but also one of the abundant streams that overflow with greatness, as David said: [There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God] (Ps 4:46). For that city, the heavenly Jerusalem, is not watered by a canal, that is, an earthly river, but by that Holy Spirit who proceeds from the source of life. The stream that issues from Him who satisfies us seems to flow abundantly among the heavenly thrones and dominions and powers and angels and archangels, running in the fullest portion of the virtues of the seven-fold Spirit.
St. Ambrose * By the belly here (Jn 7:38) he means the heart... Where in Holy Scripture is it found that rivers of living water flow from his belly? It is not found.

What then does it mean: "He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said"? Here we must pause, for the saying "out of his belly shall flow rivers" may be an affirmation that it is about Christ. For many said: "This is the Christ," and "When Christ cometh, will he do more miracles?" He shows the need for right knowledge, and that they be convinced not by miracles but by the Scripture...

He had said before: "Search the scriptures" (Jn 5:39) and also: "It is written in the prophets," [And they shall be all taught of God] (Jn 6:45), [there is one that accuseth you, even Moses] (Jn 5:45), and here he says: "As the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers," hinting at the greatness of grace and its overflow... And elsewhere he called it "eternal life," but here he calls it "rivers of water"...
For the grace of the Spirit, when it enters the mind and dwells, overflows more than any spring.
It will not cease and will not run dry...
In order to mean that it offers inexhaustible help, and at the same time an energy that does not fail, He called it a "well" and rivers, not one river, but countless rivers.
A person can clearly grasp what it means if he considers the wisdom of Stephen and the tongue of Peter and the zeal of Paul.
St. John Chrysostom * Which of the earthly beings was created in the image of God but man?
And to whom was given authority over all nature and its creatures, to make them his own?

It is an original honor that crowns his brow and lifts him up to heaven, above the stars, higher than the sun in loftiness and dignity... And though he is lower in rank than the angels because of his bond with a material body, he was given power to understand and know his Lord and Creator.
St. Basil the Great He restraineth the trickling of the rivers, and the things that are hid bringeth he forth to light [11].

A poetic expression of God's care for man, for when man cuts channels for water among the rocks to carry on mining, God preserves man's life and does not allow these channels to seep, so that the wall or roof of the mine would fall, and He supports man in his knowledge of the metals hidden in the mines under the earth.
Pope Gregory (the Great) offers a symbolic interpretation of this phrase, seeing in these rivers the overflow of the teachings of the early Fathers.

* "He searcheth the depths of the flood, and the things that are hid bringeth he forth to light" [11]. What are those called a flood but the sayings of the ancient Fathers? Who can estimate the mighty overflow that issued from the breast of Moses himself when he delivered the Law? What great overflow issued from the heart of David? What streams of water flowed from the lips of Solomon and the lips of all the prophets?
Pope Gregory (the Great)

12 "But where shall wisdom be found? and where is the place of understanding? 13 Man knoweth not the price thereof; neither is it found in the land of the living. 14 The depth saith, It is not in me: and the sea saith, It is not with me.
"But where shall wisdom be found?
and where is the place of understanding?" [12]
If the treasures of precious metals are hidden beneath the earth, how much more is the wisdom of God. Who can perceive by himself where it is, or from where he may acquire true understanding?
Wisdom is the treasure hidden within the Gospel. No man can enjoy it unless the Spirit of God shines upon him with His light and reveals to him the mysteries of the Word.
* True wisdom is the Gospel, the means of salvation through the Cross of Christ.
St. John Chrysostom "Man knoweth not the price thereof; neither is it found in the land of the living" [13].

Wisdom is the Second Hypostasis, "the wisdom of God." While we are still in the flesh, we cannot grasp the depths of the mystery of Wisdom or know the Person of Wisdom, since He is in the bosom of the Father. He became incarnate so that He might meet us, and we might meet Him in our world.
* Paul does not mean here (1 Cor 2:7) that he proclaims secret matters and riddles, but that the message he preaches was formerly hidden.

Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrus * Wisdom is not in a time or in a place, for time would mean that it came into being. But how could it be in time, when it is from the beginning? How could it be in a place, when it was with God? If anyone is searching for the Only-Begotten Son, then according to the sense of the Gospel He is in the bosom of the Father. Do you think that the bosom of the Father is a place? Do you seek to know how wisdom was born, when the man of prophecy says, "Man knoweth not the price thereof" (Job 28:13)? Do you think that its origin is among men, while Job says that it is not found among men? Do you ascribe wisdom to death, when it is that of which "the depth saith, It is not in me: and the sea saith, It is not with me" (Job 28:14)?

St. Ambrose * Paul testifies (1 Cor 2:7) that he was sent to proclaim the mystery of the wisdom which the rulers of this world do not know, and for this reason they are called foolish. The wisdom of God is hidden, because it is not words but power. It is impossible to speak of it in human expressions, but we believe in it by the power of the Spirit.

Ambrosiaster * "Neither is it found in the land of them that live delicately" [13]. What does the land signify in this phrase but the soul of man? The Psalmist says, "My soul thirsteth after thee, as a thirsty land" (Ps 143:6). But this wisdom cannot be found in the land of those who live in luxury, for the man who still feeds on the pleasures of this life is deprived of the perception of eternal wisdom.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"The depth saith, It is not in me: and the sea saith, It is not with me" [14].

It is as though nature, with all the creativity, beauty and possibilities within it, speaks with man and directs his gaze to the Creator as the source of true wisdom, so that man does not seek it from nature, nor from books, nor from events, but from God Himself.
St. Augustine sees that God made wisdom hidden, not because He wants to deprive us of it, but to arouse our longing for it so that we may seek it earnestly.

* "The depth saith, It is not in me: and the sea saith, It is not with me" [14]. Holy Scripture often personifies many lifeless things, for example, "The sea saith, It is not with me," and so on. "The depth saith, It is not in me," "The heavens declare the glory of God" (Ps 19:1). The command is also given to the sword (Zech 13:7), and the mountains and hills are asked about their skipping with joy (Ps 114:6). We do not make a pretext of any of these, although some of our predecessors used them as strong proof. Let us reckon that this expression was used of our Saviour Himself, the true Wisdom.

Father Gregory of Nazianzus * When Job was asked about the place of wisdom he answered, "The depth saith, It is not in me," pointing not to the place where it is found, but to the place where it is not.

Again, when he said that its price is not known by man [15], and then went on, "It cannot be gotten for gold," he did not show what its price is, but what is not its price. It is clear to all that no man can find this wisdom in any place, nor buy it with riches. But the holy man, being full of mystical thoughts, leads us to discover other matters; he does not seek created wisdom, but the Wisdom who is the Creator. For unless we search the hidden depths of the symbolism in these words, what is said would certainly be of no value if it were interpreted from the historical side alone...
So then, what is the wisdom that the holy man contemplates but that of which the Apostle Paul says, "Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God" (1 Cor 1:24)?

Solomon wrote of her, "Wisdom hath builded her house" (Prov 9:1). And the Psalmist says of her, "In wisdom hast thou made them all" (Ps 104:24). Of this very Wisdom, "man knoweth not the price thereof" (c), for he finds nothing by which he can value it... There is no means of obtaining it...

What do we give so that we may be worthy to receive this Wisdom, who is Christ? For by grace we are saved... Man deserves one thing by way of justice (namely death), and receives another by grace... Paul says, "While we were yet sinners, Christ died for the ungodly in due time" (Rom 5:8, 6). So we who were found ungodly when Wisdom came, what good thing did we offer by which to receive this Wisdom? "Man knoweth not the price thereof" (c)... "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast" (Eph 2:8-9). And he speaks of himself, saying, "But by the grace of God I am what I am" (1 Cor 15:10).

* To what does the "sea" point but to worldly minds that suffer bitter turmoil, so that they enter into foolish hostility with others, and proceed in enmity from one person to another in turn, and minds shatter one another like waves dashing against each other? Rightly the life of worldly persons is called a sea, because it is in a state of agitation by stirring storms, and it is deprived of the calm and steadfastness of inner wisdom. In contrast to this it was well said by the prophet, "To whom will my Spirit look, but to him that is humble and quiet, and trembleth at my word" (see Isa 66:2)... The Lord calls us, while we are in these wounds of turmoil, saying, "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Mt 11:28-29).

What is more exhausting than for a man to be feverish with earthly passions? Or what is more restful here than for a man not to desire anything of this world? For this reason the Israelites were given the keeping of the Sabbath as a gift... For the people who follow God receive the Sabbath, that is, the rest of the spirit, by not being entangled in this life, that is, by not being absorbed in carnal pleasures...
But how can we know that most of the ancient Fathers held fast to this wisdom in their inner life, while outwardly they were managing the affairs of the world?

Shall we reckon Joseph deprived of receiving this wisdom, he upon whose shoulders were laid the affairs of all Egypt in the time of famine, not only to provide for the needs of the Egyptians, but who, by his surpassing skill, also took care to preserve the lives of the foreign people who came to him?

Was Daniel a stranger to this wisdom, he who, when he was set as ruler over the governors by the king of the Chaldeans in Babylon, was occupied with great responsibilities...? It is therefore clear that often even the righteous are engaged in earthly obligations without being entangled...

Those who have this calm, however troublesome their outward occupations may be, these troubles will not enter into their inner depths... For their hearts are filled with this wisdom, so they are neither entangled nor troubled... The minds troubled by worldly matters cry out simply because they are not at rest and are cut off from true wisdom.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

15 It cannot be gotten for gold, neither shall silver be weighed for the price thereof. 16 It cannot be valued with the gold of Ophir, with the precious onyx, or the sapphire. 17 The gold and the crystal cannot equal it: and the exchange of it shall not be for jewels of fine gold. 18 No mention shall be made of coral, or of pearls: for the price of wisdom is above rubies. 19 The topaz of Ethiopia shall not equal it, neither shall it be valued with pure gold.
"It cannot be gotten for gold, neither shall silver be weighed for the price thereof" [15].

Since the wisdom of God is the Hypostasis of the Word, whoever acquires it acquires the Creator Himself, and there is no ground for comparison between Him and created things, however great their value.

* To what does pure gold point but to the angels, who are rightly called pure gold? They are gold because they shine with the splendor of righteousness, and pure gold because no stain of sin has ever touched them. As for human beings, as long as they are in the corruptible flesh and subject to death, they can be gold, but they cannot be pure gold. "The corruptible body presseth down the soul, and the earthly tabernacle weigheth down the mind that museth upon many things" (Wis 9:15). Even in this life they may shine with surpassing splendor of righteousness, and yet they will not be wholly free from the dross of sins. The Apostle John bears witness to this when he says, "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us" (1 Jn 1:8). James confirms it, saying, "In many things we offend all" (Jas 3:2). In the same way the prophet pleads, saying, "Enter not into judgment with thy servant, O Lord: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified" (Ps 143:2).

So Wisdom reveals Himself by Himself, so that the human race may be saved from sin. An angel is not sent in place of Wisdom, for it is necessary that the creature be set free by the Creator. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel, "If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed" (Jn 8:36).

But the holy man (Job), being filled with the spirit of this wisdom, foresaw that Judaism would become the condition of those who put their hope in the giver of the Law and make Moses the source of their salvation, for they spoke evil even to the one who had been healed: "Thou art his disciple; but we are Moses' disciples" (Jn 9:28).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"It cannot be valued with the gold of Ophir, with the precious onyx, or the sapphire" [16].

In the Septuagint it reads, "It shall not be compared with the dyed colors of India." Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the wisdom of God is not tainted by the ornament of rhetoric; it would be pleasing like a garment without dye. Paul made light of dye when he said, "Which things also we speak, not in the words which man's wisdom teacheth, but which the Holy Ghost teacheth" (1 Cor 2:13). The Apostle chose to use this wisdom in the simplicity of pure truth alone, without staining it with the dye of speech.
"The gold and the crystal cannot equal it: and the exchange of it shall not be for jewels of fine gold" [17].
Since the Word of God became incarnate and became man, no man equals Him, whether gold or crystal, however brilliant like gold or transparently pure like crystal.

* John saw this in the Revelation when he said, "The building of the wall of it was of jasper: and the city was pure gold, like unto clear glass" (Rev 21:18). This is because all the saints will shine in the splendor of surpassing blessedness; therefore (the heavenly Jerusalem) is described as a building of gold... But as long as we are in this life, and our hearts cannot be seen by others, they are not vessels of glass but vessels of earthenware. In this clay, which can corrupt the mind, the prophet fears lest he sink, when he says, "Deliver me out of the mire, and let me not sink" (Ps 69:14). Paul himself calls the tabernacle of our bodies "our earthly house of this tabernacle," and says, "For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens" (2 Cor 5:1)... Yet all the saints shine with such wonderful splendor, and gleam with such surpassing purity, that they become in the likeness of Wisdom, but they do not equal it. For this reason all the saints are brought into the eternal joys so that they may become in the likeness of God, as it is written: "When he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is" (1 Jn 3:2). And yet it is written: "O Lord God of hosts, who is like unto thee?" (Ps 89:8, 6). Also: "Who among the sons of the mighty can be likened unto the Lord?" How can they be like Him, and yet not be like Him, except that they will be like this Wisdom in likeness, but they are not equal to it? They are like Him because they become blessed, and they are not like Him because He is the Creator; they do not equal Him since He is incomprehensible, while they are comprehensible beings. Therefore it may be said with justice, "The gold and the crystal cannot equal it." For however great the splendor and purity with which the saints shine, this belongs to men as those who are wise in God, whereas He is the Wisdom of God, which is another matter...

"And the exchange of it shall not be for jewels of fine gold" [17]... The Church will not exchange this Wisdom for precious and lofty vessels of gold, for she holds fast to Christ the Son of God, not as one of the prophets, but as the one Lord of the prophets.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* The Son gives Himself, so that He Himself, being righteousness, removes evil from us; Wisdom offers Herself that She may take the place of folly.
St. Jerome "No mention shall be made of coral, or of pearls: for the price of wisdom is above rubies" [18].
"The topaz of Ethiopia shall not equal it, neither shall it be valued with pure gold" [19].
Wisdom is the Lord of glory Jesus, who is more precious than all pearls, coral, crystal, and everything precious.

* We have often said that Christ is wisdom, justice, peace, joy, gentleness, and the rest of such things. Note that the names of all these virtues are loved even by those who do not pursue them. There is no criminal who declares shamelessly that he does not love wisdom and justice.
St. Jerome

20 "Whence then cometh wisdom? and where is the place of understanding? 21 Seeing it is hid from the eyes of all living, and kept close from the fowls of the air. 22 Destruction and death say, We have heard the fame thereof with our ears. 23 God understandeth the way thereof, and he knoweth the place thereof. 24 For he looketh to the ends of the earth, and seeth under the whole heaven; 25 To make the weight for the winds; and he weigheth the waters by measure. 26 When he made a decree for the rain, and a way for the lightning of the thunder: 27 Then did he see it, and declare it; he prepared it, yea, and searched it out. 28 And unto man he said, Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding.
"Whence then cometh wisdom? and where is the place of understanding?" [20].
The men of God often cry out, asking for wisdom from the Heavenly One, for whence does wisdom come, and where is the place of understanding, if not from the heavenly God?
* He gives knowledge not by a book that we learn from, but by the enlightenment of the Spirit.

Ambrosiaster * Those who become small in the flesh, leaving their own knowledge, are the wise in the world... They become of their own free will like infants, learning the wisdom that is not acquired through the toil of study.

St. Mar Isaac the Syrian * It comes from the One from whom it proceeds. Now its way is hidden, since it is begotten of the Invisible One, who is co-eternal with the Father. The prophet expressed the "whence" by saying, "Who shall declare his generation?" (Isa 53:8). Now the place of understanding has become the mind of man, the man whom the wisdom of God fills and makes holy...
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"Seeing it is hid from the eyes of all living, and kept close from the fowls of the air?" [21]

The desire of the heart of every believer and every true theologian is that it may be the right of the chosen to enjoy the vision of God in eternal life. This is what St. John the Apostle declares: "For we shall see him as he is" (1 Jn 3:2). Yet in the same epistle he says, "No man hath seen God at any time" (1 Jn 4:12). And the Apostle Paul affirms: "Dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto; whom no man hath seen, nor can see" (1 Tim 6:16). This raises many questions, among them: 1. Is this vision reserved only for eternal life? Or can it begin here in an inner experience in the depths of the soul? 2. Is the vision of God by the heavenly beings a vision of His essence? And do the believers in heaven enjoy the vision of the divine essence?

St. John Chrysostom wrote a treatise entitled "The Incomprehensible Nature of God," in which he shows the impossibility of seeing God in His essence as He is. The councils of Constantinople in the fourteenth century (1341, 1351, 1368 AD) affirmed that God cannot be approached with respect to His essence; He is not the object of the knowledge of the angels or the saints, nor the object of their vision, but this divine essence is seen through His uncreated divine energies. Father Gregory Palamas spoke at length about this teaching.

* When we hear that the Seraphim fly around the throne in its loftiness and exaltation, covering their faces with two wings... and covering their feet with two, and crying out with a voice full of trembling, do not suppose that they have feathers, feet and wings, for they are invisible powers...

Truly God is incomprehensible even to these orders, and they are not able to draw near to Him; therefore He condescends to appear in the manner that is recorded in the vision. For God is not bounded by a place, nor does He sit upon a throne... but His sitting upon the throne and His being surrounded by the heavenly powers is a matter of His love for them.

If He appeared on the throne and these powers surrounded Him, they cannot behold Him, nor have they endured to look at the splendor of His light, so they cover their eyes with their wings, and there remains for them only to praise and sing hymns full of glory and holy trembling, and wonderful songs that bear witness to the holiness of Him who sits on the throne.
He who dares to examine the providence of God, which the heavenly powers cannot touch or express, ought rather to hide himself, concealed under the hills.
St. John Chrysostom Many of the Fathers of the Church and scholars throughout the ages have been occupied with discovering whether the believers will see God as He is or within certain limits.

* If Wisdom, who is God, is hidden from the eyes of the living, then certainly none of the saints can see this Wisdom. And I hear John agreeing with this statement: "No man hath seen God at any time" (Jn 1:18).
But when I look at the fathers of the Old Testament, I learn that many of them, as the history of Holy Scripture testifies, saw God.
For Jacob saw the Lord and said, "For I have seen God face to face" (Gen 32:30).
Likewise Moses saw God, of whom it is written, "And the Lord spake unto Moses face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend" (Ex 33:11).
Job himself saw the Lord and said, "I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee" (Job 42:5).
The prophet Isaiah saw the Lord and said, "In the year that king Uzziah died I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up" (Isa 6:1).
Micaiah saw the Lord, saying, "I saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing by him on his right hand and on his left" (1 Kgs 22:19).

What then does it mean that many fathers of the Old Testament testify that they saw God, and yet it is said concerning this Wisdom, who is God, "It is hid from the eyes of all living" (Job 28:21), and John says, "No man hath seen God at any time" (Jn 1:18)? It is clear to us that, as long as we live here a mortal life, God can be seen by means of appearances, but seeing Him truly in His nature cannot be achieved.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"Destruction and death say,
We have heard the fame thereof with our ears" [22].

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that destruction and death refer to the evil spirits that cause ruin and destruction, for it is said of Satan, "His name was Death" (Rev 6:8). These spirits do not see Wisdom, since they were driven out from before Him because of their pride, and became unable to see the wisdom of God. "They are of those that rebel against the light; they know not the ways thereof, nor abide in the paths thereof" (see Job 24:13).
"God understandeth the way thereof, and he knoweth the place thereof" [23].
None knows the divine Wisdom, or the Son, except the Father. He knows the way of Wisdom, because He is begotten of Him eternally; there is no separation between the Father and the Son.

* Wisdom, co-eternal with God, has its way in one sense and its place in another... The place of Wisdom is the Father, and the place of the Father is Wisdom, as Wisdom Himself testifies, saying, "I am in the Father, and the Father in me" (Jn 14:10).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"For he looketh to the ends of the earth,
and seeth under the whole heaven" [24].

* The seeing of God is the renewal of His grace for things that were lost and corrupted. Therefore it is written: "A king that sitteth in the throne of judgment scattereth away all evil with his eyes" (Prov 20:8). By His seeing He puts an end to the evils of our folly, and grants great esteem to maturity.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"To make the weight for the winds; and he weigheth the waters by measure" [25].

* In Holy Scripture the speed and lightness of the wind generally point to souls. As the Psalmist of God says, "Who walketh upon the wings of the wind" (Ps 104:3), meaning, who goes above the virtues of the soul. Accordingly, "He makes the weight for the winds," meaning that the wisdom from above fills souls, making them heavy with maturity, and not with the weight of which it is said, "O ye sons of men, how long will ye turn my glory into shame?" (Ps 4:2) ["how long will your hearts be heavy"]. For to be weighed down by (good) counsel is one thing, and to be weighed down by sin is another; to be weighed down by obligation is one thing, and to be weighed down by transgression is another...

"And he weigheth the waters by measure" [25]. In Holy Scripture waters are used to point to the Holy Spirit, sometimes they are used of false knowledge, sometimes of calamities and swept-away peoples, and sometimes of those who follow the faith. Thus water points to the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, as it is said in the Gospel: "He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water." And the Evangelist adds, "But this spake he of the Spirit, which they that believe on him should receive" (Jn 7:38-39). Again water points to holy knowledge, as it is said: "With the water of wisdom shall she give him to drink" (Sir 15:3). Likewise water points to evil knowledge, like the woman mentioned by Solomon who bears a symbol of heresy and who bewitches with her deceiving arts, so it is said: "Stolen waters are sweet" (Prov 9:17).

Likewise the expression "waters" points to trials, as the Psalmist says, "Save me, O God; for the waters are come in unto my soul" (Ps 69:1) ("Save me, O God; for the waters are come in unto my soul").

The waters also point to peoples, as it is said by John: "The waters... are peoples" (Rev 17:15). So also not only the sweeping tide of peoples, but also the minds of the righteous who follow the preaching of the faith, as in the saying of the prophet, "Blessed are ye that sow beside all waters" (Isa 32:20), and the saying of the Psalmist, "The voice of the Lord is upon the waters" (Ps 29:3).
In this place, to what does the title "waters" point but to the hearts of the chosen, who through the understanding of wisdom receive the hearing of the heavenly voice?
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"When he made a decree for the rain, and a way (and a path) for the lightning of the thunder" [26].

* By the rains he points to the words of the preachers; therefore it is said of Moses, "My doctrine shall drop as the rain" (Deut 32:2). That is, when they present my words with gentle persuasion it is rain, and when they thunder about terrifying matters concerning the coming judgment they utter voices like crashing thunders...

The authority of speech is lost when the voice is not supported by deed. It is said by the Psalmist: "But unto the wicked God saith, What hast thou to do to declare my statutes, or that thou shouldest take my covenant in thy mouth? Seeing thou hatest instruction, and casttest my words behind thee" (Ps 50:16-17)... This was written about the law of preaching: "Whosoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, he shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven: but whosoever shall do and teach them, the same shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven," of whom it is written: "They shall gather out of his kingdom all things that offend, and them which do iniquity" (Mt 13:41). For in the heavenly Kingdom it is necessary that the "things that offend" be gathered out and cast out... Now He made [a way for the crashing thunders] [26] when He establishes contact with the hearts of men struck with dread of the coming judgment by His preachers.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"Then did he see it, and declare it; he prepared it, yea, and searched it out" [27].

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that it is fitting for us to notice that there are four things concerning wisdom, when he says, "Then did he see it, and declare it; he prepared it, yea, and searched it out" [27].

* He sees it as being "the likeness," and declares it as it is "the Word," and prepares it as it is "the remedy," and searches it out as being "hidden from sight." The eternal wisdom of God is the image of the Father and His Word, when the mind of man penetrates it. So whoever wishes to understand it must understand it as the Word without time, and the Image without limit.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
It is fitting that the wisdom of God absorb our whole being, our feelings and our senses.

* If Christ is the head of the believer, then "the wise man's eyes are in his head" (Eccl 2:14). Consequently all our senses, our mind, our thoughts, our word and our counsels (if we are wise) are centered in Christ.
St. Jerome "And unto man he said, Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding" [28].

St. Augustine comments on this phrase, saying that the Greek word θεοσέβεια (theosebeia), which is sometimes translated "godliness": [Behold, godliness, that is wisdom], means "the worship of God." The main point in worship is that the soul not be ungrateful to God. Therefore the truly excellent sacrifice is to offer thanksgiving to God our Lord. Wisdom is the inner thanksgiving of the soul toward God, which it expresses by spiritual worship of Him.
Again he affirms that whoever ascribes wisdom to himself is not thankful to God, and therefore does not bear the fear of the Lord and is not godly; he is foolish and not wise.

* "Behold, godliness, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding" (Job 28:28). Here is the distinction (between wisdom and understanding), for we must understand that wisdom belongs to contemplation, and understanding belongs to action. In this place by wisdom he means the worship of God... And what is the worship of God but love for God, by which we long to see Him, and believe and hope to see Him in part? As we progress we see as in a mirror, in a riddle, but then the vision will be in clarity... As for departing from evil, which Job says is understanding, it undoubtedly concerns temporal matters. For with regard to time (in this world) we are in evil, from which we must cease until we attain the eternal goods.

* There is another kind of wicked, who when they knew God, glorified him not as God, neither were thankful (Rom 1:21). In this "I also fell, but thy right hand held me up" (Ps 18:35), and bore me far away, and set me where I could be healed. For You said to man: "Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom" (Job 28:28), and "be not wise in thine own eyes" (Prov 3:7), for "professing themselves to be wise, they became fools" (Rom 1:22). But now I have found the pearl of great price, for which I needed to sell all and buy it (Mt 13:46), but I hesitated.

* If knowledge is of the right kind, it is the handmaid of love, for without love "knowledge puffeth up" (1 Cor 8:1), but where love is, it fills the heart with edification, so that knowledge finds nothing empty that it could puff up. Add to this that Job shows useful knowledge by defining it afterward when he says, "the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom," adding, "and to depart from evil is understanding."
* "Behold, the worship of God is wisdom." Then the mind is wise, not by its own light, but by participation in that exalted light, which is eternal, in which it reigns in blessedness.

St. Augustine * "Behold, godliness, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding" [28]. There is nothing like this practical training, nothing stronger than this wisdom. "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge, and a good understanding have all they that do his commandments" (see Prov 1:7). This is the greatest of possessions. The honoring of God is the supreme wisdom.

St. John Chrysostom * O man, return to yourself. Examine the secrets of your heart, and if you find that you fear the Lord, it is truly evident that you are full of wisdom... This wisdom, which is awesome in itself even to the angels, is called in you "the fear of the Lord." For you truly possess wisdom if you fear the Lord.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
May I acquire You, O divine Wisdom!
* You gave man a mind, that he might search and work.
By human wisdom he is able to search for precious metals, but in foolishness he does not seek the mysteries of the Kingdom of God.
Grant me to discover the silver of Your pure wisdom, and to acquire the gold, the pledge of the heavenly life.
* Man brings silver and gold out of the dust and the stones.
Let there come forth from me, who am dust, a witness to You, and let me become in Your eyes more precious than every precious stone!
You are able to turn dust into heaven,
and the heart of stone into a heart enlarged with love.
* You are the worker of wonders and miracles.
You brought forth from Saul of Tarsus a unique apostle,
and from the wicked people of Nineveh a repentant people,
and from the Gentiles a holy Church.
You made man out of dust, and from the earthy sinner You raise up a being like the angels!
* Behold, I am in Your hands; establish Your Kingdom within me.
Embrace me, as it were, among the ranks of Your angels,
that I may be in touch with Your love, and know Your divine mysteries.
You are the way that brings me into the bosom of the Father.
You are my riches and my joy!
* May I acquire You, O divine Wisdom!
In You I enter into the mysteries of heaven, and enjoy partaking of the divine nature.
In You my eyes are opened, and I see what no eye has seen.
* For the sake of acquiring wealth, man learned the craft of mining,
and because of hunger the lion came to know the ways of the forests and the wilds,
and for the sake of being fed, the eagles see the prey from lofty distances.
And for the sake of love I acquire You, and You present to me the surpassing divine mysteries.
* Your wisdom is mighty and surpassing.
You bring me into the impossible, and reveal to me wonders beyond measure!
You lift the humble up to heaven.
You turn stones into children of Abraham!
And You shake those who hold authority and power!
You cause a spring of sweet waters of love to well up from my rocky heart!
You make me very precious in Your eyes, O Lover of mankind!
* May I acquire You, O wondrous Wisdom of God,
that I may carry within me the treasure of all wisdom, knowledge and understanding.
You are my wondrous treasure.
No gold, nor silver, nor precious stones can be compared with You.
* Behold, all of nature with all its creativity cries out to me:
Acquire Creativity itself, Beauty itself, the Creator of all and the Maker of everything!
* How marvelous You are, hidden and present.
Your mysteries are hidden even from the Cherubim, who cover their faces because of the greatness of Your splendor!
You hid Yourself from me for a time, not to deprive me of You, but to inflame my heart with longing for You.
You became incarnate and came down to me, so that I find You within me!
You are very near to me!
My depths cry out to You:
Show me Your glory!

entries.section: 1. His former happiness in the Lord

paragraphs.text: 1 Moreover Job continued his parable, and said, 2 "Oh that I were as in months past, as in the days when God preserved me; 3 When his candle shined upon my head, and when by his light I walked through darkness; 4 As I was in the days of my autumn, when the favour of God was upon my tabernacle; 5 When the Almighty was yet with me, when my servants were about me; 6 When I washed my steps with milk, and the rock poured me out rivers of oil.
Moreover Job continued his parable, and said: [1]

entries.section: 1. His former happiness in the Lord

paragraphs.text: "Oh that I were as in months past, as in the days when God preserved me" [2].

Here we see the sick, grieving and bewildered man remembering the days of his success and comfort, and telling us how God preserved him, and how all people respected him, stood up for him when he went out, and made him a leader over them. But now people, even the lowest of them in the eyes of society, despise him and mock him. He affirms that he was not guilty of sensual sins, that he did not wrong the poor and the widow, that he did not withhold food from the fatherless, and that he committed no secret sins. He rejected lying, deceit, injustice, stinginess, greed, idolatry, malicious joy at another's misfortune, miserliness, hypocrisy, exploitation, and so on. By this he declares his innocence. But this is not due to any merit of his own, but to God's care for him. For the secret of the uprightness of his life is God's preserving him.

Job looked at his past and compared it with what he now was, and longed for time to return and for his state to remain as it had been. In this he does not ascribe his happiness, wealth and success to his own efforts, nor to his abilities and gifts, but to the mercies of God, saying, "God preserved me." He did not see his wealth as a stronghold for himself (Prov 10:15), nor did he trust in the abundance of his riches (Ps 52:7), but "the name of the Lord is a strong tower" (Prov 18:10) for him. Job confesses that God is a wall of fire around him and a hedge that keeps him; God is the secret of his security.

* "Then Job resumed his opening discourse: Oh that I were as in my former state for a month." What does he say? I would like to live for a month the good life that I had in former times, so that I might stop your mouths and show you what I was. He asks for one month like the former months and days. He did not ask for anything extraordinary, but to live for thirty days in the happiness of other times, and to enjoy the good things that no one had given him...

Note the piety of the man, for he ascribes everything to God. A man deprived of help from above cannot remain in an upright life. He says, "God preserved me in them," for his looking back to his former good life is only to bear witness to the providence of God.

* (The Apostle Paul) wants to say that God is the spring and source of all good things, and has no need of a partner or counselor. He is the beginning, the foundation and the maker of all good things; He is the Creator. He called that which did not exist into being. He governs all things, arranges them and keeps them according to His will!

entries.section: 1. His former happiness in the Lord

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom "When his candle shined upon my head, and when by his light I walked through darkness" [3].

The light that shone from him was the light of God, who lit his lamp upon his head, as though Job were a lighthouse, worth nothing without the divine lamp. He owes everything to God, "the true Light," who led him through the darkness, gave him divine comforts in the midst of sorrows, and kept him from stumbling.

In a spirit of humility and with thanksgiving to God, Job presents himself as a lighthouse: whatever its metal, and whatever its shape, the secret of its power is the light placed at its summit, by which ships are guided from many miles away. Job confesses that even if he is a lighthouse, the light upon his head is the light of God and not his own. It is the lamp of the Lord, the true light.

The prophet David sees in the word of God "a lamp unto my feet" (Ps 119:105) that shines for him, so that he walks through the darkness of this world, but Job sees in the word of God a divine light fixed, as it were, upon his head to lead many ships toward the harbor!

It is fitting for the believer to bow before God, that He may fill his life with the work of His Holy Spirit, the Giver of enlightenment, and so he sings, saying, "In thy light shall we see light" (Ps 36:9). He did not say "I see," but "we see," for when the believer is enlightened he draws many with him to enjoy the divine light.

* When Job explained the goodness of his works, he added: "When his candle shined upon my head" (Job 29:3). This lamp is lit with the oil of good works for each one of us. But if we practice evil, and our works become evil, we not only fail to shine, but we also put out the lamp that is ours, and the saying of Scripture is fulfilled: "He that doeth evil walketh in darkness, and he that hateth his brother is in darkness" (see 1 Jn 2:11). Does it not appear to you that whoever extinguishes the light of love has extinguished the lamp? But whoever loves his brother (see 1 Jn 4:21) abides in the light of love, and can say with assurance: "But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God" (Ps 52:8), "thy children like olive plants round about thy table" (Ps 128:3).

Origen * "By the expression [candle] he means the light of Holy Scripture, of which (the Apostle Peter) says: 'We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts' (2 Pet 1:19). And the Psalmist says, 'Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path' (Ps 119:105). Now because the upper part is the mind, and the mind is rightly called the head, it was said by the Psalmist: 'Thou anointest my head with oil' (Ps 23:5), as if he were saying plainly: You fill my soul with the fatness of love. Now the lamp shines upon the head of the Church, where the holy commandments enlighten the darkness of our minds, for in the darkness of this present life we receive the light of the word of God.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Scripture enlightens the eyes of the soul, so read it, O wise one, and be filled with love for it. For from the reading of the Holy Scriptures the sun rises upon the minds that feed on them with discernment.
God placed the Holy Scriptures in the world as a lamp of light to illuminate its darkness. He who loves his soul is enlightened by reading, and walks by its guidance.
