paragraphs.text: Upon my right hand rise the youth (the base fellows), they push away my feet, and they raise up against me the ways of their destruction [12].

Some translations have: "On the right hand the youths rise." The Jesuit translation has: "The rabble rose up at my right hand, they make my feet stumble," and also: "They make my feet stumble, and pave the way to calamity."

Rising at the right hand is an expression used for bringing accusations against a person. So they rose against him with the violence of youth, set a snare for him, and lifted him up so that he would fall in it on his heel, and then trample him with their feet. The matter does not stop at false accusations, but with violence and force they cast him down and trample upon him.

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that rising against a person on the left signifies the opposition of enemies from outside, while rising against him on the right signifies the opposition of those who ought to have been his defenders, that is, opposition from within; and this is more dangerous and more bitter.

* Calamities are presented on the left if the Church meets an enemy who persecutes her at the hands of persons outside the fold of religion, those who deny Christ. But when she suffers troubles coming from persons who appear to be believers, enrolled under the name of Christ, and who oppose His name within her. In the same way the "right hand" is used for one whom we count great: "And he shewed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the Lord, and Satan standing at his right hand to resist him" (Zech 1:3).

* [They make my feet stumble, and they press down with their paths as with waves] [12]. What does he mean by the feet of the Church but her members who are furthest away? They give themselves over to earthly works, and are quickly deceived by the enemies in proportion to their lack of understanding of heavenly things. Therefore the enemies make her feet stumble when they draw the furthest members into the errors of their teachings. The stumbling feet cannot keep the way, since all the weak are either deceived by the promises of the persecutors, or terrified by their threats, or broken by their torments, and thus they turn aside from the straight way.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
They mar my path.
They set forward my calamity.

entries.section: 2. The lowliness of those who despise him

paragraphs.text: They have no helper [13].
The Catholic translation has: "And they cut off my way, and contribute to my destruction, and need no helper."
The work of the enemy of good and his wicked followers is to spend every effort in corrupting the way, by removing the signs, so that man loses his way and loses his peace during his journey.

* Let blessed Job speak these things concerning the evil spirits, the hidden enemies. Let the Catholic Church speak concerning the wicked persecutors, the visible enemies, for these cut off her way, when they oppose the souls of the weak on the ways of truth, obstructing them with deceit.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

If the deceiver removes the signs of the way in order to mislead humanity and destroy it, the Savior has come to declare: "I am the way" (Jn 14:6), whom we acquire and in whom we walk, and so enjoy the Kingdom within us.

* This way is good; it leads the good man to the good Father, the man who brings forth good things out of his good treasure, the good and faithful servant (Mt 7:14; Lk 6:45; Mt 25:21). But this way is narrow, and the majority, who are mostly carnal, cannot travel in it. But the way is narrow also for those who strive to pass through it, since it was not said "it is confined" but narrow.

Origen the Scholar * Now the way cannot err, I mean Jesus Christ; for He says: "I am the way... and the life." This way leads to the Father, for He says, "no man cometh unto the Father, but by me" (Jn 6:14).
St. Ignatius of Antioch They came upon me as a wide breaking in of waters.

entries.section: 2. The lowliness of those who despise him

paragraphs.text: In the desolation they rolled themselves upon me [14].
They come upon him like a wide stone crusher; however firm he may be, he will not escape them, but they will crush him. They do not walk toward him but roll swiftly like a destructive storm.

If the enemy of good appears as a stone crusher to crush humanity like stones thrown on the road, the Cornerstone has come down to us (Zech 4:7; Eph 2:20), to join us together in Himself and raise up from us a heavenly temple that the enemy cannot touch.
St. Augustine sees that by the calling of the Lord Christ, the cornerstone, who is the head of the Church, the Church is the corner that has joined the Jews on one side and the Gentiles on the other.
Terrors are turned upon me.

entries.section: 2. The lowliness of those who despise him

paragraphs.text: They pursue my soul as the wind: and my welfare passeth away as a cloud [15].

In a lamentation over his condition Job says that terrors have turned toward him and weighed upon him; they removed his honor (his soul's dignity) like a wind that blew it away, and his prosperity left him like a cloud that passed and vanished.
Job is amazed at what has happened, for this befalls the wicked who wither, when calamities come upon them and they lose their success and honor.

* [As the wind has driven away my desire... and as a cloud has my health passed] [15]. The cloud floats on high, and the breath of the wind draws it away as on a swift road. So surely will be the fate of the temporal goods of the wicked. They appear in the height of honor, to pass their life as those on high, but they soon come down daily in life, like those who are blown away along with their mortal life.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. His collapse in soul and body

paragraphs.text: 16 "And now my soul is poured out upon me; the days of affliction have taken hold upon me. 17 My bones are pierced in me in the night season: and my sinews take no rest. 18 By the great force of my disease is my garment changed: it bindeth me about as the collar of my coat. 19 He hath cast me into the mire, and I am become like dust and ashes. 20 I cry unto thee, and thou dost not hear me: I stand up, and thou regardest me not. 21 Thou art become cruel to me: with thy strong hand thou opposest thyself against me. 22 Thou liftest me up to the wind; thou causest me to ride upon it, and dissolvest my substance. 23 For I know that thou wilt bring me to death, and to the house appointed for all living. 24 Howbeit he will not stretch out his hand to the grave, though they cry in his destruction. 25 "Did not I weep for him that was in trouble? was not my soul grieved for the poor? 26 When I looked for good, then evil came unto me: and when I waited for light, there came darkness. 27 My bowels boiled, and rested not: the days of affliction prevented me. 28 I went mourning without the sun: I stood up, and I cried in the congregation. 29 I am a brother to dragons, and a companion to owls. 30 My skin is black upon me, and my bones are burned with heat. 31 My harp also is turned to mourning, and my organ into the voice of them that weep.

Now that Job has offered a lamentation bewailing his state, since God has directed His arrows against him, and the wicked have taken advantage of the situation and attacked him by every means, in merciless violence, and calamities have befallen him from every side, he now reveals the effect of all this on his psychological and physical health.
"And now my soul is poured out upon me; the days of affliction have taken hold upon me" [16].
Job sees the days of affliction, which have lasted so long, as having seized him and not let him go, so that his soul has collapsed and dried up completely.
* [Now my soul is dried up within me, the days of affliction have laid hold upon me] [16]. The souls of the elect are dried up now, so that afterward they become green in triumphant eternity.
Now the days of sorrow lay hold upon them, and the days of joy follow afterward. As it is written: [For him that feareth the Lord it shall go well at the last] (Sir 13:1).
Again it is said of the Church: [She shall rejoice in the last day] (Prov 25:31).
Now is the time of sorrow for the righteous, and a day will come when glory follows them instead of tears. It is said elsewhere: [Thou hast broken us in the place of sorrows] (Ps 19:44).
[The place of sorrows] is the present life; therefore the righteous man is crushed here, but in eternal life, the place of bliss, he is exalted.
But when he said, [The soul is dried up], he rightly began it with the words, [in myself]... For in ourselves our souls truly grieve, but in God they are refreshed.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. His collapse in soul and body

paragraphs.text: My bones are pierced in me in the night season: and my sinews take no rest [17].

Here he speaks of the night as a person, as in Job (Job 3:3). The night plays a grave role: its work is to pierce his bones so that his skeleton collapses, and the sinews within him do not cease to send out the pain that gnaws at his being!
By the great force of my disease is my garment changed.

entries.section: 3. His collapse in soul and body

paragraphs.text: It bindeth me about as the collar of my coat [18].

Job lost the garments of honor, as a ruler and judge who had a role and a word in society, but what is more serious is that his clothes became tattered and altogether wretched because of the diseases and sores that befell his body. His outer garments turned into garments of perpetual mourning, or garments of grief, that encircled his body and do not leave him, like his inner garments.
* According to the historical interpretation, what does the garment of blessed Job mean if not his body? Truly the garment was worn out when his body was subjected to torment.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. His collapse in soul and body

paragraphs.text: He hath cast me into the mire, and I am become like dust and ashes [19].

In ancient times simple Easterners used to express their intense grief either by sitting on the dust, or by putting it on their heads as they mourned. Here Job pictures God as casting him into the dust to practice grief in its utmost form, and what increased his pain was that Job saw in himself that he had become like dust and ashes.

In any case, this lamentation bore an image of the contrition of soul and humility to which Job had come, since he counted himself dust and ashes. Abraham said: "Behold now, I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord, which am but dust and ashes" (Gen 18:27). And in Ben Sirach: "The Lord looketh on the host of high heaven; and all men are but dust and ashes" (Sir 17:31). So man looks at the truth of himself and finds himself dust, but in Christ Jesus he becomes a new creation after the image of his Creator.

* Scripture says: [I have despised myself, and cast myself down, and counted myself dust and ashes] (Job 19:30) (Vulgate). This is the humility of the penitent. When Abraham spoke with his God, and wished to discuss with Him the matter of the burning of Sodom, he said: "I am dust and ashes" (Gen 27:18). How is this humility always found in the great saints?

St. Augustine * O rich man, why do you exalt yourself with your wealth and boast of the glories of your forefathers? Do you boast of your homeland, take pleasure in the beauty of your body, and rejoice in a passing honor? Take heed to yourself. Remember that you are a mortal man [and that you are dust, and unto dust shalt thou return] (Gen 3:19)... Bow down and look at the tombs: can you distinguish between the bones of the poor and the bones of the rich? Between the bones of slaves and the bones of masters? Take heed to yourself, then, and give up pride, stinginess and hardness of heart.

St. Basil the Great * It is said of St. Anthony that when he entered the inner desert the demons looked at him and were troubled, and gathered against him and said to him: "O youth in age and mind, how did you dare to enter our land? For we have not seen here any human but you!" And they all began to fight him. He said to them: [O strong ones, what do you want from me, the weak and wretched? And what is my worth that you should all gather against me, when I am dust and filth and nothing, and too weak to fight one of your least?] And he would cast himself on the ground, and cry out and say: [O my Lord, help me and strengthen my weakness; have mercy on me, O Lord, for I have taken refuge in You; O Lord, do not forsake me, and let not those prevail against me who think that I am something; O Lord, You know that I am too weak to resist one of the least of these]. And whenever the demons heard this prayer, full of life and humility, they would flee from him and could not come near him.
The Garden of the Monks I cry unto thee, and thou dost not hear me.

entries.section: 3. His collapse in soul and body

paragraphs.text: I stand up, and thou regardest me not [20].

Often some believers, in the bitterness of their souls, feel as though God does not answer their prayers and cries. Yet He is called "thou that hearest prayer" (Ps 65:2). In His hearing of prayer, the answer may be the granting of the request, but at the fitting time. So it was in His answer to Abraham's request, when He gave him Isaac, but in the time of old age; and God may refuse the request because He knows that it is not for the good of the one who asks.

* When His saints suffer under the pressure of the persecution of enemies, and when they cry out without ceasing, beseeching Him to deliver them, by a great dispensation God seems as one who does not hear the voices of their supplications, so that they may be proved all the more in their sufferings.
They are proved all the more when their petition is not quickly answered... It is written: "O my God, I cry in the daytime, but thou hearest not" (Ps 2:22).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Do not grow weary in your asking. Do not think that your request returns empty.
Do not say: I have asked much and not found, and perhaps I shall never find.
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh Thou art become cruel to me.

entries.section: 3. His collapse in soul and body

paragraphs.text: With thy strong hand thou opposest thyself against me [21].

In the bitterness of his soul Job sees God as though He were harsh, using all the power of His hand against him. There is no proportion between the mighty power of God's hand and the weakness of man, so how can he bear to be opposed by God? The Jesuit translation has: "You have become a cruel enemy to me, and with the strength of Your hands You have attacked me."
Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that God appears harsh or violent toward His saints, not because there is cruelty and violence in Him, but He appears so by opposing our will, and so we count Him such.

entries.section: 3. His collapse in soul and body

paragraphs.text: Thou liftest me up to the wind; thou causest me to ride upon it, and dissolvest my substance [22].

The Jesuit translation has: "You snatched me away, and made me ride upon the wind, and the tempest dissolved me." And the NKJ translation has: "You lift me up to the wind and cause me to ride upon it; you spoil my success."

Perhaps Job counted the days of his prosperity as though God had lifted him up to the wind, so that he became very high; the winds became his supreme chariot. But as high as he rose, God allowed him to fall, so that all he had gained is shattered!

Truly the passing glory of the world is vain glory; it is a sitting on the wind, which is unsafe, for the more a man counts himself as flying on the wind, the more his fall will be utterly destructive to him.

* The glory of the present life seems to be high, but there is no stability in it, so that man is like one who has been lifted up and seated on the wind (that is, without stability, but he falls from it).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. His collapse in soul and body

paragraphs.text: For I know that thou wilt bring me to death, and to the house appointed for all living [23].

The men of the Old Testament looked toward death, which is the destiny of every man, as a passage to Hades, which is the house of every living one, his home to which he returns. But the Lord Christ came, and moved the believing dead from Hades to paradise, as spoils He rescued from the hand of the devil and from the dominion of eternal death.

* In the earlier part of this work I pointed out that before the coming of the Lord even the righteous went down to the dwellings of Hades, even though they were not fallen into woes but were at rest... Truly this was fitting for Job before the grace of the Savior, since the righteous were carried to the dwellings of Hades. The mere entering of Hades is called [the house of all the living].
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Howbeit he will not stretch out his hand to the grave?

entries.section: 3. His collapse in soul and body

paragraphs.text: Though they cry in his destruction? [24]
The Catholic translation has: "Surely no hand is stretched out against ruin, and in collapse there comes help" [24].

A wonderful insight of righteous Job, and a living attitude of faith: while God's hand appears harsh to him, and God's actions come as from an enemy, he confesses that what God permits of temporal ruin is, as it were, God's hand for eternal edification. He looks at his calamity and perceives, as he cries for help, that it is for his salvation, even if it reaches temporary collapse.

* [In any case, thou wilt not stretch out thy hand to their ruin, and if they fall to the ground thou wilt rescue them thyself]. While Job tells of his circumstances and of others not being punished... he sees that the Lord does not stretch out His hand to the destruction of those who sin, when He corrects their condition by striking them.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Did not I weep for him that was in trouble?

entries.section: 3. His collapse in soul and body

paragraphs.text: Was not my soul grieved for the poor? [25]

With living faith righteous Job calls for divine intervention. He does not justify himself, but he believes that, as he showed compassion, and as he used to weep when he found a man in distress and pitied the condition of the poor, God will surely repay him this compassion with compassion, as though he were saying to God: [Your rule: with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again](a). I offered every compassion to suffering, wounded souls, and every comfort to the poor; now my soul groans from wounds and needs divine comforts. Is it not my right to wrest them from You, O You who alone are righteous?

* Notice how he trained himself with regard to the sufferings of the body and its humiliation, for as he had never suffered anything of the kind, since he had always lived in abundant wealth and eminence, he was accustomed to take care of the misfortunes of others, one by one. This is what he declared when he said: "For the thing which I greatly feared is come upon me, and that which I was afraid of is come unto me" (Job 25:3). Again: [Did I not weep for him that was in trouble? Was not my soul grieved when I saw a man in affliction?] (cf. Job 25:30). Because of this he was not troubled by anything that befell him.

* Let our mercies overflow, and let us give proofs of our great love for man, whether by using our money or our actions. If we see someone being abused and beaten in the marketplace, then if we can give money on his behalf, let us do so, or if we can save him by words, let us not hold back. For even offering a word has its reward, and even more our sighs. This is what Job said: [I wept for every man in distress, and I sighed when I saw a man in affliction] (Job 25:30).

St. John Chrysostom * [I have wept in times past for him that was in trouble; my soul was grieved with the poor] [25]. Although it is true compassion for us to share the sufferings of our fellow creature by giving generously, sometimes when outward goods are abundant with us, our hands give generously and more easily than we offer feelings of sharing in sorrow.
Therefore it is fitting for us to know that we give in a perfect manner when we reach those who suffer, and at the same time carry within us the same feelings as theirs.
It is fitting for us first to bear within us the sufferings of the person who suffers, and afterward to share his sorrows, showing our cooperation through practical service...
The compassion of our heart reaches perfection when we do not fear to lay upon ourselves the evil of need for the sake of our fellow, in order to rescue him from pain.

This model of compassion was in fact given to us by the Mediator between God and men. For He could have come to help us without dying, but He wished to help humanity by dying. Surely if He had not borne our wounds, His love for us would have been very little... He showed how great is the virtue of compassion by placing Himself in a state that He does not want us to be in, and this for our sake...

This too is what the holy Church should do. When she sees a person bearing the tears of repentance, she binds her tears to him with constant prayer, and sympathizes with the poor man in order to help the mind stripped of virtues by her supplications and intercession. We lament for the sorrowful, sympathizing with him, when we feel that the wounds of others are our wounds, and we strive with our tears to wash away the sins of those who commit transgression.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. His collapse in soul and body

paragraphs.text: When I looked for good, then evil came unto me: and when I waited for light, there came darkness [26].

Job is amazed: he who was hoping for blessings in return for his compassion toward his brethren, and evils (trials) poured upon him. When he had lit the way for those around him, darkness surrounded him. He expected the shining of a bright morning upon his life, and found himself in deep night.
These are human feelings, even for men of God at times, when trials intensify upon them at a time when they were hoping for an abundance of blessings!

* The faithful hope for good but receive evil, and they wait for light and darkness comes upon them, because for the hope of obtaining the reward, to enjoy the joys of the angels, they are delivered into the hands of those who persecute them, even if its attainment is delayed a little here in the lower world.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
My bowels boiled, and rested not.

entries.section: 3. His collapse in soul and body

paragraphs.text: The days of affliction prevented me [27].

It is a picture of the righteous, or of the Church, as suffering, sharing her Christ's cross. Within her is a ceaseless boiling, as she lives as in days of misery. As the psalmist says: [Weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning](b).

* The boiling of the bowels of the holy Church, as regards her, is the enduring of the violence of persecution... [The days of affliction prevented me]. The Church of the elect knows that she will suffer many evils in the last tribulation, but the days of affliction hinder her, because even in time of peace she bears within her the lives of the wicked with a burdened spirit.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
I went mourning without the sun.

entries.section: 3. His collapse in soul and body

paragraphs.text: I stood up, and I cried in the congregation [28].

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that Job's speech here is the speech of every righteous man whose heart burns, not with the fire of the sun of trials, but with the fires of holy zeal and the sincere desire for the salvation of every soul. The believer will not rest until he finds all resting with him in the Lord, and enjoying with him the experience of the earnest of heaven! He cries out with the prophet Jeremiah, saying: "My bowels, my bowels! I am pained at my very heart; my heart maketh a noise in me; I cannot hold my peace" (Jer 4:19).

* [I went in mourning garb (black) without provoking wrath, I stood up in the congregation and cried] [28]. Although this man had authority over his companions, inwardly he was offering to the Lord a secret sacrifice of a contrite heart, during his mourning. [The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart] (Ps 51:17)...

He was a witness against himself that in the midst of all those circumstances (of wealth, authority, and so on) he did not take his ease, but was in mourning. For to the saint who is still in a state of pilgrimage (in the world), everything, however full of prosperity, without the vision of God is utter poverty. For the elect, seeing everything, grieve that they do not see the Creator of all things, and to them all these things are exceedingly trivial compared with their deprivation of the appearing of the Supreme Being.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. His collapse in soul and body

paragraphs.text: I am a brother to dragons, and a companion to owls [29].

Job found no man to support him in his distress, even among his household, such as his wife or his relatives, so he counted the ravening wolves his brothers, living among them like a simple lamb. He also counted his friends like the ostriches, which have a beautiful appearance but are unable to fly like most birds.

We should not wonder that we live in a world that does not separate the righteous from the wicked, and does not cleanse the wheat from the chaff, until the hour comes in which the true separation will take place before the Almighty Judge.

* He says that I have fallen to the level of the birds or the ostriches. I no longer know my nature; my state has become no better than theirs. This is also what David said: "I am like an owl of the desert... I am as a sparrow alone upon the house top" (Ps 102:6-7).

St. John Chrysostom * [I was a brother to dragons, and a companion to ostriches] [29]. To what do the dragons refer but to the lives of those with evil minds? Of these it is also said through the prophet: [They snuffed up the wind like dragons] (Jer 14:6). All the wicked snuff up the wind like dragons, when they are swallowed up by evil thoughts of pride.

But what are we to understand by those who are indicated by the ostriches but lovers of display? For the ostrich has wings but does not fly; so all lovers of display have the appearance of holiness, but lack the goodness of holiness.

This also agrees with the words of blessed Job, who was of a level of endurance and steadfastness, a good man among the wicked. For there is no perfect man who is not gentle in the midst of the evils of his relatives. He who does not bear the evils of others with composure, with his longsuffering, bears witness of himself that he is very far from the fullness of goodness.
He who has not experienced the malice of Cain refuses to be "Abel."
For on the threshing floor the wheat lies under the pressure of the chaff... and the rose with its beautiful fragrance grows among the prickly thorns.
Noah's three sons were in the ark, but two continued in humility, and one in recklessness despised his father.
Abraham had two sons, one was righteous, and the other was a persecutor of his brother.
Isaac had two sons, one was saved in humility, and the second was cast out even before he was born.
Twelve sons were born to Jacob; of these one was sold in innocence, and the rest were the sellers of their brother through their wickedness.
Twelve disciples were chosen in the holy Church, but they did not remain without testing; one mingled among them, by whose persecution (of them) they were tried.

The righteous man cleaves to the evil of the sinner, as in the furnace straw is added to the gold in the fire: the straw burns, and the gold is refined. Truly they are good people who are able to hold fast to goodness even in the midst of the wicked.

It was said to the holy Church by the voice of the Bridegroom: "As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters" (Song 2:2). And so the Lord says to Ezekiel: [And you, son of man, have unbelievers and fallen ones about you, and you dwell among scorpions] (Ezek 2:6).

Peter glorified the life of blessed Lot, saying: "And delivered just Lot, vexed with the filthy conversation of the wicked: (For that righteous man dwelling among them, in seeing and hearing, vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds;)" (2 Pet 2:7-8).

Paul glorifies the life of his disciples, and by glorifying them he strengthens them, saying: "In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world; holding forth the word of life" (Phil 2:15-16). So also through John the angel of the church of Pergamos bears witness to that in the words: "I know... where thou dwellest, even where Satan's seat is: and thou holdest fast my name, and hast not denied my faith" (Rev 2:13)
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. His collapse in soul and body

paragraphs.text: My skin is black (turned black) upon me, and my bones are burned with heat (the fever in me) [30].

In referring to the Church, Pope Gregory (the Great) sees the sorrow of the Church over the weak souls whose skin the sun of tribulations burns and whose bones it scorches, so that she counts what befalls them as befalling her, since they are members of the Church.

* [My skin is black upon me, and my bones are burned with the heat within me] [30]... By the skin he indicates the weak, those who serve in her for an outward benefit. And the bones represent the strong, since through them the whole body is held together.

The weak in the Church fall away from steadfastness in the faith, either by the temptation of money or by being broken by persecutions. And after their fall they themselves persecute her, so the Church suffers from the blackness of her skin.

[And my bones are dried up with heat]: the strongest bone of the holy Church, Paul, was burned, and dried up with anxiety for others, when he said concerning some who had fallen: "Who is weak, and I am not weak? who is offended, and I burn not?" (2 Cor 11:29). So the skin turned black and the bones dried up with heat, because the weak leap toward evil, and the strong are tormented by the fire of their zeal.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* To what shall we compare Paul, who groans daily for every man in this world, for every nation and city, for every soul? His resolve was stronger than iron and firmer than steel, so with what words shall we describe this spirit?!
* What a wondrous feeling in the shepherd! Others fall and he says: I affirm my grief. Others stumble and he says: The fires of my sufferings burn!

Would that all to whom the leadership of the rational flock has been entrusted would imitate this, and not show themselves to be less than the shepherd who for many years cares for an irrational flock.

For in the case of the irrational flock no appreciable harm occurs even if there is neglect, but in our case, if one sheep perishes or is devoured, the harm will be very grave and terrifying, and the punishment unspeakable; above all this, since the Lord had first endured the shedding of His blood for it, what excuse can this man offer, who allows himself to neglect the one for whom the Lord cared and for whose sake He gave every effort on His part for the care of the flock?

entries.section: 3. His collapse in soul and body

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom My harp also is turned to mourning, and my organ into the voice of them that weep [31].

St. Augustine sees that Job here looks to the Holy Spirit who strikes the strings of the human soul and makes of it a harp and a pipe; the soul melts with love for humanity in the Lord. Man spends his life grieving for every suffering soul and weeping with those who weep. This is the wisdom of God working in man, so that he shares the feelings of all, and in this he feels a surpassing peace while grieving for others.

And Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the believer is like a string on a lute or harp: if it is struck very lightly it gives no sound, and if it is struck hard it causes a disturbance. Therefore it befits man to walk in moderation in everything: in his asceticism he should not exaggerate lest he destroy his vitality, nor abandon asceticism altogether so that he cannot control his body.

We are different strings on the harp of God, working together, and a joyful symphony comes forth that God receives as an acceptable sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving, pleasing to Him. By this the believer enjoys the heavenly life as a communal life in the Lord; each member by himself feels the touches of the hand of God playing upon him, but with the same hand He strikes the other strings in wondrous harmony and concord!
* It is hard for us to doubt, I think, that Job in this expression means the Holy Spirit.
The subject of the discussion is wisdom, where it comes to men from; it does not come from many years, but the Holy Spirit who dwells in mortals, and the breath of the Almighty, is what teaches...

It is perfectly clear that he is not speaking of the spirit of man in the expression "the Spirit who is in mortals." He wanted to show from where men receive wisdom, for it is not from themselves... In the same way in another passage in the same book he says: [The understanding of my lips shall not meditate purity. The divine Spirit that formed me, and the breath of the Almighty teaches me] (cf. Job 33:3-4) LXX.

St. Augustine * "My harp also is turned to mourning, and my organ into the voice of them that weep" [31]. Let it be considered that if the string of the harp is struck very lightly it gives no sound, and if it is struck with great force it produces a harsh sound. So the virtue of asceticism becomes altogether nothing if a man does not discipline his body as far as he can. But it is wrongly used if a man wears out his body beyond what it can bear. For by asceticism the deficiencies of the body are consumed, not the body itself, and it befits each one to control himself with exact discipline, so that the body does not grow proud and sin, and yet is sustained to practice righteousness. The great preacher says: "Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth" (Col 3:5). And yet he wrote to the preacher who was very dear to him: "Use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities" (1 Tim 5:23).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
My soul groans in bitterness!
* I often look at my life and see that it has passed quickly without fruit.
I wanted to bear witness to You each time that time passed over me.
But my soul is bitter, for I see no spiritual fruits in my life and my service!
Who removes the spirit of despair from me, except Your cross, O Giver of hope!
Let me cling to You, and carry me on Your arms, and let my soul be assured by You, O Savior of souls from corruption!
* Many mock me even in my old age!
They reflect what is in their hearts of want, hunger and shame, and pour it upon my soul to shatter it.
But You are my heavenly bread, my satisfaction and my glory!
Fix my eyes upon You, that I may rise above the dunghill from which I suffer.
* Around me have gathered those who have not tasted the truth nor been satisfied by Your grace, and behold, they mock me.
They went out against You as against a thief, and behold, they do the same work with Your Church!
Grant me that my soul be not troubled!
* They left the city of God with all its blessings.
Instead of returning to it, they gloat over the suffering men of God.

* They went out to the wastelands and the wildernesses, depriving themselves of the divine planting and the waters of the Holy Spirit; they thought themselves strong, and came to mock the divine plants, the wondrous vineyard of God!
* Why does my soul groan at the mockery of the world.
Your love satisfies my soul!
Your sufferings and the shame of Your cross and Your death for me are my true comfort!
Who is worthy to share with You in Your glorious shame?
Who is qualified to carry Your cross with You?
* In the distress of my soul I see that You have loosed the reins for those who trouble me; You seem as one who aims arrows against me.
But You, who are all love, turn my bitterness into sweetness.
You turn the troubles of my opponents into eternal glories.
You leave them to mock with their tongues, to pour out accusations against me.
And to practice injustice as though without restraint!
And in all this Your eyes are upon me, taking pity on me!
You are my salvation and my glory!
* When I fall under sufferings, You are revealed before me, O You who suffered for me, and I forget my sufferings in the sight of You that gladdens my heart.
And my lamentation is turned into a heavenly song and unceasing rejoicing.
* The deceiver has no work but to lead me astray from the truth.
He thinks he is cutting off my way, so that I shall not pass into the Kingdom.
How foolish he is. You are the Way that no power can hide from me.
He seeks my destruction, and has not realized that You are my almighty Savior.
* The enemy moves toward me as in a storm to destroy me.
He thinks he is crushing me like a stone under a wide stone crusher.
He has not realized that You are the cornerstone, joining me by You to the heavenly temple!
There is no power that can crush me while I am in Your hands!
* My life has become like a passing wind or a cloud that soon vanishes.
It has become as though without aim or taste!
It has dried up completely like a tree without life or fruit.
The night rushed upon me, and began to gnaw my bones.
My veins within me know no rest.
I wrapped myself in sufferings like a garment clinging to me.
I was cast into the midst of the mire.
And my life turned into dust and ashes.
* My life has lost all stability and security.
My eyes have turned to the grave, as a house in which every man settles!
The light has turned to darkness for me.
My bowels within me have melted from boiling.
I no longer have anyone to comfort me, nor anyone to share my sufferings.
I have become a brother to the savage wolves, and to the ostriches that cannot fly!
I no longer play on the harp of my soul a song or a hymn.
Rather, my whole being has turned into a harp that plays perpetual laments!
* This is my lamentation; who can comfort me but You?
Who can raise me from the grave except the One who rose from the dead?
Who lifts me from the dunghill but the Heavenly One who by His love came down to me?
Who gives my life taste except the One who turns bitterness into sweetness; my lamentation does not shatter my soul, but gives me hope in You, O Gladdener of hearts!
"I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?" [1]

Job, in the era before the Law of Moses, was able to rise, with divine help, to a surpassing Gospel-like height. For he did not abstain only from adultery and abominations, but shut the door on sin at the very start of its advance, namely the evil glance. He did not allow himself to look at a virgin in order to desire her, counting this an inward adultery creeping into his senses.

God has given us the senses to use as is fitting, a holy gift for which we give thanks to God. But if we misuse them through recklessness and carelessness, we thereby open the door for sin to creep in little by little.

For this reason the Fathers of the early Church forbade dwelling together with virgins, however lofty the lives of both parties, not by looking on them as a source of defilement, but for the sake of purity of the eyes, the mind and the heart.

* Jeremiah says: [For death is come up into our windows, and is entered into our palaces] (Jer 9:21). This happens when desire enters through the senses of the body, and enters into the dwelling of the mind. In contrast to this Isaiah speaks of the righteous: [Who are these that fly as a cloud, and as the doves to their windows?] (Isa 60:8), for the righteous are said to fly like a cloud, because they rise above the filth of the earth...
In order to keep the thoughts of his heart in chastity, Job "made a covenant with his eyes," lest he should see without caution what he might love...

Eve would not have touched the forbidden tree if she had not first looked at it without caution, as it is written: "And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to look upon, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat" (Gen 3:6). Therefore we who live a mortal life must set great restraint to limit our gaze toward forbidden things, since the mother of all living (Eve) came to death through the eyes. The prophet also says: [Mine eye affecteth mine heart] (cf. Lam 3:51)... Our Lord said: "Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery: But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery in his heart" (Mt 5:27-28).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Christ has removed this cause (adultery), since we pay attention even to what is in the heart alone. Now what can they say who share dwelling with virgins? For according to this rule they are guilty of the sin of adultery tens of thousands of times every day, as they look upon them with desire. For this reason blessed Job also laid down this rule from the beginning, removing this kind of glance from himself on every side.

St. John Chrysostom * "Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery: But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart" (Mt 5:27-28).

The lesser righteousness is not committing adultery in deed, while the greater righteousness of the Kingdom of God is not committing adultery at all; then the last commandment came confirming the first, for the Lord did not come to destroy but to fulfill the Law.

We must note that He did not say "whosoever desires a woman" but "whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her," that is, looks at her with this intention; this look is not the stirring of bodily pleasure but its carrying out, for even though it is restrained, it will be carried out if circumstances permit.
For sin is completed in three stages: its provocation, delight in it, and then its satisfaction (its execution).

The provocation occurs by means of memory or the senses, such as sight, hearing, smell, taste or touch. If pleasure results from these, it must be restrained. If we were fasting, then at the sight of food the desire to taste is aroused, and this desire produces pleasure. We must not satisfy it but restrain it, if our mind, which keeps us from satisfying it, has the mastery. But if we satisfy it, the sin will be complete in the heart, and God knows of it even if men do not.
So these are the steps of sin:

The provocation creeps in by means of the bodily senses, as the serpent crept in with the provocation of Eve, for wherever wrong thoughts and imaginations seep into our souls, they spring from outside, from the bodily senses. And if the spirit perceives any hidden sensation apart from these five senses, that sensation is temporary and fleeting. So these imaginations creep into the thought with the cunning of the serpent.

The three stages of sin resemble the fall of man recorded in the Book of Genesis: the provocation comes from outside, from the senses, as the serpent caused it; the delight in sin occurs in the bodily desire, as Eve took delight; and the satisfaction of sin occurs in the mind, as in Adam. And because of sin man was expelled from paradise, that is, from the light of the greater righteousness, into death.

He who offers pleasure does not force man to accept it, so man must not come down from his lofty rank, in which the mind has the mastery, to a lower rank, for God created man in a rank higher than the animals. Man is not forced to accept pleasure; if he accepts it, he is punished by the just law of God, because he sinned by his own will.

However, before sin turns into a habit, there is no pleasure in it, or it is of a slight kind that is made light of, and yielding to it is a great sin as long as this pleasure is forbidden. For he who yields to it does evil in his heart. And after yielding to it and carrying it out, it seems to him that he has satisfied his desire and the matter is finished, but when what provokes it comes again, the pleasure is aroused more strongly than the first time. Yet it is less than the pleasure that results from habit. The pleasure the second time is hard to overcome; nevertheless if he is true to himself, ready for the spiritual war, he will be healed of it, and even of the habit, by the help of his Christ, the Commander of the spiritual battle. Thus the man is subject to Christ and the woman to the man (1 Cor 3:11; Eph 23:5), according to the natural order.
St. Augustine

entries.section: 2. His preoccupation with God as his eternal portion

paragraphs.text: "For what portion of God is there from above? and what inheritance of the Almighty from on high?" [2]
The translation of the Jesuit Order has: "What then is the portion from God above, and the inheritance from the Almighty on high?"

What is the portion of God, or the heavenly portion on high for the soul, but that the soul sing, saying: "The Lord is my portion, saith my soul" (Lam 3:24)? He who enjoys fellowship with the Lord, and counts the Lord Himself his eternal portion that he enjoys, will not allow his depths to find their delight in earthly things and bodily desires.

Many Fathers of the Church see that the virtues are different, interrelated aspects of one truth, which is the enjoyment of fellowship with God. Here Pope Gregory (the Great) links the two verses [1-2] and says that whoever sets in his heart to live pure and chaste, and does not allow the evil glance, enjoys God's support for him in the practice of humility, and his depths are lifted up to seek God Himself as his portion.
Every virtue supports the others, and even reveals the beauty of the virtues together, like a heavenly pearl of many facets.

* It is as though he were saying clearly: If I defile my mind with thought, I shall not be able to be an heir of Him who is the Author of purity. For nothing can be of any benefit if it is not proved in the eyes of the hidden Judge by the witness of purity. For all the virtues lift themselves up in the eyes of the Creator by mutual help, that is, a virtue without the others becomes either nothing at all, or the least of the virtues. The virtues must be supported by their alliance together. If humility abandons chastity, or chastity leaves humility, before the Author of humility and chastity, what is the use to us of a proud chastity or a defiled humility?
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Origen the Scholar sees that all the virtues in their essence are the acquiring of the Lord Christ Himself, for man becomes one with Christ; He is the virtue that fills him, He is justice, wisdom and truth. So he who practices virtue shares in the divine nature, or in the characteristics of Christ, as far as the believer can bear.
* To seek Christ is like seeking the Word, wisdom, justice, truth and the omnipotence of God. For Christ is all of these.
Origen the Scholar
"Is not destruction to the wicked? and a strange punishment (a hideous thing or calamity) to the workers of iniquity!" [3]
The Jesuit translation has: "Is not calamity for the unjust, and disaster for the workers of iniquity?"

If chastity, represented in the believer's earnestness not to allow an evil glance to creep in upon him, moves him to long for the heavenly reward, where the Lord is his portion, then on the negative side, what does evil or defilement, especially adultery, offer but eternal destruction?

By practical experience we taste what the prophet Isaiah said: "There is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked." For sin draws from what is its own, namely corruption, bitterness and ruin, and gives it to those who possess it. It offers to the one who practices it what he has chosen for himself.
The wicked man, by his determination upon evil, isolates himself from the holy Church, and so deprives himself of the blessings of the Lord for her, and of her eternal portion in glory.
* Let sinners go now, and satisfy the desires of their pleasures. For in the judgment at the end they will feel that in their evil life they were in love with death...

Now the righteous man is scourged and corrected with the rod of discipline, because he is being prepared to receive the inheritance of the Father. But let the unjust man go after his pleasures, for he is satisfied with temporal goods to the extent that he is deprived of eternal goods. The unjust man runs toward the death prepared for him, enjoying pleasures without restraint, just as calves prepared for slaughter are left free in the pastures...
Let the righteous man weigh well the evils that await the wicked, and not envy him his passing happiness...

[Is not banishment for the workers of iniquity?] What we call banishment is exile or "anathema" among the Jews. It will be banishment for the wicked when they find themselves deprived (anathema) of the inheritance of the stern Judge.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* The things of grace are accompanied by joy, peace, love and truth... But the forms of sin are accompanied by disturbance, and neither love nor joy toward God.
St. Macarius the Great What is meant by sin in Origen's mind?
(a) Since Christ is our virtue, the lack of His company and of union with the Father is sin.
(b) Virtue is the restoration of the nature of the soul, as the image of the Logos. And sin is the lack of this image.

(c) Virtue ascribes the soul to God as one of His children. And sin is its ascription to Satan. The soul that rejects its Father and its heavenly Bridegroom becomes forsaken like Jerusalem. Such a spirit easily becomes a prey to its enemies.

entries.section: 4. God examines the ways of man

paragraphs.text: "Doth not he see my ways, and count all my steps?" [4]

In Job's examination of himself he declares that he speaks only by the witness of God Himself, who knows his conduct, his life, his thoughts, his feelings and all his intentions. The ways of man are laid bare before God, the visible and the hidden ways, for He is the searcher of hearts and reins.

When a man examines his depths, it befits him to realize this truth, that God is the examiner of his ways, not to catch his faults, but to sanctify him completely. God's concern even for our intentions and hidden thoughts consists of touches of surpassing divine love. For He desires to raise up even from our depths a living icon of heaven!
* Is not what he calls "ways" nothing but the ways of working? Therefore it is said through Jeremiah: "Amend your ways and your doings" (Jer 7:3)...

The Truth calls us to Himself [by walking in steps], saying: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden" (Mt 11:28). For the Lord commands us, "Come unto me," certainly not with the steps of the body but with the advance of the heart... So human works the Lord reckons as steps in the strict sense...

The prophet saw His exactness in examination when he said: "The Great, the Mighty God, the Lord of hosts, is his name, great in counsel, and mighty in work: for thine eyes are open upon all the ways of the sons of men: to give every one according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings" (Jer 32:18-19).

So (the Lord) praised the angel of the church of Pergamos in some things, and rebuked him in others, saying: "I know thy works, and where thou dwellest, even where Satan's seat is: and thou holdest fast my name, and hast not denied my faith" (Rev 2:13). Afterward He says: "But I have a few things against thee, because thou hast there them that hold the doctrine of Balaam" (Rev 2:14). And it was said to the angel of Thyatira: "I know thy works, and charity, and service, and faith, and thy patience, and thy works; and the last to be more than the first. Notwithstanding I have a few things against thee, because thou sufferest that woman Jezebel, which calleth herself a prophetess, to teach and to seduce my servants to commit fornication, and to eat things sacrificed unto idols" (Rev 2:19-20)...

Note how He records the good things and does not let them go without punishment for the evil things that call for cutting off. This truly happens because He sees the ways of everyone and holds them to account for their steps...

The saints themselves bind themselves to the strictest scrutiny of the thought of the heart, seeing that the heavenly Judge examines their life with all exactness, and so they test the mind in the depths of the depths, watching lest they be carrying any wrong thought.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"If I have walked with vanity, or if my foot hath hasted to deceit" [5].

After Job spoke of his care to sanctify his glances so as not to lose the eternal inheritance, he speaks of sanctifying the tongue, for he takes care not to utter a word of falsehood or deceive with his tongue, speaking what contradicts what is in his heart.

If God is the Truth, and is simple, with no deceit or crookedness in Him, then whoever takes care to enjoy fellowship with the Truth must give the devil no place in him, who is called the liar and the father of lies (Jn 44:8), and is also called the deceiver (2 Jn 1:7) or the beguiler.
* Everyone must give great attention lest "lying" rob him, for the liar is not united with God.
The liar is a stranger to God. And Holy Scripture says that the liar is of Satan, for he is "a liar, and the father of it" (Jn 44:8).
So Satan was called the father of lies, while the Truth is God, for He Himself says: "I am the way, the truth, and the life" (Jn 6:14).

Do you not see, then, how we become strangers to God by lying, and with whom we are united (through it)?! Therefore, if we truly want to be saved, we must love the truth with all our strength and all our zeal, and guard ourselves against all lying, lest it separate us from the Truth and the Life.
Father Dorotheus * People use lying not as something fitting for them but as something foreign to them.

* Let no one deceive his neighbor, as the psalmist says here and there: "with flattering lips and with a double heart do they speak" (Ps 12:2). For there is nothing that brings enmity more than deceit and malice.
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 6. Let us be weighed in the Savior's scales

paragraphs.text: "Let me be weighed in an even balance, that God may know mine integrity" [6].

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the balance here is the Mediator between God and men, for in Him all our merits are weighed in the balance of His love, even though we see in ourselves the weaknesses of our life.

We are weighed in His balances so that we may imitate Him in His life. As the Apostle Peter says: "Because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps: Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth: Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not" (1 Pet 2:21-23). And the Apostle Paul says: "let us run with patience the race that is set before us, looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame" (Heb 12:1-2).

Truly all humanity in the scales goes up; there is none justified before the all-holy God. But when we are weighed in the balance of truth, who is the Lord Christ our Savior, He covers us in Him, and we bear His righteousness, and by Him we are justified before the Father, and are counted the object of His pleasure. "But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption" (1 Cor 1:30).
* God has not made us merely wise and righteous and holy in Christ; He has given us Christ for our salvation.
St. John Chrysostom * If Christ is the way of the righteous, then Satan is the way of the wicked.
St. Jerome

7 "If my step hath turned out of the way, and mine heart walked after mine eyes, and if any blot hath cleaved to mine hands; 8 Then let me sow, and let another eat; yea, let my offspring be rooted out.
"If my step hath turned out of the way, and mine heart walked after mine eyes, and if any blot hath cleaved to mine hands" [7].

Righteous Job believes in not tearing life apart into an inner life and an outer life; man has one life, and everything within and without interacts together. There is no separation between the glance of the eye and the inner insight, nor between what is in the heart and outward conduct. It befits the believer to be sanctified inwardly and outwardly, in his thought, feelings, heart, words and conduct.

He feared sins whether in practical conduct, where his steps would turn aside from the way of truth, or through the glance, so that his heart would turn aside because of his looks, or in the practice of injustice, where a blot would cleave to his hands.

* Look also at how, by keeping watch over the inner activity, he returned to training the outward members. If it happens that the heart covets something forbidden, the eye must be kept by teaching and discipline until it refuses to look at it... Let us look into our consciences through these points, and see the loftiness of this man in comparison with the lowliness into which our breasts have sunk. If it happens that he imagines improper things, he quickly rises to kill them while they are still in the depths of the heart, with the sword of holy zeal. He does not allow this imagination to turn into action... Sin is not allowed to turn into action if it is killed inwardly in the place of its birth.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"Then let me sow, and let another eat; yea, let my offspring be rooted out" [8].

Job declares his commitment to walk in everything in the spirit of truth, for he who does not walk so loses the divine blessing, and sows and reaps nothing, but another reaps it and enjoys it. He has no fruit in his life or in his offspring, since [his offspring are rooted out].

* According to Holy Scripture we call the preaching of the words of life a sowing. The prophet says: "Blessed are ye that sow beside all waters" (Isa 32:20). The preachers of the holy Church are seen sowing beside all waters, as they offer the words of life, like the wheat of the heavenly Bread, to all peoples, far and wide.

The Truth says: "My meat is to do the will of him that sent me" (Jn 4:34). So if Job abstains from doing something he says: [Let me sow, and let another eat]. He says plainly: what my tongue utters I do not practice myself, but another does. For the preacher whose ways differ from his words sows and goes hungry, while another eats. For he does not feed on his harvest when his conduct is wrong, when it does not agree with the uprightness of his words.
And since disciples, when they often hear from their teacher what is good without works, perish because of their conduct, he rightly added: "yea, let my offspring be rooted out" [8].
Pope Gregory (the Great)

9 "If mine heart have been deceived by a woman, or if I have laid wait at my neighbour's door; 10 Then let my wife grind unto another, and let others bow down upon her. 11 For this is an heinous crime; yea, it is an iniquity to be punished by the judges. 12 For it is a fire that consumeth to destruction, and would root out all mine increase.
"If mine heart have been deceived by a woman, or if I have laid wait at my neighbour's door" [9].

After speaking of his flight from the evil glance, the evil tongue, deceit, caution regarding the way of the wicked, corruption of the heart and the practice of injustice, he speaks at greater length about fleeing from the enticement of the heart toward another's wife or falling with her into sin, for it is a grave crime. On the one hand it corrupts man's purity and chastity, and on the other hand it is an encroachment on the rights of the neighbor, and an intrusion into his bedchamber.

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that fornication differs from adultery (1 Cor 6:9), and that Job's heart was not enticed to fornication with a woman, and that he took care not to lie in wait at his neighbor's door and so commit adultery.

Job sees that defilement by fornication or adultery is a crime, and not merely a sin, though there is no one without sin. Job did not commit the crime of fornication or adultery, for it exposes a man to the court so that he may be sentenced to death. This crime is a consuming fire that destroys man's life and wipes out his fruits from their roots.

* The demon of fornication stirs up bodily desire, launches his attack on the ascetics, and strives that they abandon their asceticism, sowing in their souls that this asceticism of theirs is of no use.
And if he is able to defile the soul, he begins to prepare it to say and hear some (evil) talk, until it seems as though the (evil) deed itself were present before their eyes.
Father Evagrius the Monk * Is he counted to have been delivered from the sin of fornication in his heart, he who wanted to do evil with her because she was chaste?!
Is he not counted to have committed adultery in his heart with the harlot, he who sought her and did not find her in the brothel?!

St. Augustine * A brother came to Abba Matoes and asked him: "Is slander (or defamation) worse than fornication?" The elder said to him: "Fornication is worse." The brother asked him: "How can that be?" He answered: "Slander is a bad thing but can be healed quickly, for the slanderer often repents, saying: I have spoken evil and cruelly; but fornication of the body is death in his very being."

The Garden of the Monks * When night comes be vigilant that you are not drawn by bodily lust, but increase your prayer also as it leaves you. And if you are sitting and this lust attacks you anew, do not stay sitting for a long time but get up and pray. So also if the demon of fornication tempts you a thousand times, pray a thousand times with frequent prostrations, and God will rebuke the devil when you pray and he will depart from you.

Pope Theophilus * Abba Isaiah was also asked: [Why does fornication harm a man and press upon him so much?] He answered: [Because the devil knew that fornication makes us naked of the Holy Spirit. And hear the saying of the Lord: My Spirit shall not abide in these men, because they are flesh] [(Gen 6:3) LXX].
Abba Isaiah "Then let my wife grind unto another, and let others bow down upon her" [10].

He who breaks into his neighbor's bed to transgress against his wife falls into humiliation instead of the pleasure of bodily desires, for he becomes so poor that his wife is taken from him as a slave who works in the houses of others, doing the work of slaves and maidservants, such as grinding grain, which is hard labor. And as a slave she cannot prevent her master from having bodily relations with her.
A bitter picture of the sin of adultery, which robs a man of his freedom and dignity and the purity of his wife, and brings him into the humiliation of slaves.
"For this is an heinous crime; yea, it is an iniquity to be punished by the judges" [11].
He who breaks in upon his neighbor's wife deserves death (Gen 38:24).
"For it is a fire that consumeth to destruction, and would root out all mine increase" [12].

Job compares adultery to the fire that consumes everything belonging to the adulterer, rooting out all the fruits of his labor and striving until he becomes poor, and even destroying his soul so that he perishes.

The Apostle John distinguishes between two kinds of sins: "There is a sin unto death: I do not say that he shall pray for it. All unrighteousness is sin: and there is a sin not unto death" (1 Jn 5:16-17). Perhaps he means by the sin not unto death the involuntary human weakness committed without knowledge, while the sin unto death is persistence in sin knowingly, in stubbornness and determination not to repent. Such a sin is a destroying fire for those who commit it.

* When the great preacher described him who is qualified for the grace of the priesthood, he did not say: [if any man be without sin] but [if any be without crime] (cf. Titus 1:6). Who is without sin, since John says: [If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us] (1 Jn 1:8). By this distinction between sins and crimes it may be said that venial sins defile the soul, while crimes kill it. This is the reason for which he says of the crime of lust that it is "a fire that consumeth to... destruction" [12]
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* If the lustful man knew the effect of his lust on the poor victim, he would not do what he does. If the fear of God is in him it prevents him from that, and natural compassion obliges him to change his mind. Without doubt he knows it, but in the way in which one who has experienced injustice personally knows it.
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 9. The right of dialogue with all

paragraphs.text: 13 "If I did despise the cause of my manservant or of my maidservant, when they contended with me; 14 What then shall I do when God riseth up? and when he visiteth, what shall I answer him? 15 Did not he that made me in the womb make him? and did not one fashion us in the womb?
"If I did despise the cause of my manservant or of my maidservant, when they contended with me" [13].

In wondrous humility righteous Job gave his menservants and maidservants not only their human rights, which the world at that time ignored, as he lived before the Law of Moses, but he gave them the right to dialogue with him, and even their right to defend themselves even if they put him in the position of the accused!
* O masters, be kind to your servants, as holy Job taught us, for there is one nature and one family of humanity. For in Christ there is neither bond nor free (Gal 3:28).

St. Ignatius of Antioch * Job was righteous and practiced every human virtue, and did not abstain from one vice while clinging to another. We too count the weight just if it is a true and comprehensive weight, so that we do not weigh gold uprightly and lead otherwise, but our weights for all materials are honest, every weight like the other with justice in every case. This is the way by which Job was righteous and just in all cases, not only with regard to money and matter, but he kept this equality in all matters without exaggeration in measures. He avoided that vice with great care. Here he says: [If I rejected the right of my manservant and maidservant in their complaint against me, or supposed in myself that I was not of human birth like them] (Job 31:13, 15).
St. John Chrysostom * He who does not refuse to be judged together with his menservants and maidservants shows clearly that pride against his fellows has not at any time swallowed him up...
Behold, you see how he appeared lofty in his authority among the rulers in a wondrous way, and yet he holds dialogue with his servants.

In the assembly of the rulers he remembers his work, and in his dialogue with his servants he remembers that he is a creature (like them). He sees himself a servant under the true Master, and so he did not exalt himself with a haughty heart over his servants.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
"What then shall I do when God riseth up?"

entries.section: 9. The right of dialogue with all

paragraphs.text: "And when he visiteth, what shall I answer him?" [14]

There was no written Law, nor laws protecting menservants and maidservants, but the faith of righteous Job in God the Judge, who is no respecter of persons, moved him to esteem every person, even if he was a servant of his.

* He who thinks of the coming Judge prepares his accounts for the better day after day without ceasing. He who looks to the eternal Lord with a trembling heart is bound to put a limit to his temporary lordship over those under him. For he looks well to the fact that there is no way for him to be above others temporally, because of the account he will give as one under Him who exercises authority without end. He knows who are under him, so it befits him to know that One (the Lord) who is himself over him, and by knowing the true Master, the vanity of his lordship, which bears vanity, dies in him. So blessed Job, fearing the judgment of Him who is over all, exercised temporary judgment as one equal to his servants.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* He who seeks the Lord with pain of heart, his petition is heard, if he asks with knowledge and care and a sorrowful heart, and is bound to nothing of the world except himself alone, in order to present it before the Lord without blemish as far as he is able. Like a lowly, despised man eager to please God his Lord, for if a man performed many wonders and healed difficult diseases, and had knowledge of all the sciences, yet as long as he has fallen into sin he cannot be without care for it, for he is still in repentance. And if he sees a man with all sins and negligence and judges him and despises him, let him know that his repentance is of no avail, for he has cast off from him a member of Christ and condemned him, and has not left the judgment to the Lord the Judge.

entries.section: 9. The right of dialogue with all

paragraphs.text: Abba Isaiah "Did not he that made me in the womb make him? and did not one fashion us in the womb?" [15]

* For persons who hold authority, the great work of humility is to keep in their thoughts the equality of creation. For we men are all equal by nature, but the distribution of the dispensation has been added to us so that we appear to have authority over certain persons. If we set aside our imagining of what happens temporarily (that we have authority over others), we shall very quickly find ourselves what we are by nature...

By nature we were all born equal, and since the dispensation of merits is varied, some have become above others by a hidden dispensation. This variance, which was added to our nature through a defect, is rightly ordered through the judgments of God; therefore, since not all walk in this life in the same way, one is judged by another. But the saints do not look at the authority of their positions within themselves, but at the equality of nature, for they know well that our ancient fathers lived not as kings so much as shepherds of flocks...

Since man by nature rules over the irrational animals, and not over the rest of men, it was therefore said to him that he must be an object of fear to the wild beasts, and not an object of fear to men. When you seek to be feared by one who is your equal, you are swallowed up by pride against nature... Therefore when Cornelius bowed down to the shepherd of the Church, and saw that the honor offered him was more than he deserved, he hastened to point to the equality of creation, saying the words: "Stand up; I myself also am a man" (Acts 10:26). Who does not know that it befits man to bow down to his Creator and not to a man...? So also the angel, when John bowed down to him, confessed that he is a creature, saying: "See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren" (Rev 19:10).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* If we are masters, it befits us not to despair of our servants and so be harsh with them, but to learn to forgive their offenses...
Likewise Paul was not ashamed to call the servant his son and his bowels and his brother and his beloved, so it befits us not to be ashamed of them.

And why do I say Paul? For the Lord of Paul was not ashamed to call us His servants His brethren... See how He honored us, and called us His servants and brethren and friends and heirs with Him, and that we appear beside Him and are counted workers with Him, and that the Master Himself works to be a servant! Hear and tremble!
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 10. His care for orphans, widows and the poor

paragraphs.text: 16 "If I have withheld the poor from their desire, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail; 17 Or have eaten my morsel myself alone, and the fatherless hath not eaten thereof; 18 (For from my youth he was brought up with me, as with a father, and I have guided her from my mother's womb;) 19 If I have seen any perish for want of clothing, or any poor without covering; 20 If his loins have not blessed me, and if he were not warmed with the fleece of my sheep; 21 If I have lifted up my hand against the fatherless, when I saw my help in the gate: 22 Then let mine arm fall from my shoulder blade, and mine arm be broken from the bone. 23 For destruction from God was a terror to me, and by reason of his highness I could not endure.
"If I have withheld the poor from their desire, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail" [16].
Job believed in the Creator who creates all men in their mothers' wombs without distinction, who forms every embryo without partiality between one social class and another.

God permitted righteous Job to enter into this severe affliction and to reproach God openly so that all generations might learn how there were righteous men, even in the era before the Law, who by living faith, through the natural law, rose above many who lived under the Law of Moses, and even in the era of grace.

He lived free, not enslaving himself to the practice of injustice or cruelty. He longed to provide the poor with all their needs and all they desired, whatever it cost him. He did not allow a widow to beseech with her tears, but hastened to give to all as much as he could!

* [He did not deprive the poor of all their desire, nor did he make the eye of a widow seek for anything] [16]. Do you see how he avoided arrogance, walking in moderation, as a physician to all, a common harbor and shared refuge for all who were in distress.

He says: [all their desire]. This does not mean saying yes to this need and not to that, but not depriving them of any need without distinction, even if it was fraught with danger and very costly. Note that he helped those from whom he expected nothing: widows and orphans and those without help. He was not occupied with boasting and glory, but gave for God's sake.

St. John Chrysostom * By these words the holy man shows that he not only serves the needs of the poor, but also grants them their desire... He adds [or made the eyes of a widow wait]... For it is written elsewhere: "Say not unto thy neighbour, Go, and come again, and to morrow I will give; when thou hast it by thee" (Prov 3:28)
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 10. His care for orphans, widows and the poor

paragraphs.text: "Or have eaten my morsel myself alone, and the fatherless hath not eaten thereof!" [17]
His compassion reached the point that he could not eat alone, so that he not only called his wife and children to eat with him, but at every meal looked for an orphan to share his meal!

It was among the manners of fellowship and the rules of custom among the Easterners to invite others to share their food. In some desert regions, after the food was prepared, a member of the household would stand on a high place and call out in a loud voice that someone should come and share the food with the household. Sometimes he would wait for the arrival of a guest he had heard from a long distance, to share the family's meal.

entries.section: 10. His care for orphans, widows and the poor

paragraphs.text: "For from my youth he was brought up with me, as with a father, and I have guided her from my mother's womb" [18].

The care he enjoyed even for the servants was not issuing from a binding law or deterring statutes, but it was a matter that touched his depths, issuing from a divine work within him. From his youth, while still not bound by family matters, he treated the servants in his house as his own children, practicing tender fatherhood toward them while still young.

Again he does not mention how he trained himself in compassion toward servants, orphans, widows and all who were in need, but counted that what he practiced he had received from God while still in the womb before his birth.

* He counts it an injustice to his compassion to eat alone what was created for the common people... But as for these surpassingly compassionate bowels, did he draw them to himself by himself, or did he receive them by the grace of his Creator? Let us know it. [But from my childhood compassion grew with me, and from my mother's womb it came forth with me] [18]. Although he undertook the matter by his own command (that is, his struggle) so that compassion might grow in him, it is clear that it was not in his power for it to come out with him from the womb. It is clear that he did not ascribe anything to his own goodness, since he bears witness that he received this through the gift of his Creator. He received the goodness he practices from his creation. By this he settles his praise of the Creator, for what he has he received from Him, and he did not receive his compassion from another.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 10. His care for orphans, widows and the poor

paragraphs.text: "If I have seen any perish for want of clothing, or any poor without covering" [19].

entries.section: 10. His care for orphans, widows and the poor

paragraphs.text: "If his loins have not blessed me, and if he were not warmed with the fleece of my sheep" [20].

His care for the poor did not stop at offering them food, but when he saw a man groaning from nakedness because of cold or heat, having no clothing, he did not wait for him to ask, but counted it a blessing to himself to give them costly garments from the wool woven from the fleece of his sheep.

* By not despising the poor man he showed the virtue of humility, and he also clothes him out of compassion. For these two virtues must cleave to each other, and be supported by their mutual action. With regard to the need of a fellow creature, let humility help compassion, and compassion help humility, in a way that when you see a person who shares your nature lacking the necessities of life, you must not cease to clothe him, neither without compassion, nor out of pride failing to honor the one you clothe.

James rebukes strongly: "If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food, and one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit?" (Jas 2:15-16). This is what John the Apostle advises: "My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth" (1 Jn 3:18). For tender love must always appear in fitting words and at the same time in the service of giving...

Paul says: "But by an equality, that now at this time your abundance may be a supply for their want, that their abundance also may be a supply for your want" (2 Cor 8:14). This means that in our concern we consider those whom we now see in want as ones we see some day in plenty, and we who are seen in plenty, if we neglect giving, will some day be in want...

Now he who is without a garment is less in need than he who is without humility. Therefore, when we see those who are sharers with us in our nature lacking outward things, let us consider our own lack of many great things within us, so that the thoughts of our hearts may not be puffed up against the poor. Thus we shall see with a penetrating eye that we ourselves are in truth in greater want with regard to our inner need. Blessed Job says well in this: [If I despised a passer-by because he had no clothing], for he shows compassion to the fellow creature unknown to him, since he calls him a "passer-by."
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 10. His care for orphans, widows and the poor

paragraphs.text: "If I have lifted up my hand against the fatherless, when I saw my help in the gate" [21].
