Job did not take advantage of his position as ruler and judge, lifting his hand in injustice against an orphan.

* [If I have lifted up my hand against an orphan, I would not have seen myself the most exalted at the gate] [21]. The custom was that the elders sat at the gate to settle disputes during judicial sessions, so that everyone in the city might be in harmony, and no one might enter it at odds with another. Therefore the Lord says through the prophet: "Establish judgment in the gate" (Amos 5:15)...
It is as though he were saying: even when I see myself, justly, as the best of those who exercise judgment, I do not take advantage of that for my own benefit by using my authority over the orphan.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 10. His care for orphans, widows and the poor

paragraphs.text: "Then let mine arm fall from my shoulder blade, and mine arm be broken from the bone" [22].

If the arm signifies work, then the man who wants to work by himself, ignoring his unity with his brethren, is like one whose shoulder, which joins the arm to the body, has fallen off, so that he cannot do what befits him as a living member in the body of Christ. Our holy dealings will not be accomplished without our union together as a holy Church, and at the same time through our personal relationship with God.

* Since bodily works are accomplished by the shoulder and the arm, he wished his shoulder to fall and his arm to be broken into pieces if he spoke with his mouth of good things without practicing them in deed.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 10. His care for orphans, widows and the poor

paragraphs.text: “For destruction from God was a terror to me, and by reason of his highness I could not endure” [23].

After speaking of his exceeding tenderness toward all the deprived classes, and his esteem for all who were rejected by society, even the slaves, he lifts his eyes with all reverence toward God and wonders why God allowed him to suffer these harsh trials.
When Job felt the weight of the afflictions he was filled with terror, and felt that the hand of God had become heavy upon him.

entries.section: 11. His trust is in God, not in his wealth

paragraphs.text: 24 “If I have made gold my hope, or have said to the fine gold, Thou art my confidence; 25 If I rejoiced because my wealth was great, and because mine hand had gotten much;
“If I have made gold my hope, or have said to the fine gold, Thou art my confidence” [24].

Had he relied on his wealth and possessions, there would have been a reason for all this to be taken from his hand. But he had focused all his feelings, emotions and intentions on the Creator and not on the creature, so why were these blessings taken from him?
* It happens that a man stops placing his hope in the Creator, so that hope in the creature takes His place.

That rich man fixed his hope on uncertain things when he said: [Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry] (Lk 12:19). But the voice from on high rebuked him, saying: “Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?” (Lk 12:20)... For God stands forever, and all these things pass away. What, then, is this, that we fly from Him who alone stands, and cling to passing things?
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 11. His trust is in God, not in his wealth

paragraphs.text: “If I rejoiced because my wealth was great, and because mine hand had gotten much” [25].

St. John Chrysostom sees that the victory won by righteous Job during his trial was not the product of the moment, but the fruit of practical spiritual training that he lived by divine grace even before the trial came, among which was his training in despising temporal blessings and earthly wealth.

* Such was blessed Job. Had he not trained himself well before entering the struggles, he would not have shone in splendor in this way. Had he not experienced freedom from despondency, he would have uttered words in a rush when his sons died. But as he was before, so he stood against all the assaults: against the destruction of his wealth and the great ruin that came upon him, against the loss of his sons, the consolation of his wife, the plague that struck his body, the reproaches of his friends, and the insults of his servants.

If you also want to see his ways on the (spiritual) path, listen to him telling how he despised wealth, saying: “If I rejoiced because my wealth was great, if I gathered gold in huge quantities, if I trusted in precious stones” (Job 31:25, 24) LXX. Therefore he was not troubled when he lost these things, because he did not desire them when he had them.

* Job was rich, but he did not serve the demon of greed, mammon; rather he reigned over wealth and mastered it, so he was a lord and not a slave. Therefore he possessed all these things as a steward of another’s money, not only not seizing from others, but giving what was his to the needy. And what is more, when he had these possessions they did not make him glad, for he declared, saying: [If I rejoiced when my wealth was great] (Job 31:25), nor did he grieve when they were gone from him.

St. John Chrysostom * The saints, in this pitiable journey, long for that appearing of their Creator which they cannot now contemplate, and so they count the whole fullness of the present life as if it were poverty. Nothing outside God satisfies the mind that truly seeks after God.

Such persons often count abundant goods an excessive burden, for they carry many things with seriousness while they hasten toward their homeland. Therefore they devote their energy so that their needy relatives may share with them...
The elect will not rejoice in many goods, because out of love for the heavenly inheritance they give away and distribute what is in their hands, despising it and renouncing it.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

26 If I beheld the sun when it shined, or the moon walking in brightness; 27 And my heart hath been secretly enticed, or my mouth hath kissed my hand: 28 This also were an iniquity to be punished by the judge: for I should have denied the God that is above.
“If I beheld the sun when it shined, or the moon walking in brightness” [26].

As his wealth was not his trust, but the Giver of wealth, so the sun and the moon, with their beauty and splendor, took no place in his heart; rather he was enlightened by God, the Creator of the sun and the moon, the true eternal Light.
The sun and the moon were objects of worship for many in the days of Job, who honored them as soldiers of heaven. This act was counted the height of evil and ingratitude toward God the Creator.
* Job tells us that he did not look at the sun as it rose, nor at the moon as it walked in brightness, showing that he did not seek the present light.

As the soul pours itself out in contemplation outside itself, so much the more does it do so in order to return to inward things. Thus all who have wise hearts avoid falling toward outward things through the bodily senses. Instead they make continual effort to gather themselves within by hidden discipline, guarding their own selves, so as to be found wholly in what is inward.
Jeremiah bound himself to the depths of his heart in earnest discipline, and fled from longing for the outward life, when he said: [I did not desire the day of man, thou knowest] (cf. Jer 17:16).
* Just as the “gold” of understanding did not make Job proud, so also the light of outward works did not make him exalt himself before the eyes of men...

The sun in its brightness is the good works displayed outwardly. It is written: “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven” (Mt 5:16). Again: “Let your loins be girded about, and your lights burning” (Lk 12:35). For what is said in this passage about the rising sun means the Gospel, which is indicated by the burning lamps. When good works shine among unbelievers, the lamp is lit in the night; and when they shine in the Church, the sun shines in the day.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Many have strayed from the One in many ways. Some deified the sun, so that when it set they dwell at night without a god.
And some worshiped the moon, so that they have no god by day.
And some worshiped the parts of the rest of the world.
And some worshiped the arts.

And some worshiped various kinds of foods, and some their pleasures, and some took delight in women, so they set up a statue of a naked woman and called her Aphrodite, and worshiped their lusts in a visible form.
And some were dazzled by the glitter of gold and worshiped it, and others worshiped other kinds of these things.
St. Cyril of Jerusalem “And my heart hath been secretly enticed, or my mouth hath kissed my hand” [27].

Righteous Job affirms that idols, gold, precious stones and abundant wealth could not, all of them, deceive his heart in secret; that is, not only did he not practice any kind of arrogance, pride or idolatry in deed, but none of it even crept stealthily into his heart.

Putting the hand to the mouth and kissing it is a custom practiced by many when their hearts are occupied with something very dear to them or when they greatly admire it, and so they express what is in their hearts by sending kisses from the mouth through the hand, pointing to whom or what they love. Thus neither wealth nor idols occupied him, nor did he love these things, nor send them his kisses.

* Stretching the hand to the mouth is the harmony between voice and practice. He who praises what he does kisses his hand with his mouth, and so bears witness to his speech by the merits of his practical deeds. In this case, who is the despiser if not the one who receives the very same gifts for doing them (and ascribes them to himself)? The great Preacher says well: “What hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?” (1 Cor 4:7). Now the saints themselves know that they are of the stock of a corrupt origin, since from the fall of our first father it is grace that changes us for the better in desires and works... They perceive that they have received strength for the struggle. So blessed Job tells of the good things that he practices, but he never ascribes them to his own work. On the contrary, he praises his Creator, and denies that he kissed his hand with his mouth.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
“This also were an iniquity to be punished by the judge: for I should have denied the God that is above” [28].

The love of the world did not creep into Job’s heart, nor did idol worship creep into it. Had he fallen into either, he would have deserved what came upon him as a divine punishment. He did not deny his God by clinging to creation or by deifying it.

entries.section: 13. No thought of gloating enters him

paragraphs.text: 29 “If I rejoiced at the destruction of him that hated me, or lifted up myself when evil found him: 30 Neither have I suffered my mouth to sin by wishing a curse to his soul.
“If I rejoiced at the destruction of him that hated me, or lifted up myself when evil found him” [29].

Job was careful not to deny his Creator, nor to wrong his brother or hate him, even if his brother hated him. No thought of gloating over an opponent or one who hated him crept into his mind. Solomon the Wise says: “Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth: Lest the LORD see it, and it displease him, and he turn away his wrath from him” (Prov 24:17-18).

* The ways of the wicked who devise harm are death (Prov 12:28). “Thou shalt not devise harm against thy brother” (Lev 19:18) LXX. And also: [If you see the ass of him that hateth you fallen (in the mire), you shall not pass by it until you have first lifted it up] (Ex 23:5). On this point each one must bear in mind that he may not leave his enemy’s ass in the mire, so how can a man hate or ignore a human being created in the image of God?

I have noticed in blessed Job a true, perfect love, in all faithfulness, even toward his enemies, so that he could rejoice and say with a clear conscience to the Lord: [If I rejoiced at the destruction of him that hated me, or lifted up myself when evil found him, and said in my heart: Well done!] (Job 31:29-30).

Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles * Keeping love is the only proof that we are disciples of Almighty God. The Truth says: “By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another” (Jn 13:35).
This love, if it truly fills our hearts, is usually shown in two ways: we love our friends in God, and we love our enemies for God’s sake...
If we rejoice at the misfortunes of one who hates us, it is clear that we do not love him, since we do not wish him to be better than ourselves...
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 13. No thought of gloating enters him

paragraphs.text: “Neither have I suffered my mouth to sin by wishing a curse to his soul” [30].

Not only did he not stir himself to harm the one who hated him, nor gloat when distress or disaster came upon him, but he did not dare to ask God against his brother. He did not seek vengeance on those who harmed him, nor did a word of cursing come out of his mouth against them!

* Those who attack an enemy with curses, what do they want God to do to him but what they are unable to do, or are ashamed to do...? In that same place, did those who read “Love your enemies” not also read “Bless, and curse not”? Again: “Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing” (Lk 6:27; Rom 12:14; 1 Pet 3:9).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 14. Marvelous love for the people of his household

paragraphs.text: 31 “If the men of my tabernacle said not, Who will bring one who has not been satisfied with his food? 32 The stranger did not lodge in the street: but I opened my doors to the traveller.
“If the men of my tabernacle said not:
Who will bring one who has not been satisfied with his food?” [31]

Job’s nature was wonderful: he gave continually and generously, especially to the needy and the poor, giving others their needs not merely to the point of sufficiency but until they were satisfied. This was a cause of amazement to the people of his tent; even the hired servants, the slaves and the maidservants marveled at his tenderness toward all. He was admired by everyone who dealt with him!

This saying points to the Savior, whom the men of His tent, or His Church, long to have enter, that each one may enjoy the Body of the Lord and be spiritually satisfied by it, whether of the persecuting Jews or of the Gentiles who accept the faith.

St. John Chrysostom comments on what is said here: [Oh, that we were filled with his flesh!], that this is an expression of the intense love binding Job to his servants, and that the Lord Christ gives us His Body to eat as a declaration of the intense love between Him and His believers: [This Body He gives us to eat, which befits intense love. For those who have warmth in their hearts, we often bite with our teeth. Therefore Job, pointing to the love of his servants for him, said that they often did this because of their strong affection for him, saying: ‘Oh, that we were filled with his flesh!’ (see Job 31:31). So Christ gives us to be filled with His Body, drawing us to a greater love.]

* [If I have allowed the poor man to go out of my house empty-handed] [31]. He did not say “I gave when he begged,” but “I gave even to the one who refused to take.” Those who entered his house had to leave only after receiving... Job used pressure on those he gave to, so that they would take.

* This too Christ does, to lead us to close friendship and to show His love for us, for He gives those who long for Him not only to see Him, but also to touch Him, to eat Him, to fix their teeth in His flesh, to embrace Him, and to satisfy all their love. Let us return from that table like lions breathing fire, becoming a terror to Satan, thinking of our Head and of the love He shows us.
St. John Chrysostom “The stranger did not lodge in the street.”

entries.section: 14. Marvelous love for the people of his household

paragraphs.text: “I opened my doors to the traveller” [32].
St. Ambrose offers us a symbolic interpretation, seeing in the true believer one who imitates Job and brings those who are strangers to the faith into his house, which is the Church of God.

Righteous Job is a type of the Lord Christ, and his house is a type of the Church. The Lord Christ longs for the doors of His Church to be opened so that every stranger may enter it. All are washed by His precious Blood, enjoy the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and become members of the household of God. If all humanity is a caravan ever on the move, then the doors of God’s mercies are open to them, that they may enjoy the blessings of God’s saving work during their journey in this world.

* Take away good will from men and it is like taking the sun from the world. Without it men no longer care to show the way to the stranger, or to bring back the one who has strayed, or to show generosity. This is no small virtue. Because of it Job praised himself, saying: [The stranger did not lodge (outside my gates), I opened my door to the traveller] (Job 31:32)... Thus good will is found in all these things, like a spring of water that refreshes the thirsty, and like a light that shines on others and does not withhold its brightness from those who give light to others.

St. Ambrose * He says: I gave generously to every needy person. I offered my roof that they might share it with me. When I noticed that they were in a public place, I offered my house, my table, and all that I had to be held in common. I counted myself as a treasurer for the needy, without looking on my possessions as personal property, but as the property of the Master (the Lord). “The LORD gave” (Job 1:21), and accordingly let us be partners with all His servants.

* Poverty and wealth are two similar weapons, with which we serve virtue if we wish... To learn that this is true, let us recall the case of Job, who became rich and also poor, and used these two weapons in a similar way, conquering with both. When he was rich he said: [I opened my door to every traveller] (Job 31:32). And when he became poor he said: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it seemed good in His eyes, so He has done” [(Job 1:21) LXX and the Vulgate]. When he was rich he showed generous hospitality, and when he was poor he showed much patience.

* Not only what we give as alms, but also what we bear steadfastly when others rob us of what is ours, both of these yield us great fruit. And that you may know that the latter is truly greater, I offer as witness what befell Job. When he possessed wealth he opened his house to the poor, giving them what he had. But he was not as famous when he opened his house to the poor as he became when he heard that his house had fallen and did not receive the news with a troubled heart. He did not gain fame when he clothed the naked with the fleece of his sheep, as he became famous and known when he heard that fire had fallen on his flocks and burned them all, and yet gave thanks. Before, he was a lover of men; now he became a lover of wisdom. Before, he was compassionate to the poor; now he gives thanks to the Lord... He knew that God was ordering all things for good.
St. John Chrysostom
“If I covered my transgressions as men do, by hiding mine iniquity in my bosom” [33].

A beautiful picture of the humility of righteous Job. For with all the preceding amazing traits of a man living in the midst of a pagan world, who holds fast to his Creator, into whose heart the love of possessions does not creep, but who gives and bestows with marvelous generosity, and esteems and honors even the male and female slaves, he does not deny that he has faults and sins; he does not hide them in his bosom but confesses them openly.

* These are the proofs of true humility, that a man affirms his own evil, confirming it by disclosing it with the voice of confession. This is contrary to the habit of the human race, that a man practices sin while keeping himself hidden from sight. And when it is discovered he denies it, hiding it, and when he is accused of it he multiplies his sins by falling into defending himself. Since the fall of man we have been drawn down to these degrees of evil... And as the sin of concealment grew, it reached a frightful extent in the human race, and blessed Job said: [If I hid my transgressions], adding the words “as a man,” since he saw that taking the likeness of the first parents had become a pattern for man...

Blessed Job displayed a singular humility, for he knew that he lived among adversaries, and yet he did not fear to disclose his faults with the voice of confession. Note that he first tells of his virtuous traits, and after that confesses his sin.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* He was not turned aside by the crowds of the people, that is, those subject to him, who knew his natural faults. This indeed is wisdom: [Confess first your transgressions, that you may be justified] (cf. Isa 43:26). Thus I have not taken anyone as a witness to my good works, while I wish everyone to know my faults and transgressions. This is the height of wisdom, a pattern of virtue, that a person hide his good works and expose his faults to the public. In any case, this is contrary to what is practiced in reality.

St. John Chrysostom * When you are occupied with some sin, be an accuser of yourself (Prov 18:17), and do not wait for others to bring the accusation. Thus you become like a righteous man who accuses himself at the start of his speech in court, or like Job, whom the crowd of the people in the city did not hinder from declaring his offense before all.
St. Basil the Great

entries.section: 16. The clans rise up against him without cause

paragraphs.text: “Did I fear a great multitude, or did the contempt of families terrify me, that I kept silence, and went not out of the door?” [34]

Although he was accustomed to confess his sins openly and not conceal them within him, the situation had completely changed, for the tribes had risen up against him, and it was as though the clans had no work but violent attack against him, without cause. As for him, he did not allow his mouth to utter anything for a time. His words became like words that do not go out of the door of his mouth.

* It is as though he says plainly: While others did not cease attacking me outwardly, I myself remained free from disturbance within my soul. For what are we to take the door to be here but the mouth? By it we come forward, as it were, to disclose the secrets of our hearts. While we remain within in the conscience, we go out through the tongue.
But there are some who fear above all to be despised, and aim to appear wise when accused of deserving contempt...

When the saints are on trial, they abstain completely from appearing (to defend themselves), and when they cannot benefit those who listen to them, they keep silence, even to be despised, lest they boast by displaying their wisdom... It is written: [And when Herod saw Jesus, he was exceeding glad: for he was desirous to see him of a long season, because he had heard many things of him; and he hoped to have seen some miracle done by him]. And I add: “Then he questioned with him in many words; but he answered him nothing.” But how greatly the Lord was despised because He kept silence was shown by the words that follow immediately: “And Herod with his men of war set him at nought, and mocked him” (Lk 23:8-9, 11).

It befits us to hear and learn that those who listen to us often want to be known through matters that concern us, and not that they may correct their faults. Therefore it befits us to hold to silence, lest, if we speak the word of God openly, the faults of these persons do not cease, and we ourselves sin...

The Preacher says: “For we are not as many, which corrupt the word of God: but as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God speak we in Christ” (2 Cor 2:17)... To speak as of sincerity is to seek nothing beyond what is necessary and needful...

He speaks as of God who knows that he himself has nothing of his own, but speaks only what he receives from God. He speaks in the sight of God who does not seek what belongs to men in all that he utters, but is occupied with the presence of Almighty God, and looks toward the glory of his Creator, not his own glory.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

35 “Oh that one would hear me! behold, here is my signature. Let the Almighty answer me, and that mine adversary had written a complaint. 36 Surely I would take it upon my shoulder, and bind it as a crown to me. 37 I would declare unto him the number of my steps; as a prince would I go near unto him. 38 If my land cry against me, or that the furrows likewise thereof complain; 39 If I have eaten the fruits thereof without money, or have caused the owners thereof to lose their life: 40 Let thistles grow instead of wheat, and cockle instead of barley.” The words of Job are ended.
“Oh that one would hear me!
Behold, here is my signature.
Let the Almighty answer me.
And that mine adversary had written a complaint” [35].

In the end Job returns to ask what he had asked before, repeating his request to find someone who would enter into a trial with him and hear him. He himself signed the request to enter into the trial, and to be ready to accept whatever punishment he deserves.

He asks that the Almighty Himself, the Searcher of hearts and reins and the Knower of secrets, rise up to judge him, and that the matter not stop at accusations brought against him by his adversaries with no established facts against him.
“Surely I would take it upon my shoulder.”
“I would bind it as a crown to me” [36].

Job asks for a public trial, reckoning that while being tried as a criminal he receives honor, and he considers the accusations leveled against him a crown that wreathes his head, because God will surely justify him!
“I would declare unto him the number of my steps; as a prince would I go near unto him” [37].
Righteous Job declares that he will hide nothing of the steps of his whole life. For he knew that his life bore witness to him as a prince and not as a criminal.
“If my land cry against me, or that the furrows likewise thereof complain” [38].

In his certainty that he never wronged anyone, but showed tenderness as far as he could and gave constantly, he therefore asks them to look at the land, for it bears witness, it and its produce, to his love; it finds no single complaint against him, and neither weeps nor laments over any conduct of his.

* The earth does not sigh or grieve. What, then, does he mean by this? It is not that the earth truly (in the literal sense) sighs, but these lifeless things are offended by injustice, as the prophet says: [The earth shall be broken, and struck with terror] (Jer 4:28)(a). In any case the earth sighs every time we use its fruits unjustly.
St. John Chrysostom “If I have eaten the fruits thereof without money, or have caused the owners thereof to lose their life” [39].
“Let thistles grow instead of wheat, and cockle instead of barley.”
“The words of Job are ended” [40].

Job challenges his friends, saying that if he had wronged anyone and taken produce (wheat or barley) without paying the price, he would not grieve if those subject to him offered thorns and tares instead of grain for food and refreshment.

He affirms that if he were unjust he would not deserve to eat bread of wheat like the poorest of mankind, nor barley like the animals, but that men should offer him words sharp as thorns or worthless words like tares, since he would deserve only to be cast into the fire.

The words of Job in his dialogue with his friends are ended, and in his speech he felt that he was speaking in the presence of God; indeed he often directs his speech to God Himself, for he seeks God’s approval, not that a man should justify him.
Shine with Your light in my depths
* Grant me, with Your devout servant Job, to discover my depths.
I know the weight of my sins, but who can sanctify me but You?
Without You I am struck by the darkness that has reigned within me.
In You I am filled with hope for Your salvation, O You who shine upon me with Your glory!
You gave the face of Moses radiance; give my depths a radiance from You.
* I do not allow my eyes to look at a virgin.
But who gives my heart, my mind and my emotions a virgin purity but You?
You are my portion and my eternal inheritance; I possess You, so that the love of lust does not creep into my depths.
* You are the Searcher of hearts and reins; You know all my hidden secrets, not to condemn me but to sanctify me.
* You are the Truth; whoever possesses You does not make peace with falsehood, nor enters into dealings with the devil, the liar and the father of liars.
* The heavens are not clean in Your sight, and You charge Your angels with folly, so how shall I be justified before You?
Let me be weighed in the balance of Your love, and Your Cross will support me.
Let me put on Your free righteousness, that I may appear before the divine throne.
* In You I possess purity, tenderness and truth.
Then adultery will not come near my body, nor my soul!
I will respect every man, and see You in every person!
I will not care for wealth or authority, for You are my wealth and my glory!
I will love even my enemies and my opponents, and desire the peace of the whole world and its glory in You.
Let the world rise up against me, for I desire to wash its feet!
Finally, grant me, with righteous Job, that You may be my all!

1 So these three men ceased to answer Job, because he was righteous in his own eyes. 2 Then was kindled the wrath of Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram: against Job was his wrath kindled, because he justified himself rather than God. 3 Also against his three friends was his wrath kindled, because they had found no answer, and yet had condemned Job. 4 Now Elihu had waited till Job had spoken, because they were elder than he. 5 When Elihu saw that there was no answer in the mouth of these three men, then his wrath was kindled.
So these three men ceased to answer Job, because he was righteous in his own eyes [1].

The three friends stopped speaking, either because they saw God Himself defending Job as righteous, or because Job counted himself righteous, so that there was no profit in debating with him. The real fact is that they failed to prove their accusations against Job because they carried in their hearts and thoughts an insincere intention, so their accusations had no weight.

"Because he was righteous in his own eyes": this text reads in the Septuagint, the Syriac, the old Arabic and the Chaldean, "because he was righteous in their eyes." They were convinced that he was righteous and that their accusations had no basis.
The text reads in the translation of Symmachus, "because he appeared more righteous than they."

In the previous chapters we saw that Job did not deny that he had sins, and that he confessed them; but he was suffering because of what had befallen him, which had disfigured his image and caused his friends to stumble over him.
* They had no answer to this (that is, to what Job said), so Job fell silent to give them the word. And since he had received testimony from God (that he was blameless), they shut their mouths.

[Because Job was righteous before them]... They changed their former opinion, for by speaking against Job they condemn God. Note that in both cases there is a lack of proportion. They condemned Job as they did God also, and testified against both. But God did not defend Himself; rather He defended Job, ignoring the defense of Himself. He drew all eyes to him (Job 1:8), and He also said of Job: [You have not spoken of Me what is right, as My servant Job has] (see 42:8). In all this God bore the utmost degree of injustice.

St. John Chrysostom God, in His love for His believers, defends them, whether as individuals or as a community. The psalmist says: "I cry... to God who defends me" (Ps 57:2). "The Lord will defend me. O Lord, thy mercy endureth for ever: forsake not the works of thine own hands" (Ps 138:8). As for the community, it is said: "For I will defend this city to save it for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake" (Isa 37:35; 38:6; Zech 9:15).
In the midst of the accusations of those nearest to us, we lift our eyes to our Lord Jesus, as the fortress in which we take refuge, the refuge of our salvation and our defender.

* [You have become my hope, and a tower in the face of the enemy] (Ps 61:3). He says: My heart is troubled, for they have gathered together from the ends of the earth, and I have come to suffer in the midst of trials and attack... Inside the Church the wheat suffers from the violence of the chaff. In the midst of all these things, since my heart is troubled, I cry out from the ends of the earth.. Christ Himself is the tower. He makes Himself a tower from the face of the enemy, and He is also the rock on which the Church is built. Do you wish not to be struck by Satan? Flee to the tower. The arrows of Satan will not be able to weary you in that tower. There you take shelter and stand firm... The tower is before you. Call Christ to your minds, and enter the tower!
St. Augustine Then was kindled the wrath of Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram.
Against Job was his wrath kindled, because he justified himself rather than God [2].
"Elihu" is a Hebrew name meaning "He is my God." The wrath here indicates his inner emotion and his great zeal to defend God's justice, His righteousness and His care.

* [Against Job was his wrath kindled, because he counted himself righteous before God] [2]. Elihu was angry, not because Job declared that he was righteous, but because he did this before the Lord, whom he counted as a witness, or he thought that Job wanted to condemn God. His justifying himself was of no importance; but to do so with the purpose of condemning God is wrong. Scripture says: [Justify not thyself before the Lord] (Sir 7:5)...

Did this happen? Job's thought was not so. It was Elihu who understood it in this way; Job did not say that he was more righteous than God, but rather his thought was that God was responsible for his calamities. Even so, he did not wrong God by accusing Him of injustice; this is only what Elihu understood.

St. John Chrysostom "Elihu," or "He is Jehovah, God." His name and his character announce his role as a messenger between God and Job, preparing Job to enjoy the vision of God coming in the whirlwind. He bore a shadow of the true Mediator, our Lord Jesus (Job 33:23-26).
Barachel: it means "God blesses." The name of Elihu and the name of his father indicate that this family was marked by godliness and did not practice idol worship.

The Buzite: Buz was the second son of Nahor, the brother of Abraham (Gen 22:21), and this region in the Arabian desert was called by his name; the name of the city of Buz occurs in (Jer 25:23); perhaps it took its name from the family. Pope Gregory (the Great) holds that the word "Buzite" is translated "contemptible."

Some rabbis and St. Jerome hold that Elihu is Balaam the son of Beor. Pope Gregory (the Great) holds that Elihu, as an example of arrogant preachers, offers us an interpretation of his name, the name of his father and the name of his kindred: for although they do not live according to the commandments of the Lord, they know God as their Lord. And while they enjoy the blessing of divine grace in the eloquence of their speech, in their arrogant conduct they show that they are despised. Dr. Hodges holds that Elihu is one of the appearances of the Second Hypostasis, and that the aim of the whole book is to focus on the person of Elihu and to bring out his role in convincing Job that his justification does not rest on reliance on his good works and clinging to his own righteousness, but on faith in the One who is able to justify.

None of the Fathers of the Church has proclaimed this opinion, but it may be said that he was a type of the Lord Christ, who comes to accomplish mediation and reconciliation, and so justifies the believers who walk in Him in spirit and truth.

Ram: Ram - Aram was the nephew of Buz, and perhaps Job was of a generation earlier than Elihu, since he was older than he. Pope Gregory (the Great) holds that the word "Ram" means "exalted." True believers are exalted, for they can say with the Apostle Paul: [For our conversation is in heaven] (Phil 3:20).

"Because he justified himself rather than God": perhaps he means "because he counted himself righteous before God." The literal translation is: "he justified his soul before God." He defended not only his conduct, but also his thoughts and inner motives.

Elihu differed from the three friends as to the intention of the two parties, for Elihu bore no malice or envy toward Job like these friends. On the other hand, he did not accuse him of committing grave hidden evils or of being a hypocrite; what he criticized in him was that in his speech he did not justify God, but what occupied him was justifying himself before God as well as before men, even if he feared that they would stumble over him as a man of God.
Also against his three friends was his wrath kindled, because they had found no answer, and yet had condemned Job [3].

They had condemned Job, but they were unable to answer his arguments in general, and his justification of himself. Truly they sat silent, but they did not change their thoughts about him, and at the same time they failed to answer him.

What Job's friends did wrong was that they lacked a spirit of compassion toward a man who was tried and suffering like Job. They accused him of hypocrisy and of being wicked, and though unable to prove it, they did not wish to retreat. They reached a conclusion and a verdict on a man beforehand, before conversing with him, and their dialogue had no aim except to crush him completely.

Perhaps among the wonderful traits of Elihu is that, though his heart was filled with compassion for Job, as a mediator between the two parties he did not take a position of favoritism toward Job at the expense of his friends, but with gentleness and prudence he brought out the error of both parties. He began with Job so as to give the friends the opportunity to receive his words seriously and to reassess their dialogue with Job.
Now Elihu had waited till Job had spoken, because they were elder than he [4].

Elihu waited until the elders were silent and stopped speaking. By waiting he showed the wisdom of the elders while still a young man; he kept silent when they spoke, not because they were wiser than he, but because they were older than he. He kept to good order and fitting management, and when they fell silent in failure, while insisting on what was in their minds, he spoke with the spirit of truth, with boldness and prudence. Holy Scripture has commanded honoring the elders, but in the Lord:
"Despise not a man in his old age: for even some of us wax old" (Sir 8:7).
"Rebuke not an elder, but entreat him as a father; and the younger men as brethren" (1 Tim 5:1).
"Against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses" (1 Tim 5:19).
When Elihu saw that there was no answer in the mouth of these three men, then his wrath was kindled [5].

Elihu was jealous for the Lord, for Job had sinned by not leaving the matter to God, counting that an injustice had been done to him. And Elihu regarded the silence of the three elders as a kind of consent and agreement with Job's opinion, so he was jealous for the glory and wisdom of the Lord.

6 And Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said, I am young, and ye are very old; wherefore I was afraid, and durst not shew you mine opinion. 7 I said, Days should speak, and multitude of years should teach wisdom. 8 But there is a spirit in man: and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding. 9 Great men are not always wise: neither do the aged understand judgment. 10 Therefore I said, Hearken to me; I also will shew mine opinion.
And Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said:
I am young, and ye are very old; wherefore I was afraid, and durst not shew you mine opinion [6].

In ancient times, especially in the region of Asia, the young were not permitted to enter into dialogue with those older than themselves; sometimes the young man kept silent as far as possible on any subject.

His saying, "I am young in days," is an expression indicating a difference in age, whatever its extent; it may also indicate that he has less experience across the days because of his young age, but it does not mean he is less than they in wisdom.
I said, Days should speak, and multitude of years should teach wisdom [7].
Elihu holds that wisdom does not depend on the mere experience of years. We can distinguish three kinds of wisdom:
Wisdom acquired through the experience of life; this grows with the years, and the elders hold it dear.

And wisdom as a natural gift which God has given to man in general, since He gave them reason by nature [8]. Often some of our children are wiser and more intelligent than we, even if they do not enjoy the same experience as ours.
And finally wisdom is the gift of the Spirit of God, which He gives to His godly ones.

While we hold dear and esteem the first two kinds of wisdom, the surpassing wisdom of God remains the object of our continual asking of God. [Give me wisdom, that sitteth by thy throne; and reject me not from among thy children] (Wis 9:4).

* All this wisdom and prudence are found in Christ, and through Christ we understand God (the Father) and see Him; so whatever wisdom remains in the world, any wisdom of this kind outside Christ and without Him is counted vain, worthless and base.

Fr. Marius Victorinus * Solomon says in Ecclesiastes that the eyes of the wise man are in his head (Eccl 2:14). Paul understood the importance of headship. He knew why the eyes are in the head. If Christ is the head of the believer, and the eyes of the wise man are in the head, then all our senses, our mind, our thought, our speech and our counsel (if we are wise) will be in Christ.
St. Jerome But there is a spirit in man: and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding [8].

The Hebrew text is translated literally "the Spirit Himself," meaning that man is given the Spirit, the giver of wisdom, or the spirit of inspiration. Elihu had earlier honored the elders for their experience; now he brings out that wisdom is a gift of God, which the old man can enjoy as the young man can. True wisdom, though it does not ignore experience through life, is fundamentally an inspiration from the Almighty, or a breath from the Almighty, "nishmat Shaday."
Some hold that the word "spirit" here refers to the breath which God gave to man (Gen 2:7), which gives him understanding.
Great men are not always wise: neither do the aged understand judgment [9].

With the multitude of days a man may gain useful experience, whether in his own life or in the lives of others whom he meets and deals with; he may also gather many proverbs full of wisdom and memorize some of them by heart, and yet he may not practice wisdom, nor enjoy the spirit of discernment and understanding.

This is the argument by which Elihu justifies his position, that he has intruded into the situation to speak among elders, and to point out to them some judgments and counsels, and even to rebuke them.

Some hold that he is speaking of the wisdom granted by God, since He gave man the breath of a rational life. "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it" (Eccl 12:7). "Thus saith the Lord, which stretcheth forth the heavens, and layeth the foundation of the earth, and formeth the spirit of man within him" (Zech 12:1).
Therefore I said, Hearken to me.
I also will shew mine opinion [10].
Elihu asks the elders not to despise him because of his young age, but rather to listen to him first and then examine his words.
It is fitting for us not to look lightly on those younger than ourselves, but to listen to them. The wise man says: [Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king] (Eccl 4:13).

entries.section: 3. With patience he bore what had been said

paragraphs.text: 11 Behold, I waited for your words; I gave ear to your reasons, whilst ye searched out what to say. 12 Yea, I attended unto you, and, behold, there was none of you that convinced Job, or that answered his words: 13 Lest ye should say, We have found out wisdom: God thrusteth him down, not man.
Behold, I waited for your words.
I gave ear to your reasons, whilst ye searched out what to say [11].

It is as though he says to them: "I was listening to your words and attending to your arguments, and I found you lovers of disputation, searching for bare words here and there; and all that concerned you in the matter was to find words, whatever they might be, to carry out what was within you toward Job, rather than to touch the truth and offer love. By this he accuses you of your manner of dialogue. It is the manner of one who wants to win and excel with words, not of one who builds up himself and others. What occupied them throughout their whole dialogue was to contend with Job, and here they have failed in their barren contention.
* When you meet a man who loves disputes, and he begins to argue with you about what is self-evident and true, cut off the conversation and withdraw quickly, for his mind has turned to stone.
For as water spoils the finest wines, so foolish discussions spoil the virtuous in their conduct and in their characters.
St. Anthony the Great * Always flee from every man who does not cease from argument in his speech.
* If the soul withdraws from all discussion, disturbance and agitation, then the Spirit of God enters into it, and that which was barren becomes fruitful.

entries.section: 3. With patience he bore what had been said

paragraphs.text: Abba Poemen Yea, I attended unto you, and, behold, there was none of you that convinced Job, or that answered his words [12].

He made clear their failure in the dialogue, for they were unable to persuade Job's mind and change it, and they also failed to give convincing answers to his questions. They uttered a huge quantity of words, which were powerless to remove what was in Job's mind.
Lest ye should say, We have found out wisdom.

entries.section: 3. With patience he bore what had been said

paragraphs.text: God thrusteth him down, not man [13].

Here Elihu brings out what lay behind their dialogue and discussions, for they supposed in themselves that they were able to convince him by their own wisdom, whereas man needs an inner conviction coming from God, who alone overcomes the mind and subdues it, a thing of which man is incapable, whatever his linguistic and philosophical abilities.
God did not allow them victory in their dialogue, lest they rely on their own wisdom.

entries.section: 4. His inner depths impel him to intervene

paragraphs.text: 14 Now he hath not directed his words against me: neither will I answer him with your speeches. 15 They were amazed, they answered no more: they left off speaking. 16 When I had waited, (for they spake not, but stood still, and answered no more;) 17 I said, I will answer also my part, I also will shew mine opinion. 18 For I am full of matter, the spirit within me constraineth me. 19 Behold, my belly is as wine which hath no vent; it is ready to burst like new bottles. 20 I will speak, that I may be refreshed: I will open my lips and answer. 21 Let me not, I pray you, accept any man's person, neither let me give flattering titles unto man. 22 For I know not to give flattering titles; in so doing my maker would soon take me away.
Now he hath not directed his words against me: neither will I answer him with your speeches [14].

Elihu says: [I am not a party to the dialogue, for Job has not uttered a single word against me; therefore my speech carries no emotions and does not issue from inward agitation, but springs from the desire for the truth. At the same time I will not speak to him in your manner, full of violence and harshness, which bore a folly that came out of your mouths. So, without partiality and without bias, I speak with him and also with you].
They were amazed.
They answered no more.

entries.section: 4. His inner depths impel him to intervene

paragraphs.text: They left off speaking [15].

It seems that he turned his gaze to those present and began to speak with them about the position of the three friends, how they were bewildered and could not answer a word, for they felt that their words were worthless babble.

"Good" holds that the talk here is not about the friends, but about their words, which no longer carried any effectiveness, going out of their mouths to be dissipated in the air, carrying no meaning and offering nothing new.
When I had waited, (for they spake not.

entries.section: 4. His inner depths impel him to intervene

paragraphs.text: But stood still, and answered no more;) [16].
Elihu says that he was waiting for the friends to utter a word and answer Job, and since they had become mute, he came forward to speak.

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees in Job's friends a type of the heretics who stir up many disputes, accuse the Church and resist her, but in the end the Lord upholds His Church and silences the heretics.

entries.section: 4. His inner depths impel him to intervene

paragraphs.text: I said, I will answer also my part, I also will shew mine opinion [17].

The time had come for Elihu's turn. Now he became like one receiving his portion, by revealing the knowledge that he had kept hidden throughout the dialogue that went on between Job and the friends. He counted this as his portion, which came to him as a gracious gift offered to him.

Some hold that his saying, "I also will shew mine opinion," carries in the Hebrew original a touch of gentleness and humility that does not appear clearly in translations into other languages. It is as though he says: [Even I, the young man, a humble man like me, am permitted to express my opinions, while the elders and the great have nothing left to say].
For I am full of matter.

entries.section: 4. His inner depths impel him to intervene

paragraphs.text: The spirit within me constraineth me [18].

The true believer bears a fiery spirit, in the likeness of God the consuming fire, or a fire of love that is not quenched (Ex 24:17; Deut 4:24; Heb 12:29), and so he becomes like one of the servants of God of whom it is said: "His ministers a flame of fire" (Heb 1:7).

The believer carries the word of God - the blazing fire of love - and so becomes like our teacher the Apostle Paul, who was "pressed in the spirit" (Acts 18:5), full of blazing spiritual zeal, who says: "For I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ" (2 Cor 11:2). And he cries out with the prophet Jeremiah: "My bowels, my bowels! I am pained at my very heart... I cannot hold my peace" (Jer 4:19), "Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay" (Jer 20:9).

So Elihu felt like one constrained by the Spirit of God, who kindles the fires of his love toward Job as toward his friends and all who were present, seeking in blazing zeal from his depths what is for their edification and their eternal glory.

The three friends fell silent and found no word to utter, because they had emptied out the words that issued from their envy of Job, and became like those who have emptied what was in their quiver; but Elihu, who was silent for a time, had within him words of love that are not emptied. He wished to speak, not as one who desires to teach, nor from the seat of authority, but from the position of love and compassion for all, his words overflowing from his bowels, or as he says: "the spirit within me."

* Paul here uses a word much stronger than mere "love." For zealous souls burn with ardor toward those they love. Jealousy presupposes strong affection. Therefore, lest they suppose that Paul seeks authority, wealth or honor, he adds that his jealousy is godly. For God is said to be jealous, not in a human way, but so that each one may know his right of lordship over those whom He loves, and that what He does is for their increasing profit.
Human jealousy rests basically on selfishness, but divine jealousy is strong and pure.

Note the difference between the human bride and the Church. In the world, the virgin woman before marriage loses her virginity by her marriage. But in the Church, those who were virgins to some extent before returning to Christ enjoy virginity in Him. Therefore the whole Church is a virgin.

* God is also said to be jealous, lest anyone suppose that (the Godhead) has passion, but so that all may know that He does everything only for the sake of those over whom He is jealous, not to acquire anything but to save them.
St. John Chrysostom Behold, my belly is as wine which hath no vent.

entries.section: 4. His inner depths impel him to intervene

paragraphs.text: It is ready to burst like new bottles [19].

Since Elihu offered an excuse for speaking in the presence of the elders, he entered into a soliloquy with himself, saying that his inside was filled with blazing zeal, so that his soul almost burst like new wineskins full of wine, or like a smith's bellows full of air. In his soliloquy he declares that he shows partiality to no one and flatters no man!
Elihu's speeches came not as one seeking an answer to questions or to accusations, but as one looking at the problem with a general view, to prepare the way for the dialogue between God and Job.

We can interpret Elihu's words symbolically: the belly indicates the depths of the heart, and the new wine the Spirit, as the Lord Christ's saying that new wine is put into new bottles (Mt 9:17). For when the disciples were filled with the Holy Spirit who came down upon them on the day of Pentecost, they became like new bottles filled with new wine, and their tongues were loosed to speak as the Spirit gave them utterance. And since the Jews did not grasp the divine truth, they accused the disciples of being full of new wine, like drunkards (Acts 2:4).
I will speak, that I may be refreshed.

entries.section: 4. His inner depths impel him to intervene

paragraphs.text: I will open my lips and answer [20].

Elihu could not keep silence, so he burst out in speech that his soul might find rest. This is what happened with the prophet Jeremiah, who was filled with intense compassion toward the people of God; how he longed to be silent, but the fires of his love and the flame of the word of God in his depths compelled him to speak.
I do not think we blame Elihu for his position; rather we learn from him when to be silent and when to speak, as the wise man says: "A time to keep silence, and a time to speak" (Eccl 3:7).
* The wise man is the one who strives to please God and is much given to silence, and if he speaks, he speaks little, uttering what is necessary and pleasing to God.

* In silence you see your mind, but when you use your mind you are speaking within yourself. For during silence the mind gives birth to the word, and the word of thanksgiving offered to God is the salvation of man.
* He who speaks foolishly has no mind, for he speaks without thinking about all matters. Therefore examine what is profitable to you, for the sake of your soul's salvation, so that you may do it.

entries.section: 4. His inner depths impel him to intervene

paragraphs.text: St. Abba Anthony the Great Let me not accept any man's person, neither let me give flattering titles (flatter) unto man [21].

It is as though he says: "I beseech you, let me not show partiality to a man for his person, nor flatter people for their titles." This is not speech addressed to those present, nor a prayer offered to God, but an expression revealing the determination of his heart to speak with the spirit of truth, without respect of persons and without flattering anyone, whatever his position or abilities. He wishes to utter the truth without fear, courtesy or personal gain for himself.
"These things also belong to the wise. It is not good to have respect of persons in judgment" (Prov 24:23).
"To have respect of persons is not good: for for a piece of bread that man will transgress" (Prov 28:21).
"And, ye masters, do the same things unto them, forbearing threatening: knowing that your Master also is in heaven; neither is there respect of persons with him" (Eph 6:9).
"But he that doeth wrong shall receive for the wrong which he hath done: and there is no respect of persons" (Col 3:25).
"I charge thee before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the elect angels, that thou observe these things without preferring one before another, doing nothing by partiality (1 Tim 5:21).
"My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons" (Jas 2:1).
"And if ye call on the Father, who without respect of persons judgeth according to every man's work, pass the time of your sojourning here in fear" (1 Pet 1:17).
"For there is no respect of persons with God" (Rom 2:11).
"For there is no iniquity with the Lord our God, nor respect of persons, nor taking of gifts" (2 Chr 19:7).

Since God sent His only-begotten Son out of His love for the whole world, without partiality, and gave Him up for all of us, we perceive God's lack of partiality. And since we are members in the body of Christ, the Lover of mankind, it is fitting for us to have no partiality. Concerning God's lack of partiality it is said:
* God has no partiality toward persons; He judges by works.

St. John Chrysostom * If anyone doubts this, it is enough for him to read what Peter said when he visited the Gentile Cornelius: "Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons: but in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him" (Acts 10:34-35). We go further than this and quote what our Lord says in the Gospel: [He that believeth not is condemned already, because he hath not believed in the name of the only begotten Son of God] (Jn 3:18).
Origen * All of us were born equal, emperors and paupers, and we die equal. Our humanity is equal.
St. Jerome Solomon the Wise himself offers us a living example of lack of partiality, as he looks upon himself, a king of great wealth and honor, as no different in anything from any pauper.

[I myself also am a mortal man, like to all, and the offspring of him that was first made of the earth, and in my mother's womb was fashioned to be flesh in the time of ten months, being compacted in blood, of the seed of man, and the pleasure that came with sleep] (Wis 7:1-2).
For I know not to give flattering titles (flattery).

entries.section: 4. His inner depths impel him to intervene

paragraphs.text: In so doing my maker would soon take me away [22].

His defense of Job did not issue from partiality or flattery, nor to seek some profit for himself, for Job no longer had any authority or resources for Elihu to flatter him; rather he defends one who is in the midst of the dunghill, even if in his defense he points to the error of Job who, with his righteousness, when accused was wholly occupied with defending himself, even at the expense of affirming God's care for him and His compassion toward him.

Elihu enjoyed the sense of the divine presence, so he feared no man, a thing in whose snare many fall, as the wise man says: "The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the Lord shall be safe" (Prov 29:25). What occupied Elihu's heart was his sense of the swiftness of the Lord's coming, when he would be taken from this world and stand before Him, and give an account of all that was in his heart and thought as well as of his conduct, before the Creator who knows all the secrets of man, and from whom nothing is hidden.
This is what impelled him to silence, to listen and study with deliberation, and it is what impelled him to speak, to present the truth in simplicity and without embellishment.

Here he calls God "my maker," for He is God the Creator who is personally concerned for him and who knows his depths. He is the God of truth, and He is love; He gives the truth to His believers, reveals it to them more and more, and upholds them to speak the truth and to walk in it.

So Elihu concludes the introduction of his long speech by affirming that he flatters no one and shows no partiality to those with titles, but presents the truth in simplicity for the sake of his Maker, before whom he stands on the great day of the Lord.
Let my heart be kindled with the fire of Your word, that I may speak Your truth!
* My God, You who gave me thought and tongue!
Sanctify my depths, my words and my actions.
Let me know how to keep silent with my tongue, so that my heart speaks with love for You and for all mankind.
Let my soul groan with the groans of every heart.
And let my depths cry out with the cries of every wronged one.
Hear the cries of my soul rising to Your throne!
* Grant me to speak at a good time, to utter what You give me of words, so that I fear no man, nor flatter a rich man or one in authority.
Grant me the wisdom that sits by Your throne, so that I speak Your word, kept by Your wisdom.
* You gave me a breath from You, that I may receive Your wisdom and walk by Your Holy Spirit.

I am jealous for the salvation of every soul, and I long for You to be glorified in every man, yet in my zeal I do not rely on my bare experience, nor do the years of my life concern me, however long or short.
Rather I carry You within me, that You may speak through me, and work by Your Spirit in me and in my brethren!
Who can renew my life but You?
Who can set right the mind of my brethren except Your Spirit?
* My depths groan for every wandering soul, my bowels pain me, my heart has melted like wax for all mankind!
Let me speak, but rather You speak in me and through me.
Let me utter Your word, and my soul will rest and be comforted in You!
Let me speak, awaiting my departure to You!
Let me enter into the divine embrace, and let my soul rejoice for all those who enjoy the glories!
Yes, come, Lord Jesus!
Come, to carry every believer to Your glories!
Our hearts will not cease to long for Your coming!

entries.section: 1. In God's name he invites Job to dialogue with him

paragraphs.text: 1 "Wherefore, Job, I pray thee, hear my speeches, and hearken to all my words. 2 Behold, now I have opened my mouth, my tongue hath spoken in my mouth. 3 My words shall be of the uprightness of my heart: and my lips shall utter knowledge clearly. 4 The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life. 5 If thou canst answer me, set thy words in order before me, stand up. 6 Behold, I am according to thy wish in God's stead: I also am formed out of the clay. 7 Behold, my terror shall not make thee afraid, neither shall my hand be heavy upon thee.
Wherefore, Job, I pray thee, hear my speeches, and hearken to all my words [1].

None of the elders dared to address Job, mentioning his name, but this young man, despite the difference in age, says: [Hear now, O Job, my speeches, and hearken to my words] (Job 33:1). There is a difference in age, but both are creatures, and it is fitting for each of them to listen to the other.

If it is fitting for the young in age to obey their elders, then everyone must listen to one another. So we need not wonder that the young Elihu begins his speech to the godly old man Job saying: [Hear now, O Job, my speeches, and hearken to my words] (Job 33:1). He also says with courage and courtesy: "Behold, in this thou art not just" (Job 33:12). He repeats again: [Mark well, O Job, hearken unto me: hold thy peace, and I will speak... for I desire to justify thee] (Job 33:31-32).

A wonderful picture on both sides: the godly old man of God listens to a young man, with no arrogance on his part and no disdain for his youth. And on the part of the young man, though he converses with the old man frankly, with an open heart and courage, he was extremely courteous and gentle. He wants to justify one who is of his father's age!
As Elihu presents his plea to Job, he asks him to listen to him as a sincere friend who loves him, who does not speak to criticize him or terrify him.

Elihu quoted some expressions from Job and made clear to him that God is greater than man, and that man has no right to demand an explanation from God for His actions. What Job should realize is that God seeks the salvation of man, not his destruction.
Elihu begins by directing his speech to Job, and in the next chapter he directs the speech to Job's friends.

This chapter is regarded as an introduction to prepare the hearts of these three friends to listen to him. In this he did not slander Job, but addressed blame to him from the reality of his words in the previous dialogues.

He asks him to listen to his words, or his speeches, not only what he addresses to him, but also to [all his words], for he utters divine truth for the benefit of all. He asks him to be long-suffering, to hear the speech to its end, and to keep in mind that what is said is not meant to criticize him and lay blame on him, but for his benefit.
Behold, now I have opened my mouth.

entries.section: 1. In God's name he invites Job to dialogue with him

paragraphs.text: My tongue hath spoken in my mouth [2].

In Barnes's notes on this phrase, Elihu speaks with the words that are in his mouth, uttered by his tongue which moves toward the roof of his palate, because pronunciation in the Hebrew language uses mostly the larynx, the throat and the tongue, whereas in the European languages (Latin and English) it uses mostly the teeth and the lips.

He speaks with him from his throat, as one who brings out words carrying a special flavor and a taste full of love. All men speak with their mouths, but few taste their words and examine them first, so that they utter what is good for edification.

Elihu was silent throughout the period of the dialogue, interacting inwardly with the dialogue. He did not hasten to criticize or to answer some of the questions, but with wisdom and deliberation he tested the words that were in his mind, so as to utter what is fitting.

In a wonderful discourse St. Mar Jacob of Serugh directs us to train ourselves in holy silence and holy speech. Wherever we are occupied with the divine Word, His Holy Spirit leads us to constructive silence as well as constructive speech.
* You are the Word who gives a word to those who speak; by You all who speak speak for Your sake.
A ray, a radiance and a great light has shone in me, so that I look at You.
For by looking at You, the soul is enlightened and acquires goodness.
And when the soul departs from You it is filled with darkness, but if it gazes upon You it puts on light, to utter the words of Your news...
Silence and speech stand over me and make demands of me.
O Lord, order my life according to Your will.
If I am silent I marvel, for I feel my insufficiency (for speech). I am silent in wonder, and not in vain arrogance.
And if I speak, may my word be according to Your glory and for Your sake.

When the soul is filled with silence in wonder at You, this silence is a speech full of all benefit. And when the soul is moved to glorify You with love... it is with love that I move, and I move to glorify You. And in wonder I am silent and do not cease from glorifying You.
Grant me, O Lord, wonder (in silence) and the word, and I will be enriched. Every day I marvel, and every day I am moved to speak!

entries.section: 1. In God's name he invites Job to dialogue with him

paragraphs.text: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh My words shall be of the uprightness of my heart: and my lips shall utter knowledge clearly [3].

Elihu says that God, who gave him His Spirit, enables him to speak with a pure heart and to present sincere knowledge, without deceit. It is as though he asks Job to look not at the bare words, but at what is in Elihu's heart of purity toward him, and the uprightness of his aim in the dialogue. His words issue from pure love, without hypocrisy; he speaks in sincerity from his heart, and does not display hollow words. What he utters expresses truthfully what is in his heart.
He wanted him not to include him with the three friends, even if the words were similar, because the intentions are entirely different.

* He wants to say: It is not out of envy or jealousy that I use this means. Even if the three say the same things as he says, it seems that they did not speak with the same spirit, nor did they do this in defense of God. Judas and the twelve(a) all expressed themselves in the same way concerning the alabaster box of ointment (Jn 12:5-6), but not with the same spirit. Therefore it is fitting for us to examine not the words, but the intention with which each of them expressed himself: how some wanted to crush Job, while the other wanted the opposite.

entries.section: 1. In God's name he invites Job to dialogue with him

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life [4].

Many of the Fathers of the Church used this phrase to affirm the divinity of the Holy Spirit as the Creator and Giver of life. If the Father is the Creator and Giver of life, then the three hypostases share together in every divine work. Here he speaks with Job in a spirit of sincere brotherhood, making clear to him that he is the work of the Spirit of God, who gave him life. He is an instrument in the hand of God, who also created Job and gave him life. So Job need not fear dialogue with his fellow in creation and in life, since both owe their existence and life to the Spirit of God. He assures him that both are God's creation, with the same nature, and with its weaknesses that have crept into human nature.

* How did (the Book of) Job show clearly that the Spirit is Creator, saying: [The Spirit of God made me]? In a short phrase he showed that He is divine and Creator. If the Spirit is the Creator, then certainly He is not a creature, for the Apostle separates the Creator from the creature, saying: [They worshipped the creature rather than the Creator] (Rom 1:25).

St. Ambrose * The Holy Spirit shared with the Son in the work, whether in creation or in resurrection, as Holy Scripture shows: [By the word of the Lord were the heavens made; and all the host of them by the breath of his mouth] (Ps 33:6). And also: [The Spirit of God made me, and the breath of the Almighty teacheth me] (Job 33:4). And also: "Thou sendest forth thy spirit, they are created: and thou renewest the face of the earth" (Ps 104:30).

St. Gregory of Nazianzus * When words of folly are mixed with wise sayings, even wisdom is not kept in the mind, because their folly becomes an object of contempt to the hearer... Here he speaks in fitting order concerning his creation and his receiving of life. He says that he was created by the Spirit, and received life by the breath of God. It is written of Adam at his creation: [He breathed into his face the breath of life; and man became a living soul].
Pope Gregory (the Great)
If thou canst answer me.
Set thy words in order before me.

entries.section: 1. In God's name he invites Job to dialogue with him

paragraphs.text: Stand up [5].

Elihu assures him that if he wishes to enter into dialogue with him, he should know that he has not come as one who rebukes and teaches, but as two equals, made by the Spirit of God. He speaks not to prevail or to dominate, but in a spirit of brotherhood. It is as though he says to him: I am a man like you, and I wish for you what I wish for myself. Receive my words in a spirit of friendliness.
Behold, I am according to thy wish in God's stead.

entries.section: 1. In God's name he invites Job to dialogue with him

paragraphs.text: I also am formed (molded) out of the clay [6].

Umbreit translates it: "I am like you from God"; Noyes: "I am like you, God's creature"; Wemyss: "I am equal to you in the eyes of God"; and Coverdale: "Behold, I am before God as you are; I was formed from the same clay." The Vulgate translation reads: "Behold, God made me as He made you, and from the same clay I was formed." And the Septuagint: "From clay I was formed as you are; we were formed from the same clay."
Some hold that the meaning of the phrase in Hebrew is: "I am, according to your mouth, a man of God," that is, I speak in His name as His representative, His ambassador.
Since Job was beseeching God to summon him to trial so that he might find his opportunity to defend himself, Elihu came to him asking him to speak with complete frankness as in a court before God.

Elihu goes on to reassure Job that though he speaks in the name of the Lord, he is made of frail clay like him, of the dust of the earth. Though God speaks through him, there is nothing in himself to frighten or terrify.

* When we are urged to practice some virtue, we must not say that these were partakers of a nature other than ours, or that they were not men. For this reason it was said of the great Elijah: "Elias was a man subject to like passions as we are" (Jas 5:17). Do you see that Elijah showed by his very partaking of sufferings that he was a man like us? Again it was said: [I too am a man subject to the same sufferings as you] (see Wis 7:1). This gives reassurance concerning the sharing of nature.

* The nature of Paul the Apostle was no different from our nature; nor was his soul different from our souls, nor did he live in another world, but he dwelt in the same world and was subject to the same laws and customs, yet he surpassed in virtue all men, past and present.
Now, where are those who object to the difficulty of virtue and the ease of sin?
For this man condemns them by his words: "For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory" (2 Cor 4:17).
If his afflictions were bearable and light, how much more so ours, which, compared with his afflictions, become as nothing or mere pleasures?

entries.section: 1. In God's name he invites Job to dialogue with him

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom Behold, my terror shall not make thee afraid, neither shall my hand be heavy upon thee [7].

With intense longing Job wanted to present his case before God directly, but he felt the awe of God, which made him unable to speak frankly with Him. He says: "Withdraw thine hand far from me: and let not thy dread make me afraid" (Job 13:21), and he says: "Let him take his rod away from me, and let not his fear terrify me" (Job 9:34).

Elihu says: {We are equal; there is no fear that will come upon you, and no terror of me that will surprise you, so that you would be unable to take a position of defense with me. My hand will not be heavy upon you, for I am weak like you, and I have no authority over you}.
The word "heavy" here is used of a man while he leads an animal that carries loads, and it also indicates a person who is very heavily burdened and so stoops because of the weight of the load.

Perhaps because of this meaning Pope Gregory (the Great) felt that Elihu overstepped the bounds of propriety. For while admitting that he bears the same nature as Job, and that he is equal to him, he speaks with surpassing boldness, demanding that Job answer and converse without fear or trembling.

entries.section: 2. His rebuke of Job for using violent expressions

paragraphs.text: 8 "Surely thou hast spoken in mine hearing, and I have heard the voice of thy words, saying, 9 I am clean without transgression, I am innocent; neither is there iniquity in me. 10 Behold, he findeth occasions against me, he counteth me for his enemy, 11 He putteth my feet in the stocks, he marketh all my paths.
Surely thou hast spoken in mine hearing, and I have heard the voice of thy words [8].

It is clear that Elihu attended all the dialogues, and his ears listened to every word with full attention. Now he begins to comment on what he thinks Job erred in, in his attempt to justify himself. He quoted the following three expressions from Job's words in his speeches.
Saying, I am clean without transgression.

entries.section: 2. His rebuke of Job for using violent expressions

paragraphs.text: I am innocent; neither is there iniquity in me [9].

The first error Elihu raised is Job's justifying himself. It is true that Job told God that he knows he is not wicked, and that he holds fast to righteousness, and other similar expressions, but at the same time he confessed that he is a sinner and that he would not be justified before God (Job 7:21; 9:29-30; 13:23, 26).
Elihu did not quote Job's words as they were, nor did Job's words carry a justification of himself, but rather a facing of the accusations against him, that he is a hypocrite and that he is wicked.
"I am innocent": the Hebrew word here is chap, derived from Chopap, and it means to cover, to protect, and also to wash or purify.
Behold, he findeth occasions against me.

entries.section: 2. His rebuke of Job for using violent expressions

paragraphs.text: He counteth me for his enemy [10].

Elihu accuses him of having said of God that He picks out faults against him, and watches for every opportunity against him as if he were an enemy. Perhaps he concluded this from Job's saying to God: "For now thou numberest my steps: dost thou not watch over my sin? My transgression is sealed up in a bag, and thou fabricatest against me beyond mine iniquity" (Job 14:16-17). "Wherefore hidest thou thy face, and holdest me for thine enemy?" (Job 13:24). "He hath also kindled his wrath against me, and he counteth me unto him as one of his enemies" (Job 19:11).
He putteth my feet in the stocks.

entries.section: 2. His rebuke of Job for using violent expressions

paragraphs.text: He marketh all my paths [11].
He took this accusation from Job's saying: "Thou puttest my feet also in the stocks, and lookest narrowly unto all my paths; and upon the roots of my feet thou hast dug" (Job 13:27).

Thus Job pictures God as one who is occupied with his sin, scrutinizing it and sealing it up, so that it may stand as a witness against him, and that He deals with him as an enemy, bearing wrath against him; He binds him in the stocks so that he may not escape the coming judgment and the divine verdict against him.

entries.section: A. God has authority over man

paragraphs.text: 12 "Behold, in this thou art not just: I will answer thee, that God is greater than man. 13 Why dost thou strive against him? for he giveth not account of any of his matters.
Behold, in this thou art not just.
I will answer thee.
That God is greater than man [12].

To one who does not know that God is greater than man, this saying seems to need no recounting, but Elihu said it for a particular purpose. For he directed it to a man suffering grave successive calamities, without Job knowing what lay behind these calamities. What Elihu meant was that Job, the weak man, must submit to the divine chastisements, even if he does not grasp God's judgments concerning these chastisements. All that is fitting for him to know is that God is just, and that there is no injustice in Him, and that what befell Job is the fruit of his errors.
