St. John Chrysostom holds that when Job cried out to God, saying: [He would not answer me] (Job 9:15), Elihu answered him: {Tell me, He whom you reproach for not inclining His ear to your entreaty, what is the proof that He does not hear you? He chastens and punishes! This is His rule for the reform of the condition of men}.

* The prophet David was compelled, under the weight of the blows, to utter exaggerated words, and then he returned to contemplate his origin, saying: [I was dumb, I opened not my mouth; for thou hast made me] (Ps 39:9). For he considered in what rank he was created, and learned the justice of the blow that had fallen on him.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* If we had no adversaries there would be no battle and no reward set apart for the victors, and the Kingdom of Heaven would not have been offered to us. "Our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory" (2 Cor 4:17). And none of us would have hope of the great glory in the coming life as the result of patience in bearable afflictions.
* The temporary sorrow was no small matter for anyone, since they have perfect love for God in Christ Jesus, shed abroad in their hearts by the Holy Spirit.
Origen Why dost thou strive against him?

entries.section: A. God has authority over man

paragraphs.text: For he giveth not account of any of his matters [13].
Elihu reproaches Job because he enters into a quarrel with God; he questions Him and awaits a quick answer.

God loves man as His creature made in His image, and does what pleases (God), even if man does not grasp His divine plan. God does what is for man's edification, even if in many circumstances man does not grasp what lies behind the divine dealings.

It is fitting for man to trust in God's love and His surpassing fatherhood, wisdom and power, and so to receive everything from God's hand with joy and trust, as a child receives from his parents' hands what they do with him, until day by day he comes to understand the parents' plan for him.

Instead of entering into a quarrel with God, it is fitting for us to trust that He will not err, that He is a doer of good things, and that one day we shall mature spiritually and come to know His plan toward us.

Our part is submission and obedience with joy and trust in His wisdom, not entering into a quarrel with Him. For woe to him who strives with his Maker, a potsherd among the potsherds of the earth. Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou? or thy work, He hath no hands?" (Isa 45:9).

entries.section: B. By the use of dreams and visions

paragraphs.text: 14 For God speaketh once, yea twice, yet man perceiveth it not. 15 In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falleth upon men, in slumberings upon the bed.
For God speaketh once, yea twice, yet man perceiveth it not [14].

Perhaps Elihu means that God spoke with Job when he was in prosperity and had many good things, and since he did not listen to God, He spoke with him in the language of successive afflictions, and yet Job did not grasp God's purposes and did not understand His words. So God sometimes speaks to us in the language of pain and affliction in order to purify us, so that we hear His voice and see Him revealed in our lives.
"Every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit" (Jn 15:2).
"God hath spoken once; twice have I heard this; that power belongeth unto God" (Ps 62:11).

He uses every means to speak with us: at times through the many good things He gives us, at times through His holy word, and sometimes through dreams and visions, and when we do not listen to Him, He speaks to us in the language of afflictions and sufferings, such as illnesses or troubles at work or material or moral losses, and so on.

Pope Gregory (the Great) holds that it is natural for the suffering heart, when it sees matters going contrary to what it desires, to long to hear an answer from God as to why things go this way and not that. It longs to find an explanation for the events that pass over it. Elihu answers him that God does not answer man in a private, solitary talk with man's heart, but gives the answer through the Holy Scriptures once and not twice, that is, there is no need for God to give us the answer directly, as though repeating what He had already announced through the Holy Bible, but man has not noticed God's answer to him. It is fitting for us to grasp God's answer through His dealings with those who went before us, as examples for those who come after them, and not to expect Him to repeat the answer a second time (Job 33:14)..

He gives us an example of this: when an affliction comes upon us we find our consolation in what befell St. Paul, who suffered from weakness of the body, and heard the divine voice: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness" (2 Cor 12:9). This was said to St. Paul when he suffered pain, so that it would not be said to each one individually, but that this saying be counted as offered beforehand to every sufferer.
The Father spoke once, when the divine Word was begotten eternally, and there is no other word that He begets that shares with Him the divine essence and is equal to Him in the same essence.

entries.section: B. By the use of dreams and visions

paragraphs.text: In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falleth upon men, in slumberings upon the bed [15].
By slumbering he means light sleep, in which a man is in a state between sleeping and waking.

Job had said earlier: "Then thou scarest me with dreams, and terrifiest me through visions" (Job 7:14). It was fitting for him to realize that God wished to give him a certain message through these frightening dreams and fearful visions. The Syriac version reads: "Not by lips does He teach, but by dreams and visions in the night."

When a man is in quietness, far from the confusions of life and the daily preoccupations, like one in a doze of sleep, he can listen to the divine voice amid the calm of his thoughts and inner emotions.

* What is meant by the word of God being made known to us in a dream, except that we do not learn the secret things of God while we are awake in worldly desires? In a dream the outer senses rest, and inner things can be discerned. So, if we wish to contemplate inner things, let us rest from outward occupations. Truly the voice of God is heard as in a dream when our minds are at rest, we rest from the noise of this world, and we reflect on the divine commandments in their depths, in the deep stillness of the mind.

So when the saints are obliged by the necessity of duties to busy themselves with outward things, they always return with longing to study the secrets of their hearts. Thus they ascend to the height of hidden thought, and learn as though from the Law on the mountain, when they put aside the disturbances of temporal affairs and meditate on the judgments of the divine will. So Moses himself often withdrew to the tabernacle of the congregation in doubtful matters, asking God secretly, and learning the decisions he had to make... So in the Song of Songs, the bride who says: "I sleep, but my heart waketh" (Song 5:2) heard the voice of the bridegroom in dreams...

And since all the saints, as long as they are in this life, see the secrets of the divine nature only through likenesses (for they have not yet acquired a clearer view of it, to see it as it is), therefore, after Elihu said that God speaks to us in a dream, he rightly added: "in a vision of the night." For the night is the present life, and as long as we are in it, we are covered with a light mist of uncertain imaginings, in so far as we are concerned with inner things. He added fittingly: [slumbering upon their beds]. For to the saints slumbering upon their beds is to rest in the chambers of the mind. So it is written: [Let the saints be joyful in glory: let them rejoice upon their beds] (Ps 149:5).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* The Lord commands (man) to leave his confused life and cleave to the One, to draw near to the grace of Him who offers eternal life.

St. Clement of Alexandria * Martha was concerned to feed the Lord, while Mary was concerned that the Lord should feed her. Through Martha the feast was prepared for the Lord, this feast in which Mary rejoiced.

* I say that in these two women the two lives were represented: the present life and the life to come; the life of striving and the life of rest; the life of sorrow and the life of blessedness; the temporal life and the eternal life...

What does this life bear? I am not speaking of a wicked, evil, malicious, luxurious, ungrateful life, but a life of striving filled with sufferings and fears, whose peace trials take away... And I say that the two lives are not harmful, indeed both are worthy of praise, but one is full of toil and the other is easy...
In Martha we find a picture of present things, and in Mary the things to come.
What Martha does we do now; what Mary does we hope to do. Let us do the first work well, so that we may receive the second in its fullness.

St. Augustine * The greatest good does not lie in works in themselves, however great their importance, but in contemplation of the Lord, who is truly "the one thing"... As for his saying, "shall not be taken away from her," he revealed that the other's portion can be taken away from her, because bodily services cannot remain with man eternally, whereas Mary's longing will have no end.
Abba Moses

16 Then he openeth the ears of men, and sealeth their instruction, 17 That he may withdraw man from his purpose, and hide pride from man. 18 He keepeth back his soul from the pit, and his life from perishing by the sword.
Then he openeth the ears of men, and sealeth their instruction [16].

In the calm of the soul, far from the confusions of life, God opens the ears of man to hear, with the prophet Samuel, the divine voice that Eli the priest did not hear. In the stillness of the night Samuel lifts up his heart, saying: [Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth].

God opens the ears of man to hear what those around him do not hear. God reveals to him some of His divine secrets, uncovers the truth to him, and shows him His divine will. "And sealeth their instruction," that is, He puts a seal on His warnings and chastisements to them, meaning that they are precious in God's eyes for their benefit; He treasures them for the edification of His children, so He seals them as one who confirms them.

In ancient times contracts were sealed so that they would be kept safe, with no hand stretched out to change them. So God regards chastisement as a covenant of love between God and His children, and seals it with His heavenly seal, as though He sealed a will He had given them to enjoy an inheritance or a share of it.
God seals their instruction, that is, He promises that behind it are many blessings that cannot be revoked. Behind afflictions are sealed divine promises that do not change.
* [Then he openeth the ears of men, and their teaching, and trains them by chastisement] [16]. There are four ways by which a man is strongly moved to practice remorse:
When he remembers his sins and sees where he is.
Or when he fears the judgments of God's judgment and examines himself, and so knows where he will be.
Or when he observes carefully the evils of the present life, and grieves over where he stands.
Or when he contemplates the blessings of his heavenly homeland, which he does not yet enjoy, and grieves that he has not yet reached it.
Paul remembered his sins and grieved over what he had been, for he said: "I am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God" (1 Cor 15:9).

Again, when he carefully weighed the divine judgment, he feared lest his position should be bad in this matter, for he says: "Lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway" (1 Cor 9:27).

Again he contemplated the evils of the present life, for he said: "Whilst we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord" (2 Cor 5:6). And: "I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members. O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" (Rom 7:23-24).

He also contemplated the blessings of his heavenly homeland, for he says: "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known" (1 Cor 13:12), "For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens" (2 Cor 5:1). Looking to the blessings of this house, he says to the Ephesians: "That ye may know what is the hope of his calling, and what the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints, and what is the exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who believe, according to the working of his mighty power" (Eph 1:18-19).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
That he may withdraw man from his purpose, and hide pride from man [17].

Since man's nature has become corrupt, what occupies him is sin, and what dominates him is pride. So God allows chastisements and seals them in order to draw the believer away from his sin so that he may enjoy God's righteousness, and pride may be hidden from him lest it creep into his heart and mind, and he may live in a spirit of humility.
"Pride" is a dangerous pit into which even the religious often fall, like the Pharisees; therefore God covers the pit and fills it in, so that believers may not fall into it.

* What is man's own work, if not sin? It is rightly said, then, that when man is turned from what he does, he will be freed from pride. In disobeying the commandments of our Creator by sin, we exalt ourselves against Him. It is as though man throws off the yoke of God's authority whenever he disdains to submit to Him in obedience. On the other hand, he who wishes to avoid what he does calls to mind what he was made by God, and in humility returns to the order of his creation when he flies from his own works, and loves himself as God made him in the beginning.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
He keepeth back his soul from the pit, and his life from perishing by the sword [18].

While the wicked spend every effort to achieve their evil goals and satisfy their pride, their souls fall into the pit of pride and perish in this present world and in the age to come. But God intervenes by every means, especially by allowing chastisements, to rescue them from this eternal death.
The word "soul" refers to the whole man, for death overtakes the body as well as the soul, the whole being of man.

The word "pit, shaachat" perhaps means a trap set by hunters for wild animals to fall into (Ps 7:15; 9:15), or a hollow filled with mire (Job 9:31), or a prison (Isa 51:14), or a tomb in the shape of a great cave (Job 17:13; Ps 30:9). It is clear that what is meant here is the grave, where man's life on earth ends.

* [Rescuing his soul from corruption, and his life from perishing by the sword] [18]. For every sinner, because of his corruption here by sin, is bound to pass over to the sword of punishment, so that he is justly punished in that world with the very sins in which he delighted in this world.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

19 He is chastened also with pain upon his bed, and the multitude of his bones with strong pain: 20 So that his life abhorreth bread, and his soul dainty meat. 21 His flesh is consumed away, that it cannot be seen; and his bones that were not seen stick out. 22 Yea, his soul draweth near unto the grave, and his life to the destroyers.
He is chastened also with pain upon his bed, and the multitude of his bones with strong pain [19].

God allows sufferings to befall some of His believers so that they are confined to bed, and in this He does not seek their pain, but to restrain their desire toward sin. In moments of affliction a man rethinks his life, and is given the opportunity to think about his eternal destiny.

Elihu makes clear here that affliction is a work of chastisement for edification, which God uses in a spirit of tender fatherhood, for the repentance of His children, their return to Him, and their enjoyment of fellowship in the glories.

The bed, the couch, or the resting place indicates either bodily pleasures, or rest in the practice of good works, or temporary rest. When the Lord Christ healed the paralytic He told him to take up his bed and walk (Mt 9:6), that is, no longer to sleep in the pleasures of the body, but by the word of the Lord to carry the bed of his sickness and be rid of his sins.

Here he declares that God chastens the man who has fallen into the pleasures of the body on his bed, so that the pleasures themselves become the source of his pain and chastisement. What he thinks the secret of his joy becomes for him the cause of his sorrow.

As for the bones that stick out, they indicate in Holy Scripture the virtues, for it is written: [The Lord keepeth all their bones: not one of them is broken] (Ps 34:20). They do not indicate here the bones of the body but the powers of the mind. For many bones of the martyrs were broken, in the bodily sense, as the legs of the thief to whom it was said: "Today shalt thou be with me in paradise" (Jn 19:32; Lk 23:43) were broken. For when He chastens us through our bodily desires, the boasting in our virtues is dispelled within us, and we confess our weakness. Through chastisement we realize our weakness, and without it we count ourselves strong in the life of virtue by our own abilities.
So that his life abhorreth bread, and his soul dainty meat [20].

Among the chastisements that God uses is the permitting of illness which makes a man lose his appetite even for eating bread, for his soul loathes it; and this is a profitable chastisement for sufferers, for they no longer find pleasure in delights and luxury.
A man loathes the sumptuous foods that he used to desire, and now finds repugnant.

The psalmist says of the foolish who are humbled by their iniquities: "Their soul abhorreth all manner of meat; and they draw near unto the gates of death" (Ps 107:18). And the wise man describes the state of the dead: "And desire shall fail: because man goeth to his long home, and the mourners go about the streets" (Eccl 12:5).

After speaking of the power of divine chastisement, which lifts man from the bed of bodily pleasures and dispels his boasting in a virtuous life as though it were the work of his own hands, he says here that He makes his bread defiled in his lips, so that his life abhors bread, and his soul loathes dainty meat. What does he mean by bread and dainty meat but the pleasures in which he found a special delight that he could not do without? Through chastisement his bread turns for him into a loathsome defilement, as he realizes the vanity of bodily pleasures, and the sweetness of the dainty food turns into a bitterness he cannot bear.
His flesh is consumed away, that it cannot be seen; and his bones that were not seen stick out [21].

The body that man prized and took pride in for its beauty and strength is consumed as though it had vanished, and becomes as though it did not exist, and the bones which were hidden, clothed with flesh, stand out from extreme thinness and illness, as though they had become bare.

Pope Gregory (the Great) comments on this phrase, which in his writings is translated: "His flesh is consumed, and his bones that were covered are laid bare," that the flesh here indicates the desires of the flesh, and the bones the virtues of the soul. For through the rod of chastisement the desires of the flesh are consumed and have no authority over us, and the virtues that were hidden are uncovered, and shine forth amid the divine chastisement.

* No one learns how far he has progressed except in affliction, because in prosperity desires cannot be distinguished from spiritual strength. When the Apostles were chastised they were commanded not to speak any more in the name of Jesus. But they rejoiced greatly that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for the name of Jesus. And with confidence they answered their adversaries saying: [We ought to obey God rather than men] (see Acts 5:29). Behold, you see the power of faith shine more vividly in the midst of affliction. Behold, you see the soundness of (the desires of) the flesh cut off, and the bones of their virtues laid bare. It was said of them by Wisdom: [God proved them, and found them worthy for himself] (Wis 3:5). For when they are tested by the blasts of the adversary they are found worthy by the baring of their bones. For the strength of every man is known only in affliction.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Yea, his soul draweth near unto the grave, and his life to the destroyers [22].

Here he means that the man who has fallen into affliction becomes like one suffering severe pains that almost end his life, and he is led to the destroyers, that is, the angels of death, the angels appointed by God to take men's spirits.

* [His soul draweth near unto corruption, and his life to the destroyers] [22]. To the extent that he is led by affliction and realizes that his strength is drawing near to death, he works to find a solution, finds the true foundation of life, by flying to the protection that comes from trust in God.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
If there be a messenger with him, a mediator, one among a thousand, to shew unto man his uprightness [23].

Opinions differ in the interpretation of this phrase. It reads in the Septuagint: "If there be a thousand angels of death, not one of them can wound him mortally. If he is determined in his heart to return to the Lord, when his accusation against him appears to man and his folly is shown, He will help him so that he does not fall into death, and will renew his flesh like smooth plaster on a wall, and will fill his bones with marrow, and make his body tender like a child's." The Vulgate translation reads: "If there be an angel speaking for him, one of a thousand, to declare man's righteousness, it will weigh upon him and he will say: Deliver him who falls into corruption; I have found this one for whom I am suitable." And in the Chaldean version: "If there be found merit in him, an angel is prepared, a comforter, one among a thousand accusers, to declare to man his uprightness; I have found a ransom." 1. The first opinion: that this angel is a man. Munster and Isidore hold that he is an excellent teacher sent to the sick to teach the will of God. Junius and Termillius hold that he is a prophet. Codurcus holds that he refers here to the case of Abimelech, who was struck with sickness because of Sarah, and that the angel is a prophet sent to declare to him that God is righteous (Gen 20). Umbreit holds that the angel here is Elihu himself, whom God sent to Job to declare the truth concerning the divine dispensation and the mystery of allowing sorrows to befall men. Others hold that the speech here concerns the faithful servant of God who visits the sick and the suffering and declares to them God's plan, without naming a particular person. 2. The second opinion: that the speech concerns God's sending His angels to declare His will to men, especially to sufferers, and to assure them that God wants to show them His mercy if they return to Him in repentance. St. Jerome, for example, holds that the speech here refers to an angel standing in God's presence, whose work is to guide mankind and set its affairs right. 3. The third opinion: that the speech here is a prophecy about the person of the Lord Christ, and among those who proclaimed this opinion is St. Augustine.
* Who is this messenger (angel), but he whom the prophet called: "the Angel of Counsel, the Mighty"?

* Our Physician from above, since He found us under the weight of many diseases like this... came to us as man, but as righteous to those who are in sin. He agreed with us in the truth of His nature (His humanity), and differed from us in the power of His righteousness.

A sinful man cannot be set right except by God. But it was necessary that He (Christ) who accomplishes his healing should be visible and perceived by the senses, in order that He might set right our former evil life by setting before us a pattern to imitate. It was not possible for God to be seen by man. Therefore He became man in order to be seen. The holy, invisible God appeared as a visible man like us, so that, appearing as one like us, He might teach us by His holiness and put an end to our sickness by the power of His skill...

Since there was in Him no admixture of sin, He was not subject to any punishment as a matter of necessity. He subdued our transgression by overcoming it. He submitted to our punishment because of His compassion for us, and as He Himself says: [I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again] (see Jn 10:18). Again, He did not rise like other men, for our resurrection will be accomplished at the end of the world, but His resurrection was celebrated on the third day. We indeed rise by Him, but He rises by Himself.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Then he is gracious unto him, and saith, Deliver him from going down to the pit: I have found a ransom [24].

As Elihu refers to the Mediator, our Lord Jesus Christ, he speaks of His role in the salvation of man and his enjoyment of redemption, rescuing him from descending into the abyss of the kingdom of darkness, and giving him eternal life instead of eternal destruction.

* He will be gracious to him, and say: [Deliver him from going down to corruption: I have found a way to his ransom] [24]. The Mediator between God and man, the man Christ Jesus, since He took the form of a man. In His compassion His Father says on behalf of the man who is saved: [Deliver him from going down to corruption].

We are set free by the righteousness of the Almighty Savior, as He Himself says: "If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed" (Jn 8:36). It is well said on behalf of this redeemed man: [His soul draweth near unto corruption] (see Job 33:22), and now he declares that he does not go down to corruption. It is as though he says: Since he realizes, through the sense of his weakness, that he is not far from corruption, therefore may he not go down to the death of corruption, for he truly goes down to corruption if he counts himself by his own strength to have gone far from it. But since he draws near in humility, he must be received with mercy. For as he confessed his weakness by nature, he is strengthened against the sins that wrestle with him. For he who boasts of himself beyond what he is goes down by the weight of his pride, and sinks to greater depths...
Since the Lord took weakness upon Himself and bore our punishment by His death, He restored our corruption by His resurrection.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

"Deliver him" is the literal translation of the Hebrew word "redeem him," that is, to rescue a person by a ransom or by paying a price on his behalf. The Greek word means paying a price or a ransom, and it is used in (Mt 20:28): "The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many."

The speech here is a clear prophecy of the eternal redemption whose price the Lord Christ paid with His precious blood. As the Apostle Paul says: "Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood he entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us" (Heb 9:12).

"I have found a ransom": our Lord Jesus has found this redemption. The expression "found" points to His burning zeal for the salvation of the world, His faithfulness, His joy, and His striving for the salvation of man. He works like one who searches until he finds, and then rejoices!
"Go after that which is lost, until he find it. And when he hath found it, he layeth it on his shoulders, rejoicing" (Lk 15:4-5).
"Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost" (Lk 15:6).
"What woman... if she lose one piece... seek diligently till she find it" (Lk 15:8).
[Rejoice with me; for I have found the piece which I had lost] (Lk 15:9).
"I have found David my servant; with my holy oil have I anointed him" (Ps 89:20).

* The Mediator between God and man, the man Christ Jesus, shows mercy to man, having taken the form of a man. Through His tenderness He says to His Father on behalf of the man who is saved: [Deliver him from going down to corruption]...

entries.section: 4. The sweetness of enjoying God's salvation

paragraphs.text: 25 His flesh shall be fresher than a child's: he shall return to the days of his youth. 26 He shall pray unto God, and he will be favourable unto him: and he shall see his face with joy: for he will render unto man his righteousness. 27 He shall sing among men, and say, I have sinned, and perverted that which was right, and it profited me not. 28 He will deliver his soul from going into the pit, and his life shall see the light. 29 "Lo, all these things worketh God oftentimes with man, 30 To bring back his soul from the pit, to be enlightened with the light of the living.
His flesh shall be fresher (more flourishing) than a child's: he shall return to the days of his youth [25].

When Elihu spoke of Christ the Redeemer, he lifted our eyes from tribulations, sorrows, and sicknesses to what we enjoy through this wonderful redemption. Instead of speaking about sicknesses, Elihu marvels as he sees, in the spirit of prophecy, the man who was descending toward eternal destruction not only enjoying health, but his body becoming fresher than the body of a child, changed from the state of helpless old age to strong youth, full of vitality and energy.

Through redemption he enjoys a new birth, and the believer becomes a new creation after the image of his Creator. He becomes a son of God in the waters of Baptism, by his union with the Only-Begotten Son. He becomes a new Naaman, of whom it was said: "Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God: and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean" (2 Kgs 5:14). The saying of the Lord Christ to Nicodemus is fulfilled in him: "Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God. That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit" (Jn 3:5-6).

* [His flesh was consumed by punishments, that it may return to the days of his youth] [25]. When the first man fell from the presence of God, we were driven out from the delights of Paradise and bound to the miseries of this perishable life. And we feel the pain of our punishment, how grave is the fault we committed through the serpent's deception. For having fallen into this state, we find nothing outside God but sorrow... We suffer daily sorrow in the flesh, with its torment and death. Therefore the Lord, by His wonderful dispensation, changes what befell us through our commission of sin, by means of punishment....

[His flesh was consumed by punishments, that it may return to the days of his youth]. It is as though he said: Through the punishment of death (the death of man) he has sunk down in his old age; let him return to the days of his youth, that is, let him be renewed to the fullness of his former life, and not remain in the state into which he fell, but by his salvation return to the delights of the state in which he was originally created... Since we were brought to this power of new life not by our own strength but by the Savior, may the Messenger (the Lord Christ) say in His mediation for this man who is under punishment: [Let him return to the days of his youth].
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 4. The sweetness of enjoying God's salvation

paragraphs.text: He shall pray unto God, and he will be favourable unto him: and he shall see his face with joy: for he will render unto man his righteousness [26].

By this new birth the believer enters into a relationship with God, as a son who has boldness before his father. He prays, confesses, praises, and gives thanks, offering sweet incense that God smells as a fragrance of delight and acceptance, by virtue of the sacrifice of Christ. He looks to God his Father with joy of heart, seeing His face with shouting and rejoicing. He does not fear meeting Him, for he knows the truth of the reconciliation accomplished by the Cross.
God pours out on His believers the fruits of the Spirit in abundance, so that they bear the icon of Christ and His righteousness.

Thus Elihu moves us from crying out because of sorrows to shouting as sons of the heavenly Father, bearing the new nature crowned with glory, enjoying the sight of God's face, sharing with the heavenly beings in their praises and shouts, and being covered by the righteousness of Christ, which we put on as a radiant heavenly garment.

* [He shall pray unto God, and he will be favourable unto him]. He says that the Messenger (the propitiating Intercessor) intercedes first and then man. For if the Lord had not interceded with His Father through His incarnation and prayed for our life, our living stiffness could not have been moved to seek the eternal things... But because the light of truth bursts forth with hidden joy in our hearts after trials, often after great sorrows, it is rightly added concerning this man who has been tried and who pleads with God: "And he shall see his face with joy" [25]. It was said earlier how God works by revealing Himself to us; here it shows how He delights us when He makes Himself known.

Thus Jacob, after his struggle with the angel, said: "I have seen God face to face" (Gen 32:30), as one who says: {I know the Lord because He Himself condescends to make me know Him}. But Paul declares that this knowledge will be accomplished in its utmost perfection at the end, where he says: "then shall I know even as also I am known" (1 Cor 13:12). After the struggle in toils and the waves of trials, the soul is often carried away rejoicing as it contemplates the knowledge of the divine presence (which it can sense but cannot enjoy in its fullness). Therefore it is rightly said of this man who has been tried after many toils: "He shall see his face with joy" [26]. The more a man contemplates divine things, the more he is repaid for his earthly deeds by the grace of contemplation; therefore it is fitting that it be added for his works: "for he will render unto man his righteousness" [26].

It is called "our righteousness" not as though it were from ourselves, but because it has become ours by divine gift, as we say in the Lord's Prayer: [Give us this day our daily bread](b). Behold, we call it "our bread" although we pray that we may receive it. It becomes ours when we receive it, but it belongs to God, because it is He who gives it.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
He shall sing among men, and say:

entries.section: 4. The sweetness of enjoying God's salvation

paragraphs.text: I have sinned, and perverted that which was right, and it profited me not [27].

The phrase in the Hebrew is "he sings among men," and the translations of the Hebrew word Shiyr שִׁיר, meaning "to sing," differ. Man is transformed from his crying out under the intensity of the trials and sufferings that befell him into rejoicing and praising, singing of the grace of this Mediator who redeemed him, renewed his nature by His Holy Spirit, and granted him eternal life. He sinned and perverted the straight way, but grace covered him, so he received forgiveness and was not repaid for his past.

Some have seen that the Hebrew word is derived from שׁוּר Shuwr, meaning "to look around" or "to regard" or "to observe." Therefore the English translation (KJ*) came: [He looketh upon men, and if any say, I have sinned, and perverted that which was right, and it profited me not]. This phrase seems to point to the divine Mediator, the Savior of the world, who looks upon corrupted humanity; if anyone confesses that he has sinned and has spoiled what is good of the abilities and possibilities, and of the mercies and blessings given to him by the Savior, and that this has not profited him at all, the Savior will work in him.
Whether under the pressure of trials or in the enjoyment of seeing the Mediator, if anyone confesses the sins and crookedness of his conduct, he enjoys the divine mercies.

In this Elihu presents to us his view of trials as discipline from the Lord, whose aim is that man may return to himself, discover his faults, and feel his need of the Redeemer, and so enjoy the divine mercies.

By saying "perverted that which was right," he may mean: I misjudged God's plan toward me. Trials are permitted me for the uprightness of my life, but because of the corruption of my heart I looked upon them as an injustice that had befallen me. For this reason "it profited me not" or "I was not repaid for it." The fault is not in the coming of trials but in my not profiting from them because of my murmuring against the Lord, and I reckoned that I did not deserve all these harsh sufferings.

* [He looketh upon men, and saith, I have sinned] [27]. He could not have known that he was a sinner if righteousness had not come to him. For no one discovers his faults unless he has begun to be upright. One who is wholly deformed cannot perceive the truth about himself. But the one who feels that he is a sinner has already, to some degree, begun to become upright. Being upright, he blames his conduct where he is still not righteous. And by accusing himself he begins to cleave to God. And as he passes on to accusing himself in truth, he condemns himself in what he perceives does not please God.
But if a sinner looks at himself without having learned the character of the righteous man, he cannot by any means perceive that he is a sinner...
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the believer, as he looks upon men (the saints), reads in their lives as in an open book, and so perceives that he is a sinner and offers repentance so that he may live in the righteousness of Christ. In his comment on this phrase he says: [The lives of the righteous are a living study; therefore it is not without merit that the righteous are called "books" in the language of Scripture, as it is written: "And the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works"

(Rev 2:12)... To acquire the knowledge of heavenly things we study the examples of the saints who went before us. It is said that they feed among the lilies (see Song 4:5-6). For what is meant by the lilies but the conduct of those who say in all sincerity: "For we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ" (2 Cor 2:15)... For as long as we pass through the shadows of this perishable life until we reach the dawn of the eternal day, we need to be nourished by the examples of the righteous.]

* [He looketh upon men, and saith, I have sinned, and perverted that which was right, and it profited me not, as I deserved] [27]. Even those who do not believe that they sin confess in a general way that they are sinners. So it is with men. They often confess openly that they are sinners, but when they hear someone truthfully mention their sins when they attack them, they boldly defend themselves and seek to show themselves innocent. Whoever has this character, when he says that he sins, does not speak the truth; he declares himself a sinner, but not from the depth of his heart, only uttering words, because it is written: [The righteous man is first in his own cause] (see Prov 18:17). He wishes to gain a good reputation, not to be humbled by confessing his sin. By accusing himself he desires to appear humble while he is not so... But the righteous man, when he accuses himself for his conduct, knows the depth of his heart, through the examples of the saints, that he is truly as he confesses. And in pain he completes: that he was not repaid as he deserved.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 4. The sweetness of enjoying God's salvation

paragraphs.text: He will deliver his soul from going into the pit, and his life shall see the light [28].

This is the song of those who come out of the great tribulation (Rev 7:14), as they praise God for His surpassing mercies, who lifted them from the pit of hell to the heavenly Jerusalem, and brought them across from the kingdom of darkness to dwell in His bosom forever in the divine light. As it was said of the heavenly Jerusalem: [And the city had no need of the sun, neither of the moon, to shine in it: for the glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb is the light thereof] (Rev 21:23).

* [He will deliver his soul from going into destruction] [28]. When divine grace goes before us in good works, our free will follows it, and when we submit our consent to God who saves us, it is said of us that we redeem our own souls. Paul says: "I laboured more abundantly than they all" (1 Cor 15:10). And fearing that he might ascribe his labors to himself, he immediately added: "yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me." For since by his free will he followed the grace of God that went before him and protected him, he truly added: "which was with me," so that he might not be ungrateful for the divine grace, nor remain estranged from being made fit for free will...
"And his life shall see the light" [28], meaning the light of truth which he could not see when he was dead in his heart, or it means the Lord who said: "I am the light of the world" (Jn 8:12)...
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 4. The sweetness of enjoying God's salvation

paragraphs.text: Lo, all these things worketh God oftentimes with man [29].

Some translate "twice and thrice" as "many times," meaning that God does not cease to work for salvation once, twice, and thrice, and by every means, in order to draw the wicked to salvation, that they may enjoy sonship to Him and revel in His righteousness, His holiness, and His heavens.
Some see that Elihu mentions "thrice" as an indication of God's work with sinners, in which He uses three ways:

First He pours out good things in abundance, that man may be touched by the love of the Giver; if he does not return to God, He uses divine inspirations, whether through dreams, visions, or divine revelation; if he does not return, He uses sorrows and tribulations so that he may reconsider his life and realize the truth of his position.

* [Lo, all these things worketh God thrice with every man] [29]... If we observe carefully, we shall find that there are three stages of sorrow and joy, one following the other, in his conversion, in his trial, and in his death.

In the first occasion, his conversion... man's sorrow is great, because he takes his sins into account, and desires to cast off forcefully the bonds of worldly cares and to walk in the way of God throughout the period of his conversion. He wishes to remove the weight of heavy temporal disturbances in order to bear the easy yoke of the Lord. It is a bondage that bears freedom... But then comes pain of heart and its turmoil, as the Spirit calls from one side and the flesh calls him from the opposite side... Rightly it is said of this embittered man: "So that his life abhorreth bread, and his soul dainty meat. His soul draweth near unto the grave, and his life to the destroyers" [see 2, 22]. But divine grace does not allow us to be exposed to these hardships for a long time. It looses the bonds of our sins and leads us quickly to the consolations of the freedom of our new life. The joy that follows removes the former sorrow. And so the mind of the one who is converted rejoices very much more than it desires...

And lest man think that he is a saint, immediately upon his conversion... he is permitted by God's dispensation to suffer the assaults of trials. By his conversion he crosses the Red Sea, but the enemies continue to oppose him in the wilderness of this present life. We have left our past sins behind us, as the Egyptians died on the shore, but destructive vices still attack us like new enemies to obstruct our way by which we enter the Promised Land... Our enemy is more zealous against our victory as long as we are in this life, the more he perceives that we are rebelling against him. He does not care that he strikes those whom he knows to be in his possession. Rather, he is in a state of greater fury against us, since he has been driven out of our hearts, as though it were his right to possess us as a dwelling for himself... Truly there are three stages for the converted: the beginning, the middle, and the end. In the beginning they experience the charm of sweetness, in the middle the resistance of trials, and at the end the fullness of perfection...

After passing through these two stages, conversion and testing, in sorrow and joy, the third stage remains, whose sorrows he still fears, but whose delights he receives... David says: [And enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified] (Ps 143:2). And Paul says after that: "For I know nothing by myself; yet am I not hereby justified" (1 Cor 4:4). James says: "In many things we offend all" (Jas 3:2), and John says: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us" (1 Jn 1:8)
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 4. The sweetness of enjoying God's salvation

paragraphs.text: To bring back his soul from the pit, to be enlightened with the light of the living [30].

Elihu here confirms what he had pointed out earlier as a song that man sings in enjoying God's salvation (Job 33:28): that it is a gift offered to every man without partiality, for God is "not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance" (2 Pet 3:9). So every believer sings: "For thou hast delivered my soul from death: wilt not thou deliver my feet from falling, that I may walk before God in the light of the living?" (Ps 56:13).

* Because the mind of every elect person suffers in each of these three stages, that is, the pain of conversion, the trials of testing, or the horror of dissolution, and is purified and set free by that very pain, it was said: [To bring back his soul from corruption, to be enlightened with the light of the living] [30].

For this is the light of the dead, which we behold with our bodily eyes... But those who are enlightened by the light of the living despise the light of the world and return to the height of the inner splendor, so that they may live in that place where they see and feel the true light, where there is no difference between life and light, for where there is light there is life also...
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 5. An appeal to Job to listen to him

paragraphs.text: 31 Mark well, O Job, hearken unto me: hold thy peace, and I will speak. 32 If thou hast any thing to say, answer me: speak, for I desire to justify thee. 33 If not, hearken unto me: hold thy peace, and I shall teach thee wisdom."
Mark well, O Job, hearken unto me:
hold thy peace, and I will speak [31].

Elihu asks Job to examine deeply what he has said and to listen with very close attention to what he is about to say. He has much to say, a matter that touches Job's life, which deserves that he be longsuffering and patient in earnest, to listen to what Elihu will say to him.
If thou hast any thing to say, answer me.

entries.section: 5. An appeal to Job to listen to him

paragraphs.text: Speak, for I desire to justify thee [32].
Before Elihu continues his speech, which comes in the next chapter, he wanted to pause thoughtfully, asking Job to answer him or to offer his comments on what he has said.

Here Elihu's calmness stands out. Although he exaggerated in accusing Job, he stops to hear his comments in a good spirit. For his aim is neither to rebuke nor to heap accusations, but to open the door of salvation and righteousness so that Job may be justified before God. So it is fitting for us in our preaching to realize the truth of our message: not criticism and rebuke, but support and tenderness together with frankness and without flattery. Elihu had already said to Job that he too was formed out of the same clay, and that both of them need the Savior who helps. And the Apostle Peter says in his preaching to the first Gentile: "I myself also am a man" (Acts 10:26).

A man does not need someone to terrify him, but someone who is tender and gentle with him, and who makes him feel that he is a companion with him in human weakness, and needs with him the divine help.

In humility, love, and tenderness Elihu asks Job, if he has any objection or asks for clarification, to speak freely, for he wishes to explain in love all that is in his mind for the sake of Job's justification.
Just as Elihu asked Job to listen with longsuffering and patience to what Elihu has said and will say, he also declares his own readiness to listen with an open heart and longsuffering.

By saying "I desire to justify thee," Elihu feared that he might have misunderstood Job's statements, or attributed to him words with meanings that Job did not intend; therefore he gives him the opportunity to speak frankly.
If not, hearken unto me.

entries.section: 5. An appeal to Job to listen to him

paragraphs.text: Hold thy peace, and I shall teach thee wisdom [33].
If Job has nothing with which to object to Elihu's words, the latter demands that he listen to him and pay attention, and he will teach him wisdom.
Since Job kept silent, and none of the three friends intervened, Elihu wanted to continue his speech (as it comes in the next chapter).
Let my soul sing aloud to You,

entries.section: 1. A call to those present to listen

paragraphs.text: 1 Furthermore Elihu answered and said, 2 "Hear my words, O ye wise men; and give ear unto me, ye that have knowledge. 3 For the ear trieth words, as the mouth tasteth meat. 4 Let us choose to us judgment: let us know among ourselves what is good.
Furthermore Elihu answered and said: [1]

"Answered": this does not mean that someone asked and Elihu answered him. Scripture is accustomed to begin speeches with this word, "answered," even if no one has spoken before, as in (Job 3:2; Isa 14:10; Zech 1:10; 3:4; 4:11-12). Sometimes this word is used to express an answer to a hidden question in the mind of another person, an opponent, who has not disclosed it openly.

entries.section: 1. A call to those present to listen

paragraphs.text: Hear my words, O ye wise men; and give ear unto me, ye that have knowledge [2].

In the previous chapter Elihu addressed his speech to Job, answering his questions about sorrows and tribulations, explaining that they are by God's permission for the benefit of believers, since the believer is given the opportunity to withdraw into himself, discover his faults, and seek the one divine Mediator. Job did not answer him, nor did he comment on his words. Now he addresses his speech particularly to his three friends, calling them wise, men who have been given knowledge. In this he wanted to prepare them to listen to him attentively and without hostility. Perhaps he looked upon them as truly wise, able to follow his words and his explanation of some difficult matters.

entries.section: 1. A call to those present to listen

paragraphs.text: For the ear trieth words, as the mouth tasteth meat [3].

Elihu calls us to have a spirit of discernment. As the mouth tastes food and distinguishes what is good from what is spoiled, so it is fitting for our ears to separate good words from evil ones. Here he speaks to those present, especially the three friends, and he speaks not only of the inner ears but also of the bodily ears, so that believers may not leave the doors of their ears open to receive all words without discrimination.

Just as we shall be judged for an idle word that wastes our time, we must be on guard against every word we hear, and flee as far as we can from listening not only to what is evil but also to what is vain and useless.

Many of the Fathers see that negligence in listening to the dissolute or to heretics may corrupt the purity of the soul and the uprightness of faith. Therefore it is fitting for the believer to test what is said and not allow his ears to listen without discernment.
"Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?" (2 Cor 13:5).
"Prove all things; hold fast that which is good" (1 Thess 5:21).
"Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world" (1 Jn 4:1).
"Do nothing without discretion" (Sir 33:30).
"To another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discerning of spirits; to another divers kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of tongues" (1 Cor 12:10).
"But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil" (Heb 5:14).
* "Be not carried about with divers and strange doctrines" (Heb 13:9). This is the meaning of discerning between good and evil. [The mouth tastes food, but the soul tests words] (see Job 34:3).
St. John Chrysostom * Discernment is better than all the virtues.

The Spiritual Elder * [Lord, by thy favour thou hast made my mountain to stand strong] (Ps 30:7)... Some ask about the results of virtue... Some say that every virtue has a cause (reason), while others reject this explanation... For example, the aim or cause of wisdom is to distinguish between good and evil... and by discernment we are able to choose and to refuse, and by justice we perceive what we ought to give and what we ought not to give... by courage we perceive what we ought to fear and what we ought not to fear... As for the virtues of beauty and strength, they have no cause... rather their value comes from other virtues that have a cause... For the wise perceive what beauty is through the harmony and order within their souls... and they perceive strength through the practical carrying out of theoretical virtue.

St. Basil the Great * My son, do not speak in anger, but let your speech be with wisdom and knowledge, and likewise your silence, because the speech of our wise fathers was full of wisdom and discernment, and likewise their silence.

entries.section: 1. A call to those present to listen

paragraphs.text: St. Anthony the Great * Let us choose to us judgment: let us know among ourselves what is good [4].
Let us test matters for ourselves, not concerned with the praise of others; what occupies us is to reach the truth, to know the facts, and to strive to find what is good.

It is fitting for the believer to strive to discover what is true, what is just, and what belongs to the sons, amid conflicting opinions and concepts, testing everything with seriousness and sincerity, without partiality to his own opinions or the opinions of those who love him.

St. John Chrysostom sees that it is fitting for us to examine ourselves, listening to the voice of the Lord Christ who is within us, as well as to His voice in the holy Church through our Church teachers.
* Look within yourselves, and you will find Christ in you. But if Christ is in you, how much more is He in your teacher.

St. John Chrysostom * If we do not know how one is to examine another, we do not know whether Christ is in us or not. Failure to practice examination is ignorance of the faith inherited in the declaration of our faith. Whoever has the sense of faith in his heart knows that Jesus Christ is in him.

Ambrosiaster * As in ancient Israel there were some prophets who spoke the word of God and others who did not, so too, as soon as the apostles appeared speaking in Christ and having the Holy Spirit whom the Lord sent to them, Satan sent many false apostles who falsified the teaching of the Gospel. It is vital that you have the gift of the Holy Spirit that is called the discerning of spirits, so that you may test the spirits and see what you must believe and what you must reject.

St. Didymus the Blind * We must observe this threefold matter with all care: let us examine the thoughts that attack us with insight and wisdom, so that we may know the source of the thought and its causes from its beginning. In this way we can consider whether we should yield to it, according to the kind of one who proposes it, and so be like the wise money-changers, as the Lord teaches us. By their skill and experience they distinguish the pure gold that has been purified by fire as it ought to be, and by their skill they are not deceived by pieces of copper coated with a thin layer of gold which appear to be of great value... By their intelligence and skill they perfectly recognize the counterfeit coins minted by the great deceivers...

So we must first examine with all care every thought that enters our hearts and every teaching that we receive, to see whether it has been purified by the fire of the divine, heavenly Holy Spirit, or belongs to the error of the heretics, or is the fruit of the pride of human philosophy, which has nothing but the outward appearance of religion.

We can do this if we walk by the counsel of the Apostle who says: "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God..." (1 Jn 4:1). Some are deceived by this kind of thing, enticed by fine arrangement and by philosophical teachings that deceive at first glance with some pious meanings that agree with religion, just as the gleam of gold deceives the eyes. Appearances attract these people, but they soon feel that in fact they have come away empty-handed, and they fall into despair, like those who have been deceived by counterfeit copper coins.
Abba Moses

entries.section: 2. A reply to Job's justifying himself

paragraphs.text: 5 "For Job hath said, I am righteous: and God hath taken away my judgment. 6 Should I lie against my right? my wound is incurable without transgression. 7 What man is like Job, who drinketh up scorning like water? 8 Which goeth in company with the workers of iniquity, and walketh with wicked men. 9 For he hath said, It profiteth a man nothing that he should delight himself with God. 10 "Therefore hearken unto me, ye men of understanding: far be it from God, that he should do wickedness; and from the Almighty, that he should commit iniquity. 11 For the work of a man shall he render unto him, and cause every man to find according to his ways. 12 Yea, surely God will not do wickedly, neither will the Almighty pervert judgment.
For Job hath said:
I am righteous: and God hath taken away my judgment [5].

These words came in Job (Job 13:18; 27:2), but he said them to clear himself, because his friends had attacked him personally, so he wanted to affirm his innocence of the false accusations, without meaning that he was justified before God or that he was free from error. He never hinted that he was always pure of heart or that he never sinned against the law of his Creator. He truly said that God had taken away his judgment, but he never meant that he wished to take God to court, accusing Him of injustice; rather, what he meant was that God was dealing with him in a secret, mysterious way, and not as he had been accustomed to feel in his relationship with Him before, in terms of His surpassing divine providence. What was mysterious to him was not the trials that had befallen him, but how He allowed his friends to stumble over him.

Job had confessed his sins, but he bears a relative righteousness when compared with his brothers in humanity, not when compared with God. For it has been said: "For there is not a just man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not" (Eccl 7:20).
* I know no man perfect in anything... being still a man, except the One who alone for our sake put on our humanity.

St. Clement of Alexandria * God is good, perfectly good alone, and since you are His image, it is fitting for you to be good. He is generous to all, so you ought to be generous, avoiding greed, and not withholding from your neighbor anything material and transitory, for this is the gravest disaster and folly.
Father John of Kronstadt * First return to yourself from what is outside you; then present yourself again to Him who created you. For He is the source of all our happiness and perfect goodness.
St. Augustine * Should I lie against my right?

entries.section: 2. A reply to Job's justifying himself

paragraphs.text: My wound is incurable without transgression [6].
Perhaps Job is asking: Should he lie and accuse himself of evil as his friends think, and so become a liar against his declaration of innocence of what they ascribed to him?

He cries out, for his wound has become incurable though he committed no iniquity. They accused him of being the worst criminal and treated him in the most terrible way, although God Himself testified to his perfection, and that Satan had incited Him against him without cause (Job 1:1; 2:3).
By his wound here he means the calamities that befell him, which seemed incurable, with no remedy for them and no possibility of mending the situation.

The picture here is that Job is like an animal struck by a deadly arrow through no fault of its own. What Job complains of is not that he is without sin, but of the calamities that have befallen him, which completely distorted his image, especially in the minds of his friends.

entries.section: 2. A reply to Job's justifying himself

paragraphs.text: What man is like Job, who drinketh up scorning like water? [7]

Some see that this proverb suits the ancient desert environment, as it likens the man to a camel that drinks a huge quantity of water that enables it not to feel thirst for a long time during its journey in the dry wilderness. So Job drank huge quantities of trials, whose effect continues throughout his whole journey here in the wilderness of this world.
Eliphaz cited a similar phrase when accusing Job (Job 15:16).

entries.section: 2. A reply to Job's justifying himself

paragraphs.text: Which goeth in company with the workers of iniquity, and walketh with wicked men? [8]

Elihu reckoned Job a companion of the wicked, because he bore thoughts like theirs in his complaint with God (Job 9:22-23, 30; 21:7-15), at least in saying that those who do evil are not punished. It seems as though he denied God's justice because of his not knowing what lay behind the tribulations that befell him while they did not befall the wicked, so Elihu counted him as one who by his thoughts befriended the wicked.

entries.section: 2. A reply to Job's justifying himself

paragraphs.text: For he hath said, It profiteth a man nothing that he should delight himself with God [9].

Since Job adopted this thought in the bitterness of his soul, saying that there is no profit in serving God, and that a man's walking in righteousness profits him nothing, because God does not defend the righteous against those who oppose them, Elihu therefore reckoned Job to be in friendship with the wicked.
Therefore hearken unto me, ye men of understanding.

entries.section: 2. A reply to Job's justifying himself

paragraphs.text: Far be it from God, that he should do wickedness; and from the Almighty, that he should commit iniquity [10].

Elihu calls those present to listen to his answer to what he thought were mistaken concepts on Job's part, showing that Job used improper expressions in his complaint with God concerning His judgments.

"Ye men of understanding": the Hebrew word means "hearts," for the Jews considered the heart to be the center of all mental processes and their throne. They did not speak of the mind or the head as the throne of mental processes. So Elihu reckons those present to be wise, and able to grasp the thought he presents concerning God's righteousness and justice in His judgments.
Elihu wants to affirm that far be it from God to err or to do evil.

Elihu says: We must not place God's actions on human scales, so that we sometimes accuse Him of injustice. Rather, it is fitting for us to trust that all God's ways are true and just, because they are His ways and He is holy, and not because we see them so.
"What shall we say then? Is there unrighteousness with God? God forbid" (Rom 9:14).

"That be far from thee to do after this manner, to slay the righteous with the wicked: and that the righteous should be as the wicked, that be far from thee: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?" (Gen 18:25).
"He is the Rock, his work is perfect: for all his ways are judgment: a God of truth and without iniquity, just and right is he" (Deut 32:4).
"Righteous art thou, O Lord, and all thy judgments are right, and all thy ways mercy and truth and judgment" (Tob 3:2).
"God judgeth the righteous, and God is angry with the wicked every day" (Ps 7:11).
"For the righteous Lord loveth righteousness; his countenance doth behold the upright" (Ps 11:7).
"The fear of the Lord is clean, enduring for ever: the judgments of the Lord are true and righteous altogether" (Ps 19:9).
"The righteousness of thy testimonies is everlasting: give me understanding, and I shall live" (Ps 119:144).
"Seeing then that thou art righteous thyself, thou orderest all things righteously: thinking it not agreeable with thy power to condemn him that hath not deserved to be punished" (Wis 12:15).
"Therefore the Lord hath watched over us for evil, and the Lord hath brought it upon us: for the Lord is righteous in all his works which he hath commanded us" (Bar 2:9).
"For thou art just in all that thou hast done, and all thy works are true, and thy ways right, and all thy judgments truth" (Additions to Dan 3:27).
"The just Lord is in the midst thereof; he will not do iniquity: every morning doth he bring his judgment to light, he faileth not; but the unjust knoweth no shame" (Zeph 3:5).
"And this is what Nehemiah prayed: O Lord, Lord God, Creator of all things, who art fearful and strong, and righteous, and merciful, and the only and gracious King" (2 Macc 1:24).
"The only giver of all things, the only just, almighty, and eternal, thou that deliverest Israel from all trouble, and didst choose the fathers, and sanctify them" (2 Macc 1:25).
"And I heard the angel of the waters say, Thou art righteous, O Lord, which art, and wast, and shalt be, because thou hast judged thus" (Rev 16:5).
"And I heard another out of the altar say, Even so, Lord God Almighty, true and righteous are thy judgments" (Rev 16:7).
"For true and righteous are his judgments: for he hath judged the great whore, which did corrupt the earth with her fornication, and hath avenged the blood of his servants at her hand" (Rev 19:2).

* If He whom you call Father is our Judge, and if He is no respecter of persons, then let us hasten and give all diligence during our journey here on earth, in all fear and holy conduct... By this we know that this same Father is the One who gives us the promises, and He is the One who keeps us without any punishment.

St. Didymus the Blind * God is a righteous, strong, and longsuffering Judge. Do you not understand why He does not punish although He is able and ready? He says: Learn that He is longsuffering, and does not give vent to His anger every day. Behold, you see that, lest some fool think that God holds back out of weakness, He shows that the reason for His delay is His very wide longsuffering. I mean that He is longsuffering in order to lead you to repentance, and if you do not benefit from this remedy, He will take action also. Be sure that we deserve punishment every day... Does a day pass without our praying with indifference and a dangerous distraction of mind?

St. John Chrysostom * Those who forsake God, despise His commandments, and bring shame on their Creator by their deeds and by their thoughts that blaspheme the One who sustains them, gather just judgment against themselves.

entries.section: 2. A reply to Job's justifying himself

paragraphs.text: St. Irenaeus * For the work of a man shall he render unto him, and cause every man to find according to his ways [11].
God always acts with justice; He will not forget the righteous, nor allow the wicked to prosper in the end. He will deal with every man according to his deserving.

He did not mean by this that he judges Job to be wicked because of what has befallen him, as his three friends accused him, but he thinks he is correcting an obscure or mistaken concept of Job that he expressed in the bitterness of his soul.

Let us wait, for God will reward the righteous and also repay the wicked if they persist in their evils, at the proper time. The Lord said of the wicked king Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah: [They shall not lament for him, saying, Ah my brother! or, Ah sister! they shall not lament for him, saying, Ah lord! or, Ah his glory! He shall be buried with the burial of an ass, drawn and cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem] (Jer 22:18-19). It was also said: "But after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God; who will render to every man according to his deeds" (Rom 2:5-6). "And if ye call on the Father, who without respect of persons judgeth according to every man's work, pass the time of your sojourning here in fear" (1 Pet 1:17). "And, behold, I come quickly; and my reward is with me, to give every man according to his work shall be" (Rev 22:12).

* Why does God not punish all men with mercy in such a way that He allows no one to harden himself against Him? (This question arises) because of the evil to which those who have become hardened have qualified themselves, or because of God's mysterious judgments, which are often hidden but will never be unjust.

entries.section: 2. A reply to Job's justifying himself

paragraphs.text: Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles * Yea, surely God will not do wickedly, neither will the Almighty pervert judgment [12].

Elihu repeats this principle, affirming that God does no evil, and speaking of it at length. Under all circumstances this principle cannot be breached, not even for a single moment. He found fault with Job because, although he embraced the same principle, under the pressure of intense sufferings he thought that God could err in His judgment, so that injustice would take the place of justice (Job 34:5; 8:3).

The Lord said to Satan: "Thou movedst me against him, to destroy him without cause" (Job 2:3). And as Pope Gregory (the Great) says, God may allow sorrows without a cause (that man deserves), but He will not condemn him without a cause.
God allows His righteous ones sorrows for their purification or their approval, but He does not allow them sorrows on the Day of Judgment.
* You will obtain the world of light in place of a bitter pain that you bear for Him for one day.
If you endure hunger a little for His love's sake, then your desire to see His face will be kindled.
If darkness appears on your face from the works done for Him, He will adorn you with His glory forever without end.
If you strip yourself of what is yours, He will clothe you with His light, and hide from you what is yours.
If you leave what you possess, you will possess it in yourself eternally.
The Spiritual Elder (John of Dalyatha)
* The evils that come upon you will pass, and what you wait for with patience will come.
He will wipe away the sweat of toil. He will dry every tear, and there will be no more weeping.
Here below we must groan amid trials, as Job asks: [Is there not an appointed time to man upon earth?] (Job 7:1).
St. Augustine

13 Who hath given him a charge over the earth? or who hath disposed the whole world? 14 If he set his heart upon man, if he gather unto himself his spirit and his breath; 15 All flesh shall perish together, and man shall turn again unto dust. 16 If now thou hast understanding, hear this: hearken to the voice of my words. 17 Shall even he that hateth right govern? and wilt thou condemn him that is most just? 18 Is it fit to say to a king, Thou art wicked? and to princes, Ye are ungodly? 19 How much less to him that accepteth not the persons of princes, nor regardeth the rich more than the poor? for they all are the work of his hands. 20 In a moment shall they die, and the people shall be troubled at midnight, and pass away: and the mighty shall be taken away without hand. 21 For his eyes are upon the ways of man, and he seeth all his goings. 22 There is no darkness, nor shadow of death, where the workers of iniquity may hide themselves. 23 For he will not lay upon man more than right; that he should enter into judgment with God. 24 He shall break in pieces mighty men without number, and set others in their stead. 25 Therefore he knoweth their works, and he overturneth them in the night, so that they are destroyed. 26 He striketh them as wicked men in the open sight of others; 27 Because they turned back from him, and would not consider any of his ways: 28 So that they cause the cry of the poor to come unto him, and he heareth the cry of the afflicted. 29 When he giveth quietness, who then can make trouble? and when he hideth his face, who then can behold him? whether it be done against a nation, or against a man only: 30 That the hypocrite reign not, lest the people be ensnared.
Who hath given him a charge over the earth? or who hath disposed the whole world? [13]

He is the Creator of heaven and earth and the Ruler of the whole world; He did not receive His authority from another, nor is He subject to anyone; heaven and earth are the place of His care and delight.

If the earth were not the work of His hands, but had been entrusted to Him by another greater than He, He could do wrong and rule unjustly, as one who suffers no harm; but since it is His own, and He is its Creator and the One who cares for it, He governs everything that takes place on earth by His divine justice and His providence that surpasses human understanding. "Behold, God exalteth by his power: who teacheth like him? Who hath enjoined him his way? or who can say, Thou hast wrought iniquity?" (Job 36:22-23).

* Note how Elihu proves the justice of God: [He made the earth] and heaven and all the other creatures. Are His works foreign to Him, that He should be unjust to us...? He is just, not only because these are His works, but because He is their Lord. In fact this happens even with the wicked, for they do not accept harm (from another) coming upon those subject to them. Ordinarily everyone cares for those who are his and what is his. As for Him who is the Creator and Lord, how should He not exercise justice in all His governing, if He has poured out upon it such splendor? You cannot say that He does no injustice out of weakness, for He could easily destroy all men.

St. John Chrysostom * He truly governs the world Himself, He who created it Himself. He needs no help from another in governing it, He who needed no help in creating it... If Almighty God did not disdain to govern the world He Himself created, how much more does He govern well what He has created well. He is not harsh toward what He brought into being in His mercy. And He who cared for them before He created them does not abandon them after He has created them.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
If he set his heart upon man, if he gather unto himself his spirit and his breath [14].

Some see that this phrase and the one following mean that if God sets His heart upon a man, He gathers his spirit to Himself, because he is a being very dear to Him. He allows the body to return to dust, but He cherishes the breath He gave him and gathers it to Himself. What intercedes for us all is the love of God who created us and gave us a breath from His mouth. As the wise man says: "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it" (Eccl 12:7).

God, in His love for man, sets His heart upon him and focuses His divine plan on his salvation. Truly it is within God's authority to destroy the whole human race, because "They are all gone out of the way, they are together become unprofitable; there is none that doeth good, no, not one" (Rom 3:12). Man no longer has the right to live, and has no standing to ask anything good from God because he disobeyed Him. So whatever befalls man, even death, he cannot complain and accuse God of injustice, for who is justified before Him? As the psalmist says: "Enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified" (Ps 143:2). Yet in His love God allowed the body to die and return to dust, and gathers in His love the spirit of man, granting it the first resurrection with Him, so that in the second resurrection the body also rises with the spirit, and man returns to the divine embrace.

In this Elihu answers Job and says to him: Why do you seek a trial before God, for if God examined the life of any man, He would find him a criminal who deserves to be cut off from life completely. It is as though Elihu says to Job: I know that if you are compared with men you are reckoned righteous and perfect, but how do you dare ask to be tried before God, since like all men you deserve death.

* [If he set his heart upon him, he will gather unto himself his spirit and his breath] [14]. When the heart seeks lower things it becomes crooked. It becomes upright when it is lifted up to the heavenly things. For if a man sets his heart toward the Lord, the Lord draws his spirit and his breath to Himself. Here he uses the expression "spirit" for the inner thoughts, and the breath that comes out of the body for outward deeds. Thus God draws the spirit and the breath to Himself, in order to change what is within and what is without, making us turn toward Him in our longings... The whole man has burning inner desires toward Him who brought him into being.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
All flesh shall perish together, and man shall turn again unto dust [15].
If God willed, it is His right to remove all humanity; so why do people complain of the loss of health, of temporal goods, or of relatives, and think that God is unjust?

* [All flesh shall fall together, and man shall return to dust] [15]. For all flesh falls completely when it is no longer a slave to its passions... So the more a man begins to live for the heavenly things, the more he dies to the lower things... Paul's flesh perished completely when he said: "I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me" (Gal 2:20).

Rightly Elihu added in this matter: "man shall turn again unto dust." For everyone who is occupied with sin forgets his mortal condition, and while he is puffed up with pride he does not remember that he is dust. But after the grace of conversion touches him with a spirit of humility, then he recalls to his mind that he is dust.

David returned to dust when he said: [Remember, O Lord, that we are dust] (Ps 103:14). And Abraham returned to dust, saying: [I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord, which am but dust and ashes] (Gen 18:27). Although death had not yet dissolved the living body into dust, in their own view they were so, as they had foreseen and looked upon it without doubting what would happen.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
If now thou hast understanding, hear this: hearken to the voice of my words [16].
