At the beginning of the chapter Elihu addressed his speech to men of wisdom and understanding; now he addresses it rather to Job, if he has understanding. He wanted to rebuke him for the expressions that came from him that were unfitting regarding God and His judgments.
Shall even he that hateth right govern? and wilt thou condemn him that is most just? [17]
Elihu marvels at man's attitude toward God, that one who is subject to law dares to condemn God, who is all justice and righteousness and the Giver of the law to men.

How strange! One who needs a law to govern him puts himself in the position of judge to condemn the Lawgiver. Or one who hates the law and tries to be rid of it wishes to pass judgment on the founder of the law.
* He hates evil and loves mankind. He is not like us who leave evil not out of hatred for vice, but out of fear of the coming punishment.
St. John Chrysostom * Is it fit to say to a king, Thou art wicked? and to princes (to nobles), Ye are ungodly? [18]

If God established authorities, it was that they might be honored in the Lord and for the sake of the Lord, and not that they might occupy the Lord's place (Sir 32:1). For a ruler or one in authority whose heart is lifted up in pride falls into apostasy, as happened with Satan. The Apostle Paul, as a leader who feared lest he fall into pride, says: "Nor of men sought we glory, neither of you, nor yet of others, when we might have been burdensome, as the apostles of Christ. But we were gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children" (1 Thess 2:6-7). The glory of the leader is to bear the Spirit of the Lord, who embraces all who are subject to him with love and treats them as his sons.
If man does not dare to accuse an earthly king of wickedness and evil, how can he ascribe injustice and evil to the King of kings and Lord of lords?

It is fitting for man to give honor to whom honor is due, for it is hard for a man to judge his rulers, because he does not perceive the hidden causes and secret reasons behind their actions; how then can he condemn the plan of God that is without limit and His plans that surpass the mind.

* Now concerning the passages in the Gospel that seem to carry something of contradiction, it is better for each one to rebuke himself that he has not yet attained to understanding "the riches both of the wisdom" (Rom 11:33), and to remember in truth that it is hard to grasp God's mysterious judgments, rather than to accuse them with insolence and rashness, and so hear the words: "It is a lawless one who says: You transgress the law" (Job 34:18) LXX.
St. Basil the Great * That accepteth not the persons of princes, nor regardeth the rich more than the poor (nor regards the wealthy above the needy).
For they all are the work of his hands [19].

If it is not fitting for us to judge kings and rulers, who as men often show partiality, how can we condemn God, who treats the rich and the poor on the same level, without respect of persons (see Gal 2:6; Acts 10:34; 2 Chr 19:7; Prov 22:2; Rom 2:11; Eph 6:9; Col 3:25). For all are His creation, and all need His divine providence and mercies in order to enjoy salvation. A man's abilities or position have no bearing on God's dealings with him.

* By the ruler or tyrant here is understood every arrogant person, while the humble are indicated by the needy (poor). Therefore God does not favor the tyrant when he opposes the needy, for He declares that He does not know, in the judgment, the proud who trouble the lives of the poor, as it is written: "I know you not whence ye are" (Lk 13:25). If He wished, He could destroy him by His power, since He created him by His power when He willed. Therefore it was fitting to add: "for they all are the work of his hands."
Pope Gregory (the Great)
In a moment shall they die, and the people shall be troubled at midnight, and pass away: and the mighty (those with power) shall be taken away without hand [20].
Here he speaks of three classes in order for Elihu to bring out that God shows no partiality.

The first class: the kings and the rich who depend on authority and money, and so are reckoned more secure than others. God not only does not favor these, but sometimes allows their souls to be taken suddenly, something to which the people are not exposed in the same way.

The second class: the wicked people, who depend on their great numbers and the strength of walls, when suddenly they suffer troubles and are drawn away from their land, taken captive at midnight. At midnight God struck the firstborn of the Egyptians while they were at ease, mocking the people of God.

The third class: the mighty, such as men of war who take pride in their military capabilities; they are sometimes taken away or fall captive from where they do not know, as though without a hand. They are defeated not by a human arm, just as the strong and righteous are not saved by it. As it was said: "This is the word of the Lord unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts" (Zech 4:6). It was also said: "There is no king saved by the multitude of an host: a mighty man is not delivered by much strength. An horse is a vain thing for safety: neither shall he deliver any by his great strength" (Ps 33:16-17).
* Let God be your hope, your power of endurance, your strength. Let Him be your atonement, your praise, your goal and place of rest, and your help in your striving...

The mighty man is the arrogant man who exalts himself (haughtily) against God, as though he were something in himself and in what is his. Such a man is not saved by his own strength. Now, he has a swift and strong horse, sound and quick of step; if an attack occurs, can it deliver its rider from the danger that besets him? Let him hear: [The horse is a vain thing for safety](a)... You must not let the horse promise you deliverance...

We can take the horse as a symbol of any possessions in this world, or any kind of honor on which we rely in pride, wrongly reckoning that the higher you rise, the more your security and your height increase. Do you not realize with what violence you will be thrown down? The higher you climb, the heavier your fall will be... How then is safety achieved? It is not achieved by strength, nor by authority, nor by honor, nor by glory, nor by a horse.
St. Augustine * For his eyes are upon the ways of man, and he seeth all his goings [21].

God does not need someone to give Him a report about a person, as Job thought when he said: "Am I a sea, or a whale, that thou settest a watch over me?" (Job 7:12). Rather the prophet Jeremiah says of Him: "Whose eyes are open upon all the ways of the sons of men" (Jer 32:19), and it was also said of Him: "For the eyes of the Lord run to and fro throughout the whole earth" (2 Chr 16:9).
All things are open before Him, for He is present everywhere, caring for all, exercising divine righteousness and justice. No one escapes from Him (Ps 139:2-3).

St. John Chrysostom sees that Elihu affirms God's justice without aiming to harm Job with false accusations as the other three friends did, for he did not say of him that he broke the widows and orphans (Job 22:9). Elihu knows how to blame Job without making accusations against him.

"The Lord looketh from heaven; he beholdeth all the sons of men. From the place of his habitation he looketh upon all the inhabitants of the earth. He fashioneth their hearts alike; he considereth all their works" (Ps 33:13-15).
"Can any hide himself in secret places that I shall not see him? saith the Lord. Do not I fill heaven and earth? saith the Lord" (Jer 23:24).

* God is reckoned as one who does not know the deeds of the wicked, because He justly postpones their judgment, so that the greatness of His longsuffering toward them appears as a kind of overlooking of them. And the wicked man, each time he sins without being punished, thinks that God does not see him, as a result of not being punished immediately as he deserves. He reckons that his conduct is not hateful to God... But there the punishments will fall upon him suddenly, with an eternal blow. Then he will know that God watches everything, when he finds himself punished by an unexpected death as an eschatological punishment for all his iniquity...

* He calls [all the goings of men] either the separate works with which we are occupied, or the successive motives of our deep thoughts, since they are like steps by which we are separated from the Lord or draw near to Him in holiness. For the mind draws near to God as by many steps (degrees) when it advances in many holy affections. Again it is separated from Him through many evil thoughts.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
There is no darkness, nor shadow of death, where the workers of iniquity may hide themselves [22].

Usually the criminal wants to hide from sight. Elihu says that there is no dark cave here in which the wicked can hide from the eyes of God, and in the world to come there is no deep darkness to which they can flee from His face. A man can hide from the face of his fellow man so that his affair is not exposed, but with God everything is open, whether in this world or on the great day of the Lord. There is a hidden eye that sees the wicked, and a strong hand that draws them to their recompense.
"Shadow of death" points to dense darkness (Amos 9:2-3; Ps 139:12).

* What does he mean by darkness but ignorance, and by the shadow of death but forgetfulness? Of the ignorance of certain people it is said: "Having the understanding darkened" (Eph 4:18). Again, of the forgetfulness that comes upon us at death it was said: [In that very day his thoughts perish] (Ps 146:4). For all that he thinks of during his life is given over to forgetfulness by death; forgetfulness is a kind of shadow of death, for as the coming of death puts an end to the works of life, so the coming of forgetfulness destroys what is in the memory...

No one hides from (God's) judgment; therefore it is impossible for Him not to see what we do, or to forget what He sees... It is the mark of the divine nature alone not to suffer shadows of ignorance or change... For since the eternal light in its shining, which is God Himself, does not change, He sees with a piercing gaze, and is not ignorant of what is hidden, for He penetrates all things, and does not forget what He penetrates since He is unchangeable...
When we think that we are not seen, we keep our eyes closed to the light of the sun, meaning we shut it out from us, and do not shut ourselves out from it.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
For he will not lay upon man more than right; that he should enter into judgment with God [23].

Some see that the meaning here is: God does not call man again to trial; He does not look into a case twice, for His judgments are just and need no appeal; the sentence is issued and there is no one to appeal for a fresh pleading.

And some translate it: "Behold, no man is given a set time to come to judgment with God." Man's time is not in his hand, nor is his lot fulfilled by his wisdom and strength. When God sees that the time is right, He judges man.
He shall break in pieces mighty men without number, and set others in their stead [24].
He crushes and shatters those who think themselves great, for He cares nothing for their huge wealth, their standing in society, and their great numbers.
"Without number," that is, God does not need long procedures to examine matters and make sure of them. He judges at once, directly, and removes the wicked and sets up those who take their places.
In many cases God presses down the proud who are self-reliant, and lifts up the humble and the meek.

* [He shall break in pieces many without number, and set others in their stead] [24]. This happens every day, but because the end of the two groups (the righteous and the wicked) has not yet been seen, the awe is less. For the wicked will not know their faults until they fall under punishment... By examining the hearts of men individually, or placing them under justice and mercy, He drives some outside and leads others inside. These others are inspired to seek the inner delights, and He leaves the former to inherit the outer pleasures.
He lifts the minds of some toward the heavenly things and casts down the pride of others into the depths of pleasures...
He drives out one with firmness, and draws another with His mercy...

It is well said by the prophet: "He casteth the wicked down to the ground" (Ps 147:6). For since they lose heavenly things, all they thirst for is earthly, and everything they pursue and that seems greater to them, they seek through it what is lower in value.

It is well said of them by Jeremiah: [They that depart from thee shall be written in the earth] (see Jer 17:13). While on the other side it is said of the elect: "Rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven" (Lk 10:20).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Therefore he knoweth their works, and he overturneth them in the night, so that they are destroyed [25].

God knows their works, and what they plan, without need of examination; so He gives them many opportunities, perhaps they will turn back from evil, and in a single night He shatters them. Clear examples in the Old Testament are what happened to all of Egypt's people when all the firstborn died in one night, and also Belshazzar king of Babylon (Dan 5:30).

"He overturneth them in the night": the literal translation is "He overturns the night." That is, He turns it upon them, so that a grave disaster they do not expect befalls them. The word "night" often indicates an unexpected disaster, hard to face.

* It is understood in particular that every wicked man is crushed in the night in two ways: either when he is struck from outside with the torment of punishment, or when he is stricken with a sentence, when he loses forever the light of life by the final judgment. As it is written: "Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness" (Mt 22:13). Then he is sent by force into the outer darkness, since by his own will he has become blind with the inner darkness...
Every sin that is not quickly wiped out by remorse is either a sin and the cause of a sin, or a sin and a punishment for a sin.
The sin that remorse does not wash away at once leads, by its weight, to another sin. So it is not only a sin, but in addition it is the cause of a sin.

This sin is followed by the stirring up of faults, as the blind mind is led to suffer slavery from sin to another sin(b); but the sin that arises from a sin does not merely return after the sin, but becomes a sin with the punishment of a sin added.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
He striketh them as wicked men in the open sight of others [26].

The wicked often want to disappear from sight as in darkness, because their works are darkness that cannot bear the light; therefore the Lord chastises them openly so that they tremble and realize their inability to escape the divine justice, and so that they become a practical lesson to others, who will not imitate them.
Perhaps Elihu was fixing his eyes on the calamities that had befallen Job in public.
Pope Gregory (the Great) holds that the onlookers are the godly who stand as witnesses against the wicked on the day of judgment.
* "He striketh them as wicked men in the open sight of others" (Job 34:26)...

Holy Scripture calls unbelievers in particular wicked. For sinners are distinguished from the wicked by this difference: every wicked man is a sinner, but not every sinner is wicked. For even a man who is godly in the faith can be a sinner. John says: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us" (1 Jn 1:8). But a man is rightly called wicked if he is estranged from the holiness of religion... The very calm of the Church's peace hides many under the Christian name and the plague of their wickedness envelops them. But when they are struck by a light breath of persecution, it sweeps them away at once like chaff from the threshing floor.

Some people desire to bear the mark of the Christian calling, because the name of Christ has been exalted, so that nearly everyone looks to appear as believers. When they see others called so, they are ashamed to appear unbelievers, but they neglect to become what they boast of being called...

Some keep the faith inside their hearts, but they do not care to walk faithfully in life... Since they ignore the exacting life, they fall into unbelief without anyone persecuting them... These are hidden from the eyes of men but exposed in the sight of God.

Many die unbelieving while dwelling in the faith itself. It is rightly said: "He striketh them as wicked men in the open sight of others" (Job 34:26). For they show themselves before men in the Church as godly persons, but since they cannot escape the divine judgments, they are struck as wicked men.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Because they turned back from him, and would not consider any of his ways [27].

He gives an explanation for their chastisement in public, namely their forsaking of the Holy God in secret, within their hearts and thoughts as in their hidden conduct, and they did not accept the way of the Lord, that is, they did not keep His commandments nor give any consideration to God Himself in their lives.

* "Because they turned back from him, and would not consider any of his ways" [27]. What will befall the wicked on the day of judgment has its secret in their turning away from God, or turning back from him, and their indifference to His divine ways.
* [Who turned aside from him, as if deliberately]. We should understand that sin is committed in three ways: either from ignorance, or from weakness, or deliberately.
Our sin becomes graver if it is from weakness and not from ignorance, but the danger is greater if it is deliberate and not from weakness.
Paul sinned from ignorance when he said: "Who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious: but I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief" (1 Tim 1:13).

Peter sinned from weakness when the word of the maid shook the strength of the faith he had spoken of with the Lord, and when he denied with his voice the Lord whom he held fast in his heart (Mt 26:69).

But those sinned deliberately of whom the Lord Himself said: "If I had not come and spoken unto them, they had not had sin: but now they have no cloke for their sin" (Jn 15:22). To sin deliberately means that you do not love goodness and do not do it. Therefore sometimes the guilt is heavier to love sin than to practice it. Likewise it is a greater sin to hate righteousness than not to do it. Therefore there are some in the Church who are far from goodness and even persecute it, and also those who hate in others what they themselves practice in negligence.

* [And would not consider any of his ways]. He does not say that they do not understand from weakness, but that they do not want to understand, because men often despise the knowledge of things which they greatly boast of doing... since they reckon that their ignorance of them gives them immunity concerning their sins...
To understand the ways of the Lord is to bear with humility the passing things (afflictions) and to wait with steadfastness for the abiding things (the eternal things).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
So that they cause the cry of the poor to come unto him, and he heareth the cry of the afflicted [28].

By forsaking the way of the Lord and rejecting His commandments, they opened the way for the cries of the poor whom they wronged to ascend to the Lord, and the cries of the afflicted (the sorrowful) to reach Him. In other words, when the wicked man rejects the way of the Lord and stops his ears from hearing the divine commandment in his practical life, he causes loss and bitterness to his brethren, so their cries ascend to heaven and reach the ears of God.

There is nothing more terrifying in the heavenly court than the hardness of man's heart toward his brother because of his rejection of the commandment of divine love. For even if he prays to God, He stops His ears until man opens his ears to those whom he has grieved and troubled. For the tears and sighs of the sufferers go before and complain against the wicked wrongdoers.

* [So that the cry of the needy comes to him, and he hears the voice of the poor] [28]. While these (the wicked) boast, those whom they oppress cry out to God, or it certainly means that they cause the cry of the poor to reach God... This also refers to the leaders of the Church who cease from the work of preaching and busy themselves with worldly concerns. They leave the obligations of preaching. By this they oblige the flock under them to rush into complaint and murmuring. Everyone whom you urge complains, as if with justice, of the conduct of the false shepherd, asking: Why does one who does not practice the work occupy the place of the teacher?
Pope Gregory (the Great)
When he giveth quietness, who then can make trouble?
And when he hideth his face, who then can behold him? whether it be done against a nation, or against a man only? [29]

Elihu says: {When God hears the groans of the people and the sighs of the suffering man, He gives rest or comfort or prosperity to the poor, the suffering and the wronged; then who dares to cause them trouble or hardship?} Elihu wants to affirm that all things are under His authority, He hears the voice of the sufferers and acts, and the wicked, with all their abilities and authority, cannot touch them!

"And when he hideth his face" is a biblical expression indicating the coming of a disaster, as though announcing that God has hidden His face from man, so no one can see him, that is, care for him and lift from him the disaster that has befallen him, and give him peace and joy.

It is as though Elihu invites Job to return to God, for He alone, when He gives him divine comfort and inner peace, can keep trials and men's troubles from harming him. But if he does not return to God, He will hide His face from him, and all the faces of men cannot look upon him and give him rest.
This principle, that the secret of man's rest is in God's hand and not in men's, applies to the people as a whole as well as to the individual person.

If God justifies us by His love, no one can condemn us, and if He is angry with us, no one can give us peace! Then let us enjoy perfect peace by centering our depths on God, the source of peace and the gladdener of hearts (Prov 16:7; Isa 26:3).

* [When he giveth peace, who then can condemn? and when he hideth his face, who then can behold him?] [29]... He also says this when He gives the laborers in the vineyard their wages... "Didst not thou agree with me for a penny?... I will give unto this last, even as unto thee. Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own?" (see Mt 20:13-15)...

"Whether it be done against a nation, or against a man only"... The divine judgments are set forth in the same manner concerning one soul or one city, and also concerning one city or one nation, and in the same manner concerning the human race. The Lord cares for particular persons in the same manner as He cares for the whole world.

Again, He directs His care toward all at the same time as if He did not care for individuals. For He who fills all things by His providence fills all. And when He cares for one thing alone, He is at the same time present in all. Again, while He governs the whole world, He is present with each individual. In fact, He does everything by the power of His nature without moving. What is marvelous is that while He is intent on something, He is not limited by it, He who works even while at rest.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
That the hypocrite (the ungodly) reign not, lest the people be ensnared [30].

All human affairs are in the hand of God, under His surpassing care, so that the wicked hypocrite may not reign and rule over his brethren, thinking himself possessor of irresistible authority, with no one able to restrain him or check him from wronging them. And lest this wicked man become a snare into which the people fall, as they feel as though God does not care about the injustice that has come upon them.

So it is fitting for leaders - at all levels - to realize that though they have received authority, God is above all, the controller of all. The psalmist says: "For the rod of the wicked shall not rest upon the lot of the righteous; lest the righteous put forth their hands unto iniquity" (Ps 125:3).

* "Who makes the hypocrite reign for the sins of the people" [30]. Judea did not want the true King to reign over her, so she brought a hypocrite to reign over her as befitted her deserts. As the Truth Himself says in the Gospel: [I am come in my Father's name, and ye receive me not: if another shall come in his own name, him ye will receive] (Jn 5:43). Paul says: "Because they received not the love of the truth, that they might be saved. And for this cause God shall send them strong delusion, that they should believe a lie" (2 Thess 2:10-11).

By saying: [Who makes the hypocrite reign for the sins of the people] he perhaps means the Antichrist, the chief of all hypocrites. For the deceiver pretends to holiness in order to draw men to evil...

This Antichrist reigns over the wicked, not because of the injustice of the judge, but because of the sin of those who are obliged to bear the punishment. Although most of them do not see his ruling power, they are enslaved to him because of the state they have reached by their sins. Without doubt they honor him by their wicked lives, these who do not see his tyranny over them. Are these not his members who seek, by displaying holiness, what they are not...? For it is written: "Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin" (Jn 8:34). For to the extent that they commit sins by this will of theirs which they desire, they bow down to the service of (the Antichrist), enslaved to him.

May whoever suffers under such a ruler not blame the wicked ruler... but blame the faults of his own wicked deeds and not the injustice of his ruler. It is written: "I gave thee a king in mine anger" (Hos 13:11).

Why then do we mock the one who is set up as ruler over us, who received his authority from God's wrath? If we receive rulers according to our deserts from God's displeasure, we infer from their conduct what our own condition truly is...! The characteristics of rulers are fixed according to the deserts of those subject to them. Even those who appear to be good are changed by the power they receive. Observe Scripture! Saul's very heart changed with his dignity. It is written: "When thou wast little in thine own sight, wast thou not made the head of the tribes of Israel?" (1 Sam 15:17).
The conduct of rulers is shaped according to the characteristics of those subject to them, for the conduct of even a good shepherd becomes evil because of the evil of his flock.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* The wicked are scattered bitterly like light tares, but the righteous are saved like heavy wheat. So note what the Lord says to Peter: "Behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat: but I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not" (Lk 22:31-32). Those who are scattered like tares perish, but he who does not perish is like the seed that falls and grows and increases and brings forth much fruit (Lk 8:8)... Evil is likened to the chaff that burns quickly and becomes dust.
St. Ambrose * Here is the remedy for your sickness: "Fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way"(c). Yes, he prospers, but in his own way. But you labor, yet in the way of God.
He travels on his journey recklessly, but where is he going?
If Christ had promised you the good things of this world, you would have reason to be angry, because the unbeliever overflows in his ways.

What has He promised you? Eternal happiness when the dead are raised, and in this life He promised you His own portion. I repeat, His portion is the way that He walked. Do you despise what your Master walked, you who are a servant and disciple? You have heard that the servant is not better than his master, for He suffered! A thing which that Righteous One did not deserve, so what do you deserve, O sinner?

* "For the rod of the wicked shall not rest upon the lot of the righteous; lest the righteous put forth their hands unto iniquity" (Ps 125:3). At present the righteous suffer to some extent, and at present the wicked sometimes oppress the righteous. In what ways? Sometimes the wicked attain temporal honors, and when they attain them and become judges or kings, God permits this for the chastening of His flock, for the chastening of His people; here the honor that befits them must be shown... And sometimes there are authorities who are good and fear God, and some of them have no fear of God in them.

Julian was an unbelieving emperor, an apostate, wicked and an idol worshiper. And the Christian soldiers served an unbelieving emperor.... Whenever he called them to worship idols and offer incense to them they pointed to God, but when he commanded them to deploy in the lines of soldiers and move against this nation or that, they obeyed at once. They distinguished between their eternal Master and their temporal master, and for the sake of their eternal Master they submitted to the temporal. But do the wicked always hold authority over the righteous? The rod of the wicked remains for a time upon the lot of the righteous, but it will not last forever. A time will come when Christ will appear in His glory and gather all the nations before Him.
St. Augustine

31 "Surely it is meet to be said unto God, I have borne chastisement, I will not offend any more: 32 That which I see not teach thou me: if I have done iniquity, I will do no more. 33 Should it be according to thy mind? he will recompense it, whether thou refuse, or whether thou choose; and not I: therefore speak what thou knowest. 34 Let men of understanding tell me, and let a wise man hearken unto me. 35 Job hath spoken without knowledge, and his words were without wisdom. 36 My desire is that Job may be tried unto the end because of his answers for wicked men. 37 For he addeth rebellion unto his sin, he clappeth his hands among us, and multiplieth his words against God."
But hath any said unto God:
I have borne chastisement, I will not offend any more [31].
Elihu demands that he return to God, and in a spirit of repentance say: I have borne the chastisement, I will not sin any more!

The conclusion came bearing more violence than all the speeches of the three friends, but it seems that Elihu's intention and sincere zeal are what distinguished him from them, for he did not share their envy.
Some translate it: "Surely it is fitting to say to God: I have been chastised, I will not disobey any more." Thus Elihu demands that he walk in a spirit of humility before God.

It is fitting for the suffering man to go beyond the limits of pain to meet God in a spirit of humility and understanding, without murmuring or complaint, realizing that behind the pain is a divine plan for his edification. He presented to him a general truth, that it is fitting for the sufferer to come to know God's plan toward him.

"I have borne": some hold that the Hebrew word here means "I repented" or "chastisement," so I will not do corruption any more. Thus sufferings become a way of reviewing the soul and seeking reform by returning to God.
Indeed Job said so to God (Job 40:3-5; Mic 7:9; Lev 26:41).
That which I see not teach thou me.
If I have done iniquity, I will do no more? [32]
Elihu presents to us a wonderful picture of repentance, and at the same time brings out what is within him concerning Job.

Job was not, as his friends had said to him before, a hypocrite covering his sins with deceptive formalities and hiding his buried evils with displays of giving and service; rather he says to him: "There are in your life - as in the life of every believer - sins hidden from your eyes, which you practice involuntarily, which you cannot see or perceive. Ask God and He will reveal them to you."
God teaches His people (Job 10:2), giving them inner knowledge even of their faults which they had not perceived if they come to Him repentant (Ps 32:8; 19:12; 139:23-24).
It is fitting for the believer to set in his heart that if the Lord reveals his sins to him, he will not return to them again (Prov 28:13; Eph 4:22).
Will He recompense it according to thy mind, saying:
Because thou hast refused? thou choosest, and not I.
And speak what thou knowest? [33]

This text came out obscure, so the interpretations differ. Some hold that God will recompense for the deed whether the person accepts it or refuses, and that God does not act according to man's point of view, but as He sees what is right and profitable, so man should not expect God to consult men and act according to their opinions or feelings.

It is as though man says to God: Do You, O God, work as You see fit; it is You who choose and take, not I, You work and speak as You know. As for me, for my part I trust in Your decisions and submit to Your plan.
Let men of understanding tell me, and let a wise man hearken unto me: [34]
Elihu wishes to enter into dialogue with men of understanding and wisdom, because he wishes to find one who will listen to him and weigh his words and evaluate them.
Job hath spoken without knowledge, and his words were without wisdom [35].

Elihu sees in Job that he has kept silent, so he counted him rigid in his thought, holding fast to his will and to himself, so there was no profit in speaking with him. He counted him as one without knowledge or wisdom.
My desire is that Job may be tried unto the end because of his answers for wicked men [36].
Elihu wishes to bring Job to a just trial, so that his words and concepts may be tested, for he gave his answers to the men of iniquity (his friends), and he must correct what he said.
For he addeth rebellion unto his sin.
He clappeth his hands among us, and multiplieth his words against God [37].

Besides his former sins, he added a graver sin during his dialogue, namely the sin of complaint with murmuring against God. If God permitted him chastisement for his sins, he ought not to have murmured, even if his friends provoked him with unjust and violent accusations.

[Clapping] is either a sign of approval and victory, or of anger and distress (Num 24:10), or of mockery (Job 27:23). It seems that he is speaking here of clapping as a symbol of contempt and mockery of his friends' concepts. It is as though Job - instead of studying matters objectively, in a calm spirit and with a desire to know the truth and benefit from it - had all that occupied him in making light of his friends who accuse him unjustly.
"And multiplieth his words against God": instead of resorting to God for His support, he ascribed injustice to God, and went on at length in it.
Grant me the spirit of discernment!
* Grant me from You the spirit of discernment, O Wisdom of God.
So that by Your Spirit I may test every thought and every word and every action.
Let me test my words, so that no idle word comes out.
Let me test what I listen to, so that I do not waste my time with idle words.
Let me hear Your voice in everything, in Your holy Gospel, in beautiful nature, and in past and present events.
* In You I experience virtue and delight in it. In You I cannot bear evil, nor converse with it.
Let the deceitful wisdom of the world not deceive me, nor the winds of vain philosophy move me.
Let me taste Your wisdom, Your love and Your care all the day long, so that my soul rejoices even in the midst of the flames of trials.
* Grant me the spirit of discernment, so that men's praise does not deceive me, nor their sharp criticism crush me.
Rather in You let me know the divine truth and live it!
Let me hear Your voice in my depths, as in Your Church!
Let me enjoy You in the midst of Your children!
* Grant me the spirit of discernment, that I may welcome Your pure word and hold fast to it, that I may listen to You through Your servants and reject the voice of deceivers.
In You let me become a skilled money-changer, distinguishing true coins from counterfeit!
* Grant me the spirit of discernment, that I may realize that no one is perfect but You, in You let me be perfect and holy!
In You I long for the whole world to cleave to Your righteousness.
So that mankind becomes perfect and good in You!

* Grant me the spirit of discernment, so that in the midst of affliction and in the bitterness of my soul, I do not think that righteousness does not profit its possessor, nor that evil does not harm its doer.
Let me not ask: Where is Your care for Your believers?
Nor weigh matters with human, temporal scales.
Rather let me trust in Your love, Your care and Your justice.
Let me wait, for tomorrow the secrets of Your wisdom will be revealed!
* By Your dwelling in my heart, it expands to embrace every man with love.
It expands, and is not narrowed before any trial. And all trials turn to my good.
Let me perceive the secret of Your love behind every affliction!
In the midst of sufferings my soul rejoices in You, and sings always of Your righteousness!
My soul will not be troubled by the cruelty of the wicked toward me, nor do I fear the rod of sinners, for it will not rest upon me.
I bear witness to Your righteousness, You who show no partiality!
* I see You as a Father who has compassion on me as on Your son.
You do not forget a cup of cold water that I offer in Your name.
I see evils passing quickly, and my soul rejoices in Your hands as they wipe away my tears.
* Grant me the spirit of discernment, that I may realize Your care for me, Your creature.
If a man does not bear an insult that touches those subject to him, will You not care for me, Your creature and the work of Your hands?
In Your mercy You brought me into being, O Almighty, wonderful Father, so how would You not care for me with Your love?!
You gave me life by a breath from You, so how very dear I am to You?!
Will You not open Your fatherly arms to me?
* You created me from nothing, so I am the work of Your hands.
You loved me and created me, and redeemed me freely with Your precious blood; would You then let injustice befall me, O Lover of mankind?
* Let my body return to the dust from which it was created, but will my spirit not return to You, for it is a breath from Your mouth?!
You took my body by Your Incarnation, and hope returned to me that I shall not perish.
I look forward to the day of my resurrection, when my body will be glorified with my spirit!
* Your Spirit carries me from glory to glory, lifts me from the dunghill and the dust, and takes me away to heaven!
So what can the events of the world do to me?!
* Grant me the spirit of discernment, that I may realize that with You there is no partiality!
You will not show partiality to a rich man because of his wealth or his authority.
Nor will You show partiality to a people because of the multitude of its number.
Nor will You show partiality to an army because of its military capabilities.
Rather You care for every man as if there were no one else on earth.
And You care for all without distinction or bias!
* Your eyes watch every man, not to destroy him but to save him.
Your eyes behold what is in the mind and the heart.
You have no need of anyone's testimony, for everything is open before You!
* In Your love You do not wish the destruction of anyone, but deliberately the wicked insisted on turning away from You.
They left You and held Your commandment in contempt.
So evil reigned over their hearts.
Violence became their constitution, and their ears were struck with deafness, so they do not hear the cries of the wronged poor.
But You continue to hear the groans of inner hearts.
You lift them up, uphold them and glorify them!
* Is there no man who can insult a ruler or a king?
Then who dares to condemn Your divine plans?
You are King of kings! You are Lord of lords!
Your eyes are on the ways of all mankind. They look even into what is in our hearts and thoughts.
As if You had no work but to care for the sons of men.
You desire that all be saved, and come to the knowledge of You!
* Let the world rise against me, for its Creator embraces me.
Let the wicked rage with all their strength. Their spirit goes out and they return to their dust.
They mock me, and they become a spectacle, a proverb and a derision!
They turned away from You with their hard hearts, and lost their life and their glory!
* They mocked the cries of the afflicted, and did not realize that You listen to the groaning of their hearts.
They hid their faces from the wronged, and did not realize that You Yourself look upon them.
They thought the poor were tares that burn, and did not realize that You make them gold refined by fire.
* Grant me the spirit of discernment, that I may grasp the secrets of Your plans, and learn how to converse with You, and distinguish between heavenly and earthly things.
And let me hasten to You, and enjoy You within me.
* Finally, teach me and train me, that I may learn by the spirit of discernment how to speak with You!

entries.section: 1. Job thinks he is more righteous than God

paragraphs.text: Elihu answered and said:
Thinkest thou this to be right?
Thou saidst, My righteousness is more than God's [1-2].

Elihu addresses Job, asking: Do you think it right to say that you are more righteous than God? This is blasphemy! Job did not say this, either openly or by implication. But perhaps Elihu sensed it in Job's talk about his sincerity and the uprightness of his life, and that he had committed no crime that would qualify him for these calamities (see Job 9:17, 30-35; 10:13-15; 16:12-17; 34:18-19). He interpreted all this to mean that Job thinks himself more righteous than his Creator.

Pope Gregory (the Great) holds that Elihu did not grasp what was in Job's mind or what lay behind his words. Though Job seemed to justify himself before the Lord, Elihu took him to be calling himself more righteous than the Lord. In truth, Job did not yet understand that his trials were meant to prove him more and more for the sake of receiving greater glories, and were not a punishment for sins. So he asks: What sins have I committed that all these trials, which have not come upon anyone else, should come upon me? It is a question rather than a justification of himself!

entries.section: 1. Job thinks he is more righteous than God

paragraphs.text: * “Thinkest thou this to be right, that thou saidst, My righteousness is more than God's?” [2]... It should be noted that the blessed Job did not say that he was more righteous than God. But he says: [Let justice contend with me, and my trial will result in victory] (see Job 23:7).

In examining Job's life and the reasons for his being struck, we often notice that he believed his scourgings were to remove his sins and not to increase his merits. Therefore he was confident that his trial would result in victory, since he found nothing in himself that deserved the blows that had befallen him. Indeed, the Lord Himself said of him to Satan: “Thou movedst me against him, to swallow him up without cause” (Job 2:3).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

What Job did even before the Law, many have done even in the age of grace, asking: “Why does God permit afflictions for the saints?” Many of the Fathers of the Church faced such a question. We mention as an example the sixth Conference of St. John Cassian with Abba Theodore (Tadros), which we have already published, and from which we quote the following:

* Some asked: Why are these men of great merit and abundant virtues slain by these robbers?! Why does God permit crimes to be committed against His servants, so that they fall into the hands of the wicked?!

In our grief we came to St. Theodore, who excelled in the (grace of) discernment. This Father lived in the region of the Cells, Calle, between Nitria and Scete, five miles from Nitria and eight from the desert of Scete where we were dwelling. When we came before him, distressed because of their death, and showing our astonishment at God's great long-suffering in permitting these men to be killed in this way, those who by their holiness were able to keep others from such trials, yet could not themselves be saved from falling into the hands of the wicked, we asked him: Why does God permit such crimes against His servants?!
Abba Theodore (Tadros)
In the introduction to his treatise “No One Can Harm a Man Unless He Harms Himself,” St. John Chrysostom wrote:

[Just as it is impossible to count the waves of the sea, so it is impossible to count the victims who fall under the burdens of plots, insults and sufferings. Neither by amending the law, nor by terror through the courts, nor by anything of the kind, can anyone stop the course of this plague and confusion; rather, evil increases more and more every day, until the sighs, laments and weeping of the sufferers have become a common and familiar thing...

And there are those who cling to a new kind of folly, accusing the providence of the Lord when they see the chaste man often held captive under violence, beaten and shamefully treated, while the shameless, cruel and base man pours countless troubles upon those who are chaster than he, and wrongs those in the city, in the country, in the desert, at sea and on land.
This discourse that I deliver is necessary in order to correct what they claim... proving that whoever has sinned is harmed only by his own hands, and no other man has driven him to sin.]

entries.section: 2. Is righteousness of no profit, and evil of no harm?

paragraphs.text: 3 For thou saidst, What advantage will it be unto thee? and, What profit shall I have more than by my sin? 4 I will answer thee, and thy companions with thee. 5 Look unto the heavens, and see; and behold the clouds which are higher than thou. 6 If thou sinnest, what doest thou against him? or if thy transgressions be multiplied, what doest thou unto him?
For thou saidst, What advantage will it be unto thee?
What profit shall I have more than by my sin? [3]
Some think that Job is speaking to himself, asking: What have you gained (O my soul)? And what do I gain by not practicing sin?
Others think that Job is saying to God: My righteousness does not profit You in anything, and it does not profit me.
Perhaps he took this from what Job said (Job 9:30-31; 10:15). The psalmist expressed this too in the Psalm (Ps 73:13).

Job did not say this openly. What he said was that he had expected these calamities not to befall him because of his upright conduct, yet this conduct did not spare him, as though he had gained nothing from it (see Job 19:28).
St. John Chrysostom made clear that nothing harms a man except his own evil, and nothing profits him except the uprightness of his life.

* What, then, is man's good? Man's good does not lie in wealth, that we should fear poverty; nor in bodily health, that we should dread sickness; nor in the way people look at you, that you should beware of what people say evilly about you; nor in life here for its own sake, that you should tremble at death... Rather, his good lies in holding fast to the true teachings and in uprightness of life, which no one, not even Satan himself, can take from a man as long as he guards it as he ought.

And this is fully understood even by the most wicked and fierce of the demons. Therefore Satan stripped Job of his possessions, not to make him poor, but to compel him to utter a word of blasphemy against God. He tormented his body, not to humble him by sickness, but to frustrate the goodness of his soul. But when he had exhausted all his devices, and had made this rich man poor... and deprived him of his children... and tore his body with a savagery that torturers could not equal, for instruments of torture cannot rend every side of the body as the worms that were in his body did, and Satan ruined his reputation, so that his friends who were with him declared that this was the recompense for the sins he deserved, directing many accusations against him, and drove him out of his city and his home, not to another city, but the dunghill of his city became his home...
None of this harmed Job; on the contrary, he was glorified the more because of these plots which Satan poured out against him.

Satan took much from him, but he did not rob him of any of his goodness. Rather, he drove him the more to increase the strength of his goodness. For after these things befell him, he enjoyed greater confidence, in proportion to the strength of the adversary who fought him.

Now if one who endured sufferings such as these, which were not the work of a man but of Satan, who is more wicked than all humankind, suffered no harm, would you say that some man has harmed or destroyed you...

If Satan, filled with such great cunning, after emptying all that was in his bag, using all his weapons, and pouring all his evils against a man of exalted standing in his family, and righteous, yet caused him no harm, but rather, as I have said, benefited him, how can you accuse one man or another of bringing harm in his hands upon another, and not upon himself?!

entries.section: 2. Is righteousness of no profit, and evil of no harm?

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom I will answer thee, and thy companions with thee [4].

I will show you the evil that the wrong way causes, or that sin causes, and the blessings that righteousness causes, and I will bring forward what your friends did not mention in their discussion with you.
Look unto the heavens, and see; and behold the clouds.

entries.section: 2. Is righteousness of no profit, and evil of no harm?

paragraphs.text: Which are higher than thou [5].

God created the heavens that you might look at them, and they would bear witness to you that God's wisdom and His boundless loftiness are beyond your understanding. Look at the clouds and you will perceive the perfections of God.

Here Elihu begins to answer Job, showing that it is impossible for him to comprehend God's wisdom, as the height of the heavens bears witness. It is as though he asks him: Can you soar in the heavens and reach the clouds? For God, who is their Creator, is higher, greater and loftier than the heavens and the clouds.
Thus Elihu, like Eliphaz, shows that God is loftier than nature, which itself rises above the thought of man.
He who cannot look with his eyes at the heaven and comprehend its secrets, how can he reach with his mind the throne of God and understand the secrets of His plan?

“For the works of the Lord are for the most part hidden; who shall declare the works of His justice, or who shall endure them? For the covenant is afar off, and the examination of all is at the end” (Sir 16:22).
“O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!” (Rom 11:33)
“For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts” (Isa 55:9).
* The works of our Creator must always be honored without examination, for they will never be unjust.
For whoever searches for the cause of His secret counsel is counted as nothing other than a man resisting His counsel in pride.

So when man cannot discover the motive of God's works, we must be silent in humility, submitting to His works, because the bodily senses are not on a level that can penetrate the secrets of His majesty...
Paul adds later: “Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus?” (Rom 9:20)
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Elihu speaks of God's surpassing loftiness. For man's conduct, whether good or evil, does not affect God [6-8]. Though man's righteousness or evil is not to serve God and does not offend Him, yet both have their effect on human life. Therefore there is no need to treat righteousness as though it were a sin that must be punished.
If thou sinnest, what doest thou against him?

entries.section: 2. Is righteousness of no profit, and evil of no harm?

paragraphs.text: Or if thy transgressions be multiplied, what doest thou unto him? [6]
Nothing of your practice of sin will hurt Him, even if you multiply it many times over (Jer 7:19; Prov 8:36).
* Such words ought not to be said to the blessed Job, who knows greater truths; yet what was said is true, namely that our sins do not harm God, nor do our good works help Him in anything.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 3. God has no need of our righteousness

paragraphs.text: 7 If thou be righteous, what givest thou him? or what receiveth he of thine hand? 8 Thy wickedness may hurt a man as thou art; and thy righteousness may profit the son of man. 9 By reason of the multitude of oppressions they make the oppressed to cry: they cry out by reason of the arm of the mighty.
If thou be righteous, what givest thou him? or what receiveth he of thine hand? [7]
God will gain nothing from your practice of righteousness; you have nothing that God needs for you to give Him (Ps 16:2; Prov 9:12; Lk 17:10).

entries.section: 3. God has no need of our righteousness

paragraphs.text: Thy wickedness may hurt a man as thou art; and thy righteousness may profit the son of man [8].

Your evil harms you as a man, and does not harm God, because your evil separates you from God, the source of happiness. As a man you harm yourself, and you may harm other human beings, by your evil; and by your righteousness, as a son of man, you profit and benefit your brethren.
* The evil of man harms the one whom evil corrupts by leading him astray; again, our righteousness profits the one who turns from his evil.

* When the wicked grieve the righteous, they set them free the more from the desires of this world. While they heap savage deeds upon them here, they urge them on to hasten toward heaven... This is the reason why the righteous are allowed to be wronged by the wicked, so that they may listen to the blessings to come and long for them, and bear the dreadful evils of the present; and while love calls them, the sufferings draw them into a swift flight.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* What then?! Is the man who is slandered and suffers the plundering of his goods not harmed, deprived of his possessions, driven from his inheritance, and struggling in crushing poverty?!

No, he is rather profited, if he is dignified. For did these things harm the Apostles? Did they not always struggle with hunger, thirst and nakedness?! And because of these things they became glorified and renowned, and gained for themselves more help from the Lord?!
* I have not said that no one harms another, but that no one is harmed by another. And how can no one be harmed by another, when many harm others...?!
The brothers of Joseph, for example, wronged Joseph, but Joseph himself was not harmed.
And Cain cast his nets for Abel, but Abel did not fall into them. And this is the reason why disciplines and punishments exist.

For God does not lift the punishment from the one who devised the harm merely because of the goodness of the one who bore it, but confirms his punishment because of the evil of the doer of iniquity. For although those upon whom the evil falls become more glorified because of the plots devised against them, this was not in the intention of those who devised the evil, but is due to the courage of those who are their victims. Therefore crowns of wisdom are prepared for the latter, but for the former, the recompense of their evils.

Have your possessions been taken from you? Remember those words: “Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither” (Job 1:21). And add to them the words of the Apostle: “For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out” (1 Tim 6:7).

Has your reputation been wronged, and have some loaded you with countless insults? Remember the saying: “Woe unto you, when all men shall speak well of you!” (Lk 6:26). And also: “[If they] say all manner of evil against you... rejoice, and be exceeding glad” (Mt 5:11-12).
Have you been taken into exile? Remember that you have no place here, but if you are wise you must look upon the whole world as a land of sojourning.
Have you been struck with a serious illness? Recall what the Apostle says: “Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day” (2 Cor 4:16).
Is a man suffering a violent death? Let him remember John, whose head was cut off in prison and taken on a platter and given as a reward for the dancing of a harlot.

Consider the reward you receive on account of these things, for all these sufferings, when they fall unjustly from one man upon another, take away our sins and our evil (since we accept the injustice without murmuring, believing in God and hoping for the other life, and these things work to prove us). Great, then, is the benefit of these labors for those who bear them courageously!
St. John Chrysostom By reason of the multitude of oppressions they make the oppressed to cry.

entries.section: 3. God has no need of our righteousness

paragraphs.text: They cry out by reason of the arm of the mighty [9].

Though evil does not harm God at all, it harms the children of men, for the oppressed cry out in the midst of the crowds because of the violence of the powerful, those who hold authority (the mighty). The wicked rich press with their violent hands upon the poor and wretched, who cry aloud from their persecutors, and there is no one to calm their souls, because they do not turn to God.

It is difficult to connect this statement with the preceding discourse. But it seems that Elihu is reviewing a general question in society, to which Job himself had referred (Job 24:12), where he sees that God does not intervene quickly to rescue the poor from the hands of the cruel wicked. Many are crushed by tyrants, and God does not intervene. Job considered that this general question touched him personally, since his friends had almost crushed him under their feet. And Elihu considered this thought an insult directed against Almighty God, His care and His love. He found himself obliged to give an explanation of this phenomenon.

Elihu answers the question: Why does God not respond to the cries of the suffering righteous, to help them against the oppressors? Elihu declares that the secret of God's not answering prayer is that the one who prays does not care about enjoying God; all that concerns him is to benefit from God. It is not true prayer, whose aim is to enjoy the light of the divine Presence, but a natural cry that comes out of pain, as the bird and the animal cry [10-11]. Our prayers for deliverance from the wicked are empty prayers [12-13].
When a man cries out in his distress he supposes that God does not hear; but He hears, and He may not answer because of the pride of the one crying out, or his falsehood.

* Rightly we may call the wicked “oppressors,” not only those who corrupt our outward goods, but also those who strive by their evil habits and the example of their corrupt life to scatter our inner treasures. They do not attack the things around us, but seek to devour us from within.

He who attacks our virtues by his evil conduct is a more dangerous oppressor than he who harms our goods by violent injustice against us. For though he takes nothing of our resources, he sets before us examples of destruction.

He practices a heavier injustice, for he stirs our quiet hearts with temptation. Even if he does not compel us to fight his evil conduct, he presses upon us by stirring up temptation, so that we suffer severe injustice from his life, suffering within by things that we overcome with difficulty.

Since the life of the wicked man, bound to the world, harms us, it was well said: [By the multitude of oppressors they cry out] [9]... [They wail by reason of the arm of the tyrants] [9]... For he who wishes to terrify us in order to push us into sin rages against us with the arm of a tyrant. To urge toward vice through the conduct of (an evil man) is one thing, and to compel to it by terror is another.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 4. Let us cry out to God in distress

paragraphs.text: 10 But none saith, Where is God my maker, who giveth songs in the night; 11 Who teacheth us more than the beasts of the earth, and maketh us wiser than the fowls of heaven?
But none saith, Where is God my maker, who giveth songs in the night? [10]

The secret of this problem, that is, of God's not intervening to rescue the poor from the hands of the oppressors, is that they do not turn to God, but turn to complaint and murmuring against God, and to reliance on human arms. Elihu says that none of those who have fallen under the feet of the cruel in bitter calamities cries out, saying: Where is my God who made me, that He may turn the night of calamities into a joyful feast and a song that fills my heart with gladness?

God is ready to intervene, but He does not force Himself in; rather He waits to be called upon by the poor, that He may give them His divine consolations and break the snares set for the poor (see Acts 16:25; Ps 126:1-2).
Night in the Holy Bible sometimes signifies sin, and sometimes the afflictions and calamities that turn a man's life into a dark and frightening night.
The Septuagint reads: “Who appoints the watchers of the night,” that is, He sends His angels in the midst of the night of calamities to rescue those who take refuge in Him.
He who takes refuge in God in his joys and in his afflictions enjoys heavenly peace by day as by night, and his life is turned into a joyful symphony and a ceaseless praise.

entries.section: 4. Let us cry out to God in distress

paragraphs.text: Who teacheth us more than the beasts of the earth, and maketh us wiser than the fowls of heaven? [11]

Elihu grieves over the state to which rational man has come by ignoring his Creator, the giver of understanding and wisdom, who is able to save to the uttermost. In folly he rejects God's teaching, guidance and leadership, and so has become less than the beasts of the earth and the fowls of heaven.

The Lord says through Isaiah: “The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib: but Israel doth not know, my people doth not consider” (Isa 1:3). The beasts of the earth, the birds, and sometimes the fish know the hand that is stretched out to feed them and give thanks for it; but rational man, who receives much from his Creator, pays no heed to Him and does not look to His compassionate hands.
The Holy Bible calls us to learn even from the ant, which sometimes behaves with more wisdom than man, who has a mind and surpassing abilities.

The blows of the enemy of good are dangerous. He wishes to draw us to temporal pleasures and enslave us to lusts through the carnal life; and if we do not respond to him and seek true knowledge, he strikes our hearts with pride, and so corrupts our understanding and wisdom. Therefore the psalmist stresses the need for understanding and wisdom together with humility: “Man that is in honour, and understandeth not, is like the beasts that perish” (Ps 49:20). And on the other hand the Apostle Paul says: “Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened”... Therefore “God also gave them up to uncleanness through the lusts of their own hearts, to dishonour their own bodies between themselves” (Rom 1:21, 24).
* The beasts of the earth are those who seek lower things through the carnal life, while the fowls of heaven are those who seek higher things in the zeal of arrogant curiosity.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 5. Let us cry out in humility without murmuring

paragraphs.text: 12 There they cry, but none giveth answer, because of the pride of evil men. 13 Surely God will not hear vanity, neither will the Almighty regard it. 14 Although thou sayest thou shalt not see him, yet judgment is before him; therefore trust thou in him. 15 But now, because his anger does not punish, neither does he regard the multitude of transgressions, 16 therefore Job openeth his mouth in vain; he multiplieth words without knowledge.
There they cry, but none giveth answer [12].
Sadly, these poor afflicted by calamities cry out and are not answered, because they do not cry out to God in a spirit of humility, but in complaint and murmuring, in evil pride.

Here he gives us another reason for God's not intervening: the first, as we saw, is that they do not cry out to Him; the second is that they cry out, but in a spirit of murmuring, and so they obtain nothing. God does not hear them until humility takes the place of pride in their hearts, and they offer prayers of contrition and repentance (Ps 10:4; Jer 13:17).

* It often happens that, when they are engulfed in temptation, they expect heaven to give them consolation even during their lifetime. They desire deliverance, not for their own sake, but for the sake of their opponents. They want Almighty God to deliver them from the dangers surrounding them by working a miracle, so that God may show His power even to the unjust. They long that God should save their adversaries eternally by the same means by which He saves one like them in this world. As the prophet also says in the person of the martyrs: [Deliver me because of my enemies] (Ps 69:18). It is as though he says: “For my own sake I do not ask deliverance from temporal trial, but I ask deliverance for the sake of my opponents.”
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Prayer has conditions for it to be answered, among them:

That our request be according to the will of God (Mt 26:39), with perseverance and importunity (Lk 11:8), and that we realize it is God's will that we amend our ways before the answer comes (Isa 1:15).
Among them also is the sense of our unworthiness of what we ask (1 Job 17:4), or the unworthiness of the one for whom we ask (Jer 14:11).
Among them too is that not being answered is better than being answered (2 Cor 12:7)... But if all the conditions are met, there is no doubt that God answers our prayer.

entries.section: 5. Let us cry out in humility without murmuring

paragraphs.text: St. Basil the Great Surely God will not hear vanity, neither will the Almighty regard it [13].

Surely God does not listen to vain or false cries or requests, or to ungrateful, thankless hearts. Where there is no sincerity, faith or thanksgiving, the petition does not rise to God. The prophet says: “Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil, and canst not look on iniquity” (Hab 1:13).

entries.section: 5. Let us cry out in humility without murmuring

paragraphs.text: Although thou sayest thou shalt not see him, yet judgment is before him; therefore trust thou in him [14].

Elihu asks Job to trust in God. Here he seems to refer to an observation Job made (Job 23:8), where he said that he could not approach God, nor present his case to Him. He went east, west, north and south, and could not see Him, nor did he find an opportunity to present his case before Him. Here Elihu makes clear that in truth God is unseen, but this does not mean that He does not care about the affairs of men, or that He does not deserve our trust and love. God cares for humanity and judges with justice and righteousness, and all things are open before Him. It befits us to wait patiently, for He will surely judge at the proper time.

* Because the Lord does not wish to look upon faults, being Almighty, He observes all who practice deeds against the Law, and saves me. You plead before Him if you are able to praise Him, which is possible even now (see Job 35:13-14). For the Lord not only does not wish to examine faults, but does not even wish to look upon them, as another prophet says: “You who have eyes that are purer than to behold evil, and cannot look upon wrong”(a)... See what divine care this is! What protection! What tenderness! For He does not take vengeance, nor is He disgusted by the deeds!

entries.section: 5. Let us cry out in humility without murmuring

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom But now, because his anger does not punish, neither does he regard the multitude of transgressions [15].

Some think that the meaning here is that what befalls a person in the way of calamities seems as nothing beside the punishment that man deserves. If God visits man in anger through the chastisements He permits, these are very light and small compared with the transgressions we commit.

“Neither does he regard (know) the multitude of transgressions”: here the talk is of God, who does not repay here for all the transgressions we commit, as though He overlooks them or does not know them, lest the hand of chastisement grow heavy upon us. In His chastening of us He is tender and compassionate, even if we count this chastening very harsh.

* God, who judges forever, is long-suffering for a long time. If He is long-suffering in bringing His wrath, it is because He keeps it to pour out later without end. Pain here is the portion of the elect, to prepare them to receive the heavenly reward. It is our portion to receive scourgings here, for He keeps eternal joy for us.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Rejoice while you are under the scourgings, for the inheritance is kept for you, because He does not cast off His people. He chastens for a while, and does not condemn forever.

St. Augustine * I choose that the Lord visit my sins and correct my transgressions here in this world, so that Abraham may say to me there what he said about poor Lazarus in his talk with the rich man: “Son, remember that thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things, and likewise Lazarus evil things: but now he is comforted, and thou art tormented” (Lk 16:25). For this reason, when the Lord rebukes and chastens us, we must not be ungrateful. Let us understand, then, that our rebuke in the present time is so that we may receive comfort in the future. And as the Apostle says: [But when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world] (1 Cor 11:32). For this reason Job also accepted all his sufferings willingly, saying: “What? shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?” (Job 2:10).

entries.section: 5. Let us cry out in humility without murmuring

paragraphs.text: Origen Therefore doth Job open his mouth in vain; he multiplieth words without knowledge [16].

Elihu came to this conclusion, that Job opened his mouth and cried out, but by his murmuring his words and cries were counted vain and without understanding. Job's complaint, in Elihu's eyes, is worthless babble, without knowledge or understanding, because it carried accusations against God's dispensation.
Why has Your hand been heavy upon me?!
* In my human weakness I often ask:
Why has Your hand been heavy upon me?
Why do You permit affliction for Your believers?
Why do You permit the wicked to triumph and exult?
* You answered me, O All-loving One, in the language of deed, not of dialogue; in my name and on my behalf You entered the garden of Gethsemane.
And You, the Ruler of all, began to be amazed and sorrowful.
In my stead You said: My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death.
You fell on the ground, You before whom all the heavenly powers bow down.
You said to God Your Father: Abba, Father, all things are possible unto You; take away this cup from me.
“Nevertheless not what I will, but what thou wilt” (Mk 14:36).
* Establish me in You, that I may utter what You uttered, and ask what You asked, and bear Your mind within me!
Then I will accept affliction with You, even the shame of the Cross!
I will accompany You on the road to Golgotha, and my soul will find rest.
* What do You ask of me in the midst of the furnace of affliction?
You ask to see my face and hear my voice.
I confess to You: I have turned my face to the world.
May Your Holy Spirit turn it back, that it may look to You.
I turned my converse to men; I thought they were able to save me, but their spirit goes forth, and they return to their dust.
Let me cry out to You, for You are my strong tower.
Affliction surrounds me, but it does not steal into my soul!
Outwardly there is bitterness and gloom, but inwardly there is exultation in You, O Heavenly One!

* In humility You cried out, O only-begotten Son, though You are one with Your Father in the same essence, and Your will is the same as His will; You surrendered Your will to Him, that He might do His will in You.
Grant me the spirit of humility, that my heart may cry out to You:
Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth!
* Welcome to affliction, as long as it is by Your permission.
I experience fellowship in the sufferings and the Crucifixion with You.
I taste the turning of my face to You; I see You and exult, and no power can separate me from You!
I cry out to You from my depths, asking that You do Your will in me!
Glory to You, O wonderful in His goodness, and all-wise in Your plans toward me!

1 Elihu also proceeded, and said: 2 “Suffer me a little, and I will shew thee that I have yet to speak on God’s behalf. 3 I will fetch my knowledge from afar, and will ascribe righteousness to my Maker. 4 For truly my words shall not be false: he that is perfect in knowledge is with thee.”
Elihu’s description of God’s power in the storm comes immediately before God’s own coming and speaking with Job. The storm and the rain are God’s agencies for judgment and for blessing [31].
Elihu also proceeded, and said: [1]
Suffer me a little, and I will shew thee that I have yet to speak on God’s behalf [2].
Elihu asks Job to be patient with him a little and to listen to him, for he has further arguments to bring concerning the justice of God and His providence.
I will fetch my knowledge from afar, and will ascribe righteousness to my Maker [3].

Elihu declares that he carries his knowledge, or engraves it like an inscription that cannot be erased. He brings it from afar, not from a distant place, but from the mighty works of God. He ascribes righteousness to God, whereas he believes that Job ascribes injustice to Him (Job 34:10-12).

It is as though he says: What I am about to tell you is not the common talk that many people know. It is the fruit of searching and of understanding the surpassing works of God, which have escaped many.
Perhaps he means that he enjoys his knowledge from afar, that is, from God, as a special gift.
For truly my words shall not be false:
he that is perfect in knowledge is with thee [4].
He assures Job that he will not speak idle words like his three friends, but will utter the truth, and that he is a man of complete knowledge.

God does not despise anyone who is earnest, but glorifies the righteous, even if they fall under afflictions. He shows them their sins and sets their affairs right if they repent, and He permits their destruction if they refuse repentance [5-12]. God permits suffering for the sake of instruction and discipline [15].
Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that Elihu tried to commend himself, as St. Paul did, in order to affirm that he was presenting great truths, and that Job would know this afterwards.

* Even the righteous often incline to praise what they say when they see that weak hearers do not take in their words. This is not because they are eager for their own praise, but in order to kindle in their hearers a burning desire to listen to them... So St. Paul, after speaking of many wonderful things, says to the Corinthians: “O ye Corinthians, our mouth is open unto you, our heart is enlarged” (2 Cor 6:11).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 2. How God deals with His children

paragraphs.text: 5 “Behold, God is mighty, and despiseth not any: he is mighty in strength of heart. 6 He giveth not life to the wicked, but executeth judgment for the afflicted. 7 He withdraweth not his eyes from the righteous: but with kings are they on the throne; yea, he doth establish them for ever, and they are exalted. 8 And if they be bound in fetters, and be holden in cords of affliction, 9 then he sheweth them their work, and their transgressions that they have behaved proudly. 10 He openeth also their ear to discipline, and commandeth that they return from iniquity. 11 If they obey and serve him, they shall spend their days in prosperity, and their years in pleasures. 12 But if they obey not, they shall perish by the sword, and they shall die without knowledge. 13 But the hypocrites in heart heap up wrath: they cry not when he bindeth them. 14 Their soul dieth in youth, and their life is among the unclean. 15 He delivereth the poor in his affliction, and openeth their ears in oppression.”
Behold, God is mighty, and despiseth not any:
he is mighty in strength of heart [5].

God is mighty in strength and in wisdom. There is no one, whatever his standing, whom God despises. He seeks everyone and cares for all, to secure justice for each person and not leave him wronged. Elihu confirms what he declared earlier (Job 35:14).

The work of the mighty Lord Christ is to support the weak and give them strength, and He does not belittle the strong. The Lord does not cast out the strong, for He Himself is the Almighty. But if He casts down those who seek their own glory, it is to grant them the grace of humility, so that they receive from the fullness of His power and strength and sing: “For the LORD JEHOVAH is my strength and my song; he also is become my salvation” (Isa 2:12).

Almighty God wishes to see in His children a spirit of leadership and strength, for He does not despise the mighty who hold authority. The humble Apostle Paul understood this, and says with full assurance: “Shall I come unto you with a rod, or in love, and in the spirit of meekness?” (1 Cor 4:21).
* A leader (a ruler) truly desires to imitate God if he uses his lofty power for the benefit of others.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 2. How God deals with His children

paragraphs.text: He giveth not life to the wicked, but executeth judgment for the afflicted [6].

The wicked think they are living when they seize the rights of others, enjoy pleasures and mock the righteous, but in truth they do not live, for eternal death comes upon them. As for the righteous and humble, though their lives may seem bitter because of afflictions, they will surely enjoy divine justice.

By the afflicted he means here the poor and the weak, who think that no one will support them and defend them against the rich and the powerful. God Himself judges for them and restores their rights to them.

* [But He does not save the wicked, and executes judgment for the poor] [6]. Holy Scripture is often inclined to call the humble [the poor]. They are referred to in the Gospel in this way, with the addition “in spirit,” where it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Mt 5:3)... God destroys the proud and sets the humble free by His judgment. Or He judges for the poor, because they are now wickedly wronged, and afterwards they come as judges over those who wronged them.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 2. How God deals with His children

paragraphs.text: He withdraweth not his eyes from the righteous: but with kings are they on the throne; yea, he doth establish them for ever, and they are exalted [7].

The eyes of the Lord never leave the righteous, whether they are rich or poor, in high positions or low. They are like a precious treasure in God’s eyes. He may permit trials to come upon them, but He will not forget them or ignore them. They enjoy a kind of honor and authority, and are counted as kings, while the world looks at them as people who are despised, rejected and without honor.
