God grants them authority in this world, and He also establishes them forever in a surpassing heavenly peace.
He does not forsake the godly (1 Pet 3:12), but honors them (1 Sam 2:8; Ps 113:7-8). They receive partial honor here (1 Pet 2:9; 1:6), and complete honor in the age to come (Rev 5:10; Job 22:5).

* It is sometimes thought that God turns His eyes away from the righteous because they are wounded here by the injustice of the wicked without His taking vengeance on them. In fact He dwells with His servants all the more when the injustice of their persecutor comes upon them, since He sees them bearing it in humility. Without doubt He looks to the reward that He will grant them there. Thus He does not turn His eyes away from the righteous.

Look how the one groans in his humility, while the other exalts himself and flourishes in his wickedness. One has his heart wounded, while the other boasts proudly in his evil. From which of them do God’s eyes turn away more: from the one who suffers injustice, or from the one who inflicts injustice on those he persecutes...?

Fittingly, the saints are called kings in the language of Scripture, because they rise above fleshly passions, restrain the pleasures of lust, soften the flame of greed, bend the haughtiness of pride, crush the suggestions of envy, and quench the fire of passion.
They are kings because they learn not to surrender to the emotions of temptations by accepting them, but to rule over them...

They are set forever on the throne of the kingdom of eternal glory, and receive the authority to judge others... So the Lord says to the church of Laodicea: “To him that overcometh will I grant to sit with me in my throne, even as I also overcame, and am set down with my Father in his throne” (Rev 3:21)...

It is not a contradiction that He declares in another place that His disciples will come on twelve thrones (Mt 19:28), and says here that they sit on His throne. By the twelve thrones He shows the general judgment, and by the throne of the Son He shows the particular loftiness of judicial authority.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 2. How God deals with His children

paragraphs.text: And if they be bound in fetters, and be holden in cords of affliction [8].

Elihu corrects the notions of Job’s friends, saying that even if the righteous are thrown into prison, subjected to harsh trials and troubles, bound in chains, laid as it were on a bed of pain and crushed by heavy calamities, the eyes of the Lord remain upon them. What they have come to should not be regarded as proof that they were hypocrites or that God does not care for them. For God has a wise plan for disciplining mankind, which ends in the happiness of those who accept discipline and in their glory at the proper time.

* The fetters of bondage are the detention in the present journey. Paul saw himself bound with these fetters when he said: “having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ” (Phil 1:23). He realized that he was bound with the bonds of poverty, looking to true riches and asking this for his disciples too: “that ye may know what is the hope of his calling, and what the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints” (Eph 1:18)... When we learn with much love about the heavenly glory, we feel more burdened when we commit sins.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 2. How God deals with His children

paragraphs.text: Then he sheweth them their work, and their transgressions that they have behaved proudly [9].

He shows them their lives and their evil works, by sending them messengers or prophets who declare to them their evil state (Job 33:23), or through their quiet reflections and their examination of themselves (Job 33:27), or by the work of the Holy Spirit, who reveals their lives to them. The purpose of their sorrows and afflictions, as Elihu says, is that they may find the opportunity to discover their lives and mend their shortcomings.

He also shows them how great and grave their transgressions have become. They thought themselves strong and great, instead of trusting in the living God; therefore He does not support them when afflictions come upon them.

entries.section: 2. How God deals with His children

paragraphs.text: He openeth also their ear to discipline, and commandeth that they return from iniquity [10].

By saying “He openeth their ear” he means that He gives them understanding, or teaches them, or gives them the desire to learn, so that they may grasp the reason for which they are disciplined; and He commands them to return from those evils that made Him visit them with sorrows and afflictions.

entries.section: 2. How God deals with His children

paragraphs.text: If they obey and serve him, they shall spend their days in prosperity, and their years in pleasures [11].

If they listen to His voice and serve Him as is fitting, they spend their lives in success and their lives are filled with joy. In other words, if afflictions bear the fruit of repentance for their sins, and they seek God’s mercies and serve Him, they live in prosperity. It is as though the purpose of afflictions is not to crush them, but for them to return to God, to enjoy His blessings and mercies and to have true happiness.

It is as though Elihu demands that Job not fix his eyes on his friends’ accusations so that his spirit is broken, and at the same time not suppose that God is violent and harsh, and not justify himself before God, but seek repentance and so enjoy the happiness he has lost.

* By “prosperity” he means upright conduct, and by “glory” (pleasures) he means the heavenly reward. Those who learn to obey the divine commandments spend their days in prosperity and their years in glory.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 2. How God deals with His children

paragraphs.text: But if they obey not, they shall perish by the sword, and they shall die without knowledge [12].

But if a man grows insolent and murmurs against God because of afflictions, the spear of death or the sword of death strikes him and he perishes. He dies not because of the afflictions, but because of lack of knowledge, or because of their folly.

A man’s murmuring against afflictions instead of repenting does not remove them from him, but makes them heavier, so that he is crushed by his murmuring. God does not withdraw His hand, which seems heavy with severe trials, until the man returns to Him and stops murmuring and complaining.

God usually begins with light chastisements; if they bear the fruit of repentance He removes them, but if a man’s heart grows hard by murmuring against God, the trial intensifies and increases until he realizes his weakness and returns to God with wisdom.

* There are some whom not even torments turn back from their corrupt habit. The prophet says of them: [Thou hast stricken them, but they have not grieved; thou hast consumed them, but they have refused to receive correction] (Jer 5:3). It is said of them under the figure of Babylon: “We would have healed Babylon, but she is not healed” (Jer 51:9). And also: [I will destroy my people; they return not from their ways] (see Jer 15:7). These become worse by being punished, because when pain comes upon them they either grow more hardened in their stubbornness, or, what is worse, they rush into blasphemy in wrath.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
But the hypocrites in heart heap up wrath:

entries.section: 2. How God deals with His children

paragraphs.text: they cry not when he bindeth them [13].

Elihu calls those who murmur against God hypocrites in heart, that is, the wicked. Instead of removing God’s wrath from themselves by repentance, they gather up more of His wrath. Although God in His love permits them to be bound by afflictions so that they may cry to Him in a spirit of humility, in their stubbornness they do not turn to Him and do not humble themselves before Him.

Through afflictions God calls them to accept His friendship, to know His secrets and to enter with Him into a fitting dialogue; but whoever exalts himself enters into enmity with God and condemns himself to destruction.
By the hypocrites he means here a class of the wicked who practice evil in defiance of God and with open stubbornness, so that they gather up for themselves the wrath of God (Rom 2:5).
Some, such as Umbreit, see that what is meant here is not God’s wrath, but that the hypocrites gather up wrath against God; instead of crying to Him they rebel against Him openly.

Since he speaks here of hypocrites, by their hypocrisy they not only deserve to fall under the wrath of God, who hates evil, but by trying to hide under the cover of self-righteousness and deceiving people into thinking they are righteous, they provoke God’s anger; for they practice evil knowingly and add deceit to evil, which is the mark of the deceiving enemy of good. Such hypocrites fall under chastisements, in the hope that they may turn from their evils, but often they do not care about chastisements however severe, just as they do not care about eternal punishment; so they do not cry to God to return to Him and abandon their hypocrisy. All that concerns them is to fix people’s view of them that they are righteous.

We can divide people into three classes: 1. The class of the wicked, who persist in evil and are not ashamed of their evils, whatever chastisements come upon them. 2. The class of the hypocrites, whose only concern is how people look at them, so they hide their evils and do not confess them even while under chastisement. 3. The class of true believers, who confess that they are sinners and believe in God who forgives sin; chastisement pushes these toward spiritual growth, a pledge of eternal glory.

* [The hypocrites and deceivers provoke God’s wrath] [13]. Whoever is a hypocrite is constantly troubled by two points: to learn how to conceal the truth of what he is, and to display what he is not, covering up his real faults and showing a goodness that is not real... When he speaks of hypocrites and deceivers he adds, very fittingly, not that they deserve God’s wrath but that they provoke it; for whoever sins in ignorance deserves God’s wrath, but whoever deliberately resists His commandments, knowing what is good and making light of it, though able to do good and unwilling, provokes God’s anger...

[They cry not when they are bound] [13]. Every wicked person who does not seek to appear holy, when severe chastisement comes upon him, is not ashamed to confess that he is wicked. But the wicked person who is held back by human judgments to show holiness, even when he is beaten with the rod, refrains from showing his evil, because he has grown accustomed to appearing holy... But we are “bound” when the blows of the rod come upon us. We cry out loudly when we are bound, whenever we confess our sins while under the blows. When the blows of chastisement fall upon hypocrites they do not bring them to sincere confession. They fear to be exposed as sinners if people look. When they are now beaten to the end, and aware that they are being led to eternal punishment, they still want to remain in the sight of people as they are, since they have learned to make a show of themselves.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Everyone sees the thief “hypocrisy” carrying everything off before their eyes, and rejoices in it! What a new kind of robbery, which attracts people and delights them while they are being robbed!

* There may be one who gives his alms before people but avoids showing it off, and there is also one who does not give it before people but boasts of it in secret. For God does not repay a charitable deed according to how it is done, whether before people or not, but according to the intention of the one who does it.

St. John Chrysostom * They are accustomed to walk about in honored garments so as to receive great honor because of them, and they follow the same course in many things that lead them to temporal glory.

entries.section: 2. How God deals with His children

paragraphs.text: Father Theophylact Their soul dieth in youth (they die in youth), and their life is among the unclean [14].
This is what the Psalmist says in the Psalm (Ps 55:2).

The literal translation: “They shall die in the youth of their souls.” They may live to old age according to the body, but their souls are counted immature; they spent most of their lives without spiritual growth and without benefit to themselves or to their brethren; their years are counted as a single day (Ps 90:4), or as a few hours.

[Their life is among the unclean], among adulterers, fornicators and the ungodly. The word translated “unclean” came to mean those whose lives were devoted to idol worship for the practice of sinful fleshly relations. In the Septuagint it reads: “Their life is wounded by angels.”

They are counted like the people of Sodom and Gomorrah, to whom no more tenderness or mercy is shown, for they ought to have borne witness to true righteousness, practicing it and preaching it, but they devoted their lives to corruption.

* [Their soul dies in a storm, and their life is among the effeminate] [14]... Their souls have become accustomed to human praise in a deadly calm, but they die in a sudden storm... For human praise torments the righteous, while it puffs up the wicked.

The righteous are tormented (by human praise of them) and so are purified, while the rejoicing of the wicked (in human praise of them) qualifies them for eternal punishment. Since they do not seek the glory of their Creator, they rejoice in their own praise; but those who seek the glory of their Creator are tormented by people’s praise of them, lest what is said of them outwardly have no existence inwardly; and lest what is said, even if it exists inwardly, become vain in God’s eyes because of these very honors; and lest people’s praise draw their hearts away from firmness and bring them down to a feeling of self-satisfaction.

But if they see that their praise leads to the glory of God, they long for it and welcome it. It is written: “That they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven” (Mt 5:16)...
The proud devote their effeminate hearts to human praise, because they are corrupted by self-love. Of these it is said in another place: “For men shall be lovers of their own selves” (2 Tim 3:2)..
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 2. How God deals with His children

paragraphs.text: He delivereth the poor in his affliction, and openeth their ears in oppression [15].
The word “poor” here does not mean merely the destitute, but the suffering and the tried, as Elihu explained.
Those who repent and return to God, God rescues from their trials and restores them to their life before the trials came.
“He openeth their ears,” giving them understanding of His divine dispensation. This principle occupies Elihu’s mind; he repeated it several times.

* The poor man is saved from his affliction when the humble man is freed from the troubles of this journey. For he is under pressure in continual trials so that he may long to seek the joy of true comfort. Therefore it follows: [and openeth their ears in oppression]... Tribulation opens the ears of the heart that the prosperity of this world had closed.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

16 “Even so would he have removed thee out of the strait into a broad place, where there is no straitness; and that which should be set on thy table should be full of fatness. 17 But thou hast fulfilled the judgment of the wicked: judgment and justice take hold on thee. 18 Because there is wrath, beware lest he take thee away with his stroke: then a great ransom cannot deliver thee. 19 Will he esteem thy riches? no, not gold, nor all the forces of strength. 20 Desire not the night, when people are cut off in their place. 21 Take heed, regard not iniquity: for this hast thou chosen rather than affliction.”
Even so would he have removed thee out of the strait into a broad place, where there is no straitness; and that which should be set on thy table should be full of fatness [16].

In the midst of affliction God snatches believers as from the lion’s mouth and lifts them into freedom, as into a broad place, more than they had before the trial (Ps 18:19; 31:8; 118:5), and He supplies them with a rich table (Ps 23:5; Isa 25:6).
The phrase “where there is no straitness” appears in the text cited in the writings of Pope Gregory (the Great) as: “which has no foundation beneath it.”

* Everyone who forgets the way of life and throws himself into the darkness of sin pushes himself into a pit or a hole, whatever it may be. And if he becomes very weighed down by the habit of committing sin and unable to climb out, he becomes like one shut up in a pit; and when, after being in the strait of an evil habit, he is brought into the spacious chamber of good works, it is said of him: “He would remove thee out of the strait into a broad place.” For a person is led safely out of the strait into the broad place when he returns by repentance from carrying the heavy yoke of evil to the freedom of good works.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
But thou hast fulfilled the judgment of the wicked: judgment and justice take hold on thee [17].

Some see that Elihu rebukes Job, telling him that if, while under sufferings and chastisements, he imitated the murmurers, he falls with them under the same sentence. All that Elihu saw in Job was that he murmurs against God, so that he is like one who completes what the wicked do and adopts their spirit and thought, and so qualified himself to fall with them under divine justice.
* Every sin has no foundation, since it has no being in its nature. Evil has no being in itself... The corruption of evil has no power to stand on its own.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Because there is wrath, beware lest he take thee away with his stroke:
then a great ransom cannot deliver thee [18].

Elihu warns Job against behaving like the murmurers, lest God draw him away with a stroke from Himself, and no ransom of any amount could save him, even if Job has become destitute and has no ransom to offer.

The murmurer is not redeemed by his wealth or his brothers; as the Psalmist says: “They that trust in their wealth, and boast themselves in the multitude of their riches, none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give to God a ransom for him” (Ps 49:6-7). The stubborn man who is always complaining and murmuring keeps for himself the terrible divine wrath, with nothing to redeem him and no one to redeem him. His life is taken away and he throws himself into hell.

“Therefore beware of murmuring, which is unprofitable; and refrain your tongue from backbiting: for there is no word so secret that shall go for nought: and the mouth that belieth slayeth the soul” (Wis 1:11)
“Unto a wise servant shall they that are free do service: and a man of understanding will not murmur” (Sir 10:28)
“Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer” (1 Cor 10:10)
* The man who has a grievance (or murmuring) rising up in his heart is far from God’s mercy.

Father Isaiah * If food is lacking to you, first pray and ask God, then go out of your cell and do not put your hope in the one to whom you go, thinking: A man will give me; but say: {God will supply my need}(a). If you go to someone and ask for something and he does not give it to you, do not murmur, but understand that God did not command him to receive your blessing.

St. Arsenius * The man who has known his weakness and helplessness has reached the limit of humility. What directs God’s favors to man is thankfulness that continually stirs in the heart. And what directs trials upon the soul is murmuring. God bears all of man’s weakness, but He does not bear the man who always murmurs without disciplining him. The mouth that always gives thanks receives blessing from God, and grace dwells in the heart that holds fast to praise and thanksgiving.

* He who disputes against discipline drives fatherly mercies away from himself. He who murmurs against trials has them multiplied upon him. He who is not disciplined here and crushed by trials is tormented there without mercy.

St. Isaac the Syrian * An elder said of poor Lazarus: “We did not see that he did any virtue, except that he never murmured against that rich man who had no mercy on him, and he was thankful to God for what he was in; and for that alone God had mercy on him.”
Garden of the Monks Will he esteem thy riches?
no, not gold, nor all the forces of strength [19].
Does the wicked man think that God fights him on account of his wealth and his gold, or all the sources of strength on which he relies?

Perhaps he refers here to the wealth in which Job lived, which did not rescue him from God’s hand. He also refers to the sources of his strength, for Job was known for his wisdom, his reputation, his authority, his social position and the dignity of his old age; none of these was able to rescue him from God’s wrath, as Elihu says. And as the wise man says: “Riches profit not in the day of wrath: but righteousness delivereth from death” (Prov 11:4).
Desire not the night, when people are cut off in their place [20].

It is clear that he means the night of death, which Job had long desired in order to be freed from what he was in. The Lord Christ spoke of death as the night, when no one can any longer do any work (Jn 9:4).
If Job desired death to be freed from his sufferings, Elihu invites him to review his accounts, for death does not rescue the wicked from pain; only repentance and return to God do.
Some see that this phrase means that some of the wicked long for the night of death, to pass out of the present world so that others may take their place and receive their share of sufferings.

Some see that Elihu is reproaching Job, telling him: Do not long for death, but leave the matter in God’s hands, lest God hear you and send death to you while you are in this state, and you be cut off and your soul be in terror and trembling.
Take heed, regard not iniquity: for this hast thou chosen rather than affliction [21].

Elihu says: You insult God’s providence, which permitted sorrows to come upon you to discipline you, and you longed for death instead of the sorrows. This longing is sinful, for it offends God’s providence and wisdom.

Man often prefers iniquity to pain, for he does not care about his iniquity while exerting every effort to be rid of troubles and pains. It is stupidity and ignorance, for man adds to his pains ever more sins and iniquities.

entries.section: 4. God teaches and does not compel the acceptance of His teaching

paragraphs.text: 22 “Behold, God exalteth by his power: who teacheth like him? 23 Who hath enjoined him his way? or who can say, Thou hast wrought iniquity?”
Behold, God exalteth by his power:
who teacheth like him? [22]

Elihu’s aim is to draw Job’s thought to God, so that he contemplates His power, wisdom and fatherhood and accepts Him as a divine, heavenly Teacher, and does not direct blame or accusations at Him or complain of Him.

In the Septuagint: “Who teaches like Him?” “Who is mighty like Him?” As the prophet Micah says: “Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and passeth by the transgression of the remnant of his heritage? he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy” (Mic 7:18).
The heavenly Teacher is mighty; He disciplines, and He is able to give life and raise up. It is not right for us to sin against His tenderness and fatherhood!

God in His fatherhood teaches and disciplines: “Blessed is the man whom thou chastenest, O LORD, and teachest him out of thy law” (Ps 94:12). And since He is all-powerful and all-wise, He does not at once explain what lies behind His teaching and discipline, because of the human mind’s inability to grasp the divine plan. Therefore it is fitting for the believer to receive God’s teaching, not to suppose that he is teaching God: “Who hath measured the Spirit of the LORD, or being his counsellor hath taught him? With whom took he counsel, and who instructed him, and taught him in the path of judgment, and taught him knowledge, and shewed to him the way of understanding? Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance: behold, he taketh up the isles as a very little thing” (Isa 40:13-15). And the Apostle says: “For who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor?” (Rom 11:34). “For who hath known the mind of the Lord, that he may instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ” (1 Cor 2:16).
God teaches, but He compels no one to accept the teaching [22-23].

*The art of medicine, according to Democritus, heals the diseases of the body, and wisdom frees the soul from its anxieties. But the good Teacher, Wisdom, who is the Word of the Father who took a human body, cares for the whole nature of His creation.
He is the Physician of mankind, in whom is all sufficiency, the Savior, who heals body and soul together.

* The heavenly Guide, the Logos, is called the Leader when He calls mankind to salvation... But when He acts as physician or tutor His name becomes “the Instructor”... For the sick soul needs an instructor to heal its passions. Then it needs the teacher who gives it understanding... “the revelation of the Logos.” Thus, since the Logos wishes our salvation step by step, He uses an excellent method: at the beginning He guides, then He corrects, and finally He teaches.

* Who is He? Learn briefly that He is the Word of truth, the Word of incorruption, who renews man by restoring him to the truth. He is the goad that urges to salvation. He is the destroyer of perdition and the one who drives death away. He builds the temple of God in men, taking them as a dwelling for God.

The sick need a Savior, and the lost need a guide; the blind need one to lead them to the light, and the thirsty need the living spring from which whoever drinks will never thirst; the dead need life, the sheep need a shepherd, and children need a teacher; all mankind needs Jesus!

St. Clement of Alexandria * A great lawgiver came down from heaven and became a teacher of the world. The world was enlightened by His teaching, so that no one would any longer desire the perishing possessions. (The First Epistle)

St. Jacob of Serugh * Moses was a lawgiver, and Joshua was a lawgiver, and the prophets also were lawgivers. We can call them all lawgivers, but there is no one like this Mediator among the lawgivers.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Christ appears to each one according to his need. To those who need joy He comes as a vine; to those who need to be in the Father’s presence He comes as a door; to those who need someone to present their prayers He is the Intercessor among them, the High Priest; and to sinners He is the Lamb (slain) for their sanctification.

He is everything to everyone without His nature changing, but remaining as He is. He remains, and the work of His sonship will not change, yet He adapts Himself to our weakness, as an excellent physician or a teacher full of tenderness. He is the Lord Himself; He did not receive lordship by advancement, but the work of His sonship is natural.

entries.section: 4. God teaches and does not compel the acceptance of His teaching

paragraphs.text: St. Cyril of Jerusalem Who hath enjoined him his way? or who can say, Thou hast wrought iniquity? [23]
Does God take instructions from any man while He governs the world and cares for all creation? Is there any man who obliges God to some command? God always does what is right; He will never err.
Job dared to explain to the Lord what ought to be done (Job 34:10, 13).

* It is as though it were said: How can he be blamed whose works cannot be examined? For no one can judge what he does not know. Therefore we must rather remain silent under His judgments, the more we see that we do not understand the reason for His judgments.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

24 “Remember that thou magnify his work, which men behold. 25 Every man may see it; man may behold it afar off. 26 Behold, God is great, and we know him not, neither can the number of his years be searched out.”
Remember that thou magnify his work, which men sing of [24].

Instead of accusing God, praise Him and glorify Him in His works (Ps 111:2-8; Rev 15:3); by this you will realize that His works are unseen and beyond comprehension, and that He is wise and good. As the Apostle says: “For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse” (Rom 1:20).

Since we are called to fellowship with the heavenly ones forever, so as to be counted as having taken the rank from which the devil fell, we must train ourselves in inward praise of God and in glorifying Him without ceasing for His dealings with us.

* In Holy Scripture angels are sometimes called “men,” and perfect persons also are called “men.” As for an angel being called a man, Daniel bears witness to it, saying: [Yea, the man Gabriel, whom I had seen] (Dan 9:21).

Men sing to the Lord when the heavenly spirits or the perfect teachers show us God’s power; yet His work is not known, and even those who preach Him revere His judgments that cannot be comprehended. They know the One whom they preach, but they do not know the reason for His works; by grace they know Him who created them, but they cannot grasp His judgments, which are done by Him and are beyond their understanding. The Psalmist bears witness that Almighty God is not clearly seen in His works, saying of Him who “made darkness his secret place; round about him” (Ps 18:11).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Every man may see it;
man may behold it afar off [25].

Every person looks at the visible creation and sees in it the wisdom and power of God revealed. So it is fitting for us to follow God’s wisdom and power through His works, and so to perceive what the men of God have set down, saying: “O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!” (Rom 11:33).

* Since man was created rational, it was fitting for him to conclude by reason that the One who created him is God. He now sees through reason the power of His authority. But when it is said: [All men may see it], it is rightly added: [man may behold it afar off]. For to see Him afar off is to see Him as present not in His person, but to think of Him wholly with wonder at His works.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Behold, God is great, and we know him not, neither can the number of his years be searched out [26].
God is all-powerful; we cannot examine Him. He is eternal; His existence has no set time that limits it. Our knowledge of God is partial (1 Cor 13:12), because He is unlimited (Ps 90:2; 102:24, 27).

He speaks to us of His eternity, without beginning and without end, in human language so that we can touch it. “The number of his years cannot be searched out,” for He is not subject to time, but is its Creator.
* Since God is present everywhere, it is said of Him: “Behold.” He is said to be present even to those who do not see Him.

He rightly says that He is beyond our knowledge, although he said before that all men see Him. This means that although He is seen by the mind, His greatness cannot be penetrated by our senses. For what we know of the splendor of His majesty is little, and the more we think we grasp His power, the further we move from knowing Him. Our mind is caught up on high, but it is surpassed by the immensity of His majesty, and we know Him only in part when we feel that we are unable to know Him through our own merits.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

27 “For he maketh small the drops of water: they pour down rain according to the vapour thereof: 28 which the clouds do drop and distil upon man abundantly. 29 Also can any understand the spreadings of the clouds, or the noise of his tabernacle? 30 Behold, he spreadeth his light upon it, and covereth the bottom of the sea. 31 For by them judgeth he the people; he giveth meat in abundance.”
For he maketh small the drops of water (for he draweth up the drops of water).
They pour down rain according to the vapour thereof [27].

Elihu offers a practical example that man lives with, especially in that age: how water evaporates from the sea and then descends as rain used in farming, and also the growth of the herbage on which the flocks graze. God in His wisdom draws up the vapor to become clouds moved by the winds, and turns the clouds into rains that let fall small drops, so that man and beast may live.

*He who planned everything by measure and weight, who, according to Job, numbers the drops of rain (Job 36:27) [LXX], knows how long His work remains, and how long He permits fire to destroy (the world).

St. Basil the Great * There are two kinds of righteous in this life: those who live uprightly and teach nothing, and those who live uprightly and teach according to how they live. It is as on the face of the sky: some stars come without storms following them, and other stars come and pour water on the thirsty earth in abundant rains.

Often there are persons in the holy Church who live uprightly but do not know how to preach uprightness. They are truly stars, but they appear in a dry atmosphere. They can give light to others by the example of their good lives, but they do not rain by the word of their preaching. And there are other persons who live uprightly and rain this uprightness on others by the word of preaching; so the stars appear in the heavens and bring rains that change others by the merits of their lives, and they rain well by the word of preaching. Did not Moses appear as a rain-star? Did he not appear in this heaven...? Did not Isaiah appear as a rain-star, he who first saw the light of truth and held fast to it, and watered the dryness of unbelief by proclaiming the word of prophecy?

When the Lord removed the prophets He sent the apostles to take their place, to rain like downpours, after the preaching of the outward (literal) Law had ceased, when the early fathers withdrew... It is said by Jeremiah of the rejection of Judaism: [The rain-stars have stopped and there is no longer a latter rain] (see Jer 3:3).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* A short while ago the floods swept over us late and destroyed us. Count the drops of rain that fell on this city alone. No, I say, if you can, count only the drops that fell on your own house, and not on the city, in one hour! You cannot!
Then know your weakness, and learn from this moment the power of God [who counts the drops of rain](b) over the whole world, not only now, but throughout all times.

And the sun is God’s handiwork. For all its greatness it is like a point in the midst of the heavens. Contemplate the sun, and then look in amazement at the Lord of the sun. “Seek not out the things that are too hard for thee, neither search the things that are above thy strength: but what is commanded thee, think thereupon” (Sir 3:22).
St. Cyril of Jerusalem Which the clouds do drop and distil upon man abundantly [28].

In the Septuagint: “The rains come down, and the clouds overshadow multitudes of people. It has been appointed for the animals to know the ordering of their dwellings. When you contemplate these things, is not your mind stirred, and your heart made ready to leave your body?”

As the clouds receive the vapor that rises toward heaven, they return it as drops of rain that come down on many multitudes for their benefit. This thing, which happens abundantly in the world, comes to pass without men thinking about it, and it is one of the countless natural laws that God established for the benefit of man and beast. He gave the beasts of the wild to know their dwellings, where there is water through the rains or the springs, though they are not rational beings able to think and plan.

* “Which the clouds do drop” [28]... In Holy Scripture clouds sometimes signify changeable people, sometimes the prophets, and at other times the apostles. Solomon expresses the changeableness of human thought by saying: “He that observeth the wind shall not sow; and he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap” (Eccl 11:4). He calls the unclean spirit “wind” and those who are subject to him “clouds,” whom he drives back and forth, here and there, since temptations often follow one another in their hearts from storms of suggestions...
By clouds he also means the prophets, as said by the Psalmist: [darkness of waters in the clouds of the air] (see Ps 18:11), that is, the wisdom hidden in the prophets.

By clouds the apostles are also meant, as said by Isaiah: “I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it” (Isa 5:6). They are stars, since they shine by the merits of their lives, and they are clouds, since they water the thirsty earth of our hearts with streams of heavenly knowledge. Were they not clouds, the prophet would not say when looking at them: [Who are these that fly as a cloud] (Isa 60:8)...

* [And they cover everything from above] [28]. When the cloud covers the air from above, if we lift our eyes to heaven we do not see the sky but the cloud... Because we are carnal, when we seek to obtain heavenly things we lift our eyes to the sky, as though our sight were bound to bodily things, and so we wish to learn spiritual things through them. But our reasoning is not allowed to pass over divine things unless it is first formed by examples of earlier saints; therefore our eyes, as it were, look toward heaven, but they see through the cloud. They seek to grasp the things that belong to God, but only with effort can they marvel at the things given to men.

Look, we are aflame with zeal for consecration to the Lord and love of Him, yet we are formed in this consecration and love by our contemplation of these clouds. For who is as consecrated as Peter? And who is as full of love as John?

We are also covered by the lives of the fathers (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Joshua, Samuel and David) like clouds spread over us, so that we are watered and bear abundant fruit. We see the clouds first when we look to heaven, for we first see with wonder the works of the righteous, and afterwards we go deeper by our experience of heavenly things. But the lives and virtues of these clouds, that is, these early fathers, would not have been opened to us unless other clouds, that is, the Apostles, explained them to us by the light of their preaching.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Also can any understand the spreadings of the clouds, or the noise of his tabernacle? [29]
Elihu asks: {Who is able to understand the mystery of the spreading of the clouds and the noise of a pavilion, or the sound of thunder?} (Ps 18:11; Isa 40:22; Ps 105:39).

At the beginning of history man was not able to understand the causes that form the clouds and bring down the rains. Now, with the advance of science, man has discovered some of these secrets, and his amazement at the wonderful Creator has increased; he has also realized that, however far his knowledge reaches, it is difficult, indeed impossible, for him to control the natural phenomena.
Behold, he spreadeth his light upon it, and covereth the bottom of the sea [30].

The Jews see in the clouds, the thunders and the lightning wonders that bear witness to God’s power and care. These phenomena appear like God’s pavilion or tent. The clouds spread across the sky, and the light, or lightning, also appears spread out for moments. It is as though these phenomena reveal wonderful things that seem opposed to one another. The spreading cloud casts shadows on the earth, while the lightning that is produced by the clouds spreads lights that pierce the clouds.
Dense clouds with lightning present a striking and creative picture.

The Psalmist sees in the dense clouds and the lightning something like a creative heavenly garment, and says: “Who coverest himself with light as with a garment: who stretchest out the heavens like a curtain: who layeth the beams of his chambers in the waters: who maketh the clouds his chariot: who walketh upon the wings of the wind” (Ps 104:2-3).

While God reveals the falling of the rains through the shining lightning, He covers the depths of the seas with the abundance of the rains that fall and pour into the seas as though covering their depths.
God’s hand extends to work on high in the heavens amid the dense clouds, on the earth where the rains fall, and in the depths of the seas. He is the Controller of all.

* [For when He has spread the cloud as His tent, and lit it with His light from above, He will cover the sea also.] The Lord spreads out His cloud when He opens the way of preaching for His servants, scattering them in every direction over the whole world. He says well: “as His tent,” because a tent is usually pitched on a journey. And when the holy preachers were sent into the world, they made a way for God. On this journey the tents of God are the hearts of the saints, with which He covers Himself on the way while resting...
These clouds are now rightly called His tent, because when God comes to us by His grace He is hidden in the hearts of His preachers.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
For by them judgeth he the people; he giveth meat in abundance [31].

God uses the clouds, rains, dew, storms, whirlwinds, winds, hurricanes and tornadoes, thunder, lightning, drought and flood for discipline, out of His tenderness toward man and for his upbuilding. And these same things God uses to provide mankind and the animals with food and drink in abundance.

The Psalmist says: [Thou crownest the year with thy goodness; and thy paths drop fatness. They drop upon the pastures of the wilderness: and the little hills rejoice on every side. The pastures are clothed with flocks; the valleys also are covered over with corn; they shout for joy, they also sing] (Ps 65:11-13). And as the Apostle Paul says: “Nevertheless he left not himself without witness, in that he did good, and gave us rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness” (Acts 14:17).

* [For by these He judges the peoples, and gives food to many mortals] [31]. By the words of the preachers, that is, the drops of the clouds, and by the lightning of miracles, God without doubt judges the peoples, for He calls their terrified hearts to repentance. For when they hear heavenly things, and when they listen to the miraculous works, they turn back in their hearts and grieve over their former evils, and fear the eternal torments...
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 7. A hymn to the almighty Wisdom

paragraphs.text: 32 “He covereth his palms with light, and commandeth it against the enemy. 33 His thunder telleth concerning him, the cattle also concerning his rising.”
He covereth his palms with light, and commandeth it against the enemy [32].
God uses the lights (and the lightning) in His hands; with the lightning He disciplines the wicked, and with the lights He shines upon the righteous.
The Septuagint reads: “He covers the light in His hands.”

It is as though God holds in His hand the lightning, over which we have no authority, and directs it as He wills. The lightning, which appears to move very swiftly, moves only at God’s direction; it is a natural instrument in His hand.
If God permits His light to be withheld from the proud, His grace works in them by allowing trials to come upon them, so that they return to Him with their hearts and are enlightened by His light.

* [He gives light concerning the mighty (the powerful)] [32]. The mighty in fact are those who boast of haughty thoughts. It is said by Isaiah against them: [Woe unto them that are wise in their own eyes, and prudent in their own sight!] (Isa 5:21). And Paul says against them: “Be not wise in your own conceits” (Rom 12:16). The light is hidden from these mighty ones, because without doubt He withholds the knowledge of the truth from the proud... There are many in the Church who disdain to be little, and do not cease to be great in their own eyes instead of humble.
* Here also, after it was said that the light withdraws from them, he added: [and commandeth it to return again].
Pope Gregory (the Great)

entries.section: 7. A hymn to the almighty Wisdom

paragraphs.text: His thunder telleth concerning him, the cattle also concerning his rising [33].

The thunder that accompanies the lightning bears witness to God’s authority and greatness. Even in the sound of the thunders God cares for the flock; His greatness appears not only in His great and mighty works, but in His tenderness even toward the flock and all creation.

Some see that he is speaking here of the sound of the water of heavy rains, for the irrational flock senses by instinct the coming of rain as it approaches, and so flees to find a shelter for itself, while man sees evil coming toward him and does not flee from it.

* [He declares to his friends that it is his, and that he ascends to it] [33]. A friend of the truth is one who loves upright conduct. The Truth Himself says to His disciples: “Ye are my friends, if ye do whatsoever I command you” (Jn 15:14). For the friend is called [a keeper of the soul](c), and so he strives to observe God’s will in His commandments, and so deserves to be called His friend. Therefore the Truth Himself says to these same disciples: “I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you” (Jn 15:15)...

The promise is rightly added: [that he ascends to it]. What is harder than for a man born on earth, who bears frail earthly members, to ascend to the heights of heaven and penetrate the secrets of the highest spirits? But the Creator of these very spirits came to us, and declared Himself man, and even became less than we... He who became lower than the angels for our sake makes us equal to the angels by His humility. By His death He also taught us not to fear death, by His resurrection to trust in life, and by His ascension to cherish the inheritance of the heavenly city...

Since we have become one with Him, He returned alone, in us, to the same place from which He came alone. He who is always in heaven ascends daily to heaven, because He who remains in His divinity above all things raises Himself up daily in the body of His becoming man. May human weakness not despair, but rejoice in the blood of the Only-Begotten Son, since the cost is so great... Let mankind, in its zealous care, make for itself the place where its Head has gone before it, and let those who are bound to His commandment for a good life be strengthened in hope by His example, so that mankind may feel assured of heaven! Let it hope for the heavenly city. Let it know that it is the angels, and rejoice that, being joined to its Head, it has come to be preferred even above the angels!
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Teach me, train me, that I may enjoy You!
* Teach me, O wonderful heavenly Teacher.
Though Your hand seems severe, Your heart is wide with love for me; You are the wise and almighty Father.
* You permit Your children to be in distress, but the rod of sinners will not rest upon them.
You carry them in Yourself; You raise them from the dunghill to sit with the nobles of Your people.
* The wicked stretch out their hands against me, supposing that You do not see and do not care!
In Your love You permit injustice for a time, to prepare my depths for surpassing glories.
You prepare me as a king, that I may enjoy Your eternal kingdom.
* The wicked think they are binding me with the fetters of injustice.
They did not realize that I am set all the more free, that my depths may soar to You and I may be with You!
* In the midst of distress I listen to Your voice; my soul is filled with joy, and my heart exults in You.
I discover my sins, and my soul groans.
But I see You, the Savior of the world, and I cling to Your cross.
* In the midst of the world’s humiliation You open my ear by Your Holy Spirit, and I enjoy Your divine promises.
You bring my heart out of the strait into the broad place.
My soul grows wide with love, even for those who trouble me.
I enter into the table of love.
I enjoy the richness of Your feast.
And my soul is satisfied with You!
* Instead of murmuring at the multitude of those who oppose me, my soul rejoices in You, and does not cease to offer unceasing sacrifices of thanksgiving.
I possess You, O heavenly Treasure.
So the gold of the world becomes dust in my eyes.
And the wealth of the world is nothing!
* Who is like You, wonderful Teacher!
You teach me by Your commandment, train me by Your love, carry me in Yourself, and raise me to the throne of Your grace!
* What teacher is like You, O heavenly Father!
You bring me into discipleship to You.
I meet You as Teacher, and You pour out upon me the treasures of Your learning and knowledge.
You heal the wounds of my soul, my heart and my mind.

You raise me from the death of sin and grant me immortality; You take away my shame and give me fellowship in the heavenly glory; You open my eyes so that I do not stumble in the valley of this world.
You water me with Your Holy Spirit, so that I do not thirst for the life of the world.
* Who can search out Your wisdom, O wonderful Wisdom of God!
Can the clay converse with the potter?
Can the earthly one grasp the secrets of the heavenly Creator?
Yet in Your fatherhood and humility You ask me to reason with You!
I speak with You and delight in You!
* Blow like the storm upon my soul, and let it be filled with strength.
Rain with the waters of Your Holy Spirit, and turn my wilderness into Your garden!
Spread Your light over me, and my darkness will be scattered.
Glory to You, my loving and good Teacher!

1 “At this also my heart trembleth, and is moved out of his place. 2 Hear attentively the noise of his voice, and the sound that goeth out of his mouth. 3 He directeth it under the whole heaven, and his lightning unto the ends of the earth. 4 After it a voice roareth: he thundereth with the voice of his excellency; and he will not stay them when his voice is heard. 5 God thundereth marvellously with his voice; great things doeth he, which we cannot comprehend.”
At this also my heart trembleth, and is moved out of his place [1].

As the features of the storm began to appear, Elihu felt that an inner storm was sweeping over his heart, and he trembled at his sense of the divine presence. He felt a disturbance not from anxiety and loss of peace, but from the trembling of his heart as it was struck with wonder before the greatness of the Creator. It was as though his heart had become a temple of the Lord, shaking before the glory of God.
By saying “at this” he means: “when I heard the thunder of the divine majesty.” Perhaps the storm through which God spoke with Job had already begun.

Although Elihu spoke at length in describing these natural phenomena, the storms, thunder and lightning, as bearing witness to God’s greatness, power and authority, yet as soon as the storm began his inner being shook. Thunder and lightning often terrify not only the wicked but at times even some of the righteous.
It is said of the Emperor Caligula that he used to run to hide in a corner of his palace or get under the bed when he heard thunder and saw lightning.

* Here, after contemplating the light of the eternal city, it is rightly said: “At this my heart trembleth.” It is as though he says: I went out of myself in excess of wonder, and because the mind was inspired with a spirit of new hope, it abandoned its old ways of thinking.

It is well said: “and is moved out of his place,” because the delight of the present life is the place of the human heart. But when our heart is touched by divine inspiration, the love of eternity takes its place. For this reason the mind moves from its place by contemplating eternal things. It leaves the lower things and fixes its thought on the higher.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* A brother told me: When my mind was caught up to this glorious vision, I saw it gazing into the sea of life, swimming in depths of light, breathing in the fragrance of life, marveling and transfigured with great joy, covered with light, and boiling with the working of love and joy in a wonderful radiance... And at the time when this gift is in the soul, even if all creation were voices and tumult, it could not make the mind come down from its place or return to itself, so absorbed is it in wonder and amazement, and so cut off from every link with the senses of the body.

* When you look upon Him thus united with you, He takes your own self captive from before your mind, so that He alone appears to your mind, if your power of sight is able to do so. And if you are not able, let it remain in continual remembrance. Thus the mind of man is gathered in itself by the remembrance of God and by gazing upon Him. This is what our fathers call guarding the mind, and there is nothing as high as it among all the virtues and works.
The Spiritual Elder Hear attentively the noise of his voice, and the sound that goeth out of his mouth (and the roar that goeth out of his mouth) [2].

“Hear attentively”: he repeats the word hearing twice, and likens his words to a storm of thunder and lightning, as though it were a continual pounding upon his house and lightning shining before the eyes. So Job and those with him have no excuse, but must listen with all their senses.
The storm continued until the Lord Himself spoke from heaven to Job.

The Lord’s speaking with His people or His believers is often linked with the storm, and as the Psalmist says: “The God of glory thundereth... The voice of the LORD shaketh the wilderness; the LORD shaketh the wilderness of Kadesh” (Ps 29:3, 8). “God in the storm,” not only in nature, but also in the inner storm of the soul; in our depths He declares Himself through the storms that sweep over our inner nature. The Word of God came to enter the soul and stir up in it an inner revolt against evil, to destroy in us the old man and give us the new man.

Surely Adam and Eve joyfully awaited the voice of God as He came walking in the garden, but after their fall into sin the voice of the Lord God became a cause of fear and terror to them, and when they heard it they hid themselves from the presence of the Lord (Gen 3:8). Because of our attachment to earthly things we have come to hear His voice in the storm and through the thunder: “The LORD thundered from heaven, and the most High uttered his voice” (2 Sam 22:14). When Moses the prophet received the Law, it is said: “And all the people saw the thunderings, and the lightnings, and the noise of the trumpet, and the mountain smoking: and when the people saw it, they removed, and stood afar off” (Ex 20:18; see Ex 19:16). And the Psalmist says: “The voice of thy thunder was in the whirlwind: the lightnings lightened the world: the earth trembled and shook” (Ps 77:18; see Ps 97:4; 135:7). It is also said: “When he uttereth his voice, there is a multitude of waters in the heavens, and he causeth the vapours to ascend from the ends of the earth; he maketh lightnings with rain, and bringeth forth the wind out of his treasures” (Jer 10:13, 16).

* By this saying (Ex 29:18-19) Scripture established that creatures have no strength to hear the voice of the Creator. And if they hear it they almost die from fear of it. Therefore He graciously gave us the Incarnation at the end of time, so that the sons of men might hear His voice and not die.
St. Ephrem the Syrian * Heaven stands trembling, growing weak until it becomes nothing before Your greatness, yet the womb received You and contained You and bore Your glory.

St. Jacob of Serugh * It is fitting for us to note that the voice of God is said to be heard not in joy but in trembling. Certainly every sinner who thinks only of earthly things and carries a heart sunk in lowly thoughts, when he is suddenly touched by the inspiration of divine grace, realizes above all else that all his deeds are punished by the eternal Judge. Therefore the voice of the Lord is at first in trembling, to be turned afterwards into sweetness...

So we can understand from the thunder of His voice the power of fear, and from the sound of His mouth the sweetness of consolation. For those whom the Holy Spirit fills He warns about their earthly deeds, and afterwards comforts them with hope in heavenly things, so that they may rejoice the more afterwards in the certainty of the reward, to the extent that they were in fear when they looked only at the punishments. Paul says: “For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father” (Rom 8:15)... Behold, you see that the trembling of conversion has turned into strength; they punish their sins with remorse, and rise even to the exercise of rule, to receive this power from God, the power at whose hands they used to tremble.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

The Psalmist says: [The voice of the LORD breaketh the cedars; yea, the LORD breaketh the cedars of Lebanon] (Ps 29:5). The voice of the Lord in the thunder often breaks the cedar trees, even the cedars of Lebanon, the strongest and hardest of their kind. The winds of the storm sometimes uproot them with their roots and shatter their lofty, towering crowns, so that they are laid flat on the ground. These trees represent the proud, self-reliant souls; the voice of the Lord, or the incarnate Word of God, came to bring these souls into a life of humility through the sorrow of repentance.
And God chose the weak things of the world to confound the mighty (1 Cor 27:1), so that they too might enjoy Him who for their sake, though Almighty, took the form of weakness.

* [The voice of the Lord breaketh the cedars]. By repentance the Lord breaks those who glorify themselves by the honor of their temporal origin, and who stand ashamed when He chooses the lowly of this world to reveal His divine power in them.
St. Augustine He directeth it under the whole heaven, and his lightning unto the ends of the earth [3].
His speech is like the lightning that, as man sees it, darts from one end of the world to the other, so that in the twinkling of an eye all see His tenderness and all hear His voice.

[Unto the ends of the earth]: the Hebrew text reads “to the wings of the earth,” likening the whole earth to a bird that spreads its wings and flies; and behold, it enjoys the voice of the Lord and His light, to soar in the very heavens.

Although the Lord’s speaking is personal to the believer, yet as a lover of His creation He speaks openly under all the heavens, and His voice is heard in the four corners of the world, so that the heavenly and the earthly all hear His voice and grasp His secrets. In His speaking He cares for the righteous who are great in faith, as He does for sinners, purifying them even from the slightest weaknesses.

* It is as though he says plainly: He who manages the high matters does not forget even the very small things... He cares for everything equally, and governs everything equally. He who is present in all places is not limited to any one place, and does not care for different places with partiality...

He cares even for the most trivial of our weaknesses. His light is seen as at the ends of the earth under the heavens. After passing over the lofty works of those who stand before Him, He cares for the ways and deeds of sinners by enlightening them with His grace. And although He does not show wonderful signs in the lives of the believers, He does not forsake these believers, but works in them... Certainly the end of the earth is the end of sinners. For many forget God during their lives, bound to fleshly lusts, but when the grace of God works late in their lives they return to God.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

St. Jacob of Serugh sees that the thunder that accompanied the divine presence when Moses received the Law points to the sound of the trumpet that goes before the bridegroom coming to the wedding, as though the aim of the Law or the divine commandment were our joyful union with the heavenly Bridegroom.

* He blew into the mist as into a horn, and thunder came forth that split the earth with its power; by this too the order of that wedding was honored, for the bridegroom enters his chamber at the sound of the horn...
Moses gave this sign, which he alone knew, before he came down to the people...

Creatures were shaken by the voices and dreadful visions, for the Lord of the wilderness had come down upon Sinai in the mist; the thunders spread far over the top of the mountain, and cried out and signaled: The King is here. The trumpets cried out mightily on the height of Sinai, that the earth might gather at the appointed time of the sound: The Lord is there.
St. Jacob of Serugh After it a voice roareth: he thundereth with the voice of his excellency; and he will not stay them when his voice is heard [4].

“After it,” that is, after the lightning or the illumination, where the light of the lightning is seen accompanied by the sound of thunder. This is what the Lord in His loftiness does toward man: He shines with His light and thunders with His voice, that man may enjoy the divine promises or respond to His chastisements of him.

“He will not stay them when his voice is heard” perhaps means that He does not delay His lightning with which He shines upon the heart and mind of man, or does not delay the rain that accompanies the storms, so that the earth may be watered with the waters of divine grace, and the wilderness be turned into a joyful garden bearing the fruit of the Spirit.

Some see that although man is sure of the appearing of the lightning and the hearing of the thunder, it is very hard for him to trace these phenomena, and to determine their places and movements exactly. So the Word of God touches the believer; his eyes are opened to see God’s love and to hear the divine promises, but they remain beyond his grasp, for they surpass the human mind.
“He will not stay them when his voice is heard”: when man hears the sound of the thunder, he cannot seize the lightning and delay it so as to determine its place or its distance, and so on.

* O you who have been bitten by the sin of death, behold, life is hung up before you. Look to the cross and live. If you do not look to it you die. Fall upon it like the dead man upon the bones of Elisha (2 Kgs 13:21). Hear His voice like Lazarus from the clefts of destruction. Do not cut off the hope of your life, for your hope is fixed in Him. The dead man does not loathe relying on the Giver of life. It is not good for one who has a wound to keep away from the door of sorrow... It is the duty of the sinner who persists not to cease asking for mercies even if he does not obtain forgiveness. If the sinner supposes himself unworthy of mercies, and knows that he is unworthy to receive them, yet does not cease to beseech, he is the one who deserves mercies.
St. Jacob of Serugh God thundereth marvellously with his voice;
great things doeth he, which we cannot comprehend [5].

In a wonderful description he says that God is present in the whole storm, directing it as He wills, doing wonders that the human mind cannot comprehend. “Marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well” (Ps 139:14). It is as though he says that the sound of His thunder is exceedingly astonishing, declaring His power, majesty and wisdom. Not only in the thunder and lightning, but in everything we perceive the wonderful work of God.

So Elihu was preparing the minds of all those present for the appearing of the Lord and His speaking through the storm. The Psalmist says: “The waters saw thee, O God, the waters saw thee; they were afraid: the depths also were troubled. The clouds poured out water: the skies sent out a sound: thine arrows also went abroad. The voice of thy thunder was in the whirlwind: the lightnings lightened the world: the earth trembled and shook” (Ps 77:16-18).

* God thunders marvellously with His voice, for He pierces our hearts with His secret power in an inexpressible way. While His voice masters us with fear by His secret working and forms us in love, He declares in a silent way how He longs for us to follow Him...

“Great things doeth he, which we cannot comprehend (mysterious).” The man who has surrendered to earthly things and been tyrannized by evil lusts suddenly becomes zealous for new pursuits and cold toward his old habits; he renounces outward concerns and is passionate for inward contemplation. Who can express the power of this high voice...? He speaks with His voice even by the Apostles, and He Himself enlightens within the hearts of the hearers. Paul gives his testimony, saying: “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1 Cor 3:6). For although they do not grant the hearing of the divine voice in the minds, they were sent to deliver the words from outside.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

What are the great things that we cannot comprehend, when God thunders with His wonderful voice, other than the work of His hidden grace in us, by which He makes a wonder of us through His effective word and His rich grace? For the Word of God thunders with wonderful power and works richly within us, and as the Psalmist says: “He sent his word, and healed them, and delivered them from their destructions” (Ps 107:20).

* He who sees the wonders of God (Ps 1:9) fulfilled not only openly in his body but also invisibly in his soul declares them, and indeed these wonders are higher and loftier. For men, being earthly and led by what they see with the eye, marvel more that the dead Lazarus rises in the body than that Paul the persecutor rises in the spirit (Jn 11; Acts 9). But the visible wonder calls the soul to enjoy the light, whereas by the invisible wonder man passes on to speak of all the wonders of God.
St. Augustine * Do not be ashamed of the gift of grace, for it is more wonderful than the power to raise the dead and work miracles.
St. John Chrysostom

6 “For he saith to the snow, Be thou on the earth; likewise to the small rain, and to the great rain of his strength. 7 He sealeth up the hand of every man; that all men may know their Creator. 8 Then the beasts go into dens, and remain in their places. 9 Out of the south cometh the whirlwind: and cold out of the north. 10 By the breath of God frost is given: and the breadth of the waters is straitened. 11 Also by watering he wearieth the thick cloud: he scattereth the cloud of his light. 12 And it is turned round about by his counsels: that they may do whatsoever he commandeth them upon the face of the world in the earth. 13 Whether it be for correction, or for his land, or for mercy, he causeth it to come.”
For he saith to the snow, Be thou on the earth;
likewise to the small rain, and to the great rain of his strength [6].

Elihu speaks of snowstorms, where heavy snow falls, not hail. Because of the intense cold of the air, the rain turns to snow, which falls and settles on the earth, making of it a dazzling white carpet that reflects the light in a creative way. This snow points to God’s wisdom, which He grants to His Church and in which the believers share, so that they bear the pure righteousness of Christ and reflect His splendor.
At His command the light rain falls, as do the heavy rains; for all the phenomena move only at His command, since they are under His authority.

* When the Psalmist says: [Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow] (Ps 51:7), what do we understand by the snow but the hearts of the saints that have become white with the light of righteousness...? The water then is the minds of the preachers, which stand firm in high meanings of things when they are lifted up by contemplating heavenly things...

Certainly Paul was raining water on the earth when he knew the Law in a carnal way. But when he was lifted up to heavenly knowledge he was turned into snow. He changed his former feeble knowledge into the firmness of true wisdom, and returned and came down to his brethren, for he returned as snow to the earth. For even after reaching the heights of virtue, he knew how unworthy he had been, saying: “Who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor” (1 Tim 1:13). See how he took care to call his mind to remember his weakness, in order to bear the weaknesses of others. Paul returned, as one who had been in heaven, to the earth from which he was taken, he who after reaching the great mysteries of his contemplations remembers that he had been a sinner, so that he might benefit sinners by his humility....

[The rains of the strength of His power] are the preaching of His humanity, of which Paul spoke (1 Cor 1:25), and also: “For though he was crucified through weakness, yet he liveth by the power of God” (2 Cor 13:4). But the saints preached the weakness of His humanity in this way so that they might also enter into the hearts of the hearers with the power of the divinity.

May we hear through the thunder of the cloud the rains of His power: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (Jn 1:1). Let us hear the rains of His weakness: “And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us” (Jn 1:14).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* For we have been renewed by the renewal we received in Baptism, and renewed through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, and we shall be renewed also by the resurrection, as it says in another text of David: “so that thy youth is renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps 103:5). Know then the manner of our renewal: [Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow] (Ps 51:7), and in Isaiah: [though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow] (Isa 1:18). And whoever is changed from darkness (the darkness of sin) to the light of virtue and to grace has indeed been renewed. Therefore he who was formerly stained with foolish filth now shines more brightly than snow in whiteness.
St. Ambrose He sealeth up the hand of every man; that all men may know their Creator [7].

In the lands where snow falls during snowstorms, everyone, especially the farmers, had to stay in their houses during the winter period, as though God in His love sealed their hands so that they might rest in the bitter winter season from work outside the house, and go out after the winter to work with energy and strength.

Nature, which God created to serve us, has become a teacher to us. Through the succession of the seasons mankind perceives God’s plan toward man. Man learns that there is a time for work and a time for rest. So it is fitting for man from time to time to enter into the rest of contemplating God’s work and to seek the shining of God’s Spirit upon him, to reveal to him God’s love as well as his own weaknesses and faults, so that he may always offer continual repentance with joyful hope and thanksgiving to God, the forgiver of sins.
* Since men make light of thinking about the sins they commit, when they hear forcefully the heavenly firmness they realize the weight of their evil deeds that waste their lives...

This passage (Job 37:7) can be understood in another sense. For the Creator is almighty over all creatures that have no feeling or reason, so that man is bound not to be ignorant of what he does. He is bound by the law of nature, so that he knows whether what he does is right or wrong. For why would he be condemned for his conduct if he were ignorant of what he did...? Therefore it is well said: [For wickedness shows cowardice, when it judges itself that its conduct deserves condemnation] (see Wis 17:10)... Over against this John said: “If our heart condemn us not, then have we confidence toward God” (1 Jn 3:21).
Pope Gregory (the Great)

St. John Chrysostom sees that God’s hand, manifest in nature and bearing witness to His surpassing power, drives man to discover his own weakness together with his mighty possibilities in Almighty God, and while he is weak he realizes that in God he is strong. “Let the weak say, I am strong” (Joel 3:10). As the Apostle Paul says: “for when I am weak, then am I strong” (2 Cor 12:10).

* He says this is the reason for His creative works, the reason for the existence of cold and heat, and for the blowing of the winds in a way that seems aimless. Could He not have provided a harmonious whole? God did not do so, in order to prevent by every means the proud and arrogant mind.

He does this so that every man may know his weakness. In contrast to this, the formation of the body and the course of our life have been arranged in a way that leads us to humility, so that we learn to behave with moderation and to realize our weakness. Let us say like Abraham: “I am but dust and ashes” (Gen 18:27), and like David: [I am a worm, and no man] (Ps 22:6), and like the Apostle: “And last of all he was seen of me also, as of one born out of due time” (1 Cor 15:8).
He created man weak, but man counts himself strong, and therefore became weaker. Yet God sometimes shows His power in order to give us understanding (and strength) within us.
St. John Chrysostom * God the Word urges us and strengthens us to keep away from the demons and to follow the living God alone through His Son.
We who were for a time immersed in fornication now accept purity alone.
We formerly used the arts of magic, and now we consecrate ourselves to the good, living God.
Our chief concern above all was to gain riches and possessions, and now we bring what we have to be common property, from which every one in need may take.

We hated one another and destroyed one another because of the difference of our ways, refusing to live with those of another tribe, but today, since the coming of Christ, we live together in harmony. Today we pray for our enemies, and try to persuade those who hate us without cause to submit to the good principles of Christ and His commandments, so that they may share with us the same joyful hope of receiving a reward given by God, the Ruler of all.
St. Justin Martyr Then the beasts go into dens, and remain in their places [8].

Elihu sees God’s wisdom not only with regard to man, but even with regard to the wild beasts of prey. In the winter period, with its bitter cold, these animals are bound to remain sluggish in their dens and caves, almost without movement, and so they do not need much food to feed on.

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that Elihu is speaking of the beasts of prey, the devil and his hosts, who enter the hearts and thoughts of the wicked and settle in them as their kingdom. As for the righteous, the demons attack them, and may break into their depths for a time, but they will not be able to settle in them.

* What is meant by the beast but our ancient enemy, who violently set out to deceive the first man and mar the perfection of his life by his evil counsel? Against this one the promise came in the words of the prophet concerning the restoration of the Church of the elect to her former state: “No lion shall be there, nor any ravenous beast shall go up thereon” (Isa 35:9)...

I think it should be noted that of this beast it is said not that it enters its lair, but that it settles in it. For it sometimes enters the minds of the good and suggests unseemly thoughts, terrifies them with temptations, and seeks to corrupt the uprightness of the spirit with the pleasures of the flesh. It also strives to carry pleasure as far as the person accepts it. It enters the minds of the good, but cannot settle in them, because the heart of the righteous man is not a lair for this one.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Out of the south cometh the whirlwind: and cold out of the north [9].

In the Bible, where most of the events recorded took place in the Middle East, the south winds are regarded as hot, while the northern are cold. When the cold north winds come, the sky is filled with clouds with thunder and lightning, and when the hot south winds blow, the clouds are scattered and the mist disappears.

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the hot whirlwinds come from the south and the cold from the north; the first point to believers who are fervent in faith, on whom the sun shines as at midday, and the second to unbelievers who are deprived of the sun and so remain in spiritual coldness.

* Whoever learns to do God’s work in this world, this valley of tears and toil, becomes joyful like the diligent farmer who sows the seed even in the death of winter. Can the cold winds and the harsh weather keep him from his work? Surely not! So it is fitting for us to look at the troubles of this life. Amusements are thrown in our way by the evil one, with the aim of making us turn aside from the good works we were created to do. Look what the Psalmist says: [He that goeth forth weeping...](a) Truly he finds cause for weeping; each one of us finds it. Yet we must go on, doing God’s good works on our way.
How wretched we would be if we were called to work earnestly only to weep, without looking to any fruit of our labor. How wretched we would be if we found no one to wipe away our tears.

But we know that the Holy Spirit works so that we continue sowing amid our tears. For the Spirit promises us through the Psalmist that we shall return astonished with joy! We shall bring the fruit of our labor as an offering to Him.

St. Augustine * “Awake, O north wind; and come, thou south” (Song 4:16)... Let us direct our attention to the way in which the queen makes the north wind go away from her and then return to her. She does not command it to be still, as the Lord Christ commanded the storm to be calm when He was walking on the waters (Lk 8:23-24), but she commanded the south wind to blow and that no contrary wind should oppose her; she said to the north wind: “Awake.” What is the reason for the movement of these winds? The Proverbs speak of these winds: “Whosoever hideth her hideth the wind, and his right hand grasps oil” (Prov 27:16), but the north wind does not blow from a person’s right hand toward the west... and the movement of the sun is toward the west. You understand the truth of what these words contain of mysteries: the sun rises from the east and hastens toward the west, that is, toward the powers of darkness; the north lies on the right of the sun and receives insults during its journey that ends in darkness. Therefore the undisciplined person finds himself, like the north wind, behaving and doing shameful deeds. This evil wind on the right is filled with covetousness when it raises heaps of money matters, as if they were sand or dust, and as a result the north wind cooperates with each person’s faults and blows on his right side; but if this wind is very strong, it changes and overturns things and removes the enjoyment of joy. Therefore the bride makes the north wind, whose strength comes from the passions, flee on her own responsibility: “Awake, O north wind.”

The north wind points to the opposing powers (to God), and this is clear to anyone who examines the nature of the visible truth. For who does not know the course of the sun after its rising? It appears to move toward the south and sets in the west. And the experts say that the earth is spherical, so that if half the earth is lit by the sun, the opposite half is dark, lying in the region of the earth’s shadow. And since the north pole of the earth is continually cold and is neither warmed nor lit by the rays of the sun, the power that controls darkness holds souls captive and makes them rigid; the Song calls this freezing “the north,” that is, the influence of the darkness of winter.
