If God cared for the lifeless creation that He brought out of nothing, and cared for the laws of the sky, the falling of snow or the blowing of winds or the falling of rains, and cares for the wild animals and the birds of prey, how then should He not care for the affairs of man, for whose sake He created all these?

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the lioness here refers to the proud Judaism, when it accepts faith in the Lord Christ through the preaching of the Church, for the Lord Christ Himself satisfies the souls of its children.

entries.section: 9. God's care for the irrational animals

paragraphs.text: When they couch in their dens (when they crouch in their lairs), and abide in the covert to lie in wait? (and lurk in their thicket to lie in wait?) [40]

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that he speaks here of the period between the passion of the Lord Christ and the descent of the Holy Spirit on the feast of Pentecost, when the apostles and disciples ceased from ministry, so they were like the lioness that crouches in her lair and lurks in the thicket in a state of lying in wait. They were waiting, in fear of those who opposed them, until they should be clothed with power from on high to begin the preaching.
They resemble the lioness who stays in her lair with the little cubs until the lion brings the prey to them.

entries.section: 9. God's care for the irrational animals

paragraphs.text: Who provideth for the raven his food? when his young ones cry unto God, they wander for lack of meat? [41]

Wonderful is God in His care and providence for His creation, for He cares even for the young ravens, and gives them their food (Ps 147:9). Man cares for the creatures useful to him, but God cares for all creation. He listens even to the cry (croaking) of the young ravens.

It is said that ravens do not care for their young, so the young croak as though to God, and God gives them their food. They teach us to cry "Abba, Father" (Rom 8:15), for He hears us even if our parents do not hear us. As the psalmist says: [When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up] (a).

If He likened the Jews who were coming to faith to the lioness whose cubs' needs God satisfies, then He likens the Gentiles to the ravens, and God cares for these and those: "He giveth to the beast his food, and to the young ravens which cry" (Ps 147:9).

* The animals receive their food when beastlike minds feed upon Holy Scripture. But food is given to the young ravens, that is, to the sons of the Gentiles, when their longings are refreshed by our conversations with them... The young ravens, that is, the holy preachers coming from the Church of the Gentiles, truly do not rely on themselves but on the power of their Savior; therefore it was well said: [when his young ones cry unto God], for they realize that they can do nothing by their own strength.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Grant me to perceive the greatness of Your providence
* For my sake You laid the foundations of the earth, and set it up as upon pillars.
None knows its hidden mysteries but You.
The heavenly beings looked upon Your works for my sake, and came forward like a harmonious chorus, sang and praised with a spirit of exultation, and all shouted because of Your love and care!
You set boundaries for the sea.
You shut it in as with barricades and doors.
You broke its haughtiness and the pride of its deeps!
Let me go down to the depths of the sea and walk about, and be amazed by its hidden treasures.
* With every dawn I stand in amazement, I see the sparks of light begin to shine.
Who can determine its place? Who can measure its dimensions?
What a mighty and wonderful Creator You are!
* The sun rises to give joy to the earth; with every morning I see it as though it were new!
I touch in the rays of the sun the splendor of Your grace.
My soul exults in Your daily works!
* I look at the clouds; who can comprehend their size!
Who knows precisely their weights?
Even the storms and the snow and the ice, all of them do not escape Your hand.
They work by Your permission!
* All nature You make subject to me, You care even for the rains to water the earth for me.
How wonderful! You do not ignore even the wild beasts of the wilderness!
You care for me as a king whom You set up on the earth, and You care for the animals and the birds; even lifeless creation is an object of Your care!
You provide the beasts of prey with food in the wilderness or in the forest.
And You hear the croaking of the young ravens, and You sustain them!
Glory to You, O Shepherd of all, in Your love!

1 "Knowest thou the time when the wild goats of the rock bring forth? or canst thou mark when the hinds do calve? 2 Canst thou number the months that they fulfil? or knowest thou the time when they bring forth? 3 They bow themselves, they bring forth their young ones, they cast out their sorrows. 4 Their young ones come to maturity, they grow up in the wilderness; they go forth, and return not unto them.
Knowest thou the time when the wild goats of the rock bring forth? or canst thou mark when the hinds do calve? [1].

Most of mankind is not occupied with the wild animals that roam the desert or the forests, but what occupies it is its own work and its own animals, such as flocks, horses, dogs, cats, etc. But God, the Creator of all, cares even for the animals of the wilderness, for their preservation, their bearing of young, their food and drink and their dens.

When a man and his wife realize that the wife has become pregnant, they are concerned to know the time of the birth and to observe the labor. And they often turn to specialist doctors to follow the pregnancy until the birth takes place. Thus the birth of a child costs man much care and material expense and psychological and financial preparation; so who cares for the wild goats and hinds when they are pregnant? God Himself tends them and cares for them; will He not then care for man, His beloved creature, so very dear to Him?

We can say, after the example of the Apostle Paul who said: "Doth God take care for oxen?" (1 Cor 9:9), [Doth God take care for the bringing forth of the wild goats and the labor of the hinds?] Yes, He is concerned with the human wild goats and hinds who work by His Holy Spirit, and strive to bring forth souls for the Lord. They strike with their feet the heads of serpents to kill them, and each puts its head on the other, and all work together for the gaining of every soul for the Kingdom of God. Then the spiritual teacher sings with the Apostle Paul, saying: "For though ye have ten thousand instructers in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel" (1 Cor 4:15). "I beseech thee for my son Onesimus, whom I have begotten in my bonds" (Phlm 1:10).
Pope Gregory (the Great) offers us a symbolic interpretation of the conception of the wild goats and hinds.

* It is the custom of the hinds (the females) to kill the serpents they find, and the serpents try to bite their feet. It is said that when crossing rivers each of them rests her head on the hind in front of her, and so does not feel the weight of her head. Why was Job asked about the bringing forth of the wild goats and hinds, unless because they refer to the character of the spiritual leaders?

For they are truly like the wild goats that bear young among the rocks, because through the teachings of the Fathers, who are called rocks, they bring forth souls by their guidance... It was said by Jeremiah of the teachers who in negligence leave the children born to them: "Yea, the hind also calved in the field, and forsook it" (Jer 14:5).

They are like the hinds who live by destroying sins, that is, dead serpents, and by destroying their sins they burn all the more with longing for the fountain of life. Therefore the psalmist says: "As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God" (Ps 42:1).

It is as though it were said to Job: You think that you are working on a high level, yet you have not known beforehand the time in which the spiritual masters are sent into the world to bring forth children by the teaching of the early Fathers, and by their striving gather for me the souls that are won.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Canst thou number the months that they fulfil? or knowest thou the time when they bring forth? [2].

Man is not concerned with counting the months that the wild animals complete while pregnant, nor does he care about the time of birth, and even if he were concerned, he would not know the exact time of the birth.

If man is ignorant of these things that surround him on the earth he inhabits, does he think he is able to comprehend what is in the mind of God and in His heart? Can he comprehend God's plan toward him and the extent of His love for him?
They bow themselves, they bring forth their young ones.
They cast out their sorrows [3].
The birth of the young of wild animals is hard, and no man helps them, yet their young are born safe through God's care for them, and they forget their weariness and pains.

The birth of children, especially in advanced countries, takes enormous effort, whether at the level of states or families or individuals, and costs the world much. But the birth of wild animals costs almost no one anything.
For the animals "rise early and bring forth their young ones. They cast out their sorrows."
May the spiritual teachers trust in the wonderful work of God who works through them to bring forth sons for Him in the Gospel through the riches of God's free grace!

* When the saints think of the progress of their hearers, they come into a state of conception, as in the womb. For I present one among many who resembles the hinds, Paul, who speaks like one roaring from the intensity of the pain of labor. He says: "My little children, of whom I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you" (Gal 4:19).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Their young ones come to maturity.
They grow up in the wilderness.
They go forth, and return not unto them [4].

The young of the wild animals soon reach maturity, that is, they grow. For the young of wild animals, or of most animals in general, need no long time nor anyone to teach them suckling and walking and movement, etc. Unlike man, who needs a long period of training to learn to walk and to depend on himself. It is a wonderful divine gift for the animal as for man. The animal needs no one to teach it, because its mother is unable to arrange that, but man needs someone to teach him and a long period in which, while he learns to walk and the manner of eating, etc., he absorbs from the family many customs, enjoys a collective culture, and benefits from the experience of those before him! God has set everything in wisdom, both for the animal and for man!

"They go forth, and return not unto them": the young of animals go out after a short time to seek their own food, and do not remain a burden on their mothers. But for human beings it continues for years extending to tens, the family supporting him until he completes his practical studies or his training for a certain profession and becomes independent of his parents.

5 "Who hath sent out the onager free? or who hath loosed the bands of the wild ass? 6 Whose house I have made the wilderness, and the salt land his dwelling. 7 He laugheth at the multitude of the village. Neither regardeth he the crying of the driver. 8 The range of the mountains is his pasture, and he searcheth after every green thing.
Who hath sent out the onager free? or who hath loosed the bands of the wild ass? [5]
Some of the Fathers see in the onager and the wild ass, which frolic in the wilderness without hindrance, symbols of those who walk in the life of solitude in the freedom of the Spirit.

* The wild ass that dwells in solitude means the life of those who dwell far from the press of people. It is fittingly said "free" also, because the toil of worldly conduct is great, the mind is confused by it, even if its labors are acceptable to them. To be freed from this state of bondage it is necessary to desire nothing in this world. For men seek after riches, and the enemy presses with a kind of terrible yoke of bondage.

But he who frees the neck of his mind from the dominion of temporal desires enjoys a kind of freedom in this life... The Lord saw this heavy yoke when He said: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Mt 11:28)... For the Lord looses the bands of the wild ass when He tears from the mind of His chosen ones the fetters of weak dangers, and in His mercy tears to pieces all that binds their brilliant thought.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* The wilderness is the mother of stillness, it is the calm and the harbor that saves us from all troubles.
St. John Chrysostom * The mere sight of the wasteland gives the soul stillness, and kills in us the passions of the body.

Mar Isaac the Syrian * Abba Mark said: "This is the reason why stillness is good: that a man does not see in it what is harmful to his soul, and the thing that is not seen does not reach the soul, and what is not in the soul does not stir up in it the memory of sights nor make the passions (that is, the inclinations of the soul) rise up in it, and a man enjoys within himself a deep calm and a manifold peace [or delights in the abundance of peace (Ps 37:11)]".

* An elder was asked: "Why did Abba Anthony say to Abba Paul his disciple: Go and dwell in silence until you receive the temptations of the demons?" The elder said: "Because perfection comes to the monk from spiritual conduct, and spiritual conduct arises from the inclinations of the heart, and purity of heart comes from the inclinations of thought, and the manner of thinking is built upon unceasing prayer and the struggle with demons. But unceasing prayer and the struggle with demons, whether in thoughts or in visions, have no opportunity to exist without stillness and solitude".

* A brother asked Abba Cronius: "What shall I do to cure the forgetfulness (or negligence) that enslaves my spirit, since before I perceive anything I am led into sin?" The elder said to him: "When the strangers seized the ark of the covenant because of the sins of the children of Israel, they took it to the house of their god Dagon, and then Dagon fell to the ground" (1 Sam 5). The brother said: "What does this mean?" The father said to him: "If the demons try to capture a man's spirit by their own means, they push him so as to lead him to an unknown hidden passion (that is, an inclination of the soul), and here if his spirit returns to seeking God and remembers the eternal judgment, the passion is driven out at once and disappears. It is written: In returning and rest shall ye be saved; in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength" (Isa 30:15).
The Garden of the Monks Whose house I have made the wilderness, and the salt land his dwelling [6].

The tame ass is often shut up in a stable inside the field or the house, not moving in it, but the wild ass finds freedom of movement so that it counts the wilderness its own house, and dwells in a suitable region.

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that for him who practices the life of solitude and stillness the whole desert becomes his house, he moves in it in safety and tranquility, and dwells even in the salt places that inflame man with thirst, so that he is ever hungering and thirsting for fellowship with the Lord.

* [Whose house I have made the wasteland, and the salt land his dwelling (tent)]... Those who live in isolation, that is, those who are freed from bodily passions, dwell in stillness of heart, just as the Lord gave the wilderness as a house to the wild ass, so that the crowds of bodily passions do not press upon him...

Saltiness suits the burning of thirst, so since the saints live in the dwellings of this life (that of stillness of heart), and burn with the daily warmth of their longing for the heavenly city, it is said that they make their dwellings in the salt land. They are burning with thirst continually, as it is written: [Blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness: for they shall be filled].
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Of this number of the perfect, or, if I may call them so, the tree of the saints that has budded and brought forth blossoms and fruits, are the "ascetics"...

The Lord spoke of them with Job in a symbolic way, saying: "Who hath sent out the onager free? or who hath loosed the bands of the wild ass? Whose house I have made the wilderness, and the salt land his dwelling. He laugheth at the multitude of the village. Neither regardeth he the crying of the driver. The range of the mountains is his pasture, and he searcheth after every green thing" (Job 5:39-8). The book of Psalms also says: "Let the redeemed of the LORD say so, whom he hath redeemed from the hand of the enemy" then continues saying: "They wandered in the wilderness in a waste where there was no way. They found no city to dwell in. Hungry and thirsty also, their soul fainted in them. Then they cried unto the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them out of their distresses" (Ps 2:107, 4-6). Jeremiah also describes them, saying: "It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth. He sitteth alone and keepeth silence, because he hath borne it upon him" (Lam 27:3, 28). And the words of the psalmist come from the heart: "I am like an owl of the ruins. I watch, and am as a sparrow alone upon the house top" (Ps 6:102, 7).
Father Piamun He laugheth at the multitude of the village.
Neither regardeth he the crying of the driver [7].

The wild ass laughs at the multitude of the village when they try to catch him and surround him, for he quickly slips from their hands. "Neither regardeth he the crying of the driver," for he is not like the tame ass which fears the wrath of him who drives it, being exposed to beating. The wild ass feels that he is in a happier state than the tame ass.

If we take the symbolic interpretation of Pope Gregory (the Great), who says that the wild ass refers to those who walk the way of stillness and solitude, then these cannot be shut up by the crowds in narrow concepts, nor can any desire or sin drive him according to its whim.
The range of the mountains is his pasture, and he searcheth after every green thing [8].
He who walks in the spirit of true stillness lives as in a circle of holy mountains, seeking the heavenly pasture.

* The mountains of pasture are also the heavenly powers of the angels, since they support us by their ministry to us and their help... We can also take the mountains of pasture to be the lofty sayings of Holy Scripture, of which the psalmist says: "The high hills are a refuge for the wild goats" (Ps 104:18). For those who know how to practice the leaps of contemplation ascend the high peaks...
"And he searcheth after every green thing," for he truly dries up all the things that take shape for a time and wither and lose the sweetness of the present life.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

9 "Will the wild ox be willing to serve thee, or abide by thy crib? 10 Canst thou bind the wild ox with his band in the furrow? or will he harrow the valleys after thee? 11 Wilt thou trust him, because his strength is great? or wilt thou leave thy labour to him? 12 Wilt thou trust him that he will bring in thy seed, and gather it into thy threshing floor?
Will the wild ox be willing to serve thee, or abide by thy crib? [9]

"The wild ox," in the writings of Pope Gregory (the Great), is the rhinoceros, and he sees that it refers to the pride of this world or the powers of its evil kingdom which destroy men with a spirit of pride. The believer does not expect the powers of evil to serve him, nor does he lodge at his crib, where the word of God is as food for the soul. Pride destroys the believer and does not build him, and corrupts his understanding of the word of God, so that his depths are not satisfied by it.

* The rhinoceros is often understood as pride, as we have been taught by the testimony of the prophet who says: [I said unto the boasters (the wicked), Do not boast (do no evil), and to the sinners, lift not up the horn] (Ps 75:4). To what then does the rhinoceros refer but to the power of this world or the very powers of darkness belonging to its kingdom, who exalt themselves in the pride of vain arrogance...

Here it is rightly said to the blessed Job, as a representative of the holy Church: [Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve thee? or abide by thy crib?] By the crib here is understood Holy Scripture itself, upon which the holy animals feed with the food of the word, of whom it was said by the prophet: "Thy congregation hath dwelt therein" (Ps 68:10). Therefore our Lord also, when He was born, was found by the shepherds in a manger, because His incarnation, which refreshes us, we recognize in the Scripture of the prophets.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

Since Job thought he was able to subdue everything to his will, God said to him: {Begin with the rhinoceros, show me your intelligence and your power, can you make the rhinoceros a tame animal that serves you instead of the animals you lost of camels and donkeys? Show me your power: can you make this animal approach your crib, and eat of the food you used to provide?} Canst thou bind the wild ox with his band in the furrow (Canst thou bind the wild ox with a rope to the line of the plow?)
Or will he harrow the valleys after thee? [10]

It is as if He says to him: If you cannot use the rhinoceros instead of camels and donkeys, can you use it instead of oxen, binding it to the plow to till the land (the furrow is the line of the plow)?
Wilt thou trust him, because his strength is great? or wilt thou leave thy labour to him? [11]
The rhinoceros as a wild animal is stronger than the donkey and the ox, so can man replace his donkey or his ox with a rhinoceros to serve him?

It befits man to realize that if he has lost the service of the wild beasts, it is only because of his sin, for since he rebelled against God these animals rebelled against him. And if the tame animals submit to him and serve him, that is only from God's mercies upon him and His love.

Some see that most of the tame animals that serve man are in general weaker than the wild ones. It is as though dealing with man deprives the animal of its strength and ability. In a symbolic story a tiger was amazed when it saw a cat bearing its same form, but small of body and weak. It asked it the secret of its great weakness. The cat answered: Living with man has humbled me and weakened me.
Wilt thou trust him that he will bring in thy seed, and gather it into thy threshing floor? [12]

Man can entrust tame animals; he leaves a small boy to lead his donkey or his ox, and lays burdens on the donkey, and ties the ox to the arms of a plow led by a boy. But he does not entrust a rhinoceros to do such works, by bringing it to the harvest and laying the load on it.

13 "The wing of the ostrich flaps. Is it a kind pinion, or plumage? 14 For she leaveth her eggs in the earth, and warmeth them in the dust, 15 And forgetteth that the foot may crush them, or that the wild beast may tread upon them. 16 She is hardened against her young ones, as though they were not hers: her labour is in vain without regret. 17 Because God hath deprived her of wisdom, neither hath he imparted to her understanding. 18 What time she betakes herself on high, she laugheth at the horse and his rider.
The wing of the ostrich flaps.
Is it a kind pinion, or plumage? [13]

As for the ostrich, it is a very large bird that some call a winged camel. He who sees it flapping its great wings thinks that it is able to fly, and with surpassing speed, but with the size of its wings and the beauty of its plumage it is unable to fly.
*The wings of the ostrich are like the wings of the "heron" and the wings of the falcon; who can be ignorant how the heron and the falcon surpass the rest of the birds in the speed of their flight?

The ostrich has two wings resembling theirs, but not their speed of flight. For truly it cannot rise from the earth and practice true flight. So are all the hypocrites who pretend to the conduct of the righteous and have the same good appearance, but have no true good conduct. It is as if God says: You have the appearance of your wings, so you seem like one who can rise, but the weight of your conduct drags you down to the lowest depths.

The bodies of the falcon and the heron are small, but they are supported by dense wings. Therefore they fly swiftly because what weighs them down is little and what supports them for flight is much... The character of the chosen man is well indicated by the heron and the falcon. As long as the chosen live in this life they cannot be free of some sin, however small it may seem. But as long as what weighs them down is little in them, they have an abundance of the virtue of good work which lifts them to the heights.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
For she leaveth her eggs in the earth, and warmeth them in the dust [14].

With the beautiful plumage the ostrich has, she struts like the peacock in pride, but she acts in stupidity without wisdom. For neither her beauty nor the largeness of her size is joined with wisdom. She does not care for her young, for she exposes her eggs to danger. She does not hide in a secluded place to make herself a nest like the sparrow and the swallow (Ps 84:3), nor does she sit on the eggs until they hatch. She leaves her eggs on the ground anywhere, they can hatch by the warmth of the sun and the sand, and she does not trouble herself to warm them.

It is a painful picture of some believers who do not care for the salvation of their children, whether according to the flesh or those whom they have begotten in the Gospel, but leave them as in the dust of this world, yet the grace of God often seeks them and supports them with the warmth of the Sun of righteousness, so that they enjoy the risen life.

* To leave the eggs on the ground is not to care for the upbringing of the children they have begotten through conversion, by raising them above earthly work by giving counsel. To leave the eggs on the ground is not to support them by giving the children an example of the heavenly life.

What is meant by dust but the sinner...? What does dust indicate but the instability of the wicked? Therefore the Lord warms the eggs that are left in the dust, kindling the fire of His love for the little souls deprived of the earnest care of the preachers, even when they dwell among sinners.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
And forgetteth that the foot may crush them, or that the wild beast may tread upon them! [15]

In stupidity the ostrich leaves her eggs in the dust, without considering that the foot of a man might tread on it or an animal might shatter it. Yet God in His love sends the heat of the sun to warm it until it hatches.

Pope Gregory in his symbolic interpretation sees that some preachers, after presenting to God children through their preaching, leave those who have accepted the faith as in the dust, in the midst of the wicked, and do not care about the trampling of feet to which they are exposed when the wicked try to discourage them, and when they are exposed to a beast of prey that shatters them, that is, to the trials of the wicked devil.
She is hardened against her young ones, as though they were not hers.
Her labour is in vain without regret [16].

We are not surprised if the ostrich is hardened against her young as though they were not hers, so that all her labor is fruitless, in contrast to the majority of birds and animals that expose themselves to danger even to death for their young. But what surprises us is that the rational man ignores his children according to the flesh or the spirit, as though they were not his, and his whole life becomes tasteless.
* He who does not enjoy the grace of love looks at his neighbor as a stranger, even if he has begotten him for God.

What tender compassion Paul had when he ran for the sake of his children with the warmth of such great love: "(God) is my witness how without ceasing I make mention of you, always making request in my prayers, if by any means now at length I might have a prosperous journey by the will of God to come unto you. For I long to see you" (Rom 1:9-11)... For he was not like the ostrich, forgetting her children, but he feared greatly for his disciples as they suffered persecutions during their preaching, making light of the faith... He counted the wounds of his body in him as nothing, for fear lest the hearts of his children be wounded.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Because God hath deprived her of wisdom, neither hath he imparted to her understanding [17].
God permitted that the huge, beautiful ostrich should not enjoy wisdom, while the tiny ant, which we despise, enjoys it. He wished us to learn from both to seek wisdom and cherish it and practice it.
Since the ostrich represents the hypocritical person who has the beautiful, good appearance without the holy heart, she was not made worthy to receive wisdom.

For God in His love wishes all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, offering wisdom to everyone who seeks it with sincerity and longing. But if we do not care for it, even natural wisdom is taken from us.
What time she betakes herself on high, she laugheth at the horse and his rider [18].
In spite of the ostrich's neglect of her young, when some danger encircles her she lifts her wings and sets off with surpassing speed, so that she mocks the horse and his rider.
* Let God be your hope, your ability to endure, your strength. Let Him be your atonement, your praise, your goal and resting place, and your help in your striving...
The mighty man is the arrogant man who exalts himself (in pride) against God, as though he were something in himself and what belongs to him. Such a man is not saved by his own strength.

Now, he has a nimble and strong horse, sound and swift of foot; if an attack takes place, can it not save its rider from the danger that surrounds him? Let him hear: "The salvation of the horse is a lie"... You must not let the horse promise you escape...

We can take the horse as a symbol of any possessions in this world, or of any kind of honor in which we trust in pride, counting mistakenly that the higher you rise the more your safety and your height increase. Do you not perceive with what violence you will be cast down; the higher you ascend, the heavier will be your fall... How then is safety achieved? It is not achieved by power nor by authority nor by honor nor by glory nor by the horse.
St. Augustine

19 "Hast thou given the horse strength? hast thou clothed his neck with a mane? 20 Canst thou make him leap as a locust? The snorting of his nostrils is terrible. 21 He paweth in the valley, and leapeth with might. He goeth forth to meet the weapons. 22 He mocketh at fear, and is not affrighted; neither turneth he back from the sword. 23 Against him the arrows rattle, with the point of the spear and the javelin. 24 In his leaping and his rumbling he devoureth the ground, neither believeth he that it is the sound of the trumpet. 25 At the blast of the trumpet he saith, Aha! and from afar he scenteth the battle, the shouting of the captains and the cry.
Hast thou given the horse strength? hast thou clothed his neck with a mane? [19]
After speaking of the wild animals and the birds of the wilderness, He presents to him as an example a tame animal serving man, the horse.

He asks him if horses are used to protect man in battles, who gave them the strength? It is not a gift from man, but from God. Yet he who depends on horses without looking to God the giver of strength loses the victory. The psalmist says: "An horse is a vain thing for safety: neither shall he deliver any by his great strength" (Ps 33:17), as it is said: "He delighteth not in the strength of the horse" (Ps 147:10; cf. Hos 14:3; Ps 20:7; Isa 31:1, 3).

Horses are used in Holy Scripture to carry many meanings, among them: 1. Reliance on temporal honor: "I have seen servants upon horses, and princes walking as servants upon the earth" (Eccl 10:7). The servants here refer to the wicked enslaved to sin, who exalt themselves with temporal positions and vain honor.

b. It carries a good meaning, as it is said: "The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but victory is of the LORD" (Prov 21:31). The horse here refers to the believer's abilities and powers that face the opposition of the devil and prevail through the work of God in them.
c. Horses also refer to the preachers: "Thou didst walk through the sea with thine horses, through the heap of great waters" (Hab 3:15).
Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the horse in this place (Job 39:19) means the good preachers who win souls by God's work through them and in them.
With the strength a horse has, man relied on it to defend himself and his country and his possessions, yet a small boy can lead it without rebellion on its part.
Canst thou make him leap as a locust? The snorting of his nostrils is terrible [20].
God asks Job if he is able to hide him like a small locust, for the snorting of his nose in battles is terrifying! He attacks the enemy and does not fear danger to his life.
He paweth in the valley, and leapeth with might.
He goeth forth to meet the weapons [21].

He had previously spoken of the rhinoceros which by its strength mocks man and does not serve him, but here he presents the horse which with its great strength submits to man, and works in his service at the expense of its very life. It goes out to meet the weapons without fear of death!

The text in the Septuagint reads: "He paweth with his hoof in the plain, rejoicing." He is like one who seeks heavenly things, and strikes the earth with his hoof with all strength and boldness, not subject to the passions of his body. Truly Solomon the Wise says: "Prepare thy work without, and make it fit for thyself in the field; and afterwards build thine house" (Prov 24:27).
He mocketh at fear, and is not affrighted; neither turneth he back from the sword [22].
Against him the arrows rattle, with the point of the spear (and the lance) and the javelin [23].

Out of loyalty to his master the horse laughs at death, and is not frightened by the attacks of the enemies, whether by sword or spear, and does not retreat but continues his advance into the midst of the battle, inspiring his rider with the spirit of courage!
Truly man stands in shame when he does not make light of death for the sake of his loyalty to and love for his Creator!

The Apostle Paul himself offers us a wonderful example of love unto death, when he says: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? As it is written, For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter" (Rom 8:35-36).
In his leaping and his anger he devoureth the ground (in his leaping and his rumbling he devoureth the ground), neither believeth he that it is the sound of the trumpet [24].
If the horse in battle is full of zeal and enthusiasm and composure, devouring the ground, should not the believer in his spiritual battle be marked by courage and certainty of God's work with him?

"Neither believeth he that it is the sound of the trumpet." What does this mean? When the apostles preached the Gospel, the high priest sounded the trumpet, not to work for the Lord, but to nullify the work of preaching the Kingdom. "And when they had called the apostles, and beaten them, they commanded that they should not speak in the name of Jesus" (Acts 5:40). But the apostles realized that this was not the sound of the true trumpet, so they said: "For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard" (Acts 4:20).
At the blast of the trumpet he saith, Aha!
And from afar he scenteth the battle, the shouting of the captains and the cry [25].

* When (the believer) obtains the weapon of the Lord, then as soon as he hears of the existence of wars and feels them, he advances [with shouting and a cry] as it says in Job (Job 39:25), because the very voice of his prayer makes the enemies fall to the ground.
St. Macarius the Great

26 "Doth the hawk take flight by thy understanding, and stretch his wings toward the south? 27 Or doth the eagle soar at thy command, and make his nest on high? 28 He dwelleth and abideth on the rock, upon the crag of the rock, and the stronghold. 29 From thence he seeketh his food; his eyes behold afar off. 30 His young ones also suck up blood: and where the slain are, there is he."
Doth the hawk take flight by thy understanding, and stretch his wings toward the south? [26]

The hawk is marked by the speed of its flight and strength; it is among the birds of prey; it spreads its wings and flies toward the south, escaping from the cold regions in the north, especially when it sheds its feathers and replaces them with new feathers. Who gave it this wisdom but God?

* What then is the falcon(b) that enjoys its (new) plumage in the south but every saint who burns when touched by the breath of the Holy Spirit, and so casts off the old habit of dialogue, and takes the form of the new man? Paul advises, saying: "Ye have put off the old man with his deeds, and have put on the new" (Col 3:9-10). And also: "Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day" (2 Cor 4:16).

To spread our wings toward the south means to open our hearts in confession, by the descent of the Holy Spirit, so that we no longer find our pleasure in hiding ourselves by defending ourselves, but expose ourselves by accusing ourselves.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* Who can distinguish the nature of the birds of the air?! How some of them enjoy melodious voices, and another is speckled with all colors in its wings, and some hover in the air as though motionless like the eagle. For by divine command "he (the hawk) stretcheth his wings toward the south." Who can see the lofty height of the falcon...?! How then do you wish to understand the Creator of all?!
St. Cyril of Jerusalem Or doth the eagle soar at thy command, and make his nest on high? [27]

The eagle - the king of birds - offers us an example of the mighty capacities that God gives even to this bird, as a symbol of the capacities of man, who can use them for building for the Kingdom of God within him and in the hearts of others, or for destruction and violence and predation.

Here the characteristics of the eagle stand out, and they are: 1. His soaring very high during his flight by the strength of his wings. Where did he get this ability, is it a gift from man to the eagle? But it is a natural instinct God gave him.

He who created the eagle among the birds for man's sake and gave him the ability to soar on high, will He not grant man to rise by the Holy Spirit of God to enjoy the flight toward the heavenly things?

The eagle uses flying high in order to be hidden from sight, and with the power of his vision and the swiftness of his movement he suddenly swoops upon the prey. So the wicked man uses the capacities offered to him to harm others instead of helping and supporting them. 2. He makes his nest in the high rocks on the crag of the rock, so that no one reaches his young.
He dwelleth and abideth on the rock, upon the crag of the rock, and the stronghold [28].
It befits the believer to make his nest in Christ Jesus, the true Rock, so that evil does not approach him.

But he who in arrogance and pride exalts himself and thinks he has set up for himself a rock which no one approaches, and walks in evil securely, hears the voice: "Though thou shouldest make thy nest as high as the eagle, I will bring thee down from thence, saith the LORD" (Jer 49:16). 3. The keenness of his sight: the believer's inner sight is opened to see the earnest of heaven and enjoy it. But the wicked uses the keenness of his sight to look downward, and his heart is full of violence and predation.
From thence he seeketh his food.
His eyes behold afar off [29]. 4. His young ones suck up blood from their youth and live with the great eagle on the prey.
His young ones also suck up blood: and where the slain are, there is he [30].

All thirst for the shedding of blood as their daily food. But the believers gather like holy eagles around the slain Lord Christ for the sake of their eternal resurrection. Christ becomes their spiritual food: "For wheresoever the carcase is, there will the eagles be gathered together" (Mt 24:28).

* In Holy Scripture the word eagle sometimes refers to spiteful spirits, corrupters of souls; and sometimes to the powers of the present world. But at times it refers to the sharp understanding of the saints, or to the incarnate Lord, flying swiftly above lower things and seeking the things above.

Jeremiah bears witness to the spirits resting in expectation: "Our persecutors are swifter than the eagles of the heaven" (Lam 4:19)... It also symbolizes earthly power, as it was said by the prophet Ezekiel: "A great eagle, large of wings, long of pinions, broad of shoulders, full of splendors, came unto Lebanon, and took the branch of the cedar, he cropped off the top of its young twigs" (Ezek 17:3-4). For this eagle in truth to whom does it point but Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon...?

By the word "eagle" is indicated the sharp understanding of the saints, or the flight of Christ's ascension. Therefore the same prophet (Ezekiel), in describing the four Evangelists whom he saw under the appearance of living creatures, declared that they appeared to him in the form of the face of a man and a lion and an ox and an eagle; he surely indicated by the eagle the fourth living creature, John, who in his flight left the earth, and through sharp understanding penetrated inner mysteries by his vision of the Word...

Let us look at the very structure of the eagle, the nest of hope in heavenly things. Paul says: "For our conversation is in heaven" (Phil 3:20). And also: "And hath raised us up together with him, and made us sit together with him in heavenly places" (Eph 2:6)... For as he who climbs a mountain looks downward and sees lower things as small, so the more a man advances to higher stages, striving to fix his care on the heavenly things, he finds with the same effort that the glory of the present life is nothing, and rises above the places of the earth.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Your creation calls me to meet You!
* For my sake You created the earth and all that is on it.
Behold, even the animals and the birds call me to meet You!
Grant me, with the wild goats of the rocks, to run to You, and to hide in You, O Rock of Ages.
* Grant me, with the hinds, to thirst for You.
That I may strike with You the head of the serpent.
And the devil shall not have dominion over me.
By You I crush him, for You cast him down from heaven like lightning, and though he appears luminous, it is only for a moment, and his deceit is exposed.
* Grant me to be a fruitful hind.
That I may bring forth for You children by the Gospel!
It is Your work, O Shepherd of all!
* Let me learn even from the wild ass the freedom of the wilderness.
Why should I confine myself in the animals' stall?
Let me go forth to the wilderness of the Spirit, and let my soul fly to You with joy and exultation.
* I see the rhinoceros, and my soul trembles at falling into pride.
Why should I be arrogant about the strength and abilities and gifts You have given me?
Why do I not commit myself, in a spirit of humility, to draw near to the manger?
You are the food of my soul.
You are my satisfaction and my joy!
* I see the beautiful, huge ostrich, and I fear that I may be occupied with outward appearances without the wisdom of the Spirit.
I fear that I may act in stupidity and leave the little ones in the dust.
And not offer the weak the warmth of love and the power of the Spirit!
* Count me as a holy horse, bearing You in my heart, O unique Rider.
I do not fear spiritual battles, nor take account of the death of the body.
I am not troubled by the enemy's spears, nor do I fear the sword of the devil!
By You I prevail and am crowned!
* Let me renew my plumage always with the falcon.
I put off always the old man and all his deeds, and put on always the new man.
May he be renewed every day by the work of Your Holy Spirit.
Let me sing to You, saying:
Behold, all things have become new!
* Let me fly with the eagle in the heavenly places.
Let my depths soar to the earnest of eternity.
Let the eyes of my heart look to the crowns prepared.
Let me throw myself into Your arms and live by You and with You!

1 Moreover the LORD answered Job, and said, 2 "Shall he that reproveth contend with the Almighty? he that argueth with God, shall he answer him?" 3 Then Job answered the LORD, and said, 4 "Behold, I am vile; what shall I answer thee? I will lay mine hand upon my mouth. 5 Once have I spoken; but I will not answer: yea, twice; but I will proceed no further."

God gave Job the opportunity to answer his questions, but Job could not answer any question. He knew his own weight. For in the days of his greatness and wealth, "the princes refrained talking, and laid their hand on their mouth. The nobles held their peace, and their tongue cleaved to the roof of their mouth" (Job 29:9-10). Now Job realized the truth about his weight. He said, "Behold, I am vile; what shall I answer thee? I will lay mine hand upon my mouth" (Job 40:4). The word vile here comes in Hebrew to be translated as trifling or light in weight (without weight, lightweight). What occupied him was not his sins, for he did not say, "I have sinned," but he was like one caught up into the divine mystery, so that he realized the truth about himself before his Creator and the Ruler of his life.
Moreover the LORD answered Job, and said, [1]
Shall he that reproveth contend with the Almighty? He that argueth with God, shall he answer him? [2]

God asks Job: Is it for the creature to dictate his will to his Creator? Or to object to His wisdom and will? It is fitting for a person to answer quickly, rejecting the thought of contending with the Almighty or standing before the wisdom of the Creator.

It is as if God were saying to him: Until now you have not grasped My wisdom in My permitting the trial to come upon you. You look at your own loftiness and righteousness, and you have not taken into account My wisdom and My care for you. Did you not learn from the beasts of the wild and the birds of prey to cleave to Me?
Then Job answered the LORD, and said, [3]
Job was convinced, for his vision of God had passed all bounds, and he now had a worthy appreciation of God's world, with its new horizons, its harmony and its concord.

Job now confesses that God can do everything and that His purposes are fulfilled. This melted Job's heart, and he saw himself called to bow beneath the mighty hand of God. Now he submits humbly to the wisdom of God, and by entering into communion with Him he passes into the realm of light and hope. The Lord spoke and His power came, and it brought man's helplessness into true wisdom. When God revealed Himself to Job, He made Job reveal himself. Job gave up his human wisdom, so he left the image of God as a warrior and returned to the image of God as the Friend who came to him in the midst of the tempest. And God became silent again after Job had seen Him.
Behold, I am vile; what shall I answer thee?
I will lay mine hand upon my mouth [4].

Job surpassed all the people of his time in virtue, and in the dialogue he was able to overcome his friends. But when God spoke with him, he confessed his lowliness and weakness, and was compelled to lay his hand upon his mouth to keep silent in an awesome stillness.

Job offers us a lesson in dialogue with God: even if we are righteous in His eyes, we keep silent so that we may not justify ourselves with words, but rather leave our life and practical conduct, by His grace, to speak with Him. Speaking with Him in the language of deeds is better than with the tongue.
* The saints have learned to restrain slips of the tongue before the eyes of God, by presenting a good life. They learn to refrain from exaggerated words through the weight of their good works.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* Job himself did not keep silent about his sins... Since he is a true worshipper of God, without doubt he made his confession in truth.

St. Augustine *Let us consider what man is. The pagans say that he is a rational, mortal animal, capable of reasoning and knowledge. Let us not take our definition of him from them, but from where? From the Holy Scriptures... Hear its words: "That man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil" (Job 1:1). This is truly man! Again another says: "Man is a great thing, and a merciful man is precious" (Prov 20:6) LXX. Those who do not respond to this description will not be able to attain knowledge, and Holy Scripture refuses to recognize them as human beings, but calls them dogs, horses, serpents, foxes and wolves, or any base animal. If this is what man is, then he who lives in pleasures is not a man, for how can he be such who thinks of nothing that befits him? Luxury and dignity cannot be joined together; the one destroys the other. Even the pagans say: {A stuffed belly does not bear a keen mind}.
St. John Chrysostom Once have I spoken; but I will not answer: yea, twice; but I will proceed no further [5].
In sincere repentance Job says that he spoke once about the trials that had come upon him, without being able to explain the wisdom behind them.

I reproached God, and I wanted to enter, as into a trial, and present my case to Him. Perhaps I repeated that, instead of once, twice, but now "I will proceed no further"; I will not repeat what I said before.
Job, who had been insisting on a meeting with God in order to dispute with Him, now that he has seen the Lord, falls into an awesome silence.

* If we examine the earlier words of the blessed Job, we find that he never uttered anything evil... But when he weighed himself in the perfectly exact balance of God, he confessed that he had sinned in his speech for the second time...
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* If you confess that you are a sinner, the truth is in you, for the truth itself is light. Your life does not shine with full brightness, because there are sins in you, but when you begin to be enlightened, you come to the confession of sins... First of all, then, confession, and then love. For what is said of love? "Charity shall cover the multitude of sins" (1 Pet 4:8)... Pride quenches love, and humility strengthens it; love extinguishes sins, and humility goes in the company of confession.

Tell men who you are, tell God who you are. If you do not tell God who you are, He will judge you for what He finds in you... Do you want Him to forgive you? Know how to say to God: [Hide Thy face from my sins]. Say to Him also the words of the psalmist himself: [I acknowledge my transgression] (Ps 51:3, 9).
St. Augustine

6 Then answered the LORD unto Job out of the whirlwind, and said, 7 "Gird up thy loins now like a man: I will demand of thee, and declare thou unto me. 8 Wilt thou also disannul my judgment? wilt thou condemn me, that thou mayest be righteous? 9 Hast thou an arm like God? or canst thou thunder with a voice like him? 10 Deck thyself now with majesty and excellency; and array thyself with glory and beauty. 11 Cast abroad the rage of thy wrath: and behold every one that is proud, and abase him. 12 Look on every one that is proud, and bring him low; and tread down the wicked in their place. 13 Hide them in the dust together; and bind their faces in secret. 14 Then will I also confess unto thee that thine own right hand can save thee. 15 Behold now behemoth, which I made with thee; he eateth grass as an ox. 16 Lo now, his strength is in his loins, and his force is in the navel of his belly. 17 He moveth his tail like a cedar: the sinews of his stones are wrapped together. 18 His bones are as strong pieces of brass; his bones are like bars of iron. 19 He is the chief of the ways of God: he that made him can make his sword to approach unto him. 20 Surely the mountains bring him forth food, where all the beasts of the field play. 21 He lieth under the shady trees, in the covert of the reed, and fens. 22 The shady trees cover him with their shadow; the willows of the brook compass him about. 23 Behold, he drinketh up a river, and hasteth not: he trusteth that he can draw up Jordan into his mouth. 24 Can one take him before his eyes? or bore his nose with a snare?"
In His second discourse with Job He made clear to him that there is no ground for comparison between the creature and his Creator, and that it is not the creature's right to interrogate his Creator.
Then answered the LORD unto Job out of the whirlwind, and said, [6]
Gird up thy loins now like a man.
I will demand of thee, and declare thou unto me [7].

The Septuagint rendering of verse [8] is: "Dost thou think that I have dealt with thee for any other purpose than that thou mightest appear righteous?" It is as if God were revealing to Job, with all power, His transcendent care and His love for him: if He permitted him trials of such magnitude, their aim was only that Job might be justified and enjoy victory over the devil.

When Job defends himself against the blows that God permitted to come upon him, he accuses divine justice; but if he accepts the trial with thanksgiving, God justifies him and glorifies him, and it is reckoned not as his chastisement but as his approval.

* He who struggles in defending himself against the blows of God seeks to ignore the judgments of God who inflicted the blows. And when he says that he was not struck on account of his faults, what does he do but accuse the One who strikes? The blows from heaven did not fall upon the blessed Job to remove his faults, but rather to add to his merits, so that he who in time of calm shone with such great holiness might thus declare the virtue of patience hidden within him... But he thought that he had been struck unjustly when he found nothing in himself that required correction. So that he might not be puffed up with pride in his innocence, the divine voice rebuked him, while his mind was free from evil but he was weighed down with blows, and he was called to the mysteries of the divine judgments... So the saint was not at variance with God in any sin, but was in agreement with Him, though with some difficulty because of the blows.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Wilt thou also disannul my judgment?
Wilt thou condemn me, that thou mayest be righteous? [8]

* At the end of the struggles He (God) proclaimed the victory of the wrestler in a sublime declaration, and revealed the mystery of his sorrows, saying: ["Dost thou think that I have dealt with thee for any other purpose than that thou mightest appear righteous?"] This is the balm of his wounds, this is the crown of the struggle, this is the reward of his patience.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus *The righteous endure trial here, because they are sojourners and strangers, and in a foreign city. The righteous endure those things for the sake of testing. What did God say to Job? [Do you not suppose that I warn you for any other purpose than that you may appear righteous?] (Job 40:8) LXX. But sinners, when they suffer any affliction, suffer only the punishment for their sins. Therefore in all circumstances, whether bitter or not, let us give thanks to God. For both conditions are profitable. For God does nothing out of hatred or enmity toward us, but what He does is out of His care and concern for us.

St. John Chrysostom *Had Job not fought in the battle and gained the victory, he would not have received the crown of righteousness, and would not have heard the Lord say: Do you not think that I speak with you for any purpose other than that you may appear righteous? (Job 40:8 LXX).

St. Jerome *I think that the wind means trials. For trials show that in the heap of believers some are like chaff and others like wheat. When your soul is overcome by some trial, the trial does not turn you into chaff. Rather, because you are chaff, light in weight and unbelieving, the trial reveals what you are and what you had hidden. On the contrary, when you bear trials courageously, the trials do not make you a believer and a patient man, but rather reveal the virtues of patience and courage which were hidden in you. The Lord says: "Dost thou think that I warn thee for any other reason than that thou mayest appear righteous" (Job 40:8 LXX).
Origen Hast thou an arm like God? or canst thou thunder with a voice like him? [9]
God reproaches Job, saying that there is no ground for comparison between the arm of the Lord and His voice, and the arm of Job and his voice. For God is mighty in His work and mighty in His words.

* When speaking of the voice of God and His arm, let us take great care lest our mind imagine something material in Him. For he who confines within the frame of a body Him who is immaterial, who fills all and embraces all, falls into the heresy of the Anthropomorphites (likening the Godhead to man). But Almighty God, in drawing us near to Himself, humbles Himself to teach us the high things and condescends to the lowly things... Therefore in His Holy Scripture He sometimes uses likenesses taken now from human bodies, now from our minds, and sometimes even from birds...
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Deck thyself now with majesty and excellency; and array thyself with glory and beauty [10].
A man may adorn himself with a garment of glory and splendor, so that he awes other men and draws the great to himself as friends, but this is worth nothing before the glory and majesty of God.

* God surrounds Himself with beauty, of which it is written: "The LORD reigneth, he is clothed with majesty" (Ps 93:1). He is exalted on high in us when we are sure that His nature cannot be searched out by our minds. He is glorious, He who contains joy and has no need of praise. He is wrapped in beautiful garments, for He appoints the orders of the holy angels to the service of His beauty. He created them and established His Church as a glorious garment, without spot or wrinkle. Therefore it was said to Him by the prophet: "Thou art clothed with honour and majesty: who coverest thyself with light as with a garment" (Ps 104:1-2).
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Cast abroad the rage of thy wrath: and behold every one that is proud, and abase him [11].

It is as though He were saying to him: "There is no ground for comparison between Me and you; if you were in a state of anger and wrath, could you, with a look from you, shatter your arrogant opponents?" For it is said: "For the day of the LORD of hosts shall be upon every one that is proud and lofty, and upon every one that is lifted up; and he shall be brought low" (Isa 2:12). No proud man can stand before His gaze.
If Job silenced his friends to some extent in the long dialogue and for a long time, then a single look from God shakes the whole being of the proud who exalt themselves against Him.
Look on every one that is proud, and bring him low; and tread down the wicked in their place [12].

It is as though God were saying to Job: "I know that your request was not out of arrogance and pride. I know your humble heart, even if you reproached Me in your distress and asked for an explanation of what had befallen you. If you were distressed because of your friends' arrogance toward you and their unjust accusation of you, do not fear. If you wish, I have permitted you to look at them with the eye of faith, and you will overcome them. You can overcome the wicked and proud in their places before they move to face your gaze.

If they think that they are more honorable or richer or happier than you, because what befell you did not befall them, they will be crushed, and their temporal glories, their material resources and their offspring will not profit them.

* The proud are confounded at the look of the Lord, whether here, where in His mercy He reveals their faults and condemns them, or there, where He punishes them by His justice. But pride itself is the place of the wicked. It is written: [Pride is the beginning of all sin] (Sir 10:15), for it dwells in the place where evil dwells, though it is very hard to distinguish between evil and pride. He who is very proud thinks evil of our Creator. The wicked man, then, is trodden down in his place, for he is shattered by the very pride that lifted him up... Often, while the proud man advances in his vain glory against God, he sinks inwardly into real misery.
Pope Gregory (the Great)

* I do not want you to be proud on account of anything, but rather to be fearful. You travel like a young girl with gold. Let her fear the thief. This temporal life is a race. Here we compete so that we may be crowned afterward. No one enters among serpents and scorpions while sure that he will be safe.
* Not only fornication and prostitution defile those who practice them, but pride also defiles a man more than they do.
* Humility is given to each person according to the measure of his greatness. Pride is harmful to everyone. It seeks to corrupt, above all, those who are great!
St. Jerome * It is clear that excessive boasting was one of the marks of the false apostles.

* Arrogance together with sin is a great calamity... If he who does good loses his labor if he becomes puffed up, how great is the iniquity of him who adds to his sins the sin of arrogance? For such a one cannot practice repentance.
St. John Chrysostom Hide them in the dust together; and bind their faces in secret [13].

While the proud think that they have overcome and triumphed, God asks Job not to fear them, but to hide them in the dust, to bury them as in a dark tomb, so that their names are no longer remembered. It is like Moses the prophet, who hid the proud Egyptian in the sand (Ex 2:12).
Their faces are bound in the darkness, where they cannot stand before God, the true Light, but go down into the outer darkness, the darkness of Hades.

* God, by His just judgment, hides the proud and the wicked in the dust, by permitting their hearts to be swallowed up by earthly things according to their own choice, as they despise the love of their Creator.

Fittingly He adds: [and at the same time I bind their faces in the pit]... since He brings down the intention of their hearts when it wants to exalt itself over men. For he whose face is turned down toward Hades looks upon the lowly things.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
* What madness! Does this proud man not know that his glory passes away and evaporates like a dream, and that greatness and authority are nothing but a deceptive mirage?
St. Basil the Great Then will I also confess unto thee that thine own right hand can save thee [14].

God wants to praise His creature; He treasures him and seeks his honor. But can Job, despite God's testimony to his uprightness, save himself by his arm or by his right hand, that is, by his own strength? He who makes light of God's support of him relies on his own strength, and so does not receive praise from God.

It is fitting for the believer to sing: "For they got not the land in possession by their own sword, neither did their own arm save them: but thy right hand, and thine arm, and the light of thy countenance, because thou hadst a favour unto them" (Ps 44:3).
* At the moment when we are still in the midst of the battle, fighting and being wounded, we ask ourselves: Who is the victor?

The victor, brethren, is the one who relies on God, who supports him as he fights, and does not rely on his own strength. Satan has his experience in war, but if God is with us we shall overcome him. Satan fights by himself, and if we try to do the same, he will overcome us. He is an experienced fighter, and so it is fitting for us to call upon the Almighty to stand against him.
Let Him who is never overcome dwell in you, and you will overcome him who is accustomed to conquer. Whom does he overcome? Those whose hearts are empty of God.
* God knows your striving and your good will, and awaits your struggle, and supports your weakness, and crowns your victory.
St. Augustine Behold now the sea horse (behemoth), which I made with thee.
He eateth grass as an ox [15].

Behemoth comes in the plural form of "behemah," that is, an animal. It is still used in Egypt to mean a tame animal such as sheep, donkeys, horses and so on, and it differs from the Hebrew word chaytow, which is for the wild beasts of the field.
Some see that it refers here to the sea horse, the barniq, or the sea buffalo, the hippopotamus.
Adam Clarke considers this animal to be one of the extinct animals, called the mammoth.
This animal is distinguished by the hugeness of its body together with its strength, so that no man can enter into a wrestling match with it; how then does he wish to resist his Creator?
Some thought that it refers here to the elephant because of the hugeness of its body and its strength, but many scholars have rejected that.
St. John Chrysostom says that some interpreters interpreted this passage in a spiritual sense, and that this animal refers to Satan.
If it refers to Satan, then he eats grass like the ox, meaning that when the body dominates the human soul, man becomes like the grass of the field, food for Satan!

God dwelt at length in His discourse with Job on behemoth, a symbol of the enemy of good, the devil. Perhaps He wanted to direct Job's gaze to this enemy. Instead of murmuring against the judgments of God, it is fitting for Job to realize that there is a dangerous enemy who wants to devour all mankind, and that it was he who asked permission to tempt him; but these trials turn the devil into a plaything that even little children mock.

* The demon of fornication stirs up bodily lust, and launches his attack upon the ascetics, and strives to make them abandon their asceticism, sowing in their souls the thought that this asceticism of theirs is of no use.
And if he is able to defile the soul, he begins to prepare it to speak and to hear certain (evil) conversations, so that it seems as though the (evil) act itself were present before their eyes.
St. Mar Evagrius of Pontus Lo now, his strength is in his loins, and his force is in the navel of his belly [16].
He refers here to its surpassing power despite the hugeness of its body: its strength is in its loins (the hips), and its force in the navel of its belly.

The strength of the elephant is in its neck, of the lion in its claws, of the horse and the ox in their chests, but the main strength of this animal is in its loins. It was said in Nahum: "Make thy loins strong, fortify thy power mightily" (Nah 2:1).
It is fitting for the believer to mortify his loins, and not allow the flesh to lust against the Spirit (Gal 5:17).

* If we want to eat the flesh of the Lamb, we must mortify our loins, that is, the works of the flesh, and destroy in ourselves what Job said of Satan: "Lo now, his strength is in his loins, and his force is in the navel of his belly" (Job 40:16). It is fitting that we not allow the flesh to lust against the Spirit (Gal 5:17), but through the Spirit mortify the deeds of the flesh, and by this purification enjoy the body of the Lamb.
St. Jerome In a letter to Eustochium, St. Jerome wrote, explaining that asceticism is not of value in itself, but is an important means for self-control and chastity.

* The Creator, the Lord of all, takes no pleasure in rumbling and an empty stomach..... but these are necessary as a means of preserving chastity. Job was dear to God, perfect and upright before Him (Job 2:3), and yet hear what he says about Satan: [His strength is in his loins (his sexual organs), and his force is in the navel] (Job 40:16). I chose these expressions for the sake of delicacy of speech, but what is meant by them is the reproductive sexual organs of both sexes. The descendant of David, who sits on his throne according to the promise, is said to be of the fruit of his belly (his loins) (Ps 132:11). And the seventy-five souls of the family of Jacob who came into Egypt are said to have come out of his loins (Gen 46:26). So when the hollow of Jacob's thigh was put out of joint as he wrestled with the Lord, he ceased to beget children. Again the Israelites were commanded to celebrate the Passover with loins girded and mortified (Ex 12:11). God said to Job: "Gird up now thy loins like a man" (Job 38:3). John wore a girdle of a skin (Mt 3:4). And the Apostles were bound to gird their loins in order to carry the lamp of the Gospel (Lk 12:35). When Ezekiel told us of Jerusalem that she was found in the open field, covered with blood, he used the words: [thy navel was not cut] (Ezek 16:4-6). Therefore Satan, in his attack on men, has his strength in his loins, and in his attack on women his force is in the navel. Do you want proof of these assertions of mine? Take examples of it. Samson was more courageous than a lion and steadier than a rock..... but in the presence of his guide his resistance vanished and was blotted out. David was a man whose heart was after the likeness of God's heart, whose lips were always praising the Holy One, the Christ who was to come, and yet, as he walked on the roof of his house, the temptation of Bathsheba's nakedness caught him, and he added murder to the crime of adultery. Observe how a man, even in his own house, cannot use his eyes without danger staring him in the face.

St. Jerome * And it is also clear to all that adultery is committed only by a bodily act, for God says of this blessed husband Job: "Lo now, his strength is in his loins, and his force is in the navel of his belly" (Job 40:16).
Abba Serapion He moveth his tail like a cedar.
The sinews of his stones are wrapped together [17].
He moves his tail like a strong cedar tree, and it was said of the dragon: "His tail drew the third part of the stars of heaven, and did cast them to the earth" (Rev 12:4).
He is strong; when he treads upon a man with his feet he crushes him, for "the sinews of his stones are wrapped together."

St. Mar Jacob of Serugh portrays for us how the devil cannot bear the salvation of man. When he sees a sinner walking the path of repentance, he asks his soldiers to intensify their efforts to shatter him by evil thoughts and vain glory and by every possible means. The saint wrote to two harlots named Lantia and Maria, who had repented and become recluses, warning them of the devil's wars and his resistance to them with all violence.
* Now the commander of the harmful forces of the left (the devil commands his soldiers) orders because of his enmity toward you both:
Do not fight the pure, nor the perfect, nor any of my strong enemies, but these two who were my own, and despised me and mocked me. And they stand in the rank of the saints.
Bring upon them pieces of despair, fill them with sloth.
Sow envy in them toward one another, that they may submit to weakness and burn with the desire for food.
Awaken their thoughts to love their former deeds. Trouble them with thoughts of fornication.
Hinder their prayers, lest they be strong enough to fulfill their vows...
Set them on the edge of the precipice of greatness, and bind them with love of glory...
Lead them to think that they have become good.
Send the sick to them that they may pray for them, and urge others to say: We were healed by your prayers; deceive them into thinking that they are not penitents but virtuous women.
St. Mar Jacob of Serugh His bones are as strong pieces of brass; his bones are like bars of iron (and his ribs are like beaten iron) [18].
No one can break his bones, nor tear his ribs apart; his bones are like pipes of brass, and his ribs like beaten iron.

* What does the Book of Job say about him? He is fearful and terrifying (Job 40:18; 41:7). His sides are brass, and his back is cast iron, his bowels are of sharp stones. This and more the Holy Scripture says about him. This is the great and mighty leader of the satanic hosts. But what does the One who has the true and unique power call him? He is a "little fox!" (Song 2:15). All who are with Satan, his whole force, are an object of mockery. God calls them by the same name, "the little foxes," and urges the hunters against them.
St. Gregory of Nyssa He is the chief of the ways of God.
He that made him can make his sword to approach unto him [19].

The text in the Septuagint reads: [This is the first of the works of the Lord, made to be mocked by His angels]. Some have relied on this passage in claiming that Satan was created evil and did not fall by his own will. St. Augustine refuted this view in his book "The Literal Meaning of Genesis."
Who denies that God created the devil from among the greatest of the heavenly orders, but by his own will he became a laughingstock and an object of mockery to the angels?

* It is said of Satan [the beginning of the works of the Lord, made to be mocked by His angels], not because he is the first creature that God brought into being, nor because he was an evil creature from the beginning. But God, knowing that he would come to have an evil will inclined to harm the good, created him to be of use to the good. This is the meaning of the words [His angels mock him], for Satan is mocked when he tries to destroy the one whom he chose by his own will, who proves useful to the servants of God despite his evil intent. Truly God saw that when He created him.

St. Augustine The devil was a great and distinguished star among the heavenly beings, "Lucifer, son of the morning" (Isa 14:12). He not only enjoyed light but shone with his light on others as a bright light in the morning, as a divine gift. But he exalted himself against God, his Creator and the Giver of light, and thought that he could rise to the level of God Himself, even to become greater than He, so he fell and became darkness instead of light, having separated himself by himself from God, the source of light. He wanted to sit upon the mount of Zion (Ps 48:2), the holy mountain of God, reckoning himself as God in greatness, and so he exalted himself above the clouds!

* Those who say that Satan is not God's creature are mistaken. Insofar as he is Satan he is not God's creature, but the being himself (as a creature) is God's creature. It is like saying that a murderer is not God's creature, but as a man he is God's creature.

*It is perfectly clear from these words (Isa 14:12) that he who was formerly Lucifer, who appeared in the morning, fell from heaven. For if he were - as some claim - a being of darkness, why was it said of him that he was like Lucifer, or the light-bearer? Or how does he who has no light at all rise in the morning?

Origen * The saying of the Lord Christ: "The prince of this world," means by it the devil, and wicked men have called him by this name, not because he rules heaven and earth, for otherwise he would overturn and reverse creation, but because he rules those who have surrendered themselves to him.

St. John Chrysostom * We understand from these words that there is one King, who is the Creator of the whole universe. On the other side there is the prince of this world, who calls himself the king of darkness. Myriads of angels serve the true King, while myriads of demons surround the prince of the powers of darkness (Col 1:13). The principalities and powers and virtue follow the King of kings and Lord of lords. And in the end, when Christ delivers up the kingdom to God the Father, after He has put down all rule and all authority and power of the enemy, it is necessary that He reign till He has put all enemies under His feet (1 Cor 15:24-25).
St. Gregory of Nyssa Surely the mountains bring him forth food, where all the beasts of the field play [20].

Some see here the marvelous goodness of God: for despite the hugeness of this animal's body and its power, it is not a predator like the lion or the leopard. Were it a predator living on the flesh of animals, then with the hugeness of its body it would need to devour many animals, because it needs an enormous quantity of food. But its food is the grass which is found in abundance on the mountains. And since it lives on vegetation, the beasts of the field, which are weaker than it in body, do not fear it, but play with it.
He lieth under the shady trees, in the covert of the reed, and fens [21].

* The great trees shade him (Satan), and he sleeps beside the reeds and the rushes and the papyrus (Job 40:21). He is king over all the things that are in the waters, that is, over the throne of pleasure and luxury.
St. Jerome The shady trees cover him with their shadow.
The willows of the brook compass him about [22].

Since the beasts of the field play with him, he has no need to lurk in dark places or hide in caves in order to pounce suddenly upon his prey. Rather he lies down in safety under the shady trees. He sleeps in peace, and the animals gather around him rejoicing, playing with him.
Since he harms no one, he has no need of caves to protect him, but is covered by the reeds and other plants that grow beside the waters.

Pope Gregory (the Great) offers us a symbolic interpretation of this passage, saying: [Behemoth finds a kind of rest in those who become cold by withdrawing from the light of the true Sun, and so it is said of him, "he sleeps under the shade"... The moist places (the willows of the brook) are the minds of earthly men, where there is the moisture of fleshly lusts. In these minds he plants the footprints of his wickedness, and he sinks into their minds as into moist ground. The moist places are the works of lust. For the foot does not slip on dry ground, but only when it walks on slippery ground, where it is hard to be supported. Those who cannot stand upright pass through this life in moist places].
Behold, he drinketh up a river, and hasteth not.
He trusteth that he can draw up Jordan into his mouth [23].

Since this huge animal needs an enormous quantity of water, one imagines that it is able to drink a whole river. If the river overflows, it does not flee, but deliberately drinks from it without fear or alarm.
Behemoth thinks that he is able to drink up the whole river Jordan if it were poured into his mouth.

Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the waters refer to the peoples. The devil opened his mouth to drink the whole river, that is, the whole human race, as his drink, and it is his right to swallow them up. And when the Lord Christ came to the river Jordan, the enemy opened his mouth to drink up the Jordan with the Lord descending into it. In vain the enemy tried to catch the Lord Christ; rather the Lord Christ crushed the head of the dragon in the waters of the Jordan.

The enemy still opens his mouth to swallow the whole river Jordan, that is, to catch those who have received the sacrament of Baptism and become children of God, but in their negligence he deceives them into returning to sonship to the devil.

St. Cyril of Jerusalem spoke of the gift of Baptism as liberation from the authority of the devil, the beast who dwells in the depths of the waters, saying: [It is written in Job that there was in the waters the beast who "trusteth that he can draw up Jordan into his mouth" (Job 40:23), and his heads had to be broken (Ps 74:14). Therefore the Lord went down and bound the strong one in the waters, that we may receive strength in them, since we have authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions (Lk 10:19). The beast was great and terrifying, "a thick vessel could not bear one scale of his tail" (Job 41:7) LXX, raging against everyone who met him.
